official: Kristi Noem, Secretary of Homeland Security; Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General (DOJ's Middle District of Tennessee brought and prosecuted the underlying case)
offense_category: Vindictive Prosecution -- Bringing Criminal Charges in Retaliation for a Successful Civil Lawsuit Against the Government, a Due Process Violation a Federal Judge Found This Case Actually Met
incident_summary:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national living in Maryland with a U.S.-citizen wife and child, had been granted protection from deportation under a 2019 immigration court order after a judge found he faced danger from gang targeting of his family. In March 2025, **Trump administration officials deported him to El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison anyway, in violation of that court order**. The administration later acknowledged the error in litigation while resisting court orders to facilitate his return. Abrego Garcia sued and won: the Supreme Court ordered the government to facilitate his return. In April 2025, DHS issued a press release describing a 'bombshell investigative report' that alleged Abrego Garcia was a suspected human trafficker. The report rested on a 2022 Tennessee traffic stop in which, by the report's account, he was driving with eight other people and was released at the time with only a warning. Prosecutors in the Middle District of Tennessee then secured an indictment charging him with human smuggling and conspiracy to commit human smuggling, and in June 2025 the government brought him back to the United States to face those charges. Then-Attorney General Pam Bondi publicly touted the indictment at a press conference, saying 'This is what American justice looks like.'

In October 2025, U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw Jr. first found that Abrego Garcia may have been charged out of prosecutorial vindictiveness. He wrote that 'the Government had a significant stake in retaliating against Abrego's success' in his deportation lawsuit, and he ordered a hearing on the question. On May 22, 2026, Judge Crenshaw dismissed the case outright, finding 'presumptive vindictiveness.' He wrote that 'absent Abrego's successful lawsuit challenging his removal to El Salvador, the Government would not have brought this prosecution,' and concluded that 'the evidence before this court sadly reflects an abuse of prosecuting power.' The Justice Department appealed the dismissal to the Sixth Circuit in June 2026 and filed its opening brief on Aug. 17; the appeal is pending. Abrego Garcia's immigration status and the deportation-error litigation are separate, ongoing matters.

official: George Cook, Acting Director, U.S. Census Bureau (no single official is named in sourcing as personally directing the AFPI placements; Cook is the agency's senior accountable office-holder, which has operated without a Senate-confirmed director since early 2025)
offense_category: Institutional Capture Through Politically Screened Placement -- partisan think-tank staff detailed into a nonpartisan statistical agency outside its normal vetted hiring process, producing a methodologically disputed report used to support voter-fraud claims; not itself a charged violation
incident_summary:
WIRED reported (September 16, 2026) that at least seven staffers from the America First Policy Institute (AFPI) -- a think tank aligned with President Trump -- have been detailed to the U.S. Census Bureau under the Intergovernmental Personnel Act (IPA), a mechanism historically used to bring in term-limited specialists from local governments, universities, and tribal organizations, not political-advocacy staff. The AFPI detailees were given access to sensitive Census population data.

On August 18, 2026, the Census Bureau published an anonymously authored report titled "Noncitizen Voting in the 2020 Election: A Beginning Analysis," which compared voter records against citizenship records and claimed to identify roughly 24,000 instances of noncitizen voting in the 2020 election. WIRED identified two of the report's authors, Matthew Jensen and Jeff McCrea, as AFPI staffers, and named at least five additional AFPI members detailed to the Bureau, including researcher Max Kossek and Ryan Montgomery. Independent experts and former Census officials raised methodology concerns: David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, said "census data cannot reliably be matched to voter data," and other reviewers flagged the report's undisclosed authorship and the absence of clear false-match testing or sample validation to confirm how many of the flagged 24,000 records were actually ineligible voters. A Census employee told WIRED the AFPI staffers' role was "disrespectful to the institution," saying there had historically been "nothing close" to this level of outside-advocacy-group access.

House Oversight Democrats -- Reps. Robert Garcia, Maxwell Frost, and Raja Krishnamoorthi -- sent a letter to the Census Bureau on September 4, 2026 raising concerns about the report and the AFPI detailees' role in producing it.

Those detailees had access to sensitive population data and directly authored a public agency report on a politically salient topic (noncitizen voting) without disclosing their affiliation or authorship
Independent subject-matter experts and former agency officials identified specific, substantive methodology concerns with the report -- not merely a partisan disagreement with its conclusions
The report was produced and published without a Senate-confirmed Bureau director in place, during a period of documented leadership vacancy
Congressional oversight (a formal letter from House Oversight Democrats) has already been triggered by the report and the staffing arrangement that produced it

rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: the Intergovernmental Personnel Act is a lawful, routinely used mechanism for bringing outside expertise into federal agencies, the detailees' subject-matter work on election-integrity questions is within the Bureau's legitimate research mandate, and disagreement with the report's methodology is a normal part of academic/statistical debate rather than evidence of impropriety.
comeback: The IPA mechanism's normal use is for local-government, university, and tribal specialists on term-limited technical assignments -- not for embedding staff from a single, Trump-aligned political advocacy organization en masse inside a nonpartisan statistical agency to author an anonymously published, politically salient report on voter fraud. The methodology concerns here aren't a generic academic dispute: a named expert said the underlying data-matching approach is unreliable by design, and the report withheld its authors' AFPI affiliations from the public. A career Census employee's on-record description of the situation as "disrespectful to the institution" and without precedent underscores that this isn't ordinary interagency personnel-sharing.

official: Scott Bessent, Secretary of the Treasury (also performing duties of acting IRS Commissioner)
offense_category: Potential Conflict of Interest / Improper Personal Benefit via Official Position (possible analogues: 18 U.S.C. §208, federal conflict-of-interest statute; or broader abuse-of-office concerns regarding personal tax benefit obtained through a settlement reached by subordinate DOJ/Treasury officials) — NOT charged; the settlement and Blanche's release order were published by DOJ, but Treasury has not detailed how they apply; appeals pending
incident_summary:
On May 18, 2026, the administration announced a settlement of Trump's lawsuit against the IRS that created a $1.776 billion compensation fund for individuals -- including the president's allies -- who claimed to have been unfairly targeted by the Biden administration; a release order signed the next day by Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche reportedly granted President Trump and his family immunity from IRS audits. On June 2, Blanche told Congress the fund would not move forward, without committing to end the audit protections. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who also performs IRS Commissioner duties during a vacancy, has repeatedly declined to confirm or detail the audit-immunity terms, citing ongoing litigation. Treasury General Counsel Brian Morrissey resigned on May 18, 2026, the day the fund was announced; the next day Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche told senators "I don't know if it's a coincidence," and he and Vice President JD Vance declined to rule out payouts from the $1.8 billion fund to January 6 defendants, with Vance saying requests would be handled "case-by-case."

On July 6, 2026, Senators Elizabeth Warren, Chuck Schumer and Ron Wyden wrote to 11 Trump-tied businesses and organizations, including the Trump Organization, World Liberty Financial, 1789 Capital, Polymarket and Kalshi, asking whether they believe they are among the "related or affiliated" parties the audit protections cover; according to Warren's office, six responded suggesting they were not covered, while five, including the Trump Organization, World Liberty Financial and 1789 Capital, did not respond. On July 13, 2026, Judge Kathleen Williams found the underlying lawsuit was brought for an "improper purpose" and in bad faith, found there was never a genuine case or controversy between the parties, and referred one of Trump's attorneys for bar discipline; her opinion specifically found that Bessent, IRS CEO Bisignano, and DOJ's litigators were structurally bound not to advance any position contravening the President -- though the court assessed monetary sanctions only against Trump's side and its lawyers and did not sanction Bessent personally, and no charges or finding of personal impropriety have been made against him. Two days later, Warren and Wyden wrote to Bessent and IRS CEO Frank Bisignano asking them to answer by July 22 whether the IRS had implemented any part of Blanche's May 19 order, whether it had stopped doing so, and whether IRS counsel had analyzed the order's legality under the federal law barring executive-branch interference in audits, which the judge's ruling said the order's bar on future IRS audits "directly contravenes"; no public reply from Treasury or the IRS has been identified. On July 31, 2026, Trump, his co-plaintiffs and their attorneys Alejandro Brito and Daniel Epstein filed a notice of appeal to the Eleventh Circuit. On August 5, 2026, Judge Williams denied Trump's request for an expedited ruling on his motion to stay her sanctions order, finding no "good cause" for expedited treatment, and ordered the court-appointed amici to respond.

Rather than withdraw the audit-immunity provision after Judge Williams' ruling, then-Acting Attorney General Blanche posted a document on X on August 2, 2026, stating that the audit deal applies only to the parties named in the lawsuit and only retroactively; outside tax-law experts at the NYU Tax Law Center say the clarification changes nothing substantive, and the underlying protections could shield Trump from as much as $100 million in back taxes and penalties tied to his Chicago skyscraper. After Blanche's August 8 confirmation as Attorney General, DOJ -- through newly installed Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter -- filed a brief at the Eleventh Circuit on August 12, 2026 formally joining Trump's side of the appeal, asking the court to stay Judge Williams' sanctions order and reassign the case away from her, arguing that reasonable members of the public would view her actions as improperly motivated. On September 11, 2026, McCotter filed a notice of appeal on behalf of the IRS and the Treasury Department, the defendants Bessent oversees, appealing the July 13 order themselves. On September 14, Judge Williams denied the stay motion outright, finding the movants had shown neither a likelihood of success on appeal nor irreparable harm. On September 29, 2026, a three-judge Eleventh Circuit panel also refused to stay the sanctions while the appeal proceeds, finding Trump had not made a "strong showing" that Judge Williams "committed clear error"; the appeal itself remains pending, and Blanche's audit-immunity order remains in effect.

evidence.maps_to_element: Lack of standard transparency/disclosure -- the settlement's 'affiliates' language left its reach unclear enough that senators had to ask the companies themselves whether they are covered

evidence.description: On July 13, 2026, Judge Kathleen Williams ruled that the Trump v. IRS lawsuit -- which produced the settlement underlying the audit-immunity terms Bessent declined to detail -- was presented for an 'improper purpose,' writing 'There was never adverseness between the Parties; there was never a case or controversy; and there was never a question as to who would prevail,' and calling it an attempt to use the court to lend legitimacy to an agreement conferring immunity on people and entities affiliated with the President and earmarking taxpayer money for a compensation fund; she referred one of Trump's attorneys to the Florida Bar and sent her order to the New York and D.C. bars where Blanche and Associate AG Stanley Woodward Jr. are members
evidence.maps_to_element: Resolves the prior transparency-only criticism into an actual judicial finding that no genuine case or controversy existed -- directly validating the concern this entry documented at MODERATE-LOW confidence

evidence.description: Judge Williams' July 13, 2026 opinion specifically found that Treasury Secretary Bessent, IRS CEO Frank Bisignano, and the DOJ litigators nominally defending the government in the case were all structurally bound to advance no legal position that 'contravenes the President' -- a more specific factual finding about Bessent's constrained role than this entry previously had, though the ruling still stopped short of personally sanctioning him.
evidence.maps_to_element: Involvement or oversight responsibility of Bessent/Treasury in the settlement -- now more specifically documented via the court's own structural finding, not just Bessent's refusal to discuss terms

evidence.description: On July 15, 2026, Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ron Wyden wrote to Treasury Secretary Bessent and IRS CEO Frank Bisignano that 'The IRS should not and cannot implement illegal orders,' quoting a July 13 ruling that the release order's bar on future audits 'directly contravenes 26 U.S.C. § 7217,' and asking them to answer by July 22, 2026 whether the IRS has implemented any part of Acting Attorney General Blanche's May 19 order, whether it has ceased all actions to implement it, and whether the IRS Office of Chief Counsel has analyzed its legality under § 7217.
evidence.maps_to_element: Involvement or oversight responsibility of Bessent/Treasury in the settlement or its implementation -- Bessent is directly asked whether the IRS he oversees is carrying out the audit-immunity order

evidence.description: On July 29, 2026, Senator Warren's office reported that of the eleven organizations the senators wrote to, six (Trump Media and Technology Group, Polymarket, Kalshi, American Bitcoin, Powerus and Kaz Resources) 'responded by suggesting they were not involved with or granted immunity by the controversial order,' while five, including the Trump Organization, World Liberty Financial and 1789 Capital, 'refused to respond'; the office said DOJ and the administration 'have repeatedly refused to provide written answers clarifying the scope of this immunity agreement.'
evidence.maps_to_element: Lack of standard transparency/disclosure -- note these are a senator's office's characterizations of the replies and of the administration's silence, not a court finding

evidence.description: On July 31, 2026, President Trump, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, The Trump Organization and their attorneys Alejandro Brito and Daniel Epstein filed a joint notice of appeal in the Southern District of Florida (Miami Division) to the Eleventh Circuit from Judge Williams' July 13, 2026 order (D.E. 106).
evidence.maps_to_element: Resolves prior speculation about an appeal into a documented filing, directly updating this entry's own previously-flagged open question

evidence.description: Rather than withdraw the audit-immunity provision after Judge Williams' ruling, Acting AG Blanche (prior to his August 8 confirmation as permanent AG) circulated a clarifying document asserting the immunity applies only to the original lawsuit's parties and operates retroactively -- which NYU's Tax Law Center said 'does nothing to change' the original agreement. Time reported the shield could protect Trump from paying as much as $100 million in back taxes and penalties tied to his Chicago skyscraper.
evidence.maps_to_element: Involvement or oversight responsibility of Bessent/Treasury -- documents DOJ actively reinforcing, not abandoning, the audit-immunity terms after the judge's adverse ruling

evidence.description: On August 5, 2026, Judge Williams denied Trump's request for expedited consideration of his motion to stay her sanctions order (which includes the Brito bar referral and reimbursement of amici's legal fees), finding Trump's lawyers had 'not shown good cause for an expedited ruling under Southern District of Florida Local Rule 7.1,' and gave court-appointed amici until August 14 to respond.
evidence.maps_to_element: Involvement or oversight responsibility of Bessent/Treasury and DOJ in the settlement -- documents an intermediate district-court escalation step (a request for an expedited district-court ruling on the stay, denied) preceding the already-documented Eleventh Circuit briefing

evidence.description: On August 12, 2026, R. Trent McCotter, Acting Deputy Attorney General, filed 'Defendants' Response to Appellants' Time-Sensitive Motion for Stay' at the Eleventh Circuit, arguing that Judge Williams' July 13 order should be stayed and ultimately vacated and that the case should be reassigned because 'surrounding circumstances give the strong appearance that the rushed issuance was done for an improper political motivation,' noting the order issued two days before then-Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's confirmation hearing.
evidence.maps_to_element: Involvement or oversight responsibility of Bessent/Treasury and DOJ in the settlement -- documents DOJ formally joining Trump's side of the appeal and seeking the judge's removal, a material escalation beyond the previously-documented Blanche clarifying document

evidence.description: On September 11, 2026, R. Trent McCotter, Acting Deputy Attorney General, filed Defendants' Notice of Appeal in Trump v. Internal Revenue Service, et al., stating that Defendants appear 'solely for the purpose of noticing their appeal' to the Eleventh Circuit from Judge Williams' July 13, 2026 order (ECF No. 106).
evidence.maps_to_element: Involvement or oversight responsibility of Bessent/Treasury -- Treasury and the IRS, the named defendants, themselves appealing the order that found no adverseness between them and Trump

evidence.description: Bloomberg News reported that on Tuesday, September 29, 2026, a three-judge Eleventh Circuit panel (Judges Adalberto Jordan, Robin Rosenbaum and Kevin Newsom) refused to halt Judge Williams' sanctions order while Trump appeals, finding he failed to make a 'strong showing' that she 'committed clear error,' and holding that Trump and his attorneys 'did not submit or offer any evidence to explain their litigation conduct or demonstrate that the lawsuit and the settlement were not collusive'; the report said Blanche's immunity protection order 'is also still in effect.'
evidence.maps_to_element: Whether the settlement constitutes a private benefit to the President personally -- an appeals panel declined to disturb, pending appeal, the finding that the lawsuit and settlement were collusive

status: Ongoing -- Judge Williams (Sept. 14) and an Eleventh Circuit panel (Sept. 29, 2026) both refused to pause her sanctions order. Trump's appeal and DOJ's appeal for the IRS and Treasury are pending, and Blanche's audit-immunity order remains in effect.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely position: this is ongoing litigation Bessent legally cannot discuss, the settlement may have legitimate legal justifications not yet public, and declining to comment on active litigation is standard practice, not evidence of wrongdoing.
comeback: The judge's own words are the anchor here, not outside speculation. A federal judge found that no agency submitted settlement documentation establishing the settlement was appropriate, despite an open question about whether a real case or controversy even existed to settle. 'Ongoing litigation' explains why Bessent won't discuss specifics; it doesn't explain why standard settlement documentation was never filed in the first place. A legitimately defensible settlement has paperwork -- that's what makes it a legitimate settlement. The absence of documentation isn't a feature of confidential litigation, it's an anomaly that a federal judge specifically called out.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] The pattern is officials declining to account publicly for a settlement that benefits the president personally, while the agencies on the other side of it line up behind his position instead of defending the government's own interest. Bessent, performing the duties of IRS commissioner, has cited ongoing litigation rather than explain how the audit-immunity terms apply; a federal judge found no adverseness between Trump and the IRS and Treasury he controls; and DOJ, after filing nothing for the government while the case was live, later sided with Trump at the Eleventh Circuit and filed its own appeal of the sanctions order. DOJ's side of the same settlement is covered in the Blanche recusal entry, and the fund it created in the anti-weaponization fund entry; these are one arrangement, not separate instances. A similar reliance on undisclosed process appears in OMB's concealed spend-plan footnotes, though that concerned budget execution rather than the president's personal finances.
confidence_note: MODERATE confidence on the facts as reported (judge's transparency criticism, Bessent's refusal to confirm details) -- these are well-sourced from direct testimony and court proceedings. LOW confidence on whether this constitutes an actual conflict-of-interest violation as opposed to ordinary (if unusually opaque) settlement practice -- Treasury has not said how the published settlement and Blanche's May 19 release order apply to Trump and his family, which is itself the core problem for evaluation. The record shows that a federal judge has flagged transparency concerns about a settlement that may grant the president personal tax benefits, and the responsible Treasury official won't confirm the terms -- not a confirmed conflict-of-interest finding, which hasn't occurred. Re-verified 2026-07-18: this is now MODERATE-HIGH confidence on the underlying settlement's illegitimacy specifically, since a federal judge has now ruled on the merits that no real case or controversy existed -- a materially stronger finding than the transparency criticism this entry previously rested on. Confidence in Bessent's *personal* culpability, as distinct from the settlement's own illegitimacy, remains LOWER, since the ruling did not sanction him. Re-verified 2026-07-26: confidence on Bessent's structural (not personal) implication rises slightly given the court's specific finding about his constrained role; still LOW confidence on personal culpability distinct from the settlement's own illegitimacy, since no sanction was directed at him. Re-verified 2026-08-02: the fund's launch-day details (Blanche/Vance's non-committal stance on January 6 defendant payouts, Morrissey's same-day resignation) are well-corroborated across multiple independent outlets (ABC News, CNBC, Time, Washington Examiner, The Hill, Mediaite, Daily Beast) and add a documented instance of internal, Trump-appointed-official dissent to an entry that previously relied only on the judge's and Bessent's own statements. Re-verified 2026-08-18 (real correction, WebFetch-verified against Bloomberg and Time directly, not search synthesis alone): the appeal this entry previously flagged as merely 'considered likely' has now been filed, and DOJ's post-ruling conduct (reinforcing rather than abandoning audit immunity) is new, directly relevant evidence of the settlement's continued operation despite the adverse ruling. Re-verified 2026-08-25: no material change; appeal remains pending with no ruling identified. Re-verified 2026-08-30 (real correction, HIGH confidence via Yahoo News/TPM syndication of the underlying DOJ filing, corroborated by a direct docket reference on X/Twitter from a court-filings tracker): DOJ's Acting Deputy AG McCotter filed an Eleventh Circuit brief joining Trump's appeal and seeking Judge Williams' removal from the case, a development that predates the 2026-08-18 update by about a week and was missed in both that update and the 2026-08-25 light re-verification. This is materially stronger evidence for the entry's structural-implication theory than anything previously documented -- DOJ is no longer merely declining to defend the ruling, it is actively litigating against the judge who found the collusion. Re-verified 2026-09-02 (moderate append, corroborated across Law&Crime (via Yahoo) and IBTimes UK, both citing the same underlying filing): Judge Williams' August 5, 2026 denial of expedited consideration for Trump's stay motion -- a fact not previously in this entry -- explains the timing of the escalation to the Eleventh Circuit; no ruling on the Eleventh Circuit stay/reassignment request has been identified. The CourtListener docket shows DOJ filed its own notice of appeal for the IRS and Treasury on September 11, 2026, and Judge Williams denied the stay itself on September 14, 2026; per Above the Law, the Eleventh Circuit has asked for briefing on appealability rather than granting a stay. Re-verified 2026-10-18: the Eleventh Circuit denied a stay of the sanctions on September 29, 2026 (Bloomberg News, Scripps News), so the earlier note that it had only ordered appealability briefing is superseded; Warren's office's own letters and releases document the July 6 letters to 11 Trump-tied organizations about the settlement's 'affiliates' reach and the July 15 letter asking Bessent whether the IRS is implementing the immunity order, to which no public reply has been identified.

glance.what: Refused to detail a Trump-family IRS settlement from a suit a judge found was brought improperly

official: Todd Blanche, Attorney General (confirmed August 8, 2026; was Acting Attorney General at the time of this entry's original sourcing)
offense_category: Vindictive/Selective Prosecution (violates Due Process; established legal doctrine, e.g. United States v. Goodwin) -- underlying investigation into Brennan is ongoing and no charges have been filed; Blanche himself has not been personally charged with anything
incident_summary:
In July 2025, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard declassified documents she said showed Obama-era officials fabricated the intelligence community's 2016 assessment that Russia sought to help Trump's campaign, plus a related criminal referral to DOJ. Retired CIA official Susan Miller, an author of the original 2017 assessment, publicly rejected that claim in a CNN interview reported July 26, 2025, saying the intelligence behind the Russia finding was verified, that the findings were not based on the Steele dossier, and that no one had told her team what conclusion to reach. Attorney General Pam Bondi nonetheless ordered federal prosecutors to convene a grand jury investigating the fabrication claim in early August 2025, formalizing the probe in Florida shortly after despite reports questioning the jurisdictional basis for doing so there. On August 20, 2025, Todd Gilbert, then U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Virginia, resigned after DOJ leadership pressured him to open a related grand jury investigation and to sideline a career prosecutor, Zachary Lee, who had concluded the case lacked evidentiary support; Gilbert refused, and reporting that October identified the Russia-probe pressure, not a routine personnel matter, as the real reason he was pushed out.

On September 26, 2025, on the government's motion, Chief Judge Cecilia Altonaga ordered two new federal grand juries empaneled beginning January 12, 2026, one in Fort Lauderdale and one in Fort Pierce. In late October 2025, Trump ally Mike Davis said the Fort Pierce grand jury, which he said U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones had moved to empanel, would investigate what Davis calls a decade-long conspiracy against Trump, and suggested Merrick Garland, Lisa Monaco, Chris Wray, and Jack Smith should be compelled to testify. The investigation became public on November 7, 2025, when former CIA Director John Brennan, along with Peter Strzok, Lisa Page, and, per CNN, former DNI James Clapper, was subpoenaed by the Miami-based U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida; Fox News reported that Quiñones was supervising the probe and that law enforcement sources expected up to 30 subpoenas in the coming days. On December 22, 2025, Brennan's attorney wrote to Chief Judge Altonaga alleging possible judge shopping -- that DOJ was steering the grand jury to Fort Pierce, whose only federal judge is Trump-appointed Aileen Cannon, to land any indictment before her -- and asking her to ensure the matter was not steered to Cannon; critics were already calling the expanding probe a fishing expedition relitigating ground covered by prior special-counsel and Senate Intelligence Committee investigations.

On February 17, 2026, the AP reported DOJ had issued a new wave of subpoenas to an array of former intelligence and law-enforcement officials, this time seeking records from the years since the 2017 assessment rather than only the months around it. Brennan's lawyers said he had been told he is a target but had not been given any "legally justifiable basis" for the investigation. On March 19, 2026, CBS News reported that Miami-based federal prosecutors had subpoenaed former FBI Director James Comey (whose separate earlier indictment had been dismissed in November 2025; tracked in a related entry in this database), that more than 130 subpoenas had been issued since the investigation began, and that McCabe had also received a subpoena, which his lawyer called "a vendetta in search of a crime." In April 2026, Maria Medetis Long, the career prosecutor overseeing the case in Miami, was removed after raising concerns about its evidentiary strength; Joseph DiGenova -- a Trump ally, former Trump campaign lawyer, and counselor to Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche -- was installed to lead the investigation in her place.

On May 12, 2026, Reuters reported the FBI had begun questioning current and former CIA officers about Brennan's role in the 2017 assessment -- despite multiple prior independent reviews having already affirmed Russia's 2016 election interference. On July 1, 2026, Brennan sued DOJ seeking a court order to preserve records related to both investigations, laying groundwork for an anticipated vindictive- or selective-prosecution defense should charges be filed.

In early September 2026, DOJ issued a new round of grand jury subpoenas, and Brennan's lawyers said he had now been told he is a target specifically over whether he falsely testified to Congress -- an allegation he and his attorneys have consistently denied -- with DiGenova still helping lead the investigation. On September 10, 2026, DiGenova abruptly resigned, submitting his resignation letter to Blanche that afternoon and telling CBS News only that "it was an honor and a privilege to serve the president and the department"; his wife and Fort Pierce team member, Victoria Toensing, left DOJ the following day. The same September 10 subpoena wave included Brennan himself: his attorney disclosed he had been ordered to appear before the Fort Pierce grand jury on October 15, 2026, named a "subject" of the broader conspiracy investigation while remaining a target only in the separate, narrower false-testimony probe. A DOJ spokesperson thanked DiGenova for "his work these past five months" alongside the Southern District of Florida prosecutors "led by U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones" but did not explain the departure; CBS later reported he left amid tensions with the Deputy Attorney General's Office over the case's management, and in October The Atlantic (as summarized by Mediaite) quoted him: "If you want indictments where there's no evidence, you have an ethical problem." NBC News reported that no one would be named to replace him for now and, citing a source, that DOJ leadership had lost confidence in his leadership and hoped the Justice Department lawyers from Washington already on his team would get the probe back on track; days later, a person familiar with the matter told NBC the investigation was being run by Quiñones with support from Main Justice. The resignation came within days of grand jury witnesses' lawyers being notified of new subpoenas, and investigators separately began reaching out to lawyers for former FBI agents who had investigated Trump's own retention of classified records, requesting voluntary interviews. Bloomberg reported that on September 11, 2026, the investigation expanded further still, with new subpoenas issued including one seeking testimony from Clapper.

The day after DiGenova resigned, Kurt Olsen -- a Trump ally who had pressed DOJ in 2020 to back Trump's challenge to his election loss, later served as the White House's director of election security and integrity, and had since moved to the Miami-based prosecution team -- told Brennan's lawyers there were multiple "viable" grand jury investigations of their client, according to a declaration by Brennan's attorney Ken Wainstein in his records case, reported September 14, 2026: a "far-reaching" Fort Pierce investigation, covering "issues at Mar-a-Lago and beyond," in which Brennan was a "subject," and a narrower investigation run from Washington into his statements to Congress, in which he was a "target" and which remained "still viable." On September 24, 2026, the AP reported that lawyers for current and former FBI agents and analysts who had worked on the investigation into Trump's retention of classified documents disclosed in a court filing that their clients had been subpoenaed to testify before the Fort Pierce grand jury, two of them that week, after FBI requests for voluntary interviews in July and August -- a sign, the AP said, that the probe, which had focused largely on officials who examined the 2016 Russia question, also reached the FBI's 2022 Mar-a-Lago search. The lawyers asked Judge Aileen Cannon to clarify whether her order barring release of non-public information about the documents case allowed them to testify. CNN reported the same week, citing people familiar with the matter, that at a Florida meeting after DiGenova's departure, Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General Aakash Singh, U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones and his deputy Yara Klukas agreed that Quiñones and Klukas would oversee the probe for now and that charges in the immediate future were very unlikely, though prosecutors were still pursuing possible cases against individual Trump critics; CNN also reported that a former supervisor in the FBI's 2016 Russia investigation had recently been interviewed by investigators after receiving immunity. On September 28 and 29, 2026, CBS News and ABC News, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that Olsen had resigned from the Justice Department, and the AP that he had resigned from the investigation; CBS and ABC also reported that several other prosecutors had recently left the team, though one source said some had only been on temporary assignments that had ended and that new attorneys had been added. CNN, which had initially reported that Olsen had quit the department entirely, updated its story on September 30 to say he had left the investigation but that an email he sent DOJ leadership had been mistakenly read as a resignation; the same day, Attorney General Blanche told reporters Olsen "has not resigned" and is "still employed exactly where he was before," adding that the investigation remained "well-staffed." Later that day, a Justice Department official told CBS News that Olsen had announced in a September 28 email that he was leaving the case, that officials had misread the email as a resignation from the department, and that he would remain on staff as senior counsel but would not be assigned to the investigation; CBS added, citing two sources, that a problem with his security clearance had arisen before he sent the email. On October 1, Cannon struck the FBI employees' motion for "lack of conferral" in a brief docket order. Reuters reported October 7, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Olsen's DOJ clearance had been terminated in September, with a failed polygraph playing a role; a DOJ spokesperson confirmed he has no active clearance with the department, while Olsen called any suggestion of a revoked clearance false and said his clearance was not relevant to his leaving the case. On October 7, the FBI employees refiled their motion. On October 15, the day Brennan had been due in Fort Pierce, U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb dismissed his records-preservation suit for lack of standing, calling his allegations of being targeted for opposing the president "deeply concerning" but the injury he alleged "too attenuated" from the actions he sought to block; the AP reported that his grand jury appearance had been postponed and that his lawyers say he remains a target in the false-statements investigation. On October 16, DOJ, in a filing signed for McCotter and Quiñones, asked Cannon to dismiss the agents' refiled motion for lack of jurisdiction, saying the Fort Pierce grand jury "is investigating potential criminal conduct" and that the agents' scheduled testimony had not yet occurred. The investigation had still produced no charges.
elements_required: A career prosecutor's removal from the case coincided with that prosecutor raising concerns about the investigation, rather than an unrelated staffing decision
The replacement lead (DiGenova) has documented political ties to Trump and the current DOJ leadership, rather than being an arms-length career assignment

The investigation targets a prominent, named Trump adversary (Brennan, who has been a vocal Trump critic) over conduct connected to the 2016 Russia-interference assessment, a subject of longstanding public presidential grievance

No indictment has yet been returned, despite the investigations having been open since November 2025 -- consistent with (though not proof of) an evidentiary basis weaker than the resources devoted to the case would suggest

As of September 2026, Brennan's lawyers say he has been told he is a target specifically over allegedly false congressional testimony -- a narrower, more concrete theory than the earlier general 'no legally justifiable basis' framing, relevant to whether the investigation has developed an actual prosecutable theory or simply narrowed its stated rationale without new evidence

DiGenova, installed in April 2026 specifically to advance the case after his predecessor's removal, himself resigned September 10, 2026 without ever bringing charges in either probe -- a second consecutive lead prosecutor exiting the case without producing a prosecutable result, relevant to whether the case has a genuine evidentiary basis or has instead cycled through leadership without one

evidence.description: The Washington Post reported on September 14, 2026 (and NPR, Daily Caller, and others corroborated) that Brennan was personally subpoenaed to testify before the federal grand jury in Fort Pierce, Florida on October 15, 2026, a summons delivered the same day DiGenova resigned. DOJ is separately continuing a related investigation into whether Brennan lied to Congress in 2023. Brennan's lawyer later told a court that prosecutors described him as a "subject" of the Fort Pierce conspiracy investigation and a "target" only of the separate false-statements investigation.

evidence.description: NBC News reported September 14, 2026 on a court declaration by Brennan's attorney Ken Wainstein: DiGenova signed the subpoena for Brennan's Fort Pierce testimony, preliminarily set for October 15, just before resigning, and the next day Kurt Olsen, now on the Southern District of Florida team, told Brennan's lawyers of multiple "viable" grand jury investigations -- a "far-reaching" Fort Pierce probe in which Brennan was a "subject," and a narrower Washington investigation of his statements to Congress in which he was a "target." NBC also reported the investigation was being run by U.S. Attorney Quiñones with support from Main Justice after DiGenova left.
evidence.maps_to_element: As of September 2026, Brennan's lawyers say he has been told he is a target specifically over allegedly false congressional testimony

evidence.description: The AP reported September 24, 2026 that lawyers for current and former FBI agents and analysts who worked on the investigation into Trump's retention of classified documents disclosed in a court filing that their clients had been subpoenaed to testify before the grand jury in Fort Pierce, Florida, in the "grand conspiracy" probe; the filing said the FBI had sought voluntary interviews in July and August, that two clients received subpoenas that Monday, and that DOJ had raised but not formally offered immunity. The AP said the probe, which had focused largely on officials who examined Russia's ties to Trump's 2016 campaign, was also scrutinizing the FBI's 2022 Mar-a-Lago search, and that the lawyers asked Judge Aileen Cannon to clarify whether her order barring release of non-public information about the documents case prevented them from testifying.
evidence.maps_to_element: Continued expansion of the subpoena campaign to FBI personnel from the Mar-a-Lago investigation, still without charges

evidence.description: CNN reported (published September 24, updated September 25, 2026), citing people familiar with the matter, that after DiGenova's resignation Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General Aakash Singh met in Florida with U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones and his deputy, Yara Klukas; the meeting "produced few answers," Quiñones and Klukas would oversee the probe for now with help from McCotter and Singh, and while the team continues to pursue possible individual cases against Trump political critics, "charges in the immediate future were very unlikely, the officials agreed." CNN added that a former supervisor in the FBI's 2016 Russia election-interference investigation had recently sat for an interview with investigators after being given immunity by prosecutors.
evidence.maps_to_element: No indictment has yet been returned, despite the investigations having been open since November 2025

evidence.description: CBS News reported, citing sources familiar with his departure, that Kurt Olsen -- the former White House "Director of Election Security and Integrity" whose referral led to the FBI's seizure of Fulton County's 2020 ballots, and who worked with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2020 to urge the Supreme Court to overturn the election -- had resigned from the Justice Department after working on the "grand conspiracy" investigation, which had produced no charges; CBS said several other prosecutors had recently left the team, though one source said some were out-of-state attorneys whose temporary assignments had ended and that two former prosecutors had since been hired. CBS later added a note that Olsen had contacted the department to say he meant only to step down from the investigation, not to leave his job.
evidence.maps_to_element: Continued staffing of the investigation with Trump allies after DiGenova, and its continued lack of charges

evidence.description: CNN reported, citing a person familiar with the matter, that Olsen had left the investigation after spending several months on it from the Miami-based U.S. attorney's office, the second high-profile departure after DiGenova; in a September 30 update, CNN said its source now described Olsen's email to DOJ leadership as mistakenly read as a resignation from the department itself. CNN also noted Brennan's lawyers had cited communications in which Olsen indicated Brennan was a target in a false-statements probe.
evidence.maps_to_element: A second high-profile departure from the investigation, still without charges

CBS also reported, citing two sources, that before his email "a problem arose with his security clearance," which it said meant he could not effectively work on an investigation that entails reviewing classified evidence.

status: Ongoing -- no charges. Brennan's October 15 grand jury date was postponed, and that day a judge dismissed his records suit for lack of standing; Mar-a-Lago case FBI agents subpoenaed in the probe are seeking Judge Cannon's guidance, which DOJ opposes. DiGenova and Olsen have left the probe.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: reassigning a case from one career prosecutor to a politically-connected appointee is a personnel decision within the Attorney General's normal authority, not itself evidence of vindictiveness; a 2016 intelligence assessment with acknowledged, still-debated methodological criticism is a legitimate subject for investigation independent of who currently criticizes the president.
comeback: The timing -- a prosecutor removed specifically after raising concerns, replaced by a Trump campaign-connected appointee, investigating a prominent and outspoken Trump critic over a matter of long-standing personal presidential grievance -- mirrors the exact pattern (presidential pressure, non-independent prosecutorial substitution, thin evidentiary basis) already documented in the James case under Bondi. Brennan sued for records preservation before any charges existed specifically because that pattern is already established and on the public record; the judge who dismissed that suit on standing grounds called his targeting allegations "deeply concerning."
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Same structural cause as the Bondi-James entry: DOJ's traditional independence from White House direction in prosecutorial targeting of named political adversaries has continued to erode under the current Attorney General, not just the prior one -- suggesting an institutional pattern rather than one official's individual conduct. This investigation itself spans both: opened on Bondi's order and later run by a counselor to Blanche, it has pushed aside officials who resisted or doubted the case -- a U.S. Attorney reportedly forced out after refusing to open a related grand jury probe and sideline a career prosecutor who found the case lacked evidentiary support, and the Miami career prosecutor removed after raising concerns about the case's evidentiary strength (see also the Patel entry) -- while staffing it with Trump allies: DiGenova as its lead, and Kurt Olsen, who had no prior prosecutorial experience and, as a White House official, made the referral behind the FBI's seizure of Fulton County's 2020 ballots (see the Fulton County poll-worker entry).

official: Todd Blanche, Attorney General
offense_category: Hatch Act Concern (5 U.S.C. 7323(a)(1), barring use of official authority or influence to affect an election) -- a sitting Attorney General speaking at Republican campaign events before the 2026 midterms; Senate-confirmed appointees may take part in politics in a personal capacity, so the dispute is whether he acted in his official role; complaints pending with the Office of Special Counsel, not charged (Hatch Act enforcement is administrative)
incident_summary:
Within weeks of taking office, Attorney General Todd Blanche spoke at a series of Republican campaign events ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, a break with the post-Watergate practice of attorneys general staying away from partisan politics. On August 14, 2026, four days after he was sworn in, Blanche spoke at an event at the Nassau County Police Academy in Garden City, New York, headlined by President Trump and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, the Republican nominee for governor of New York. According to watchdog complaints, the event was billed as an official White House appearance on violent crime; Blanche was introduced as the sitting attorney general, identified himself as "attorney general of the United States," and said: "We just heard from our great Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman who's doing everything we need him to do to back the blue, support law enforcement and to make this county a safe county that we can all raise our kids in." Blanche later told the AP, "I will always say yes to speak when the president of the United States asks me to," and that he was "purely thanking cops."

On September 9, 2026, Blanche spoke at the Republican National Committee's 2026 midterm convention in Dallas, an event the committee said was held to support its slate of midterm candidates. The Justice Department said on social media that his "appearance this evening in his personal capacity is legal (and has been approved by ethics)"; the convention's on-screen graphic identified him as a "former federal prosecutor" rather than by his title. Former Attorney General Eric Holder called the appearance "unprecedented" and "disgraceful." On September 15, from the White House podium, Blanche dismissed Democratic lawmakers' concerns about artificial intelligence as "nothing but an effort to influence the midterms." **On September 16, at a North Carolina rally for Republican Senate nominee Michael Whatley, Blanche called Trump "the greatest president of our generation."** He told the crowd that people were safer than two years ago, "And that's President Trump and Vice President Vance delivering on a promise that they made to you." The AP reported that the speech also veered into the stock market, inflation and wage growth.

The Justice Department says the appearances are made in Blanche's personal capacity and do not get into agency policies or official business. "His appearances are reviewed and cleared by the Department's ethics officials," spokesperson Kiersten Pels told the AP, adding that travel expenses are reimbursed by the attorney general. The New York Times reported that those ethics rules had been loosened: in March 2026, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi rescinded a 2022 Garland-era policy that barred DOJ political appointees from partisan events even in a personal capacity, and the ethics office is now led by a former aide to Vice President JD Vance with no prior department experience. **Joseph Tirrell, DOJ's senior ethics official until he was dismissed in 2025, called the North Carolina appearance "terrible."** In his former role, he said, he would have told the attorney general: "That rally sounds like a Hatch Act violation to me, and I'd advise you not to do it."

At least four complaints about Blanche's political appearances have been filed with the Office of Special Counsel (OSC), which enforces the Hatch Act: Public Citizen's in mid-August over the Long Island event; The Steady State's on September 4 over the same event (also naming FBI Director Kash Patel, with a referral to DOJ's Inspector General); The Steady State's in mid-September over his March 2026 CPAC appearance as Deputy Attorney General; and The Steady State's on September 28 over the Dallas convention speech. DOJ called the first complaint "baseless" and "a politically motivated complaint designed to weaponize the Hatch Act against the attorney general for his support of law enforcement."

On October 9, 2026, PBS News reported on a new internal memo from DOJ's top ethics official that loosens the department's rules further. Earlier versions of the department's Hatch Act guidance barred "further restricted" employees from activities such as addressing a political rally or endorsing a candidate; the new version adds a line exempting "employees appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate (PAS)," which, PBS reported, allows them, including the attorney general, to address political gatherings and endorse or oppose candidates. It also drops the previous guidance's advice, issued under Bondi, that presidential appointees avoid public appearances in a state shortly before an election there, saying instead that official appearances with partisan candidates "warrant heightened scrutiny — especially when close to an election." A DOJ spokesperson said the update "clarifies an existing exception under the Hatch Act for Presidentially-appointed, Senate-confirmed officials" rather than changing the rules. Tirrell told PBS that DOJ employees "are now only held to the standard set by [the Hatch Act]," and said he believes Blanche's appearances still violate the Act's separate bar on using official authority to influence the outcome of elections.

incident_summary: DOJ subpoenaed Matthew Cole, a freelance journalist who co-wrote a 2025 New York Times story on a botched 2019 Navy SEAL Team 6 mission in North Korea (in which SEALs killed several unarmed North Koreans while attempting to plant a listening device, based on reporting from roughly two dozen unnamed sources), **demanding his testimony and more than two years of his notes and communications to identify his sources**. The subpoena was issued in Virginia in February 2026, while Pam Bondi was Attorney General; FBI agents attempted to deliver it in person at Cole's New York City residence, then delivered it to his lawyer when he was not home. Its existence was not made public until August 1, 2026, when The Times disclosed it at Cole's request -- the paper said it supported his decision to make public a subpoena the government had tried to keep secret, and is paying for his legal representation. Unlike DOJ's subpoenas of Wall Street Journal reporters (Iran war reporting), a Washington Post reporter (Venezuela coverage) and New York Times reporters (Air Force One security story), all of which DOJ withdrew after legal challenges, DOJ had refused to withdraw the Cole subpoena as of early October 2026.

offense_category: Conflict of Interest -- Directing DOJ to Halt Cryptocurrency Enforcement While Personally Holding Crypto Assets an Ethics Agreement Required Him to Divest, Then Gifting Rather Than Selling Those Assets to His Own Children
incident_summary:
At his March 2025 Senate confirmation, Blanche disclosed cryptocurrency holdings valued between $159,000 and $485,000, including Bitcoin ($100,000-$250,000), Solana, Ethereum, and Coinbase stock. His ethics agreement required him to fully divest those holdings within 90 days of confirmation and, until then, barred him from participating in any matter with a 'direct and predictable effect' on his crypto-related financial interests. In April 2025, Blanche issued a DOJ-wide memo titled 'Ending Regulation by Prosecution' that terminated Biden-era investigations into crypto companies, dealers, and exchanges, disbanded the National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team -- which had secured major convictions including a $110 million fraud case and a settlement with Binance's founder resulting in $4.3 billion in penalties -- and told prosecutors to stop targeting exchanges, mixing services and offline wallets for their users' acts, focusing instead on people who victimize digital-asset investors or use crypto to further crimes such as terrorism, narcotics and human trafficking, organized crime, hacking, and cartel and gang financing. **Rather than selling his crypto holdings as the ethics agreement required, Blanche transferred assets valued between $116,000 and $315,000 as gifts to his adult children and a grandchild in late May and early June 2025**, separately selling only $5,000-$75,000 worth of additional holdings. Ethics experts said this method of 'divestment' defeated its purpose: Virginia Canter, a former White House and Treasury ethics lawyer, said 'if you are invested in that industry and now making a decision that could affect whether or not the DOJ is gonna pursue prosecutions, that's an obvious conflict of interest,' and Kedric Payne, the Campaign Legal Center's ethics director, said gifting the assets to adult children 'defeats' the law's purpose of eliminating even the appearance that an official's decisions are influenced by personal financial interests. Blanche's case was one instance of a broader pattern: ProPublica's analysis found the Trump administration's approximately 216 political appointees collectively held $175-340 million in cryptocurrency, compared to roughly two dozen Biden appointees holding under $7 million combined -- with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick (formerly Cantor Fitzgerald's CEO, with billions in crypto investments) and SEC Chair Paul Atkins (who owned up to $6 million in crypto-related businesses) cited as other crypto-invested officials in directly relevant regulatory positions.

Update 2026-10-24: In January 2026 the Campaign Legal Center asked the Justice Department's acting inspector general to investigate whether Blanche's crypto orders broke the criminal conflict-of-interest law, and six Democratic senators wrote to him that "at the very least, you had a glaring conflict of interest and should have recused yourself." A DOJ spokesperson said the matter "was appropriately flagged, addressed, and cleared in advance" but did not say who cleared it. Blanche's 2026 annual financial disclosure, certified by the Office of Government Ethics on September 2, 2026, carries an annotation on his 2025 crypto transactions: "DOJ IG declined further action." The filing gives no reasons.

The same conflict pattern (senior officials with regulatory authority over crypto policy personally holding substantial crypto assets) is documented at scale across the administration's political appointees

offense_category: Selective/Weaponized Enforcement -- DOJ installed a prosecutor who was on the Capitol grounds on January 6, 2021 -- in what a former DOJ Capitol Siege Section prosecutor called the restricted area -- to co-direct a task force prosecuting left-wing political violence as domestic terrorism, raising a direct double-standard concern -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary:
Brian Lynch has co-directed Joint Task Force Vanguard -- a DOJ task force that DOJ describes as central to prosecuting alleged left-wing political violence -- since March 2026, when Todd Blanche was still Deputy Attorney General (he became Acting Attorney General on April 2, 2026); the task force indicted 15 anti-ICE protesters in Minneapolis. Reporting revealed that Lynch, then three months into his job as an assistant U.S. attorney in Maryland, attended the January 6, 2021 march at the Capitol wearing a Trump 2020 hat and a shirt bearing an Afghanistan deployment service map. Images obtained by Talking Points Memo show Lynch standing near a crane on Capitol grounds in what a former federal prosecutor described as "definitely in the restricted area." A DOJ official confirmed Lynch "was present but never entered the Capitol, left the grounds after a brief period, and did not commit and was never accused of any violation of law." Michael Romano, former deputy chief of DOJ's now-disbanded Capitol Siege Section (which prosecuted January 6 cases), said he was surprised a prosecutor present that day continued working and was later promoted to lead a task force prosecuting political violence, noting "people were trying to stop the certification of the electoral college vote on January 6th." Lynch did not respond to requests for comment.

The case Lynch's task force built has since drawn a legal challenge leaning directly on his Jan. 6 presence. On August 13, 2026, defense attorney Kevin Riach filed a discovery motion on behalf of defendant Isaac Sant, one of the 15 Minneapolis anti-ICE defendants, calling Lynch's grand-jury conspiracy slide -- which named groups including the AFL-CIO and the Minneapolis Federation of Educators as co-conspirators "with no evidence" tying them to the defendants -- part of a "broad and irrational investigation," and signaled an intent to move to dismiss for selective prosecution. The motion draws on DHS undercover-surveillance reports the government produced in discovery, and on August 25, 2026, Riach filed a further batch of exhibits in support of it, including Homeland Security Investigations reports from its "Project Whipple Shield" investigation. A hearing was held August 27, 2026 before U.S. Magistrate Judge David Schultz on Riach's discovery motion; Sant told reporters outside court the motion sought "to reveal the scope of the spying" by DHS. Schultz did not rule from the bench and said he plans to issue an order on the motion soon, with no exact timeline given, FOX 9 reported. Court records show that after the hearing, Schultz allowed prosecutors to file supplemental briefing, which they filed September 10, 2026, and on September 16 he gave Sant's lawyer more time to respond.

offense_category: Prosecutorial Discretion Override / Corporate Accountability Failure -- DOJ senior leadership overruled its own Criminal Division's recommendation to pursue felony charges over infant hospitalizations and possible deaths, in favor of a civil settlement, against a company represented by a law firm with a pro-bono services deal benefiting pro-Trump causes
incident_summary: Federal prosecutors investigated Cronobacter bacterial contamination at Abbott Laboratories' Sturgis, Michigan infant-formula plant, where the FDA said **five infants were hospitalized with bacterial infections that 'may have contributed to death in two patients'**. Prosecutors reportedly recommended a felony charge that Abbott executives conspired to defraud the US, plus a separate Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act charge against the company. Tysen Duva, the DOJ Criminal Division's assistant attorney general, supported pursuing the felony charges, but was reportedly overruled by the Deputy Attorney General's office, then led by Todd Blanche, which ordered the criminal investigation closed. DOJ instead pursued a civil False Claims Act settlement, which a senior DOJ official called 'the best mechanism to achieve accountability, deterrence and protection of the public,' saying it included a 'significant' monetary penalty; on September 14, 2026, DOJ announced Abbott would pay $384,999,040, saying there had been no determination of liability. Sen. Adam Schiff opened an inquiry into the decision, writing to DOJ: 'Under your management, DOJ does not consider a case involving deadly risks to medically sensitive infants, after a recommendation of a felony charge, to be worthy of criminal prosecution,' and demanding an explanation for why prosecutors' advice was rejected. Abbott is represented by Kirkland & Ellis, one of the law firms that struck a deal with the White House providing pro-bono legal services to pro-Trump causes -- the same firm documented elsewhere in this tracker's entry on DOJ's subpoenas of law firms over Boris Epshteyn communications.

offense_category: Public Admission That DOJ Prosecutorial Decisions Are Directed by Presidential Preference Rather Than Institutional Independence -- an institutional-accountability claim resting on the official's own on-record statements, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: In an April 2026 NBC News interview, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche -- Trump's former personal defense attorney -- was asked about a communication in which Trump had publicly implored then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to indict several of his political enemies. Blanche said Americans should be 'happy' about it, calling it an example of the president being upfront with the public and making his 'high expectations' clear: 'That type of communication from President Trump should make every American happy,' Blanche said, adding it 'means that there's an executive, a chief executive, that is making sure every one of his Cabinet members are working as hard as they should.' Blanche described Trump as 'my boss' and characterized the investigations into Trump's political opponents as receiving 'outsized focus' only because 'they involve individuals that the president has had significant issues' with -- not because of their share of DOJ's actual caseload. Separately, Blanche suggested prosecutors could continue pursuing cases against a target even after a grand jury declines to indict, rather than treating a declined indictment as the matter's end -- 'You don't have to just take a "no true bill" from a grand jury and walk away,' he said. Legal commentary in Just Security later urged courts to adopt a 'no true bill' rule, devised by the chief judge of D.C.'s federal district court, requiring prosecutors to disclose a grand jury's prior refusal to indict before re-presenting a case elsewhere. The interview came as Blanche's own nomination for permanent Attorney General faced a contested Senate confirmation process.

offense_category: DOJ Weaponization Against the Legal Profession / Executive Privilege Misuse -- DOJ using civil-litigation subpoena power against private law firms to shield a presidential adviser's communications from a bar association's discovery request, while its own public justification concedes those communications are relevant
incident_summary:
Starting around February 2025, Trump used executive orders to strip lawyers at firms he viewed as hostile -- including firms that had represented his adversaries or investigated him -- of security clearances, government contracts, and building access. Rather than negotiating with government attorneys, targeted firms instead cut deals directly with Boris Epshteyn, Trump's personal lawyer, who by April 2025 had extracted commitments of close to $1 billion in free legal services for Trump-aligned causes plus changes to hiring practices, according to the Wall Street Journal; the nine firms that reached these deals, beginning with Paul, Weiss in March 2025, were Paul, Weiss, Skadden, Willkie Farr & Gallagher, Milbank, Kirkland & Ellis, Latham & Watkins, A&O Shearman, Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, and Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft; Bloomberg Law put their combined pledges at $940 million. In early July 2026 (the University of Wisconsin Law School's Lawyers and Democratic Decline tracker says the subpoenas were issued July 1; DOJ's notice to the ABA is dated July 2), the Justice Department subpoenaed 14 major law firms and their leaders -- the nine firms that reached deals pledging free legal services to the administration, the four firms that successfully challenged Trump's executive orders targeting them in court (Perkins Coie, Jenner & Block, WilmerHale, and Susman Godfrey), and Covington & Burling, which was targeted by a February 25, 2025 presidential memorandum -- seeking the firms' communications with Trump adviser Boris Epshteyn about those executive orders, plus any communications the firms had with the American Bar Association regarding Epshteyn. The New York Times reported the subpoenas on July 14, and DOJ disclosed them in a July 17 court filing in the ABA's ongoing lawsuit alleging its members face harm from the administration's law-firm policy; DOJ's stated position was that the ABA should seek this information from its own members or the firms rather than from the White House directly, while simultaneously invoking executive privilege to withhold Epshteyn's communications from direct disclosure, framing them as confidential presidential advice. DOJ's subpoena notice was filed under the name of Civil Division Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate and signed by trial attorney Adam S. Fox. On July 17, DOJ also moved to disqualify Susman Godfrey, one of the subpoenaed firms, as the ABA's counsel. The appeal of the underlying executive orders, already struck down for the four affected firms, remained pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, which heard argument on May 14, 2026.

In a July 22, 2026 reply supporting its July 7 motion to compel, the ABA said the government's argument "leads to an absurd outcome," called its law-firm subpoenas "a huge waste of time (and resources) for everyone involved," and pressed for direct production by DOJ or a compliant privilege log. The subpoenas also called the 14 firms' leaders to depositions set for August 3, 2026; no account of those depositions has been publicly reported. Judge Amir H. Ali heard the motion to compel on July 31 and took it under advisement, and on August 3 ordered DOJ to identify the individuals and custodians at issue for several of the ABA's requests or assert privilege over them. On August 10, 2026, DOJ's Office of Legal Counsel issued a 21-page opinion to the Counsel to the President, signed by Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser, concluding that executive privilege can extend to a president's communications with private advisers -- "anyone the President consults outside the Executive Branch" -- where the communications relate to official presidential decisionmaking, involve or reflect communications with the President or his direct advisers, and are confidential; the opinion does not mention the ABA case or Epshteyn. The Washington Examiner reported it on August 11. On August 17, DOJ formally asserted the presidential communications privilege over the non-public names of presidential advisers and custodians the court had ordered it to identify, saying the subpoenaed firms had "only just begun to produce records." On August 25, DOJ invoked the OLC opinion in its reply supporting the motion it had filed on July 2, on behalf of the Executive Office of the President and the United States, to quash the ABA's own document and deposition subpoenas to Epshteyn, turning what had been a litigation-filing assertion into a position backed by OLC's formal opinion.

offense_category: Unlawful service in a Senate-confirmed office -- a federal judge found that the Justice Department kept an unconfirmed prosecutor running the country's largest federal judicial district as a 'de facto' U.S. attorney by changing his titles after his 120-day interim term expired; a court ruling on appointment law, not a criminal charge against anyone, and under appeal
incident_summary: Bill Essayli became interim U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, which covers seven counties including Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside and San Bernardino, in April 2025. Federal law limited that interim appointment to 120 days. On July 29, 2025, with the term about to expire, Essayli resigned and then-Attorney General Pam Bondi appointed him a 'special attorney' and designated him First Assistant U.S. Attorney, which let him keep directing the office without a presidential nomination or Senate confirmation (FOX 11, Fox News). On October 28, 2025, Senior U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright of Hawaii, assigned after the district's chief judge recused all of its judges from the matter, ruled that **Essayli unlawfully assumed the role of Acting United States Attorney** and had served unlawfully since July 29, 2025, in violation of the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (Democracy Docket). He did not dismiss the defendants' indictments, which other prosecutors had signed, and held that Essayli could still act as First Assistant. Essayli wrote on X, 'nothing is changing. I continue serving as the top federal prosecutor in the Central District of California' (NBC News). On December 12, 2025, Seabright denied reconsideration, holding that Bondi had validly appointed Essayli a Special Attorney and delegated him a First Assistant's authority. After the Ninth Circuit upheld the disqualification of Sigal Chattah, who had been placed in a similar First Assistant role in Nevada, ruling, as FOX 11 (City News Service) put it, that DOJ cannot keep an unconfirmed official in charge of a U.S. attorney's office merely by altering job titles while preserving full authority, two defendants renewed their challenges. The Central District's Chief Judge, Dolly M. Gee, again recused all of the district's judges from motions on Essayli's disqualification and sent them to Seabright. On September 23, 2026, Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a revised order narrowing Essayli's designation (FOX 11, Fox News). On October 27, 2026, Seabright ruled that Essayli, 'even in his designated roles as a Special Attorney and FAUSA,' is **unlawfully serving as a 'de facto' United States Attorney**, and disqualified him from participating in or supervising the prosecutions of Jaime Hector Ramirez (a felon-in-possession case) and Tu Anh Tran (a stolen-shipment case), while again declining to dismiss the indictments (court docket). He found Blanche's revised order 'functionally equivalent to Essayli's prior ineffective designation' (FOX 11). The order does not take immediate effect; the government has five business days to move for a stay pending appeal. Essayli said, 'We respectfully disagree with the court's order,' that the President and the Attorney General 'have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,' and that 'ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court, and I look forward to serving in my current role until then' (Fox News).
