incident_summary: On July 17, 2025, amid mounting pressure over DOJ's withheld Epstein files, Trump publicly directed Attorney General Pam Bondi to "produce any and all pertinent Grand Jury testimony"; the next day, July 18, DOJ under Bondi asked the Southern District of New York to unseal grand jury materials from Maxwell's criminal case; a parallel DOJ motion to unseal grand jury materials in the original Florida Epstein criminal case was denied on July 23, 2025 by U.S. District Judge Robin Rosenberg, who ruled that DOJ's rationales "are no exceptions" to grand jury secrecy under binding 11th Circuit precedent and wrote that the government itself "has effectively conceded that the Court's hands are tied." Amid mounting public and congressional criticism over DOJ's refusal to release the full Epstein files, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche -- Trump's own former personal defense attorney -- personally interviewed Ghislaine Maxwell, Jeffrey Epstein's convicted co-conspirator serving 20 years for sex trafficking, over two days (July 24-25, 2025) in Tallahassee, Florida, under a grant of limited/proffer immunity; Blanche had announced the outreach on July 22 in a statement Bondi posted on X: "President Trump has told us to release all credible evidence." Maxwell's attorney said she "answered every single question" and had been cooperating "100%." Asked in July 2025 about clemency for Maxwell, Trump said, "I'm allowed to do it, but it's something I have not thought about." Roughly a week after the interview, on August 1, 2025, Maxwell was quietly transferred from a low-security facility to FPC Bryan, Texas -- one of only three minimum-security federal prison camps in the country, ordinarily reserved for low-risk, often white-collar offenders -- a transfer multiple former federal prison officials called "highly unusual" for a convicted sex offender. On August 5, 2025, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced H.Res.635, expressing that Maxwell should not receive a pardon, commutation, or other clemency; it drew 14 Democratic cosponsors in all, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and has received no floor vote. Victims were given until August 5, 2025 to submit letters on DOJ's SDNY unsealing motion; on August 5 and 6 the court docketed six letters that representatives of victims and other witnesses had submitted. One victim, in a letter reported by CNN on August 4, called the push "political warfare" that shields powerful men while ignoring survivors and wrote that the government's continued handling of the matter was "eating at me day after day." A second, in a letter reported August 10, objected specifically to what she called Maxwell's impending "public legitimization," separately criticizing Maxwell's prison transfer, DOJ's private meetings with her, and clemency speculation, and accused the administration of retraumatizing survivors by moving to unseal without consulting them first. On August 11, 2025, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer -- the same judge who later denied Maxwell's habeas petition -- denied DOJ's unsealing bid in a scathing 31-page order, calling the government's central premise that the materials would reveal meaningful new information about Epstein's or Maxwell's crimes "demonstrably false," and separately faulting DOJ for failing to notify Epstein's and Maxwell's victims of the request in advance. On August 19, 2025, Democracy Forward sued DOJ and the FBI to force release of communications about the investigation, including any Epstein-Trump correspondence. On August 20, 2025, U.S. District Judge Richard Berman likewise denied DOJ's bid to unseal grand jury records from Epstein's 2019 New York case, finding that the information in them "pales in comparison to the Epstein investigative information and materials in the hands of the Department of Justice." On August 22, 2025, DOJ released the July 24-25 interview transcript (263 pages for day one, 66 for day two) and audio; in it, Maxwell said she "never saw" Trump "in any inappropriate setting" and disputed aspects of her own conviction, casting doubt on accuser Virginia Giuffre's allegations -- prompting Giuffre's family to say DOJ had given Maxwell "a platform to rewrite history." The Supreme Court declined to hear Maxwell's direct appeal on October 6, 2025. Reps. Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia each wrote to FPC Bryan Warden Tanisha Hall on October 30, 2025 seeking answers about her treatment; on November 8, 2025, NBC News reported on Maxwell's own emails from her first months at FPC Bryan, obtained by the House Judiciary Committee, in which she called herself "much much happier" and "safe," while separate Wall Street Journal reporting documented additional perks (dormitory meal delivery, late-night workouts, priority shower access) and inmates alleging retaliation, including one transfer, for discussing Maxwell with reporters. On November 10, 2025, House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Rep. Jamie Raskin disclosed that a whistleblower had come forward describing extensive special treatment FPC Bryan's warden was arranging for Maxwell: customized meals delivered to her cell, private visitor meetings in a cordoned-off area with refreshments, visitors permitted to bring computers (described as unprecedented), the warden personally handling her documents and correspondence, after-hours private exercise time in staff-only areas, and access to a service-dog-in-training for recreation that other inmates and staff were not normally permitted to touch. Raskin said the same whistleblower reported Maxwell was actively preparing a formal commutation application for submission to Trump with the warden's assistance. Raskin publicly demanded written answers from Trump on the extent of any clemency discussions and requested Blanche testify publicly before the Committee; no response from Trump, Blanche, or the Bureau of Prisons was identified in reporting reviewed. In November 2025, Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One, "I don't talk about that. I don't rule it in or out." On December 9, 2025, after Congress passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, Engelmayer granted DOJ's renewed request to unseal the Maxwell-case grand jury materials, citing the Act, while again criticizing DOJ for moving without notice to victims. On February 9, 2026, appearing virtually for the House Oversight Committee's subpoenaed deposition, which Chairman James Comer had postponed in August 2025 until the Supreme Court acted on her appeal, Maxwell invoked the Fifth Amendment rather than answer questions; her attorney, David Oscar Markus, said she was "prepared to speak fully and honestly" if Trump granted her clemency. On July 29, 2026, the Senate agreed by unanimous consent to S.Res.608, sponsored by Sen. Jacky Rosen, expressing that Maxwell should not be granted a presidential pardon or any form of clemency. On August 25, 2026, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer denied her self-represented habeas corpus petition in a 67-page opinion calling her claims "meritless" and warning that further appeals would not be considered made in good faith. On October 26, 2026, House Judiciary Committee Democrats, the committee's minority, released a staff report alleging that Blanche likely knew of certain survivors' claims against Trump when he interviewed Maxwell -- an FBI "Prominent Names" slide deck compiled in the weeks before the interview referenced the account of one of them -- yet asked no questions about the allegations of that survivor, who testified at Maxwell's trial under the pseudonym "Jane" and who, according to DOJ documents the report cites, alleged that Epstein introduced her to Trump at Mar-a-Lago in 1994, when she was 14. According to the report and the transcript pages it reproduces, when Maxwell said "I believe you're talking about Jane," Blanche answered "yeah" and then cut her off, and "on at least three separate occasions" he directed Maxwell not to discuss Jane, saying "I don't want to get into … he said, she said" and, when she raised Jane again, "Let's not talk about individuals"; the report argued "the whole point of the conversation was not to uncover information but to create a conspiracy of silence." Noting that the House Oversight Committee had scheduled an interview with Maxwell for August 11, 2025, the report argued that his instructions "potentially constituted witness tampering and obstruction of an official proceeding" and that he "may have engaged in criminal obstruction of justice." The report, a minority-staff allegation rather than any finding, called for an independent special counsel under 28 C.F.R. § 600.1, an appointment that regulation assigns to the Attorney General -- now Blanche himself -- or, if he is recused, the Acting Attorney General, and said there was "little reason to believe this Administration will take even this minimal step." A Justice Department spokesperson called the report "nothing more than a last-ditch effort by House Judiciary Democrats to mislead the public."

Whether this sequence constitutes an implicit or explicit clemency-for-favorable-testimony arrangement, versus legitimate investigative cooperation and a prison-classification decision made on independent grounds -- not independently adjudicated as of this entry

status: Maxwell remains at FPC Bryan (projected 2037 release) with no clemency granted; S.Res.608 is non-binding. rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: the interview was legitimate investigative fact-finding conducted under standard, narrow proffer immunity that did not affect Maxwell's underlying conviction or sentence; the prison transfer was a routine Bureau of Prisons classification decision unrelated to the interview's content or timing; and no pardon has actually been granted, meaning the clemency concern remains speculative. DOJ and the White House have publicly framed the process as transparency-driven, responding to bipartisan calls to release more information about Epstein's associates. Responding to House Judiciary Democrats' October 2026 staff report alleging possible obstruction by Blanche, a DOJ spokesperson called it "nothing more than a last-ditch effort by House Judiciary Democrats to mislead the public."
comeback: The timing is the hardest fact to explain away: a minimum-security transfer highly unusual for a convicted sex trafficker followed the interview by about a week, and the interview itself was conducted not by a career prosecutor but by the president's own former personal defense attorney -- while the resulting testimony specifically and uniquely exculpated Trump ('never saw him in any inappropriate setting'). The Senate's unanimous-consent adoption of S.Res.608 on July 29, 2026, opposing clemency for Maxwell before any had been granted, reflects that lawmakers across party lines saw the same pattern as concerning enough to get ahead of. Whether or not a formal quid-pro-quo is ever proven, the sequence -- interview by a conflicted official, unusual benefit, favorable testimony, open clemency speculation -- is the kind of appearance-of-impropriety pattern accountability frameworks exist to flag even without a provable explicit deal.

official: Todd Blanche, Deputy Attorney General
offense_category: Weaponizing the Federal Clemency Process for Political Loyalty -- firing DOJ's career Pardon Attorney for declining a personal favor for a Trump ally, then installing a political appointee who has used the office to fast-track clemency for MAGA-aligned figures
incident_summary:
Elizabeth Oyer, DOJ's career Pardon Attorney since 2022, was fired on March 7, 2025 -- two days after Todd Blanche was confirmed as Deputy Attorney General. Oyer later testified, including before the Senate Judiciary Committee on July 16, 2026 during Blanche's own confirmation hearing to become Attorney General, that Blanche's office had asked her to recommend restoring gun rights to actor Mel Gibson, who lost that right after a 2011 misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction and who has a personal relationship with President Trump; Gibson's attorneys had written directly to senior DOJ officials citing a special appointment he had received from Trump. When Oyer declined and was pressed to reconsider, she was fired without any stated reason in a termination letter signed by Blanche.

On May 14, 2025, Trump appointed Edward "Ed" Martin Jr. -- previously interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, known for openly blending Trump's political goals with DOJ's clemency function -- as the new Pardon Attorney. Within two weeks of Martin's appointment, Trump pardoned more than two dozen MAGA-aligned loyalists and wealthy donors, including Culpeper County, Virginia Sheriff Scott Jenkins, convicted in December 2024 on federal bribery charges in a "cash-for-badges" scheme and sentenced to 10 years (Martin posted "No MAGA left behind" after the Jenkins pardon); reality-TV stars Todd and Julie Chrisley, pardoned May 28, 2025 after a 2022 conviction for defrauding banks of more than $30 million and evading federal taxes, after their daughter Savannah, a Trump-aligned media figure and RNC speaker, publicly and personally lobbied for their release and Trump called her directly to tell her the pardons were coming; and a commuted sentence for Larry Hoover, a Chicago gang leader (Gangster Disciples) serving multiple life sentences for conspiracy and drug-trafficking convictions -- a notable outlier from the wave's otherwise white-collar/MAGA-loyalist pattern, since Hoover's case is neither a fraud conviction nor an obvious political-donor connection. Martin went on to organize symbolic pardons for participants in the 2020 fake-elector scheme and to grant clemency or pardons to a number of Trump-connected officials and campaign donors; ProPublica reporting found no comparable path forward for ordinary clemency applicants under the restructured office. A June 17, 2025 House Judiciary Committee Democrats analysis, led by Ranking Member Jamie Raskin, quantified the pattern's scope beyond named individual examples: Trump's pardons and commutations -- more than 1,600 recipients, including white-collar and fraud convictions well beyond the MAGA-loyalist cases above -- had eliminated roughly $1.3 billion in restitution and fines owed to crime victims and taxpayers.

On December 3, 2025, Trump pardoned Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-TX) and his wife, ending a sitting Democratic member of Congress's active federal prosecution mid-case -- a materially different scenario from the wave above, which involved already-convicted or symbolic beneficiaries rather than a pending indictment against a sitting lawmaker. Cuellar and his wife had been indicted in 2024 on 12 counts of bribery, conspiracy, and money laundering centered on an alleged roughly $600,000 in bribes from Azerbaijan and a Mexican bank; two Foreign Agents Registration Act-related counts had already been narrowed under a separate Trump-driven policy sharply limiting FARA prosecutions before the pardon voided the remaining charges entirely. Cuellar's response undercuts any "reciprocal loyalty" framing of the pardon: he announced he would run for re-election as a Democrat, prompting Trump to publicly call the decision "a lack of LOYALTY" on social media -- itself evidence that the administration frames pardons as transactions expecting political fealty in return. Government watchdog group CREW sued for records on the pardon's origin, and Cuellar continued to face a separate House Ethics Committee investigation, opened May 2024 and reauthorized July 2025, unaffected by the federal pardon.

Martin's tenure as Pardon Attorney ended when Trump announced on August 21, 2026 that Martin was "leaving to go outside to fight Legal Battles for the upcoming Midterm Election, and the Presidential Election of 2028"; the announcement named no successor Pardon Attorney, with no reporting indicating a change of direction for the office's clemency practices. Martin's January 1, 2026 removal as head of DOJ's Weaponization Working Group, which CNN's sources tied in part to a DOJ review finding he improperly handled grand jury material -- a related but factually distinct episode from the clemency-favoritism pattern described here -- is tracked separately in this database. On September 3, 2026, Oyer filed suit in federal court in Washington, D.C. against DOJ and Blanche, seeking a declaration that her removal was unlawful, reinstatement to federal service, and back pay.

official: Todd Blanche, Attorney General (sued in his official capacity; was Acting Attorney General when the suit was filed and the June 2026 injunction issued, and as Deputy Attorney General signed DOJ's 2025-2026 letters to Congress on the files' production)
offense_category: Resisting a Federal Court's Orders to Comply With the Epstein Files Transparency Act -- a judge rejected DOJ's reasons for withholding FBI interview notes and never reviewing foreign-language files; no contempt finding has been made
incident_summary:
The Epstein Files Transparency Act, signed November 19, 2025, required the Attorney General to publish the Justice Department's unclassified Epstein and Maxwell files by December 19, 2025, with a written justification for every redaction published in the Federal Register. In a January 30, 2026 letter to Congress, then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche said foreign-language materials had not been reviewed or produced because "it was not practicable for a first-level reviewer to determine the responsiveness of a foreign-language document." On April 27, 2026, lawyer and journalist Katie Phang sued Blanche, then Acting Attorney General, in federal court in Washington under the Administrative Procedure Act (Phang v. Blanche, No. 26-cv-1417), alleging DOJ had improperly redacted and withheld records the law required it to release, including notes of FBI interviews with a woman who alleged that, when she was about 13, Epstein introduced her to Trump, who then assaulted her.

On June 25, 2026, U.S. District Judge Emmet G. Sullivan granted Phang a preliminary injunction. DOJ had argued that Phang lacked standing and a right to sue but did not respond substantively to her merits arguments, which the court treated as conceded. The order required DOJ, by July 2, to unredact names in eight emails and two DOJ documents or show cause why not; to produce the handwritten FBI notes behind four FD-302 interview reports or show cause; to begin reviewing and producing foreign-language materials and notify the court; and to publish the redaction log in the Federal Register or explain why it could not. DOJ answered that the notes were "substantially similar" to the typed reports and hard to redact, and that the court should not "supplant Congress's acceptance" of its foreign-language explanation. At an August 13 hearing, where a DOJ lawyer could say only that the Federal Register publication was "forthcoming," Sullivan said "the public has a right to know what the hell is going on in this case," recalled holding Justice Department prosecutors in contempt in the Ted Stevens corruption case, and said "I don't want to do it, but I will do it to ensure justice is fairly administered." DOJ filed a notice of appeal on August 24 and, on August 27, published its February 14 report to Congress in the Federal Register as its redaction justification.

On September 16, 2026, after reviewing documents privately, Sullivan discharged the show-cause orders for seven documents and for the redaction log but **rejected DOJ's reasons for withholding the handwritten FBI interview notes and for never reviewing foreign-language Epstein files, and on the foreign-language files wrote that DOJ "cites no authority for the proposition that administrative inconvenience excuses him from meeting his statutory obligations."** He called a civil contempt finding "premature" because DOJ had now stated its rationale, set out the legal standard for contempt, and ordered Blanche, by September 24, to give the court redacted and unredacted copies of the notes and documentation for three disputed victim redactions, and to begin the foreign-language review and notify the court, seeking clarification by September 21 if he considered that order not "clear and unambiguous." In a separate order the same day, Sullivan found DOJ had missed its June 26 deadline to answer the lawsuit without seeking an extension, and ordered an answer by September 24.

DOJ appealed again and, on the evening of Friday, September 18, asked Sullivan to pause the foreign-language requirement, arguing that once documents are produced they "cannot be unproduced." On September 21 he denied the request because DOJ had not conferred with Phang's lawyers as local rules require, said he would have denied it on the merits anyway, and temporarily stayed only the foreign-language deadline so DOJ could ask the D.C. Circuit for a stay, which it did on September 22, arguing Phang has no right to sue. DOJ filed its answer on September 24, denying that it had failed to comply with the Act. MeidasTouch reported that Phang said on September 25 that a DOJ lawyer had told her by email that DOJ had given the judge the FBI notes by the deadline, though DOJ filed no public notice of what it submitted; the same report said, per Phang, that no foreign-language Epstein-file document had been publicly produced. The foreign-language deadline remains paused under Sullivan's temporary stay while the D.C. Circuit weighs DOJ's stay request; on September 25 Phang opposed that request and asked the appeals court to dismiss the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.

official: Todd Blanche, Attorney General (confirmed August 8, 2026; former personal defense attorney to President Trump)
offense_category: Conflict of Interest / Breach of Sworn Recusal Commitment (relevant standards: DOJ ethics regulations on personal/substantial participation in matters involving a former client; professional conduct rules, New York Rules of Professional Conduct, subject of a grievance complaint before New York's Attorney Grievance Committee, declined at staff level with reconsideration pending) — NOT charged criminally; this is a professional-ethics and conflict-of-interest matter, addressed via attorney grievance complaint and congressional inquiry, not criminal prosecution
incident_summary:
At his February 12, 2025 Senate confirmation hearing for Deputy Attorney General, Todd Blanche testified under oath: "I will follow the rules as told to me by the experts, career prosecutors in the department, if it comes to ever recusing." In March 2025, less than two weeks after he took office as Deputy Attorney General, DOJ's top career ethics lawyer, Joseph Tirrell, formally advised him that his recusal from cases involving Donald Trump in his personal capacity was necessary, given Blanche's prior work as Trump's personal defense attorney, CNN reported in May 2026. Reporting indicates he did not recuse himself from matters including a May 2026 settlement (Trump v. IRS), reached while he was acting Attorney General, that granted Trump and his family an IRS audit shield and was connected to a proposed $1.776 billion compensation fund; DOJ never contested Trump's claims in that litigation and never made a court appearance before settling. On June 22, 2026, Democracy Defenders Fund, Lawyers Defending American Democracy and 101 former federal and state judges filed a 73-page grievance complaint against Blanche with New York's Attorney Grievance Committee (Appellate Division, First Department), covering the settlement, the $1.776 billion fund and related conduct. Separately, the New York City Bar Association's July 13, 2026 letter urged the Senate Judiciary Committee to reject his nomination as Attorney General, calling him "unfit to lead the U.S. Department of Justice" and saying he had breached his confirmation commitment to follow career ethics staff's recusal guidance.

On July 13, 2026, Judge Kathleen Williams found the underlying IRS settlement was brought for an improper purpose and referred Trump's attorney to the Florida Bar for discipline; the personal tax-liability release for Trump and his family was left intact. By July 24, 2026, the New York Attorney Grievance Committee's chief attorney had declined to open an investigation into the grievance complaint, instead directing it to DOJ's own Office of Professional Responsibility; DDF and LDAD filed a request for reconsideration with the Committee's chair, arguing OPR's lack of independence given it reports to Blanche's own chain of command. On August 2, 2026, after Sens. Thom Tillis and John Cornyn demanded written assurances, Blanche issued an order stating that the May 18, 2026 order establishing the fund "is rescinded and shall have no force or effect"; DOJ also said that day that the settlement's audit protections apply only retroactively (CBS News, NPR) and are limited to Trump, two of his sons and the Trump Organization (NPR). Neither change was signed by the settlement's parties, which Senate Judiciary ranking member Richard Durbin said left them unenforceable (Roll Call).

The Senate confirmed Blanche as Attorney General by a 50-49 vote in the early hours of August 8, 2026. Sens. Collins and Murkowski (R) voted no alongside every Democrat, both citing independence concerns given Blanche's history as Trump's personal lawyer. With Sen. McConnell absent, the outcome came down to Sen. Bill Cassidy (R), Roll Call reported; NPR called his vote "crucial." In an August 7 floor speech, Cassidy cited what he called Blanche's "poor judgment in approving the anti-weaponization slush fund and exempting the president from IRS audits" and "episodes of apparent lawfare [with the] DOJ bringing suits against political enemies," then announced he would vote to confirm. The IRS settlement and fund were directly debated on the Senate floor and did not prevent confirmation, but the vote was not a finding on the merits of the recusal question.

Formal ethics advice received (from DOJ's top career ethics lawyer) that recusal was required for matters involving the former client personally
Subsequent participation in such a matter despite that advice (the IRS settlement)
Resulting personal benefit to the former client (Trump) from the matter in question

incident_summary: For about a decade, Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt was investigated by the Justice Department in a probe of an alleged scheme to embezzle more than $1 billion from Venezuela's state oil company PDVSA and launder it through Miami real estate and bank accounts in Malta and Switzerland. Ten people were indicted; Betancourt was never charged, but people briefed told CNN he is listed as a co-conspirator in at least one charged transaction, and six sources told Reuters he was an unnamed unindicted co-conspirator in the scheme. He was also under investigation in Switzerland and Spain, and was arrested in London in 2025 on a Swiss warrant. After the U.S. military seized Nicolas Maduro on January 3, 2026, administration officials sought Betancourt's help in talks with interim leader Delcy Rodriguez, CNN and Reuters reported. Earlier in 2026, Reuters reported, federal prosecutors in Florida paused their investigation of him, and two sources said prosecutors were then discouraged by supervisors from pursuing it, without being given a rationale. Switzerland withdrew its request to extradite him from the UK in May, after U.S. officials pressured it, according to four people; Zurich prosecutors said the withdrawal concerned UK extradition law and their case continues. On August 28, President Trump announced an oil deal in which the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital takes a stake of up to 35% in Betancourt's company, North American Blue Energy Partners (Reuters reported a 35% stake; the New York Times, an option on up to 35% of its parent through warrants), and the U.S. gets preferential access to its oil, about one-fifth of Venezuela's reserves per Reuters, in a venture Trump says covers 65 billion barrels. On September 2, Semafor reported that an unnamed U.S. official said the United States had recently intervened in an international money-laundering investigation into Betancourt in order to finalize the deal. On September 4, CNN reported, citing two people briefed on the matter, that **Miami prosecutors closed the Betancourt investigation on orders from the office of then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, they were told** (CNN gave no date for the order; Blanche was Deputy Attorney General and, from April 2 to August 8, Acting Attorney General), as part of an effort by White House officials and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to enlist him for the deal. A person briefed said Rubio and White House officials pressed DOJ, first under then-Attorney General Pam Bondi and later under Blanche, to clear the way, and CNN reported that Blanche also reached out to Swiss authorities to drop warrants that kept Betancourt in the UK. A Justice Department spokesperson called this "a complete fabrication," saying Blanche never discussed the case with the Miami office or told anyone to close it. The Washington Post reported in August, per El Pais, that Bondi, Blanche and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau pressured Swiss prosecutors directly; in Spain, a judge investigating Betancourt said in August he would wait no later than December for U.S. legal assistance before possibly closing his case. Rubio said publicly that U.S. authorities had checked and found "no investigation within our system against him." Reuters said it could not determine when the probe was paused or whether that was in exchange for Betancourt's cooperation. On September 18, Semafor reported that the top Democrats on the House Oversight, Foreign Affairs and Natural Resources committees had written to the State and Justice departments asking about reports that U.S. officials intervened in an international money-laundering investigation into Betancourt; the administration has no legal obligation to respond. On October 20, ProPublica, which reviewed the 18-page agreement Rubio and Hegseth signed, reported that it safeguards Betancourt's position as chief executive of NABEP, requiring a supermajority vote of five to oust him, and that the U.S. takes its 35% stake in a Barbados-registered parent company whose owners and investors the document says little about. Signing for that parent company, alongside Betancourt, Hegseth and Rubio, was Orlando Alvarado, a name the administration had not disclosed as a party, who has held senior roles in multiple Betancourt businesses; ProPublica, citing the Miami Herald, wrote that federal prosecutors identified Alvarado as an unindicted co-conspirator in a scheme to embezzle money from Venezuela's national oil company. A NABEP spokesperson said neither man "has ever been charged with any crime in any country."

incident_summary:
Alexander Smirnov, a former FBI confidential informant, was convicted and sentenced to six years in prison after admitting he fabricated a claim that Burisma, a Ukrainian energy company, paid Joe Biden and Hunter Biden a $10 million bribe. Prosecutors later wrote that when he was re-interviewed in September 2023, Smirnov changed parts of his account and "promoted a new false narrative after meeting with Russian officials"; DOJ stated in February 2024 that Smirnov admitted "officials associated with Russian intelligence were involved" in developing that new Hunter Biden narrative. The fabricated bribery claim had circulated among congressional Republicans and fueled impeachment-related attacks on President Biden before it was exposed as false.

In April 2025, prosecutor David Friedman told the court, with minimal explanation, only that "the United States intends to review the government's theory of the case underlying Defendant's criminal conviction," and jointly moved with Smirnov's own attorneys for his release pending appeal, which Judge Wright rejected from the bench with visible skepticism ("Seriously?"). Smirnov was nonetheless furloughed from custody by the Bureau of Prisons later in 2025, despite that denial, and was reported missing from the facility for months; his lawyer called it a medical furlough, and the Bureau of Prisons said in March 2026 that he was back in custody at Terminal Island. On March 4, 2026, DOJ filed its answering brief in the Ninth Circuit under the name of Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche (signed by Assistant U.S. Attorney Alexander P. Robbins), siding with Smirnov and asking the court to vacate the judgment and let him withdraw his guilty pleas. The Wall Street Journal noted that if an appeals court vacated the sentence, DOJ could then drop the charges entirely -- erasing Smirnov's own admission that the Biden bribery claims were fabricated.

The Ninth Circuit appeal (Nos. 25-400 and 25-408) proceeded with DOJ's active support. After briefing, the panel on July 31, 2026 ordered supplemental briefs on whether it had jurisdiction over the appeals and on the sentencing-guideline adjustment the government had described, then decided the case without oral argument, submitting it on September 17, 2026. On September 22, 2026, Judges Jacqueline Nguyen, Ryan Nelson and Roopali Desai dismissed the custody-credit claim for lack of jurisdiction, holding that a recommendation to the Bureau of Prisons is not part of a sentence and cannot be appealed, and affirmed the rest, finding that the plea agreement did not require a sentencing adjustment. The ruling rejected the argument Smirnov and DOJ had jointly pressed and left his guilty pleas and six-year sentence in place.

offense_category: Vindictive/Selective Prosecution (violates Due Process; established legal doctrine, e.g. United States v. incident_summary:
On April 21, 2026, a federal grand jury indicted the Southern Poverty Law Center on 11 counts -- six counts of wire fraud, four counts of false statements to a federally insured bank, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering -- announced by then-Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche. The indictment alleges that between 2014 and 2023, SPLC secretly funneled more than $3 million to "field sources" affiliated with extremist groups including the Ku Klux Klan, the National Socialist Movement, and the American Front, characterizing this as defrauding SPLC's own donors. In an April 30, 2026 letter reported May 1 by MS NOW and CNN, House Judiciary Democrats Jamie Raskin and Mary Gay Scanlon wrote that, according to whistleblower information, Associate Deputy Attorney General Aakash Singh ordered the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Middle District of Alabama to rush through the indictment despite serious concerns about the strength of the case.

On May 26, 2026, SPLC moved to dismiss the indictment, arguing the charges are "vindictive" and part of a broader "retribution campaign" against organizations and individuals the administration perceives as its enemies, and separately sought discovery into DOJ's prosecutorial motives. On June 2, 2026, the grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging the same 11 counts and alleging that $4.1 million in tax-exempt funds were used to pay informants inside extremist organizations (CBS News). U.S. District Judge Emily C. Marks denied both the motion and the discovery request in an order issued August 7, 2026, finding SPLC had not shown evidence of prosecutorial animus resulting in the prosecution -- a ruling that resolves this procedural motion but does not reach the underlying fraud charges, and does not foreclose SPLC raising the same argument again at trial or on appeal; no appeal of that denial has been identified.

On August 11, 2026, the grand jury returned a second superseding indictment adding former SPLC official Heidi Beirich as the first individually-named defendant (unsealed August 12, when she was arrested), charged with wire fraud conspiracy, conspiracy to submit false statements to a bank, and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering -- bringing the case to 14 counts. It alleges SPLC funneled at least $4.1 million in tax-exempt donor funds between 2007 and 2023 (Fox News). Beirich was arraigned August 25. On August 31, Judge Marks denied SPLC's motion to be tried separately from Beirich and, on Beirich's motion, continued the joint trial from October 5, 2026 to February 1, 2027; on September 2, after SPLC's lead counsel said the February term was unworkable, she reset jury selection and trial for April 19, 2027 in Montgomery (court orders, Docs. 160 and 168). SPLC's lawyers argue law enforcement agencies have long known the organization paid informants to monitor hate groups' movements as part of its investigative and watchdog work, and separately allege that Blanche made a false statement, at a news conference and in interviews, when he claimed SPLC had not shared informant-derived information with law enforcement.

incident_summary: **Boeing's 2021 deferred prosecution agreement over the fatal 2018 Lion Air and 2019 Ethiopian Airlines 737 MAX crashes (346 deaths combined) was found violated** after the January 2024 Alaska Airlines door-plug blowout revived scrutiny of the company's compliance record. That put Boeing back on track for prosecution on the underlying fraud-conspiracy charge: deceiving FAA regulators about a flight-control system (MCAS) implicated in both crashes. U.S. District Judge Reed O'Connor rejected an initial revised plea-deal version in December 2024. Reuters reported May 17, 2025 that crash victims' families were preparing to formally object to a new tentative nonprosecution agreement the Trump-era DOJ had reached with Boeing, which would let the company avoid a felony conviction. Sen. Elizabeth Warren wrote Attorney General Bondi May 22, 2025 questioning the deal's adequacy. DOJ formally announced the agreement May 23, 2025, and the parties filed the final written Non-Prosecution Agreement on May 29, 2025. Under it, Boeing avoids trial and any felony conviction. It pays a $487.2 million criminal fine (crediting $243.6 million already paid under the 2021 agreement), contributes $444.5 million to a new victims'-families compensation fund, and commits at least $455 million more to compliance, safety, and quality programs, a total 'pay or invest' commitment DOJ said exceeds $1.1 billion. Boeing must retain a DOJ-selected Independent Compliance Consultant and cooperate with authorities for two years, but the agreement does not include the court-supervised independent monitoring the 2021 deal's compliance-oversight regime nominally provided. Victims' families, relatives of those killed in both crashes, formally objected; their lawyer Paul Cassell had called the deal 'a step backward from last summer, when Boeing was going to plead guilty.' On November 6, 2025, Judge O'Connor granted DOJ's motion to dismiss the underlying criminal case, approving the agreement. He wrote that the families opposing it 'are correct' that it 'fails to secure the necessary accountability to ensure the safety of the flying public' and 'disregards the need for Boeing to be subject to independent monitoring.' He also wrote that he 'disagrees with the Government that dismissing the criminal information...is in the public interest,' but concluded he lacked legal authority to override DOJ's charging decision. Families' attorneys said they planned to appeal to the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals. On March 31, 2026, a unanimous three-judge panel of the Fifth Circuit denied the families' petitions to overturn the agreement, finding that DOJ did not violate victims' rights laws when it struck the deal and moved to dismiss the case. The families then asked the full Fifth Circuit to rehear the case. On May 22, 2026, the court denied rehearing en banc, with no judge requesting a poll, and the panel denied rehearing as well.

Reuters reported September 25, 2025 that Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche's office was pressuring career prosecutors in the Maryland U.S. Attorney's office and DOJ's National Security Division to present the case to a grand jury within days, despite those prosecutors' own view that more investigation was needed -- an escalation that came one week after the administration removed the top federal prosecutor in Virginia over frustration that DOJ was not moving fast enough against Trump critics including Bolton and then-FBI-Director-turned-critic James Comey (indicted around the same week). On October 16, 2025, **a federal grand jury in Greenbelt, Maryland indicted Bolton on 18 counts under the Espionage Act -- eight counts of transmitting national defense information and ten counts of unlawfully retaining it**, filed by U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes and Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas Sullivan. Prosecutors alleged Bolton used personal AOL and Google accounts to send diary-style entries containing Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information to two unauthorized family members while serving as National Security Advisor, later storing printed copies at his Maryland home; some of the alleged material reportedly also appeared in drafts of his 2020 memoir, 'The Room Where It Happened.' Bolton's attorney, Abbe Lowell, characterized the seized records as 'the kinds of ordinary records...that would be kept by a 40-year career official,' noting some dated to his Bush-administration tenure (1998-2006). Bolton pleaded not guilty at his October 17, 2025 arraignment before U.S. District Judge Theodore D. Chuang and was released on bond with standard conditions, without prosecutors seeking detention. Trump had publicly directed Attorney General Bondi the previous month to pursue his perceived enemies more aggressively; Bolton himself said Trump's retaliation 'began then, continued when he tried unsuccessfully to block the publication of my book...and became one of his rallying cries in his re-election campaign,' while Trump called Bolton 'a bad guy' in response to the indictment. On June 26, 2026, Bolton pleaded guilty, facing a maximum of 60 months in prison and agreeing to pay a $2.25 million fine.

offense_category: Concentrating Sole Certification Authority Over an Accelerated Capital-Appeals Process in the Attorney General, on an Honor-System Basis -- a proposed rule, not yet finalized; a due-process/executive-power-concentration accountability claim, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: DOJ proposed a rule making it easier for states to obtain certification for an accelerated federal review process for death penalty cases under a 1996 federal law (the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act's Chapter 154 opt-in provisions). Attorney General Pam Bondi argued that regulations implemented during the Obama and Biden administrations had improperly prevented states from using the law's fast-track option, which -- once a state is certified -- **cuts a death-sentenced prisoner's window to file a federal habeas petition from one year to 180 days and requires federal courts to prioritize capital habeas petitions over all non-capital cases**. Under the proposal, the certification decision (whether a state's system for providing competent post-conviction defense counsel meets the law's requirements) rests solely with the Attorney General, based substantially on the certifying state's own representations about the quality of its post-conviction counsel system -- a process critics, including the Death Penalty Information Center, describe as effectively an honor system that does not independently verify defense-counsel quality or consider opposing views before certification. Bloomberg reported the change is part of the Trump administration's broader push to expand use of the federal death penalty. Critics quoted by Davis Vanguard and other outlets warned the accelerated timeline and reliance on state self-certification increase the risk of executing people without adequate review of wrongful-conviction claims.

incident_summary: A ProPublica investigation, examining two decades of DOJ case-declination data, found **DOJ under Attorney General Pam Bondi closed more than 23,000 criminal investigations without prosecution in the first six months of the administration -- including cases involving terrorism, fraud, corruption, labor racketeering, drug trafficking, and environmental crimes** -- while ramping up immigration prosecutions. The majority of the declined cases had been referred to DOJ by law enforcement agencies, including under prior administrations, whose investigators believed a federal crime may have been committed. February 2025 alone, covering the first weeks of Bondi's tenure, saw nearly 11,000 declinations -- the most in a single month since at least 2004, when comparable data begins, and far exceeding the prior monthly high of roughly 6,500 declinations set in September 2019 during Trump's first term. ProPublica's analysis found the increase was not attributable to a larger inherited caseload or increased referral volume from law enforcement, indicating a deliberate shift in prosecutorial priority rather than a passive resourcing effect.

ProPublica's analysis ruled out caseload inheritance or referral-volume increases as explanations, supporting a characterization of the decline as a deliberate prioritization shift toward immigration enforcement

offense_category: Deliberate impairment of federal public-corruption enforcement combined with a pattern of pardons for politically-connected allies -- no criminal charge against Bondi or Blanche personally; this is an institutional-capacity and accountability-evasion claim, not a completed prosecution
incident_summary:
In late March 2025, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche circulated a memo proposing to reorganize DOJ's Public Integrity Section, reassigning most of its personnel to individual U.S. Attorney's offices while keeping a core team of supervisory attorneys to administer the Justice Manual. The Washington Post reported May 17, 2025 that DOJ was considering, and Bloomberg Law reported it was reviewing, ending the longstanding requirement that federal prosecutors obtain the Public Integrity Section's approval before bringing charges against members of Congress, and ending the requirement that prosecutors consult the section's career lawyers during key steps of investigations of public officials -- a Watergate-era safeguard designed to prevent politically motivated prosecutions by letting career, non-political attorneys review case merits before politically appointed U.S. Attorneys could indict. The Justice Manual's requirement of the section's approval before charging a member of Congress for conduct related to public office (JM 9-85.110) remains in place; in June 2025, however, DOJ leadership suspended a separate requirement (JM 9-85.210) that prosecutors consult the section before opening campaign-finance, patronage and election-corruption matters, pending revisions.

Under Attorney General Pam Bondi, DOJ's Public Integrity Section -- the unit responsible for prosecuting public corruption by federal, state, and local officials -- was reduced from 36 full-time attorneys (NPR put it at around 40 full-time staff) handling 175-200 open matters at the start of the second Trump term to just two attorneys by September 2025, smaller than at any point since its 1976 creation; as of May 2026 it still had two full-time attorneys and about 20 open matters, per current and former DOJ officials. The staffing cut coincided with parallel rollbacks elsewhere in DOJ's anti-corruption infrastructure: a pause in enforcing the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act against U.S. executives who bribe foreign officials, disbanding of an FBI squad devoted to investigating congressional misconduct, disbanding of a task force pursuing Russian oligarchs' assets, and a pullback in enforcing the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Over the same period, Trump pardoned at least 15 people who had been charged with or convicted of public corruption, more than half of them Republicans or Trump supporters, though Democrats such as former Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich and Rep. Henry Cuellar were also pardoned. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse sent Bondi a formal oversight letter on March 20, 2025 demanding answers on the section's dismantling. Bondi left DOJ in April 2026; Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, Trump's former personal defense attorney, became acting Attorney General and has not publicly moved to restore the section's staffing.

On June 8, 2026, Vice President JD Vance referred Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz and Attorney General Keith Ellison, both Democrats, to DOJ's National Fraud Enforcement Division -- a separate unit, not the Public Integrity Section -- for criminal investigation, citing a House Oversight Committee report alleging they failed to stop fraud in federally funded social programs; Ellison called the referral a political stunt by an administration that targets its perceived opponents. Todd Blanche was confirmed by the Senate as permanent Attorney General on August 8, 2026 (50-49, with Sens. Collins and Murkowski the only Republican defections) and sworn in; in an address to DOJ staff (August 13) and subsequent remarks (August 16) he pledged to lead with "integrity" but explicitly declined to commit to DOJ independence from the White House. Rather than restaffing the Public Integrity Section, DOJ has instead expanded the National Fraud Enforcement Division, finalizing a rule in August 2026 that lets it prosecute any federal offenses uncovered during investigations that begin with suspected fraud; no public indication of Public Integrity Section restaffing has been identified.

ProPublica reported in September 2026 on one investigation that ended in the purge. Martin Kao, the former CEO of the Hawaii defense contractor Navatek, pleaded guilty in 2022 to illegal campaign contributions and loan fraud and then sat for interviews with FBI agents and prosecutors that lasted into late 2024, telling them he had traded campaign donations for defense research funding and, at a final meeting in September 2024, handing over a 50-page document naming members of Congress, staffers and lobbyists; agents questioned him extensively about Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and her office. By late 2024 the two agents on the case, from the FBI's congressional-corruption squad known as CR-15, had come to believe there was enough evidence to warrant a broader investigation into bribery of members of Congress, according to a memo ProPublica reviewed, and agents were still examining Kao's dealings with Collins and her staff in early 2025. After Trump returned, FBI Director Kash Patel purged CR-15 agent by agent, Trump appointees ordered the remaining Public Integrity Section prosecutors to halt new corruption cases, the career attorney assigned to Kao's case quit, and the two agents were removed (one fired in October 2025, the other pushed out in early 2026). **ProPublica reported that these dismissals ended the review, which was still in its early stages, and that the investigation is now dead**; it did not report a specific order closing it. No one in Collins' orbit has been charged, and the allegations are Kao's, partly corroborated by records ProPublica reviewed. Collins denies wrongdoing and called the report "a political hit job"; her office says the matter was resolved in 2021, and an FBI spokesperson said the bureau had investigated claims against Collins years ago and "ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins' campaign"; the FBI did not respond to questions about the 2024 inquiry. A second ProPublica report, in October 2026, said the same inquiry also examined three South Carolina lawmakers. Kao told the FBI that Navatek struck campaign-cash-for-contracts deals with Sen. Lindsey Graham (R), who died earlier in 2026, Rep. James Clyburn (D) and Rep. Joe Wilson (R), and that each asked him for $100,000. An agent's December 2024 memo named two former Navatek executives as formal subjects and detailed the three lawmakers' conduct, though the FBI did not designate the lawmakers as subjects; the two executives were never charged, and Kao is the only person involved to have served prison time. Graham's office called the allegations "simply false" and the "ravings of a convicted felon"; Clyburn's office said a donation "would never cause" him to increase his support for a donor's request; Wilson's office said he "has always abided by campaign donation regulations." An FBI spokesperson called Kao's claims "half baked" and "misleading."

status: The Public Integrity Section's collapse remains unreversed under Blanche, and DOJ is expanding its fraud division instead. ProPublica reports the purge also ended an early FBI inquiry into Kao's bribery claims about Collins and three South Carolina lawmakers, which they or their offices deny.
rebuttal_anticipated: DOJ could argue the staffing changes reflect a legitimate reorganization of prosecutorial priorities, that the pardon power is constitutionally unreviewable and each pardon can be defended on its individual merits, and that reduced headquarters staffing doesn't necessarily mean corruption cases aren't being pursued through U.S. Attorney's offices instead. In statements to ProPublica for its reporting on the ended Navatek inquiry (DOJ did not answer its detailed questions), DOJ spokesperson Audrey Cook said the department "is rooting out the weaponization, corruption, and institutional rot that ran rampant under Joe Biden's two-tiered system of justice," and FBI spokesperson Ben Williamson said "personnel are only removed at this FBI if they have been found to have acted unethically, undermined the mission, or engaged in weaponization of law enforcement."
comeback: The scale of the cut (roughly 90%, from dozens of attorneys and 175-200 open matters down to two attorneys and about 20) is corroborated by multiple independent outlets citing named and unnamed DOJ officials, not a single source's characterization, and it happened in parallel with the dismantling of several other, unrelated anti-corruption units (FCPA, FARA, the oligarch-asset task force) -- a pattern harder to explain as ordinary reallocation than a single office's staffing change would be. Layering at least 15 corruption pardons, more than half of them for Republicans or Trump supporters, on top of that capacity cut is what former acting section chief John Keller describes as producing a chilling effect on prosecutors pursuing public corruption cases. And the claim that corruption work simply moved to U.S. Attorney's offices meets at least one documented counterexample: ProPublica reports that an FBI inquiry into alleged bribery of members of Congress ended after its agents and career prosecutor were purged or quit, rather than being picked up elsewhere.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Fits a broader pattern of DOJ shrinking its career-staffed corruption-enforcement capacity: the section's collapse began with the resignations over the Eric Adams case dismissal, and ran alongside a pause in foreign-bribery (FCPA) enforcement. Rather than restoring that capacity, DOJ has built up a fraud division run by a political appointee, which has since received a vice-presidential referral of two Democratic Minnesota officials. Trump's pardons of at least 15 corruption defendants (among them the Tennessee House speaker case and the Blagojevich pardon) are a separate presidential act, but they push the same way: fewer consequences for public officials, with more than half of those pardoned Republicans or Trump supporters.

offense_category: DOJ Leadership Blocking Investigation of a Federal Agent's Fatal Shooting While Pressuring an Investigation of the Victim's Widow -- potential obstruction/prosecutorial-misconduct pattern, distinct from an ordinary declination decision
incident_summary:
ICE agent Jonathan Ross fatally shot Renee Nicole Good, a 37-year-old U.S. citizen and mother of three, in south Minneapolis on January 7, 2026, during Operation Metro Surge; Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey said video evidence did not appear to support DHS's account that Good was using her SUV to run over an agent. Rather than pursuing a standard investigation of Ross's use of deadly force, top DOJ officials pressured the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Minnesota to instead investigate Good's widow, Becca Good, reportedly examining any ties she might have to activist groups. In response, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Joe Thompson -- the office's lead prosecutor on the high-profile Feeding Our Future fraud case, which had charged 78 people and secured 58 convictions -- resigned along with five colleagues (Harry Jacobs, Melinda Williams, Thomas Calhoun-Lopez, Ruth Schneider, and Tom Hollenhurst) in mid-January 2026, citing DOJ's reluctance to investigate the agent and the push to investigate Good's widow instead. In late January 2026, Tracee Mergen, a supervisor in the FBI's Minneapolis field office who had unsuccessfully attempted to investigate Ross, resigned, reportedly after pressure from FBI leadership in Washington to drop that inquiry. Eight additional assistant U.S. attorneys, including civil division chief Ana Voss, were reported in early February 2026 to be leaving the office, amid continued frustration with how DOJ was handling both the Good case and the separate fatal shooting of Alex Pretti by federal agents. CBS News reported the office's assistant U.S. attorney roster fell to as few as 17, down from 70 under the Biden administration, as the resignation wave continued into February 2026. The office lost at least 14 career prosecutors within a roughly three-week span.

The resignations extended beyond the Minneapolis U.S. Attorney's Office to DOJ headquarters itself. Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon, MS NOW reported, decided against a civil-rights investigation of Ross's shooting, and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche said there was "no basis" for a civil-rights (excessive-force) investigation into Ross's shooting -- a decision legal experts called highly unusual, noting DOJ's own manual calls for Civil Rights Division involvement in cases designated as a matter of "national interest." At least six leaders of the Civil Rights Division's criminal section, including its chief, principal deputy chief, deputy chief and acting deputy chief, announced their departures, a separate, headquarters-level wave distinct from the Minneapolis resignations; MS NOW reported they left in protest over the handling of the shooting, while a DOJ official said they had requested early retirement before it. DOJ instead treated the case as a potential assault on a federal officer, with prosecutors reportedly pressured to scrutinize Good's own conduct and her spouse rather than Ross's use of force, despite the video evidence Mayor Frey said didn't support the official account. This fits a broader documented pattern: Wired reported ICE agents have fatally shot at least 25 people since 2015 with no criminal indictments, and Fox 9 Minneapolis reported that records analyzed by The Trace showed at least 59 shootings, fatal and nonfatal, involving ICE agents from 2015 to 2021, with no evidence of an agent being indicted. The two figures measure different scopes rather than conflicting, and neither found an ICE agent indicted over the shootings it covered. Bondi was removed as Attorney General in April 2026, for reasons not confirmed by sourcing reviewed to be connected to this matter specifically.

Following Minnesota officials' March 24, 2026 lawsuit to compel access (amended June 18), federal investigators turned over previously withheld hard drives and physical evidence, including Good's SUV, to Hennepin County and the Minnesota BCA, as Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced on July 13, 2026. Moriarty said review of the evidence was ongoing, with no timeline set for a charging decision on Ross; no public update on the reported federal investigation of Becca Good was identified. ProPublica reported September 2, 2026 that federal authorities had first agreed to a joint investigation of Ross's shooting of Good, but Justice Department officials later refused to cooperate with state police, deeming any review of the shooting unnecessary. Moriarty, who leads the state's ongoing review, publicly linked this to a separate DOJ decision to downgrade planned civil-rights charges against a different agent (a federal grand jury indicted him on September 2, 2026 on six counts of making false statements to federal investigators, NBC News reported) in the legally distinct January 14, 2026 shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, who was allegedly shot in the leg by ICE agent Christian Castro.

The July evidence sharing did not last. In court filings on October 13, 2026, Minnesota investigators said an evidence-sharing agreement negotiated with the U.S. Attorney's Office over three weeks starting in late June had produced Good's vehicle, the gun used to shoot her, body-worn camera footage and officer statements, but that federal officials stopped cooperating within days of Moriarty's July press conference, offering no explanation. In a sworn statement, Moriarty said U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen repeatedly told her his office was "pausing" cooperation, then informed her on September 10 that it would stop sharing evidence "indefinitely," citing "challenges with D.C."; she wrote that "the pause on information sharing is unique to these matters." The filings say DOJ still has not turned over a statement by one of the officers who shot Alex Pretti, and, according to a sworn statement from Minnesota BCA Superintendent Drew Evans, state investigators are blocked from the cellphone of the agent who shot Good, her clothing, the firearms used to shoot Pretti, the gun he possessed, and projectiles and shell casings from that scene. CNN reported on October 15, 2026 that Minnesota is still fighting the Justice Department in federal court in Washington, D.C., for access to the evidence.

Minnesota's October 13 filings in that case included a motion for summary judgment; AP reported the state had again asked a judge to order federal agencies to hand over the evidence, arguing they "have identified no legal authority or rational basis justifying their obstruction of state criminal investigations." Evans said in a declaration that federal authorities still hold interview recordings state investigators have never been able to view, and that at no point did federal authorities assert that sharing the evidence "would harm national security or impair the federal government's own criminal investigative efforts." In a reply filed October 20, 2026, Justice Department attorneys argued that their Touhy regulations, which govern requests for official information, are triggered only by "state or federal proceedings" or "litigation," and that "at the time of their requests no proceedings or litigation had commenced." The reply said the departments, "in their discretion, have declined to share information" with the state, and that the decision not to disclose law enforcement information is committed to their discretion by law, placing it outside review under the Administrative Procedure Act; it asked the court to dismiss the suit or, accusing the state of forum shopping, transfer it to federal court in Minnesota. The case is before U.S. District Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, with no ruling yet.

official: Pam Bondi, Attorney General
offense_category: Potential Conflict of Interest / Appearance of Pay-to-Play via Selective Non-Enforcement of Federal Anti-Bribery Law -- NOT charged; a contested characterization, since the FCPA pause applied broadly and was not shown to be directed at benefiting any single donor
incident_summary:
On February 5, 2025, the day of her swearing-in as Attorney General, Pam Bondi issued a memorandum redirecting DOJ's corporate-enforcement priorities away from certain corporate crimes toward foreign bribery specifically tied to transnational criminal organizations and cartels. On February 10, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order, "Pausing Foreign Corrupt Practices Act Enforcement to Further American Economic and National Security," directing Bondi to halt new FCPA investigations and enforcement actions for 180 days and review existing matters -- the first pause of FCPA enforcement since the statute's 1977 passage.

Pilgrim's Pride, a poultry company that pleaded guilty to price-fixing in 2021 and is controlled by Brazilian billionaire brothers Wesley and Joesley Batista -- whose holding company J&F Investimentos pleaded guilty in October 2020 to conspiring to violate the FCPA itself and agreed to pay more than $256 million, over bribes paid to Brazilian officials; a parallel settled SEC order found that the Batistas' bribery scheme was carried out in part to facilitate JBS's 2009 acquisition of Pilgrim's Pride and that the brothers, J&F and JBS caused Pilgrim's Pride's violations of the FCPA's books-and-records and internal-controls provisions, with JBS paying about $27 million in disgorgement and each brother a $550,000 civil penalty -- was the single largest donor to Trump's 2025 inauguration, contributing $5 million, reported April 21, 2025. Ethics watchdogs raised concerns that a major donor with the Batista brothers' bribery history benefited from timing that coincided with the administration pausing the very federal law under which their past conduct had been resolved. On May 19, 2025, Reuters reported Sen. Elizabeth Warren sent a letter to the CEOs of Pilgrim's Pride and of JBS USA -- the U.S. arm of Pilgrim's Pride's Brazilian parent company, JBS -- asking whether company officials communicated with the Trump transition team or other Trump associates about the $5 million inaugural donation, and with the SEC, the White House or other agencies about a separate, long-delayed SEC approval for JBS's own dual-listing on the New York Stock Exchange, which had been approved just two days after a public FEC filing revealed Pilgrim's Pride as the inauguration's largest donor. Warren's letter also noted DOJ had two ongoing civil investigations into Pilgrim's Pride at the time, concerning its payment practices toward contract farmers and antitrust matters, separate from but concurrent with the FCPA-pause concern. No source reviewed confirmed whether JBS or Pilgrim's Pride ever responded substantively to Warren's letter, nor whether the SEC's own approval timeline was in fact influenced by the donation, as distinct from the appearance of the timing itself.

DOJ ended the formal pause on June 9, 2025, when Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche issued guidelines resuming FCPA enforcement with a narrower focus -- prioritizing cases touching U.S. economic/national-security interests, transnational criminal organizations and cartels, and individual (rather than corporate) misconduct. WilmerHale's year-end review counted seven DOJ FCPA actions in 2025 (only two against corporate defendants) and no SEC FCPA enforcement, the lowest level of publicly announced FCPA enforcement activity since the firm began formally tracking such actions in 2010. JBS completed its NYSE debut June 13, 2025, roughly six months after the donation.

Bondi herself, not just a donor, had a direct financial tie to a second potential beneficiary of the pause. Her financial disclosures showed $203,738 in 2024 income from the Fort Lauderdale law firm Panza, Maurer & Maynard, with Pfizer the only client she named for that work; Public Citizen noted in January 2025 that she had not disclosed the Pfizer representation on her Senate questionnaire or during her appearance before the Senate Judiciary Committee, and the Miami Herald reported the tie in early July 2025. Pfizer's own SEC filings had disclosed an ongoing DOJ investigation into potential FCPA violations tied to its China and Mexico operations; its next annual report, filed roughly three weeks after Bondi took office, no longer referenced that DOJ investigation. Public Citizen sent a letter to the Senate Judiciary Committee on June 9, 2025 requesting an oversight hearing into Bondi's Pfizer conflicts; a DOJ spokesman told the Miami Herald that Bondi's brief work for the company occurred while she was a private citizen, concerned a Florida-specific legal matter, and bore no nexus to DOJ's FCPA guidance. No source reviewed confirmed whether DOJ formally closed, is still investigating, or simply stopped publicly reporting the Pfizer FCPA matter -- the change is in Pfizer's own disclosure, not a DOJ announcement, so this is documented as an unexplained disclosure change coinciding with the broader pause, not a confirmed case closure.
elements_required: A specific, named federal anti-bribery enforcement mechanism (FCPA) was paused by executive order and DOJ memorandum
A specific named beneficiary (Pilgrim's Pride/the Batista brothers) has documented prior bribery-adjacent conduct that the paused law would be the natural tool to address
That beneficiary made a large, publicly disclosed political contribution to the administration around the same period

Absence of any pending FCPA case against Pilgrim's Pride or the Batista brothers that the pause halted (their U.S. FCPA resolution dates to 2020) -- the concern is a structural conflict-of-interest/appearance issue, not a proven quid pro quo tied to a specific enforcement decision

For the Pfizer example specifically: Bondi's own prior financial relationship with the beneficiary (not merely a donor's contribution timing), which Public Citizen says she did not disclose on her Senate questionnaire or at her confirmation hearing

rebuttal_anticipated: The administration's stated rationale was general and industry-wide -- reducing 'overexpansive and unpredictable' FCPA enforcement that DOJ argued disadvantaged U.S. companies competitively -- not targeted at any single company or donor, and Pilgrim's Pride itself was never under a specific FCPA investigation this pause is shown to have affected.
comeback: The rebuttal is accurate as far as it goes -- there is no documented FCPA case against Pilgrim's Pride the pause specifically halted -- but that is exactly why this is an appearance-of-conflict concern rather than a proven quid pro quo: a policy that broadly weakens the primary federal tool for policing the specific kind of bribery conduct the donor's controlling family has a documented history with, adopted in the same window as that donor's record-setting $5 million inauguration contribution, creates the pay-to-play appearance regardless of whether a specific case can be traced to it -- which is itself the accountability concern being documented, not a claim of a proven direct exchange.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] One instance of a broader pattern this database documents of the administration pausing or narrowing federal anti-corruption enforcement (the FCPA here; compare the Public Integrity Section entry) in ways that create appearance-of-conflict concerns. Two distinct concerns meet in this entry: a broad enforcement pause adopted while the family controlling the inauguration's largest donor had a prior U.S. FCPA resolution, and the Attorney General who implemented it having recently earned income representing another company then under disclosed DOJ FCPA inquiries. No record reviewed shows an independent review ruling out either appearance.

incident_summary:
Alina Habba, a former personal defense attorney for Trump, was installed as acting/interim U.S. Attorney for the District of New Jersey. When Habba's interim term expired, New Jersey's own federal district judges exercised their statutory authority to appoint a replacement, choosing career prosecutor Desiree Grace rather than extending Habba. Trump responded by firing Grace and withdrawing Habba's own pending nomination as permanent U.S. Attorney, keeping Habba in the post without the judges' authorization; a federal judge later ruled the arrangement violated the Federal Vacancies Reform Act and, separately, that a structure allowing the administration to unilaterally extend her tenure past normal limits amounted to "a unilateral appointment in violation of the Constitution's Appointments Clause." The dispute first surfaced publicly when defendants facing narcotics charges argued in court that prosecutors could not proceed against them without a validly appointed U.S. Attorney in charge, triggering a wave of paused trials, postponed hearings, and delayed guilty pleas across the District of New Jersey as the authority question worked through the courts. Judge Matthew Brann's 77-page order found Habba had "exercised the functions and duties of the office... without lawful authority since July 1, 2025"; Brann declined to dismiss the narcotics defendants' cases outright, instead disqualifying Habba from participating in their cases and any other ongoing matters. An appeals court upheld the disqualification ruling, and Habba resigned in December 2025.

The most prominent case Habba's office brought under this disputed authority was her June 2025 indictment of Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-NJ) on three counts of assaulting, impeding, and interfering with federal officers during a May 9, 2025 congressional oversight visit to the Delaney Hall immigration detention facility in Newark, where McIver and other members of Congress were present to inspect conditions; prosecutors alleged she physically interfered with agents attempting to arrest Newark Mayor Ras Baraka, who was also arrested (and had charges against him separately dropped) during the same visit. McIver pleaded not guilty and argued Habba's unlawful appointment should void the indictment; the Third Circuit's December 1, 2025 ruling disqualifying Habba did not retroactively dismiss the case, and an August 2026 appeals ruling allowed two of the three charges to proceed to trial despite the authority dispute. McIver's prosecution was part of a broader wave of federal and local officials facing arrest, assault, or charges in connection with immigration-enforcement protests and oversight activity in mid-2025, including Sen. Alex Padilla, NYC Comptroller Brad Lander, and Wisconsin Judge Hannah Dugan, separately charged with obstruction for allegedly helping an undocumented defendant evade arrest in her courtroom -- a pattern Time magazine's June 2025 reporting characterized as officials facing consequences for opposing the administration's immigration crackdown.

Rather than nominating a Senate-confirmable replacement, Attorney General Bondi then appointed three individuals -- Philip Lamparello, Jordan Fox, and Ari Fontecchio -- to jointly divide the U.S. Attorney's responsibilities among themselves. A federal judge ruled this arrangement was also unlawful, finding DOJ had split the power of the U.S. Attorney's office among the three-person team specifically to route around the earlier disqualification ruling. The same judge, per AP News, threw a government prosecutor out of court and ordered the top officials running the New Jersey U.S. Attorney's Office to testify under oath, condemning DOJ's leadership structure there as "chaotic" and potentially unconstitutional. After that, the district court's own judges -- in consultation with DOJ leadership, a notable shift from the prior confrontational posture -- appointed career prosecutor Robert Frazer as acting U.S. Attorney on March 23, 2026, rather than DOJ nominating a Senate-confirmable replacement itself. A defendant separately challenged Frazer's appointment as unlawful; Judge Brann rejected that challenge on April 16, 2026, affirmatively ruling the appointment lawful.

official: Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General (served 2025-2026, removed April 2026)
offense_category: Vindictive/Selective Prosecution (violates Due Process; established legal doctrine, e.g. United States v. Goodwin) and Appointments Clause Violation (U.S. Const. Art. II, §2, re: unlawful appointment of the prosecuting U.S. Attorney) — the underlying CHARGES against James were brought and then dismissed; Bondi herself was not charged with anything personally
incident_summary:
Following repeated public calls by President Trump for Bondi's DOJ to prosecute New York Attorney General Letitia James, who had brought a civil fraud case against Trump and his businesses, DOJ pursued criminal charges against James. A federal judge dismissed the case after finding the interim U.S. Attorney who secured the indictment had been unlawfully appointed, and two separate federal grand juries also declined to indict James. Congressional Judiciary Democrats opened an investigation into the matter, characterizing it as retaliatory prosecutorial abuse.

On December 22, 2025, DOJ filed to reinstate the indictments against both James and James Comey, whose cases had been dismissed on the same Appointments Clause defect; the Fourth Circuit consolidated the two appeals for oral argument and disposition on January 12, 2026. On March 25, 2026, FHFA Director Bill Pulte -- who has separately pursued mortgage-fraud referrals against other Trump critics, tracked in a related entry in this database -- sent two new criminal referrals to federal prosecutors (Jason Reding Quinones, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida, and Andrew Boutros, U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois), alleging James may have falsified information on homeowner's insurance applications to Universal Property Insurance (Florida) and Allstate (Illinois). James's attorney called the new referrals a political vendetta and accused Trump officials of recycling baseless allegations after the original federal case was dismissed and two separate grand juries had already declined to indict her. Bondi was removed as Attorney General in April 2026, for stated reasons related to Epstein files handling, not this matter specifically.

The Fourth Circuit's consolidated appeal of the dismissal remains unresolved; if the court reverses, the original indictments -- not merely the new Pulte-initiated insurance-fraud referrals -- could be reinstated and the case could proceed to trial. A three-judge Fourth Circuit panel heard argument on September 15, 2026; two of its judges questioned the government's claim that it could keep installing interim U.S. attorneys without Senate approval, and reporting described the panel as appearing poised to uphold the dismissals. No ruling had issued as of this update.

Prosecutorial action taken in response, rather than independent application of prosecutorial discretion based on evidence
Procedural/legal defect in how the prosecution was carried out (here: unlawful appointment of the prosecuting attorney)
