rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: prosecutorial decisions reflected genuine evidentiary judgment, not political direction; the Appointments Clause issue was a technical/procedural defect, not evidence the underlying case lacked merit; presidents have always commented publicly on cases of interest.
comeback: The Appointments Clause violation explains a process failure, not why career prosecutorial norms (independence from White House case selection) were abandoned to begin with, and it doesn't explain two separate grand juries -- composed of ordinary citizens reviewing the actual evidence, not partisan actors -- declining to indict. 'Technical defect' doesn't account for why the technically defective prosecutor was put in that position in the first place: to pursue a case the president had publicly demanded by name. The pattern across multiple of the administration's named political opponents (James, Comey, Schiff, Powell, Clapper, Brennan) is itself evidence against the 'isolated independent judgment' defense.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Underlying cause, well-supported by reporting: a documented shift from DOJ's traditional independence from White House direction in individual prosecutions toward direct responsiveness to presidential demands regarding named political opponents. This is a structural/institutional cause, not specific to James's case alone. It connects to related tracked matters: her dismissed indictment shares its Appointments Clause defect and a consolidated appeal with the Comey case (see the Halligan-Comey entry), and the new insurance-fraud referrals come from the same FHFA director whose referrals against other Trump critics are tracked in the Pulte entry.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the documented facts: presidential public pressure, the Appointments Clause dismissal, and the two grand jury non-indictments are all corroborated by direct reporting and court action, not contested. MODERATE confidence on directly attributing personal culpability to Bondi for the prosecutorial decision-making itself, since the congressional investigation into DOJ conduct was not concluded as of this entry's last update. This is one of the stronger-evidenced entries in the dataset -- the judicial dismissal and grand jury pattern give it firmer footing than entries relying solely on press reporting or contested testimony. The House Judiciary investigation into DOJ's conduct in the James matter remains open without a published finding, and no charges or findings against Bondi personally have emerged; a separate House Oversight civil contempt resolution against Bondi (filed April 29, 2026, over her non-appearance for an Epstein-related deposition) concerns a different matter and is not folded into this entry. The Pulte-initiated referrals and James's attorney's response are independently corroborated across CBS News, CNN, NBC News, and Fox News. DOJ's appeal and its consolidation are corroborated across The Hill, Democracy Docket, CBS News, Fox News, and Law360's court-docket reporting. The September 15, 2026 oral argument rests on the Washington Post's report of it; no ruling and no charging decision on the March 2026 referrals had been identified.

offense_category: Press Freedom / DOJ Media-Policy Reversal (rescission of the post-2021 policy restricting subpoenas, court orders, and search warrants against journalists in leak investigations) -- not itself unlawful (the Attorney General has discretion to set DOJ media policy), but the direct policy predicate for this tracker's later journalist-subpoena entries
incident_summary: On April 25, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a memorandum rescinding the policy Attorney General Merrick Garland announced in July 2021. Garland's policy shielded journalists from compelled testimony and record seizures in leak investigations; it followed the revelation that the first Trump administration's DOJ had secretly obtained or attempted to obtain records from at least nine journalists. Bondi's memo lets prosecutors more readily seek subpoenas, court orders and search warrants directed at journalists and news organizations to compel records and testimony in leak investigations, provided the measures are approved by DOJ leadership, narrowly tailored, and preceded by advance notice to the journalist where feasible. Bondi framed the reversal as necessary to 'identify and punish the source of improper leaks' that she said jeopardized DOJ's ability to 'uphold the rule of law, protect civil rights, and keep America safe.' Freedom of the Press Foundation condemned the decision and criticized members of Congress who did not prioritize passing a federal shield law in 2024. Its advocacy director, Seth Stern, said every Democrat who put the PRESS Act "on the back burner" when they could have passed "a bipartisan bill codifying journalist-source confidentiality" should be ashamed. The memo is the policy predicate for the individual journalist-subpoena episodes this tracker documents in separate entries. In February 2026, FBI agents delivered a grand jury subpoena for Times freelancer Matthew Cole; it is still active. Later in 2026, grand jury subpoenas went to Wall Street Journal reporters and a Washington Post reporter (weighed in their own entry against 28 C.F.R. Section 50.10) and were withdrawn in June. An FBI-run Air Force One leak probe led to subpoenas of New York Times reporters, withdrawn in July. There is no report of the policy being rescinded or narrowed.

The new policy's stated safeguards (DOJ-leadership approval, narrow tailoring, advance notice) are self-administered by the same department whose leadership ordered the reversal, not externally enforced
This reversal is the specific policy authority subsequently invoked in this tracker's later, individual journalist-subpoena episodes

rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: the Attorney General has clear discretion to set DOJ's internal media-subpoena policy, and this changes no statute. The new policy keeps safeguards (leadership approval, narrow tailoring, advance notice). And leak investigations into unauthorized disclosure of sensitive government information are legitimate law-enforcement business, whichever outlet receives the leaked material.
comeback: The safeguards Bondi cites are administered entirely within the same department whose leadership ordered the reversal. There is no independent or statutory check, which is precisely the gap the 2021 policy and the still-unpassed PRESS Act were designed to close. **The predecessor policy did not exist in a vacuum: it was adopted specifically because the first Trump administration's DOJ had already secretly obtained or attempted to obtain records from at least nine journalists, and this reversal restores the department's ability to do exactly that.** The later episodes this tracker documents under this authority show that self-administered safeguards did not, in practice, prevent subpoenas a court later treated skeptically. In 2026 DOJ subpoenaed Wall Street Journal reporters over Iran-war coverage and a Washington Post reporter over Venezuela coverage, then withdrew the subpoenas in June 2026, after the papers' sealed court challenges, once the judge indicated she was likely to quash them.

offense_category: Removal of an Aggressive Antitrust Enforcer Following White House Pressure Tied to a Presidential Pardon of a DOJ Antitrust Target -- raises accountability concerns about enforcement independence rather than alleging a specific criminal violation
incident_summary:
Abigail (Gail) Slater, Assistant Attorney General for the DOJ's Antitrust Division, was forced out in February 2026 after roughly a year leading the division, during which she pursued aggressive antitrust enforcement. Friction with the White House had been building for months: CBS News reported July 17, 2025 that Slater had already drawn criticism from colleagues and business leaders while leading active cases against Capital One, Apple, Google, and others, including friction over her office's handling of merger reviews -- Bondi's chief of staff Chad Mizelle had overruled her to accept a Hewlett Packard Enterprise/Juniper Networks merger settlement DOJ officials were confident was weaker than what the government could have won at trial. The two named officials who raised those concerns, Roger Alford (principal deputy assistant attorney general) and Bill Rinner (deputy assistant attorney general and head of merger enforcement), were placed on administrative leave in late July 2025 and fired outright on July 29, 2025 for alleged "insubordination" -- the officials Mizelle had overruled were themselves removed within days of that CBS News reporting. HPE had retained lobbyists with ties to the Trump White House to push the settlement through; Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison later moved to intervene in the federal court's Tunney Act review of the settlement, and House Judiciary Committee Democrats opened a probe into whether DOJ had ceded to lobbyists over its own antitrust experts' advice. Business leaders were reportedly unhappy after Slater warned them not to engage with the administration through Trump-aligned lobbyists and consultants seeking to influence pending antitrust matters; some administration officials defended her as principled and appropriately distrustful of well-connected allies attempting to sway confidential legal decisions.

In December 2025, Trump issued a "full and unconditional pardon" for Oak View Group co-founder Tim Leiweke, who had been indicted by Slater's own division earlier in 2025 -- undercutting an active enforcement action from within her own department. She had also lost the confidence of AG Bondi and Deputy AG Blanche, with a source telling reporters officials felt new leadership was needed to advance the President's agenda; a separate travel-rules dispute (an unauthorized trip to a Paris conference) led DOJ to cut off Slater's government credit card access. Slater suggested in a public post that she was leaving voluntarily, but CNN's sourcing characterized the departure as a firing. Bondi publicly thanked Slater for her service; DOJ named Omeed Assefi acting antitrust chief. House Judiciary Democrats sent a formal letter to Bondi regarding the Antitrust Division following Slater's departure; the letter's outcome was not confirmed in sourcing reviewed.

The Antitrust Division's Live Nation/Ticketmaster case -- the matter Slater had been pursuing aggressively before her departure -- was settled by DOJ in March 2026 for a $280 million payment and divestiture of roughly a dozen venues, short of the Ticketmaster breakup that had been the division's stated goal. A federal jury in a parallel case brought by a coalition of state attorneys general -- who continued litigating because they viewed DOJ's settlement as inadequate -- found Live Nation and Ticketmaster liable for illegal monopolization on April 15, 2026, with a separate remedies trial (potentially including a breakup) to follow before Judge Arun Subramanian. Former DOJ antitrust attorney Roger Alford testified before Congress in May 2026 criticizing the settlement on the record as enabling political-ally lobbying.

Live Nation and Ticketmaster have moved to overturn the April 15, 2026 jury verdict entirely (Rule 50(b) judgment as a matter of law) or, failing that, for a new trial (Rule 59); briefing closed July 2, 2026, and Judge Subramanian had not ruled as of the most recent reporting reviewed, with his questioning at a post-trial hearing focused on whether the states proved a legally distinct large-amphitheater market. Separately, the states' Tunney Act bid for discovery into the DOJ settlement's own adequacy was denied without prejudice by Judge Subramanian on August 4, 2026, with the states invited to return with narrower requests; the court's own Tunney Act ruling on the settlement is expected mid-September to mid-October 2026. The Rule 50(b)/59 post-trial motions remained unruled following a July 31, 2026 hearing.

official: Pam Bondi, Attorney General
offense_category: Retaliatory Firing of Career DOJ Staff Over Association with Special Counsel Jack Smith's Trump Prosecutions -- undermining internal ethics oversight and eroding a structural check (the Merit Systems Protection Board) that would ordinarily let the fired employees contest it
incident_summary:
**On July 11, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi fired Joseph Tirrell, the career director of DOJ's Departmental Ethics Office, in a four-sentence termination letter that gave no reason.** Tirrell had spent nearly 20 years at the department and had led the ethics office since 2023, reviewing and approving financial disclosures, recusals, and conflict-of-interest waivers for DOJ leadership including Bondi herself, Deputy AG Todd Blanche, and FBI Director Kash Patel. His portfolio had also included advising then-Special Counsel Jack Smith on ethics matters during Smith's prosecutions of Trump, including approving roughly $140,000 in free legal fees Smith received from a major Washington law firm -- and, before the firing, requiring Bondi's own office to either pay for, return, or destroy gifts (cigars from Conor McGregor, a soccer ball from FIFA) that federal employees are barred from keeping; a DOJ spokesperson told the New York Times the ball was accepted and the cigars were destroyed after consulting ethics officials. Tirrell was fired the same day Bondi dismissed at least 20 other DOJ employees with ties to Smith's prosecutions team, as part of a broader purge. In the same November 2025 Times account, Tirrell said he also believed leadership "didn't want the ethics office calling them up and telling them what to do." A DOJ spokesperson responded that "any ethics advice received from career ethics officials has been followed and not overruled."

Tirrell, along with two other fired former DOJ officials (Michael M. Gordon and Patricia A. Hartman), filed a lawsuit in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Gordon v. Executive Office of the President, D.D.C. 1:25-cv-02409, before Judge Jia M. Cobb) seeking immediate reinstatement and back pay -- noting that fired federal employees would normally appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board, but that the board had been left without a quorum after Trump removed one of its members, leaving them without the administrative appeal process Congress designed for exactly this situation; the complaint called MSPB review futile, though each plaintiff also filed a protective MSPB appeal. The Board's quorum was restored when a newly confirmed member was sworn in on October 28, 2025. The government moved to dismiss on November 25, 2025, arguing the Board is the proper forum; the plaintiffs opposed on December 23, 2025, arguing MSPB review would still be futile because the President now claims the power to fire Board members and its administrative judges and to direct how they construe the law, and the government replied on January 20, 2026. Tirrell has continued to write publicly on DOJ ethics policy, including a March 9, 2026 op-ed in Above the Law criticizing DOJ's decision to stop treating its senior political appointees as Hatch Act "further restricted" employees, which had limited their political activity. In April and July 2026 the plaintiffs flagged rulings in other Article II firing cases (Comans in the Eastern District of Virginia and Comey in the Southern District of New York) holding that such employees need not go to the MSPB first; on August 18, 2026 Judge Cobb ordered the government to address those rulings, and on September 15, 2026 the government responded that they were wrongly decided. The motion to dismiss remains undecided.
elements_required: Tirrell held a career, non-political ethics-oversight position with direct responsibility for DOJ leadership's own conflict-of-interest compliance
His termination letter, signed by Bondi, gave no stated reason and came the same day as a broader purge of at least 20 other staff connected to Jack Smith's prosecution team

Tirrell's own prior work included ethics oversight of Jack Smith specifically, tying his firing directly to his association with the Trump prosecutions rather than to any identified performance or misconduct issue

The normal administrative check on such a firing -- appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board -- was, the plaintiffs argued, futile when they were fired because the board itself had been left without a quorum by a separate Trump personnel action (the quorum was restored in October 2025; the plaintiffs argue MSPB review remains futile because the President claims control over the board)

Per Tirrell, his office told Bondi's office the items had to be paid for, returned, or destroyed; a DOJ spokesperson confirmed to the Times that the soccer ball was accepted and the cigars were destroyed following ethics consultation. This documents a concrete instance of Tirrell's ethics office overseeing Bondi's own conduct specifically, distinct from the Jack Smith-association rationale already documented as this entry's central thesis.

rebuttal_anticipated: DOJ leadership could argue that political appointees and their chosen staff serve at the Attorney General's discretion and that a change in administration routinely brings staff turnover, without needing to allege individual misconduct by any specific employee.
comeback: Tirrell was a career civil servant, not a political appointee serving at the AG's pleasure in the ordinary sense, and the ethics office he ran exists specifically to provide independent oversight of DOJ leadership's own conduct -- firing its head without stated cause, on the same day as a broader purge of Jack-Smith-associated staff, and doing so while the one structural check against improper removal (MSPB appeal) had been separately disabled, describes a coordinated effort to eliminate independent ethics oversight and retaliate against association with the Trump prosecutions, not routine staff turnover.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Illustrates a pattern of removing internal accountability checks at DOJ -- here the career official who enforced ethics rules on the Attorney General's own office, including over gifts -- on the same day as a purge of staff connected to Jack Smith's Trump prosecutions, and weeks after the firing of co-plaintiff Michael Gordon, a January 6 prosecutor, while the MSPB appeal route that would normally review such firings was first left without a quorum by the firing of MSPB Chair Cathy Harris and is now, the plaintiffs argue, under presidential control. The firing letter gave no reason, so the link to the Smith work rests on timing and circumstance. Related to, but a distinct mechanism from, this database's Trump IG-firing entry, which covers a different set of independent-oversight officials (agency Inspectors General) removed without the statutorily required congressional notice. Five days after Tirrell's firing, the department fired SDNY prosecutor Maurene Comey under the same claimed Article II power, and the judge whose April 2026 Comey jurisdiction ruling these plaintiffs cite later held that firing unlawful (see the Maurene Comey firing entry).

incident_summary:
Denise Cheung, the top criminal prosecutor in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia, resigned on February 18, 2025 after refusing an order from her Trump-appointed superiors -- acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove, directing Ed Martin (Trump's nominee for permanent D.C. U.S. Attorney) -- to open a grand jury investigation into a Biden-era Environmental Protection Agency funding decision and then use DOJ's authority to freeze the associated bank assets. Cheung and other experienced white-collar prosecutors in her office assessed the evidence on hand -- Bove's office cited a Project Veritas video as its basis -- and concluded it did not meet the legal threshold required to justify a grand jury investigation or an asset freeze. After she and her colleagues pushed back on the grand jury request, DOJ shifted to freezing the bank assets instead; the FBI in Washington, looped into the plan, sought legal backing from Cheung and ultimately wrote to the bank itself, and Martin objected that the FBI's letter was not explicit enough about a criminal investigation. In her resignation letter, Cheung wrote that she believed she lacked the legal authority to issue such a letter, cited her oath of office and legal-ethics obligations, and said that when she declined, she was asked to resign.

After Cheung left, then-Interim U.S. Attorney Ed Martin personally submitted a seizure warrant application without any other prosecutors in his office joining it; a D.C. magistrate judge rejected it, ruling, according to the Washington Post's sources, that the application and an accompanying FBI agent's affidavit failed to establish a reasonable belief that a crime had occurred. Bove then approached at least one other U.S. Attorney's office, in the southeastern United States, about opening a grand jury investigation and seeking a court order to freeze the Citibank funds, and prosecutors there also declined, the Post reported. The FBI also questioned EPA employees about the program, reportedly at the request of the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida. Separately, in the parallel civil litigation over the underlying Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund grants (Climate United Fund v. Citibank and related suits by the grant recipients), U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan told a DOJ lawyer at an April 2, 2025 hearing: "Here we are, weeks in, and you're still unable to proffer me any information with regard to any kind of investigation or malfeasance" -- a judge's remark from the bench, separate from the prosecutor's own assessment, that DOJ had shown her no evidentiary basis. No indication in sourcing reviewed that the underlying grand-jury investigation into the EPA funding decision itself (as opposed to the asset-freeze mechanism) was ever formally opened or closed.

A divided en banc U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit ruled 6-4 on August 4, 2026 that EPA likely acted unlawfully in terminating the GGRF grants and clawing back disbursed funds, affirming the district court's preliminary injunction that a three-judge panel had set aside in September 2025. On August 6, 2026, the government filed an unopposed motion to stay the mandate pending a forthcoming Supreme Court cert petition; the court granted it, extending through November 9, 2026 the partial stay, in place since April 16, 2025, of the injunction's requirement that Citibank disburse funds, and directed that the stay continue pending the Supreme Court's final disposition if a petition is filed. No cert petition has been confirmed filed.

offense_category: Ordering Dismissal of a Pending Federal Corruption Indictment in Exchange for a Sitting Official's Cooperation on Unrelated Policy Priorities -- a federal judge found the arrangement carried the appearance of an improper quid pro quo; addressed here as an institutional-integrity and prosecutorial-independence matter rather than a criminal charge against Bove
incident_summary:
New York City Mayor Eric Adams had been federally indicted on charges including bribery, wire fraud, and illegal foreign campaign contributions. On February 10, 2025, acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove ordered federal prosecutors to move to dismiss the case without prejudice -- preserving DOJ's ability to revive the charges later -- citing concerns that the prosecution would interfere with Adams's ability to assist the administration's immigration-enforcement priorities and with his reelection campaign, rather than any evidentiary or legal weakness in the case. The order triggered a cascade of resignations: Acting U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York Danielle Sassoon, who had held the post only three weeks, resigned rather than comply, writing that Adams's attorneys had effectively proposed a quid pro quo in a meeting with DOJ -- that Adams would cooperate with the administration's enforcement priorities only if the indictment were dropped. The then-acting chief of DOJ's Public Integrity Section and a deputy assistant attorney general also resigned rather than sign the dismissal motion.

U.S. District Judge Dale Ho ultimately dismissed the case on April 2, 2025 -- but with prejudice, permanently barring its revival, rejecting DOJ's request to dismiss without prejudice. Judge Ho wrote that "everything here smacks of a bargain: dismissal of the Indictment in exchange for immigration policy concessions," calling DOJ's claimed "virtually unreviewable" license to dismiss charges on that basis "disturbing in its breadth, implying that public officials may receive special dispensation if they are compliant with the incumbent administration's policy priorities," and that dismissing without prejudice would create "the unavoidable perception that the Mayor's freedom depends on his ability to carry out the immigration enforcement priorities of the administration." Senators Whitehouse and Blumenthal had filed ethics complaints against Bove with DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility and New York's attorney grievance body on February 27, 2025. On May 28, 2025, shortly after Bove's Third Circuit nomination was announced, the senators were notified that New York's Attorney Grievance Committee was transferring the matter to DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility as "better suited" to investigate and would take no further action. A June 2025 NBC News analysis situated the episode within a broader four-month pattern in which the new administration dismantled key parts of federal anti-corruption enforcement, including the Inspectors General purge and a pause in foreign-bribery enforcement documented elsewhere in this database.

Sens. Whitehouse and Blumenthal filed a renewed ethics complaint with the New York State Courts' Attorney Grievance Committee in September 2025 -- after Bove's confirmation -- that folded in the Adams dismissal, the separate GGRF/Cheung episode tracked in a related entry in this database, and his alleged instruction to DOJ attorneys to prepare to defy adverse court orders in immigration cases. Separately, because Bove is now a sitting Article III judge, a different accountability mechanism became available: in December 2025 the watchdog group Fix the Court filed a judicial-misconduct complaint against him under the Judicial Conduct and Disability Act, after he attended a December 9, 2025 Trump rally in Mount Pocono, Pennsylvania, citing Canons 2 and 5 of the judicial conduct code. In a June 25, 2026 letter to DOJ's acting inspector general, Whitehouse wrote that OPR had yet to respond to the senators' February 2025 complaint. As of late July 2026, Fix the Court listed its complaint against Bove as still under consideration.

official: Doug Burgum, Secretary of the Interior
offense_category: Statutory Violation — Commemorative Works Act (40 U.S.C. §§8901-8909) and 40 U.S.C. §8106 (unauthorized construction of a monument on federal land in the National Capital area) — NOT charged; this is a planning/permitting-stage dispute, not yet a completed unauthorized construction, and is most likely to be resolved via litigation or congressional action rather than criminal process
incident_summary:
The Interior Department, under Burgum, has advanced planning and historic-preservation review (a Section 106 Assessment of Effect and draft Programmatic Agreement) for a 250-foot "Triumphal Arch" at Memorial Circle on Columbia Island, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery -- nicknamed the "Arch de Trump" by critics -- although the Commemorative Works Act allows a new commemorative work on National Park Service land in the capital only as specifically authorized by law, and Congress has enacted no such authorization for this project. In February 2026, three Vietnam veterans and architectural historian Calder Loth sued the President, the Executive Office of the President, Domestic Policy Council Director Vince Haley and the National Park Service (Lemmon v. Trump) to block construction absent congressional authorization, also objecting that the arch would obstruct the view between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. In court, the government has claimed its authority from a 1925 law that authorized the Arlington Memorial Bridge; the plaintiffs call that reading meritless.

At an April 2, 2026 hearing, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan said she did not want ground broken while the case was pending, or to "wake up in the morning" to bulldozers at Memorial Circle. On April 8, she entered a consent order under which NPS may not authorize construction before posting notice on its planning website and must give at least 14 days' notice on the court docket before construction, or demolition in preparation for construction, begins; the plaintiffs' preliminary-injunction motion was denied without prejudice. The U.S. Commission of Fine Arts approved the arch's concept on April 16, 2026. On May 13, 2026, Burgum told the House Natural Resources Committee, under questioning from its top Democrat, Rep. Jared Huffman, that there was "no final agency action around building something" at the site and "not a proposal." The next day, as workers operated drilling equipment inside fenced-off areas of Memorial Circle -- site surveys such as geotechnical work, according to Interior -- Huffman accused Burgum of coming "pretty damn close" to perjuring himself and offered him the chance to revise his statements; Interior called the testimony "100% accurate." No perjury referral or charge has been identified. On May 21, the Commission of Fine Arts gave final design approval, except for the sculpture and statuary, after the design dropped an eight-foot base and four lion sculptures.

In a June 15, 2026 comment letter on the Section 106 review, Senators Angus King, Martin Heinrich and Jeff Merkley and Representatives Jared Huffman, Maxine Dexter and Yassamin Ansari, writing as ranking members of committees with jurisdiction over capital monuments, told Burgum and NPS officials that Congress has never authorized the arch, that Congressional Research Service analysis they requested in January reached the same conclusion, and that NPS has "no power to build" it, citing the Commemorative Works Act, 40 U.S.C. §8106 and the 1910 Height of Buildings Act. On July 9, 2026, the National Capital Planning Commission voted 8-1, with three members voting present, to give preliminary approval to the site and building plans, with comments to be addressed before final review; it suggested cutting the mezzanine to 130 feet and the observation level to 20 feet to meet the Height of Buildings Act, adding the 40 feet to the arch's Lady Liberty statue (bringing it to 100 feet) so the arch would still reach 250 feet. NPS issued a revised Section 106 Assessment of Effect on August 28, 2026.

On September 3, 2026, Burgum announced on X that Interior was "preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck." The plaintiffs sought a temporary restraining order the next day. The government answered that the planned work -- four archaeological test pits, starting no earlier than September 21 with the land restored by October 31 -- was predecisional information-gathering, not construction, and that NPS had issued no final agency action authorizing construction. On September 4, Chutkan ordered 48 hours' notice before any activity on Memorial Circle other than that archaeological information-gathering, warning that construction before a final NPS authorization or without 14 days' notice would violate her orders. On September 17 she denied the government's request to dissolve that order, clarifying that it covers only arch-related activity, and denied the restraining-order motion as moot; on September 18 the government gave notice that nine geoarchaeological borings would be added to the testing. A government motion to dismiss and cross-motions for summary judgment are fully briefed and pending. On September 24, 2026, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation notified NPS that it was terminating consultation on a Section 106 agreement for the arch -- before consultation was finished, according to the National Trust for Historic Preservation -- and said it would send formal comments to the Secretary of the Interior, whose response would conclude the review; it asked for public comments by September 29. NCPC has not given final approval, and the arch is not on the agenda for its October 1, 2026 meeting.
elements_required: Commemorative Works Act requires congressional authorization, via specific enacted law, before a new commemorative work may be placed on federal land in the National Capital region (40 U.S.C. §8902(a)(2))
No such congressional authorization has been enacted for this specific project
Interior/NPS proceeded with planning, historic-preservation review, and permitting processes for the project despite the absence of authorization
Separate violation alleged under 40 U.S.C. §8106 (a related capital-construction statute)

status: No act of Congress authorizes the arch. NCPC approval is only preliminary (July 9); final review is not on its Oct. 1 agenda. In Lemmon v. Trump, dispositive motions are pending and court orders require notice before construction or non-archaeological site work. No charges.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: the project remains in a preliminary planning/environmental-review phase, not actual construction, so no violation has technically occurred yet; in court, the government has claimed authority from a 1925 statute that authorized the Arlington Memorial Bridge, and it describes the current site work as archaeological testing, not construction, with no final NPS decision authorizing construction.
comeback: The 'planning phase, not yet a violation' framing inverts how the Commemorative Works Act works in practice: every comparable memorial built over the last forty years went to Congress first, before construction was permitted -- not as a post-hoc formality, but as the threshold requirement that opens the door to everything else. Proceeding with a formal Section 106 historic-preservation review and a draft Programmatic Agreement before securing that authorization isn't a minor sequencing issue to be cleaned up later; it's the documented departure from the Act's established practice. A CRS analysis -- nonpartisan, written for Congress, not an advocacy document -- concluded, according to the lawmakers who requested it, that building the arch without congressional authorization would not comport with the Act. The government's answer in court has been a 1925 statute that authorized the Arlington Memorial Bridge, and it has kept proceeding.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] The arch fits a pattern of the administration advancing capital projects the president favors in Washington through executive review processes while disputing that Congress must authorize them: here, the government offers a 1925 bridge statute in place of the specific authorization the Commemorative Works Act requires, site testing proceeds as what the government calls predecisional information-gathering, not construction, and Section 106 consultation was ended with the public given days to comment. The White House ballroom, where the East Wing was demolished before courts could weigh in, is a separate project on a separate legal track, but it is the precedent Judge Chutkan and the plaintiffs pointed to in demanding advance notice here. The arch has also advanced in the same budget cycle in which the administration's fiscal 2027 request proposed a 40 percent cut to the National Park Service's maintenance budget and a $736 million cut to park operations; Burgum told senators the proposed $10 billion presidential capital fund would not pay for the arch, so the parallel is one of priorities, not a documented transfer of money. Burgum's role is that of the cabinet officer carrying out and publicly championing the project, including through his May 2026 testimony that there was no final agency action; he did not originate it.

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (institutional attribution -- a Marine Corps 250th-anniversary demonstration held under DoD auspices and attended by Hegseth and Vice President JD Vance; no specific individual was named in sourcing as personally authorizing the decision to fire live artillery over the highway)
offense_category: Authorizing Live Artillery Fire Directly Over a Major Public Interstate Highway for a Televised Political Spectacle, Resulting in a Malfunctioning Round Striking a State Patrol Vehicle
incident_summary:
On October 18, 2025, the Marine Corps staged a live-fire demonstration at Camp Pendleton, California, to commemorate the Corps' 250th anniversary. The event was recorded for a future prime-time broadcast and attended by an estimated 15,000 invited guests, including Vice President JD Vance and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The day before, California Gov. Gavin Newsom called the demonstration 'dangerous' and 'unnecessary,' saying 'firing live rounds over a busy highway isn't just wrong -- it's dangerous,' and accused the administration of prioritizing spectacle over public safety. Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA) countered that Newsom had improperly interfered with Marine Corps planning and staged 'a spiteful publicity stunt.'

The demonstration included Marine forces moving from Navy ships offshore onto Pendleton's Red Beach, and howitzer artillery firing directly over Interstate 5, a major corridor between Los Angeles and San Diego that was closed to traffic during the exercise. The rounds were meant to land far to the east, in the base's Whiskey Impact Area. **One M795 high-explosive round detonated prematurely, at an altitude of roughly 1,480 feet, scattering shrapnel onto the closed roadway that struck and damaged a California Highway Patrol vehicle and motorcycle**. The patrol vehicle was part of Vice President Vance's own security detail. No injuries were reported. California Highway Patrol Border Division Chief Tony Coronado called live fire over an active freeway 'highly uncommon.'

Issa's spokesperson dismissed media coverage as 'comic exaggerations.' Rep. Mike Levin led 26 House members and two senators in a formal letter demanding to know who had authorized firing over the freeway and how the safety risk had been assessed beforehand. State Sen. Catherine Blakespear called the event 'posturing with militaristic bluster at the expense of the safety and well-being of the community.'

A Marine Corps investigation, detailed in a 666-page report dated December 19, 2025 and publicly reported in March 2026, concluded there was 'no definitive answer' for why the round detonated early. It characterized the malfunction as a 'one in a million' occurrence and found no negligence or wrongdoing by the Marine Corps personnel involved. In the sourcing reviewed, the investigation did not appear to separately evaluate whether the underlying decision to fire live artillery over a public interstate was itself a sound safety judgment, and Levin's question of who specifically authorized that plan has no public answer.

A round malfunctioned and detonated over the highway, scattering shrapnel that struck a state law-enforcement vehicle assigned to protect the sitting Vice President

A state governor and dozens of members of Congress from both chambers formally characterized the underlying decision (not merely the malfunction) as reckless and demanded accountability for who authorized it

The military's own investigation, while finding no personnel negligence in the malfunction itself, could not identify why the round detonated early and did not address whether firing over a public highway was itself a sound safety decision

official: Brendan Carr, Chairman of the Federal Communications Commission (early-renewal order issued by the FCC's Media Bureau under his chairmanship); Donald Trump, President (public demands that ABC fire Jimmy Kimmel and lose its licenses)
offense_category: First Amendment Retaliation and Government Coercion of Speech (NRA v. Vullo, 2024: the government may not 'use the power of the State to punish or suppress disfavored expression') -- alleged use of the FCC's power to call broadcast licenses in for early renewal (47 C.F.R. § 73.3539(c)) to punish ABC for its programming; the FCC says the order serves a discrimination investigation -- civil litigation (ABC v. FCC, D.D.C. No. 1:26-cv-02902), not criminal
incident_summary: In September 2025, after Jimmy Kimmel's on-air remarks following the killing of Charlie Kirk, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said on a podcast, "Look, we can do this the easy way or the hard way," and warned of "additional work for the FCC ahead"; Disney briefly suspended Kimmel's show and reinstated it six days later. On April 23, 2026, Kimmel joked in a sketch that First Lady Melania Trump had "a glow like an expectant widow." After a shooting at the White House Correspondents' Dinner on April 25, the President wrote on Truth Social on April 27 that the joke was a "despicable call to violence" and that Kimmel should "be immediately fired by Disney and ABC." **The next day, April 28, the FCC's Media Bureau ordered all eight ABC-owned television stations to file license renewal applications within 30 days, although none of their licenses expires before December 2028 and two run to 2031.** The FCC had not called a license in early for more than half a century until the day before, when it did so for one small licensee, and according to ABC's complaint it had never called in a network's owned stations together. The order said early renewal was essential to the agency's investigation of Disney's employment and diversity practices, and Carr criticized Disney's diversity policies on a podcast as the order went out. The stations filed on May 28 under protest, and the public comment period closed August 5 with more than 150,000 comments, according to ABC's complaint. **After ABC declined to carry his July 16 address live, the President said during the speech that this "should mean a revocation of their licenses," and on July 22 Carr said he expected ABC's decision to be part of the agency's early review of the stations' licenses.** On August 18, ABC, Disney and the eight stations sued the FCC in federal court in Washington, alleging a retaliatory campaign against ABC "for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts," and moved for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction to stop the FCC from designating the licenses for a hearing. Carr called it "a meritless case." On September 3, the FCC moved to dismiss, arguing that only a federal appeals court can review its licensing actions and that Disney's deficient responses to the discrimination inquiry, not ABC's speech, prompted the early renewals; it agreed to give at least 48 hours' notice before referring the licenses for a hearing. In a September 17 filing, ABC argued that Carr is carrying out the President's "specific directives aimed at curbing speech critical of the Administration," citing the President's August 30 post that NBC's Kristen Welker would be "reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment." The FCC replied on September 24, and Judge Loren L. AliKhan heard ABC's motion and the FCC's motion to dismiss on October 6, 2026. During the two-hour hearing the judge challenged the government to justify the unusual licensing requirements, according to JURIST. ABC's lawyer likened the review to a looming execution by guillotine that was already chilling the network's editorial decisions weeks before the midterm elections, according to the Associated Press; the government argued that the court lacks jurisdiction because the case belongs in a different venue, challenged ABC's First Amendment arguments and said ABC had failed to show irreparable harm. The judge took both motions under advisement without ruling and allowed supplemental briefs on the other tools the FCC could use to compel Disney to answer its discrimination inquiry, due October 9 from the government and October 14 from ABC. The FCC's October 9 brief listed alternatives such as administrative subpoenas and monetary penalties, but said the Media Bureau had determined that early renewal was "the best tool for the task."

The government took adverse action likely to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness: an unprecedented order calling all eight ABC-owned stations' licenses in for early renewal, with a possible hearing that could lead to non-renewal

Causal link: retaliatory motive was a but-for cause of the action (timing relative to the President's demands, and the Chairman's own statements tying the license review to programming decisions), rather than the discrimination investigation the FCC cites

incident_summary: The FCC's news distortion policy, which the agency describes as covering broadcasters who "have deliberately distorted a factual news report," was rarely invoked for decades until FCC Chairman Brendan Carr cited it in disputes with networks the agency regulates. In November 2025, a bipartisan group of former FCC chairs and commissioners petitioned the agency to repeal it. On August 30, 2026, after NBC's Kristen Welker said President Trump had had "mixed results" with his primary endorsements, Trump wrote on Truth Social that she would be reported to the FCC for "rebuke or punishment" and that he hoped Carr and his commission "will take this Threat to our Country very seriously." Asked about Welker on Fox News on Sunday, September 6, Carr said "President Trump is over the target, and we're looking at a lot of actions," adding that "the FCC may put guidance out soon to remind broadcasters about their obligations with respect to not airing fake polls, particularly if they're done to suppress people heading into the fall." On Tuesday, October 20, a self-described polling firm, Wedgewood Polls, admitted it had fabricated its survey data after the poll tracker FiftyPlusOne asked it to comment on an investigation; The New York Times, among others, had included its numbers in election coverage. The next day, Wednesday, October 21, as the latest Reuters/Ipsos and Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos polls put Trump's approval at 31% and 33%, record lows by CNN's and Reuters' accounts, **Carr posted on X that there had been "a significant surge in entirely Fake Polls and Suppression Polls designed to do nothing more than interfere with the regular functioning of the electoral process and alter the normal patterns of voter turnout and enthusiasm,"** and that "many journalists and broadcasters" had been airing them. He wrote that "broadcasters are prohibited by the terms of their federal licenses from engaging in News Distortion or promoting Broadcast Hoaxes" and advised them "to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes by airing Polls that would violate their regulatory obligations." He named no poll or broadcaster and offered no evidence, according to Reuters and TheDesk, and did not respond to CNN's request for comment. Commissioner Anna Gomez, the commission's lone Democrat, replied that "FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith." A bipartisan group of former FCC officials, including former chairs Mark Fowler and Tom Wheeler and former commissioner Gloria Tristani, said Carr was "seizing on reports about fabricated political polling as an excuse to once again try to scare broadcasters into self-censorship" and that "the FCC has zero authority to dictate editorial decisions." The midterm elections are on November 3.

incident_summary:
In September 2024 Paramount asked the Federal Communications Commission to approve its merger with Skydance Media. On July 24, 2025 the commission approved it 2-1: Chairman Brendan Carr and Commissioner Olivia Trusty voted in favor and Commissioner Anna Gomez dissented, saying the deal was "linked to a payout to settle a baseless lawsuit and other troubling concessions." Carr said the approval "advances the public interest."

On December 5, 2025, Warner Bros. Discovery accepted a bid from Netflix for its studio and streaming business. Two days later, on December 7, Carr and Trusty attended the Kennedy Center Honors gala, which President Trump hosted and CBS sponsors. Trusty's financial disclosure lists two tickets from Paramount worth more than $12,000. Carr and his wife sat in a private skybox with Paramount CEO David Ellison and other Paramount and CBS executives; such seats sold for $125,000 a ticket, according to Kennedy Center guidelines cited by ProPublica. Carr's disclosure, which the FCC released only after the complaints described below were filed, lists tickets from Paramount for himself and a guest to the 2025 gala and reception worth $12,390, and he did not respond when ProPublica asked about the gap. His disclosures show **he has reported accepting gala tickets from CBS or its parent company eight times since his 2017 appointment, totaling over $75,000.** Hours after the gala ended, Paramount launched a hostile takeover bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, which later produced a merger agreement.

On March 3, 2026, after Netflix dropped out, Carr told CNBC that Paramount's bid was "a lot cleaner" than Netflix's, that any FCC role would be "pretty minimal," and that "this is a good deal, and I think it should get through pretty quickly." On March 23, Senator Cory Booker and six other Democratic senators wrote to Carr that his statements "indicate that the Commission has no intention of conducting a meaningful inquiry" into the merger's foreign investment. In April, Paramount petitioned the FCC to allow foreign investors to hold more than the 25% benchmark in its broadcast-licensee parent.

In July 2026 ProPublica reported the gala tickets. Four ethics experts told it that Carr and Trusty had compromised the FCC's impartiality and should not take part in any decision on the merger. The FCC said agency ethics officers had for years cleared commissioners' attendance, and an FCC official told ProPublica the commissioners were advised the event met the "widely attended gathering" exception; ProPublica reported that a 2007 Office of Government Ethics memo said performing arts presentations do not qualify. On July 16, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) asked the FCC's inspector general to investigate whether the commissioners were properly authorized to accept the gifts and whether accepting them violated their ethical duties regardless. On July 30, Democracy Defenders Fund filed a complaint with the Office of Government Ethics, the FCC inspector general and the FCC ethics office, asking whether Carr and Trusty broke the gift rules or the criminal illegal-gratuities statute (18 U.S.C. 201(c)), that they repay the gifts' "fair market value," and that Carr be disqualified from the Warner Bros. decision. The complaints do not allege that the gifts influenced any FCC decision, though Democracy Defenders Fund wrote that the gala's timing "raises serious questions about whether Paramount had an intent to influence" the commission. The FCC called the accusations "unfounded," and the inspector general declined to comment.

On September 17, 2026, the FCC's Media Bureau issued a declaratory ruling allowing up to 100% indirect foreign equity ownership of Paramount, including stakes for funds from Saudi Arabia, Abu Dhabi and Qatar. Gomez said she had called for the issue to go to a full commission vote and that "the FCC snuck this ruling out as a staff-level decision, with no public vote and no accountability for a call of this magnitude." After a judge approved Paramount's September settlements with the 12 states that had sued to block the deal, the merger closed on October 6, 2026. No recusal by Carr or Trusty, no inspector general or Office of Government Ethics finding, and no public response from Carr himself was identified in sourcing reviewed.

official: Lori Chavez-DeRemer, then-Secretary of Labor (resigned April 2026)
offense_category: Retaliation Against Employees Who Reported Sexual Misconduct by the Secretary's Own Husband, Alongside a Broader Inspector General Misconduct Investigation -- an EEO-complaint-based accountability claim distinct from her husband's underlying alleged conduct or the IG's separate personal-conduct/travel findings, both of which are separate matters
incident_summary:
Two female political staffers at the Department of Labor alleged that Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer's husband, Dr. Shawn DeRemer, an anesthesiologist, subjected them to unwanted sexual touching at the department's Washington headquarters in late 2025, including an incident on December 18 captured on office security cameras. DeRemer was barred from the building, reportedly on the Labor Department Inspector General's recommendation; federal prosecutors ultimately declined to bring charges against him after reviewing the evidence, including the security footage. Separately, at least three people filed formal EEO discrimination/retaliation complaints against Chavez-DeRemer herself, alleging she created a hostile workplace, retaliated against the female staffers who reported her husband's conduct, fostered a climate in which staff feared punishment for speaking out or resisting directives they considered inappropriate, and directed staff to perform personal errands for her (including cleaning her closet).

The Inspector General's investigation broadened well beyond the husband incident: whistleblowers alleged Chavez-DeRemer had an affair with a member of her own security detail, used department resources for personal trips, and sent inappropriate personal messages to young staffers; the IG separately investigated her chief of staff Jihun Han and his deputy Rebecca Wright for alleged "travel fraud" -- setting up professional events as pretexts for her personal travel. According to witnesses the Inspector General later cited, after a New York Post article on January 9, 2026, Chavez-DeRemer directed Han and Wright to identify employees they believed had given information to the media, and the two told staff they had advised her to fire three suspected sources; those firings were never carried out because Han and Wright were themselves placed on administrative leave on January 11, 2026. Both were terminated on March 2, 2026, as the broadened probe proceeded. Chavez-DeRemer resigned as Labor Secretary on April 20, 2026 amid the mounting allegations -- the third member of Trump's Cabinet to leave within two months -- and, per reporting, falsely claimed a "deep state" conspiracy was behind the scrutiny on her way out. Deputy Secretary Keith Sonderling became acting secretary. She had resigned the day before the Inspector General was scheduled to interview her; her attorney then declined to make her available.

IG D'Esposito's May 2026 estimate that the investigation would be finalized by the end of June was not met; as of August 10, 2026 reporting, the investigation remained open with no completion date, and by early August investigators had interviewed over 65 people. No findings had been publicly released, and congressional Education and Workforce Committee staff on both sides said they had not received an update. The IG's 44-page report, dated and released September 3, 2026, found Chavez-DeRemer's office was "toxic, intimidating and humiliating" per interviews with 53 current/former DOL staffers and one employee from another agency, and substantiated the inappropriate-relationship, alcohol-policy, unauthorized personal/official travel-combining, personal-task-misuse, and unreported-gift allegations. It also recounted witness statements that career employees who raised travel-rule concerns were removed from travel-preparation duties at her direction. It concluded she violated department policy and federal ethics standards but stopped short of saying she violated federal law, and it found insufficient evidence to establish that her inappropriately close relationship with the assistant special agent-in-charge of her protective detail was romantic or sexual. The report also details a specific incident: during personal travel to Oregon in April 2025, Chavez-DeRemer allegedly directed her security-detail driver, over his repeated objections, to give cash from her purse to a partially nude performer at a strip club. The report did not address the allegations against her husband or the separate EEO retaliation complaints.

official: Adm. Kevin Lunday, Coast Guard Commandant / Kristi Noem, then-Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: Repeated Policy Flip-Flopping on Classifying Swastikas and Nooses as Hate Symbols, Followed by an Actual Swastika Incident at a Recruit Training Center -- documents an institutional policy failure rather than any single official's criminal conduct
incident_summary:
In November 2025, The Washington Post reported the Coast Guard would no longer classify swastikas and nooses as hate symbols under a new workplace-harassment policy, instead labeling them merely "potentially divisive." Within a day, the Coast Guard reversed course and said both would again be classified as hate symbols. Despite that public reversal, Commandant Adm. Kevin Lunday's order to maintain the hate-symbol classification was never actually incorporated into the policy for reasons that remain unclear, and the more lenient "potentially divisive" language was allowed to take effect in mid-December 2025 despite objections from members of Congress. Facing renewed uproar, the Coast Guard deleted the downgraded language again on December 18, 2025, restoring the hate-symbol classification for a second time.

Roughly two months later, on February 19-20, 2026, an instructor found a swastika hand-drawn on a bathroom wall at the Coast Guard's primary recruit training center in Cape May, New Jersey; Lunday personally flew to the base to address roughly 900 recruits and staff, condemning the symbol's use, and the Coast Guard referred the incident to its Investigative Service. The Coast Guard Investigative Service has not publicly released findings, identified a suspect, or announced any disciplinary/legal action from the Cape May incident; no further policy reversals have been identified since the December 2025 restoration of the hate-symbol classification.
elements_required: The Coast Guard's official written policy classified swastikas and nooses as merely 'potentially divisive' rather than hate symbols for a period in December 2025, despite the Commandant's own stated intent to maintain the stricter classification
This downgraded language took effect and remained in place for a period despite congressional objections, indicating a governance failure in how the Commandant's order was (or wasn't) implemented
The policy was reversed twice in response to public and congressional pressure rather than through a considered, stable policymaking process

An actual swastika incident occurred at a Coast Guard training facility within about two months of the second reversal, providing a concrete test of whether the final policy and its enforcement culture were adequate

official: Doug Collins, Secretary of Veterans Affairs
offense_category: Administrative Procedure Act Violation — Final Rule Issued Without Required Notice-and-Comment (5 U.S.C. §553) — NOT charged criminally; this is a civil administrative law matter; the rule was withdrawn following public backlash, and at least one lawsuit was filed seeking review before the withdrawal
incident_summary: In February 2026, the VA issued a regulation -- with no advance public notice, as an interim final rule in immediate effect -- requiring medical examiners to factor in the effects of medication when determining veterans' disability ratings, departing from prior practice. **The rule had a documented potential economic impact of $100 million per year and would have affected some 350,000 pending claims across more than 500 conditions**. After fewer than 60 hours of public reaction (more than 10,000 Federal Register comments) and condemnation from major veterans service organizations (VFW, Disabled American Veterans, American Legion, Paralyzed Veterans of America), at least one lawsuit was filed, and Collins announced within two days that the rule would not be enforced, and VA formally rescinded it effective February 27, 2026.
elements_required: APA generally requires agencies to publish proposed rules for public notice and comment before issuing them as final, with limited exceptions
The rule was issued as an interim final rule with immediate effect, invoking the APA 'good cause' exception to skip prior notice and comment
Documented substantial impact (350,000 claims, $100 million/year) establishing this was not a minor technical rule eligible for any narrow procedural exception
Subsequent litigation/legal challenge specifically contesting the rule's procedural validity

evidence.description: On March 12, 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims decided Ingram v. Collins (38 Vet. App. 130), holding that 'because the applicable diagnostic codes (DCs) and special musculoskeletal regulations do not reference medication, the Board must discount beneficial medication effects when assigning an evaluation,' and setting aside the Board's denial of higher ratings for the veteran's back and ankle disabilities -- the decision VA's February 2026 rule was written to counter
evidence.maps_to_element: Establishes the pro-veteran ruling at issue: the litigation context the rule was issued to override, and the ruling left standing when VA later dropped its appeal

evidence.description: The VA introduced the medication-disability-rating rule with no public notice, two days before backlash forced its pullback; American Legion national commander Dan K. Wiley welcomed the reversal as 'allowing the litigation to proceed in court and for your voices to be heard prior to the rule taking effect' -- underscoring that the rule took effect before any public input
evidence.maps_to_element: Rule issued without standard notice-and-comment process

evidence.description: The regulation itself documented a potential $100 million/year economic impact and said it would affect 350,000 claims and more than 500 conditions (VA argued that without it, Ingram would force it to readjudicate those claims), establishing the rule's substantial regulatory significance
evidence.maps_to_element: Scale establishing this was a substantive rule, not eligible for narrow procedural exceptions

evidence.description: Within the first 60 hours of the rule's posting, the Federal Register comment section drew more than 10,000 responses, and the rule drew formal condemnation from the VFW, Disabled American Veterans, American Legion, and Paralyzed Veterans of America, along with newer organizations like Burn Pits 360 and Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America
evidence.maps_to_element: Establishes the practical harm of bypassing notice-and-comment -- affected stakeholders had no opportunity for input before the rule took final effect

evidence.description: Collins did not disavow the underlying policy itself even while pulling back enforcement, initially calling criticism 'fake news' and maintaining the rule merely formalized VA's longstanding practice since 1958, before reversing course days later
evidence.maps_to_element: Context on Collins's own characterization and the inconsistency between his initial defense and the subsequent reversal

evidence.description: Less than 48 hours after the rule took effect, MilVet Law Firm, attorney Derek Debus and disabled Vietnam veteran Andrew Laffoon, among others, petitioned the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit to vacate the rule -- MilVet Law Firm PLLC v. Secretary of Veterans Affairs, No. 26-1469, a case separate from Ingram v. Collins
evidence.maps_to_element: Formal legal challenge to the rule

evidence.description: The VA formally rescinded the rule effective February 27, 2026, via publication in the Federal Register -- resolving what this entry previously described as an unconfirmed formal rescission
evidence.maps_to_element: Confirms formal rescission occurred, correcting this entry's prior 'did not confirm formal rescission' status

evidence.description: On March 5, 2026, the Federal Circuit dismissed MilVet Law Firm PLLC v. Secretary of Veterans Affairs (No. 26-1469), the petition for review of the rule under 38 U.S.C. § 502, under Fed. R. App. P. 42(b), 'The parties having so agreed,' with each side bearing its own costs; the order does not address the rule's validity
evidence.maps_to_element: Formal legal challenge to the rule -- ended by agreed dismissal, without a ruling on the rule's procedural validity

evidence.description: On March 30, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit dismissed Ingram v. Collins -- the related litigation over whether VA may use medication's ameliorative effects to lower a veteran's disability rating -- after DOJ and VA abandoned their appeal, leaving in place the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims' March 2025 ruling that VA must discount medication's beneficial effects where the rating criteria do not mention medication
evidence.maps_to_element: Resolves this entry's prior 'resolution not confirmed' status on the litigation -- the case concluded with VA abandoning its appeal, a substantive outcome favoring the veteran

evidence.maps_to_element: Re-verification confirming continued resolution, no change

status: Concluded -- VA formally rescinded the rule effective February 27, 2026, and on March 30, 2026 the Federal Circuit dismissed Ingram v. Collins after DOJ and VA abandoned their appeal, leaving the pro-veteran ruling intact; no court ruled on whether the February issuance violated the APA.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: the rule formalized a longstanding practice (since 1958) rather than creating new policy, which could qualify for an APA exception for rules that are 'interpretive' rather than substantive; the rapid responsiveness to public concern, withdrawing within 48 hours, demonstrates good-faith engagement rather than disregard for proper process.
comeback: A rule with a documented $100 million/year economic impact, affecting some 350,000 pending claims, is hard to characterize as merely 'interpretive' rather than substantive under APA case law -- scale matters to that distinction, and both of those figures are Collins's own agency's numbers, not critics' estimates. As for the 48-hour withdrawal: if the rule genuinely formalized longstanding practice as Collins initially claimed, it wouldn't have generated immediate, near-universal opposition from the entire veterans advocacy spectrum. Quick withdrawal after massive backlash is better evidence the agency knew the rule was vulnerable than evidence it acted in good faith. Good-faith rulemakers use the comment period precisely to catch these problems before, not after, a rule goes out.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] VA's own Federal Register notice said the rule was 'needed immediately to minimize the negative impact of an erroneous line of cases culminating in the recent decision of Ingram v. Collins' -- the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims ruling requiring VA to discount beneficial medication effects under rating criteria that do not address medication -- and rested its case for skipping notice and comment on that ruling. The rushed, notice-bypassing rollout was a deliberate response to unfavorable litigation rather than routine policy formalization. That shifts the characterization from 'procedural oversight' to 'deliberate end-run around litigation,' which is a materially more serious process failure.
confidence_note: MODERATE-HIGH confidence on the documented facts (the rule's issuance, scale, and rapid withdrawal) -- these are well-corroborated by multiple outlets and Collins's own public statements. LOWER confidence on the ultimate APA legal characterization, since VA withdrew the rule before any court ruled on the procedural question; the direct court challenge to the rule stayed open after the February 27 rescission until the parties agreed to dismiss it on March 5, 2026. The record shows a bypass of standard rulemaking procedure for a substantial regulatory change, reversed only after significant public backlash and litigation -- a real and concerning process failure, even though it didn't result in a final adverse court ruling given the rule's quick withdrawal. official: Doug Collins, Secretary of Veterans Affairs
offense_category: Defiance of a Federal Court Order -- Re-Terminating a Union Contract 13 Days After a Judge Ordered Its Reinstatement, on the Eve of an Enforcement Hearing -- a district court's contempt inquiry, held in abeyance and not a finding; VA disputes the characterization
incident_summary:
Government Executive reported that the administration, following Office of Personnel Management guidance, had assured federal judges that agencies would hold off on formally terminating union contracts until litigation over the underlying executive order concluded; in August 2025, the VA canceled its collective bargaining agreement covering roughly 320,000 employees (the figure Reuters and Federal News Network report; Government Executive has put it at more than 300,000, and the figure of more than 400,000 in some August 2025 reporting covers all five unions whose VA contracts were terminated that day) anyway, implementing Trump's executive order stripping collective bargaining rights from large parts of the federal workforce on stated national-security grounds -- drawing immediate accusations from labor leaders (AFGE President Everett Kelley among them) that the move was retaliatory, the same retaliation theory the contempt dispute below revisits in a more acute form. The employees' union sued, and on March 13, 2026, U.S. District Judge Melissa DuBose of the District of Rhode Island (a Biden appointee) issued a preliminary injunction ordering the VA to reinstate the bargaining agreement, finding the union likely to succeed on its claim that VA had canceled it in retaliation for the union's opposition to administration policies, and that VA had provided no evidence supporting its claimed national-security rationale. VA formally reinstated the agreement but, the union told the court, did not honor its terms, and the union moved on March 20 to enforce the injunction. On the night of March 26, 2026, the eve of the hearing on that motion, VA filed an after-hours status report announcing it had re-terminated the same contract, and argued at the hearing that the enforcement motion was now moot. At that March 27 hearing, DuBose said the position was "a blatant disrespect for not just this court's order but for the rule of law," granted the enforcement motion, gave the administration until Tuesday, March 31, to explain why VA should not be held in contempt, and scheduled a contempt hearing for April 3, 2026.

VA appealed the injunction and the March 27 enforcement order to the First Circuit that same day and on March 29 asked DuBose to stay both; on March 30, DuBose held the contempt proceeding in abeyance pending the appeal, and on April 6 she denied VA's stay request. In early April, VA's Central Office instructed facilities to return AFGE-represented employees to the contractual status quo, and no contempt ruling has been issued. On May 16, 2026, a unanimous First Circuit panel (opinion by Chief Judge David Barron) refused to stay the injunction, leaving the reinstatement in place, but stayed the enforcement order's directives that VA comply with the agreement "in both form and substance" and keep processing pending grievances and arbitrations, finding VA likely to succeed in challenging that part.

The dispute did not end there: Government Executive later reported this was VA's third attempt to scrap the same union contract. After VA itself moved in May 2026 to open negotiations on a successor agreement, it told AFGE on July 24 that it would terminate the agreement for all bargaining-unit workers on its scheduled August 8 expiration date, claiming the union had not met within 30 days of VA's request; AFGE disputed this, citing the contract's rollover clause and a series of negotiation letters exchanged in June and July. On August 7, 2026, Judge DuBose again ruled for AFGE, calling VA's 30-day claim "not well-taken" and its plan "in direct contravention" of her orders, and enforced the injunction in an order amended August 11. VA appealed that enforcement order to the First Circuit and asked DuBose to stay both it and the March injunction; she denied that request on August 28, 2026. No First Circuit ruling on that second appeal has been identified, and no ruling on the merits has been issued; DuBose's March finding that the union was likely to succeed on its retaliation and APA claims rested in part on Secretary Collins having exempted some unions, but not AFGE, from the executive order. The contempt proceeding remains in abeyance.
elements_required: A federal judge issued a specific, dated order (March 13, 2026) requiring VA to reinstate the union bargaining agreement

VA's re-termination of the same contract came 13 days after that order and hours before a hearing on the union's motion to enforce it, announced via an after-hours court filing rather than through any new factual or legal basis addressing the court's findings
The judge's original ruling found VA had provided no evidence for its stated national-security justification, meaning the re-termination was not accompanied by newly cured evidentiary support
The judge treated the timing and manner of the re-termination as serious enough to initiate a formal contempt inquiry, not merely to note continued legal disagreement

evidence.description: Reuters's March 27, 2026 report (syndicated copy) that Judge DuBose said VA's re-termination, announced in an after-hours filing the night before, was openly defiant of her March 13 ruling; that her earlier ruling found VA had provided no evidence for its national-security justification; and that she gave the administration until Tuesday to explain why VA should not be held in contempt and set a hearing for April 3
evidence.maps_to_element: The court order, its evidentiary finding, and VA's re-termination on the eve of the enforcement hearing

evidence.description: The union's March 20, 2026 memorandum supporting its motion to enforce the preliminary injunction, arguing that while VA asserted the master agreement had been reinstated, it was not complying with its terms and continued to deny employees the benefits and protections due under it
evidence.maps_to_element: VA's continued resistance to the reinstatement order

AFGE disputed this, invoking the contract's rollover clause (triggered when VA itself opened negotiations for a successor agreement in May 2026) and documenting a series of negotiation letters exchanged June 5 through July 8, 2026 that contradict VA's non-engagement claim; AFGE's motion to enforce DuBose's prior injunctions was pending as of this reporting

evidence.description: Government Executive's May 21, 2026 reporting that a unanimous three-judge First Circuit panel (Biden, Obama and Trump appointees; opinion by Chief Judge David Barron) denied VA's request to pause Judge DuBose's March injunction reinstating the AFGE contract, but agreed with VA that the requirement that it 'comply' with the contract 'in both form and substance' should be put on hold, siding with VA's argument that the enforcement order created a mechanism 'utterly foreign' to labor-relations lawsuits.

evidence.description: Government Executive's August 6, 2025 reporting that VA terminated most of its union contracts in a move that appeared to violate OPM guidance, and the Justice Department's assurances to judges, that agencies would not formally terminate union contracts until litigation over the executive order concluded, and that AFGE President Everett Kelley called the move retaliation against AFGE members for speaking out.

status: All three of VA's attempts to end the AFGE contract (August 2025, March 2026, August 2026) have been blocked by court order; the First Circuit refused in May to stay reinstatement, VA's appeal of the August enforcement order is pending, and the merits and the contempt question remain unresolved.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: VA retains independent authority to make new, legally distinct determinations about national-security-based contract terminations even after an adverse ruling on a prior determination, and re-filing to assert a modified legal basis is a normal, if aggressive, litigation posture rather than defiance of the court itself.
comeback: The judge's own characterization -- 'blatant disrespect' -- of VA's claim that its after-hours re-termination, which offered no new evidentiary basis addressing the specific deficiency (lack of evidence for the national-security claim) her ruling identified, had mooted the case distinguishes this from an ordinary good-faith re-filing; a court treating conduct as warranting a formal contempt inquiry, rather than simply another round of ordinary litigation, is itself a significant judicial signal independent of the contempt hearing's eventual outcome.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with the broader pattern this tracker documents of agencies implementing Trump's federal-workforce collective-bargaining executive order aggressively even where courts have preliminarily found specific implementations likely unlawful (see also the Hegseth union-contracts entry and the Trump entry for the underlying EO litigation). Here the pattern took a sharper form: after each adverse order, VA sought a new route to end the same contract -- a re-termination filed the night before an enforcement hearing, then a claimed expiration -- rather than first asking the court or an appeals court for relief, the course the judge said, after the March re-termination, was open to it.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the March 13, 2026 order, VA's re-termination, and the judge's contempt inquiry are all independently corroborated across Reuters, the union's own court filings, and Government Executive, with the judge's 'blatant disrespect' characterization directly quoted. The later course of the case -- the contempt proceeding held in abeyance on March 30, 2026, VA's early-April restoration of the contract, the First Circuit's May 16, 2026 stay ruling, the third termination attempt and the August 7 enforcement order, and VA's second appeal and the August 28 stay denial -- rests on the court docket, the First Circuit's opinion, Government Executive, and Federal News Network. No contempt ruling and no merits ruling had been identified. The August 2025 detail that the administration had assured judges agencies would wait rests on Government Executive's contemporaneous reporting. The 320,000 figure covers the AFGE master agreement; the more than 400,000 figure in some August 2025 reporting (Newsweek, citing The New York Times) covers all five unions whose VA contracts were terminated.
