official: Donald Trump, President (said he directed the suit); Todd Blanche, Attorney General; Stanley Woodward Jr., Associate Attorney General (signed the complaint)
offense_category: Executive interference in a state-run federal election -- a Justice Department lawsuit, which the President said he ordered, asking a federal court to bar Alaska from certifying its U.S. Senate result if the President's favored incumbent loses narrowly, on a name-confusion theory, after Alaska's courts had already ordered the second candidate kept on the ballot (the state Supreme Court summarily affirmed); not alleged to be a crime, an accountability concern about using federal litigation authority on behalf of one candidate in a pending election
incident_summary:
On October 22, 2026, less than two weeks before the November 3 election, the Justice Department sued the State of Alaska, its Division of Elections director Carol Beecher and its election boards in federal court in Anchorage (United States v. State of Alaska, No. 3:26-cv-00376, D. Alaska, assigned to Judge Sharon L. Gleason). The complaint, signed by Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. and an Assistant U.S. Attorney, says a second candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, is on the ballot with 'the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan' and that 'some supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan.' It asks the court to bar certification of any result that 'may be impacted by voter confusion,' defined as one where Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan does not win but would have won had 'all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan,' **pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan**. It rests on the National Voter Registration Act's stated purpose of protecting 'the integrity of the electoral process.' The complaint itself notes that an Alaska trial court had already held the Division erred in removing Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, and that the Alaska Supreme Court summarily affirmed on June 29, 2026. The ballot lists the senator as 'Dan S. Sullivan,' a registered Republican and the incumbent, and the other candidate with no party label. On October 23, Trump told reporters, 'I'm the one that said do it' (CNN, NBC News). Blanche said that weekend that DOJ 'does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska's election' and did not coordinate with any campaign. The campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola (Alaskans for Mary) and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee moved to intervene on October 23 and, on October 25, sought leave to file a motion to dismiss and asked the court to expedite, saying they fear Trump and Blanche will use the suit to 'lay the groundwork for unlawful efforts to challenge a potential Peltola victory' (CNBC); Common Cause and the League of Women Voters of Alaska, which had also moved to intervene on October 23, joined the request to expedite on October 26.

Update 2026-10-28: On October 24, The New York Times reported that Trump had demanded legal action 'even as some department officials raised concerns about the merits and constitutionality of the case,' according to two people with knowledge of the situation, and that the suit came amid a wider push in which Blanche 'has abandoned departmental norms by promoting prosecutions and investigations of politicians, within 60 days of the election,' and that, according to former officials, Woodward's name on a filing at times 'indicates that subordinates were unwilling to do so themselves.' On October 26, Alaska's own election officials, who had tried to keep Daniel J. Sullivan off the ballot, moved to dismiss, saying the United States 'lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate.' Judge Gleason expedited both the intervention motions and the State's motion, with briefing due by October 30. On October 27 DOJ opposed intervention, calling Daniel J. Sullivan 'a sham candidate.' On October 28 the Times reported that people working with Peltola's campaign and senior DSCC aides took part in recruiting him, citing interviews, texts and documents and Peltola's former campaign manager, who was fired in August and later tried to retract her statements; Peltola's campaign and the DSCC deny involvement (CNBC, CNN). Trump then demanded that both Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan be removed from the ballot, and Blanche cited the report as proof DOJ was right to sue and said it has a civil investigation. The same day, DOJ withdrew its objection to the campaign's intervention, citing the Times report, and said it will seek expedited discovery from the campaign; Judge Gleason then let the campaign, the DSCC, Common Cause, the League of Women Voters of Alaska and two Alaska voters intervene.

Update 2026-10-30: On October 29, DOJ filed an amended complaint, signed by Woodward, that leans on the Times report ('Although what the New York Times reports is not always true, its reporting here aligns with what the United States has been alleging on information and belief'), adds a second claim under the Supremacy Clause, and again asks the court to bar certification of any result 'that may be impacted by voter confusion' pending an investigation. Rather than argue the merits of the three motions to dismiss by the court's deadlines that day, DOJ asked that they be denied as moot. Alaska's election officials called this 'gamesmanship,' moved to dismiss the amended complaint and asked for a decision by November 2; Peltola's campaign, the DSCC and the voter groups also moved to dismiss it, the campaign and the DSCC calling the new claim 'Count I in a costume.' The same day, people familiar with the matter told CNN and ABC News that federal prosecutors had issued a wave of grand jury subpoenas in a separate criminal investigation of the recruitment (more than 40 subpoenas and preservation notices, one official told CNN), and one federal official told CNN the civil suit is a 'preservation lawsuit' that 'will allow us to challenge the election if a challenge becomes necessary.' Trump, who on October 28 said Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan 'should be prosecuted' (CNN), was asked on October 29 whether Republicans should refuse to seat Peltola if she wins and said, 'You're going to have to see what happens' (NBC News). DOJ's filing also cited Gov. Mike Dunleavy's order that the Alaska Department of Public Safety investigate whether the recruitment broke state law; House Oversight Chair James Comer requested interviews with Peltola's former campaign manager and a Democratic operative. Peltola said she 'knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot.'

Update 2026-10-31: On October 30, Judge Gleason denied the three original motions to dismiss as moot in light of the amended complaint, granted Alaska's request to expedite the renewed motions, and ordered DOJ to respond by 1:00 p.m. that day, with replies due at noon on October 31. DOJ asked the court to deny the renewed motions, saying it 'is not asking for any change to how voters may vote, who may vote, where they vote, or who they may vote for.' The same day DOJ moved for expedited discovery and a preliminary injunction, filed proposed discovery requests and Rule 30(b)(6) deposition notices for Peltola's campaign and the DSCC, and asked for a decision by November 2. It seeks an order directing the State 'to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan' for a possible investigation into voter confusion, and discovery of the campaign's and the DSCC's 'internal and external conversations' about their efforts to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan. Alaska's election officials, joined by both intervenor groups, opposed expediting it, saying the Division already preserves federal election ballots for 22 months and that election workers cannot segregate ballots during voting without violating ballot secrecy.

status: Pending before Judge Sharon Gleason (D. Alaska). The first motions to dismiss were denied as moot after DOJ amended its complaint; replies on the renewed motions are due Oct. 31. On Oct. 30 DOJ sought discovery from Peltola's campaign and the DSCC and a ballot-segregation order. No ruling yet.
rebuttal_anticipated: DOJ would argue that the National Voter Registration Act charges it with protecting 'the integrity of the electoral process,' that Alaska's own Division of Elections first found Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy was filed 'to confuse or mislead,' and that the suit asks only for ballots and information to be preserved for Alaska officials, not to stop any vote or certification -- Blanche said DOJ 'does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska's election' and that the lawsuit 'was written by Justice Department attorneys' without coordination with any campaign or candidate. After The New York Times reported on October 28 that people working with Peltola's campaign and DSCC aides helped recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, Blanche cited the report as proof DOJ was right to sue and said the department has a civil investigation. In its October 29 amended complaint, DOJ argues that the Times reporting 'aligns with what the United States has been alleging on information and belief' and that certifying a result 'that may be impacted by the scheme' would frustrate Congress's objectives, making it preempted under the Supremacy Clause. In its October 30 filings, DOJ says it 'is not asking for any change to how voters may vote, who may vote, where they vote, or who they may vote for,' only that ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan be preserved and segregated pending a possible investigation, and that it needs fast discovery from Peltola's campaign and the DSCC because early voting is under way.
comeback: The complaint's own prayer for relief asks the court to bar certification of any result that 'may be impacted by voter confusion' pending an investigation, which is a request to stop certification in exactly one outcome: a narrow loss by the candidate the President backs. Trump said 'I'm the one that said do it.' Alaska's courts, including its Supreme Court, had already decided under state law that Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan,' **pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan**. Sullivan from the ballot, and that the Alaska Supreme Court summarily affirmed on June 29, 2026. The ballot lists the senator as 'Dan S. offense_category: DOJ Moving to Erase a Political Ally's Criminal Conviction for Defying Congressional Oversight -- a discretionary prosecutorial decision benefiting a Trump ally, analogous in kind to this tracker's pardon-power entry on the Kidan donor pardon though pursued through a motion to dismiss rather than clemency
incident_summary:
A jury had convicted Bannon on two counts in July 2022 of criminal contempt of Congress for defying a lawful subpoena from the House January 6 committee; he served prison time and paid a $6,500 fine. Bannon, a former senior Trump adviser and ally, had been one of the most prominent defendants prosecuted for defying the House's Jan. 6 investigation. On February 9, 2026, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro filed an unopposed motion in D.C. federal district court to dismiss Bannon's indictment, stating only that the government "has determined in its prosecutorial discretion that dismissal of this criminal case is in the interests of justice." The same day, Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the Supreme Court, where Bannon's petition challenging the D.C. Circuit's affirmance of his conviction was pending, to vacate that ruling and send the case back so the district court could grant the motion; his filing described the Jan. 6 committee as "a putative congressional committee." On April 6, 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the D.C. Circuit's ruling and remanded the case to that court "for further consideration in light of the pending motion to dismiss" -- clearing a path toward dismissal without itself dismissing the conviction. On July 16, 2026, the D.C. Circuit directed the parties to file motions to govern further proceedings; Bannon and the government jointly asked it to send the case back so the district court could address the pending, unopposed motion and terminate the prosecution, and on August 12, 2026 the D.C. Circuit remanded the case with instructions to address the motion to dismiss the indictment with prejudice under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 48(a).

U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols denied DOJ's motion to dismiss on August 26, 2026, finding that the motion did not explain DOJ's motivations for seeking dismissal and that its single sentence of explanation was the kind of "conclusory statement by the prosecutor" that D.C. Circuit precedent holds insufficient under Rule 48(a), which requires a statement of reasons. The denial was without prejudice -- DOJ is free to submit a renewed motion that complies with Rule 48(a) -- but Nichols directed any renewed motion to address whether the D.C. Circuit's 2025 decision in United States v. Thorpe, which held that the government may dismiss a prosecution only while it is pending, bars dismissal here, noting that his own judgment of conviction has not been vacated. As of late September 2026, no renewed motion appears on the court docket, and the district court's judgment of conviction remains in place.

The conviction was for defying a lawful congressional subpoena -- itself a mechanism for enforcing legislative oversight -- which dismissal would effectively nullify as a deterrent
The beneficiary, Steve Bannon, is a prominent ally of President Trump, distinguishing this from a case-specific legal-merits reassessment unconnected to political relationships

offense_category: Reviving Historically Racist Legal Arguments in Official U.S. Government Supreme Court Briefing -- a legal-strategy and characterization dispute; not a criminal charge
incident_summary:
The Washington Post reported that Trump administration lawyers, defending the administration's effort to end birthright citizenship for children of undocumented immigrants and temporary visa holders, cited historical legal arguments originally made by Alexander Porter Morse -- a Confederate officer and Louisiana attorney who argued for legalized segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) and who was, over a century ago, part of a trio of legal advocates who spearheaded a failed, explicitly anti-Black and anti-Chinese effort to narrow the 14th Amendment's citizenship guarantee. The government's January 20, 2026 merits brief in Trump v. Barbara, like its September 26, 2025 petition for certiorari, quoted Morse's 1881 Treatise on Citizenship for the proposition that the Citizenship Clause "exclude[s] the children of foreigners transiently within the United States." A friend-of-the-court brief from the Chinese American Legal Defense Alliance called the arguments "built on a racist foundation," and a historian and a law professor quoted by the Post said the government's arguments echoed that first push to end birthright citizenship, while another law professor, Ilan Wurman, called the racism charge "a classic logical fallacy." The Post reported that if the Supreme Court adopted the administration's interpretation and reversed the long-settled reading of the Citizenship Clause, it could render hundreds of thousands of children born to immigrant parents stateless.

The Supreme Court decided Trump v. Barbara on June 30, 2026, with Chief Justice Roberts' majority opinion rejecting the administration's historical argument for narrowing 14th Amendment birthright citizenship as resting on "scant evidence," and holding (in practical effect 6-3, counting Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence in the judgment) that children born in the U.S. to undocumented or temporarily-present parents remain citizens at birth. The majority opinion itself traced the parental-domicile theory to commentators of the 1880s, citing Francis Wharton and Morse's 1881 Treatise on Citizenship, and noted that Wong Kim Ark (1898) had rejected that view; Justice Thomas's principal dissent relied on the same Morse passage. The interpretation DOJ was defending did not prevail, and the feared mass-statelessness outcome did not occur.

On August 6, 2026, Trump signed a new Executive Order 14418, "Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship," again restricting birthright citizenship. Where neither parent is a citizen, it bars agencies from recognizing the citizenship of children whose parent is an "alien enemy" (defined to include members of designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations and Specially Designated Global Terrorists); whose parent is a foreign-government employee (including ambassadors, foreign embassy or consulate staff who are nationals of that country, and immunity-holding international-organization staff); or whose parent engaged in a commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship (including paid travel to give birth here or a paid surrogate) or in fraud to obtain citizenship; and of children born in U.S. territories where federal statute does not confer citizenship. The order says these categories fall outside the rule of birthright citizenship the Court announced in Trump v. Barbara, and directs agency heads to issue implementing guidance within 30 days, by September 5, 2026. It is a new executive action, distinct from the 2025 order (EO 14160) DOJ defended in Trump v. Barbara, but continues the same policy dispute after the Court ruled against the administration. On August 11, 2026, the ACLU-led Barbara plaintiffs asked the New Hampshire federal court to clarify or modify its existing injunction, arguing the new order tried to strip citizenship from members of the certified class. In the parallel Maryland class action, CASA v. Trump, Judge Deborah Boardman on September 2, 2026 preliminarily enjoined enforcement of EO 14418 against the certified class, which her order describes as identical to the Barbara class, finding the plaintiffs likely to succeed because the Supreme Court had held those children citizens at birth; she left the territory provision and the issuance of agency guidance unenjoined. DOJ moved on September 8 to dissolve that injunction or stay it pending appeal. In New Hampshire, after Judge Joseph Laplante indicated at a September 22 status conference that the supplemental complaint effectively represented a new case, the Barbara plaintiffs withdrew their pending motions on September 23, saying the new plaintiffs would refile elsewhere.

incident_summary: On April 7, 2025, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche issued an internal memorandum instructing federal prosecutors to stop pursuing 'litigation or enforcement actions that have the effect of superimposing regulatory frameworks on digital assets.' **The memo disbanded the DOJ's National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team (NCET), created in 2021 to address criminal misuse of cryptocurrency, and directed the Fraud Section's Market Integrity and Major Frauds Unit to stop pursuing cryptocurrency-related enforcement matters.** Under the new policy, DOJ said it would still prioritize cases where digital assets were used to defraud investors or to further other crimes: terrorism, narcotics and human trafficking, organized crime, hacking, and cartel and gang financing. It would no longer pursue enforcement actions premised on treating unregistered exchanges or unlicensed money transmission as crimes in themselves, the theory behind many earlier crypto-industry prosecutions. On April 10, 2025, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Mazie Hirono, Dick Durbin and colleagues sent DOJ leadership a formal letter urging reversal of the policy, warning it greenlit cryptocurrency-based crime. The disbandment followed, and was reported alongside, a wave of Trump pardons for crypto executives convicted under the enforcement regime being wound down, including Ross Ulbricht (Silk Road) and the BitMEX founders, and later Binance's Changpeng 'CZ' Zhao (see the Trump Family tracker's entry on that pardon pattern). It also came as the Trump family's own crypto ventures, the $TRUMP/$MELANIA meme coins and World Liberty Financial, were generating substantial personal wealth. The policy remains in effect and has not been reversed.

official: Donald Trump, President; Chad Mizelle, Chief of Staff to the Attorney General
offense_category: Executive nullification of a federal civil-rights protection statute (the FACE Act, 18 U.S.C. §248) via pardon and enforcement-policy directive, effectively decriminalizing most future clinic-blockade/harassment conduct the statute was written to punish
incident_summary: On January 23, 2025, Trump granted full pardons to 23 people convicted under the FACE Act (Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act) for blockading, invading, or harassing patients at reproductive-health clinics. Among them: Lauren Handy, sentenced to nearly five years for directing a clinic blockade in which protesters chained themselves to clinic doors -- Handy separately made national news in 2022 after D.C. police found five fetuses in her apartment during the same investigation. The next day, January 24, 2025, Chad Mizelle -- chief of staff to the Attorney General's office, more than a week before Pam Bondi was confirmed as Attorney General on February 4, 2025 -- issued a DOJ memorandum directing that future abortion-related FACE Act prosecutions and civil actions 'will be permitted only in extraordinary circumstances' or cases with 'significant aggravating factors, such as death, serious bodily harm, or serious property damage,' and that no new abortion-related FACE Act action of any kind could proceed without sign-off from the Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division. In practice, this pairs a mass clemency for past violations with a policy directive sharply curtailing prosecution of future ones -- addressing both ends of enforcement in the same 24-hour window. **Since the pardons, at least two of the pardoned individuals have been separately charged with trespassing at a Pennsylvania abortion clinic, and at least three have been rearrested multiple times for clinic blockades**, according to reporting reviewed by the Center for Reproductive Rights.

The enforcement curtailment has correlated with documented recidivism among specific pardoned individuals

The administration's own subsequent framing (an April 2026 DOJ 'weaponization' report characterizing Biden-era FACE Act prosecutions of anti-abortion activists as themselves biased) supplies its stated rationale for the rollback

official: Theodore Hertzberg, U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Georgia (Trump-appointed)
offense_category: Federal Grand Jury Investigation Opened Into the State Prosecutor Who Indicted Trump -- clemency and prosecutorial discretion are lawful, but the accountability claim concerns using federal law-enforcement power to investigate the specific state official whose 2023 indictment targeted the President
incident_summary: In late September 2025, the New York Times reported that **federal prosecutors had subpoenaed travel records belonging to Fani Willis, the Fulton County, Georgia District Attorney who brought a 41-count racketeering indictment against Trump and 18 co-defendants over alleged 2020 election interference.** The subpoena, issued via a federal grand jury, sought records concerning Willis's travel in the fall of 2024, around the time of the presidential election, and was led by Theodore Hertzberg, the Trump-appointed U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Georgia. It was not publicly disclosed whether Willis herself was a formal target of the investigation, and her spokesperson said the office had 'no knowledge of any investigation.' The subpoena followed years of separate, parallel congressional scrutiny of Willis -- House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan had subpoenaed her for records related to her office's use of DOJ grant funds beginning in 2024, and Senators Chuck Grassley and Ron Johnson opened a related Senate inquiry -- but the September 2025 grand jury subpoena marked the first known instance of the Trump administration's own DOJ directly investigating Willis using federal compulsory process, rather than Congress. As of the most recent reporting reviewed, no charges had been filed against Willis and the investigation's scope and findings remained undisclosed, consistent with grand jury secrecy requirements.

offense_category: Federal Law Enforcement Resources Redirected to Re-litigate a Settled, Court-Confirmed 2020 Election Result -- expands a documented pattern with the earlier Fulton County, Georgia ballot seizure (and the later Fulton County poll-worker subpoena)
incident_summary:
A federal grand jury subpoena, confirmed by Arizona Senate President Warren Petersen, sought records related to the Arizona Senate's 2020 partisan "audit" of Maricopa County's presidential election results -- an audit conducted by Cyber Ninjas and its subcontractor Cyfir that was widely discredited by election experts and produced results confirming Joe Biden's victory despite the audit's methodology. The subpoena follows and expands a broader federal pattern of using DOJ and FBI resources to re-examine 2020 election administration more than five years after the election, after multiple independent audits, recounts, and court rulings in Arizona and nationally confirmed Biden's victory and found no evidence of the fraud the audit was commissioned to find; it follows the January 2026 FBI seizure of Fulton County, Georgia's 2020 ballots and precedes the April 2026 Fulton County poll-worker-data subpoena, both documented in this tracker's separate Fulton County entry, indicating a multi-state pattern rather than an isolated action.

Reporting based on emails obtained by American Oversight shows that Maricopa County Recorder Justin Heap -- an elected Republican official -- wrote to the county manager after, by his account, learning in mid-August 2025 that county elections and IT staff planned to delete certain 2020 and 2022 election records, had a meeting arranged with U.S. Attorney Timothy Courchaine for Aug. 27, 2025, and in September 2025 wrote to DOJ Civil Rights Division head Harmeet Dhillon that his office was "committed to full cooperation with the Department of Justice as it conducts its investigation" -- months before the March 2026 subpoena became public.

On the morning of March 7, 2026, an FBI agent took more than three dozen hard drives and servers containing audit-related data and Cyfir subcontractor material from the Arizona Senate building, according to a property receipt obtained by ProPublica; a copy of the subpoena later obtained by Votebeat confirmed that a federal grand jury was conducting a criminal investigation. Petersen said he complied with the subpoena "late last week." The Maricopa County Board of Supervisors and Recorder's Office, who jointly administer the county's actual election operations, said they had not received subpoenas as of this reporting, though the Board said it would cooperate if one arrived. ProPublica reported election-security experts warned the seized audit records could be "fatally flawed" as evidentiary material given the audit's own documented chain-of-custody and methodological problems.

On the morning of March 9, before Petersen's announcement, President Trump shared a Just the News article claiming the FBI had used a grand jury subpoena to obtain 2020 election data from Maricopa County itself (not just the Senate); the county's Elections Department said no records had been seized by the FBI, and Petersen, sharing a screenshot of Trump's post, said the subpoena was to the Senate for its audit records. In April 2026, Votebeat reported that Courchaine's office issued the Senate subpoena and is overseeing a grand jury impaneled in Phoenix.

A copy of the subpoena released under Arizona's public records law showed it sought virtually all of the audit's records, including Cyber Ninjas' forensic reports, clones of the county's election equipment software and data, and the Senate's communications with county election officials; KJZZ reported that, according to an FBI property receipt, Petersen turned over servers, USB drives and other devices holding more than 200 terabytes of data, and that a letter from Courchaine let him hand over the documents instead of testifying before the grand jury. Attorney General Kris Mayes said what the administration appeared to be pursuing was "not a legitimate law enforcement inquiry" but "the weaponization of federal law enforcement in service of crackpots and lies"; she and Secretary of State Adrian Fontes urged county recorders not to give confidential voter data to federal investigators even under a grand jury subpoena, and Mayes's office asked Petersen what exactly he gave the FBI. Petersen did not answer that letter and instead referred Mayes and Fontes to Courchaine for "obstruction of justice and tampering with a witness"; Courchaine replied that his office was "carefully reviewing the facts," and Mayes called Courchaine's letter "all nonsense."

In September 2026, CNN reported that Kurt Olsen, who as the White House's presidentially appointed Director of Election Security and Integrity made the referral behind the FBI's Fulton County ballot seizure, also "played a role" in the Justice Department's move to subpoena the Maricopa 2020 election records, and CBS News, citing a single source with direct knowledge, reported that Olsen had made several other 2020 election-related referrals to the Justice Department, including one in Arizona. In October 2026, Reuters reported, citing three people familiar with his work, that Olsen "oversaw the Justice Department's acquisition of Maricopa records through a subpoena to the Arizona Senate," records that included voter rolls, 2.1 million ballot images and signature-verification data; it reported that Olsen's wider search found no evidence of foreign manipulation of the 2020 election. The Justice Department has not publicly described Olsen's role.

official: Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General / Kash Patel, FBI Director
offense_category: Non-Compliance With a Statutory Deadline for Epstein-File Disclosure, Alongside FBI Compilation of Unverified Allegations Against Other Prominent Figures -- raises accountability concerns distinct from any single named individual's conduct within the files themselves
incident_summary:
The Epstein Files Transparency Act required DOJ to produce its Epstein/Maxwell-related files by December 19, 2025; DOJ said the process was delayed by the volume of material and the need to redact survivors' personal information. Following the broadly-criticized rollout of a partial release ("The Epstein Files: Part 1") on February 27, 2025, Attorney General Bondi directed the FBI to deliver the complete files within 24 hours and ordered FBI Director Kash Patel to produce a comprehensive report within 14 days; as of the reporting reviewed, 74 days had passed since that directive without the report's release.

On July 9, 2025, FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino -- himself a former prominent Epstein-conspiracy podcaster before joining the administration -- had a heated clash with Bondi at the White House after Bondi publicly stated evidence confirmed Epstein died by suicide and that DOJ found no incriminating "client list," triggering backlash from both Democrats and Bongino's own MAGA-aligned base who felt they had been overpromised disclosures. Bongino told colleagues he was considering resigning and did not report to work the following Friday; Bondi separately accused him of leaking stories that blamed her for the public backlash. The Daily Beast reported Bongino left a subsequent West Wing meeting abruptly amid the tension. Reporting on Vice President JD Vance's role was less specific than other aspects of the episode -- Vance, along with Bongino and Patel, had each separately hinted at forthcoming disclosures that never materialized, but no sourcing reviewed confirmed Vance directly mediated between Bongino and Bondi. Bongino ultimately remained in his post through this episode.

On July 18, 2025, Sen. Dick Durbin, ranking member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said his office had received a protected FBI whistleblower disclosure alleging Bondi had roughly 1,000 FBI personnel placed on 24-hour shifts starting in March 2025 to comb through approximately 100,000 Epstein-related documents and flag any mention of Trump. Independent journalist Allison Gill separately reported anonymous FBI sources corroborating the account, saying they were directed to log Trump mentions in an Excel spreadsheet. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said on July 21, 2025 that she was not aware of any effort to flag Trump's name and directed inquiries to the FBI. Durbin sent formal letters to DOJ leadership demanding an explanation, characterizing the deployment as a potential effort to identify and manage information about Trump within the files rather than the neutral, comprehensive review the department had publicly described; no source reviewed confirmed DOJ's or FBI's on-the-record response to the specific whistleblower allegation itself, distinct from the general denial reported through Leavitt.

In the run-up to the Transparency Act's December 19, 2025 deadline, Trump directed Bondi to open a new DOJ investigation into several of his political opponents' own links to Epstein; Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) publicly warned on November 15-18, 2025 that the new probe could function as a "smokescreen" and "last-ditch effort to prevent the release of the Epstein files," explaining the underlying mechanism: "If they have ongoing investigations in certain areas, those documents can't be released." Former U.S. Attorney Barbara McQuade confirmed the legal basis for that concern, telling reporters that with a pending investigation, DOJ "can assert executive privilege and try to prevent any more documents from being released."

As pressure mounted for full disclosure, CNN reported that FBI employees assembled a 21-slide internal presentation compiling what one employee described as "salacious statements" about 13 prominent men in Epstein's orbit -- including Donald Trump, Bill Clinton, Prince Andrew (Mountbatten-Windsor), Leon Black, and Harvey Weinstein -- drawn from unverified allegations in the investigative files. DOJ ultimately released more than 3 million pages of documents and photos, including the 21-slide presentation itself, as part of the broader disclosure; DOJ subsequently removed a photo showing Commerce Secretary Lutnick with Epstein from its own Epstein files website after the photo had already been part of the public release.

On March 17, 2026, a bipartisan House oversight committee subpoenaed Attorney General Bondi to testify about DOJ's handling of the Epstein files. Lawmakers from both parties alleged DOJ improperly redacted key information, failed to fully comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act's disclosure requirements, and exposed sensitive details about survivors in the process. On April 2, 2026, Trump removed Bondi as Attorney General after a 14-month tenure, with sources citing her Epstein-files handling as one of several frustrations; Todd Blanche became acting Attorney General. Days before Bondi's scheduled April 14, 2026 deposition, DOJ told the committee the subpoena "no longer obligates" her testimony now that she is out of office -- a position bipartisan committee members rejected, with Democrats moving toward a contempt-of-Congress resolution.

Rather than face a contempt vote, Bondi agreed to a transcribed interview -- not a sworn, videotaped deposition, and one that let her decline individual questions -- held May 29, 2026. She defended DOJ's handling, calling the release process "an enormously complicated and labor-intensive process" and saying "justice and transparency in this matter have been delivered at the direction of President Trump," while acknowledging redaction errors occurred. Committee Chair James Comer said she could face prosecution if she lied to Congress and that a transcript would be released publicly. The House Oversight Committee released the full 111-page transcript on June 4, 2026. It shows AAG Harmeet Dhillon repeatedly invoking executive privilege to block questions about Bondi's own White House conversations, Bondi declining to say whether Trump directed DOJ's handling of the files or what he knew before the files' release, and Bondi attributing the release and redaction decisions to Todd Blanche by name more than 30 times. No outcome of the underlying files-compliance dispute, and no further public developments beyond the transcript's release itself, have been identified.

As of September 10, 2026, four European law-enforcement bodies (Poland, Norway, Latvia, Britain) say DOJ has not responded to their own formal evidence requests tied to their domestic Epstein-linked investigations -- a related but legally distinct compliance gap from the domestic statutory-deadline dispute this entry otherwise documents, since these are foreign mutual-legal-assistance requests rather than the Transparency Act's own release mechanism. DOJ says it has "not refused to assist any jurisdiction."

official: Kristi Noem, Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: DOJ Criminal Subpoenas and FEMA Data and Affidavit Demands Targeting Migrant Shelters and Their Funders, Alongside DHS Immigration Conditions on State Grants That a Federal Court Struck Down as Unlawful Coercion
incident_summary: In March 2025, federal prosecutors served criminal subpoenas on at least three New York City shelter buildings -- the Roosevelt Hotel and the Stewart Hotel, both used as migrant shelters, and the former Hotel Chandler, a homeless shelter that the AP reported does not primarily house migrants -- demanding the names, birth dates, and nationalities of residents, as well as the identities of the entities and individuals funding the shelter programs. In parallel, FEMA required recipients of its Shelter and Services Program grants nationwide to submit, within 30 days, lists of names and contact information for every migrant they had assisted, and **told each recipient organization's executive officers to personally sign sworn affidavits attesting they had no knowledge or suspicion that anyone in their organization had violated federal human-smuggling law -- with funding withheld during the review -- effectively conditioning continued shelter funding on self-incriminating attestations and mass data handover with no individualized suspicion**. In a separate case, a coalition of 20 states led by Illinois, later joined by the District of Columbia, sued DHS, FEMA, and Secretary Kristi Noem in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island (State of Illinois et al. v. FEMA), arguing the administration was withholding congressionally appropriated emergency-preparedness funds unless states diverted resources to federal civil immigration enforcement. On September 24, 2025, Senior U.S. District Judge William E. Smith granted the states summary judgment and permanently enjoined DHS and FEMA from enforcing the immigration-related conditions across 40 separate federal grant programs, finding the conditions unlawful. That ruling covered immigration-cooperation conditions DHS had added to its standard grant terms in March and April 2025; the states' case did not involve the New York subpoenas or FEMA's Shelter and Services Program letter, and no court ruling on the subpoenas was identified.

offense_category: Halting a Criminal Investigation Into Alleged Improper Payments Connected to a Presidential Clemency Grant -- no charges have been filed against anyone involved, and the investigation itself was shut down before reaching a conclusion
incident_summary:
Federal prosecutors in Brooklyn opened a criminal inquiry into how David Gentile -- founder of GPB Capital, convicted in 2024 of defrauding more than 10,000 investors in a roughly $1.6 billion fraud scheme -- received a presidential commutation of his seven-year sentence less than two weeks after reporting to prison. The same November 26, 2025 clemency grant also eliminated Gentile's court-ordered $15.5 million restitution obligation to the more than 10,000 defrauded investors, as Politico reported December 3, 2025; the sentencing court had received thousands of victim-impact statements, many from elderly retirees who described losing their entire life savings. Investigators reportedly gathered information about jailhouse communications in which Gentile discussed paying $2.5 million or more to people or companies to help secure clemency, and the inquiry examined whether the commutation involved improper payments or communications that could support federal charges. Reporting ties Frank Mann, a retired Catholic priest from Queens, to alleged payments linked to the commutation effort; Mann denied any involvement in an email to the New York Times, though people with knowledge of the prison communications said he corresponded with Gentile about lobbying the president on his behalf. The inquiry was halted before it reached a conclusion: by May 2026, Associate Deputy Attorney General Aakash Singh expressed concern about the investigation in a phone call with Joseph Nocella Jr., the U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of New York, and shortly afterward the career prosecutors were told to abandon their efforts, the New York Times reported June 21, 2026, citing two people with an understanding of the sequence of events.

At Blanche's July 15, 2026 confirmation hearing, Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked whether he had any involvement in the commutation or in stopping the investigation. Blanche said the president had not discussed the commutation with him, called the reporting the product of leaks containing "falsehoods," and declined to say whether an investigation had existed. The same day, Blumenthal and Sen. Ruben Gallego wrote to the Justice Department's acting Inspector General asking for an investigation into the closure, citing the reported Singh call to Nocella. DOJ has not confirmed or denied the reported Singh call. Singh was promoted to Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General by Attorney General Todd Blanche in late August 2026, giving him a broader portfolio overseeing operations at DOJ field offices and the litigating divisions at headquarters -- reported by Bloomberg Law (September 3, 2026) and relayed by Talking Points Memo the next day; Bloomberg noted that past officials in this role have wielded significant law-enforcement power behind the scenes. The promotion does not resolve the unanswered congressional referral to the DOJ Inspector General regarding Singh's reported role in halting the Gentile investigation.

official: Pam Bondi, Attorney General
offense_category: Unlawful Removal of a Career Federal Prosecutor in Violation of the Civil Service Reform Act, the Separation of Powers and Due Process -- as found by a federal district court (the department says it will appeal); the claim that she was fired for being James Comey's daughter or for her perceived politics is an allegation the court has not decided
incident_summary:
**On July 16, 2025, the Justice Department fired Maurene Comey, a career Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Southern District of New York, by a one-page memorandum that cited only "Article II of the United States Constitution and the laws of the United States" and gave no reason.** Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, had served in the office since November 2015 and worked on the prosecutions of Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell, Sean "Diddy" Combs and former Sen. Robert Menendez; the department has admitted she was rated "outstanding" in every annual review from 2019 through 2024. She received no notice and no chance to respond. When she asked why, then-Interim U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton told her, "All I can say is it came from Washington," and the White House press secretary said the decision was "made by the Department of Justice."

Comey filed a protective appeal with the Merit Systems Protection Board on August 14, 2025, then sued in federal court in Manhattan on September 15, 2025 (Comey v. U.S. Department of Justice, S.D.N.Y. 1:25-cv-07625, before Judge Jesse M. Furman). Her complaint alleges she was fired "solely or substantially" because she is James Comey's daughter, or because of her perceived political beliefs, or both, and points to social media posts in which social media influencer Laura Loomer had demanded her firing and, the day it happened, claimed credit. On April 28, 2026, Furman denied the government's motion to send the case to the Merit Systems Protection Board, holding that because she was fired under Article II rather than under the civil service law, her case fell outside that board's scheme. In its May 26, 2026 answer, the department said for the first time that then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had "authorized and directed" the removal, and it attached a memorandum from Todd Blanche, then Acting Attorney General, ratifying it.

On October 26, 2026, Furman ruled that the firing was unlawful. He held that it violated the Civil Service Reform Act, which lets a prosecutor be removed only for cause and after notice and a chance to respond, and that the department's claim that Article II bars Congress from limiting such removals "flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent." He found that the department had conceded the firing "was not 'for cause' and was not based on her performance," that Blanche's ratification had no effect, and that the firing also violated the Administrative Procedure Act and her Fifth Amendment due process rights. He granted her retroactive reinstatement and back pay through December 20, 2025, when she took another job. He did not rule on her First Amendment claim, instead ordering her to explain by November 9, 2026 why it should not be dismissed now that she has won on other grounds. A department spokesperson said it "disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course."

official: Todd Blanche, Attorney General (announced the complaint); R. Trent McCotter, Acting Deputy Attorney General; Stanley Woodward Jr., Associate Attorney General (McCotter and Woodward signed the complaint)
offense_category: Use of the judicial-misconduct process against judges who ruled against the administration -- filing a misconduct complaint is lawful and is not itself alleged as illegal; the accountability concern is pressure on judicial independence and the separation of powers, by seeking to remove judges who documented ICE's noncompliance with court orders from all cases involving DHS
incident_summary:
During Operation Metro Surge, the immigration enforcement surge in the Twin Cities last winter, Minnesota's federal judges fielded a flood of habeas corpus petitions from detained immigrants, and then-Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz found that ICE had repeatedly violated court orders (tracked separately in this database). On September 17, 2026, the New York Times published an article titled "Trump's Minnesota Surge Threatened Democracy, Judge Warns," built on a 90-minute interview with Schiltz, who told the paper that what happened in the court last winter "created a grave threat to the rule of law." According to the Justice Department, six other members of the Minnesota bench also spoke to the Times. Judge John Tunheim was quoted as saying, "They weren't arresting, in my view, people who were dangerous criminals on the street." The Times wrote that Schiltz did not comment on specific cases.

On Wednesday, September 30, 2026, the Justice Department filed a judicial misconduct complaint with Chief Judge Steven Colloton of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals against Schiltz, Tunheim and "Anonymous District Judges." The complaint was signed by Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr., and Attorney General Todd Blanche announced it at a press conference, saying "seven federal judges" had spoken to the Times "in a manner that the Department of Justice views as a clear violation of their ethical duties." It asks that **the judges recuse themselves from any matters involving the Department of Homeland Security** and that the 8th Circuit open an investigation. Blanche cited the "obvious bias they have shown." Woodward accused the judges of "launching a partisan press campaign" that was "allowing criminal illegal aliens to run free in Minnesota," and McCotter said they had used their office "to pander to the press about immigration policies." The complaint, as reported by Courthouse News, says "If anything is a 'grave threat to the rule of law,' it is judges who repeatedly and brazenly exceed their authority," and blames the flood of habeas petitions and "several instances of unintentional noncompliance with court orders" on the district judges' "own legal errors." Asked about his own talk of a "war" with the judiciary, Blanche said, "I'm allowed to get really fired up when, for example, judges in Minnesota complain about us violating court orders, but the reason that we are, quote, violating court orders is because these judges are violating Supreme Court law."

The Minnesota court's spokesperson said legal-ethics experts had confirmed the judges were acting "well within the ethical rules," citing a February 2026 advisory opinion of the judiciary's Committee on Codes of Conduct that judges may speak on "core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence." Schiltz said, "That is exactly what I did." Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison called the complaint "a desperate and dangerous attack on American judicial independence." Bloomberg Law reported that DOJ had earlier filed misconduct complaints against two federal judges in Washington, including Chief Judge James Boasberg, and that appeals courts threw out both. On Friday, October 2, Schiltz told a law school symposium that he had spoken about the threat to the rule of law and judicial independence and has "not only the right, but I have the duty to do so." Under the judiciary's misconduct rules, the circuit's chief judge decides first whether to dismiss the complaint or refer it to a special committee, and the process cannot be used to obtain automatic disqualification of a judge from a case.

On Tuesday, October 20, Woodward filed motions in two cases asking Schiltz and Tunheim to disqualify themselves over their comments to the Times; he was the only government lawyer who signed them. The case before Schiltz is the government's bid to revoke the citizenship of Salah Osman Ahmed, a Somali American man who pleaded guilty to a terrorism charge in 2009. The case before Tunheim is the prosecution of Hester Sophia Weihmann, a legal permanent resident from South Africa charged with voting illegally in the 2024 election, who has pleaded not guilty. "A judge who has publicly taken sides on the political issue of immigration enforcement cannot then preside over a case concerning one of the Justice Department's key immigration initiatives," Woodward wrote in the Schiltz motion, which also cited Schiltz's remarks at the October 2 symposium. Of Tunheim he wrote, "To Judge Tunheim, the 'rule of law' apparently means ignoring the law when it comes to illegal aliens who have broken the law." Ahmed's lawyer, Daniel Gerdts, called the government's arguments "contrived and baseless." Days earlier Woodward had sought to disqualify U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes in Washington from the East Potomac golf course case, which she refused (tracked separately in this database). Schiltz has scheduled a hearing on the motion against him for November 23, and Tunheim has not yet acted on the motion against him. No action by the 8th Circuit on the misconduct complaint has been reported.
elements_required: The Justice Department, through its top leadership, filed a formal judicial misconduct complaint against named and anonymous Minnesota federal judges
The judges targeted are the ones who handled the Operation Metro Surge habeas cases and publicly documented ICE's noncompliance with court orders

The court and the judges say the comments fell within a published judicial ethics opinion, and the misconduct process cannot itself force a judge's disqualification

rebuttal_anticipated: DOJ could argue that the Code of Conduct bars judges from commenting publicly on pending cases and from political statements, that extended on-the-record interviews about immigration enforcement while related cases and appeals are still active create a reasonable appearance of bias, and that a misconduct complaint to the circuit and recusal motions in the individual cases are the proper, lawful channels for raising that concern.
comeback: The judiciary's own Committee on Codes of Conduct said in February 2026 that judges may speak on the rule of law and judicial independence, and the Times reported that Schiltz did not discuss specific cases. The complaint's remedy also goes well beyond an ethics review: it seeks to take nearly all of Minnesota's federal district judges off every DHS case, a disqualification the misconduct process cannot itself grant. And **the Attorney General blamed the government's violations of court orders on the judges who documented them.** CBS News reported that judicial-ethics experts expect the follow-up motions to disqualify Schiltz and Tunheim will likely fail, and NYU law professor Stephen Gillers called them "performative." DOJ's earlier misconduct complaints against two Washington judges were both thrown out by federal appeals courts.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of a pattern this tracker documents of the Justice Department turning its own tools against the officials and institutions that checked Operation Metro Surge. The judges named here are the ones who documented ICE's repeated violations of court orders in Minnesota habeas cases, and the complaint recasts that record as the judges' own fault. It follows the grand jury subpoenas to Gov. Walz, Mayor Frey and other Minnesota officials, which Schiltz himself quashed as meant to coerce and retaliate. What sets this case apart is its target: not elected officials but the federal bench itself, through a disciplinary process that seeks to take the judges off every case involving DHS, followed by motions to disqualify two of them case by case.

incident_summary: Task Force Vulcan, a DOJ-led interagency effort launched in 2019, spent years building a case against MS-13's top leadership, indicting 14 gang leaders in 2020 on terrorism, drug-trafficking, and conspiracy charges. ProPublica's June 2025 investigation reported that several of the indicted leaders possessed direct knowledge of a secret deal between Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele's government and MS-13 -- favorable prison conditions, judicial protections, and territorial autonomy for the gang in exchange for electoral support for Bukele's party -- which contradicted Bukele's public image as the architect of a hardline anti-gang crackdown and was itself the subject of federal prosecutorial interest, including suspected diversion of USAID funds. **On March 11, 2025, DOJ dismissed all charges against MS-13 leader César Humberto López Larios; he was repatriated to El Salvador four days later.** A DOJ prosecutor identified in reporting by surname, Durham, sought to dismiss charges against and secretly deport a second gang leader, arguing in a court filing that public disclosure before the operation was complete 'could cause harm to the government's relationship with a foreign ally.' The dismissals and repatriations coincided with the Trump administration's broader deportation partnership with Bukele, under which El Salvador agreed to detain deportees (including at CECOT) in exchange for U.S. payments and diplomatic goodwill. House Oversight Committee Ranking Member Rep. Robert Garcia sent a formal letter to DOJ, State, and DHS on August 18, 2025 demanding an accounting of the case dismissals, characterizing the administration's actions as apparently designed to undercut Task Force Vulcan by returning key witnesses to Bukele's custody before their knowledge of his MS-13 dealings could be used.

official: Todd Blanche, Attorney General (confirmed August 8, 2026; DOJ leadership overseeing the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Texas, which issued the subpoena)
offense_category: Overreaching/politically-motivated use of grand jury subpoena power implicating patient privacy and Fourth/Fifth Amendment concerns -- no criminal charges have been filed against NYU Langone, any provider, or any patient; this is a subpoena/investigative-power matter, not a completed prosecution
incident_summary:
On May 7, 2026, NYU Langone Health received a federal grand jury subpoena from the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Texas, demanding information on all patients under 18 who received gender-affirming care at the hospital system between 2020 and 2026, along with the names of the medical providers and others involved in offering that care. The hospital had already ended its Transgender Youth Health Program in February 2026. The hospital's notice indicated several other institutions had received similar subpoenas as part of the same investigation. On June 2, 2026, three families of transgender youth and two transgender young adults, represented by the ACLU, the New York Civil Liberties Union and Lambda Legal, filed a class action (Coe v. Blanche) in the Southern District of New York against DOJ and NYU Langone. On June 9, New York, California and 18 other states, plus the District of Columbia, moved to file an amicus brief supporting the plaintiffs.

Judge Katherine Polk Failla granted a temporary restraining order blocking disclosure of the requested medical information on June 24, 2026. A preliminary injunction issued July 6, 2026, with the court explicitly finding plaintiffs likely to succeed on the merits of their Fourth and Fifth Amendment claims. DOJ noticed an appeal to the Second Circuit on July 10, 2026; the district court denied DOJ's motion to stay the injunction pending appeal on July 17, 2026. DOJ then sought a stay from the Second Circuit, which denied it on August 26, 2026 -- the preliminary injunction remains in effect while DOJ's merits appeal (No. 26-1886) proceeds.

On September 18, 2026, DOJ announced an agreement with NYU Langone Hospitals resolving its investigations: NYU agreed to pay $8.5 million and to stop providing puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and surgical procedures to minors, and DOJ credited NYU for cooperation, including in DOJ's investigation of other entities. DOJ said the agreement followed similar ones with Mount Sinai Health System, another New York City provider, on September 4, and with Texas Children's Hospital, the Cleveland Clinic and Connecticut Children's. NYU denied any wrongdoing or liability and said the agreement removed the threat that it would have to turn over the patient information DOJ had demanded. Plaintiffs' counsel said no patient information had been disclosed to DOJ as part of the settlement and that the injunction remained in full effect. No criminal charges have been filed against any institution, provider, or patient.
elements_required: A criminal grand jury subpoena sought identifying medical records of minors and their treating providers based on a category of lawful medical care (gender-affirming care), rather than a specific allegation of criminal conduct by a named individual
The subpoena was issued from a district (Northern District of Texas) with no apparent jurisdictional connection to the New York hospital system it targeted
Multiple institutions beyond NYU Langone received similar subpoenas, indicating a coordinated campaign rather than an isolated, case-specific investigation
A federal court found sufficient grounds to block disclosure on an emergency basis pending further review, rather than allowing immediate compliance

incident_summary:
In December 2025 Netflix agreed to buy Warner Bros. Discovery's studio and streaming business. Asked at the Kennedy Center Honors on December 7 whether Netflix should be allowed to buy Warner, President Trump said the combined market share "could be a problem" and added, **"I'll be involved in that decision, too."** A day later, after Paramount Skydance, run by David Ellison, had launched a hostile bid for the whole company, including CNN, he said he "didn't know anything about the deal." On December 17, 2025, Senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal asked Attorney General Pam Bondi to recuse herself from DOJ's review. Their release said her former lobbying firm, Ballard Partners, represented both Netflix and Paramount, and that her ethics agreement barred her from "any particular matter involving specific parties in which (she) knows Ballard Partners is a party or represents a party" until February 4, 2026. A DOJ spokesperson told CNN that "All officials at the Department of Justice follow the guidance of career ethics officials."

In early February 2026, CNN reported, Ellison returned to the White House for two private conversations with Trump; days later Trump told NBC, "I've decided I shouldn't be involved. The Justice Department will handle it." Later that month, while DOJ was reviewing Netflix's deal, Trump posted on Truth Social that "Netflix should fire racist, Trump Deranged Susan Rice, IMMEDIATELY, or pay the consequences," linking to activist Laura Loomer, who had called to "kill the Netflix-Warner Bros. merger now." On February 26, Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos went to the White House; a White House official said the meeting was "not with POTUS." That day Warner's board declared Paramount's bid superior, and Netflix declined to match it, saying the deal was "no longer financially attractive." On March 2, Warren, Blumenthal and Representative Sam Liccardo wrote to Bondi and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles that Sarandos had reportedly met them and DOJ antitrust officials hours before Netflix withdrew, and asked what was said. In March the acting antitrust chief, Omeed Assefi, said the deal would "absolutely not" be fast-tracked for political reasons.

On June 12, 2026, with Todd Blanche as Acting Attorney General, the Antitrust Division closed its investigation, saying a "rigorous eight-month investigation led by the Division's career staff" showed the deal would "increase competition." Politico reported, as relayed by Variety, that it imposed no "divestitures, behavioral remedies or concessions." The Wall Street Journal then reported, citing anonymous sources and as relayed by Variety, that **career staff had been "leaning" toward recommending a lawsuit to block the deal and "didn't participate in writing" the statement.** Capitol Forum, also citing anonymous sources, reported that the division's front office had refused staff requests to depose Ellison and other executives, declined to "bounce" Paramount's second-request certification, let the waiting period expire in February, told staff to limit third-party engagement, and closed the review before staff could make a recommendation. DOJ disputed these accounts on the record, and Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. wrote that the career lawyers "never reached out to anyone in their leadership chain of command."

On July 13, 2026, 12 states led by California sued to block the merger under Section 7 of the Clayton Act (California et al. v. Paramount Skydance Corp. et al., N.D. Cal. No. 4:26-cv-7116-AMO), and on July 20 Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin granted a temporary restraining order. The states then settled. On September 30 the judge approved the consent decree as a "fair, reasonable, and good faith approach to address the competitive harms" alleged; its terms include more U.S. film spending, minimum theatrical releases, a $47.5 million displaced-worker fund and a "News Editorial Independence Board" for CBS and CNN. The merger closed October 6, 2026, and the combined company took the name Skydance.

incident_summary:
On July 4, 2025, a demonstration against Trump's mass-deportation push outside the Prairieland ICE detention center in Alvarado, Texas turned violent when former Marine reservist Benjamin Song shot and wounded a police officer who had just arrived at the scene. Nine defendants were tried together in a 12-day proceeding featuring testimony from more than 45 witnesses and over 210 exhibits; on March 13, 2026, a federal jury convicted all nine. Song was convicted of attempted murder of the officer and firearm counts; he and seven others were convicted of rioting, providing material support to terrorists, and explosives offenses (the explosives being fireworks), though four of those seven were acquitted of aiding-and-abetting attempted-murder and firearm charges. The ninth, Daniel Sanchez Estrada, was not at the protest and was convicted only of concealing documents and conspiracy to conceal them. Seven additional defendants, including Susan Kent, had pleaded guilty in November 2025 to one count of providing material support to terrorists. DOJ's own press releases branded the group "Antifa Cell Members." Sentences ranged widely: Song received 100 years; the other trial defendants received 30 to 70 years; those who pleaded guilty to the material-support count received 22 months to 15 years, including Kent, sentenced July 6, 2026 to 6 years for helping Song escape and hide after the shooting -- her sentencing concluded all federal district-court proceedings in the case. The Intercept reported that Sanchez Estrada received 30 years for moving a box of antifascist zines after the protest, with terrorism-linked sentencing guidelines applied to all the defendants, and Just Security separately analyzed how the terrorism statute used in the case is broadly enough defined that it could sweep in ordinary protest-adjacent conduct not involving violence.

At least four convicted defendants (Sanchez Estrada, Batten, Evetts, Elizabeth Soto) filed notices of appeal to the Fifth Circuit within a week of their June 23, 2026 sentencing, KERA News reported June 30, 2026; by July 6, 2026, court records showed all nine trial defendants, including Song, had filed notices of appeal. Southern Coalition for Social Justice and the Texas Civil Rights Project are representing Batten on appeal, describing her 50-year sentence as punishment "for attending a protest and running a book club." As of September 27, 2026, The Intercept reported, the Fifth Circuit had not yet issued a briefing notice. The same report detailed an argument Song's lawyers raised in an April 2026 new-trial motion: that the late disclosure of evidence of bullet strikes in the pavement, revealed only mid-trial, deprived them of the chance to make their case that Song, who they contend fired at the ground, never intended to shoot the officer.

rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: an officer was shot and wounded, explosives and weapons were involved, and material-support statutes properly reach anyone who knowingly assists a violent plot regardless of which specific supporting role they played; prosecutors have discretion to charge accomplices and material supporters of a violent attack under the same overarching conspiracy, and juries -- not prosecutors alone -- returned these convictions after a 12-day trial with extensive evidence.
comeback: The specific concern this entry documents is not that the shooter or direct violent participants were prosecuted -- that prosecution is not in dispute -- but that DOJ's own public communications framed the entire prosecution in explicitly ideological/organizational terms ('Antifa Cell'), and that one defendant who was not at the protest and was not charged with material support received 30 years for moving a box of literature once terrorism-linked sentencing guidelines were applied, alongside the specific concern independent legal analysts flagged: that a broadly defined terrorism statute can functionally criminalize protest-network association and non-violent material support alongside genuinely violent conduct, blurring the line between prosecuting a shooting and prosecuting a political movement.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of the administration's post-September-2025 treatment of "antifa" as a domestic-terrorism target: the material-support counts here were added only after the executive order designating antifa and NSPM-7, and terrorism-linked sentencing then reached even a defendant whose only convicted conduct was moving a box of zines. The same NSPM-7 framing recurs in this tracker's entry on the Minnesota antifa conspiracy prosecutions, though that case relies on conspiracy, assault and property-damage charges rather than terrorism counts.

incident_summary:
Erez Reuveni, a 15-year DOJ veteran immigration attorney fired in 2025 after refusing to comply with directives he believed violated court orders and his ethical obligations, filed an initial protected whistleblower disclosure in June 2025 alleging a pattern of senior DOJ and White House officials deliberately defying federal court rulings on immigration enforcement -- including knowingly violating court injunctions to carry out deportations under the Alien Enemies Act -- and retaliating against him for objecting.

DOJ later gave Reuveni's own complaint an on-record response: a short, unsigned OIG letter declining to investigate was sent one day after Reuveni asked OIG to probe former DOJ official Emil Bove and current leadership over the court-order-defiance allegations, and in January 2026 OIG told Reuveni it would refer his claims to DOJ's own Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) instead, separately citing pending litigation as a reason not to proceed. Reuveni's lawyers call both justifications pretextual: OPR itself "showed no interest" in taking up the claims, and the administration had already fired the attorney who ran OPR, which the lawyers describe as having "decapitated" that office. This response addressed Reuveni's own complaint specifically -- it does not extend to the broader set of 20+ allegations, including those raised independently by members of Congress, which remained without any confirmed OIG investigation.

In March 2026, Reuveni's lawyers told Congress that DOJ's own Office of the Inspector General had not investigated any of at least 20 serious misconduct allegations raised over the preceding 15 months, including complaints separately made by members of Congress, and that the OIG's inaction was occurring as the department's internal watchdog offices were being hollowed out, with leadership posts left vacant and internal oversight stalling department-wide.

incident_summary:
Attorney General Bondi issued a DOJ-wide memorandum on April 22, 2025 directing five enforcement priorities against pediatric gender-affirming care, including "Enforcement of Laws Outlawing Female Genital Mutilation," False Claims Act/FDCA investigations, and establishing a "Federal and State Coalition Against Child Mutilation." On July 9, 2025, DOJ announced it had issued more than 20 subpoenas to doctors and clinics providing gender-affirming care to minors nationwide, without naming the recipients or their locations. NBC News later identified the first named recipient in that wave -- Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) had received a subpoena dated June 11, 2025 (due July 9), demanding patient names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, addresses, and parent/guardian information for minors prescribed puberty blockers or hormone therapy, plus staff personnel files, patient intake procedures, and insurance billing codes for gender-affirming care; GLAD Law's Jennifer Levi called it turning "doctor-patient confidentiality into government surveillance." Neither DOJ nor CHOP responded to NBC's request for comment. The same week, the FTC held a workshop critical of pediatric trans healthcare featuring detransitioners and anti-trans activists; former FTC staff told NBC News the event was politically organized and exceeded the agency's normal jurisdiction, a parallel but institutionally separate action from DOJ's own subpoena campaign.

U.S. District Judge Myong Joun's September 9, 2025 ruling quashed DOJ's subpoena to Boston Children's Hospital, one of the Massachusetts blocks in this nationwide campaign, which had sought patient records including Social Security numbers and home addresses, billing codes, communications with pharmaceutical manufacturers about puberty blockers or cross-sex hormones, and personnel files for all 2,000 of the hospital's employees. Judge Joun found the subpoena "motivated only by bad faith," writing that "the Administration has been explicit about its disapproval of the transgender community and its aim to end GAC [gender-affirming care]" and that its true purpose was "to interfere with the Commonwealth of Massachusetts' right to protect GAC within its borders, to harass and intimidate BCH to stop providing such care, and to dissuade patients from seeking such care."

DOJ subpoenaed Rhode Island Hospital (part of Brown University Health/Lifespan) for the birth dates, Social Security numbers, and addresses of every patient who received transgender care there over the prior five years, plus all documentation of adverse side effects in minor patients, assessments for puberty blockers or hormone therapy, patient intake forms, and guardian authorizations. On May 13-14, 2026, U.S. District Judge Mary McElroy (D.R.I.) blocked the subpoena, writing that DOJ had "proven unworthy" of the trust ordinarily extended to federal prosecutors. McElroy wrote that the administration "has publicly characterized gender-affirming care for minors as abuse, directed the justice department to bring its practice to an end, and celebrated when hospitals curtailed such programs as a result of this subpoena campaign" -- tying the subpoena to a stated political goal rather than a neutral investigative need. This is one of at least seven federal districts, including Massachusetts, where judges have blocked DOJ subpoenas seeking hospitals' transgender-care patient records as part of the same nationwide campaign, including a separate subpoena issued out of the Northern District of Texas to NYU Langone, tracked in a related entry in this database.

DOJ appealed McElroy's ruling to the First Circuit on May 14, 2026 (No. 26-1568), the day after the ruling. Rhode Island's Child Advocate separately sought an emergency injunction from the First Circuit to block record production pending that appeal; the First Circuit denied it around May 19-20, 2026 on irreparable-harm grounds -- a ruling against the Child Advocate's emergency motion, not a ruling on DOJ's appeal or against the underlying injunction. The District of Rhode Island's order quashing the subpoena remains in full force. On June 5, 2026, Judge McElroy referred DOJ attorneys -- centered on Enforcement and Affirmative Litigation Branch acting director Lisa Hsiao -- for possible disciplinary proceedings, finding a sworn declaration to the court "clearly misleading, if not utterly false" and citing an undisclosed side agreement with other hospitals in the same campaign; no proceedings have been scheduled.

DOJ's broader subpoena campaign against other hospitals continues in other districts, and on August 14, 2026 won its first appellate reversal of a similar district-court block (Ninth Circuit, QueerDoc/Seattle, 2-1, on the bad-faith finding specifically, remanded for further proceedings on overbreadth) -- the pattern is no longer one of uniform DOJ losses nationwide, though the Rhode Island ruling itself stands unaffected.

incident_summary:
In May 2024 the Justice Department's Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR), which runs the immigration courts, adopted a rule through notice-and-comment rulemaking that let immigration judges and the Board of Immigration Appeals "administratively close" removal cases: temporarily take them off the active docket, for example while an immigrant seeks humanitarian protection or another legal status, without deciding or dismissing them. In April 2025 EOIR's Acting Director issued a policy memo saying EOIR "could not—and will not—defend" the rule "in good faith against legal challenge," but the memo did not rescind it, and the rule stayed binding on immigration judges.

On June 22, 2026, Texas, represented by Attorney General Ken Paxton's office and the America First Legal Foundation, sued DOJ in the Wichita Falls Division of the Northern District of Texas, where Chief Judge Reed O'Connor is the only judge. Texas alleged the rule used administrative closure "to effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country." The same day, before DOJ had entered an appearance, Texas and the defendants (DOJ, **Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche** and EOIR's director) filed a joint motion for a consent judgment, under a DOJ signature block headed by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. The parties agreed the rule authorized "indefinite administrative closure without legal justification" and was "arbitrary and capricious." DOJ set aside, for this case only, its own position that courts cannot vacate rules under the APA. O'Connor signed the judgment that day: it **vacated the rule nationwide**, declared that "no statute authorizes immigration judges to indefinitely administratively close or suspend adjudication of a case," **permanently barred DOJ and its successors from adopting a similar rule** without an express statutory basis, and recorded both sides' waiver of appeal.

On August 7, the cities of Baltimore, Columbus and New Haven and Centro Legal de la Raza, an Oakland legal-services provider, moved to intervene so they could appeal, since neither party would. Texas opposed. DOJ's lawyer, who had not entered an appearance, missed the August 17 deadline to respond, saying the motion had been served on her only on August 18; that day she told the court DOJ opposed intervention "largely for the same reasons set forth by Plaintiff." On August 21 O'Connor denied intervention, holding the cities' claimed tax losses too attenuated to give them standing and Centro Legal's added-workload theory foreclosed by Fifth Circuit precedent. The Fifth Circuit refused to stay the judgment on September 29.
