rebuttal_anticipated: DOJ and Texas say the case was a real controversy: the rule was still binding on immigration judges when Texas sued, and Texas alleged fiscal and other injuries from people staying in the country while their cases sat closed. A court ruling that a rule exceeds the agency's statutory authority, they argue, "neither substitutes for nor evades the rulemaking process," and the APA does not require a court to keep a rule the agency itself believes is unlawful. DOJ had announced more than a year earlier that it would not defend the rule, and its own data showed closed cases rising from about 278,000 to about 392,000 between 2021 and 2025. Three courts, including the Supreme Court with no noted dissent, refused to disturb the judgment, and the judgment does not order already-closed cases back onto the docket.
comeback: The courts so far have ruled only on whether the cities and Centro Legal could join the case, not on whether the judgment itself was proper. On that point the record is one-sided: Texas sued and DOJ agreed, without contest, on the same day; the motion was filed before DOJ had appeared; both sides waived appeal; and DOJ then echoed Texas in opposing anyone who wanted to defend the rule. The judgment also goes beyond what repealing the rule through rulemaking could have done, because it permanently bars any future administration from adopting a similar rule without new statutory authority. Four justices wrote in 2022 that this kind of "rulemaking-by-collusive-acquiescence" raises a "host of important questions," and the challengers' appeal of that question is still pending.

Here the agreed judgment did what a notice-and-comment repeal would otherwise have had to do, and its injunction binds future administrations. Whether that amounts to collusion is the challengers' claim, not a court finding.

official: Donald Trump, President; Yaakov M. Roth, Acting Assistant Attorney General, DOJ Civil Division
offense_category: DOJ Intervening in a State Criminal Prosecution to Advocate for a Political Ally's Early Release, Citing Alleged Political Motives Without New Evidence -- addressed here as a rule-of-law/prosecutorial-independence question rather than a criminal charge
incident_summary:
Tina Peters, the former Mesa County, Colorado clerk, was convicted in August 2024 on four felony counts for orchestrating unauthorized access to Mesa County's secured election system in 2021 as part of an effort to find evidence supporting Trump's false claims of 2020 election fraud, and was sentenced in October 2024 to nine years in state prison. On March 3, 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice, in a filing in Peters's federal habeas case signed by Acting Assistant Attorney General Yaakov Roth, announced it would "review" Peters's state conviction, questioning both the length of her sentence and Colorado's denial of bail pending her appeal as potentially "arbitrary or unreasonable" -- without identifying any new evidence or legal defect in the state proceedings. Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser, in a March 2025 court filing, called the intervention a "grotesque attempt to weaponize the rule of law." At an April 22, 2025 federal hearing on Peters's bid for release, Justice Department lawyer Abigail Stout told Magistrate Judge Scott Varholak she was not authorized to discuss any ongoing review and had no knowledge of any evidence, leaving the department's actual reason for intervening in a completed state prosecution unexplained on the record.

Trump personally escalated the matter on May 5, 2025 in a Truth Social post directing DOJ to "take all necessary action to help secure the release" of Peters, describing her as an "innocent Political Prisoner" held "hostage ... by the Democrats, for political reasons" and subjected to "Cruel and Unusual Punishment," and criticizing Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser by name for jailing her. Trump escalated the pressure further on August 21, 2025, threatening on social media, "If she is not released, I am going to take harsh measures!!!" The Federal Bureau of Prisons went further in a letter the Colorado Department of Corrections received on November 12, 2025, seeking Peters's transfer into federal custody, and Michael Flynn, national security adviser during Trump's first term, has said she should be moved into federal custody because she could be a witness in an investigation of the 2020 election; the Department of Corrections said on November 26 that it was "not currently seeking a transfer," noting state law permits transfers to federal prison only when initiated by the state. On December 8, 2025, U.S. Magistrate Judge Scott Varholak dismissed Peters's federal bid for release on bond, ruling that her pending state appeal had to play out first, and she remained in state prison. Trump announced on December 11, 2025 that he was pardoning Peters; the document her attorney shared, which appears to be dated December 5, has no legal effect on her state conviction. A December 15, 2025 email from White House staffer Emily Underwood to officials at five federal agencies, including the Energy, Transportation and Interior departments, seeking a call "to discuss immediate actions that your department or agency can take with respect to Colorado," later surfaced in Colorado's lawsuit alleging federal retaliation over how the state runs its elections; CPR News reported it was sent a month after Colorado refused to move Peters to federal custody and days after the state ignored Trump's clemency declaration, and Colorado's Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper said it showed the administration targeting the state. The email, as reported, does not mention Peters.

On April 2, 2026, the Colorado Court of Appeals -- in a unanimous, 78-page opinion by Judge Ted Tow, reached independently of DOJ's intervention -- upheld Peters's underlying conviction but ordered her resentenced, finding the trial court's nine-year sentence was based "in part on improper consideration of her exercise of her right to free speech" (the panel found the sentencing judge's comments suggested the term was meant partly to stop Peters from continuing to espouse views the court deemed "damaging"). The same opinion rejected Peters's separate argument that a hypothetical presidential pardon could nullify her state conviction, holding the President has no pardon power over state offenses. The appeals court declined to rehear the case on April 23, 2026.

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis commuted Peters's sentence on May 15, 2026 -- cutting her original nearly-nine-year term roughly in half, to four and a half years, and making her parole-eligible June 1, 2026. PBS NewsHour and ABC7 reported the commutation followed a sustained Trump pressure campaign on Polis (public attacks, exclusion from a White House governors' meeting, and administration moves against Colorado-based NCAR and U.S. Space Command); Polis had earlier said Peters would need to show "appropriate contrition, apology"; his commutation letter said her application "demonstrates taking responsibility for your crimes," though Peters has not publicly confirmed the admission Polis described. The commutation preempted the court-ordered resentencing before it occurred. Polis characterized the move as a commutation, not a pardon, and grounded it in the same disproportionate-sentencing/free-speech concern the Court of Appeals had already identified, not in the political-motive concern DOJ raised in its March 2025 filing. Peters was released June 1, 2026.

By August 2026, Peters was being considered for an elections-consultant role in Shasta County, California, with no parole condition identified that would bar it. The role did not materialize: after public backlash and a county Board of Supervisors censure of Registrar Curtis, Peters said in a September 1, 2026 statement released through her attorney, Peter Ticktin, "I have not accepted any position with the Shasta County Elections Office," only that "discussions" had occurred; Curtis offered a differing account (she declined due to travel commitments) that doesn't reconcile cleanly with his own earlier public statements that he believed she had accepted.

In a decision reported September 21, 2026, the Colorado Supreme Court declined to hear Peters's appeal of the Court of Appeals' rejection of her challenges, including her Supremacy Clause immunity and juror-misconduct claims, leaving the conviction intact.

official: Harmeet Dhillon, Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights; Todd Blanche, Attorney General; R. Trent McCotter, Acting Deputy Attorney General
offense_category: Weaponization of Federal Litigation Authority -- DOJ has sued 30 states and D.C. for sensitive voter registration data (addresses, dates of birth, driver's license numbers, partial Social Security numbers) under a legal theory federal courts have repeatedly rejected, then escalated to records-preservation letters threatening election officials with civil and criminal sanctions -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary:
Since 2025, **DOJ's Civil Rights Division has filed federal lawsuits against 30 states and D.C. seeking each state's full voter registration database, including sensitive personal data (home addresses, dates of birth, driver's license numbers, and partial Social Security numbers)**, asserting authority under the Civil Rights Act of 1960, the National Voter Registration Act, and the Help America Vote Act. Federal district courts have dismissed 26 of these lawsuits, including rulings against DOJ in California, Oregon, Michigan, New Mexico, West Virginia, New Jersey, Arizona, and Georgia; U.S. District Judge Hala Jarbou (Michigan) held the federal voting laws DOJ cited do not require states to turn over this information, and U.S. District Judge Judith C. Herrera dismissed the New Mexico suit in July 2026, finding DOJ had given no factual basis to suspect the state of violating the NVRA or HAVA. On June 24, 2026, a divided Sixth Circuit panel affirmed the Michigan dismissal, and the court later denied DOJ's petition for rehearing en banc. In early September 2026, notwithstanding this string of losses, Eric Neff, acting chief of the Civil Rights Division's Voting Section, sent letters to election officials in 29 states and D.C. that DOJ had sued, instructing them not to destroy 2024 election records, warning that failure to preserve the data 'may constitute spoliation of evidence' that could subject officials to 'civil and criminal sanctions.' Dhillon publicly characterized the letters as 'standard litigation practice, not a "threat,"' while Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested DOJ may seek Supreme Court review if its appeals fail.

Update 2026-10-11: Nevada's suit is among those dismissed: on August 14, 2026, U.S. District Judge Anne R. Traum granted Nevada's motion to dismiss, finding the statewide voter registration list is not the type of record subject to disclosure under Title III of the Civil Rights Act of 1960 and that DOJ failed to provide the factual basis and purpose required to support its demand. DOJ filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit on August 18, 2026. In early September 2026, the office of Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar said it had received 'seven voter-related DOJ subpoenas from the FBI over the last three months'; the office gave no further details, and CNN reported it was unclear what information the subpoenas sought.

Update 2026-10-13: In a separate case brought by Common Cause and four voters whose registrations were canceled after their states turned over voter rolls to DOJ, U.S. District Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan (D.D.C.) on October 9, 2026 set aside and vacated what she called the Civil Rights Division's 'Voter List Maintenance Policy': requesting states' unredacted voter rolls, disclosing them to other federal agencies, comparing them against a federal citizenship database (SAVE) to identify purportedly ineligible voters, and demanding that states remove voters based on the results. In a 78-page opinion she held that the Civil Rights Act of 1960, the NVRA and HAVA do not authorize the policy; that it is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act because DOJ 'entirely failed to consider the risk' that relying on citizenship records known to be unreliable would lead it to demand that states remove U.S. citizens; and that it violates the Privacy Act and the Paperwork Reduction Act. She wrote that the defendants 'downplay the risk of voter disenfranchisement—despite knowingly relying on an inaccurate database to check voter eligibility,' and that the court 'vacates a policy that has removed United States citizens from the voter rolls in their home states and risks disenfranchising many more.' DOJ initially said it was reviewing the decision. Reuters noted that federal law's bar on systematic voter-roll reviews in the 90 days before a federal election could blunt the ruling's effect on the November 3 midterms. In a separate case, the Supreme Court in September temporarily paused Sooknanan's June order blocking expanded use of SAVE to check voter rolls.

Update 2026-10-16: DOJ then turned to California's mail ballots for the November 3 election. In letters sent October 13, 2026, Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter gave California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder 48 hours to review a list of people DOJ 'believes are likely non-citizens' who were sent mail ballots, to segregate those voters' ballots until their citizenship was confirmed, and to stop sending them ballots; otherwise, 'the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief.' The list went to Los Angeles County on a password-protected thumb drive, with the password handwritten on what appeared to be a blue post-it note. Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said his office had not opened it: 'We do not consider the device a secure medium.' Weber's office said the administration had refused to share the methodology behind the '(still) unsubstantiated' July claim by President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its rolls. Weber put DOJ's list at 'approximately 20,000 individuals' and called the deadline 'an emergency of the DOJ's creation.' On October 15, DOJ sued California in federal court in Los Angeles, asking a judge to bar the state from tabulating mail ballots 'from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined.' ABC News reported that the suit was filed by the deputy attorney general's office rather than the Civil Rights Division and rests on the Constitution's Supremacy Clause, and that DOJ says it is not seeking a 'purge' of the rolls. David Becker, a former DOJ voting section attorney, noted that California had mailed ballots to all voters on October 5. In Nevada, state officials had found that all 185 voters DHS said it had 'confirmed' as noncitizens were citizens, a conclusion DHS disputes. Also on October 15, the Common Cause plaintiffs asked Judge Sooknanan for a status conference, arguing that DOJ's California letters and suit 'appear to implicate—and perhaps outright violate—' her October 9 vacatur order; according to their filing, DOJ's counsel had replied that the October 13 letter 'does not impact the alleged DOJ policy' because 'DHS independently reviewed California's publicly available voter roll' and did not use SAVE. The judge ordered DOJ to respond by October 19. On October 16, DOJ filed a notice of appeal of the October 9 ruling to the D.C. Circuit and asked Judge Sooknanan to stay her order pending appeal, arguing 'There is no such policy' and that her decision 'has hamstrung DOJ's ability to enforce the election laws that Congress has empowered it to enforce.'

Update 2026-10-21: On October 16, McCotter sent a further letter to Los Angeles County's counsel, copied to Weber and Logan, warning that 'Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful' and that 'If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.' Reuters reported that the letter said DOJ used 'internal immigration records' and data matching, and that President Trump shared the letter on Truth Social with the comment: 'They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!' On October 19, federal prosecutors charged 28 people in California in what DOJ called 'Operation Protect the Vote,' run by the state's four U.S. attorney's offices; the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California said 11 were arrested that day. DOJ said all 28 are lawful permanent residents, charged with crimes including making false statements on a naturalization application and submitting fraudulent voter registrations, and, according to Democracy Docket, it accused 23 of them of casting ballots in elections dating back to 2020. McCotter said each defendant 'appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week' and called the 20,000 figure 'just the floor.' California Attorney General Rob Bonta said such cases are 'a drop in the bucket' in a state with 23 million registered voters. The same day, DOJ asked the federal court in Los Angeles hearing its suit for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction ordering California to set aside mail ballots from the listed voters until their citizenship is determined, with relief by November 3; its brief argues that otherwise 'there is a significant risk that American votes will be diluted' and cites that morning's charges. California and Logan filed oppositions on October 20, the day the case was assigned to Judge John W. Holcomb, who had not ruled as of October 21. Also on October 19, DOJ answered the Common Cause plaintiffs in Washington, arguing that the California suit is 'separate from the alleged DOJ policy' Judge Sooknanan vacated because it 'originates from an independent review by DHS' of California's voter roll, which DOJ says is available for purchase, and that DHS 'did not use SAVE at any point in its analysis.' A ProPublica review published October 16 found that in all 26 final rulings, the judges -- eight Trump appointees, four George W. Bush appointees and 14 Democratic appointees -- rejected DOJ's arguments in written opinions, with four cases still pending and one state having settled; a DOJ spokesperson told ProPublica, 'Disagreement with the government's position is not evidence of bad faith. We look forward to making our case on appeal.'

Update 2026-10-25: Los Angeles County's October 20 opposition to the restraining-order request included a declaration by assistant registrar Monica Flores describing a preliminary review of 200 records with Los Angeles County addresses from DOJ's list: 112 were canceled or inactive registrations to which no general-election ballot had been mailed; of the voters whose birthplace was meaningfully reported, 38.9% indicated they were born in the United States, 'which is strong evidence of citizenship'; and 71.2% had no voting history. She wrote that DOJ's proposed process 'would risk disenfranchising voters who are validly registered.' ABC News reported that McCotter had acknowledged at an October 19 press conference that 'there may be some names on there who it turns out ultimately are citizens,' while a DOJ spokesperson accused California of 'willful blindness.' On October 21 the case was transferred to U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who in January had dismissed DOJ's earlier suit for California's unredacted voter rolls. DOJ formally filed its restraining-order application that day and, after Carter set oral argument for October 27, asked for a ruling by noon on October 22. On October 22, calling the court's silence 'a constructive denial' of its request, DOJ filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit, and on October 23 it asked for an injunction pending appeal; Carter said the court 'will rule promptly after hearing from the Parties at oral argument on Tuesday, October 27, 2026.' Separately, on October 20 the DSCC, the DCCC, the Democratic Governors Association, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the Nevada State Democratic Party and a naturalized California voter sued Trump, DOJ, Blanche, DHS and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in federal court in Washington. The complaint alleges that federal demands that states remove registered voters, refuse to issue them ballots or segregate their ballots are ultra vires and violate the separation of powers and the anticommandeering doctrine, and that threatening state election officials with prosecution violates Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act; it cites Trump's 'They will all go to jail' post. The case was assigned to Chief Judge James Boasberg. A DOJ spokesperson said every action the department has taken 'is grounded in the law and being litigated in open court.' (DHS's own voter-roll checks are covered in TAP's separate entry on DHS's voter initiative.)

Update 2026-10-26: Late on October 23 the Ninth Circuit ordered California to respond by noon the next day to DOJ's emergency request, and on Sunday, October 25, a three-judge panel (Judges Mark Bennett, Patrick Bumatay and Gabriel Sanchez) heard nearly two hours of remote argument. Bennett and Sanchez questioned whether the appeals court had jurisdiction before the district court ruled, and Bennett told DOJ, 'It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause.' Sanchez pressed DOJ on how it built its list of alleged noncitizens: 'Your claims very much depend on the reliability of that list.' DOJ attorney Matthew Donnelly said the government 'was supplied a list that was purchased' from California. Bumatay appeared more sympathetic to DOJ's argument. ABC News reported that Bennett, a Trump appointee, told Donnelly, 'I don't see how we have jurisdiction,' and asked, 'How can we, a federal court, do what is reserved to Congress, which Congress, in my view, hasn't done?', while Donnelly argued that California's handling of its election infringes on the federal government's ability to enforce the federal law barring noncitizen voting (18 U.S.C. 611). ABC News also reported that California had filed a declaration saying such an order could have a 'catastrophic' impact on tabulating the election, and that in the preceding week DOJ had sent letters to every county in California asking election officials, within 48 hours, to 'commit to working with DOJ and DHS to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not,' according to a letter described to ABC News. Bennett said the panel would try to rule as quickly as possible; Carter's hearing remained set for October 27.

Update 2026-10-28: On October 22, Attorney General Blanche told reporters in Virginia that DOJ might bring more suits like California's: 'There's a number of states that we're looking at,' adding, 'Whether we're going to do something before the election, I don't want to get too ahead of the civil lawyers working on those cases.' The county letters went out on Friday, October 23: federal prosecutors hand-delivered letters to county election offices across California (a DOJ spokesperson said every county was contacted), each with that county's subset of the 20,000-name list, giving officials 48 hours to work with DOJ and DHS 'to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not,' asking them to 'temporarily set aside' but 'not cancel' those voters' mail ballots and to provide Social Security numbers, ID copies and registration applications, and warning that 'The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring federal crimes are significant.' County lists included one name in Modoc County, 48 in Marin County and 407 in Contra Costa County; Santa Cruz County said most of its 81 records belonged to voters no longer actively registered there, and Contra Costa clerk Kristin Connelly called it 'an unenforceable 48-hour deadline delivered late on a Friday.' Also on October 23, the Democratic plaintiffs in Washington, D.C., asked Chief Judge Boasberg for expedited discovery, saying they were 'seriously contemplating a request for emergency relief.' On October 26 the Ninth Circuit panel dismissed DOJ's appeal, 2-1, holding that it lacked jurisdiction because DOJ had not given the district court an 'adequate opportunity' to consider its restraining-order application. The unsigned majority opinion said 'The United States's claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one,' faulting DOJ's delay in suing and in seeking emergency relief. Judge Bennett wrote that he would have rejected DOJ's bid on the merits as well; Judge Bumatay dissented, writing that 'the federal government has a sovereign interest in safeguarding federal elections.' The same day, federal prosecutors in Washington state, led by Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd, asked Secretary of State Steve Hobbs to set aside the ballots of more than 400 people they say are noncitizens, called the list 'only the tip of the iceberg' and said a second list would follow before November 3; Hobbs said the timing 'is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results' and that one record on the list dated to 1994. At Judge Carter's October 27 hearing, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli argued for DOJ and acknowledged of the list, 'We're never going to stand here and tell you everything's 100%.' Carter did not rule from the bench; he told DOJ, 'You've got a remedy for goodness sake. Go out and indict,' said he was considering appointing a special master to evaluate DOJ's list, a review he said could be completed before California's December 11 certification deadline, and said he would issue an order on October 28. He closed, according to the Associated Press: 'This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county election employees cease immediately.' Judge Sooknanan had not ruled on DOJ's stay motion in the Common Cause case, which was fully briefed on October 26.

Update 2026-10-29: On October 28, Judge Carter denied DOJ's restraining-order application in a 26-page order. 'Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,' he wrote. The request, he wrote, 'violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,' and if it were granted, 'either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process.' He found that the United States likely lacks standing and a cause of action, called its claimed emergency 'solely due to its own neglect,' said DOJ's matching protocol 'raises significant concerns,' and, citing the warnings to county officials, wrote that 'these threats must stop.' The same day he let the NAACP, LULAC and two immigrant-rights groups intervene. DOJ filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit and asked Carter for an injunction pending appeal, and Essayli said DOJ would seek an emergency order from the Ninth Circuit. On October 29 Carter appointed Daniel B. Garrie as special master, ordered witness lists on the reliability of DOJ's list and the method used to build it by November 6, and set a November 13 hearing on the motions to dismiss and DOJ's preliminary-injunction motion. In Washington state, Hobbs answered the federal prosecutors on October 28, the day of their noon deadline, writing that a preliminary review showed their list 'includes United States citizens and is not reliable'; no DOJ suit against Washington had been reported. In the Democrats' case in Washington, D.C., DOJ argued that its letters to states 'have no independent legal effect.' At an October 29 hearing, Chief Judge Boasberg did not rule on the restraining-order request but ordered the administration to identify, by noon Friday, every state it has pressed since July 1 to remove voters, set aside ballots or withhold ballots. He questioned whether the Democrats have standing ('The harder question for me is your standing to do it'), said DOJ could 'moot this process at any time' by filing a notice that it will not engage in the challenged conduct, and said he intends to rule by Monday, the eve of Election Day. Judge Sooknanan had still not ruled on DOJ's stay motion in the Common Cause case.

Update 2026-10-30: The Associated Press obtained copies of three subpoenas, sent October 21 and October 24, ordering employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder to appear in court on November 4, the day after the election. The San Francisco Chronicle, which also obtained subpoenas, described them as federal grand jury subpoenas from First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli and Homeland Security Investigations agents, returnable at the federal courthouse in Santa Ana, and the registrar's office confirmed to NPR that its employees had received grand jury subpoenas. The subpoenas seek documents and communications related to the letters federal officials sent state election officials in July and October alleging noncitizens on the state's voter rolls, and any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted. A letter accompanying the subpoena to the registrar's custodian of records says it was issued 'in connection with an official criminal investigation being conducted by the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Investigations.' A person familiar with the matter told AP that all four U.S. attorneys in California were issuing subpoenas; AP reported it was unclear whether DOJ intends to bring criminal charges against anyone. Registrar Dean Logan said, 'threats and intimidation have no place in elections.'

Update 2026-10-31: On October 30, a divided Ninth Circuit panel denied DOJ's request for an injunction pending appeal that would have required California to set aside the ballots. The United States 'has not made the required showing that such extraordinary relief, during an ongoing election, is clearly required by law,' the majority wrote, adding: 'As the district court found—and we discern no clear error—there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system.' Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez formed the majority; Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented, calling DOJ's proposal a 'modest' remedy. DOJ did not immediately say whether it would seek Supreme Court review. The same day, in the Democrats' case in Washington, D.C., according to a filing obtained by Democracy Docket, DOJ answered Chief Judge Boasberg's order by naming California and Washington as the states where it had sent communications within its reading of the order, while DHS listed letters to California, Nevada, Pennsylvania and New Jersey raising concerns about potential noncitizens on voter rolls; the administration argued the DHS letters fell outside the order because they asked states to verify voters' citizenship rather than remove voters or withhold ballots. In a footnote, DOJ also disclosed that on October 29 it had sent letters 'to all states' telling election officials to preserve federal election records, including 'the ballot itself,' for 22 months; copies signed by McCotter, obtained by Democracy Docket and Votebeat, warn: 'It is a crime to willfully fail to comply with Section 20701.' Also on October 30, Boasberg ordered the government to give the plaintiffs DOJ's 20,000-person list by 5 p.m. and let the plaintiffs file a supplement on standing, with the government to respond within 24 hours; he had not yet ruled on the restraining-order request, and Judge Sooknanan had not ruled on DOJ's stay motion in the Common Cause case.
elements_required: DOJ sued dozens of states demanding sensitive individual-level voter data under a specific statutory theory
Multiple federal courts, applying that same statutory theory, found DOJ lacked the legal authority it claimed and dismissed the suits on the merits
Despite that losing track record, DOJ escalated by sending the same 29 states plus D.C. formal letters warning of civil and criminal sanctions for failing to preserve the underlying records

The pattern -- pursuing sensitive individual voter data at national scale via a legal theory courts have repeatedly rejected, then threatening the same officials with sanctions -- raises separation-of-powers and voter-privacy concerns beyond the merits of any single case

status: Active, DOJ mostly losing: 26 voter-data suits dismissed, SAVE purge policy vacated (stay sought). Judge Carter and a divided Ninth Circuit refused DOJ's bid to set aside ~20,000 California mail ballots. DOJ subpoenaed LA County election staff and sent all states criminal-penalty records warnings.
rebuttal_anticipated: DOJ's Civil Rights Division has statutory authority to enforce federal voter-list-maintenance requirements, and pursuing that authority through litigation -- even litigation that loses at the district-court level -- is the normal, lawful way to test a contested legal theory; sending preservation letters tied to ongoing litigation is standard practice to prevent spoliation regardless of which side is likely to prevail, as Dhillon stated publicly.
comeback: The scale is the distinguishing feature here, not the underlying litigation tactic in isolation: DOJ is not defending one contested legal theory in one case, but pursuing the identical claim against 30 states and D.C. simultaneously, has now lost that claim in the clear majority of courts to rule on it (26 suits dismissed, and the Michigan dismissal affirmed on appeal), and only after that losing record began escalated to formal sanctions-threat letters against the same officials it is suing -- a sequence that reads less like routine litigation hygiene and more like continued pressure on state election officials despite an accumulating judicial rejection of DOJ's legal theory. On October 9, 2026, a federal judge also vacated the Civil Rights Division's underlying voter-list policy, holding that none of the statutes DOJ cited authorizes it to collect and share unredacted state voter rolls. On October 28, 2026, a federal judge in California denied DOJ's request to set aside some 20,000 mail ballots, finding that the United States likely lacks standing and a cause of action and that its claimed emergency was 'solely due to its own neglect.' On October 30, a divided Ninth Circuit panel refused DOJ's request for an injunction pending appeal, finding no clear error in the conclusion that there is 'no feasible way' to segregate specific voters' ballots without 'potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system.'
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of a broader pattern of the administration asserting federal control over state-run elections ahead of the November 2026 midterms -- alongside the separate EO 14248 citizenship-documentation litigation, DHS's SAVE-database voter-roll-scrub push, USCIS staff reportedly directed to pose as individual voters in state lookup systems, Blanche's unsubstantiated claim of hundreds of individual-voter criminal investigations, and DOJ's suit to block certification of Alaska's Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan narrowly loses -- where DOJ litigation losses have not yet translated into DOJ backing off the underlying demand for sensitive voter data.

incident_summary.base: Since 2025, **DOJ's Civil Rights Division has filed federal lawsuits against 30 states and D.C. seeking each state's full voter registration database, including sensitive personal data (home addresses, dates of birth, driver's license numbers, and partial Social Security numbers)**, asserting authority under the Civil Rights Act of 1960, the National Voter Registration Act, and the Help America Vote Act. Federal district courts have dismissed 26 of these lawsuits, including rulings against DOJ in California, Oregon, Michigan, New Mexico, West Virginia, New Jersey, Arizona, and Georgia; U.S. District Judge Hala Jarbou (Michigan) held the federal voting laws DOJ cited do not require states to turn over this information, and U.S. District Judge Judith C. Herrera dismissed the New Mexico suit in July 2026, finding DOJ had given no factual basis to suspect the state of violating the NVRA or HAVA. On June 24, 2026, a divided Sixth Circuit panel affirmed the Michigan dismissal, and the court later denied DOJ's petition for rehearing en banc. In early September 2026, notwithstanding this string of losses, Eric Neff, acting chief of the Civil Rights Division's Voting Section, sent letters to election officials in 29 states and D.C. that DOJ had sued, instructing them not to destroy 2024 election records, warning that failure to preserve the data 'may constitute spoliation of evidence' that could subject officials to 'civil and criminal sanctions.' Dhillon publicly characterized the letters as 'standard litigation practice, not a "threat,"' while Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested DOJ may seek Supreme Court review if its appeals fail.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-11: Nevada's suit is among those dismissed: on August 14, 2026, U.S. District Judge Anne R. Traum granted Nevada's motion to dismiss, finding the statewide voter registration list is not the type of record subject to disclosure under Title III of the Civil Rights Act of 1960 and that DOJ failed to provide the factual basis and purpose required to support its demand. DOJ filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit on August 18, 2026. In early September 2026, the office of Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar said it had received 'seven voter-related DOJ subpoenas from the FBI over the last three months'; the office gave no further details, and CNN reported it was unclear what information the subpoenas sought.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-13: In a separate case brought by Common Cause and four voters whose registrations were canceled after their states turned over voter rolls to DOJ, U.S. District Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan (D.D.C.) on October 9, 2026 set aside and vacated what she called the Civil Rights Division's 'Voter List Maintenance Policy': requesting states' unredacted voter rolls, disclosing them to other federal agencies, comparing them against a federal citizenship database (SAVE) to identify purportedly ineligible voters, and demanding that states remove voters based on the results. In a 78-page opinion she held that the Civil Rights Act of 1960, the NVRA and HAVA do not authorize the policy; that it is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act because DOJ 'entirely failed to consider the risk' that relying on citizenship records known to be unreliable would lead it to demand that states remove U.S. citizens; and that it violates the Privacy Act and the Paperwork Reduction Act. She wrote that the defendants 'downplay the risk of voter disenfranchisement—despite knowingly relying on an inaccurate database to check voter eligibility,' and that the court 'vacates a policy that has removed United States citizens from the voter rolls in their home states and risks disenfranchising many more.' DOJ initially said it was reviewing the decision. Reuters noted that federal law's bar on systematic voter-roll reviews in the 90 days before a federal election could blunt the ruling's effect on the November 3 midterms. In a separate case, the Supreme Court in September temporarily paused Sooknanan's June order blocking expanded use of SAVE to check voter rolls.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-16: DOJ then turned to California's mail ballots for the November 3 election. In letters sent October 13, 2026, Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter gave California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder 48 hours to review a list of people DOJ 'believes are likely non-citizens' who were sent mail ballots, to segregate those voters' ballots until their citizenship was confirmed, and to stop sending them ballots; otherwise, 'the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief.' The list went to Los Angeles County on a password-protected thumb drive, with the password handwritten on what appeared to be a blue post-it note. Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said his office had not opened it: 'We do not consider the device a secure medium.' Weber's office said the administration had refused to share the methodology behind the '(still) unsubstantiated' July claim by President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its rolls. Weber put DOJ's list at 'approximately 20,000 individuals' and called the deadline 'an emergency of the DOJ's creation.' On October 15, DOJ sued California in federal court in Los Angeles, asking a judge to bar the state from tabulating mail ballots 'from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined.' ABC News reported that the suit was filed by the deputy attorney general's office rather than the Civil Rights Division and rests on the Constitution's Supremacy Clause, and that DOJ says it is not seeking a 'purge' of the rolls. David Becker, a former DOJ voting section attorney, noted that California had mailed ballots to all voters on October 5. In Nevada, state officials had found that all 185 voters DHS said it had 'confirmed' as noncitizens were citizens, a conclusion DHS disputes. Also on October 15, the Common Cause plaintiffs asked Judge Sooknanan for a status conference, arguing that DOJ's California letters and suit 'appear to implicate—and perhaps outright violate—' her October 9 vacatur order; according to their filing, DOJ's counsel had replied that the October 13 letter 'does not impact the alleged DOJ policy' because 'DHS independently reviewed California's publicly available voter roll' and did not use SAVE. The judge ordered DOJ to respond by October 19. On October 16, DOJ filed a notice of appeal of the October 9 ruling to the D.C. Circuit and asked Judge Sooknanan to stay her order pending appeal, arguing 'There is no such policy' and that her decision 'has hamstrung DOJ's ability to enforce the election laws that Congress has empowered it to enforce.'

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-21: On October 16, McCotter sent a further letter to Los Angeles County's counsel, copied to Weber and Logan, warning that 'Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful' and that 'If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.' Reuters reported that the letter said DOJ used 'internal immigration records' and data matching, and that President Trump shared the letter on Truth Social with the comment: 'They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!' On October 19, federal prosecutors charged 28 people in California in what DOJ called 'Operation Protect the Vote,' run by the state's four U.S. attorney's offices; the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California said 11 were arrested that day. DOJ said all 28 are lawful permanent residents, charged with crimes including making false statements on a naturalization application and submitting fraudulent voter registrations, and, according to Democracy Docket, it accused 23 of them of casting ballots in elections dating back to 2020. McCotter said each defendant 'appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week' and called the 20,000 figure 'just the floor.' California Attorney General Rob Bonta said such cases are 'a drop in the bucket' in a state with 23 million registered voters. The same day, DOJ asked the federal court in Los Angeles hearing its suit for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction ordering California to set aside mail ballots from the listed voters until their citizenship is determined, with relief by November 3; its brief argues that otherwise 'there is a significant risk that American votes will be diluted' and cites that morning's charges. California and Logan filed oppositions on October 20, the day the case was assigned to Judge John W. Holcomb, who had not ruled as of October 21. Also on October 19, DOJ answered the Common Cause plaintiffs in Washington, arguing that the California suit is 'separate from the alleged DOJ policy' Judge Sooknanan vacated because it 'originates from an independent review by DHS' of California's voter roll, which DOJ says is available for purchase, and that DHS 'did not use SAVE at any point in its analysis.' A ProPublica review published October 16 found that in all 26 final rulings, the judges -- eight Trump appointees, four George W. Bush appointees and 14 Democratic appointees -- rejected DOJ's arguments in written opinions, with four cases still pending and one state having settled; a DOJ spokesperson told ProPublica, 'Disagreement with the government's position is not evidence of bad faith. We look forward to making our case on appeal.'

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-25: Los Angeles County's October 20 opposition to the restraining-order request included a declaration by assistant registrar Monica Flores describing a preliminary review of 200 records with Los Angeles County addresses from DOJ's list: 112 were canceled or inactive registrations to which no general-election ballot had been mailed; of the voters whose birthplace was meaningfully reported, 38.9% indicated they were born in the United States, 'which is strong evidence of citizenship'; and 71.2% had no voting history. She wrote that DOJ's proposed process 'would risk disenfranchising voters who are validly registered.' ABC News reported that McCotter had acknowledged at an October 19 press conference that 'there may be some names on there who it turns out ultimately are citizens,' while a DOJ spokesperson accused California of 'willful blindness.' On October 21 the case was transferred to U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who in January had dismissed DOJ's earlier suit for California's unredacted voter rolls. DOJ formally filed its restraining-order application that day and, after Carter set oral argument for October 27, asked for a ruling by noon on October 22. On October 22, calling the court's silence 'a constructive denial' of its request, DOJ filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit, and on October 23 it asked for an injunction pending appeal; Carter said the court 'will rule promptly after hearing from the Parties at oral argument on Tuesday, October 27, 2026.' Separately, on October 20 the DSCC, the DCCC, the Democratic Governors Association, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the Nevada State Democratic Party and a naturalized California voter sued Trump, DOJ, Blanche, DHS and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in federal court in Washington. The complaint alleges that federal demands that states remove registered voters, refuse to issue them ballots or segregate their ballots are ultra vires and violate the separation of powers and the anticommandeering doctrine, and that threatening state election officials with prosecution violates Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act; it cites Trump's 'They will all go to jail' post. The case was assigned to Chief Judge James Boasberg. A DOJ spokesperson said every action the department has taken 'is grounded in the law and being litigated in open court.' (DHS's own voter-roll checks are covered in TAP's separate entry on DHS's voter initiative.)

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-26: Late on October 23 the Ninth Circuit ordered California to respond by noon the next day to DOJ's emergency request, and on Sunday, October 25, a three-judge panel (Judges Mark Bennett, Patrick Bumatay and Gabriel Sanchez) heard nearly two hours of remote argument. Bennett and Sanchez questioned whether the appeals court had jurisdiction before the district court ruled, and Bennett told DOJ, 'It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause.' Sanchez pressed DOJ on how it built its list of alleged noncitizens: 'Your claims very much depend on the reliability of that list.' DOJ attorney Matthew Donnelly said the government 'was supplied a list that was purchased' from California. Bumatay appeared more sympathetic to DOJ's argument. ABC News reported that Bennett, a Trump appointee, told Donnelly, 'I don't see how we have jurisdiction,' and asked, 'How can we, a federal court, do what is reserved to Congress, which Congress, in my view, hasn't done?', while Donnelly argued that California's handling of its election infringes on the federal government's ability to enforce the federal law barring noncitizen voting (18 U.S.C. 611). ABC News also reported that California had filed a declaration saying such an order could have a 'catastrophic' impact on tabulating the election, and that in the preceding week DOJ had sent letters to every county in California asking election officials, within 48 hours, to 'commit to working with DOJ and DHS to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not,' according to a letter described to ABC News. Bennett said the panel would try to rule as quickly as possible; Carter's hearing remained set for October 27.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-28: On October 22, Attorney General Blanche told reporters in Virginia that DOJ might bring more suits like California's: 'There's a number of states that we're looking at,' adding, 'Whether we're going to do something before the election, I don't want to get too ahead of the civil lawyers working on those cases.' The county letters went out on Friday, October 23: federal prosecutors hand-delivered letters to county election offices across California (a DOJ spokesperson said every county was contacted), each with that county's subset of the 20,000-name list, giving officials 48 hours to work with DOJ and DHS 'to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not,' asking them to 'temporarily set aside' but 'not cancel' those voters' mail ballots and to provide Social Security numbers, ID copies and registration applications, and warning that 'The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring federal crimes are significant.' County lists included one name in Modoc County, 48 in Marin County and 407 in Contra Costa County; Santa Cruz County said most of its 81 records belonged to voters no longer actively registered there, and Contra Costa clerk Kristin Connelly called it 'an unenforceable 48-hour deadline delivered late on a Friday.' Also on October 23, the Democratic plaintiffs in Washington, D.C., asked Chief Judge Boasberg for expedited discovery, saying they were 'seriously contemplating a request for emergency relief.' On October 26 the Ninth Circuit panel dismissed DOJ's appeal, 2-1, holding that it lacked jurisdiction because DOJ had not given the district court an 'adequate opportunity' to consider its restraining-order application. The unsigned majority opinion said 'The United States's claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one,' faulting DOJ's delay in suing and in seeking emergency relief. Judge Bennett wrote that he would have rejected DOJ's bid on the merits as well; Judge Bumatay dissented, writing that 'the federal government has a sovereign interest in safeguarding federal elections.' The same day, federal prosecutors in Washington state, led by Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd, asked Secretary of State Steve Hobbs to set aside the ballots of more than 400 people they say are noncitizens, called the list 'only the tip of the iceberg' and said a second list would follow before November 3; Hobbs said the timing 'is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results' and that one record on the list dated to 1994. At Judge Carter's October 27 hearing, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli argued for DOJ and acknowledged of the list, 'We're never going to stand here and tell you everything's 100%.' Carter did not rule from the bench; he told DOJ, 'You've got a remedy for goodness sake. Go out and indict,' said he was considering appointing a special master to evaluate DOJ's list, a review he said could be completed before California's December 11 certification deadline, and said he would issue an order on October 28. He closed, according to the Associated Press: 'This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county election employees cease immediately.' Judge Sooknanan had not ruled on DOJ's stay motion in the Common Cause case, which was fully briefed on October 26.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-29: On October 28, Judge Carter denied DOJ's restraining-order application in a 26-page order. 'Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,' he wrote. The request, he wrote, 'violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,' and if it were granted, 'either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process.' He found that the United States likely lacks standing and a cause of action, called its claimed emergency 'solely due to its own neglect,' said DOJ's matching protocol 'raises significant concerns,' and, citing the warnings to county officials, wrote that 'these threats must stop.' The same day he let the NAACP, LULAC and two immigrant-rights groups intervene. DOJ filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit and asked Carter for an injunction pending appeal, and Essayli said DOJ would seek an emergency order from the Ninth Circuit. On October 29 Carter appointed Daniel B. Garrie as special master, ordered witness lists on the reliability of DOJ's list and the method used to build it by November 6, and set a November 13 hearing on the motions to dismiss and DOJ's preliminary-injunction motion. In Washington state, Hobbs answered the federal prosecutors on October 28, the day of their noon deadline, writing that a preliminary review showed their list 'includes United States citizens and is not reliable'; no DOJ suit against Washington had been reported. In the Democrats' case in Washington, D.C., DOJ argued that its letters to states 'have no independent legal effect.' At an October 29 hearing, Chief Judge Boasberg did not rule on the restraining-order request but ordered the administration to identify, by noon Friday, every state it has pressed since July 1 to remove voters, set aside ballots or withhold ballots. He questioned whether the Democrats have standing ('The harder question for me is your standing to do it'), said DOJ could 'moot this process at any time' by filing a notice that it will not engage in the challenged conduct, and said he intends to rule by Monday, the eve of Election Day. Judge Sooknanan had still not ruled on DOJ's stay motion in the Common Cause case.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-30: The Associated Press obtained copies of three subpoenas, sent October 21 and October 24, ordering employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder to appear in court on November 4, the day after the election. The San Francisco Chronicle, which also obtained subpoenas, described them as federal grand jury subpoenas from First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli and Homeland Security Investigations agents, returnable at the federal courthouse in Santa Ana, and the registrar's office confirmed to NPR that its employees had received grand jury subpoenas. The subpoenas seek documents and communications related to the letters federal officials sent state election officials in July and October alleging noncitizens on the state's voter rolls, and any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted. A letter accompanying the subpoena to the registrar's custodian of records says it was issued 'in connection with an official criminal investigation being conducted by the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Investigations.' A person familiar with the matter told AP that all four U.S. attorneys in California were issuing subpoenas; AP reported it was unclear whether DOJ intends to bring criminal charges against anyone. Registrar Dean Logan said, 'threats and intimidation have no place in elections.'

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-31: On October 30, a divided Ninth Circuit panel denied DOJ's request for an injunction pending appeal that would have required California to set aside the ballots. The United States 'has not made the required showing that such extraordinary relief, during an ongoing election, is clearly required by law,' the majority wrote, adding: 'As the district court found—and we discern no clear error—there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system.' Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez formed the majority; Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented, calling DOJ's proposal a 'modest' remedy. DOJ did not immediately say whether it would seek Supreme Court review. The same day, in the Democrats' case in Washington, D.C., according to a filing obtained by Democracy Docket, DOJ answered Chief Judge Boasberg's order by naming California and Washington as the states where it had sent communications within its reading of the order, while DHS listed letters to California, Nevada, Pennsylvania and New Jersey raising concerns about potential noncitizens on voter rolls; the administration argued the DHS letters fell outside the order because they asked states to verify voters' citizenship rather than remove voters or withhold ballots. In a footnote, DOJ also disclosed that on October 29 it had sent letters 'to all states' telling election officials to preserve federal election records, including 'the ballot itself,' for 22 months; copies signed by McCotter, obtained by Democracy Docket and Votebeat, warn: 'It is a crime to willfully fail to comply with Section 20701.' Also on October 30, Boasberg ordered the government to give the plaintiffs DOJ's 20,000-person list by 5 p.m. and let the plaintiffs file a supplement on standing, with the government to respond within 24 hours; he had not yet ruled on the restraining-order request, and Judge Sooknanan had not ruled on DOJ's stay motion in the Common Cause case.

official: Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General (DOJ issued these subpoenas January 20, 2026, during her tenure; no specific prosecutor named in reporting reviewed as personally directing them) -- immigration-enforcement obstruction investigation
offense_category: Grand Jury Subpoenas Quashed as Harassment/Retaliation for Constitutionally Protected Conduct -- a federal judge found the subpoenas served no legitimate investigative purpose
incident_summary:
On January 20, 2026, federal prosecutors served six grand jury subpoenas on the records custodians for Minnesota Governor Tim Walz's office, Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey's office, St. Paul Mayor Kaohly Her's office, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison's office, and the Hennepin and Ramsey County Boards of Commissioners, demanding broad categories of records on federal immigration enforcement going back to January 1, 2025, as part of a stated investigation into obstruction of federal immigration enforcement. The subpoenas came during Operation Metro Surge, the administration's aggressive immigration surge in Minnesota, which had drawn widespread protests, and four days after news first leaked that DOJ was investigating Walz and Frey. The New York Times reported the same day that the subpoenas significantly expanded an inquiry first said to focus on Walz and Frey and said to center on whether Minnesota officials had conspired to impede federal agents, and that they came as the Justice Department had all but announced it would not charge the ICE agent who fatally shot Renee Good in Minneapolis (tracked separately in this database). NBC News placed the subpoenas within a growing number of DOJ investigations of people Trump had publicly targeted -- including then-Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, Democratic lawmakers, former CNN anchor Don Lemon, and protesters, each tracked elsewhere in this database.

In an order signed June 17, 2026, and unsealed June 22, Chief U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz quashed all six subpoenas, writing that "the Department has struggled -- without success -- to identify a single plausible investigatory justification for the subpoenas," calling the requests "extraordinarily broad" and finding they sought materials "that largely if not entirely relate to constitutionally protected conduct." Resting the ruling on the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering rule, the judge found that the subpoenas' "dominant purpose" was "to coerce Minnesota officials into assisting the federal government with enforcing civil immigration law and to harass and retaliate against them for failing to do so." ABC News noted that it is almost unheard of for federal judges to quash criminal subpoenas from Justice Department prosecutors. DOJ did not say whether it would appeal, and no appeal appears on the court's docket.
elements_required: DOJ issued grand jury subpoenas -- a coercive criminal-investigative tool -- to the offices of a sitting governor, two mayors and a state attorney general, and to the boards of the state's two largest counties, an unusually broad and high-profile set of targets
A federal judge found, after DOJ's own attempt to justify the subpoenas in court, that the Department could not identify any plausible investigatory purpose for them

The court found the material sought largely or entirely related to constitutionally protected conduct (public officials' policy positions and statements), not conduct ordinarily subject to grand jury investigation

The judge made an explicit judicial finding -- not just an inference invited by advocates -- that the subpoenas were issued 'to harass and retaliate against' the targeted officials for failing to assist federal enforcement of civil immigration law, alongside a finding that the subpoenas aimed to coerce that assistance

comeback: The ruling wasn't a dispute over scope alone -- the judge made an explicit factual finding, after DOJ's own opportunity to justify the subpoenas in court, that the Department could not identify any plausible investigatory purpose at all, that the subpoenas sought materials that largely if not entirely relate to constitutionally protected conduct, and that their dominant purpose was to coerce Minnesota officials into assisting with civil immigration enforcement and to harass and retaliate against them for refusing.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of a pattern this tracker documents of the Justice Department turning grand jury subpoenas on officials the President had publicly attacked, where a court later found no legitimate investigative purpose: in March 2026 a federal judge in Washington quashed the subpoenas in the investigation of then-Fed Chair Jerome Powell as pressure on him, and Judge Schiltz cited that ruling here. What sets this case apart is its aim. The court found these subpoenas were meant to coerce state and local governments into helping enforce federal civil immigration law, which the Tenth Amendment bars, and to retaliate against them for refusing. It arose from the same Minnesota surge in which DOJ reportedly declined to pursue the agent who killed Renee Good while scrutinizing her widow.

offense_category: National-Security Document-Handling Probe Opened Into Former FBI Leadership, Followed by a Public Presidential Demand to Prosecute Named Former Officials -- prosecutorial referral and investigation are lawful DOJ functions, but the accountability claim concerns the President publicly directing DOJ to prosecute named individuals rather than DOJ reaching charging decisions independently
incident_summary: On September 29, 2025, CNN reported the Justice Department -- through prosecutors in the Western District of Virginia -- had opened a national-security investigation into FBI leadership from 2020 through 2024, during Christopher Wray's tenure as director, over alleged mishandling of documents connected to the Durham special counsel investigation, including questions about materials stored in 'burn bags' typically used to dispose of classified paper records. Investigators sought interviews with staff who worked on the FBI's seventh-floor leadership suite during Wray's directorship. The probe came in the wake of, and was reported alongside, Trump's public comments suggesting DOJ was investigating Wray following the recent indictment of former FBI Director James Comey. Less than a month later, on October 24, 2025, **Trump escalated by publicly demanding the prosecution of former Attorney General Merrick Garland, former FBI Director Christopher Wray, former Special Counsel Jack Smith, and former Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco, accusing them of 'illegal' conduct for authorizing an FBI review of Republican lawmakers' phone data connected to the 2020 election-interference investigation**. Trump's public demand followed the same pattern already documented elsewhere in this tracker: the indictments of Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James, both of which Trump had also personally pushed Attorney General Bondi to pursue.

Trump publicly and personally demanded criminal prosecution of four specifically named former officials (Garland, Wray, Smith, Monaco) for a specific investigative act (the Arctic Frost review of GOP lawmakers' phone data), rather than allowing DOJ to reach an independent charging decision

This public demand followed an already-documented pattern in this tracker (the Comey and James prosecutions) of Trump personally pressuring Bondi's DOJ to pursue charges against individuals he named publicly

incident_summary:
Following a January 29, 2025 mid-air collision near Washington National Airport and a string of other aviation incidents in the following weeks, Duffy oversaw mass firings of FAA personnel during the same period that, by his own public statements, SpaceX employees were involved in "deliver[ing] a new, world-class air traffic control system" and DOGE would "plug in to help upgrade our aviation system" -- involvement the senators described as "a cadre, unaccountable to the American people, in critical aviation safety decision making." Senators sent a formal letter requesting documentation and commitments and raising concerns about the lack of accountability and public process around this private-sector involvement in safety-critical government functions. DOT has since announced substantial, publicly detailed FAA reorganization and modernization efforts, which may represent at least a partial transparency response.

The flagship modernization software contract was formally awarded to Air Space Intelligence in June 2026, with Peraton as prime integrator -- not to SpaceX. SpaceX/DOGE personnel involvement remains at the informal advisory/facility-tour level already documented above; the senators' specific transparency questions about that informal role remain unanswered in all sourcing reviewed.

official: Pam Bondi, Attorney General
offense_category: DOJ Criminal Prosecution of a Sitting State Judge for an Official Judicial Act -- Judicial-Independence Concern -- contested; DOJ maintains the prosecution targets obstruction conduct, not judicial decision-making itself, and a federal judge has allowed the case to proceed past a judicial-immunity challenge
incident_summary: On April 18, 2025, ICE agents, FBI agents, and DEA agents entered Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Hannah Dugan's courtroom to serve an administrative arrest warrant on Eduardo Flores-Ruiz, a noncitizen facing misdemeanor domestic-violence-related battery charges. Dugan allegedly directed Flores-Ruiz to leave through a back door normally reserved for jurors, allowing him to evade the agents. **Dugan was arrested in late April 2025 and indicted by a federal grand jury on May 13, 2025, on one felony count of obstructing or impeding a federal proceeding and one misdemeanor count of concealing a person to prevent arrest.** Dugan pleaded not guilty. Her defense moved to dismiss the case on judicial-immunity grounds, arguing that a judge's in-courtroom conduct is an official judicial act immune from criminal prosecution and that immunity should bar the case at the outset rather than being litigated later at trial. A magistrate judge recommended the case proceed, and U.S. District Judge Lynn Adelman upheld that recommendation, rejecting the immunity argument and allowing the prosecution to continue. More than 150 former state and federal judges signed a letter to Attorney General Pam Bondi criticizing the prosecution as an attempt to intimidate the judiciary.

A federal district judge specifically considered and rejected that immunity argument, allowing the prosecution to proceed

A substantial bipartisan group of over 150 former judges publicly characterized the prosecution as judiciary-intimidation, a significant institutional pushback signal distinct from ordinary case commentary

comeback: The distinction DOJ draws is real but contested at exactly the point the immunity motion tested: whether directing courtroom traffic and managing who is present during a proceeding is itself judicial conduct (which historically enjoys immunity) or extrajudicial obstruction. Judge Adelman ruled against Dugan on that question before trial, and a jury then convicted her of obstruction while acquitting her of concealment; her Seventh Circuit appeal is pending and is expected to turn on whether an ICE arrest attempt counts as a 'proceeding' under the obstruction statute. None of that resolves the separate institutional concern more than 150 former judges raised -- that prosecuting a judge for conduct inside her own courtroom, whatever its merits, carries a chilling effect on judicial independence distinct from whether the prosecution is ultimately legally viable.

official: Ed Martin, former DOJ Pardon Attorney (interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia when he wrote the Georgetown Law letters)
offense_category: Formal Attorney-Discipline Charges -- violating the attorney's oath to support the Constitution (D.C. Bar Rule XI, § 2(b)) through alleged First and Fifth Amendment violations, plus ex parte communication with a judge (D.C. Rule of Professional Conduct 3.5(b)) and conduct seriously interfering with the administration of justice (Rule 8.4(d)) -- brought by D.C.'s Disciplinary Counsel; not a criminal charge, and not yet adjudicated
incident_summary:
On February 17, 2025, while serving as interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, Ed Martin wrote to the dean of Georgetown University Law Center, part of a private Catholic and Jesuit university, saying a whistleblower had told him the school was teaching and promoting "DEI," a term he did not define. He asked whether the school had eliminated DEI from its curriculum and, before receiving any reply, announced that "no applicant for our prestigious fellows program, our summer internship, or employment in our office who is a student or affiliated with Georgetown law school will be considered until this is resolved." Dean William Treanor replied on March 6, 2025 that the First Amendment "guarantees that the government cannot direct what Georgetown and its faculty teach and how to teach it," calling the threat "an attack on the University's mission as a Jesuit and Catholic institution." On March 17, 2025, Martin repeated the hiring bar and wrote to the university's interim president and board chair that answers to his questions "appear to bear directly on Georgetown University's status as a 501(c) nonprofit and its receipt of nearly $1 billion of federal tax money in recent years."

Retired judge Phillip Argento, a Georgetown graduate, complained about the letter to D.C.'s Office of Disciplinary Counsel on March 10, 2025, and the office asked Martin to respond. According to the later charges, Martin instead wrote on March 31, 2025, without notice to Disciplinary Counsel, to the chief judge and senior judges of the D.C. Court of Appeals, which has the final say on attorney discipline: he said he would not respond, complained of Disciplinary Counsel's "uneven behavior," asked for a "face-to-face meeting," and copied the White House Counsel. The chief judge told him twice in April 2025 that the court could not meet with him outside the regular process. On May 13, 2025 he wrote to her again, asking "that you not only suspend Mr. Fox immediately to investigate his conduct, but also to dismiss the case against me because of his prejudicial conduct." He answered the inquiry through counsel on June 10, 2025, and on July 31, 2025 the Board on Professional Responsibility denied his motion to disqualify Disciplinary Counsel.

On March 6, 2026, Disciplinary Counsel Hamilton P. Fox III filed a two-count Specification of Charges, made public March 10. Count I alleges that Martin "knew or should have known that, as a government official, his conduct violated the First and Fifth Amendments": acting for the government, he "used coercion to punish or suppress a disfavored viewpoint," demanded that Georgetown Law give up its free speech and religious rights to keep a benefit for its students, and gave no fair notice or chance to respond -- violating his oath to support the Constitution. Count II charges the letters to the judges as improper ex parte communication and conduct that seriously interferes with the administration of justice. CNN reported it as the first major bar discipline proceeding against a high-profile administration official in Trump's second term; possible sanctions run up to loss of his law license, though Fox did not say what sanction he would seek. A DOJ spokesperson called it an "attempt to target and punish those serving President Trump," and a source told CNN a DOJ attorney was representing Martin.

In a March 30, 2026 answer, Martin denied violating any rule. He argued the D.C. Bar has no jurisdiction because he acted under the President's constitutional authority to enforce the law, and that the charges retaliate for his complaints about and investigation of Disciplinary Counsel. A hearing committee scheduled an April 20, 2026 prehearing conference. On April 7, 2026, Martin filed notice removing the case to federal district court in D.C., saying he "is entitled to a federal forum for the adjudication of his federal defenses"; Fox moved to send it back, citing a 2023 ruling that rejected the same move by former DOJ official Jeffrey Clark, and DOJ filed a statement supporting Martin. On May 13, 2026, DOJ also sued Fox, his office, the Board and the D.C. Court of Appeals, calling the case against Martin a "retaliatory prosecution," though the relief it seeks covers only Clark. Martin left the Pardon Attorney post after Trump announced his departure on August 21, 2026. U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper set argument on the remand motion for November 3, 2026; the defendants' motion to dismiss DOJ's suit, fully briefed by September 10, awaits a ruling. No hearing-committee finding or sanction has been identified.

D.C.'s Disciplinary Counsel charges that this was government coercion against a disfavored viewpoint, without fair notice or process, that Martin knew or should have known violated the First and Fifth Amendments and so his oath as a D.C. Bar member

offense_category: Improper Disclosure of Grand Jury Material (Rule 6(e) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, which strictly limits who may access secret grand jury material and to whom it may be disclosed) -- compounded by a reported initial false denial to DOJ leadership
incident_summary:
A Justice Department internal review, overseen by Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche's office, examined whether grand jury material gathered in DOJ's mortgage-fraud investigations of Sen. Adam Schiff and New York Attorney General Letitia James -- both perceived political opponents of President Trump -- had been shared with people not authorized to possess it. At least two sources familiar with the review told CNN it found Ed Martin improperly handled grand jury material; one of them said the department found he had shared the secret grand jury material in the Schiff case. The same source said that when department leaders first asked Martin whether he had shared the material, he denied doing so; emails soon surfaced showing he had in fact shared it. CNN's sources did not say who received the material or why Martin shared it. The finding was at least part of the reason Martin was pushed out of DOJ headquarters: he was removed as head of DOJ's Weaponization Working Group on the first day of 2026 and relocated to a building across town housing the Office of the Pardon Attorney, his one remaining role. A person close to Martin said he and the Working Group "followed DOJ standards and procedures at all times." Martin has not been charged with a crime, and DOJ had not determined whether any law was broken.

In the same story that broke the internal review's finding, Deputy AG Blanche said in a statement to CNN: "there are no misconduct investigations into Ed Martin. Ed is doing a great job as Pardon Attorney" -- a present-tense denial at odds with the finding the review reportedly reached. The statement did not address whether there had ever been a review of Martin's handling of grand jury material. Martin remained active in the Pardon Attorney role as of an August 14, 2026 official Pardon Attorney announcement.

Trump announced August 21, 2026 that Martin is leaving the Pardon Attorney post entirely, to work outside DOJ on election-related legal battles for the 2026 midterms and 2028 presidential race. No outlet reviewed ties the departure to the grand jury disclosure finding; Trump presented it as a move to election legal work, though CNN's February report on the review had already said Martin was expected to leave the department within weeks. No organization or formal title for the election legal work Trump described was identified; by September 9, 2026, Martin had instead launched Firearm Rights for Americans, a group offering people barred from owning guns help in seeking restoration of their firearm rights, which he said he hoped would turn out Second Amendment voters in the midterms. The underlying accountability gap -- no termination, no referral, an on-record denial of any misconduct investigation -- stood as of his last day in the role.
