incident_summary:
In August 2024, before taking office, Ed Martin -- a "Stop the Steal" organizer who had falsely denied that Trump lost the 2020 election -- gave Timothy Hale-Cusanelli an award for embodying "God, family, and country" at a ceremony at Trump National Golf Club, calling him an "extraordinary man" and "extraordinary leader." Hale-Cusanelli was a January 6 rioter whom federal prosecutors themselves had described as a "Nazi sympathizer": he had worn a Hitler mustache to work at a naval weapons station and recorded an antisemitic rant comparing Orthodox Jews to a "plague of locusts."

After becoming interim/acting U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia in January 2025, Martin oversaw the dismissal of roughly 30 federal prosecutors who had worked on January 6 Capitol riot cases, via a memo signed by Acting Deputy AG Emil Bove. Separately, he demoted at least eight senior prosecutors who had handled those same cases to entry-level positions. CNN, citing sources, reported that the demotions were seen as retaliation meant to force the prosecutors to resign, and NPR described the demotions and firings as apparently retaliatory. Martin was also reported to have represented January 6 defendants in his own prior legal practice while simultaneously serving as the office's top federal prosecutor, an apparent conflict of interest.

When the Hale-Cusanelli award resurfaced in reporting during Martin's 2025 confirmation fight, he said in written answers to the Senate Judiciary Committee that he had been unaware of Hale-Cusanelli's antisemitic history until after giving him the award, and that he condemned those views "in the strongest terms possible." A group of former January 6 prosecutors formally asked the D.C. Bar's Office of Disciplinary Counsel to investigate Martin's conduct, and more than 100 veterans of the U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. signed a letter calling him "an affront to the singular pursuit of justice for which this Office has stood for more than two centuries." Martin had also failed to disclose at first more than 150 paid appearances on Russian state-funded RT and Sputnik networks made before taking office, including them only in a later follow-up disclosure letter. Facing opposition from Senate Republicans -- including Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC), who cited Martin's defense of January 6 rioters specifically -- Trump withdrew Martin's nomination to the permanent U.S. Attorney post on May 8, 2025. Fox News host Jeanine Pirro was named interim U.S. Attorney for D.C. in Martin's place. Rather than leaving the administration, Martin was immediately moved into two new DOJ roles: Pardon Attorney and director of DOJ's newly created "Weaponization Working Group." His later conduct in those roles, including the grand-jury-leak finding and the loyalty-driven clemency pattern, is covered in this database's separate entries.

As head of the Weaponization Working Group, Martin brought on Jared Wise, a former FBI agent, as a counselor. Wise had been charged with felony civil disorder and assault/resisting/impeding-officers counts, plus four misdemeanors, for his January 6 conduct; prosecutors cited his having yelled "Yeah, kill 'em!" to encourage the crowd to hurt police. His prosecution ended with a presidential pardon rather than a trial. On September 3-4, 2025, Senate Judiciary Democrats (Durbin, Whitehouse, Schiff, and others) sent Attorney General Bondi a letter demanding Wise's firing, calling DOJ's hiring of him "shameless." Wise was not fired. He worked on a report focused on the prosecutions of January 6 rioters, then announced his resignation in April 2026, saying he had concluded he could not complete his goal of exposing alleged prosecutorial/investigative abuses from within the department.

incident_summary: On Wednesday, January 14, 2026, the FBI executed a search warrant -- sought by Assistant U.S. Attorney Gordon D. Kromberg of the Eastern District of Virginia -- at the Virginia home of Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson, seizing six electronic devices, including her phone, work computer, personal laptop, and smart watch, in an early-morning raid. Agents told Natanson she was not the target of the underlying investigation, which concerned government contractor Aurelio Perez-Lugones, a Maryland systems administrator with top-secret clearance charged under the Espionage Act with illegally retaining classified national defense materials and indicted on January 22, 2026 on five counts of transmitting national defense information (according to the FBI's affidavit, agents searching his home and car found a SECRET-marked document in his lunchbox and more SECRET-marked materials in his basement). Trump publicly indicated the leaked information concerned a U.S. military operation in Venezuela (this database's entry on Secretary Rubio and the Maduro raid documents that operation), though court documents reviewed did not confirm the connection. Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press President Bruce D. Brown called the search 'a tremendous escalation in the administration's intrusions into the independence of the press,' and Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray called it an 'extraordinary, aggressive action' raising 'profound questions and concern around the constitutional protections for our work.' This was the first time the Justice Department had raided a journalist's home specifically in connection with a national-security leak investigation. The court quickly issued a standstill order blocking the government from reviewing the seized devices' contents pending litigation; Magistrate Judge William B. Porter subsequently ruled that the court itself, not DOJ, would conduct any review, stating this prevented 'the equivalent of leaving the government's fox in charge of the Washington Post's henhouse.' On May 4, 2026, District Judge Anthony J. Trenga sided with Natanson and The Post, affirming the magistrate's ruling and **holding that the Privacy Protection Act 'bars the Government from searching in this particular case the PPA-protected materials that were seized,'** citing 'the harassing and chilling effects such a seizure could have on a reporter.' Between February 6-9, 2026, the Freedom of the Press Foundation filed a bar complaint against Kromberg with the Virginia State Bar, alleging he 'failed to disclose key provisions of the Privacy Protection Act when seeking' the warrant; the bar declined to investigate that complaint, but in March told Kromberg it was conducting a preliminary investigation, pointing to Judge Porter's opinion, then dismissed the matter in a July 2026 letter finding the evidence did not show a rules violation 'under the required evidentiary standard of clear and convincing evidence.'

incident_summary: **FBI agents searched the Cleveland office of the Ohio Organizing Collaborative (OOC), a nonprofit that runs voter-registration drives in Ohio, on Thursday, June 11, 2026, and fanned out across the state to question people connected to the group.** MS NOW, which first reported the search, said agents showed up at the homes of the group's leaders and staff members, 'carrying some subpoenas and seeking information and electronic devices,' according to three people briefed. A spokesperson for the FBI's Cleveland Field Office confirmed law enforcement activity at the group, and CBS News, citing multiple sources, reported that the FBI executed a search warrant 'as part of an ongoing fraud-related investigation.' The Ohio Capital Journal relayed reports that agents in some cases seized phones and laptops. OOC board member and former director Prentiss Haney said agents 'asked them if they're committing voter fraud, just on their doors,' called the operation 'straight-up intimidation tactics,' and told CBS News that 'over 125 agents' went to the homes of volunteers, community leaders and staff; Rep. Shontel Brown later said at least 100 agents were involved. A Justice Department official declined to discuss the case, saying the search warrant affidavit remains under seal and that search warrants 'are authorized by a judge and anything said by any organization or others in the media is unfounded speculation, as the target of any investigation is not privy to the search warrant affidavit until after indictment.' The OOC said it stands by its program and staff and 'will not be deterred from carrying out our vital mission.' Signal Ohio reported days later that the FBI had asked Cuyahoga County elections officials in February or March 2025 about voter registrations submitted by canvassers for Black Fork Strategies, a firm owned by OOC founder Kirk Noden that the OOC's political arm paid $10.6 million in 2023 and 2024. County election boards had flagged questionable Black Fork registrations, including some in the names of dead voters, and referred them to the state, but Cuyahoga's Republican deputy elections director said officials saw no evidence that any flagged registration led to fraudulent voting. A DHS spokesperson confirmed DHS was 'providing support for an active FBI investigation in Ohio.' On June 17, Brown and four other Ohio Democratic members of Congress wrote to FBI Director Kash Patel and the Cleveland Special Agent in Charge asking for the warrant and affidavit, the legal basis for following and questioning people tied to the group, how many FBI personnel took part, and whether DOJ's election-year sensitivities policies were followed, with a response requested by June 22. The same day, America Votes, a national group that has funded the OOC, confirmed it had received a subpoena 'asking for basic records related to funding of the Ohio Organizing Collaborative' and said it had been told it is not a target. Five days after the search, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Ohio said it was 'unable to provide more information,' and federal law enforcement had given no on-the-record explanation. In October 2026, CNN, reviewing internal Homeland Security Investigations records released by Democracy Forward, reported that by late May HSI and the FBI were developing investigative plans involving seven Ohio companies described as 'consolidation centers' associated with Black Fork, and that on June 8 ICE told senior officials agents planned to execute federal search warrants and interview more than 100 current and former employees. The heavily redacted records do not explicitly identify Black Fork as the warrants' target, but the OOC raid came three days later. No charges against the group or anyone connected to it have been reported, and no court has ruled on the search.

official: Tulsi Gabbard, then-Director of National Intelligence (February 2025-June 2026; resigned and was followed by acting DNI Bill Pulte, then by Jay Clayton)
offense_category: Directing an Intelligence-Community-Wide Anti-Leak Campaign, Including Expanded Polygraph Screening on Contact With the Press, That Press Freedom Advocates Warn Chills Journalism and Whistleblowing
incident_summary:
Beginning early in her tenure as Director of National Intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard pursued a sustained campaign across the intelligence community against leaks to the press. On March 14, 2025, she announced an investigation into intelligence-agency leaks. She cited reporting by HuffPost, The Washington Post, NBC News and The Record as examples of what she called 'politically motivated leaks' that 'undermine our national security.' Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, told The New York Times that leak investigations 'threaten the free flow of information that the public needs to hold the government accountable, especially in the national security context.' On April 23, 2025, Gabbard announced referrals of two individuals to the Department of Justice for allegedly leaking classified information, stating: 'these deep-state criminals leaked classified information for partisan political purposes to undermine POTUS' agenda.' The leak investigations and DOJ referrals proceeded as announced, but no prosecution of the two referred individuals has been identified.

The campaign escalated in September 2025, when Gabbard sent a memo to intelligence agency leaders asking whether it would be feasible to conduct random polygraph examinations of both employees and contractors. **The directive specifically emphasized that polygraph questioning should include whether an individual had leaked information to members of the press as part of the standard security-clearance adjudication process.** An ODNI official told CBS News the memo reinforced existing regulations rather than creating new policy. CBS News reported on the directive October 7, 2025, after two sources, at least one of them reportedly working under Gabbard at ODNI, leaked details of it to reporters on condition of anonymity, fearing reprisal for speaking publicly. ODNI spokesperson Olivia Coleman responded to the irony directly, saying 'the fact that deep state actors leaked information about DNI Gabbard's directive, aimed at preventing leaks and protecting classified information, to the media is both deeply ironic and a powerful reminder of why her efforts to identify and deter leakers is urgently necessary.' On random polygraphs, the directive asked agencies only to assess feasibility; no random polygraph program has been confirmed as implemented across the intelligence community.
elements_required: The Director of National Intelligence publicly announced and pursued leak investigations targeting specific news organizations' reporting, characterizing sources as criminal actors with partisan motives

incident_summary: In March 2025 congressional testimony, DNI Tulsi Gabbard told Congress the intelligence community assessed Iran was not building a nuclear weapon and that Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei had not authorized resuming the program he suspended in 2003. The Washington Post reported June 18-19, 2025, in the same pre-strike window, that Hegseth was ALSO effectively outside Trump's core Iran-strike decision-making circle despite his prominent public role -- officials and advisers described Trump as relying instead on a tighter, more experienced group for the actual decision: Vice President Vance, Secretary of State Rubio, CIA Director Ratcliffe, and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Caine, with both Hegseth and Gabbard better known at that point for their Fox News profiles and 'deep state' rhetoric than for standing inside that inner circle -- a distinction between who advised the actual strike decision and who later fronted the public/congressional messaging around it (see below). Around June 17-20, 2025, as Trump prepared to strike Iran's nuclear sites, he publicly said Gabbard was 'wrong' and told reporters 'I don't care what she said' -- a direct public rebuke of his own DNI's sworn congressional testimony, days before the June 21-22 'Midnight Hammer' strikes. Gabbard reversed course on social media, saying her testimony had been taken out of context by 'dishonest media' and that she and Trump were 'on the same page,' but was reportedly left out of the Situation Room photos documenting the strikes. After a leaked preliminary Defense Intelligence Agency assessment -- produced under DIA Director Lt. Gen. Jeffrey Kruse -- suggested the strikes had only set Iran's program back by months rather than 'obliterating' it as Trump and Hegseth publicly claimed, the White House moved to limit classified intelligence-sharing with Congress and excluded Gabbard from a June 25, 2025 Senate Iran briefing, conducted instead by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Hegseth, Secretary of State Rubio, and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine; Sen. Chris Murphy said Gabbard was likely disinvited because officials knew she would not endorse the 'obliterated' characterization. Milton Sands -- with Bloomberg reporting the firing followed directly from the DIA's contradictory assessment**, tying Kruse's removal to the same dispute that had sidelined Gabbard two months earlier. The pattern extended into 2026: per Washington Post (Jan. 7) and Bloomberg (Jan. 8) reporting, Gabbard was excluded from months of administration planning for Operation Absolute Resolve, the operation to oust Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, reportedly because her past non-interventionist record raised doubts about her support for military action, with Secretary of State Rubio said to prefer keeping her out; some White House aides joked DNI stood for 'Do Not Invite.' Gabbard's office and Vice President Vance both directly denied she had been excluded, calling the reporting false.

incident_summary:
On August 20, 2025, Gabbard announced "ODNI 2.0," a reorganization she said would cut her office's workforce by more than 40%, with affected positions ending September 23, and save more than $700 million annually -- billed as the largest ODNI restructuring since its post-9/11 creation. The plan dissolved the Foreign Malign Influence Center (which tracked foreign election interference), the National Counterproliferation and Biosecurity Center, and the Cyber Threat Intelligence Integration Center, folding their functions into other directorates, while merging the National Intelligence University into the National Defense University and eliminating the External Research Council and Strategic Futures Group. The New York Times reported that Gabbard framed the changes as part of her campaign to crush "the deep state," and in a social media post she said the plan would help in "rooting out deep state actors."

The day before, on August 19, 2025, Gabbard revoked the security clearances of 37 current and former officials -- including CIA deputies and Democratic congressional staffers -- whom she linked to the intelligence community's 2016 Russia-election-interference assessments, acting on what she said was a Trump directive; the Guardian, citing three people familiar with the matter, reported that Gabbard did not inform the White House before the revocations, frustrating several of Trump's top advisers and deepening animosity with the CIA; a senior intelligence official disputed that account, saying Trump had told Gabbard to remove such officials and that the list was emailed to the White House. In publicly naming individuals in the clearance-revocation memo, Gabbard identified a senior CIA officer who was working undercover -- a Russia expert with nearly 30 years of experience, according to the Washington Post, who had helped prepare Trump's briefing ahead of his Alaska summit with Vladimir Putin and who had an overseas posting already approved by CIA Director John Ratcliffe. Losing her clearance effectively ended her career. A U.S. official told NBC News that ODNI "didn't meaningfully consult with the agency" before the clearances were revoked; ODNI's spokesperson said it had coordinated with all agencies and that the memo listed names, not agency affiliations. The episode visibly deepened tension between Gabbard and Ratcliffe over declassification decisions and Russia policy. The same clearance-revocation action also cost the NSA its chief data scientist, Vinh Nguyen, a leading government expert on AI, cryptology, and advanced mathematics who focused on using AI to scrutinize foreign communications and improve the intelligence community's quantum-computing work. In the days before the revocation, the NSA's acting director, Lt. Gen. William Hartman, called Gabbard and asked to see the evidence that Nguyen had done anything to merit losing his clearance, the New York Times reported; Gabbard rebuffed the request and proceeded with the revocation. The Times reported that many, though not all, of the 37 had tangential connections to the intelligence agencies' review of Russian efforts to meddle in the 2016 election.

In late October 2025, the FBI submitted a sharply worded unclassified letter to Congress opposing a House bill that would have made ODNI the federal government's lead counterintelligence agency -- a proposal that would have significantly expanded Gabbard's institutional authority. The FBI wrote the change "would cause serious and long-lasting damage" to national security, citing its own decades of counterintelligence experience and 53-field-office network against a proposal it said would create bureaucracy and shift authority to officials without comparable expertise; reporting indicated the CIA shared many of the FBI's concerns.

On May 22, 2026, Gabbard told Trump she would step down to support her husband after his diagnosis with a rare form of bone cancer, effective June 30, 2026. ODNI's downsizing continued under acting DNI Bill Pulte, leaving the office at roughly half its early-2025 size by July 2026; Jay Clayton was confirmed as DNI on July 28, 2026.

incident_summary:
In spring 2025, the NSA intercepted a call in which two foreign nationals (described by the whistleblower's attorney as members of foreign intelligence) discussed a person close to President Trump (later reporting from The New York Times and Wall Street Journal reported that the conversation referenced Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, which Warner and Himes said they could not confirm, and indicated the discussion involved Iran). According to the whistleblower's attorney, Andrew Bakaj, rather than allow the NSA to publish its own intelligence report through normal channels, Gabbard personally carried a paper copy of the intelligence to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, then instructed the NSA not to publish the report and to transmit details directly to her office instead. A whistleblower, represented by Whistleblower Aid, first contacted the Intelligence Community Inspector General (ICIG) about this handling in spring 2025 (April 17, according to Bakaj's account to the Guardian), filing the complaint on May 21, 2025, and in June 2025 requested the disclosure be transmitted to Congress. The complaint alleges that a highly classified report was deliberately limited in distribution for political reasons, and that an intelligence agency's legal office failed to refer a potential crime to the Department of Justice, again for political reasons. Then-Acting ICIG Tamara Johnson initially determined that the complaint met the statutory definition of an "urgent concern" if true but could not determine whether it was credible -- a determination that gave the whistleblower the right to take the complaint to Congress; three days later, a follow-up memo concluded the first allegation was not credible and that she still could not assess the second, and the complaint was administratively closed in June 2025.

The complaint was not provided to the congressional intelligence committees until the evening of February 2, 2026 -- nearly eight months later -- when ICIG Christopher Fox hand-carried it to the Gang of Eight, whose members and staff reviewed it on a read-and-return basis because of its classified contents. Fox's February 2 letter to the intelligence committees' leaders gave a specific, dated breakdown of the delay: ongoing "complexity in the classification"; the 43-day government shutdown starting October 1, 2025; ODNI leadership changes, including the confirmation of a new general counsel, Jack Dever, whom clearance issues kept from viewing the complaint until December 1, 2025; a December 4 meeting at which Gabbard said she had not previously been told that clearance to share the complaint with Congress was pending; and a subsequent White House Counsel review for a potential executive-privilege assertion, with Gabbard's final approval to share the material granted only January 30, 2026. When the complaint was finally transmitted, it also arrived heavily redacted under executive-privilege claims, further limiting congressional oversight of the underlying allegation. When Gang of Eight members then asked to see the underlying intelligence report, ODNI told them the intelligence community could not provide it unredacted "due to the assertion of executive privilege."

Senate Intelligence Committee Vice Chair Mark Warner and other Democrats publicly questioned the delay. Gabbard denied any wrongdoing, calling claims that she or ODNI "hid" the complaint "a blatant lie"; her office said both inspectors general "did not find the complaint credible," while Fox wrote that he would likely determine the allegations did not meet the statutory "urgent concern" definition; Whistleblower Aid countered that the ICIG had simply been unable to make a determination in the 14-day window. Congressional Republicans on the relevant committees rejected the complaint's substance, while Democrats continued to press over the length of the delay itself, a separate question from the complaint's underlying merits. The Guardian's February 7, 2026 reporting, citing Bakaj, detailed the handling described above -- the whistleblower's underlying allegation concerns Gabbard's handling of the intercepted call, not merely an administrative delay. Gabbard's office has said every action taken was fully within her legal and statutory authority. In a February 24, 2026 letter, Warner and House Intelligence Committee Ranking Member Jim Himes called the privilege assertion over an intelligence report "unprecedented," asked whether the President had asserted it, and said they understood Gabbard still had not given the complainant the security guidance the law requires for contacting the intelligence committees.

Whether the ICIG's itemized explanation adequately justifies the eight-month gap remains genuinely disputed; no independent body (e.g., a DOJ IG or bipartisan committee finding) has ruled on that adequacy question.

incident_summary: In June 2026, CNN reported, citing a person familiar with the matter, that the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of California was leading a criminal tax investigation into people connected to California Gov. Gavin Newsom, including his wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom. That office is headed by Eric Grant (appointed by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi in August 2025, per the Justice Department's staff profile; the San Francisco Standard names him as its head), whom CNN's account does not name. CNN says The New York Times first disclosed the probe, while the San Francisco Standard says Newsom first disclosed it. Newsom publicly blasted the probe as politically motivated and said it was focused on him and his wife; CNN's source said the governor himself was not being investigated, though the San Francisco Standard's September reporting repeats a DOJ source's statement to Politico in June that Newsom and people close to him have been under investigation for more than a year. Newsom's team told congressional Democrats the investigation was ordered by Trump specifically to damage Newsom's prospective 2028 presidential campaign, framing it as investigating a critic rather than a crime; a source familiar with the investigation told reporters it instead originated from whistleblowers and local sources in California, not from Trump or DOJ leadership in Washington, and DOJ has denied its investigations are politically motivated. The investigation escalated in September 2026: **subpoenas signed by an Assistant U.S. Attorney sought six years of records from the California State Protocol Foundation, a nonprofit that has funded Newsom's international travel, along with communications involving current and former Newsom aides and associates** -- including Rebecca Prowda, Newsom's chief protocol officer and the wife of San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie. The subpoenas sought records on the foundation's donors and fundraisers, Newsom's participation in overseas events, and spending on the governor's residence and personal expenses; one subpoena stated the records were sought for a criminal investigation pending in the Eastern District of California. Newsom has directed more than $7.5 million in outside donations to the Protocol Foundation since 2019, roughly $5.1 million of it from leftover inaugural funds. Newsom has publicly characterized the expanded investigation as continued political retribution.

official: Jamieson Greer, United States Trade Representative
offense_category: Ultra Vires Agency Action — Tariffs Imposed Without Statutory Authority (the Supreme Court ruled the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, IEEPA, did not authorize the administration's global tariff program) — NOT charged criminally; this is a completed Supreme Court ruling on the merits, the highest-authority legal finding of any entry in this dataset; remedy was invalidation of the tariffs, not personal liability for Greer
incident_summary:
The Trump administration imposed sweeping global tariffs -- including "Reciprocal" and "Fentanyl" tariffs -- relying on the International Emergency Economic Powers Act as legal authority, with Greer as US Trade Representative implementing and defending the program. On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled against the use of IEEPA as the legal foundation for these tariffs, invalidating roughly 70% of the tariffs the administration had imposed worldwide. The same day, Greer's office announced that the administration would "immediately impose" a temporary 10% global surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 and open new Section 301 investigations "to ensure continuity." Two days later, Greer told ABC's "This Week": "The legal tool to implement it, that might change, but the policy hasn't changed."

On May 7, 2026, a divided (2-1) Court of International Trade panel held that the Section 122 tariffs also exceeded statutory authority, finding the proclamation did not identify the kind of balance-of-payments deficit the statute requires. Its injunction covered only three plaintiffs, and on the government's appeal the Federal Circuit administratively stayed the order on May 12, then granted a stay pending appeal on June 11.

On July 23, 2026, USTR took final action imposing Section 301 duties on 60 economies, effective 12:01 a.m. on July 24: 10% for 17 economies, 10% or 12.5% net of the most-favored-nation rate for certain products of the European Union, Taiwan, Japan, Korea and Switzerland, and 12.5% for the rest. The Section 122 tariffs expired unrenewed at the same moment, making Section 301 the third statute used for the global tariffs. Challenges in the Court of International Trade began the day the tariffs took effect: on July 24, 2026, the Liberty Justice Center sued on behalf of Burlap & Barrel and Collective Horology (Burlap & Barrel, Inc. v. Greer), and Learning Resources and other importers filed Learning Resources, Inc. v. United States. On August 3, 2026, attorneys general from 25 states (led by Oregon, Arizona, and California) filed their own complaint. No personal liability or charges against Greer are sought in any of these suits; as with the prior two rulings, the remedy sought is tariff invalidation, not individual sanction.

On August 4, 2026, the government filed an unopposed motion asking the Court of International Trade to designate Burlap & Barrel v. Greer as the "master case" for filings, with coordinated briefing and oral argument across the three Section 301 suits. The three-judge panel (Judges Choe-Groves, Reif, and Wang) instead opened its own master docket, In re Section 301 Forced Labor Cases, and set a schedule in an August 13 procedural order; on August 19 it named Learning Resources, Inc. v. United States (brought by Learning Resources, a plaintiff in the IEEPA case the Supreme Court decided) as the sample case and stayed the other suits. The plaintiffs moved for judgment on the agency record on August 24, the government responded on September 4, and the plaintiffs replied on September 18; Burlap & Barrel and the 25 states joined as amici supporting the sample-case plaintiffs. Oral argument is set for September 30, 2026. Separately, the Federal Circuit's appeal of the Section 122 ruling is still in briefing: on September 14, 2026 it extended the government's deadline for its response and reply brief to November 12, 2026, and no argument date has been set.
elements_required: IEEPA grants the president authority to regulate certain transactions during a declared national emergency involving an unusual and extraordinary threat
Whether broad, sustained tariff programs constitute the kind of action IEEPA authorizes, versus exceeding the statute's intended scope
Supreme Court determination on the merits -- the highest possible legal authority on a question of federal statutory interpretation
USTR's role in implementing, defending, and continuing to enforce the tariff regime both before and after the ruling

evidence.description: On May 7, 2026, the U.S. Court of International Trade ruled 2-1 that the Section 122 tariffs Greer's USTR shifted to after the IEEPA ruling also exceeded statutory authority, finding the proclamation imposing them did not identify the specific type of 'balance-of-payments deficit' Congress meant when it enacted Section 122 in 1974; the ruling issued a permanent injunction, but limited to the three prevailing plaintiffs (Burlap & Barrel, Inc., Basic Fun, Inc., and the State of Washington); the government immediately appealed to the Federal Circuit, which entered an administrative stay on May 12, 2026 suspending the CIT's order while the appeal proceeds -- meaning Section 122 tariffs continued being collected from non-plaintiff importers throughout this period

rebuttal_anticipated: Greer's own stated position: the underlying policy goals (addressing trade deficits, fentanyl trafficking, reshoring manufacturing) remain valid regardless of which specific statute authorizes them, and using alternative, available statutory authority (Section 122, Section 301) to achieve the same legitimate objectives is appropriate adaptive governance, not evasion of the Court's ruling.
comeback: There's a meaningful difference between 'finding a different legal basis for a policy goal' and 'achieving substantially the same outcome the Supreme Court just said exceeded the President's authority, using a different procedural label.' Greer's own public statement is the best evidence against this defense: 'The legal tool to implement it, that might change, but the policy hasn't changed.' That's not a statement about adapting to a legal ruling -- it's a direct admission that the goal was continuity of the invalidated program. An administration genuinely responsive to a Supreme Court ruling reconsiders the scope of what it's doing; an administration that just swaps statutes while keeping the policy identical is treating the Court's ruling as a procedural inconvenience, not a substantive limit. The Section 301 workaround faces its own legal challenges for the same underlying reason -- Congress appears to have intended it for one country at a time, not blanket global tariff programs -- which, if correct, would make this a second episode of the same pattern.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] After the Supreme Court held that IEEPA did not authorize the global tariffs, the administration treated the ruling as a question of which statute to use rather than as a limit on the policy. The same day, it announced replacement tariffs under Section 122 "to ensure continuity"; after the Court of International Trade also held those unlawful (a ruling stayed on appeal) and they expired, Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies took effect at the same moment. Greer's own words ("The legal tool to implement it, that might change, but the policy hasn't changed") state this approach unusually plainly for a senior official. Whether the Section 301 tariffs are lawful is still being litigated. The posture resembles the one in the Vought impoundment entry -- act first and let legality be litigated afterward -- though that entry involves a different official, statute, and set of acts.
confidence_note: VERY HIGH confidence -- this is the single strongest entry in the entire dataset, resting on an actual U.S. Supreme Court ruling on the merits, the highest possible legal authority. The open question is whether the administration's later tariff mechanisms (Section 122, then Section 301) are themselves unlawful or a legitimate use of other authority; that secondary question is genuinely contested, but the fact that the Supreme Court rejected the original legal theory is not in dispute. HIGH confidence that the response was a repeated strategy rather than a one-off: the Court of International Trade ruled 2-1 on May 7, 2026 that the Section 122 tariffs also exceeded statutory authority (a ruling stayed on appeal), and USTR's Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies took effect on July 24, 2026 as the Section 122 tariffs expired. HIGH confidence on the Section 301 litigation's posture, taken from the Court of International Trade's own docket: Learning Resources, Inc. v. United States is the sample case, the other suits are stayed, briefing closed September 18, and oral argument is set for September 30, 2026. Greer's often-repeated "just the legal playbook" line is a headline paraphrase, not his words; what he said on ABC's "This Week" was "The legal tool to implement it, that might change, but the policy hasn't changed."

official: Richard Grenell, Special Presidential Envoy (ran a competing, uncoordinated Venezuela negotiating track that undercut Secretary of State Marco Rubio's advanced prisoner-swap talks, delaying the release of detained Americans)
offense_category: Institutional Dysfunction / Uncoordinated Foreign Policy Endangering American Hostages -- not a criminal or civil violation; an accountability claim about internal process failure that had a direct, documented human cost (Americans and Venezuelan political prisoners remained detained)
incident_summary: By May 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio's State Department had advanced talks with Venezuela toward a prisoner exchange set for late May. Roughly 250 Venezuelan migrants the U.S. had deported to El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison would be returned to Venezuela, in exchange for 11 detained U.S. citizens and legal permanent residents and roughly 80 Venezuelan political prisoners held by the Maduro government. Separately, and without coordinating with Rubio's team, Trump envoy Richard Grenell was negotiating his own track with senior Maduro officials, centered on a broader economic deal: he offered to let Chevron continue its oil operations in Venezuela as an inducement for the release of American detainees, rather than the direct prisoner-for-prisoner exchange Rubio's team was negotiating. Both U.S. tracks were dealing with the same Venezuelan interlocutor, Jorge Rodriguez, president of Venezuela's National Assembly, and neither American side was apparently aware of the other's specific terms. In May, Grenell separately won the release of one American, Air Force veteran Joseph St. Clair. The New York Times reported on July 8, 2025 that the conflicting signals left Rodriguez and the Maduro government unable to determine which offer actually spoke for the Trump administration. **The deal was never sealed, and none of the 11 Americans or the Venezuelan political prisoners it covered were freed under it; the Times calls Grenell's rival track "part of the reason."** The swap Rubio had been negotiating did not happen on the terms or timeline his track had reached. Ten days after the Times report, on July 18, 2025, a related but distinct exchange was completed: the 252 CECOT-held Venezuelan migrants were returned for 10 Americans, including Lucas Hunter and Jonathan Pagan Gonzalez, who had been among the 11 in the collapsed talks. A separate entry documents that later swap, including a serious vetting failure in how it was conducted. No source reviewed identifies a public accounting of why the two negotiating tracks were allowed to run uncoordinated, or who at the White House was responsible for allowing Grenell's parallel track to proceed without informing Rubio's team.
elements_required: Two named U.S. officials (Rubio and Grenell) ran documented, substantively different negotiating tracks with the same foreign government's same interlocutor over the same subject (detained Americans/Venezuelan political prisoners) during an overlapping window

The two tracks were not coordinated -- each involved different, incompatible terms (a direct prisoner exchange vs. a Chevron oil-related economic inducement) -- per named-source reporting, not merely inferred from outcome
The reporting itself names the rival, uncoordinated track as part of the reason the deal fell through, not merely a factor coincidentally present alongside it

A concrete, documented harm resulted: none of the 11 Americans or the Venezuelan political prisoners covered by the collapsed deal were released under it, where release had been the explicit goal of both competing tracks

status: Concluded: the State Department swap set for late May 2025 was never sealed and freed none of the 11 Americans it covered; a distinct July 18, 2025 exchange (252 CECOT migrants for 10 Americans) is covered in a separate entry. No public accounting of the coordination failure has been found.
rebuttal_anticipated: Complex, multi-track diplomacy with an adversarial government is not inherently improper. A special envoy exploring an alternative economic-leverage approach could be characterized as due diligence rather than dysfunction, and reasonable people can disagree on tactics without it being a process failure. Grenell denounced the Times account of the separate deals as false. A person close to him told the Times that Grenell did not believe a swap involving the Venezuelan migrants was going to happen, because he believed Trump would never have authorized the release of accused gang members, and that Grenell is the only authorized negotiator on any deals with Venezuela. "There is no fraction or division," White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in a statement. "The president has one team, and everyone knows he is the ultimate decision maker."
comeback: The rebuttal would carry more weight if the two tracks had been coordinated internally even while pursuing different terms, which is standard practice for parallel-track diplomacy. What the reporting documents instead is two U.S. tracks that were not coordinating while talking to the same Venezuelan official with incompatible terms, which the Times reports was part of the reason the deal fell through. The failure documented here is the absence of coordination itself, evidenced by the deal's collapse, not the mere existence of alternative approaches.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] One instance of a broader pattern this database documents of overlapping, uncoordinated envoy/agency authority within the administration's foreign-policy apparatus, where a president's use of freelance envoys alongside traditional State Department channels creates real coordination risk with direct human consequences when the subject is hostage/detainee diplomacy.
confidence_note: MODERATE-HIGH confidence on the core facts: the existence of two distinct, uncoordinated negotiating tracks, their different terms, and the deal's collapse without freeing the 11 Americans it covered. These are documented in the New York Times' original reporting (also carried in syndicated newspaper copies of the same story) and picked up by other outlets such as The Advocate citing that same underlying account, so they rest on a single news organization's anonymous-source reporting rather than independent corroboration; Grenell called the Times account "bogus." MODERATE confidence on attributing ultimate responsibility for allowing the tracks to run uncoordinated to any single decision-maker: no source reviewed identifies who at the White House was responsible for permitting Grenell's parallel track, so this entry documents the dysfunction and its consequence without assigning that specific accountability. This entry is distinct from, not a duplicate of, the separate entry on the July 18, 2025 swap and the Dahud Hanid Ortiz release, which covers a different (successful, later) exchange and a different accountability concern (vetting failure, not interagency coordination failure).

official: Lindsey Halligan, Interim U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia (appointment found unlawful by a federal court)
offense_category: Vindictive/Selective Prosecution (violates Due Process; established legal doctrine, e.g. United States v. Goodwin) and unlawful interim appointment (violated the 120-day limit on serving without Senate confirmation) -- the underlying charges against James Comey were brought and then dismissed; Halligan herself has not been personally charged with anything
incident_summary:
In September 2025, President Trump forced Erik Siebert, then-U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, to resign after Siebert concluded there was insufficient evidence to charge former FBI Director James Comey with lying to Congress ("He didn't quit, I fired him!" Trump wrote on social media afterward). In the days around Siebert's ouster, Trump publicly and repeatedly pressed for charges, warning Bondi that prosecutions of his adversaries "can't delay any longer" and, just before the indictment, demanding "JUSTICE MUST BE SERVED, NOW!!!" Siebert's deputy, Maya Song, was demoted and later pushed out of the department entirely. Trump then installed Lindsey Halligan -- a former personal attorney to Trump with no prior prosecutorial experience -- as interim U.S. Attorney, and Halligan personally secured indictments against both Comey and, separately, New York Attorney General Letitia James. Comey's charges were also reportedly rushed in part because the statute of limitations on the underlying conduct was about to expire, a detail legal experts cited as further evidence the case was driven by deadline and political pressure rather than ordinary prosecutorial judgment. After the indictment, Trump called Comey a "dirty cop," predicted "there will be others," and denied having pushed DOJ to act.

Troy A. Edwards Jr. -- Comey's own son-in-law and the EDVA office's deputy chief of national security, covering CIA and Defense Department matters -- resigned effective immediately within hours of the indictment, writing "to uphold my oath to the Constitution and country, I hereby resign," a departure distinct from the pushed-out prosecutors below in that Edwards left voluntarily and was not personally targeted, but notable for having worked in the very office that indicted his father-in-law. Michael Ben'Ary, chief of EDVA's national security section, who had no role in the Comey case, was fired on October 1, 2025 after pro-Trump activist Julie Kelly posted that he was presumably "a big part of the internal resistance to the Comey indictment," leaving a letter warning DOJ leadership was "making Americans less safe" by purging career officials; separately, an FBI agent was relieved of duty after refusing to help stage a public "perp walk" of Comey following the indictment, despite no arrest warrant having been issued. Comey was arraigned on October 8, 2025 and pleaded not guilty, calling the case a politically motivated vendetta. Letitia James's indictment, filed after Halligan took over, charged her with mortgage and bank fraud tied to a Virginia property purchase -- a case career EDVA prosecutors had also declined to bring, citing weak evidence, before Halligan advanced it herself. Beyond the two indictments, the push to prosecute Comey destabilized the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Virginia: more than a half-dozen career prosecutors were demoted or pushed out amid the fallout, other prosecutors left voluntarily rather than risk being assigned to cases they viewed as improper, and unrelated major prosecutions (including a terrorism case tied to an attack in Afghanistan) were disrupted by the turmoil.

In November 2025, the Campaign for Accountability filed a bar complaint against Halligan over the Comey and James prosecutions, and DOJ publicly defended both the appointment and the underlying charges, arguing Trump's "guilty as hell" commentary about Comey was not proof of retaliatory motive. Before the appointment-based dismissal described below, Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick had already flagged serious, independent procedural problems with the Comey case. On November 5, 2025 he criticized an "indict first, investigate later" approach and ordered prosecutors to turn over grand jury materials and evidence seized in an earlier leak investigation, which the defense had not been able to review. On November 17 he identified a "disturbing pattern of profound investigative missteps," including two statements Halligan made to the grand jury that appeared to be "fundamental misstatements of the law" and the possible use of material outside the scope of the original search warrants. At a November 19 hearing before U.S. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff, prosecutors acknowledged that the two-count indictment filed against Comey -- redrafted after the grand jury rejected one of three proposed counts -- had never been shown to the full grand jury; DOJ then argued in a filing that the foreperson had confirmed the vote, and Comey moved to dismiss over the grand jury errors. On November 24, 2025, Judge Cameron Currie dismissed both indictments without prejudice, ruling that Halligan's appointment had violated the 120-day limit for serving as interim U.S. Attorney without Senate confirmation, and that all actions flowing from her defective appointment -- including securing and signing Comey's indictment -- were unlawful exercises of executive power that had to be set aside.

The November 2025 dismissal did not end the pursuit of James: DOJ signaled plans to seek new charges against her (and potentially Comey) within days, but a grand jury declined to re-indict her on December 4, 2025, and a grand jury in Alexandria declined again the following week on a revised proposed indictment that added a third felony count -- after which Magistrate Judge William Porter refused DOJ's request to seal the failed indictment, noting it had already been returned in open court and that making it public served the interest of transparency. In January 2026, prosecutors opened a new financial-transactions inquiry into James following the repeated indictment failures.

DOJ appealed the dismissal and, as of February 2026, continued to defend Halligan's appointment; earlier, on January 6, 2026, U.S. District Judge David Novak ordered Halligan to explain why she was still identifying herself as U.S. Attorney despite Judge Currie's ruling, and on January 20 he struck the title from her filings in that case, barred her from using it before him, and warned that he would initiate disciplinary proceedings against her and any other signatory if she persisted. After the district's judges unanimously selected a new U.S. Attorney to replace Halligan, then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche fired that judicially-selected replacement, James Hundley, on February 20, 2026, leaving the office without settled leadership for months. In March 2026, a cross-ideological array of amicus briefs -- spanning a center-right rule-of-law group (Society for the Rule of Law/States United), a libertarian/conservative property-rights group (Pacific Legal Foundation), the state's criminal-defense bar, and a bipartisan group of lawmakers -- all urged the Fourth Circuit to affirm that Halligan's appointment was unlawful, several specifically invoking the circuit's own Wille v. NOAA Appointments Clause precedent against the government's ratification defense. DOJ named Theo Stamos First Assistant U.S. Attorney in mid-July 2026, which under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act made her Acting U.S. Attorney -- the office's first settled leadership since Hundley's firing. The Fourth Circuit calendared the consolidated Comey/James appeals for its September 15-18, 2026 session in Richmond, limited to whether Halligan's appointment gave her legal authority to bring the charges. A panel of Judges Albert Diaz, Julius N. Richardson and Henry F. Floyd heard the argument on September 15, 2026 and expressed skepticism about DOJ's bid to revive the prosecutions; the panel reportedly focused narrowly on whether Bondi had authority to reappoint Halligan as interim U.S. Attorney a second time, and some reporting described it as seemingly poised to uphold the dismissal. The panel has not yet ruled.

offense_category: Installing a Controversial, Discredited Figure Into a Critical Biodefense Preparedness Role, Who Was Later Fired for Misrepresenting His Own Official Title -- contested; the appointment itself is a personnel/policy judgment call, not unlawful, but the misrepresentation that led to his firing is a documented, admitted-basis accountability fact
incident_summary: In May 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s department appointed Steven Hatfill -- a virologist who had promoted hydroxychloroquine as a COVID-19 treatment and criticized mRNA vaccines, and who had previously been investigated by DOJ as a person of interest in the 2001 anthrax attacks before being exonerated and awarded a $5.8 million settlement in 2008 -- as a senior adviser in the Office of the Director at the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response (ASPR), the HHS agency responsible for coordinating the nation's disaster and pandemic response. Hatfill had worked with then-trade adviser Peter Navarro during Trump's first term promoting hydroxychloroquine. On October 28, 2025, HHS fired Hatfill; a senior department official said the firing followed Hatfill misrepresenting himself as ASPR's 'chief medical officer,' a title he did not actually hold.

HHS itself, on the record, identified Hatfill's misrepresentation of his own title as the specific basis for his October 2025 firing
The appointment and firing both occurred within the same administration and HHS leadership, reflecting on the vetting process that placed him in the role

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense
offense_category: Removal of the Army's Top Officer and Senior Generals During an Active War, Replaced by Personally-Connected Successor -- a personnel-authority action within Hegseth's legal power; the accountability concern is the pattern and its command-continuity implications, not an allegation the removals themselves were unlawful
incident_summary:
On April 2, 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth forced Gen. Randy George, the Army's 41st Chief of Staff, into immediate retirement -- roughly a year and a half before the end of his traditional four-year term -- and fired two additional senior Army generals the same day: Maj. Gen. William Green Jr., the Army's chief of chaplains, and Gen. David Hodne, commander of Army Transformation and Training Command. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell announced George's departure as effective immediately. Gen. Christopher LaNeve, who had taken office as the Army's vice chief of staff in February 2026, became acting chief of staff and was reported as the likely permanent successor; LaNeve had previously served as Hegseth's senior military assistant. The Pentagon gave no reason for George's removal; The New York Times, as relayed by Al Jazeera, reported, citing unnamed military officials, that it was related to clashes between George and Hegseth over Hegseth's blocking of the promotions of four Army officers on a list of 29, two of them Black and two women. The removals occurred during the active U.S. war with Iran and extend a broader pattern of Hegseth removing senior military leadership across the armed forces; the earlier removal of the Joint Staff Director, Vice Adm. Fred Kacher, ordered by Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, is tracked separately in this database.

The Washington Post reported that Army Secretary Dan Driscoll said he had no plans to resign following clashes with Hegseth in the aftermath of the George/Hodne/Green removals and continued reports of dysfunction inside the Pentagon; the White House publicly backed Driscoll even as tensions with Hegseth continued. The Wall Street Journal reported on August 21, 2026 that Driscoll was now planning to depart by the end of 2026 amid continued Hegseth friction; Gen. LaNeve remained only acting, not Senate-confirmed, chief of staff, with no permanent nominee identified. On August 26, 2026, Forbes, citing The Washington Post and an unnamed source, reported that George was fired shortly after LaNeve told George that Hegseth wanted to back off the Army's probe of the March 28 helicopter flyby near Kid Rock's Tennessee home; George had told colleagues the investigation should proceed, per the Post's other unnamed sources. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told the Post the reporting was a "tired, old story"; no motive for George's removal has been established.

Driscoll's departure came sooner than the Journal's report indicated: after the White House confirmed his departure on Monday, August 31, he posted on X late on September 1 that Wednesday, September 2, 2026, would be his last full day as Army Secretary, giving no reason in that post. Multiple outlets (NPR, CNN, NBC News, Axios, The Hill) attribute the resignation to his clashes with Hegseth, including feeling his modernization initiatives were being blocked and the disruption caused by the George/Hodne/Green removals and other general firings. On September 3, President Trump named Adam Telle, the assistant secretary of the Army for civil works, as acting Army secretary.
elements_required: George was removed roughly 18 months before his term's traditional end, alongside two other senior generals removed the same day
The removals occurred during active U.S. combat operations against Iran, a period when command continuity carries particular institutional weight
The acting successor, Gen. LaNeve, has a documented prior personal connection to Hegseth as his former military aide, rather than being an arms-length succession
This removal follows a documented pattern of other senior military personnel changes under Hegseth's tenure (documented in this tracker's broader Hegseth personnel-purge entries)

rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: the Secretary of Defense has clear legal and constitutional authority over senior military personnel decisions, wartime conditions can create legitimate reasons to prioritize leadership alignment with current operational needs, and selecting a successor with prior direct working experience with the Secretary is not inherently improper -- it can reflect trusted operational familiarity rather than pure loyalty-based selection.
comeback: The specific concern is not that the Secretary lacks legal authority to remove senior officers, but the cumulative pattern -- a Chief of Staff removed roughly 18 months early alongside two other generals on the same day, during active combat operations, with the acting successor being the Secretary's own former personal aide -- which mirrors the same loyalty-over-independence dynamic already documented in this tracker's broader Hegseth personnel-purge entries, raising continuity-of-command and institutional-independence concerns distinguishable from an isolated, routine personnel change.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with the broader pattern this tracker documents of Hegseth removing senior military leaders (see also the Hegseth loyalty-culture entry); here the acting successor is his own former senior military assistant. The separately tracked Joint Staff Director removal (see the Kacher removal entry) was ordered by Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, with no confirmed motive.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the removals, their timing, Parnell's on-record confirmation, and LaNeve's prior role as Hegseth's senior military assistant are corroborated across NBC News, CBS News, DefenseScoop, and Al Jazeera. MODERATE confidence on characterizing LaNeve's selection as loyalty-driven specifically, since his professional qualifications as vice chief of staff are also documented and not shown to be mutually exclusive with a personal-connection factor. The Pentagon gave no reason for George's removal; the New York Times promotions-dispute account rests on unnamed officials and is reported, not confirmed. Driscoll's April statement that he had no plans to resign, the August WSJ report of an expected year-end exit, and his confirmed departure (last full day September 2, 2026, per AP and The Hill) are each independently reported; Driscoll's own post gave no reason, so the Hegseth-friction explanation rests on outlets' sourcing rather than his statement. LaNeve remains acting chief of staff, and no permanent nominee for Army Chief of Staff has been named. The August 2026 Washington Post account (via Forbes) tying George's firing to the Kid Rock flyby probe rests on unnamed sources and was dismissed by the Pentagon, so it is reported, not established.

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense / Secretary of War
offense_category: Misuse of federal law-enforcement resources and personnel for personal/family benefit -- no criminal charge; a resource-diversion/ethics accountability claim, distinguished from an ordinary personal-security story by the scale of operational Army criminal-investigative capacity pulled off its core caseload
incident_summary:
A Washington Post investigation by Tara Copp, Alex Horton and Dan Lamothe, published August 20, 2025, found that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's personal security requirements have grown so large they are straining the Army's Criminal Investigation Division (CID). CID provides protective security for senior DoD officials, but its primary mission is investigating serious Army crimes: contracting fraud, sexual assault and other violent offenses. Of CID's roughly 1,500 agents, **about 150 typically serve on personal-protective duty; that number has been increased to 400-500 agents since Hegseth took office in January 2025**. The multimillion-dollar, multi-state operation has required weeks-long protective assignments in Minnesota, Tennessee and D.C. to guard family residences, and at times has extended to monitoring residences belonging to the Hegseths' former spouses. One CID official told the Post the diversion is unlike anything in the agency's recent history; another person familiar with the operation was quoted describing the resulting strain in stark terms: 'We have complete inability to achieve our most basic missions.' The Post reported that before publishing it withheld several sensitive details: the specific size of Hegseth's protective details and the exact locations where they are assigned.

The Pentagon's public response focused on press access and framing, not on disputing the reported agent counts or the strain the Post's sources described. Spokesman Sean Parnell wrote that when 'left-wing blogs like the Washington Post continue to dox cabinet secretaries' security protocols and movements, it puts lives at risk.' He framed the story against a stated threat environment, citing two assassination attempts against President Trump, a reported 1,000% increase in assaults on ICE agents and Iranian retaliation threats, and said Hegseth's security arrangements were made at 'the full recommendation' of CID itself. CID backed that account: it said Hegseth did not request the additional coverage, and a senior Army CID official told The Hill the agency 'operates within existing resource constraints' and 'maintains a robust security posture in both the investigative and protective realms.' Those statements sit uneasily next to the accounts the Post gathered from CID staff and others familiar with the operation, who spoke anonymously, of agents pulled off criminal investigations and an agency unable to meet its most basic missions. Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson separately told Fox News Digital that the Department had tried to get the Post to remove sensitive details about the security of Hegseth's wife, children and extended family before publication. The sourcing reviewed gives no indication that the scale of the protective detail was reduced after the report.
elements_required: Army CID agents assigned to personal-protective duty increased roughly 2.5-3x (from a baseline of ~150 to 400-500 of CID's ~1,500 total agents) since Hegseth took office, diverting capacity from CID's core mission of investigating contracting fraud, sexual assault, and violent crime within the Army

The protective operation is multimillion-dollar and multi-state (Minnesota, Tennessee, D.C.), with weeks-long assignments and, per the Post's sourcing, extension to monitoring residences of the Hegseths' former spouses -- described by a CID official as unlike anything in the agency's recent history

Documented institutional harm in the words of people inside the operation, not just outside characterization: one person familiar with the operation telling the Post 'We have complete inability to achieve our most basic missions,' and a CID official describing agents taken off investigations to 'sit on luggage' or 'sit in the cars on the driveway'

Hegseth, as Secretary of Defense, is the official whose personal and family security demands drove the reassignment of CID's operational capacity, and the Pentagon defended the arrangement's scale post-reporting rather than curtailing it or disputing the specific facts reported

That CID recommended the posture does not answer what it costs: CID's institutional statement that it 'maintains a robust security posture in both the investigative and protective realms' sits against the accounts the Post gathered from CID staff and others familiar with the operation, one of whom said, 'We have complete inability to achieve our most basic missions.'

offense_category: Potential War Crime — Killing of Combatants Rendered Hors de Combat / Denial of Quarter, Plus a Separate Potential Perfidy Violation (Using an Aircraft Disguised as a Civilian Plane in the First Strike) (Law of Armed Conflict; possible domestic analogue: 18 U.S.C. §1111, murder, or Uniform Code of Military Justice provisions if applicable to the chain of command) — NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary:
Years before becoming Defense Secretary, Hegseth repeatedly used his Fox News platform and other public statements to defend battlefield executions of captured combatants and to question the laws of war. On Fox & Friends on February 13, 2019, discussing Army Maj. Mathew Golsteyn's murder charge for killing a captured, unarmed Afghan, Hegseth said, "If he committed premeditated murder, then Duncan did as well, then I did as well. What do you think you do in war?" and "Put us all in jail." In his 2024 book The War on Warriors, he wrote, "Should we follow the Geneva Conventions? What if we treated the enemy the way they treated us?" and questioned "how can anyone write universal rules about killing other people in open conflict?" He also repeatedly lobbied on Fox for presidential pardons for service members accused of war crimes and hosted their families for sympathetic interviews.

On September 2, 2025, a U.S. strike hit an alleged drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean, leaving two survivors clinging to the wreckage. A follow-up strike then killed both survivors. The Washington Post reported, citing two anonymous sources with direct knowledge of the operation, that Hegseth gave a verbal order before the first strike to "leave no survivors," and that the Special Operations commander ordered the second strike to comply with that directive. At a September 30, 2025 Quantico address to roughly 800 assembled generals and admirals, Hegseth said: "We also don't fight with stupid rules of engagement. We untie the hands of our warfighters to intimidate, demoralize, hunt and kill the enemies of our country. No more politically correct and overbearing rules of engagement."

At a December 4, 2025 briefing, Adm. Bradley reportedly told lawmakers the boat was heading toward Suriname to transfer its drugs to a larger vessel, though he argued the shipment could ultimately have reached the U.S. -- a more indirect route than the administration's original framing; survivors were seen waving atop the wreckage after the first strike, an act lawmakers disputed the meaning of, and, by the AP's account of Sen. Cotton's remarks, the first and follow-up attacks consisted of four missile strikes in all. On November 29, 2025, a coalition of former military lawyers (the Former Judge Advocates General Working Group), responding to the Washington Post's original reporting, issued a public memo arguing that "orders to kill survivors of an attack at sea are patently illegal" and that "anyone who issues or follows such orders can and should be prosecuted for war crimes, murder, or both," citing Geneva Convention protections for those out of the fight and arguing the survivors should have been treated as prisoners of war once defenseless. Media Matters resurfaced Hegseth's years-long public record on December 5, 2025, days after the boat-strike kill-order allegation broke, framing it as a years-long public record of endorsing exactly the kind of unlawful-killing conduct now under investigation -- this does not resolve whether Hegseth in fact gave the specific "leave no survivors" order, but documents the on-the-record history described above.

CNN reported in January 2026 that the aircraft used in the September 2 first strike was painted as a civilian aircraft and was part of a closely guarded classified program; according to The New York Times, as relayed by Human Rights Watch, it had no visible military markings and carried its weapons concealed inside its fuselage, and officials were told it flew low enough that people aboard the target boat could see it before the attack. Pentagon officials told lawmakers the operation was hurried and the aircraft was the most available at the time, and administration officials said it was not pretending to be civilian -- but U.S. military law-of-war doctrine treats "feigning civilian status and then attacking" as perfidy, a distinct violation the Defense Department's own manual specifically names as an example of the practice, adding a second potential legal violation alongside the denial-of-quarter/kill-order allegation, though legal experts told CNN it is not clear the law of war applied.

The underlying strike campaign has since expanded dramatically: as of mid-2026, the U.S. military has conducted more than 60 strikes against alleged drug-trafficking vessels in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific since September 2025, killing more than 200 people. Both Armed Services Committees' Republican chairs (Rogers in the House, Wicker in the Senate) declared their own committees' probes closed in December 2025, over Democrats' public objection. Sen. Mark Warner, the Senate Intelligence Committee's vice chair, and the other Gang of Eight Democrats instead pressed for the unedited strike video to be released to the public or at least to all members of Congress. On December 9, 2025, the ACLU, Center for Constitutional Rights, and NYCLU filed a FOIA lawsuit seeking release of the DOJ Office of Legal Counsel opinion the administration has repeatedly cited as the campaign's legal basis; a federal judge heard arguments June 24, 2026, and on September 30, 2026 rejected two of the three privileges the government invoked to withhold the opinion, reserved judgment on the third, and ordered the memo produced for his private review. Congress separately made three failed attempts in November-December 2025 to force an end to the campaign under the War Powers Resolution, tracked in its own entry in this database. The Department of War Inspector General opened its own formal evaluation, set out in a May 11, 2026 letter, of whether Southern Command followed standard targeting procedure across the campaign.

The War Department's mandatory annual civilian-harm report, delivered to Congress August 11, 2026, found zero civilian deaths in the boat strikes it reviewed from 2025 -- a finding government officials themselves, speaking to The Intercept, called "a total whitewash" and said reflects the Pentagon having "absolutely no credibility" on this question; reporting also notes CENTCOM's civilian-protection team has been cut from 10 staff to 1 under Hegseth, limiting the department's own capacity to investigate harm claims. On the appropriations front, Congress withheld 25% of Hegseth's travel budget in the FY2026 NDAA to force release of the strike videos. For FY2027, the Senate Armed Services Committee's draft would raise that to 75% and also demand the Minab school-strike investigation, while the House committee's draft did not include similar language. The Senate blocked its bill on a 50-46 cloture vote on July 14, 2026, after the administration resumed airstrikes on Iran without new congressional authorization; the House passed its own FY2027 NDAA 216-212 in July 2026, leaving the two versions to be reconciled in conference.

The same cartel-FTO legal theory underlying this maritime campaign was separately pushed toward an even more expansive form -- land strikes inside Mexico -- first by DEA leadership internally in early 2025 (rejected by the Pentagon/White House as unauthorized) and later by Trump himself in a January 2026 public threat; that proposal is tracked in its own entry in this database, since it involves a different agency, target country, and no actual strikes carried out.

By October 4, 2026, the campaign's cumulative toll had grown to **at least 235 people killed across 70 strikes**; strikes on September 19 and October 4, 2026 each killed four people, with the military providing no evidence the September 19 boat was carrying drugs and citing only unspecified "confirmed intelligence" for the October 4 strike.

In a September 2026 briefing note, Ben Saul, the U.N. Human Rights Council's Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms while countering terrorism, concluded that the attacks "amount to serial extrajudicial killings in violation of the right to life" and that "there are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law." The note's count runs only to August 2026, so it does not include the September and October strikes counted above. It rejected the administration's self-defense justification, finding that the targeted groups "have not mounted any 'armed attack' on the United States" and that there was no evidence anyone aboard the vessels posed an imminent threat. It also described "at least one incident" in which "two shipwrecked survivors of an initial strike were subsequently targeted and killed, in violation of the right to life and the duty to rescue at sea" -- matching the September 2, 2025 strike at the center of this entry, though the note does not name the date. It called on the United States to investigate, to prosecute those responsible "including military and political leaders who ordered the attacks," and to provide reparation to victims and their families. Saul is an independent U.N. expert, not a court, and the note is a legal assessment rather than a judicial finding; the State Department had not responded to The Guardian's request for comment.

rebuttal_anticipated: Bradley testified there was no kill order -- this is anonymous-sourced reporting versus the actual commanding officer on record.
comeback: Set the order question aside entirely. Two facts aren't contested by anybody: there were two survivors after the first strike, and a second strike killed them. Lawmakers who saw the video -- not anonymous sources, members of Congress -- called it 'one of the most troubling things' they'd seen or said they were 'deeply disturbed.' Whoever gave the order, killing static survivors with no means of escape is the legal question, and that's the one nobody is denying happened. The scale point matters too: this is no longer a single contested incident but part of a campaign of 70 strikes and at least 235 deaths (per Stars and Stripes, as of Oct. 4, 2026) that both parties in Congress are now using appropriations leverage to force accountability on -- that escalating bipartisan response is itself evidence the underlying concern isn't a partisan characterization. offense_category: Removal of a Career Officer Reportedly Over His Past Service With a Trump Critic, Overriding the Officer's Own Service Secretary -- distinct from this tracker's Harvard entry, which concerns an academic institutional relationship rather than an individual officer's career
incident_summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered Army Secretary Dan Driscoll to remove Col. Dave Butler from his position as Chief of Army Public Affairs and chief advisor to Driscoll. Hegseth made the demand on Thursday, February 12, 2026, and Fox News first reported the ouster on February 17, while Driscoll was in Geneva serving on the U.S. negotiating team to end the Ukraine war. Butler, a 28-year Army veteran, had previously served as head of public affairs for the Joint Chiefs under Gen. Mark Milley -- who became a public critic of President Trump. A source told The Hill that Hegseth did not like that Butler had worked for Milley, and The Washington Post reported that Butler's work as Milley's senior spokesman appeared to be a factor in his removal; The New York Times reported that Hegseth also blamed Butler for news articles that compared him unfavorably to Driscoll. None of the reporting cited a performance problem in Butler's current role. Driscoll, an Army veteran and close ally of Vice President JD Vance, had reportedly resisted Hegseth's pressure to remove Butler for months because of Butler's contributions to the transformation of the Army. Butler, slated for his first star, was on an Army list of 34 officers selected for promotion that Hegseth had held up for nearly four months, reportedly over concerns about four to five officers on it whom by law he could not remove; according to an Army official, Butler volunteered to take his name off the list if that would unlock the other promotions. Butler ultimately transitioned out of his position and retired after 28 years of service, rather than being reassigned elsewhere in the Army.

Driscoll himself submitted his resignation as Secretary of the Army, confirmed by the White House on August 31, 2026, after months of friction with Hegseth. CBS News's report on the resignation does not mention Butler; it points to broader tension, including Hegseth's ouster of Driscoll's close friend Gen. Randy George as Army chief of staff and Driscoll's concerns about the Army's transformation efforts and Hegseth's pushing out of some of the generals responsible for them.
