official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense; Steve Feinberg, Deputy Secretary of Defense
offense_category: Centralizing and Restricting All Defense Department Communication With Congress, Drawing Bipartisan Accusations of Obstructing Congressional Oversight of the Military
incident_summary: On October 15, 2025 -- the same day most Pentagon press-corps reporters walked out rather than sign new Hegseth-imposed reporting restrictions -- Hegseth and Deputy Secretary Steve Feinberg signed a memo **requiring nearly all Defense Department personnel, including the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, to obtain prior approval from the Pentagon's Office of Legislative Affairs before any communication with members of Congress or state elected officials, whether in Washington or elsewhere**. The memo's scope covers congressional reporting requirements, information requests, technical assistance, drafting support, and legislative correspondence; it exempts only the Inspector General's office, the comptroller, general counsel, and personnel invoking whistleblower or other legally protected communications. The memo stated the requirement 'ensures consistency and support for the Department's priorities to re-establish deterrence, rebuild our military, and revive the warrior ethos,' warning that 'unauthorized engagements with Congress...no matter how well-intentioned, may undermine Department-wide priorities critical to achieving our legislative objectives.' Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell called it 'a pragmatic step to internally review' communications intended to 'improve accuracy and responsiveness,' insisting the review is purely internal and 'does not change how or from whom Congress receives information.' Lawmakers from both parties disputed that characterization: Senate Armed Services Committee ranking member Sen. Jack Reed (D) said centralizing all DoD-Congress communication through Hegseth's own office 'raises serious questions about transparency,' House Armed Services Committee ranking member Rep. Adam Smith (D) said he was 'deeply concerned that this memo signals the administration's intent to further restrict communication,' and Rep. Don Bacon (R), a retired Air Force brigadier general, called it an 'amateur move' that 'put a large barrier between the military and Congress.' official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (with President Trump as the removing authority)
offense_category: Politicized Removal of the Joint Chiefs Chairman, Chief of Naval Operations, and the Service Judge Advocates General Without Stated Cause -- the JAG removals specifically raise a contested statutory concern under the law protecting judge advocates' independent legal advice function
incident_summary:
On the night of Friday, February 21, 2025, the Trump administration fired Gen. CQ Brown Jr., Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and only the second Black officer to hold the post; Adm. Lisa Franchetti, Chief of Naval Operations and the first woman to hold that role; and Gen. Jim Slife, Air Force Vice Chief of Staff -- the first time in U.S. history two sitting members of the Joint Chiefs of Staff had been removed simultaneously. The same night, Hegseth announced he was removing the Judge Advocates General (the top uniformed lawyers) of the Army, Navy, and Air Force and requesting nominations for all three posts. That fired Lt. Gen. Joseph Berger (Army) and Lt. Gen. Charles Plummer (Air Force); the Navy post was already vacant after Vice Adm. Christopher French's resignation, and its acting JAG, Rear Adm. Lia Reynolds, stayed on pending a replacement -- a set of removals legal commentators dubbed the "Friday Night Massacre of Judge Advocates General." No public, on-record reason was given for any of the removals when they were announced. Hegseth announced Trump intended to nominate retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Dan Caine as the new Joint Chiefs chairman. Sen. Jack Reed (D-RI), ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, characterized the firings as "part of a broader, premeditated campaign by President Trump and Secretary Hegseth to purge talented officers for politically charged reasons," a characterization widely connected in contemporaneous and later reporting -- including The Guardian's March 15, 2025 retrospective on Hegseth's broader reshaping of the Pentagon -- to the administration's stated opposition to diversity, equity, and inclusion policies and to Hegseth's public, pre-confirmation criticism of Brown's and Franchetti's selection. This entry documents the origin point of a pattern this tracker separately documents continuing into 2026 through the removal of Vice Adm. Fred Kacher as Director of the Joint Staff, the forced retirement of Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George, and Hegseth's later interventions blocking promotions of Black and female officers -- each tracked in this database's own entries.

The pattern of removing senior women extended in July 2025 when the Pentagon reassigned Vice Adm. Yvette Davids, the first woman to lead the U.S. Naval Academy, out of that post roughly 18 months into her tenure, replacing her with Marine Corps Lt. Gen. Michael J. Borgschulte (the Academy's first Marine superintendent) and moving Davids to a deputy CNO role. The Hill reported Davids' reassignment made her at least the fifth senior female service member moved out of a leadership role since January 2025, alongside Franchetti, and cited experts warning the pattern -- combined with Hegseth's pre-confirmation record of statements opposing women in combat roles -- could have a "chilling effect" on women's enlistment and career advancement in the armed forces.

The Senate confirmed replacements for the Army JAG post (Maj. Gen. Bobby Christine) on June 29, 2025 and the Navy JAG post (Marine Maj. Gen. David Bligh) on July 31, 2025. The Air Force post stayed vacant longer. Defense One reported October 23, 2025 -- eight months after Plummer's ouster -- that acting Air Force JAG Maj. Gen. Rebecca Vernon, who had taken the role after the purge, had herself stepped down, with no one yet nominated to fill the post permanently; Hegseth had said he removed the Army and Air Force JAGs because they were "roadblocks to orders that are given by a commander in chief." Trump nominated Brig. Gen. Christopher Eason for the Air Force post in December 2025, and the Senate confirmed him on January 30, 2026.

Dan Caine was confirmed as Joint Chiefs chairman in April 2025, and the removals stand finalized with no court challenge specific to them identified -- distinguish from the separately litigated 2025 inspectors general firings, tracked elsewhere in this database, which produced an actual court finding. Brown himself has since become a public critic: in a July 3, 2026 Foreign Affairs essay co-authored with Duke political scientist Peter Feaver and attorney Andrew Kragie, Brown and his co-authors wrote that when presidents use the armed forces for "politically contentious missions, such as addressing domestic crime in cities," the military's work "becomes more fraught," and that "if you ask too much of the military, you risk the entire enterprise"; at the Aspen Ideas Festival the previous week, Brown said the pattern of Pentagon personnel firings is "not about merit," questioning whether remaining officers "are going to have a fair opportunity to advance in their career going forth."
elements_required: 10 U.S.C. provisions governing the Judge Advocates General prohibit any DoD officer or employee from interfering with a TJAG's ability to give independent legal advice to the service Secretary or Chief of Staff, or with any judge advocate's ability to give independent legal advice to commanders -- [contested application, not adjudicated] removing the service JAGs simultaneously (the Army and Air Force JAGs fired, the acting Navy JAG slated for replacement), without stated cause, is argued by legal commentators (Lawfare, Justia/Verdict) to functionally undermine this independent-advice protection, though the statute does not clearly specify removal procedure and the administration's Article II removal authority over these positions is itself a live legal question, not settled

The Joint Chiefs Chairman and service-chief removals themselves fall within the President's broad Article II authority to remove senior military leadership and are not, on their own, alleged to violate a specific statute -- the accountability concern here is the documented pattern and stated politicized motive, not an established legal violation for those two removals specifically

Multiple independent, on-record sources (Sen. Jack Reed, legal scholars writing in Lawfare and Verdict/Justia) characterized the same-night, first-ever-simultaneous scope of the removals as evidence of a coordinated, politically motivated purge rather than case-by-case performance-based personnel decisions

On March 1, 2026, an Iranian one-way attack drone struck a tactical operations center at Port Shuaiba, Kuwait, killing six soldiers of the U.S. Army's 103rd Sustainment Command and wounding more than 30 others. Soldiers told The Washington Post, which interviewed 17 people including survivors and other firsthand witnesses, that the unit's commander, Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes, and his superior, Maj. Gen. John Hinson, had been briefed that Port Shuaiba was on an Iranian target list and that the unit's own force-protection assessments advised against the move, but sent the troops there anyway; soldiers also said Army Central did not fulfill the unit's request for a truck-mounted EAGLS counter-drone system, and one said it "was denied because of lack of assets." Survivors told CBS News the facility's defenses -- T-walls designed to stop mortar and rocket fragments, not aerial drone strikes, with vertical blast barricades but no overhead protection -- were essentially nonexistent against the actual threat: one survivor rated the position's drone-specific defense as "none." CBS News reported that most other troops in Kuwait had been relocated farther from Iranian range while the unit was moved to Port Shuaiba, and survivors described a chaotic aftermath with severe injuries (perforated eardrums, heavy bleeding, head wounds) in which soldiers triaged one another with makeshift bandages and drove the wounded to Kuwaiti hospitals in commandeered civilian vehicles. A soldier ordered to flee with Barnes later told The Washington Post that the general ran to a protective bunker after the blast while dozens under his command remained behind, and none of the troops the Post interviewed recalled seeing Barnes or Hinson help carry out the dead or tend the wounded; Army Central said leadership assisted with the evacuation before being medically evacuated for their own injuries. Secretary Hegseth publicly described the attacking drone as a "squirter" that penetrated the defenses of a "fortified" position -- a characterization survivors directly dispute, with one soldier stating: "Painting a picture that 'one squeaked through' is a falsehood. I want people to know the unit ... was unprepared to provide any defense for itself." Soldiers who were present say they fear no one will be held accountable for the command decisions that left them exposed.

At an April 29, 2026 House Armed Services Committee hearing, Rep. Pat Ryan asked Hegseth whether the survivors who contradicted his account were lying; Hegseth asked whether Ryan was "just going to monologue falsehoods all over the place" and said the Pentagon had moved 7,000 troops "off of the X" based on intelligence. The Army completed its more than 350-page investigation in early July 2026, and Army officials briefed the families of the six soldiers killed privately on July 9; according to sources and officials cited by CBS News and The Washington Post, the review assigned no fault and did not address punitive action, and it has not been released publicly. An Army official told The Post that Hinson initially appointed a mid-career officer under his own command to conduct the review before Army Central took it over under a more senior officer, a choice lawmakers later questioned. At a July 21, 2026 Senate Appropriations Committee hearing, asked by Sen. Tammy Baldwin about the denial of counter-drone systems to the unit, Hegseth claimed "there was not a single drone or defense request denied at any level," according to Baldwin's later letter, which says soldiers' accounts to The Post contradict him; he also said he would coordinate with CENTCOM to provide more information to Congress. A 13-lawmaker bicameral letter led by Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Ryan, dated July 29 and released July 30, 2026, followed up on an April 2026 inquiry whose questions, the lawmakers said, Hegseth had not fully answered; it asked 23 questions, including why the investigation was first assigned to an officer under a commander's own chain of command, and set an August 12, 2026 deadline. On August 5, 2026, Baldwin wrote to CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper asking him, by August 18, to release the investigation's findings publicly and to give Congress the full unredacted report, its underlying documents and the classified Army Central review of pre-strike intelligence warnings and the post's defenses. No Pentagon response to either the August 12 or August 18 deadline, and no public release of the Army Central report, has been identified. In September 2026, CBS News reported, citing multiple sources, that Barnes had rejected at least two scouted relocation options in Saudi Arabia despite Army intelligence briefings from January onward that Port Shuaiba was a potential target, and more than 20 congressional Democrats asked the chairmen of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees to hold public hearings on the strike.

On October 5, 2026, the Associated Press reported that nine wounded service members, speaking on the record, described a military medical system that left them in many ways fighting to get treatment on their own. Lt. Col. Arturo Lincón, hit by shrapnel that severed an artery and embedded in a vertebra and left a damaged vertebral artery that put him at risk for a stroke, was not admitted to Landstuhl Regional Medical Center in Germany; he was sent to nearby Army barracks and told to schedule outpatient appointments. Chief Warrant Officer 4 Rodney Bearman said soldiers flown out of Kuwait on a cargo plane some 10 days after the attack, because Iranian missiles and drones made evacuation flights risky, learned in Germany that they had not been documented as wounded in combat, which he attributed to a coding error, and would not be hospitalized at Landstuhl. Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom said he waited over four months for his MRI results, and medical records he and another officer shared show they were not diagnosed with traumatic brain injuries until they reached Fort Hood. The Pentagon has said the medical care was appropriate, and a Pentagon official said Landstuhl's mission is to stabilize patients for transfer to U.S. military hospitals rather than admit them. The Army declined to comment, saying it had not yet briefed the families of those killed on the outcome of its investigation; it said the primary next of kin "will be scheduled for briefs on the official findings of the completed investigation," although the AP reported that Gold Star families had received a broad-overview briefing on the findings from Lt. Gen. Patrick Frank, then head of Army Central, in early July; Tina Marzan, the widow of Chief Warrant Officer 3 Robert Marzan, said there was no admission of error. An official told the AP the report has not been released, citing the need to redact sensitive information.

In a companion report the same day, based on interviews with 13 soldiers, primarily officers, the AP reported that officers overseeing protection told Hinson and Barnes, among others, in meetings that Port Shuaiba would not be safe for troops because it lacked air protection against drones, according to five soldiers who were present, and that Lt. Gen. Frank signed off on the move when Hinson briefed him, according to Lt. Col. Tim Halbur and another senior officer; the AP also reported that neither Hinson nor Barnes was empowered to change anti-air or drone defenses at the site. Maj. Billy Key, an operations planner, told the AP that on the night before the strike at least five quadcopter drones hovered over the port and appeared to be surveilling the U.S. site, and that he reported it to senior officers; intelligence briefings had warned that quadcopters were a sign of impending strikes. A medical service officer had prepared an evacuation plan, but she was among a group sent to Jordan and the plan was never briefed or put into place. One senior officer filed a complaint against Barnes and Hinson with the Army's inspector general; in a July 20 letter reviewed by the AP, the inspector general concluded, based on "the limited evidence" the officer provided, that Barnes had not engaged in misconduct or "ignored reliable intelligence," and noted that the complaint against Hinson had been withdrawn, which the officer disputed to the AP.

status: The Army's completed investigation, reportedly assigning no fault, remains unreleased; an Army IG letter, citing limited evidence, found no misconduct by Barnes. No reply to August congressional deadlines has been found, and wounded soldiers fault their medical care.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: wartime positioning and infrastructure decisions involve resource and threat-assessment tradeoffs made under uncertainty, and any forward-deployed logistics unit faces some residual risk that cannot be fully eliminated regardless of prior warnings; Secretary Hegseth's public characterization may reflect the information available to him at the time rather than a deliberate misrepresentation. In a July 20 letter, the Army inspector general found, on the limited evidence one complainant provided, that Brig. Gen. Barnes had not engaged in misconduct or ignored reliable intelligence, and the AP reported that neither Barnes nor Maj. Gen. Hinson was empowered to change the site's anti-air or drone defenses.
comeback: The specific facts distinguishing this from an inherent wartime risk are the survivors' detailed accounts, some on the record, of repeated specific warnings that went unheeded, positioning within a known threat radius while other units were relocated out of it, and post-strike conduct (generals allegedly leaving the building while soldiers tended the wounded) that is a separate and additional issue from the initial positioning decision -- none of which is explained by ordinary wartime uncertainty, and all of which directly contradicts the Secretary's own public description of the facility as 'fortified.' The inspector general's finding rested, by its own terms, on limited evidence from a single complainant who says the complaint against Hinson was not withdrawn, and the AP separately reports, from five soldiers present at briefings, that the generals were told the port was unsafe for lack of air protection against drones and, from two senior officers, that Army Central's commander approved the move -- which puts the decision to station troops at a site without drone defenses, rather than the generals' authority over those defenses, at the center of the dispute.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Fits a pattern this tracker documents during the Iran campaign of Pentagon leadership publicly contesting unfavorable accounts of specific incidents and holding completed investigations back from Congress and the public. Here, Hegseth called the Port Shuaiba post "fortified" while survivors describe it as undefended against drones, and the Army's finished review remains unreleased past congressional deadlines. The Iran school-strike entry shows the same withholding on a separate incident: a finalized Pentagon investigation not released to Congress or the public, amid reported White House pressure on Hegseth and Adm. Cooper to portray the war as successful. Neither case establishes why the findings were withheld.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the strike's occurrence and casualty figures (six killed; more than 30 wounded per CBS News's March 11 hospitalization count, The Washington Post and lawmakers' letters, though some CBS reports say more than 20). HIGH confidence that survivors have made detailed, consistent accounts of inadequate drone defenses, ignored warnings, a denied counter-drone request, missing medical support and generals leaving the building after the blast, across The Washington Post's July 12 report and several CBS News reports (a March 4 Post imagery analysis separately found no overhead protection); most are anonymous, but Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom and Master Sgt. Ann Marie Carrier spoke on the record. These remain allegations: Army Central says the post was fortified and that leadership helped evacuate personnel, and a U.S. official told The Post the investigation found a layered defense around the port. The Post names Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes and Maj. Gen. John Hinson as the generals soldiers blame for the positioning decision. HIGH confidence on the April 29 'monologue falsehoods' exchange (Truthout's hearing report) and on Hegseth's July 21 'not a single drone or defense request denied at any level' statement, which Sen. Baldwin quotes verbatim in her August 5 letter. HIGH confidence that the investigation was first assigned to an officer under Hinson's command, per an Army official quoted by The Post. HIGH confidence on the July 29/30 Warren-Ryan letter and the August 5 Baldwin letter and their deadlines, from the lawmakers' own letters. HIGH confidence that nine wounded soldiers told the Associated Press on the record (October 5, 2026) of post-evacuation care failures, including non-admission at Landstuhl, a combat-wound coding error and delayed MRI results; these are their accounts, and the Pentagon says the care was appropriate. No Pentagon response to either deadline, and no public release of the investigation, has been found. MEDIUM-HIGH confidence on the AP's October 5 companion account of pre-strike warnings (five soldiers present at briefings; Lt. Gen. Frank's sign-off per two officers; quadcopters seen the night before per Maj. Key; an evacuation plan never briefed), which is attributed to named and anonymous soldiers. HIGH confidence that a July 20 Army inspector general letter, reviewed by the AP, found on limited evidence that Barnes had not engaged in misconduct or ignored reliable intelligence -- a counterpoint to the survivors' accounts.

offense_category: Posse Comitatus Act (cited by the court as 10 U.S.C. 1385) -- a federal district judge found after trial that the 2025 Los Angeles deployment of federalized California National Guard troops and Marines violated the Act's bar on using the military to execute domestic law; the ruling is stayed and on appeal, and no criminal charge is involved
incident_summary: On June 7, 2025, after protests against immigration raids in Los Angeles, President Trump issued a memorandum calling the National Guard into federal service to protect immigration agents and federal property, citing 10 U.S.C. 12406 rather than the Insurrection Act. That night, over the objections of Gov. Gavin Newsom, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth federalized 2,000 California National Guard members; on June 9 he federalized 2,000 more and announced that about 700 active-duty Marines from Camp Pendleton were deploying to Los Angeles. The roughly 4,700 troops were placed under Task Force 51, U.S. Army North's command post. California sued on June 9. After a three-day trial in August, Senior U.S. District Judge Charles R. Breyer ruled on September 2, 2025, that **"at Defendants' orders and contrary to Congress's explicit instruction, federal troops executed the laws,"** using armed soldiers and military vehicles to set up protective perimeters and traffic blockades, engage in crowd control and demonstrate a military presence. He found that Hegseth himself approved a July 7 operation at MacArthur Park, ordering troops there as a "show of presence," and recounted a July 10 raid on a Camarillo cannabis farm, where about 80 Task Force 51 troops helped form a perimeter after the lead agency had canceled, then renewed, its request for help. Breyer barred Hegseth and the Defense Department from using troops in California for arrests, searches, traffic control, crowd control and similar law enforcement, and warned that Trump and Hegseth's stated plans to send troops to other cities risked "creating a national police force with the President as its chief." The Ninth Circuit temporarily stayed the injunction on September 4, 2025, saying the stay was not a decision on the merits. In December 2025, Breyer separately enjoined the continued federalization of the Guard, and the federalized troops were later returned to California's control. In January 2026, the Ninth Circuit put the government's Posse Comitatus appeal on hold pending related appeals; a September 8, 2026 joint status report said it remains on hold. On October 7, 2026, MS NOW reported on an Army North after-action review, obtained by the National Immigration Law Center through a public-records request, that experts said strongly suggests troops of the Guard's 49th Military Police Brigade took custody of and transported immigrant detainees at Camarillo, facts the court had not considered. Per MS NOW, the review says federal agents had no clear plan for moving detainees, the lead agent told troops the Defense Department had approved Guard "personnel to transport detainees in military vehicles," and hundreds of detainees were taken to Naval Base Ventura County; it does not say who drove. **At least 361 people were detained in the raid, and one immigrant died after falling from a roof.** U.S. Northern Command denied that its personnel detained or transported anyone. A former Defense Department lawyer told MS NOW that detention would count as executing the laws, but experts said the document alone is not enough to conclude a violation.

rebuttal_anticipated: The government argued that the President has inherent constitutional authority to protect federal property and personnel, an exception to the Posse Comitatus Act, and that troops only protected federal functions. The Ninth Circuit stayed the ruling, and the appeal is unresolved. On Camarillo, Northern Command says no personnel detained or transported detainees and no military vehicles were used to transport them, and the Army review does not say who drove; federal agents may have kept custody.
comeback: Breyer rejected the protective-power theory after a trial: the Act allows exceptions only where the Constitution or Congress "expressly authorize[]" them, and the claimed reading of the President's duty to execute the laws is one the Supreme Court rejected in Youngstown. official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense
offense_category: Demoting Deterrence of China Behind Homeland and Domestic 'Enemy Within' Priorities in the National Defense Strategy, Over the Joint Chiefs Chairman's Own Private Objection
incident_summary: The Washington Post reported September 29, 2025 that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's forthcoming National Defense Strategy, publicly branded 'America First, Peace Through Strength,' was a substantial departure from the two prior National Defense Strategies (2018 and 2022), both of which centered on deterring China as the pacing threat. **The new strategy instead emphasized homeland security and framed domestic threats -- what Hegseth and administration officials have called 'the enemy within' -- as a priority alongside or ahead of great-power deterrence, while pulling resources from Ukraine and Europe even as Russia continued its invasion**. According to the Post, Gen. Dan 'Razin' Caine, the Trump-appointed Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and a figure the administration has otherwise treated as a loyalist, personally pushed back on the strategy in private before its release. The Post said he gave Hegseth what one source described as 'very frank feedback' and specifically urged him to keep the department focused on being able to 'deter and, if necessary, defeat China in a conflict.' The same source questioned whether Hegseth grasped the strategy's stakes: 'I don't know if Hegseth even understands the magnitude of the NDS, which is why I think Caine tried so hard.' The Post reported that Caine's objection was not isolated: other career military officials described 'serious unease' with the pivot, and Hegseth's broader move away from longtime U.S. allies has alienated Pentagon seniors. The reporting came four days after CSIS began publicly asking (September 25, 2025) why Hegseth was summoning generals and admirals to Washington, and one day before Hegseth's September 30, 2025 Quantico summit of hundreds of generals and admirals. That summit is a separate event with its own entry in this tracker; its content (fitness/grooming standards, hazing rules, Trump's 'training grounds' remarks) concerned internal culture and domestic force-use policy, not the strategy's China/homeland prioritization shift. The Pentagon released the unclassified strategy on January 23, 2026. According to CSIS, it names homeland defense and the Western Hemisphere as the priority region and lists deterring China in the Indo-Pacific as the second priority, a marked shift from prior strategies, while it 'continues to emphasize the importance of deterring China in the Indo-Pacific.' No public reversal of the homeland/domestic-threat prioritization or restoration of a China-first framing has been identified in sourcing reviewed, and Caine has continued to serve as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense
offense_category: Politicization of a Merit-Based Military Promotion Process -- no criminal charge; this is an accountability claim about breaking longstanding norms insulating officer promotions from political interference, with a disparate-impact pattern along race and gender lines
incident_summary:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth personally removed officers from the Navy's slate of captains selected for promotion to one-star admiral by a board of senior Navy admirals. The New York Times reported on June 1, 2026, citing four current and former defense officials who spoke on condition of anonymity, that he had blocked at least seven of the selected officers, including at least two women, two Black men and three white men; a defense official later told Spectrum News that the board had selected 31 officers and Hegseth struck nine, including three women and two Black men. The resulting 22-nominee list, released publicly in late May 2026, includes no women, although women make up about 21% of the active-duty Navy, and appears to include only two nonwhite officers, although racial minorities make up about 38% of the active-duty Navy. The officials called the removals highly unusual: under Pentagon rules, the defense secretary is supposed to pull officers from a list only for moral, mental, physical or professional failings that raise questions about their fitness to lead. Current and former Navy officials said the officers struck appear to have been targeted for taking part in diversity-related events years or even decades earlier, and ABC News's sources said reasons included participation or involvement in military Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion initiatives. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell declined to say why the officers were removed, saying the department "will never consider the color of a service member's skin or their gender as a factor in promotions." No reversal or restoration of the removed officers has been identified.

Earlier, on March 27, 2026, The New York Times reported that Hegseth had removed four Army colonels (two Black men, two women) from a one-star general promotion list over the repeated objections of Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll, who cited what the Times called the colonels' "decadeslong records of exemplary service." A March 31 Georgetown Institute for Women, Peace and Security analysis noted that senior military officials could not recall a defense secretary selectively removing individual officers from a vetted promotion slate. Military officials also told the Times that Hegseth's chief of staff, Lt. Col. Ricky Buria, had told Driscoll during a heated exchange the previous summer, over the promotion of a different officer, that Trump would not want to stand next to a Black female officer; Buria called that account "completely false." NBC News reported April 2, 2026, citing nine U.S. officials, that Hegseth had blocked or delayed promotions for more than a dozen Black and female senior officers across all four military branches; one of the officials said no service had been immune. Appearing before the House Armed Services Committee later that spring, Hegseth acknowledged pulling names from the Army one-star list but declined to give the specific grounds, speaking instead of a need to correct years of "gender and demographic engineering."

Sen. Jack Reed (D-RI), the Senate Armed Services Committee's ranking member, has issued repeated public statements condemning the pattern and asserting that governing law reserves promotion-list removal authority to the President alone, not the Secretary of Defense -- a statutory-authority theory distinct from the disparate-impact framing above -- and cited a disparity in which women and minorities are under 20% of the general officer corps but nearly 60% of those Hegseth has fired or sidelined. Seven Democratic senators sent Hegseth a written demand for explanation on July 6, 2026, with an August 30, 2026 response deadline. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell publicly rejected the senators' letter around July 8, 2026, calling it a partisan push to "re-politicize military promotions" and stating decisions are "driven solely by merit"; no confirmation has been found either way of a separate formal written response by the August 30 deadline. On July 15, 2026, Sens. Cory Booker (D-NJ) and Brian Schatz (D-HI) asked the Defense Department's Inspector General to review Hegseth's removal of officers from promotion selection boards' lists.

The removal pattern itself continued escalating: The New York Times reported (August 28, 2026) four more Army officers selected for one-star rank blocked, in a move that appeared to target officers who had worked for generals Hegseth does not like, and a cumulative total of at least 45 officers removed from promotion lists this year, more than half female or Black -- a figure markedly larger than previously documented counts, not independently reconciled against them. NBC News reported (September 1, 2026) that Hegseth had removed at least six more Army officers from a list of 18 one-star generals selected for promotion to two-star rank.

incident_summary: Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA), Vice Chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, had a classified oversight visit to the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA) headquarters in Springfield, Virginia planned for Friday, September 5, 2025. The visit was long scheduled and weeks in the making, and it was routine: Warner said he had made visits like it regularly under both Democratic and Republican administrations. In the days before, far-right activist Laura Loomer posted a series of social-media attacks. She called Warner a 'rabid Trump hater' who had attacked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. She also criticized NGA Director Vice Adm. Frank 'Trey' Whitworth (a Biden appointee) and demanded both that the meeting be scrapped and that Whitworth be fired. Warner said Trump administration political appointees then canceled the visit. In a September 2, 2025 statement on the 'Trump Administration Blocking Congressional Intelligence Oversight,' he called it a 'nakedly political decision' that 'undermines the dedicated, nonpartisan staff at NGA and threatens the principle of civilian oversight,' and warned that the administration appeared 'desperate to please Loomer.' **Loomer publicly took credit, posting that Whitworth's 'scheduled September 5th fireside love fest...has been CANCELED!'** She also renewed her call for Hegseth to fire him. The Pentagon disputed Warner's account: a Defense Department official said the visit was 'rescheduled, not canceled...to accommodate bipartisan participation in the town hall event.' No reporting reviewed confirms the visit was ever held on a later date. On September 18, 2025, Warner took the episode to the Senate floor in a speech warning more broadly of intelligence politicization. He cited the NGA visit alongside the already-documented Loomer-driven firings of NSA Director Gen. Timothy Haugh and NSC staff (see the related entries below) as part of the same pattern, and said: 'If we continue to allow politics to dictate what intelligence is acceptable, we are effectively flying blind.' Whitworth left the NGA director post in November 2025, roughly two months after Loomer's public campaign to have him fired. No sourcing found ties his departure to that campaign specifically. He moved to a private-sector role (Satellogic) in 2026, and no reporting has characterized his NGA exit as a forced removal.

incident_summary: On August 28, 2026, President Trump announced an oil deal with Venezuela, saying Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had reached an agreement to secure access to billions of barrels of reserves "through a partnership with private business." The private partner is North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a company owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, who has been investigated for money laundering in the United States, Switzerland and Spain but never charged. The next day the Wall Street Journal reported, per Reuters, that the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital would take a 35% passive stake through penny warrants. Asked by Reuters, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said: "The Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) does not take equity stakes in private companies. Under its statutory authority, OSC's role is strictly limited to providing capital assistance in the form of a loan, loan guarantee, or technical assistance." On August 31 the White House released a fact sheet saying the deal was signed by Rubio and Hegseth and that, "At no cost to the American taxpayer, NABEP has granted the U.S. Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital a 35% equity stake in its corporate parent." It also gives the State Department the right to buy 20% of NABEP's output at production cost and first refusal on the rest, and a U.S. veto over NABEP board appointments. The terms differ by outlet: Reuters reported the office "takes a 35% stake" in NABEP; the New York Times reported an option on up to 35% of NABEP's parent through warrants, "penny warrants" convertible for very little money per two people familiar with the deal. Reuters reported on September 4 that a U.S. official said the 35% position is held as penny warrants, which guard it against dilution and still entitle the United States to dividends. The Times reported that the office reports to Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg, who approves its deals, and is run by David Lorch, formerly of Feinberg's firm Cerberus Capital Management. On September 2, Semafor reported that a U.S. official said the authority to take the stake via penny warrants "was granted to the OSC when it was created by statute" and called it "a very standard deal for OSC"; a second U.S. official said, Semafor reported, that the United States had recently intervened in an international money-laundering investigation into Betancourt in order to finalize the deal. A day later Semafor reported, citing one person familiar with the process, that Congress had declined to pass Pentagon proposals that would have given the office authority to seek equity stakes. Senator Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, whom Semafor reported was already seeking details on the legal authority, called turning the military into an investor in Venezuelan oil "a blatant abuse of power and taxpayer dollars" and demanded a full accounting of its legal authority and terms. Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Reed, Martin Heinrich and Elizabeth Warren later wrote to Rubio, Hegseth and Energy Secretary Chris Wright arguing the office's statute does not explicitly allow equity stakes in foreign companies, and House Democrats Gregory Meeks and Robert Garcia wrote to Rubio and Hegseth demanding the full documentation. On October 1 the State Department delivered copies of the agreement to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee; a briefing planned for that day was postponed after a Republican committee staffer asked to move it to November. On October 20, ProPublica, which reviewed the 18-page agreement, reported that the United States will pay nothing upfront and plans to acquire its stake at $0.01 per warrant share, on terms that expire on the 75th anniversary of closing; that the stake is in a Barbados-registered parent company whose owners and investors the document says little about; that disputes must be argued in federal court in the Northern District of Texas; and that the deal takes full force only once both sides meet its closing conditions. Signing for that parent company, alongside Betancourt, Hegseth and Rubio, was Orlando Alvarado, a name the administration had not disclosed as a party, who has held senior roles in multiple Betancourt businesses; ProPublica, citing the Miami Herald, wrote that federal prosecutors identified Alvarado as an unindicted co-conspirator in a scheme to embezzle money from Venezuela's national oil company. A NABEP spokesperson said neither man "has ever been charged with any crime in any country." Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson said the department conducts "extensive due diligence" before extending capital assistance.

incident_summary: This pattern had an earlier, documented origin. The Guardian reported August 14, 2025 that Hegseth's Pentagon had rolled out recruitment advertisements built around biblical imagery and themes, and that Hegseth had personally amplified self-described Christian nationalist pastor Doug Wilson -- who wants to repeal women's suffrage, has defended slavery, and believes homosexuality should be criminalized -- reposting a CNN segment about Wilson in which Wilson said, 'I would like to see this nation being a Christian nation, and I would like this world to be a Christian world,' with the caption 'All of Christ for All of Life,' as the Guardian reported August 9, 2025; a Pentagon spokesman told the Guardian that Hegseth 'very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson's writings and teachings.' That earlier online amplification preceded Hegseth's formal decision, roughly six months later, to invite Wilson to preach in person at a Pentagon worship service in February 2026, which CNN, the Washington Post, and Military Times each reported. Wilson, who CNN reported has advocated that the US adopt a Christian theocracy, preached on February 17, 2026 in the Pentagon auditorium in a sermon broadcast on the department's internal TV network, and the Pentagon said Hegseth 'was glad to welcome Pastor Wilson.' On March 25, 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth led a monthly Christian worship service at the Pentagon, livestreamed to Defense Department personnel, at which he read a prayer he said was first offered by a military chaplain, **asking God to 'let every round find its mark against the enemies of righteousness and our great nation,' and to give 'unbreakable unity, and overwhelming violence of action against those who deserve no mercy.'** The service was part of the monthly Christian worship services Hegseth began hosting at the Pentagon in May 2025, at which, according to the Associated Press, only evangelicals had presided and pastors from his own denomination, the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches, had appeared at least three times. On March 23, 2026, Americans United for Separation of Church and State filed suit in federal district court in Washington, D.C. against the Defense Department, with a parallel suit against the Department of Labor, seeking under the Freedom of Information Act the production of internal Pentagon communications about the recurring worship services -- including their cost, guests, any recordings, and any employee complaints received -- a request AU had first made in December 2025 that the Pentagon had not fully answered. The Defense Department answered the complaint on May 27, 2026, and Judge Trevor N. McFadden ordered the parties to report on the request's status and a production schedule; on August 28, 2026 he directed them to file joint status reports every sixty days, the next due October 27, 2026. When the suits were filed, AU president Rachel Laser said in a statement that the secretaries were 'abusing the power of their government positions and taxpayer-funded resources to impose their preferred religion on federal workers,' and that even if the services are presented as voluntary, 'there is pressure on federal employees to attend in order to appease their bosses.' AU has framed the FOIA suit as a fact-gathering step that could inform a future constitutional challenge. Former federal judge John E. Jones III, now president of Dickinson College, told The Conversation in April 2026 that 'it sure looks like they are in violation' of the Establishment Clause, while cautioning that the current Supreme Court's relaxed approach makes the outcome of any challenge uncertain; no such constitutional suit had been filed as of the most recent reporting reviewed for this entry. University of California at Berkeley historian Ronit Stahl, quoted by the Associated Press, asked, 'In a nation with no establishment of religion per the Constitution, what does it mean to have a leader being not just broadly religious or religious in a pluralistic sense, but religious in a very particular sense?'

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (policy drafted with the guidance of his personal attorney Tim Parlatore, a Navy Reserve officer then serving concurrently on Hegseth's staff and by 2026 a senior adviser to Hegseth)
offense_category: Imposing Pentagon Press-Credentialing Rules a Federal Judge Later Found Violated the First and Fifth Amendments, Drafted With the Guidance of the Secretary's Own Personal Attorney
incident_summary: In September 2025, the Pentagon distributed a new 21-page press-credentialing policy. It required journalists to sign a pledge agreeing that seeking to obtain unapproved information gathered at the Pentagon -- even unclassified information -- could be treated as 'soliciting' the disclosure of protected information, and it warned that credentials could be revoked or denied if a journalist was 'reasonably determined to pose a security or safety risk.' Journalists had until October 14, 2025 to sign the new rules; more than 30 news organizations, including The New York Times, The Washington Post, CNN, and Fox News, refused. On October 15, 2025, roughly 40 to 50 journalists turned in their Pentagon access badges together and exited the building rather than accept the restrictions, an action widely described as unprecedented in scale and near-unanimous across the ideological spectrum of outlets covering the Pentagon. The same day, The Washington Post reported that the policy had been drafted with the guidance of Tim Parlatore, Hegseth's longtime personal attorney, who had previously represented Hegseth against sexual-assault allegations and had separately represented Donald Trump and, per reporting, individuals connected to organized crime. According to the Post, Parlatore had joined Hegseth's staff in March 2025 as a Navy Reserve officer while continuing to serve as a private attorney with outside clients, an arrangement that reportedly troubled some Defense Department legal officials. In December 2025, The New York Times sued the Defense Department, Hegseth, and chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell over the policy. On March 20, 2026, U.S. District Judge Paul L. Friedman **ruled that the provisions governing when press credentials could be revoked violated the First and Fifth Amendments**. He vacated the challenged provisions and ordered the Pentagon to reinstate the credentials of seven Times reporters. The next business day, the Department issued an interim policy that closed the Correspondents' Corridor, the in-building press workspace reporters had used since the 1970s. Under it, credentialed journalists could enter the Pentagon only for five approved purposes and only with an escort at all times. Parlatore, by then a senior adviser to Hegseth, told The Times the new version used "more words to say the same thing." On April 9, 2026, Judge Friedman found the new restrictions violated his order and ordered The Times's reporters' access restored. On April 27, a divided D.C. Circuit motions panel stayed that order only to the extent it entitled journalists to unescorted access, finding the government likely to show the escort requirement fell outside the original ruling. The Times filed a second lawsuit on May 18, 2026, naming Parlatore among the defendants. On June 30, Judge Friedman preliminarily enjoined the escort requirement as likely First Amendment retaliation. On July 16, another divided D.C. Circuit panel stayed that injunction, finding the government likely to show that a generally applicable escort rule is not retaliation. The government's appeals of both sets of rulings are set for oral argument on November 16, 2026, and the escort requirement remains in effect in the meantime.

More than 30 news organizations across the ideological spectrum refused to sign, and dozens of journalists surrendered building access together rather than accept the terms
A federal court, not merely the affected press organizations, found specific provisions of the policy unconstitutional under the First and Fifth Amendments

comeback: The specific concern documented here is not that the Pentagon regulates classified information -- it does, and always has. It is that the new rules extended to unclassified information and were drafted with direct input from the Secretary's own personal attorney, who kept a private practice with outside clients while on the Secretary's staff and had earlier represented the Secretary himself in a sexual-assault matter, an arrangement Defense Department legal officials themselves were reported to have found troubling. The near-unanimous rejection by more than 30 news organizations spanning the ideological spectrum, and a federal court's own finding that specific provisions were unconstitutional (a ruling the government is appealing), are independent confirmations that this went beyond ordinary, reasonable security administration.

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense
offense_category: Failure to Warn U.S.-Flagged Vessels and American Personnel of an Imminent War Zone Before Ordering Strikes -- an institutional-accountability claim about operational conduct endangering U.S. lives, not a criminal charge against a named official
incident_summary: When the U.S. began bombing Iran on February 28, 2026, five privately-owned, U.S.-flagged vessels that work closely with the U.S. military were in the Persian Gulf, and roughly half a dozen U.S. Merchant Marine Academy cadets were aboard two of them as part of their required sea-training program. The Department of Defense broke with precedent by giving no advance warning of the strikes to the vessels, the Merchant Marine Academy, or the Department of Transportation, which oversees the academy. Three sources close to the situation told NOTUS there was no warning; one said, 'Nobody told them. They were caught unawares,' and that officials 'weren't even given a whiff, weren't even given an indication' that strikes were imminent. Without advance notice, two people familiar with the situation said, there was no clear way to evacuate the cadets or the ships. **On March 2, 2026, the U.S.-flagged Crowley tanker Stena Imperative was hit in an Iranian attack while berthed at the Port of Bahrain, and a dockworker was killed shoreside;** two sources told NOTUS that another U.S.-flagged vessel was nearly hit by a projectile. More than 800 vessels became trapped trying to exit the Persian Gulf; one of the five U.S.-flagged ships, loaded with cargo, was losing money every day it could not leave. The crews found safe harbors in the region and kept the cadets aboard for weeks; the cadets were evacuated about a month after the war started, though as of NOTUS's April 9, 2026 report it was unclear whether all had returned to the United States. The Defense Department did not respond to requests for comment on the lack of warning. On March 20, 2026, Sen. Richard Blumenthal wrote CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper that the U.S.-flagged vessels 'appear to have received no warning or direction to reposition prior to the onset of hostilities,' requesting prioritized resupply and port access, a port call plan, a communications framework, and an explanation of what steps, if any, were taken to notify or reposition the vessels, with a response requested by March 26, 2026; no public CENTCOM reply has been identified. In an interview for NOTUS's April 9, 2026 report, Blumenthal criticized the administration for failing to alert the vessels, describing his concerns as 'sky high' and saying, 'The idea that these ships would be stranded was absolutely foreseeable ...' On April 26, 2026, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Kirsten Gillibrand, Blumenthal, and Mark Kelly wrote Hegseth about a distinct incident, the March 1, 2026 Iranian drone strike on a U.S. post at Shuaiba port in Kuwait that killed six service members and injured more than 30 (tracked as its own entry in this database); the letter cited the failure to warn the U.S.-flagged vessels as part of 'a larger pattern' of failing to protect Americans in the region from Iranian retaliation, and asked what criteria DoD used to decide who needed a warning before the strikes. DoD replied to Warren on May 11, 2026, but in a September 21, 2026 letter urging the Armed Services chairmen to hold hearings on the Port Shuaiba attack, the lawmakers wrote that in its response DoD 'failed to directly answer our questions.'

The lack of warning left no clear way to evacuate, and at least one U.S.-flagged vessel was subsequently hit in an Iranian attack that killed a dockworker

A U.S. Senator with relevant oversight responsibility has called the vessels' stranding foreseeable and said warnings could have been issued, not merely an unfortunate consequence of fast-moving military operations

status: No accountability finding, public DoD explanation, or corrective action identified. CENTCOM has not publicly answered Blumenthal's March 20, 2026 letter; on Sept. 21, lawmakers said DoD's reply to four senators' April 26 letter, which asked how it chose whom to warn, did not directly answer it.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: operational security around the timing of military strikes is a legitimate and standard practice to protect mission success and force safety, advance warning to numerous private vessels risks the information reaching adversaries, and the strikes' timing was driven by broader strategic considerations rather than indifference to the cadets' or crews' safety.
comeback: Operational security concerns do not fully explain a complete absence of any warning to the Department of Transportation or the Merchant Marine Academy itself -- both part of the U.S. government -- which sourcing indicates broke with established precedent; the month-long stranding of American cadets in an active war zone, with no clear way to evacuate them, is a concrete, documented consequence of that specific gap, and the attack that hit a U.S.-flagged tanker and killed a dockworker shows the danger was real, not hypothetical.

Four senators drew the same link in an April 26, 2026 letter that paired this episode with the March 1 Port Shuaiba drone strike, where survivors say their Kuwait post had little or no defense against drones. Here the gap was coordination: by NOTUS's account, neither the Transportation Department nor its academy was told in advance, breaking with past practice. A separate entry documents the Pentagon cutting a different safeguard, its civilian-casualty prevention staff.
confidence_note: MODERATE-HIGH confidence: the cadets' presence, the precedent-breaking absence of warning, and the month-long stranding trace to a single NOTUS investigative report built on anonymous sources close to the situation plus an on-record senatorial interview. Other records back parts of it: gCaptain's March 2, 2026 report confirms the Stena Imperative strike and the shoreside death, and Blumenthal's March 20, 2026 letter, published by his Senate office, independently states that the vessels appear to have received no warning. The Merchant Marine Academy declined to confirm the cadets' presence, citing national security, and DoD did not respond to NOTUS's request for comment, which is not confirmation. No CENTCOM response to Blumenthal's letter has been identified. This is a distinct incident from the separately tracked March 1, 2026 Kuwait drone strike, although four senators linked the two in an April 26, 2026 letter.

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense
offense_category: Conflict of Interest -- appearance of conflict in appointing executives of two major Pentagon contractors to co-lead a study that will recommend future weapons and technology; naming advisers is lawful, no violation of the federal conflict-of-interest statute (18 U.S.C. 208) is alleged or charged, and the Pentagon has not disclosed the co-leads' employment status, recusal terms or any ethics waiver
incident_summary: On Wednesday, September 30, 2026, in a "State of the Force" address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced "Project Meridian," a 120-day study of future warfare. Its co-leads are **SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey** and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, working under the Pentagon's chief technology officer, Emil Michael, with a wider team from academia, policy and industry. Per TechCrunch, Hegseth's letter gave the team 120 days to propose "actionable solutions to start developing, testing, and fielding" advanced technology; GovConWire reported that findings are due to Hegseth's office by January 28, 2027, as a public unclassified report plus a classified annex. Hegseth said the project is not about new strategies or policies but about identifying "the domains that we must conquer and capabilities we must master," AFP reported. The announcement said the study would run through a partner organization without naming it; NPR later reported that Hegseth said he had directed Michael to commission it through the MITRE Corporation, a nonprofit that manages federally funded research. TechCrunch said the role seemingly marks Musk's first official return to the administration since he left the Department of Government Efficiency. Both co-leads' companies are Pentagon contractors. **SpaceX has secured over $8 billion in U.S. defense contracts in 2026 alone**, according to government contract announcements cited by NPR, and the Pentagon also uses Musk's AI chatbot Grok. Anduril builds military drones and autonomous systems and was recently awarded contracts for long-range missiles and semi-autonomous fighter aircraft, TechCrunch reported. NPR noted the announcement came days before a scheduled speech by President Trump at an Anduril facility in Baltimore. On October 6, NPR reported that the Defense Department would not say whether Musk and Luckey were hired as special government employees, as Musk was at DOGE, or as contractors. That choice decides which rules apply: executive branch employees are barred by federal criminal law from taking part in decisions that affect their own financial interests, while contractors are not. The department did not respond to NPR's questions about the co-leads' potential conflicts, and SpaceXAI and Anduril did not comment. A department spokesperson said "MITRE is responsible for the analysis and recommendations, and will evaluate all inputs with technical rigor while applying appropriate conflict-of-interest and information safeguards." Richard Painter, chief White House ethics lawyer under President George W. Bush, said of Musk, "it's not like he's doing it as a neutral public service." A former senior Defense Department official, speaking anonymously, called it "a massive conflict of interest" and said the study could favor drones or space assets, which Musk and Luckey build, over tanks, which they don't. Another former Pentagon official, also anonymous, was less concerned, distinguishing advice that Congress can accept or reject from a panel member writing a requirement and then bidding on it.

offense_category: Personal Intervention to Block Senior Military Promotions Along Racial and Gender Lines -- based on nine officials' accounts to NBC News; DoD has not confirmed the specific race/gender-motive characterization on the record
incident_summary: A named instance of Defense Secretary Hegseth's broader pattern of promotion blocking: in the spring of 2025, Hegseth declined to promote Lt. Gen. Douglas Sims over suspicions, held without evidence, that Sims had leaked sensitive information; after Sims was cleared, Hegseth briefly agreed to promote him, then reversed course again in early July 2025, maintaining that Sims was too close to former Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Mark Milley, the New York Times reported July 26, 2025. The move drew rare, direct pushback from Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine -- a break from the pattern, since most of this entry's other documented blockages did not draw comparable internal pushback from the Joint Chiefs' own chairman. On March 27, 2026, the New York Times reported, as The Hill relayed and NPR confirmed through a U.S. official, that Hegseth had struck two Black and two female Army officers from a one-star general promotion list after Army Secretary Driscoll repeatedly refused to remove them; NPR, citing a U.S. official, added that a Black colonel and a female colonel from another branch had also been taken off a promotion list. NBC News then reported on April 2, 2026, based on accounts from nine U.S. officials, that **Defense Secretary Hegseth had taken steps to block or delay promotions for more than a dozen Black and female senior officers across the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marines**. Officials told NBC some of the affected officers were seen as having been targeted because of their race, gender, or perceived affiliation with Biden-administration policies or officials; two officials said the attributes Hegseth cited for removing officers included past support for Covid vaccines or mask mandates for troops and affiliation with diversity, equity, and inclusion programs, and a second U.S. official told NPR that Hegseth has been weeding out senior officers deemed ideologically incompatible. The interventions raised concerns among officials within the affected service branches and, per NBC's reporting, within the White House itself. This entry extends the pattern of senior removals documented separately in this tracker's Army Chief of Staff purge entry to the promotion pipeline for the next generation of military leadership. One specific named instance did not succeed: Hegseth chief of staff Ricky Buria reportedly objected to Maj. Gen. Antoinette Gant's assignment to lead the Military District of Washington on the stated basis that Trump would not want to stand next to a Black female officer at public events -- Buria denies the account, and Army Secretary Driscoll pushed back at the time -- but Gant's assignment proceeded regardless, a nuance not captured uniformly by the pattern's general 'blocked or delayed' framing. Sens. Cory Booker and Brian Schatz sent a July 15, 2026 letter (released July 17) to the Defense Department Inspector General demanding an independent investigation of Hegseth's alleged intervention to block nearly 40 officers, half of them women or members of minority groups, from approved promotion lists, alleging he used personal views on race and gender to override the selection boards' merit-based process. On September 1, 2026, the New York Times reported that Hegseth had fired or blocked the promotions of more than 80 generals and admirals -- about 10% of the military's top officers -- including seven Army officers recently selected for two-star rank, two of them Black and two female, and that more than half of the officers affected by his dismissals were Black or female; Driscoll, who had complained to Trump about the firings and blocked promotions, had submitted his resignation. Days later, Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.) said on CBS that Hegseth had purged over 80 generals and admirals. On September 10, 2026, Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) urged Armed Services leaders to keep promotion-oversight provisions in the draft FY2027 NDAA and require written, justified notice within seven days to officers whose promotions are withheld or removed, citing at least 40 officers removed from one- and two-star lists since January 2025. In a September 14, 2026 report putting the figure at as many as 80, the Times reported that many current and former military leaders said Hegseth had targeted the military's most combat-tested leaders, "hollowing out an institution at war," with key leadership positions unfilled for months while the Iran war strained the force and shortfalls of critical missile interceptors raised questions about its staying power.

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (ordered a pause in offensive cyber operations against Russia, which DoD's official channel then publicly denied had occurred)
offense_category: Public misrepresentation of a national-security decision to Congress and the public -- not itself a prosecutable act, but a documented false denial issued through DoD's official channel, later contradicted by a Republican committee chairman's on-the-record confirmation
status: Unresolved: DoD's March 4, 2025 denial of any pause has not been corrected in sourcing reviewed. GOP subcommittee chairman Don Bacon confirmed a one-day pause on the record in May 2025, yet Hegseth told the House Armed Services Committee on June 12, 2025, 'We did not!', per the Kyiv Post.
incident_summary: On March 1, 2025, the Washington Post, citing one current and one former U.S. official, reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had ordered U.S. Cyber Command to halt offensive cyber and information operations against Russia, a pause meant to last as long as Trump's negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine war continued. The cybersecurity publication The Record had first reported the order, and The New York Times added its own confirmation from unnamed officials. On March 4, 2025, the Defense Department's official Rapid Response account on X publicly denied the reports, stating that Hegseth 'has neither canceled nor delayed any cyber operations directed against malicious Russian targets and there has been no stand-down order whatsoever from that priority.' At a House Armed Services subcommittee hearing on May 16, 2025, Rep. Eugene Vindman (D-VA) confronted DoD witness Laurie Buckhout with the gap between the March denial and the original reporting. Buckhout replied that she 'was not here at that time' and was 'not aware of any stand down operations ordered.' She did not defend the March denial. Subcommittee Chairman Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) then **confirmed on the record that U.S. cyber operations against Russia were in fact paused for one day in February 2025 during Trump's negotiating push**, describing it as 'typical for negotiations.' Vindman called the Rapid Response account's March 4 statement 'an outright lie,' saying 'this is not what the American people deserve.' On June 12, 2025, pressed by House Armed Services Committee members about the reports that Cyber Command had briefly stopped offensive operations aimed at Russia, Hegseth himself denied them: 'We did not!', according to the Kyiv Post. In the sourcing reviewed, DoD never formally corrected or retracted its March 4 denial.
elements_required: Contemporaneous news reporting (The Record, then the Washington Post citing one current and one former U.S. official) described Hegseth ordering U.S. Cyber Command to halt offensive cyber and information operations against Russia
DoD's official public statement (the March 4, 2025 Rapid Response Twitter account post) explicitly denied any cyber-operations pause or stand-down order had occurred
A named member of Congress from the President's own party (Bacon) confirmed on the record that a pause did in fact occur
No DoD official at the subsequent hearing disputed that a pause occurred, only disclaiming personal knowledge of it
The Secretary himself repeated the denial to the House Armed Services Committee after the pause had been confirmed on the record

It could distinguish a brief 'planning pause' from actually 'canceling or delaying operations,' or argue that no live offensive operations were underway during the one-day window regardless of any planning halt, making the categorical denial technically defensible.
comeback: The original reporting (The Record, then the Washington Post and The New York Times, the latter two citing unnamed officials) specifically described a halt to offensive cyber and information operations, not a mere rhetorical distinction. Bacon's on-the-record confirmation came from a Republican committee chairman with direct oversight access, not a partisan opponent. It corroborates that a real pause occurred as reported and undercuts a 'technically true' defense of the DoD denial.

The characterization of the denial as a deliberate 'lie' versus an imprecise or narrowly-framed statement is Vindman's own assessment, presented as his characterization rather than an adjudicated fact.

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (later 'Secretary of War')
offense_category: Policy/Regulatory Violation — DoD Instruction 8170.01 (mishandling of nonpublic DoD information) and a Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention policy violation (failure to preserve official communications), per the Pentagon Inspector General's December 2025 final report; closest criminal analogue: 18 U.S.C. §793(f), gross negligence in handling national defense information — NOT charged, included for reference only
incident_summary: On March 15, 2025, Hegseth **shared sensitive operational details (aircraft quantities, strike timing) about an imminent strike on Houthi targets in Yemen via Signal on his personal phone, in a chat that inadvertently included a journalist**. He also reportedly shared similar information in a separate personal Signal chat with his wife, brother, and personal attorney, Tim Parlatore.
elements_required: DoD Instr. 8170.01: use of personal device for official business (administrative, not criminal)
DoD Instr. 8170.01: use of non-approved commercial messaging app for nonpublic DoD information

Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention policy: failure to preserve official communications sent via Signal, an unapproved and non-archiving channel — the Pentagon IG's December 2025 final report found this violation in addition to the 8170.01 issues

[Reference only, not charged] 18 U.S.C. §793(f): lawful possession of national defense information; gross negligence permitting it to be removed from proper custody or disclosed; failure to report loss

evidence.description: Der Spiegel reported March 26, 2025 that its reporters, using a commercial contact-data provider and hacked customer data published online, found a mobile phone number and a Gmail address for Hegseth; the email address, and in some cases its password, appeared in more than 20 publicly accessible leaks, and the number led to a WhatsApp account Hegseth had apparently deleted only recently. Der Spiegel did not publish the data or test whether the passwords still worked, and said hostile intelligence services could use such data to try to install spyware on officials' devices. The Defense Department did not respond to its request for comment.
evidence.maps_to_element: Context on the exposure of Hegseth's personal contact data during the same period, not an element of any offense; Der Spiegel did not establish that the Signal chat ran on the exposed number

The pilots said they could no longer be certain the Pentagon was focused on their safety when they strapped into their cockpits.
evidence.maps_to_element: Context on the operational-security concerns raised by current and former military pilots, not an element of any offense

evidence.description: On April 21, 2025, Sen. Adam Schiff wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio in his role as acting Archivist of the United States, urging the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) to take immediate action to preserve records from Trump administration officials' use of Signal and other commercial messaging apps, and to investigate whether cabinet members and other senior officials had adequately preserved such communications. The letter cited both the original 'Houthi PC small group' chat and The New York Times's report of Hegseth's second 'Defense | Team Huddle' chat with his wife, brother and personal lawyer. Because Rubio had been in the 'Houthi PC small group' chat, Schiff wrote that he should not oversee an investigation of activity he was involved in and asked whether NARA would appoint a senior career official to oversee it, and, citing Rubio's 'evident conflict of interest', whether NARA would contact the Justice Department or appropriate inspectors general for help. The letter posed eight questions with a May 5, 2025 response deadline.
evidence.maps_to_element: Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention policy element -- documents contemporaneous congressional pressure for preservation; also adds the oversight-response landscape (Rubio's dual role as both a chat participant and acting NARA head) not previously captured in this entry

evidence.description: On April 21, 2025, the watchdog group American Oversight filed an amended complaint in its Federal Records Act suit against Hegseth, the other agency heads in the Yemen-strike chat and the National Archives (American Oversight v. Hegseth, D.D.C. No. 25-cv-883), adding Hegseth's 'Defense | Team Huddle' chat, which it said, citing The New York Times, included his wife, brother, personal lawyer, aides and advisors. The complaint noted that on March 27, 2025 the court had directed the defendants to preserve the Signal messages from March 11 through 15, and alleged, on information and belief, that none of them had preserved the Yemen-strike chat in its entirety.
evidence.maps_to_element: Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention element -- civil litigation over preservation of the chats, including the second chat (allegations, not findings)

evidence.description: CBS News reported April 25, 2025, citing sources familiar with the matter, that a computer monitor had been installed in Hegseth's Pentagon office giving him remote access to Signal and text messages on his personal cellphone, a setup two sources said bypassed standard Defense Department security protocols; Marine Col. Ricky Buria, an aide, had some oversight of the work, two sources said. CBS noted that the Associated Press had earlier reported his use of an unsecured 'dirty' internet line. A Defense Department spokesperson denied there was a 'dirty line' or any current Signal use in the office, describing a one-way line that alerts him to messages on the phone, which is kept outside the office.

Boasberg granted American Oversight's preliminary-injunction motion only in part: he ordered the agency heads, including Hegseth, to promptly notify acting Archivist Rubio of the impending deletion of any Signal chats containing federal records, and Rubio to ask the Attorney General to act to preserve them. He found American Oversight had not shown that the agencies' recordkeeping programs were inadequate or that the court could provide redress for messages already deleted. The opinion recounts a Defense Department declaration that screenshots of the existing Signal messages at issue had been preserved in a recordkeeping system in the Secretary's office.

evidence.description: Politico reported July 14, 2025, citing three people familiar with the probes, that investigators were looking at two close Hegseth aides: Ricky Buria, a senior Hegseth aide, and Tim Parlatore, Hegseth's personal attorney who also served as a top Pentagon adviser (“Ricky and Tim are some of the folks that they’re zeroing in on,” one said). In the Inspector General's probe, investigators were asking whether Buria helped set up the unsecured internet line that let Hegseth access Signal; in a separate Air Force Office of Special Investigations inquiry into leaks, they were asking whether Buria could have been a source for leaks and whether Parlatore attended meetings beyond his clearance level. The IG and OSI also asked witnesses whether they had been asked to delete Signal messages; one person said OSI investigators asked by name whether Buria or Parlatore had made such requests. Buria did not respond and Parlatore declined to comment.

evidence.description: The Pentagon Inspector General's report (DODIG-2026-021, dated December 2, 2025 and released December 4), prepared at the March 26, 2025 request of the Senate Armed Services Committee's chairman and ranking member, found that Hegseth sent sensitive, nonpublic operational information, the quantity and strike times of manned U.S. aircraft, over Signal on his personal cell phone about 2 to 4 hours before the strikes; that some of it matched a U.S. Central Command email classified SECRET//NOFORN; and that this did not comply with DoD Instruction 8170.01. It also found that Hegseth and his office did not retain the messages as federal records, as 44 U.S.C. 2911 and DoD Instruction 5015.02 require; some had auto-deleted. The IG report addressed two separate questions: (1) was classified information disclosed, and (2) were DoD's own communication-security rules followed. He may have prevailed on the first, but the report found he violated DoD Instruction 8170.01 by using a personal device and unapproved app for nonpublic operational information. Declassification authority is not the same as operational security authority -- he had the legal right to decide what was classified, not the right to send strike timing over his personal phone outside secure channels.
