offense_category: Recalling Nearly 800 Senior Commanders From Global Posts on Short Notice for a Politicized Address, Including a Presidential Proposal to Use U.S. Cities as Military 'Training Grounds' That Raises Posse Comitatus Act Concerns
incident_summary: On September 30, 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth summoned nearly 800 generals, admirals, and senior enlisted leaders -- virtually the entire senior command structure of the U.S. armed forces -- from posts around the world to Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia. He called them in on short notice for an unprecedented, in-person, mandatory address. Hegseth declared 'today we end the war on warriors' and 'the era of the Department of Defense is over.' He announced new physical-fitness and grooming standards (no more 'fat generals,' 'no more beardos'), with fitness standards raised to a uniform 'male level' regardless of service member sex. He also announced the elimination of racial hiring and promotion quotas and the loosening of restrictions on boot-camp hazing, and called for troops to stop following 'stupid rules of engagement' in combat. President Trump also addressed the assembled commanders, telling them 'we are under invasion from within' and 'it's a war from within.' **He proposed that American cities be used as military 'training grounds,' naming Chicago specifically, and said he had ordered the creation of military 'quick reaction forces' to 'help quell civil disturbances.'** The Posse Comitatus Act of 1878 generally prohibits deploying the U.S. military for domestic civilian law enforcement, absent a specific statutory exception (such as the Insurrection Act). Four weeks before the summit, on September 2, 2025, U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer had ruled that the administration violated the Act because federal troops it deployed to Los Angeles performed law enforcement there. The Ninth Circuit stayed his injunction, and the appeal is pending (see TAP's separate entry on the Los Angeles deployment). Sen. Jack Reed (D-RI), the Senate Armed Services Committee's ranking Democrat and a former 82nd Airborne officer, called the event 'an expensive, dangerous dereliction of leadership,' said Hegseth's 'words were divisive and corrosive to the force itself,' and called Trump's 'training grounds' suggestion 'a dangerous assault on our democracy.' Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) said the event 'wasted millions of taxpayer dollars by flying all of these flag officers into Washington, D.C.' A former senior defense official told DefenseScoop, 'I cannot believe 800 generals and flag officers were brought into that building to hear a pep-speech that would be better delivered by a captain to a bunch of enlisted and lieutenants out in the field somewhere.' Virginia Burger, a former Marine officer now at the Project on Government Oversight, said the exercise 'cost the American taxpayers millions of dollars to fly in every Admiral, General, and their entourages' and came 'at a risk to national security.' Experts also warned that the event's repeated references to recent senior-officer firings (part of Hegseth's broader pattern of dismissals, tracked elsewhere in this database) signaled that dissent could end careers. That atmosphere, they warned, could make commanders hesitant to offer honest counsel during an actual crisis. The Pentagon then issued a memo requiring all service members to complete a 'Warrior Ethos Tasking' -- watching the speech video and reviewing the new policy memoranda -- by the end of October 2025. Marine Col. Doug Krugman's last day in uniform, ending a 24-year career, was September 30, 2025 -- the same day as the Quantico summit. In a Washington Post op-ed published October 16, 2025, Krugman wrote that he had already decided to resign his commission before the summit took place. But he cited Trump's remarks there -- 'if you don't like what I'm saying, you can leave the room -- of course, there goes your rank, there goes your future' -- as illustrating exactly the climate that drove his decision, writing: 'I continued to serve despite all that because I believed the Constitution brought the country more success than failure, and I believed our presidents took their oaths to it seriously. With President Trump, I no longer believe that.' That month, National Guard Bureau memos carrying out the quick-reaction-force order directed the Guard in every state and territory except D.C. to form quick reaction forces trained in civil disturbance -- often 500 troops each, more than 23,000 in all -- operational by January 1, 2026. The memos cited Trump's August executive order. After the Supreme Court in December 2025 rejected his request to deploy the Guard to Chicago, Trump announced on December 31, 2025 that he was withdrawing the Guard from Chicago, Los Angeles and Portland, writing, 'We will come back, perhaps in a much different and stronger form.'

rebuttal_anticipated: The administration could argue that the summit was a legitimate exercise of the Secretary of Defense's authority to set uniform standards and communicate priorities directly to senior leadership. It could add that Trump's 'training grounds' remarks were rhetorical rather than a specific operational order, and that the remarks raise no Posse Comitatus issue on their own because they announced no specific domestic deployment.
comeback: Even accepting the administration's framing, the documented facts stand independent of intent. Nearly the entire senior military command was pulled from operational posts worldwide, at significant cost, for a non-operational address. The President explicitly proposed using domestic cities as military training grounds and described creating quick-reaction forces for civil disturbances, which the National Guard in every state was ordered to stand up within weeks. If operationalized, those remarks would raise a genuine legal question under the Posse Comitatus Act -- and they came four weeks after a federal judge ruled that the administration's Los Angeles deployment had already violated that Act. A former senior defense official and two sitting senators on the Armed Services Committee went on record criticizing the event. What this entry documents is the scale and content of the event, not merely its critics' interpretation of it.

Dan Caine's own private objection (see the Hegseth entry); the unclassified strategy released January 23, 2026 lists homeland defense and the Western Hemisphere as the priority region and deterring China as the second priority, according to CSIS -- a distinct but closely-timed thread about the strategy document's substance rather than this summit's speech content.

offense_category: Withholding Combat Casualty Information From the Public -- the Pentagon did not disclose three Iranian strikes on U.S. forces in Jordan, which injured dozens of troops and damaged helicopters, in the week before a publicly disclosed strike killed three soldiers -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary: The New York Times reported on July 20, 2026, citing several U.S. officials who spoke on condition of anonymity, that Iranian forces struck U.S. forces in Jordan three separate times in the week before the July 17, 2026 attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base that **killed two U.S. soldiers (1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan and Pvt. Isabella Gonzales) and left a third (Sgt. Angel S. Rampersad) missing; the Pentagon confirmed Rampersad's death on July 25**. The three earlier strikes injured dozens of U.S. service members and damaged several helicopters, according to the Times, but the Pentagon did not disclose the strikes, the casualties or the damage. One U.S. military official told the Times that Central Command is not required to release information about injured troops, especially when they quickly return to duty; another asked why the Pentagon would divulge information that could help Iran zero in on its ballistic-missile and drone attacks on Jordan and other bases in the Middle East, where thousands of U.S. troops are stationed. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell rejected the report on the record as "baseless and malicious accusations" and "fabrications," then said that nearly 100 service members had been "deemed to have some degree of injury since July 7, 2026," 96% of whom had returned to duty; the Times said it stood by its reporting. On July 23, 2026, all 12 Democrats on the Senate Armed Services Committee, led by Sen. Mazie Hirono, wrote to Hegseth asking for total casualty figures, an explanation of gaps in the Pentagon's casualty database, and details on the three earlier Iranian attacks in Jordan, including who authorized not disclosing them, noting that as of July 21 the database listed 14 service members killed despite wide reporting of 18; they asked for answers by July 30, and no reply has been identified. House Oversight Committee Democrats Garcia and Subramanyam opened a formal inquiry on August 4, 2026 into separate changes the Pentagon made to its own casualty-tracking database, alleging four soldiers' deaths were briefly removed from the public Iran-war casualty count before being reclassified into a newly created 'Overseas Operations' category (acting Pentagon press secretary Joel Valdez had attributed the earlier drops in the totals to "temporary data disruptions" on the database website and said the "site anomalies are currently being resolved") -- a distinct allegation from the undisclosed-earlier-strikes reporting above, though both concern the same broader casualty-transparency pattern. The lawmakers asked for a response by August 18, 2026; the Pentagon declined to comment on the letter, and no response has been identified. On August 6, 2026, Sen. Tammy Duckworth introduced S. 5300, the Honoring the Sacrifice of Troops in War Act of 2026, with 17 Democratic cosponsors including Sens. Bennet, Hickenlooper, and Rosen; the bill, referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee, would require DoD to combine all Iran War casualty records into one accurate count and notify next-of-kin of any resulting corrections -- a direct legislative response to the database-reclassification pattern. The bill has seen no action since its referral. An identical House bill, H.R. 10457, was introduced on September 16, 2026 and referred to three committees. On September 18, 2026, The Washington Post reported that five U.S. officials said **at least 22 U.S. service members had died in the Middle East since the war began on February 28 -- four more than the 18 then listed in the Pentagon's public casualty database** -- and that a sixth official put the toll at 23; the Post reported that not all of the additional deaths were directly tied to the Iran conflict, but all involved U.S. personnel in the region during the hostilities. Hegseth called the report "DISGUSTING and FAKE. A complete LIE" in a post on X. By September 22, the database total had risen to 19 after an Army officer suffered a fatal medical emergency while flying to the Middle East, but the Post reported that the gap with officials' count remained unresolved; it also noted that the Pentagon had separately announced, in news releases, the deaths of two service members at bases Iranian forces had attacked, on missions it described as unrelated to the Iran war, and that neither appears by name in the database. Hegseth, who did not address whether every death had been tallied under the Pentagon's long-standing practices, told a reporter, "Even if we wanted to attempt to hide a combat death, we never would and we never could." On September 25, the Post reported that the Pentagon had quietly added 37 wounded troops (29 sailors and eight Marines) to the database, bringing the war's wounded total to 861, without saying when or how they were hurt; Central Command declined to comment. On Friday, October 9, the Pentagon raised the totals on its public casualty database to 21 killed and 865 wounded. The Washington Post reported that the new figure adds two noncombat deaths -- Maj. Sorffly Davius, who died in Kuwait on March 6, and a Navy suicide in September, according to a U.S. official -- and that an Army sergeant's May training-accident death in Iraq, recorded under a separate operation, brings deaths in the Middle East since February 28 to 22; The New York Times described the death toll as up from 18 and the wounded as up by 98 since August, and said the cause of the increase was not completely clear. House Armed Services Democrats Adam Smith and Chrissy Houlahan, who had demanded an explanation after the committee found "a discrepancy in the Pentagon's reporting of casualty numbers" and raised it with the White House, said, "There is no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude," and that Hegseth's failure "to immediately take ownership of the problem also does a grave disservice" to service members. In a statement to the Post, the Pentagon did not acknowledge the changed numbers; it said it was making further revisions to how the database reports casualties, including a new "pending adjudication" category, and that it "continues to maintain a steadfast commitment to the transparent, accurate accounting of all Service member casualties."

cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of a broader pattern of Iran-war casualty-transparency disputes under Hegseth's Pentagon, which this entry tracks as three separate acts: the nondisclosure of three Iranian strikes on U.S. forces in Jordan in July 2026, the later removal and reclassification of four deaths in the public casualty database, and the September 2026 report that the database omits at least four deaths that U.S. officials count. official: Tom Homan, White House Border Czar (the recorded conduct predates his current role, while he was a private citizen expected to join the incoming Trump administration); Todd Blanche, Deputy Attorney General; Emil Bove, former Acting Deputy Attorney General (opposed continuing the investigation)
offense_category: Alleged Bribery/Anticipatory Influence-Peddling Tied to a Promised Future Government Role, and the Trump DOJ's Subsequent Closure of Its Own Predecessor Investigation Into a Sitting Senior Official — Contested, Not Independently Adjudicated
incident_summary:
In summer 2024, before the presidential election, the FBI and the U.S. Attorney's office in the Western District of Texas opened an undercover investigation; DOJ's Public Integrity Section joined it in late November 2024. It began after the subject of a separate investigation alleged that Tom Homan was soliciting payments in exchange for helping steer future government contracts if Trump returned to office and Homan rejoined the administration. On September 20, 2024, undercover FBI agents posing as business contractors met Homan in Texas. According to MSNBC's reporting of internal case summaries and multiple sources, hidden cameras recorded Homan accepting $50,000 in cash, delivered in a paper bag from the restaurant chain Cava, after he indicated he could help facilitate contracts once in office. Public Integrity Section supervisors initially supported continuing the investigation.

After Trump's January 2025 inauguration and Homan's appointment as White House border czar, then-Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove opposed continuing the probe, and a DOJ appointee characterized it as a 'deep state' investigation in early 2025. FBI Director Kash Patel later requested a status update, after which Trump-appointed DOJ officials **closed the case without publicly disclosing a reason, with FBI Director Patel and then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche later saying in a statement to MSNBC that a full review found 'no credible evidence of any criminal wrongdoing.'** That review's process and conclusions have not been independently verified, and no criminal charge has been filed.

MSNBC's investigative report became public on September 20, 2025, one year to the day after the recorded meeting. Homan's public response shifted over time: he first told reporters he 'did nothing criminal' without denying he received money, then at a NewsNation town hall explicitly denied taking '$50,000 from anybody.' The White House, through Deputy Press Secretary Abigail Jackson, denied the allegations and called the probe a 'blatantly political investigation.' House and Senate Democrats, led by Rep. Jamie Raskin and joined by multiple senators, formally demanded that DOJ and the FBI release the recordings and case file, including in a letter to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi. Without subpoena power in the House minority, they have been unable to compel disclosure, and no recordings or case file have been made public.

Independent fact-checkers, including Snopes, could not assign a truth rating to the core cash-acceptance claim, because the original reporting relied on anonymous sources and firsthand confirmation could not be independently obtained. The New York Times separately reported that its own anonymous sources disagreed internally on whether the evidence was sufficient to charge Homan with bribery at all.

Two nonprofits have since sued for the evidence under the Freedom of Information Act. Democracy Forward Foundation sued DOJ and the FBI in federal court in Washington on October 6, 2025, seeking any recording of the September 2024 meeting. In December 2025 the FBI issued a 'Glomar' response, refusing to confirm or deny that any recording exists, on the grounds that acknowledging one would invade Homan's personal privacy and, it later added, reveal non-public FBI surveillance techniques. DOJ moved for summary judgment on that basis in April 2026, Democracy Forward cross-moved, and briefing closed on June 30, 2026; the docket showed no ruling as of its last update in late July 2026. Democracy Defenders Fund sued the FBI on February 17, 2026, after the bureau denied in full its request for the recordings and investigative records, categorically withholding all documents under the same privacy exemptions; on September 8, 2026, Judge Ana C. Reyes directed the FBI to file a Vaughn index, an itemized justification of what it is withholding. Neither suit had produced any records as of those latest docket entries.

status: Unresolved and contested. The case is closed with no charge; DOJ's no-credible-evidence review is unverified. The recordings remain unreleased: the FBI won't confirm they exist, and two FOIA suits seeking them are pending, with no ruling on their dockets as of July and September 2026.

comeback: The dispute isn't only whether Homan accepted the cash. The officials who decided to close the investigation are appointees of the same administration whose senior official was under investigation, and career Public Integrity Section supervisors had initially recommended continuing the probe before being overruled. The core facts can't be independently verified without the recordings, which the administration controls and has declined to release even under formal congressional request. That refusal to release primary evidence that would resolve the dispute either way is itself part of what this entry documents, whichever side's account is ultimately correct.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] An example of a structural accountability gap: when an administration's own DOJ controls both the investigation of, and the case-closure decision about, one of its own senior officials, the public has no independent mechanism to verify the outcome absent congressional subpoena power or an outside legal process (e.g., a leak, a change in House majority, or a FOIA suit like the two now pending, which have not yet produced the recordings) -- a gap this entry documents regardless of whether the underlying bribery allegation itself is ultimately true.

official: Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General (directed by presidential memorandum)
offense_category: DOJ Investigation of the Opposing Party's Fundraising Infrastructure, Directed by Presidential Memorandum and Escalated by a Parallel Congressional Contempt Threat -- an institutional-accountability claim about coordinated multi-branch pressure on a single-party target, not a criminal charge against any named official
incident_summary: The congressional side of this effort began well before the DOJ probe: House Administration Chair Bryan Steil opened an inquiry into ActBlue's donor-verification practices in October 2023 and subpoenaed the platform in October 2024. By late March 2025, Republican lawmakers were asking the Treasury Department for 'suspicious activity reports' mentioning ActBlue and pressing for Treasury and FBI probes, while Elon Musk sought, without evidence, to tie ActBlue to protests and vandalism against Tesla. In April 2025, President Trump signed a memorandum directing then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate online political fundraising platforms for alleged straw-donor and foreign-contribution violations; although the memo's directive covered online fundraising platforms generally (the White House fact sheet cited 'ActBlue and other online fundraising platforms'), **ActBlue -- the Democratic Party's dominant fundraising platform, which has processed nearly $17 billion in donations since 2004 -- was the only platform named**. ActBlue called the memo a 'brazen attack on democracy in America.' In parallel, House Republicans led by Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan, Oversight Chair James Comer, and House Administration Chair Bryan Steil pursued their own year-plus congressional investigation into ActBlue's foreign-donation vetting practices. On May 7, 2025, the three chairmen wrote to Bondi, citing Trump's memorandum, sharing their ActBlue findings and saying they would like to 'work collaboratively with DOJ.' An April 2, 2026 New York Times report cited internal ActBlue documents describing the resignation of interim general counsel Aaron Ting and an internal message from former legal counsel Zain Ahmad alleging retaliation after he reported misconduct internally -- documents the House committees said ActBlue had not produced despite subpoenas. On April 14, 2026, the chairmen demanded full compliance with their subpoenas; a House Republican aide told CBS News that a contempt vote was among the options. On June 10, 2026, ActBlue CEO Regina Wallace-Jones invoked her Fifth Amendment right more than 20 times during a House Administration Committee hearing, declining to answer questions including on ActBlue's donation-verification procedures and whether it had given Congress false information. In a June 18, 2026 letter, made public on June 22 in a House Judiciary press release that called it a threat to hold ActBlue in contempt of Congress, the three chairmen called it implausible that all 422 documents on ActBlue's privilege log -- including Ting's resignation letter and Ahmad's message -- were entirely privileged, rejected the privilege claims over those two documents and over documents circulated among non-lawyers, and demanded them by June 26, 2026, saying the committees remained prepared to enforce their subpoenas 'through all available mechanisms.' The letter itself does not mention the DOJ investigation. Separately, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton had sued ActBlue in Texas state court on April 20, 2026; after ActBlue sued him in federal court in Massachusetts alleging retaliation, U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns on June 11 preliminarily barred Paxton from pursuing the Texas case, writing that the lawsuit 'was filed in retaliation,' and Paxton appealed to the First Circuit. In September 2026, Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway opened a state consumer-protection investigation of ActBlue, saying the House Administration Committee had referred its findings to her office; ActBlue called it part of a 'coordinated campaign.'

Here a presidential memorandum that named only the Democrats' main fundraising platform directed DOJ to investigate online fundraising platforms; House committees whose own ActBlue probe predated the memo offered in writing to work with DOJ and pressed toward contempt; and a Republican state attorney general sued the same target in a case a federal judge preliminarily enjoined on ActBlue's retaliation claim. official: Donald Trump, President; Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (contradicted by Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao's own public statement)
offense_category: Public Misrepresentation of a Foreign Military Sale Decision -- Trump's administration publicly characterized the pause differently than its own Acting Navy Secretary's on-record explanation; NOT charged, a characterization/transparency dispute
incident_summary: At a May 21, 2026 Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee hearing, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, answering Sen. Mitch McConnell, disclosed that the Trump administration had paused a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan to conserve munitions for U.S. operations against Iran: 'Right now we're doing a pause in order to make sure we have the munitions we need for Epic Fury -- which we have plenty. But we're just making sure we have everything, but then the foreign military sales will continue when the administration deems necessary.' He said any decision to proceed would be up to Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Cao's explanation cut against Hegseth's own assurance to lawmakers earlier that month that 'the munitions issue has been foolishly and unhelpfully overstated. . . . We have plenty of what we need.' Cao said at the hearing that he had not 'spoken to the Taiwanese' about the decision, and on May 22 Taiwan's presidential office said it had no information about any U.S. adjustment to the sale; a Pentagon spokesman said the details 'remain predecisional until finalized by the President' and that Taiwan policy was unchanged. On May 25 Taiwan's foreign minister told lawmakers that Cao was 'not the final policymaker' on foreign arms sales, and its defense minister said there had been no formal notice of a delay -- moves the Maritime Executive described as an attempt to row back Cao's comments. Six days before Cao's testimony, Trump had given a different account: asked in a May 15 Fox News interview with Bret Baier, during his trip to Beijing for talks with Xi Jinping, whether he would move forward with the package, he said, 'I'm holding that in abeyance, and it depends on China. It's a very good negotiating chip for us, frankly' -- tying the hold to leverage with China rather than to munitions supply. On May 30, at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, Hegseth said there had been 'no change' in the U.S. position on Taiwan and, asked about Cao's remarks, said, 'Hung Cao is fantastic, but I would not couple the two in any way at all,' adding that U.S. stockpiles were 'more than suited' and that any decision on future Taiwan arms sales 'will rest with' the president. In June the State Department reiterated that arms sales to Taiwan were not dependent on Beijing's consent. On July 15, 2026 the House passed a fiscal 2027 appropriations bill (H.R. 8595) with $500 million in Foreign Military Financing for Taiwan, a separate program that does not commit money to the paused package; the Senate had not passed it as of late September. Trump and Xi ended a three-day summit in Washington on September 25, 2026, after which Trump had made no public comment on the $14 billion package, which still awaited his decision.

comeback: The specific problem isn't that a pause happened -- it's that a sitting Acting Navy Secretary gave a specific, substantive reason (conserving munitions for the Iran war) in direct tension with the administration's own separate public assurances that stockpiles remained adequate, and that a treaty-adjacent security partner learned of a $14 billion sale's pause without direct notification. That gap between what officials say privately drives policy and what they say publicly to allies and the press is the accountability issue, independent of whether the pause itself is defensible on the merits. Trump's own 'negotiating chip'/'in abeyance' framing outranks a subordinate's account of the same pause -- if the President himself describes withholding the sale as China leverage, that is a materially different and more consequential explanation than Cao's stated munitions-logistics rationale, and sharpens rather than resolves the contradiction this entry documents.

offense_category: National Environmental Policy Act / Administrative Procedure Act -- a federal judge found plaintiffs likely to succeed on a NEPA claim over the removal of hundreds of trees at a public D.C. golf course on less than a day's notice to the court, and in a preliminary-injunction ruling found an official's sworn declaration misleading and the government's justification pretextual; a civil case, no criminal charge or contempt finding
incident_summary: East Potomac Golf Links is a public, historically affordable golf course in East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C. President Trump wants it remade into a championship course, and on May 8, 2026, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced that the National Park Service "will renovate East Potomac Golf Links" into "a top-tier 18-hole championship golf course capable of hosting pre-eminent tournament golf." The DC Preservation League and two residents had sued Interior, Burgum and the Park Service in February 2026, arguing that the overhaul would skip required environmental and historic-preservation reviews. U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes said she told the government at a May hearing that she did not want even 10 trees cut without notice, and at hearings in July and September 2026 she asked it to give adequate notice of any imminent, irreversible work at the course, and government lawyers agreed. At about 4:55 p.m. on Friday, October 9, before a holiday weekend, the government filed a notice that work would begin the next morning to remove "up to 529 trees" in stages, under a 2019 Park Service report recommending a return to the course's original, largely treeless "links-style" design. Superintendent Kevin Griess declared that the project "is not a renovation or redesign of the Golf Course." **Crews arrived Saturday morning, and a Justice Department lawyer later told the court that 430 trees were felled.** At an emergency hearing on Monday, October 12, Reyes told government lawyers they had done "your absolute worst" and said "What has happened has cost the government all of its credibility with me in this case." Frank Lands, the Park Service's deputy director of operations, testified that he was told at an October 5 meeting with Greg Wischer, Burgum's deputy chief of staff and a political appointee, to carry out the 2019 report's recommendations "as soon as practical," without explaining the urgency. Lands also said he had shown the course to golf architect Tom Fazio two or three months earlier. Reyes said she would examine "whether or not I've been lied to" in the government's declarations about its plans and the timing of work. She ordered Wischer and Jessica Bowron, the Park Service comptroller exercising the director's delegated authority, to testify under oath at a hearing on October 19, and warned that any violation of her order would bring contempt proceedings. On October 13 she granted a temporary restraining order, finding the plaintiffs likely to succeed on their NEPA claim, barring any further tree felling at the course through October 26, and requiring, for the same period, three business days' notice before any irreparable change to the course. On October 16 the government moved to disqualify Reyes for bias; she denied the motion on October 18, writing: "It is easy to weaponize selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion." That morning Trump posted that Interior, "in conjunction with famed Golf Course Architect, Tom Fazio," had developed a plan for a championship course, and that work on the Fazio design would begin November 15, when the course would close to play for about 15 months. Reyes took judicial notice of the post and asked whether the government still maintained that there was "no final agency action"; it replied that it did, because the Park Service had not completed its review. On October 19 Trump posted that the work would start immediately and called Reyes a "crazed lunatic." At the October 19 evidentiary hearing on the plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction, Wischer, Bowron and Griess testified under oath; Wischer and Bowron both said they had learned of the 2019 report only in September. Reyes said "There is no universe in which all of this coincidentally happened all at the same time," and that there appeared to be "a strong showing of bad faith" on the government's part. The hearing concluded that day, and Reyes took the preliminary-injunction motion under advisement. On October 22 the plaintiffs asked the court to recall Wischer to testify about text messages with Tom and Gavin Fazio, whose details, the plaintiffs said, he had testified he could not recall, and to extend the restraining order by up to 14 days; the government opposed both. Reyes denied the extension the same day and denied the request to resume testimony without prejudice, but ordered the government to ensure that Wischer had taken appropriate steps to preserve the contents of his personal phone, and widened his preservation order to "any material concerning the East Potomac Golf Course and this litigation." On October 26, as the restraining order lapsed, Reyes granted a preliminary injunction in a 70-page opinion that opens: "Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting President." She wrote that the government "asks the Court to disbelieve repeated public comments made by the President," concluded that a renovation plan, which the plaintiffs call the Washington National Plan, exists and became final "well before October 15, 2026," and called the government's reliance on the 2019 report "pretextual." Whatever "routine maintenance" means, she wrote, "it does not cover the events of October 10." She did not find Wischer credible. She found Bowron's testimony credible but her October declaration, which did not mention the tree plan, misleading, and did not fault her for it: Bowron said she had relied on government counsel's advice, and the judge wrote that counsel "must have known" the plan belonged in the declaration. She found the plaintiffs likely to succeed on their claim that Interior violated NEPA by "impermissibly segmenting its review of the Plan's environmental effects." The order bars the government from cutting or damaging any tree in East Potomac Park without a court order, except to address an imminent threat to public safety, and requires "no less than ten business days' written advance notice" before any closure of the course or irreversible change to the park; it also ordered the government to show cause why it, including relevant Justice Department attorneys, should not be ordered to preserve information about the plan and the tree removal. Late that night Trump posted that the course would close "as scheduled on November 15th." Reyes took judicial notice of the post, noted that Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward had told the court on October 19 that "there is no plan to close the course," ordered the government to explain, and said she would hold a status hearing on October 30 or November 2 at which Woodward must appear. The government filed a notice of appeal to the D.C. Circuit on October 27. On October 28 it argued that no further preservation order was needed and acknowledged that "the President has twice directed Interior and the National Park Service to close the park by November 15," saying Interior was "working to develop a plan to implement that direction" and would give the court notice under the injunction. Reyes set an in-person hearing on that response for October 30, ordered Woodward to attend, and told the government to say whether it still maintains there is no final agency action, when the President gave his two directives, and when Interior began planning the closure. That evening the government filed the notice: the Park Service would submit a Tom Fazio rendering for a championship course to the National Capital Planning Commission on October 30, for the commission's December 3 meeting, and on November 15 would close East Potomac Park south of Buckeye Drive, including the golf course, "consistent with the President's directive." A new Bowron declaration said the Park Service had signed a lease that day under which the course's operator, National Links Trust, would stop running it by November 15, and cited the crumbling seawall as a safety hazard; the notice said the closure "must occur in all events." On October 29 the government asked her to stay the injunction pending appeal and to rule by November 4, and the plaintiffs filed Trump's October 28 post calling the course "highly dangerous" and saying, "We will hold the judge, Ana C. Reyes, fully responsible for anybody who is hurt, or killed." At the October 30 hearing, which Reyes opened by reading the D.C. Bar rule against false statements to a court, Woodward told her the planning-commission submission had been in the works for several weeks, said the course was not currently scheduled to close on November 15 but that the government had filed a "notice of intent" to close it, and put the cost of seawall repairs at $150 million to $400 million. Reyes said: "For months, the court trusted, but did not verify. No longer." She announced a formal inquiry into "whether agency officials and employees, including agency attorneys and [Justice Department] attorneys, have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated applicable ethical rules," possibly led by a special master, and stressed that opening it was not a finding that anyone had done so. She ordered the government to name everyone who helped prepare the submission, to say whether it has a contract with Tom or Gavin Fazio or Fazio Design, and to brief whether privilege shields the date tree removal or a links-style design was first added to it, and directed the parties to propose a preservation order.

status: Preliminary injunction (Oct. 26) bars tree cutting in East Potomac Park without court order. The government has noticed a Nov. 15 park closure, appealed and sought a stay. On Oct. 30 the judge opened an inquiry into possible misstatements to the court. No sanctions or contempt finding.
rebuttal_anticipated: Interior says the tree removal is long-deferred maintenance under a 2019 Park Service report that recommends restoring the course's original treeless links style, made possible by a temporary workforce surge, and separate from any renovation. The government gave notice before work began, as counsel had promised, and says it completed the required NEPA and historic-preservation reviews for the project. It maintains there is no final agency action to review, because the Park Service has not completed its review and the redesign's details may change, and it has appealed the preliminary injunction to the D.C. Circuit and asked for a stay, calling the order overbroad. It says the November 15 park closure is needed regardless of the course design, because under a new lease the operator will stop running the course and the seawall is a safety hazard. It argues that no further preservation order is needed because federal records law and an Interior litigation hold already cover the records, and that because the court never issued a written order requiring notice, there is no basis for a contempt inquiry. At the October 30 hearing, Woodward likened Trump's posts to executive orders that direct an agency without guaranteeing the action, said the course is not yet scheduled to close but the government has filed a notice of intent, and said "we would never violate the court's order."
comeback: The notice came just before 5 p.m. on the Friday before a holiday weekend, about 12 hours before crews started, after the court had asked for adequate notice. **In granting a preliminary injunction, the judge found that a renovation plan exists, called the 2019-report justification "pretextual" and found the plaintiffs likely to win their NEPA claim.** The directive came, by NPS testimony, from Burgum's deputy chief of staff rather than from park staff, and Burgum had already announced a championship renovation; the NPS official who passed on the order had shown the course months earlier to Tom Fazio, whose firm Burgum's announcement named as a renovation partner. On October 18, Trump announced that Interior and Fazio had developed a championship-course plan, with work to begin November 15, and on October 28 government lawyers acknowledged that Trump had twice directed Interior and the Park Service to close the park by that date. At the October 30 hearing, Woodward said the planning-commission submission had been in the works for several weeks, although no government lawyer had mentioned it at earlier hearings, and the judge opened a formal inquiry into whether officials and Justice Department lawyers misrepresented facts to the court.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Fits a pattern this tracker documents of the administration moving fast on capital projects the president favors in Washington and treating litigation as an obstacle, as with the White House ballroom, where the East Wing was demolished without congressional authorization and construction continued while the legal challenge was pending, and the proposed arch Burgum is advancing without congressional authorization.

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (institutional attribution -- hiring authority within the Office of Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict; no specific official named on record as personally approving this hire)
offense_category: Appointment of a Convicted January 6 Participant to a Sensitive National-Security Role -- no criminal or procedural violation established in the hiring itself; this is a public-integrity/qualifications-and-vetting concern given internal Pentagon objections
incident_summary: **The Pentagon hired Elias Irizarry, a 24-year-old who pleaded guilty in 2022 to a federal misdemeanor for entering and remaining in the U.S. Capitol during the January 6, 2021 insurrection at age 19 (sentenced to 14 days in jail, later pardoned along with more than 1,500 other January 6 participants on Trump's first day back in office), to a position in the Pentagon's Office of Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict, working on irregular warfare and counterterrorism issues in a role requiring security clearance access to some of the military's most sensitive operations.** Irizarry has no prior background or career experience in counterterrorism or special operations; after his guilty plea, he was readmitted to The Citadel, graduated in 2024, and unsuccessfully ran for a South Carolina state House seat as a Republican. The Department of Defense defended the hire, stating Irizarry was 'a qualified, patriotic young professional,' despite reported concerns raised internally by Pentagon officials about the appointment.
elements_required: Irizarry has a documented federal criminal conviction (guilty plea) for conduct during the January 6 Capitol breach, a matter of public record, not contested characterization

The position to which he was appointed involves access to sensitive military operations and counterterrorism/irregular warfare policy work, a substantively different function than an ordinary administrative role

Irizarry has no documented prior professional background or experience in counterterrorism, special operations, or irregular warfare, per reporting -- relevant to assessing whether the appointment reflects standard merit-based hiring
Pentagon officials internally raised concerns about the appointment, per reporting, indicating the hire was not uncontroversial even within the department making it

official: Mike Johnson, Speaker of the House
offense_category: Obstruction of a Duly-Elected Member's Seating to Block a Discharge-Petition Vote -- a constitutional-representation and cover-up-motive claim, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: Adelita Grijalva won a special election on September 23, 2025 to fill Arizona's 7th Congressional District seat, left vacant by her late father's death. **Speaker Mike Johnson kept the House in an extended shutdown recess -- eventually a fourth straight week, per an October 13, 2025 AP report -- and refused Democrats' requests to swear Grijalva in immediately**, saying she would be sworn in once the House returned to regular session (which he tied to the government shutdown ending). Grijalva had publicly committed to signing a discharge petition seeking a floor vote to compel release of files related to Jeffrey Epstein; her signature would have been the petition's 218th and final one needed to force the vote. House Oversight Committee Ranking Member Robert Garcia said on October 15, 2025 that 'Speaker Johnson is keeping the House in recess and holding the American people hostage so Adelita is blocked from being the 218th signature on the discharge petition to release the Epstein files,' calling it a 'White House cover-up.' Johnson repeatedly and explicitly denied any connection between the delay and the Epstein petition. Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes sent Johnson a demand letter on October 14, 2025 and, when he did not act, filed suit on October 21, 2025 seeking a declaratory judgment compelling him to administer the oath, arguing the delay disenfranchised Arizona's 7th District voters ('taxation without representation'); Johnson called the suit 'patently absurd' and said Mayes 'has no jurisdiction.' Grijalva was sworn in, and signed the discharge petition as its 218th signature, on the same day -- more than seven weeks after her election win.
elements_required: An elected member-elect was not seated for an unusually extended period (over seven weeks) relative to normal House practice
The delayed member had publicly committed to providing the decisive signature on a specific, high-profile discharge petition opposed by the Speaker's own party leadership and the President

The Speaker's stated reason for the delay (waiting for the House to return to regular session) was itself substantially within the Speaker's own control, since he set the House's recess schedule during the shutdown

A state attorney general -- an independent, differently-motivated actor -- concluded the delay was legally objectionable enough to sue, on a constitutional-representation theory distinct from the Epstein-cover-up allegation

evidence.description: The Hill's reporting that Johnson denied any political motive for the delay, stating Grijalva would be sworn in once the government reopened

official: Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), Chairman, House Judiciary Committee
offense_category: Potential weaponization of congressional oversight and criminal-referral power against a former prosecutor over contested closed-door testimony -- not itself an executive-branch action, but a pattern of using investigative/referral power to pursue a perceived political adversary; the underlying perjury allegation, if pursued, would be a genuine false-statements matter under 18 U.S.C. Sec. 1001, the statute the referral cites, but no charge has been filed
incident_summary: **On December 7, 2025, House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan subpoenaed former Special Counsel Jack Smith for a closed-door deposition on December 17, 2025, seeking documents and testimony about Smith's prosecutions of Trump over the 2020 election and classified-documents cases**. Smith's team said he would comply but noted he had previously (in October 2025) offered to testify publicly so lawmakers' questions and his answers would be visible to everyone; Jordan chose the closed-door format instead, telling Fox News it gave lawmakers and committee lawyers more time to question Smith. Ranking Member Rep. Jamie Raskin criticized the closed-door format at the time, saying Republicans would 'spin, distort, and cherry-pick his remarks through press leaks.' The December 17 deposition proceeded in one-hour increments alternating between the two parties. In a letter dated July 22, 2026 and made public July 23 -- roughly seven months later -- Jordan issued a formal criminal referral asking DOJ to investigate Smith for 'willfully and intentionally false statements' made under oath at that deposition (the letter cites the federal false-statements law, 18 U.S.C. § 1001), specifically over Smith's testimony that neither he nor his team sought the contents of lawmakers' text messages, only toll (metadata) records. Records DOJ later produced showed Smith's team had obtained message content for communications involving 44 lawmakers -- but per Raskin's rebuttal, those came from a National Archives production of White House staff communications, not from a subpoena directed at the lawmakers' own phones or messages, a factual distinction Raskin says Jordan's referral elides. At his July 15, 2026 confirmation hearing, the week before the referral, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, asked by Sen. Josh Hawley whether he had thought about investigating Smith for perjury, said 'We take testimony in front of this body very seriously, yes,' and replied 'Yes, senator' when Hawley said he hoped Blanche would investigate and possibly prosecute Smith; a criminal referral is a recommendation, not a charge. Smith's counsel called the referral evidence of 'a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system' against 'a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law.' Raskin called the referral 'baseless' and predicted it would be 'laughed out of court.' Update 2026-09-30: On September 29, 2026, Smith testified publicly before the Senate Judiciary Committee, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley. In prepared remarks he said, 'I will not be silenced by the continued threats of prosecution from the President or others,' said he stood by his decision to charge Trump, and said he would prosecute a former president on the same facts 'regardless of whether that President was a Republican or a Democrat.' Grassley called Smith's operation 'a partisan weapon that broke the rules.' Smith defended the toll-records subpoenas, saying the records show who a call was to and from and its length, and that nondisclosure orders were sought because he had 'strong reason to believe that Donald Trump would destroy evidence.' ABC News reported that Blanche had said in July testimony that the department was investigating the Republicans' referral; no charge against Smith has been reported.

No DOJ charge or indictment has been reported -- the referral is a request; at his July confirmation hearing Blanche signaled DOJ might investigate Smith for perjury, and ABC News later reported Blanche had said in July the department was investigating the referral, but no charging decision has been announced

The roughly seven-month gap between the December 2025 deposition and the July 2026 referral, combined with the referral's timing well after the deposition's content was known, is presented here as a fact pattern without asserting a specific political motive beyond what Smith's counsel and Raskin have publicly alleged

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense / Gen. Dan Caine, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff
offense_category: Unexplained Removal of a Senior Military Officer From a Key Pentagon Post After Only ~90 Days -- part of a broader pattern of abrupt, unexplained senior-military personnel changes this tracker documents
incident_summary: Vice Adm. Fred Kacher, a career surface warfare officer who previously commanded the Navy's Japan-based Seventh Fleet, was removed as Director of the Joint Staff -- one of the most significant three-star posts in the Pentagon, providing key support to the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs -- after less than three months in the role, which he had assumed December 5, 2025; the Pentagon announced the removal on February 25, 2026. The removal was ordered by Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine. The Pentagon's Joint Staff spokesperson did not provide a public reason for the removal; one source told reporters only that Kacher 'was not the right fit for the position.' Kacher is returning to a Navy role rather than another Pentagon post. This follows this tracker's separately-documented removal of Col. Dave Butler from his Army public-affairs role, reportedly in part over his past service under Trump critic Gen. Mark Milley. The broader pattern this entry flagged as a possible second unexplained removal, alongside Butler's, has since grown substantially: this tracker's separate Army Chief of Staff purge entry documents Hegseth's April 2, 2026 removal of Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George and two other generals, part of a reported total approaching three dozen general officers and admirals fired or sidelined under Hegseth as of mid-2026. No source ties Kacher's own removal specifically to the same stated or reported rationale -- the Pentagon gave no reason for George's firing, and the New York Times, as relayed by Al Jazeera, reported that it involved clashes between George and Hegseth over Hegseth's blocking of four Army officers' promotions, two of them Black and two women -- so Kacher's case remains documented here as an unexplained removal within that larger, now better-documented pattern, not as a confirmed instance of the same motive.

official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services
offense_category: Whistleblower Protection Act / First Amendment Retaliation Against Federal Employees -- NOT charged criminally; challenged via a federal civil lawsuit and Office of Special Counsel complaints, not criminal prosecution
incident_summary: On September 4, 2025, two former senior NIH officials -- Dr. Jeanne Marrazzo, former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID, the position Dr. Anthony Fauci previously held), and Dr. Kathleen Neuzil, former director of NIH's Fogarty International Center -- filed a joint whistleblower complaint with the U.S. Office of Special Counsel alleging they were forced out of their positions in retaliation for objecting to the cancellation of research grants and clinical trials, the politicization of scientific decisions, and what they described as baseless hostility toward vaccines from newly installed NIH leadership. Marrazzo, who had been placed on indefinite leave in March 2025, alleged Principal Deputy NIAID Director Dr. Matthew Memoli made statements mirroring Kennedy's views that 'vaccines are unnecessary if populations are healthy' and that NIH 'should not focus on vaccines.' offense_category: Federal conflict-of-interest rules (18 U.S.C. 208 bars an executive branch official, without a written waiver, from taking part in a matter that affects his or an employer's financial interests) and contracting integrity -- a reported conflict in no-bid Pentagon consulting awards; no investigation, charge or official finding is known
incident_summary: George Kollitides, a former Cerberus executive who worked under Steve Feinberg there and spent almost 10 years as a partner at the private-equity firm Alvarez & Marsal Capital, joined the Pentagon in 2025 as a special government employee, a status capped at 130 days a year that lets holders keep private jobs. Feinberg, now Deputy Secretary of Defense, made him his co-chief of staff and senior adviser, vice chairman of the Office of Strategic Capital's investment committee, and director of two new offices, the Economic Defense Unit and the Business Operators for National Defense, or BOND. In December 2025 the Pentagon gave Alvarez & Marsal Federal, a consulting affiliate of A&M Capital, a $67.6 million deal; documents ProPublica reviewed show the firm was helping vet loan deals for the Office of Strategic Capital by late 2025. In February 2026, days after Feinberg named him to lead a new Pentagon office, Kollitides joined the board of D. Boral Acquisition I, an offshore shell company, with an indirect interest in 100,000 founder shares; an April 2026 securities filing for that company still described him as "a Senior Advisor" to A&M Capital. Bloomberg reported he left that board at the end of September. In June 2026 the Pentagon finalized a **$281 million no-bid consulting contract with Alvarez & Marsal Federal to advise BOND**. Together the two deals total almost $350 million, about five times what A&M entities received from all U.S. agencies in the two decades before Trump returned to office. Both were signed as other transaction agreements, a method meant for experimental weapons that bypasses normal disclosure rules; experts called its use for consulting extraordinary. About $31 million had been paid by October. The two A&M firms are separately managed but share back-office staff and overlapping ownership, and ProPublica reported that the fund's success depends on the consulting side's. Kollitides is now classified as a highly qualified expert, whose financial disclosures are generally confidential, and ProPublica's August request for them is unanswered. On October 8, 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported, according to a Raw Story summary, that the Pentagon had paid Alvarez & Marsal $300 million, far more than the roughly $31 million ProPublica found paid on these two deals, and that some officials privately asked why taxpayers were footing the bill; Feinberg told the paper the department lacks "capable operators." ProPublica's October 9 report quoted ethics experts saying officials are generally barred without a waiver from decisions affecting their finances, even through a salary. A&M Capital said Kollitides left days before publication, and the Pentagon said he is recused on A&M Capital matters and "in full compliance with all ethical laws and regulations." It did not say whether he was paid by A&M Capital, took part in the awards or had a waiver.

official: Scott Kupor, Director of the Office of Personnel Management
offense_category: Likely Administrative Procedure Act and First Amendment Violation -- Politicizing Nonpartisan Civil Service Hiring
incident_summary: In May 2025, OPM under Director Scott Kupor issued a "Merit Hiring Plan" that added an essay question to federal job postings across the government, asking applicants to "[i]dentify one or two relevant Executive Orders or policy initiatives that are significant to [the applicant], and explain how [the applicant] would help implement them if hired." The question appeared on more than 70,000 federal job postings for nonpartisan civil service positions. Kupor publicly defended the plan as reinforcing "the nonpartisan character of the federal workforce," and OPM guidance described the question as non-mandatory, non-scored, and not a "political litmus test." Three federal employee unions sued OPM and Kupor in November 2025, arguing the question amounted to a de facto political loyalty test that pressured applicants to signal support for Trump's agenda to be considered for hire. On September 11, 2026, U.S. District Judge George O'Toole (D. Mass.) **sided with the unions, finding they were likely to succeed in showing "there is no legitimate governmental interest in inquiring into the political beliefs of applicants to federal civil service vacancies," and that the question likely violated the Administrative Procedure Act by infringing First Amendment speech rights**. O'Toole ordered OPM to notify agencies by the end of that week that the question should be removed from active job postings.

offense_category: Federal Procurement Authority Violation -- exercising contracting authority he did not legally hold as a Special Government Employee, potentially implicating federal procurement regulations governing who may bind the government to a contract; DHS OIG (Inspector General Joseph Cuffari) was reported in July 2026 to be weighing a criminal referral, but none has been reported as made as of October 2026
incident_summary: Corey Lewandowski, a former Trump campaign manager who served as an unpaid Special Government Employee and senior adviser to then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem until both left DHS in March 2026, is under investigation by the DHS Office of Inspector General for allegedly improperly participating in the award of DHS contracts -- a function he had no legal authority to perform in his SGE capacity. In early 2026, scrutiny centered on a $220 million no-bid DHS advertising campaign featuring Noem. On March 6, 2026, Sens. Peter Welch and Richard Blumenthal wrote to the three firms involved -- Safe America Media, which signed a $143 million no-bid contract; People Who Think, which received a $77 million no-bid contract; and subcontractor the Strategy Group -- asking whether Noem, Lewandowski, or any DHS employee financially benefited. On March 10, NBC News reported that Trump had personally questioned aides about whether Lewandowski profited from the campaign. On March 19, NBC News reported, citing a person familiar with the discussions, that in September 2025 a representative of self-deportation contractor Salus Worldwide Solutions told a marketing firm owner that hiring a consultant tied to Lewandowski was a condition of a subcontract, saying 'we need to make sure we are properly thanking the person who gave it to us'; Lewandowski's spokesperson called it 'patently false' and a Salus lawyer called the accounts 'entirely false.' On March 23, **House Oversight Committee Ranking Member Robert Garcia expanded Oversight Democrats' investigation after NBC News reported that Lewandowski allegedly demanded kickbacks from private-prison contractor GEO Group tied to the value of its DHS contracts, then, after rejecting the company's counteroffer to put him on retainer, allegedly told a senior DHS official not to award it more contracts**. On March 25, House Judiciary Democrats asked Chairman Jim Jordan to subpoena Lewandowski over the ad spending, citing internal records reviewed by ProPublica indicating he approved major contracts and noting that $143 million was routed to a newly formed LLC created days before the award; no subpoena has been reported. On March 26, CNN reported that the DHS inspector general had launched a sprawling investigation into how DHS contracts were solicited and handled, including Noem's and Lewandowski's involvement; the inspector general has not said which contracts it covers, though Rep. Bennie Thompson wrote in July 2026 that the self-deportation contractor Salus Worldwide is part of the review. At a June 17, 2026 confirmation hearing, DHS management nominee Brian Cavanaugh told Sen. Maggie Hassan that DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin had begun reviewing contracts Lewandowski might have approved. On July 10, 2026, the Wall Street Journal reported that investigators led by Inspector General Joseph Cuffari had found evidence Lewandowski may have been involved in improperly awarding contracts, that people who reviewed the documents or had knowledge of the approvals said he personally signed specific contracts despite not being a full-time federal official, and that investigators were weighing a criminal referral to the Justice Department that was not imminent; DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and White House officials have been briefed on the inquiry. On September 7, 2026, the Journal reported that Lewandowski had operated as a de facto "shadow secretary" at DHS, citing an episode in which a proposed $2.7 billion Palantir agreement sat unsigned while he sought a one-on-one meeting with CEO Alex Karp and was later cut to $1 billion. The same report said he pitched officials of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates on retaining him for outside work, offering help with matters within DHS's remit such as visas; both rebuffed him. Lewandowski, through a spokesperson, has denied issuing contracts at DHS and said he has not been contacted by investigators. He called the September report "anonymous-source, politically driven reporting."

official: Kelly Loeffler, Administrator of the Small Business Administration
offense_category: Hatch Act Violation (5 U.S.C. §7323, prohibiting partisan political activity by federal employees using official resources) — NOT charged criminally, addressed via Office of Special Counsel complaint process; this entry has stronger documentary evidence (cited internal emails) than the parallel Turner/HUD entry in this dataset
incident_summary: As the 2025 federal government shutdown began, **SBA's Chief Human Capital Office emailed all SBA employees on September 30, 2025 blaming congressional Democrats for the looming funding lapse, then on October 1 sent a second email urging employees to blame congressional Democrats for the shutdown in their out-of-office replies; SBA's public website and district office voicemails carried the same partisan message**. Sen. Ed Markey, ranking member of the Senate small business committee, wrote to Loeffler citing these internal emails and called SBA's actions 'a gross misuse of federal resources and a betrayal of public trust,' noting career civil servants do not swear their oath to a political party; Rep. Nydia Velázquez, ranking member of the House small business committee, had sent a similar letter a day earlier. Public Citizen also filed a Hatch Act complaint against Loeffler personally, alleging that the SBA homepage's partisan shutdown post amounted to political activity while on duty. Update 2026-09-29: On September 25, 2026, the Office of Special Counsel closed its shutdown-messaging cases -- more than 1,000 complaints about the White House and 37 agencies, a list that includes SBA -- without seeking discipline, finding agencies had reasonably relied on an ambiguous 2024 OSC advisory. OSC made no final determination on whether any message broke the Hatch Act, did not describe SBA's messages, and said investigating individual employees' roles would not change the outcome.
elements_required: 5 U.S.C. §7323 prohibits federal employees from engaging in partisan political activity while on duty or using official government resources
Documented instruction (not merely informal/individual conduct) directing employees agency-wide to post partisan content via official channels
Content must constitute partisan political activity rather than neutral factual communication about government operations
Whether Loeffler personally directed or was aware of the Chief Human Capital Officer's emails -- a distinct, not fully resolved question from the broader agency-level conduct

evidence.description: Public Citizen, a nonprofit watchdog group, filed a Hatch Act complaint with OSC against Loeffler personally (received October 1, 2025), stating that as administrator she is responsible for SBA's web page and that it carried 'a highly partisan post targeting both employees and the public asserting that congressional Democrats are solely responsible for the shutdown,' which the complaint alleged was political activity while on duty
evidence.maps_to_element: Personal Hatch Act complaint against Loeffler, aimed at the public website post rather than the internal employee emails

evidence.description: Rep. Nydia Velázquez, ranking member of the House Committee on Small Business, wrote to Loeffler on October 2, 2025, quoting an October 1 SBA email that suggested staff use an out-of-office reply saying they were out 'because Senate Democrats voted to block a clean federal funding bill (H.R. 5371), leading to a government shutdown,' and citing a red 'Special Announcement' banner on SBA's public website; she called such directives 'at best, highly inappropriate and, at worst, a clear violation of the Hatch Act and other federal laws' and asked who wrote or directed the language
evidence.maps_to_element: Independent congressional account of the out-of-office directive and website banner, with the suggested reply text quoted

The report does not name Loeffler specifically among the six, but documents the same OSC capacity problems plausibly explaining why her and Turner's Hatch Act complaints were still undetermined at that point.

evidence.description: On September 25, 2026 the Office of Special Counsel closed its shutdown-messaging cases -- over 1,000 complaints about the White House and 37 agencies, a list that includes the Small Business Administration -- without seeking discipline, concluding agencies had reasonably relied on an ambiguous 2024 OSC advisory while OSC's Hatch Act staff were furloughed. OSC made no final determination on whether any message violated the Hatch Act, did not describe SBA's messages, and said further inquiry into 'the roles of individual employees' would not change the outcome. It called the OMB-directed pre-shutdown staff message measured, while saying inflammatory, broadly disseminated public messages 'might weigh in favor of concluding' they violated the law.
evidence.maps_to_element: Resolution of the Hatch Act complaints: closed with no discipline and no finding either way; Loeffler's personal role left uninvestigated

status: Markey and Velázquez asked who directed the messaging; no public answer found. On September 25, 2026 OSC closed the shutdown-messaging complaints, SBA's included, without discipline or a final ruling, citing agencies' reliance on its 2024 advisory. No charges; enforcement is administrative.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense, and one many agencies gave OSC: shutdown messages addressed a live funding dispute and its effect on services, never mentioned elections or voting, and followed OSC's own 2024 advisory that references to a political party, without more, typically are not political activity. OSC found that reliance reasonable in September 2026 and sought no discipline. Turner made a similar factual-information defense of HUD's banner, and the internal emails asked staff to state a funding position, not to campaign. By TAP's own comparison (OSC does not name SBA's email), SBA's September 30, 2025 staff email closely tracks the wording of the OMB-directed pre-shutdown message that OSC called measured and not prohibited; that comparison does not reach the October 1 out-of-office directive, the website banner or the district office voicemails.
comeback: OSC's closure was not an acquittal: it said reliance on its ambiguous 2024 advisory made discipline inappropriate 'even if' some messaging broke the law, made no final determination, and said inflammatory tone and broad public dissemination 'might weigh in favor of' a violation. The documentary record is what sets this entry apart from the parallel Turner/HUD entry: two congressional letters cite, by date, an October 1 agency email urging employees to put partisan shutdown blame into out-of-office replies that outside correspondents would see, alongside the same message on SBA's public website and district office voicemails. Markey's and Velázquez's questions about who directed that messaging remain, as far as available reporting shows, unanswered, and OSC chose not to examine individual employees' roles.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] This incident is part of a cross-agency pattern this tracker documents during the same shutdown period (cross-reference Turner/HUD entry, same week, similar shutdown-blame messaging on a government website; OSC later reported complaints about the White House and 37 agencies, and said a pre-shutdown staff message was sent at OMB's direction). The use of similar framing across many agencies during the same shutdown event is itself evidence this wasn't an independent agency judgment but a centrally directed communications strategy -- which would shift responsibility upward from Loeffler and Turner individually to whoever coordinated the messaging.
confidence_note: MODERATE-HIGH confidence on the underlying facts -- this entry rests on cited, dated internal agency emails referenced in formal letters from the ranking Democrats on the Senate and House small business committees, which is stronger documentary evidence than press characterization alone. LOWER confidence on Loeffler's personal, direct involvement versus institutional responsibility for staff-level conduct, since Markey's request for that specific information doesn't appear to have been answered in available reporting, and OSC declined to investigate individual employees' roles when it closed the shutdown-messaging complaints in September 2026 without a final ruling. Together with the Turner/HUD entry, this points to a cross-agency pattern during the same shutdown; the two instances carry more weight together than either alone. official: Matthew Lohmeier, Under Secretary of the Air Force
offense_category: Confirmation of a Nominee With a Documented Pattern of Threatening Reprisal Against Named Military Officers and Spreading January 6 Disinformation -- confirmation itself is not unlawful, but the underlying record raises a civilian-military-boundary concern this tracker documents (a senior DoD civilian leader on record threatening 'serious consequences' against specific officers for perceived political disloyalty)
incident_summary: Matthew Lohmeier, a former Space Force lieutenant colonel, was relieved of command of the 11th Space Warning Squadron in 2021 after publicly alleging the military was embracing Marxism and 'critical race theory.' Trump nominated him as Under Secretary of the Air Force, the Air Force's second-highest-ranking civilian position. **Sen. Jack Reed, at Lohmeier's May 2025 Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing, read aloud an October 19, 2024 social-media post in which Lohmeier warned of 'serious consequences' for senior military leaders who 'participated in the hyper-politicization of the uniformed services' if Trump won the election**. Lohmeier had also posted claims that 'undercover government agents' were present at the Capitol on January 6, 2021. He denied using the word 'hoax' but maintained that government operatives had been present during the attack. Asked at the hearing whether he disavowed the October 2024 'serious consequences' post, Lohmeier deflected: he said he wanted to examine 'the context of all of the statements' and would hold accountable only those 'who don't follow the law and who don't honor their oath to the Constitution.' Sen. Mazie Hirono pressed him on whether he would seek reprisal against named officers, including Lt. Gen. Stephen Whiting, who by then led U.S. Space Command as a four-star general. Lohmeier did not directly answer, and Hirono called his response 'totally not reassuring.' Democrats opposed the nomination, citing this record as disqualifying, but on July 24, 2025 the Senate confirmed Lohmeier 52-46 along party lines.
elements_required: Lohmeier, before his nomination, publicly and specifically threatened 'serious consequences' for named categories of senior military leaders based on perceived political disloyalty, not merely general criticism of military policy

Lohmeier separately promoted a documented false claim (undercover government agents present at the January 6 Capitol attack), consistent with broader January 6 disinformation this tracker documents elsewhere

When directly asked under oath whether he disavowed the reprisal threat and whether he would seek reprisal against a specific named officer, Lohmeier did not do so, only offering a general, non-specific accountability standard

Despite this record being raised and characterized as disqualifying by multiple senators, he was confirmed to a position with direct civilian authority over the personnel he had threatened as a category

evidence.description: Defense One reported that Sen. Jack Reed read aloud Lohmeier's October 19, 2024 social-media post warning of 'serious consequences' for senior military leaders who 'participated in the hyper-politicization of the uniformed services,' and that Lohmeier separately claimed 'undercover government agents' were present at the Capitol on January 6, 2021, while denying he had used the word 'hoax.'
