Mazie Hirono separately pressed him on whether he would seek reprisal against Lt. Gen. Stephen Whiting by name, receiving no direct answer and calling the response 'totally not reassuring.'
evidence.maps_to_element: When directly asked, Lohmeier did not disavow the threat or rule out reprisal against a specific named officer

evidence.description: Newsweek reported the background of Lohmeier's 2021 relief of command, tied to his self-published book 'Irresistible Revolution: Marxism's Goal of Conquest and the Unmaking of the American Military,' in which he criticized diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and critical race theory in the military.
evidence.maps_to_element: Background establishing the pattern predates his nomination

evidence.description: Air Force Times and Stars and Stripes reported the Senate confirmed Lohmeier as Under Secretary of the Air Force in a 52-46 party-line vote on July 24, 2025, despite Democratic senators' objections that his record -- including the reprisal threats and January 6 claims -- should be disqualifying.
evidence.maps_to_element: Despite the disqualifying characterization, he was confirmed to a position with authority over the personnel category he had threatened

status: Concluded with his confirmation: Lohmeier was confirmed and serving as Under Secretary of the Air Force as of July 24, 2025. No sourcing reviewed identifies any later reprisal action by him against named officers, or any further congressional or Inspector General inquiry into his conduct.
rebuttal_anticipated: Lohmeier's own framing at the hearing was that he made the October 2024 post as a private citizen before his nomination and that it does not reflect how he would act in office. He said he would pursue accountability only against personnel who violate the law or their oath, a legitimate standard on its face, and that his January 6 comments were about specific undercover-agent claims rather than a blanket 'hoax' characterization of the attack.
comeback: Declining to disavow a specific prior threat, or to rule out reprisal against a named four-star general, when directly asked under oath at a confirmation hearing, is materially different from actually disavowing it. The 'law and oath' standard he offered is vague enough to justify almost any personnel action he might later want to take against an officer he judges insufficiently loyal, and it does not answer Sen. Hirono's specific question about his intent toward Lt. Gen. Whiting. His January 6 'undercover agents' claim, whatever term he uses for it, is itself a documented piece of disinformation about the attack, so it corroborates rather than distances him from the broader 'hoax' framing.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern this tracker documents of installing officials with a demonstrated record of loyalty-over-independence conduct into positions with direct authority over the personnel or institutions they have publicly criticized, then treating Senate confirmation itself as resolving concerns their own hearing testimony left unresolved.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on all core facts: Lohmeier's prior statements, the hearing exchanges and the confirmation vote are corroborated across Defense One's direct hearing coverage, Air Force Times, Stars and Stripes, Newsweek and Military.com. `contested: true` reflects that Lohmeier has an on-the-record, if non-specific, defense (he would act only against personnel who violate the law or their oath). That defense is a genuine rebuttal rather than an unaddressed allegation, even though TAP's reading is that his refusal to directly answer the Whiting-specific question undercuts its reassurance value.

official: Howard Lutnick, Secretary of Commerce
offense_category: Failure to honor a legally required 31-day health-insurance continuation period for terminated federal employees, and continued deduction of health-insurance premiums from paid-through employees without corresponding coverage or refund
incident_summary: Hundreds of Commerce Department employees -- including at NOAA and the CHIPS for America program -- fired as part of the administration's probationary-employee terminations were stripped of federal health insurance without notice, despite having paid their premiums and being legally entitled to a 31-day continuation-of-coverage grace period after termination. When a court order briefly required their reinstatement, some employees were restored to payroll only to be retroactively re-fired once an appeals court allowed the firings to proceed, with Commerce basing insurance-coverage cutoffs on employees' ORIGINAL termination dates rather than treating the reinstatement period as continuous coverage -- leaving a gap in which employees believed, and in some cases were told, they were insured. **At least one NOAA employee, who had a long-planned hip arthroscopic surgery, now owes roughly $15,000 out of pocket after her coverage lapsed without her knowledge**. Half a dozen former Commerce/NOAA/CHIPS employees reported that even their final pay stubs (for the pay period ending April 19, 2025) showed continued deductions for health-insurance premiums, despite their coverage having already lapsed. Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-MA), ranking member-adjacent on House Oversight, sent Secretary Lutnick a formal letter demanding an explanation for why the department did not honor the 31-day continuation requirement, why premiums continued to be deducted after coverage lapsed, and calling for full reimbursement of employees' out-of-pocket medical costs and premium overpayments.
elements_required: Federal employees are legally entitled to a 31-day health-insurance continuation period following termination -- a specific, checkable statutory/regulatory requirement, not a discretionary courtesy

Commerce Department employees were terminated, in some cases reinstated by court order and then re-terminated, with insurance coverage administered based on original (not reinstatement-adjusted) termination dates, producing coverage gaps
At least one specific, named-circumstance harm (the $15,000 surgery bill) is documented as a direct financial consequence
Premiums continued to be deducted from pay after coverage had already lapsed, for which no refund had been issued as of the formal congressional inquiry
A formal congressional oversight demand was made directly to the responsible Cabinet secretary, not just outside advocacy criticism

evidence.description: NPR's June 4, 2025 report documents the core facts: hundreds of Commerce employees (NOAA and CHIPS for America) lost health coverage without notice despite paying premiums and being entitled to a 31-day continuation period; some were briefly reinstated by court order then retroactively re-fired once an appeals court allowed the firings, with Commerce basing coverage cutoffs on original termination dates; one NOAA employee now owes ~$15,000 for hip surgery after her coverage lapsed unknowingly; half a dozen former employees reported continued premium deductions on paystubs after their coverage had already lapsed.
evidence.maps_to_element: Establishes the coverage-gap mechanism, the named financial harm, and the continued-deduction-without-coverage detail

evidence.description: Rep. Stephen Lynch's formal letter to Secretary Lutnick demanding an explanation for the department's failure to honor the 31-day continuation-of-coverage requirement and why premiums continued to be deducted after coverage lapsed, and calling for reimbursement of affected employees' out-of-pocket costs and premium overpayments
evidence.maps_to_element: Formal congressional oversight demand directed at the named Cabinet secretary

status: Documented via reporting and a formal congressional oversight letter; no response from Lutnick/Commerce, reimbursement, or resolution identified in available sourcing as of this entry's most recent verification.
rebuttal_anticipated: Commerce could characterize the coverage gaps as an administrative error arising from the genuinely unusual whiplash of court-ordered reinstatement followed by appellate-court-permitted re-termination -- a novel, fast-moving legal situation rather than a deliberate denial of a legal entitlement.
comeback: An administrative-error explanation does not account for the continued deduction of premiums from paychecks after coverage had already lapsed -- money taken for a benefit not provided -- nor does it explain why coverage was keyed to the ORIGINAL termination date rather than treating the court-ordered reinstatement period as continuous employment, which would have naturally preserved the 31-day continuation window from whichever termination date actually applied. Both are administrable choices Commerce made, not inherent features of the legal whiplash itself.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Illustrates a downstream administrative-harm pattern distinct from headcount loss itself: the same probationary-firing/reinstatement/re-firing whiplash documented across multiple agencies in this database's other entries produced a specific benefits-administration failure at Commerce with direct financial harm to named individuals, not just projected capacity loss.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core facts: NPR's reporting is corroborated by wide public-radio syndication of the same underlying story, and Rep. Lynch's letter is a public congressional record independently confirming the demand and its specific asks. MODERATE confidence on the total scope ('hundreds' of affected employees) since the specific named/documented harm (the $15,000 case) and the paystub-deduction detail (six employees) are more narrowly sourced than the broader 'hundreds' figure. No response from Commerce/Lutnick to the oversight letter was identified in sourcing reviewed, so this entry cannot yet report the administration's own explanation beyond what NPR's contemporaneous reporting characterized as Commerce's basis for using original termination dates.

incident_summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick previously stated he cut ties with Jeffrey Epstein, his former neighbor, in 2005 and described their interactions as 'limited.' **Epstein files released by DOJ in early 2026 show Lutnick and Epstein were in business together as recently as 2014: the two signed on behalf of limited liability companies in a December 2012 agreement to jointly acquire stakes in a now-shuttered advertising technology company, Adfin.** The files also show that Epstein invited Lutnick to lunch on his private island on December 24, 2012, days before the Adfin deal was signed; that Lutnick was in email contact with Epstein, directly and through Epstein's assistant, as recently as 2018; and that Adfin correspondence continued into at least 2014, when fellow investor David Mitchell wrote to Epstein about further fundraising involving Cantor Ventures, the venture-capital subsidiary of Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnick led as CEO and chairman. Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers raised concerns following the disclosure; Rep. Thomas Massie and Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Oversight Committee Democrat, both called for Lutnick's resignation, citing what they characterized as lying about the ties. Testifying before a Senate Appropriations subcommittee on February 10, 2026, Lutnick acknowledged an hour-long 2012 lunch on the island with his wife, four children and nannies, while saying he could recall meeting Epstein only two other times after 2005 and "barely had anything to do with that person." CNN's February 15, 2026 review of the files documented further contact: calls and a drinks meeting arranged in 2011, Lutnick's invitation to Epstein to a 2015 Hillary Clinton fundraiser, and a $50,000 Epstein donation to a 2017 UJA-Federation dinner honoring Lutnick. Mother Jones' February 23, 2026 reporting found Cantor's Adfin role went well beyond the 'small minority investor' Lutnick's camp had described: Cantor lent Adfin $2 million at the end of 2013 and took majority control in 2016, with Lutnick joining the board, while Epstein kept his shares; and in May 2018 an email account identified as Lutnick's told Epstein that Adfin was "Producing revenue finally. This is their year." Lutnick appeared voluntarily for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Oversight Committee on May 6, 2026. Speaking to reporters before the session, Chairman James Comer said he had not seen wrongdoing in the email correspondence but that Lutnick 'wasn't 100% truthful' about whether he had been on the island; during a break in the interview, Comer told reporters Lutnick had 'been very forthcoming with those interactions', and he also said 'It's a felony to lie to Congress.' Committee Democrats said afterward that Comer had determined Lutnick committed no wrongdoing, while Reps. James Walkinshaw and Ro Khanna accused Lutnick of evasion and lies. The committee released the transcript on May 13, 2026: Lutnick testified that, to the best of his recollection, he met Epstein in person only three times (2005, 2011 and the 2012 island lunch), called each encounter 'meaningless and inconsequential,' and confirmed writing the 2018 Adfin email while saying he had not known Epstein was a fellow investor until the files were released. Lutnick remains Commerce Secretary.

Contemporaneous documentary evidence (signed business agreements, correspondence) shows business dealings and contact continuing through at least 2014, and communication, directly and through an intermediary, as late as 2018

comeback: The specific discrepancy is not merely that contact occurred, but that Lutnick's public 2005-cutoff claim is directly and specifically contradicted by dated business agreements, correspondence, and a documented island visit extending nearly a decade past his stated cutoff -- a factual misrepresentation distinguishable from a defensible characterization dispute, which is why the resignation calls came from members of both parties rather than being a purely partisan reaction.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern of administration appointees' past associations with Epstein surfacing only after DOJ's release of Epstein-related files under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, with the appointee's own public account or denial contradicted by those files rather than the ties being volunteered (compare the Ben Black DFC entry). Distinct from any claim that Lutnick was involved in Epstein's underlying crimes; he has not been accused of wrongdoing related to Epstein.

official: Howard Lutnick, Secretary of Commerce
offense_category: Federal Conflict of Interest (18 U.S.C. §208(a), prohibiting personal and substantial participation in government matters affecting the financial interests of organizations with which the official is associated; also 5 C.F.R. §2635.702, prohibiting use of public office for private gain) — NOT charged; congressional Democrats have sought Lutnick's ethics and recusal records on this deal (a separate Commerce Acting Inspector General request concerns AI data centers), but no completed investigation or finding identified
incident_summary: On January 26, 2026, the Commerce Department announced a tentative $1.6 billion deal with critical-minerals startup USA Rare Earth (USAR), extending up to $277 million in direct funding and $1.3 billion in loans while acquiring roughly a 10% equity stake. **On the same day, USAR announced it had separately raised $1.5 billion in private funding with Cantor Fitzgerald -- Lutnick's former firm, now chaired by his son Brandon, with another son Kyle as executive vice chairman -- serving as lead placement agent and earning a fee.** Lutnick had publicly touted the deal and reportedly was personally involved, including meeting with USAR's CEO in November 2025. In late February 2026, Sens. Van Hollen, Warren and Wyden wrote to Lutnick asking about his involvement, any ethics guidance or recusal records, and when he learned of Cantor's role, with a March 11, 2026 deadline. On June 3, 2026, Commerce's CHIPS Program Office signed the final award of up to $277 million and a loan agreement of up to $1.3 billion with USAR. In a July 6, 2026 letter, Sens. Warren, Wyden, Van Hollen and Rep. Zoe Lofgren said Lutnick had refused to provide answers and expanded the inquiry directly to Cantor Fitzgerald and USAR themselves, demanding documents by July 23, 2026; no confirmation was found that documents were produced by that deadline. On July 7, 2026, Cantor Fitzgerald issued an on-record denial specific to the USAR deal, asserting it played no role in the government negotiations and that Lutnick is fully divested from the firm. On September 2, 2026, asked on CNBC whether the deal was a conflict of interest, Lutnick said "It's just not," reportedly said he had no idea Cantor was involved, and said his sons had bought the firm from him. Later in September 2026, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the fundraising, that Cantor, with Moelis & Co. as co-placement agent, had capped the private raise at $1.5 billion and that a public filing put the fees at $50 million, without saying how they were split; a Commerce spokeswoman said neither Lutnick nor anyone else at the agency had discussed the rare earth minerals industry with Cantor Fitzgerald.

Absence of an authorized recusal or ethics-cleared waiver covering the specific participation
Private gain accrued to the official's family/associated organization as a result of the official action

A Commerce spokeswoman said neither Lutnick nor anyone else at the agency had 'interacted with or had any discussions whatsoever with Cantor Fitzgerald regarding the rare earth minerals industry.'

status: Commerce finalized the USAR deal on June 3, 2026. Lawmakers' letters (February and July) seek records; they say Lutnick refused to answer, and no document production has been confirmed. Lutnick publicly denied a conflict in September 2026. No investigation finding or charges identified.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: Lutnick formally divested his Cantor Fitzgerald stake into trusts for his adult children, overseen by his son Brandon, severing direct ownership; government investment decisions are made through standard interagency and career-staff review processes, not unilaterally by the Secretary; any benefit to Cantor is incidental to legitimate industrial policy, not the purpose of the deal. Lutnick himself disputes the "trust" description: on CNBC in September 2026 he said, "I didn't put my companies in a trust. My kids bought my company, so I am no longer involved in my old company at all."
comeback: Formally transferring a stake to trusts for one's own children, overseen by one's own son, while the firm that son runs simultaneously earns fees as paid placement agent on a deal the father's own department funds on the very same day, doesn't sever the financial relationship in any practical sense -- it restructures the paperwork while leaving the underlying family financial interest intact. That's exactly the arrangement 18 U.S.C. §208 is designed to prevent regardless of formal ownership structure. The 'standard interagency process' defense also doesn't explain the same-day timing: a $1.6 billion USAR deal announced the same day USAR announced a $1.5 billion private raise with Cantor as lead placement agent is either a remarkable coincidence or evidence that process and outcome were coordinated, and congressional oversight requests seeking documentation of that process have not been answered as of this entry's last update.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] A structural pattern rather than an isolated incident: a Cabinet secretary appointed directly from the leadership of a major financial firm transferred his ownership stake mainly to trusts for his adult children, overseen by his son Brandon, who now runs the firm with his brother Kyle, rather than selling it to unrelated buyers, so Commerce decisions can land in the family's business even where formal divestiture rules are met. Congressional Democrats have raised this same overlap in separate matters with different facts: the USAR deal (Cantor paid as placement agent for a company Commerce was funding), AI data center projects (Lutnick promoting projects his family's firms worked on), tariff-refund trades (Cantor reportedly buying refund rights while Lutnick championed the tariffs), and a Kazakh tungsten deal (Cantor reportedly helping raise $210 million for a lead investor in a mining project Lutnick helped negotiate). None has produced an investigative finding of wrongdoing; the repetition points to the ownership arrangement itself, not any single deal, as the source of the recurring conflicts.
confidence_note: MODERATE-HIGH confidence on the underlying facts (the deal timing, the family relationships, Cantor's placement-agent role, the public statements): they rest on Commerce's own announcements, USAR's disclosures as quoted in congressional letters, and news reporting. LOWER confidence on whether a technical §208 violation has actually occurred, since that depends on facts not yet public (whether Lutnick recused himself, the precise scope of his personal involvement) that congressional requests are still seeking. No completed OGE or Commerce Acting Inspector General investigation or finding has been identified, and no confirmation was found that Cantor Fitzgerald or USA Rare Earth produced documents by the July 23, 2026 deadline; the lawmakers say Lutnick has refused to answer their February letter. Commerce has denied wrongdoing on the separate AI-data-center matter ('no direct role,' 'complied with all ethics requirements') and in September 2026 said neither Lutnick nor anyone at the agency had discussed the rare earth minerals industry with Cantor; Cantor says it had no role in USAR's government negotiations and that Lutnick is fully divested; on CNBC in September 2026 Lutnick himself said the deal is not a conflict and that his sons bought the firm from him. A denial is not the same as the requested documentation being produced.
pull_quote: A Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson said the firm “had no role in USA Rare Earth's negotiations or financing arrangements with the U.S. government” and that Lutnick “is fully divested from the firm” -- yet Cantor earned fees raising $1.5 billion for USA Rare Earth on the same day Commerce announced its $1.6 billion deal with the company.

official: R. Trent McCotter, Acting Deputy Attorney General (was Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General when he filed the May 18, 2026 motion to drop the Adani charges; the judge found him the sole decisionmaker, and no fetched source shows Attorney General Todd Blanche approving the dismissal)
offense_category: Dropping a Pending Federal Fraud Indictment After the Defense, Led by the President's Personal Lawyer, Twice Floated a $10 Billion U.S. Investment as Part of a Resolution -- dismissing charges is within DOJ's prosecutorial discretion and the judge found the investment offer was not a factor; addressed here as a prosecutorial-independence and equal-justice concern over the process a federal judge called irregular, not as a criminal charge against McCotter
incident_summary:
On October 24, 2024, a Brooklyn federal grand jury indicted Indian billionaire Gautam Adani and seven others over what prosecutors alleged were schemes to pay about $265 million in bribes to Indian government officials for solar-energy contracts and to lie to U.S. investors to raise billions in financing. Adani, his nephew Sagar Adani and Adani Green Energy executive Vneet Jaain were charged with securities-fraud conspiracy, wire-fraud conspiracy and securities fraud; the five others faced Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and obstruction counts. The Adani Group has denied wrongdoing; all eight defendants are foreign nationals living abroad, and their arrest warrants remain outstanding.

In August 2025 Adani retained Sullivan & Cromwell; his lawyer Robert J. Giuffra Jr. also serves as a personal attorney for President Trump. Between February and April 2026 the firm sent the Justice Department about 600 pages of argument, and its April 17, 2026 slide deck proposed, as part of a joint defense offer, a general plan to invest $10 billion in the United States. On May 11, 2026, Eastern District of New York U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. wrote that his office "categorically rejected" that part of the offer. On May 18, 2026, R. Trent McCotter, then Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General, filed a one-paragraph motion to dismiss the indictment with prejudice, signed by him and Nocella; Judge Nicholas Garaufis noted that "no person involved in bringing the charges signed on to dismiss them." Nocella later swore that he "was not the decisionmaker" and signed at McCotter's direction.

On June 11, 2026, Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal wrote to then-Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche that the move gave "the appearance that Mr. Adani -- with the help of one of the President's personal lawyers -- bought his way to criminal immunity." On June 26 Judge Garaufis refused to grant the "terse, bland, and conclusory" motion and ordered DOJ to explain itself. McCotter's July 4 letter said the case was mainly foreign, hard to prove and outside current FCPA priorities, and called reports that the investment pledge played a part "false." In a court-ordered July 15 affidavit, Adani swore he knew of no promise tied to the dismissal but said his counsel had suggested the $10 billion pledge "might be part of a resolution," and Giuffra, in an unsolicited declaration, said he had twice told DOJ the Adani Group "would be amenable" to following through on it.

On August 10, 2026, Judge Garaufis dismissed the three Adani executives' charges with prejudice. He found McCotter was the "sole decisionmaker" and was satisfied the investment promise was a "non-consideration," but wrote that **"the irregularities in the decision to dismiss the Indictment are concerning"**: McCotter "appears to have eschewed the professional opinions of innumerable officials from various federal offices and replaced them with his singular judgment," working largely with defense counsel and seemingly without input from the FBI and SEC agents or the prosecutors who brought the case. Taking no position on "Mr. Giuffra's repeat attempts to resolve this bribery case with monetary offers," he wrote that "it is up to the public to decide what effect offers of this kind have on the equal administration of justice and the rule of law."

On September 3, 2026, the judge denied without prejudice the request to drop the FCPA and obstruction counts against the five other defendants for lack of factual support. McCotter, by then Acting Deputy Attorney General, petitioned the Second Circuit for a writ of mandamus ordering those counts dismissed, calling the ruling a "dangerous and unconstitutional arrogation of executive power"; MLex reported that on October 1 the appeals court denied DOJ's bid to expedite the petition. On September 23 Warren and Blumenthal wrote to Blanche, now Attorney General, a second time, citing the involvement of "two of President Trump's personal lawyers" and asking about any contacts by Boris Epshteyn or Donald Trump Jr.; Epshteyn's spokesperson denied any involvement in Adani's defense, and Trump Jr.'s said his November 2025 meeting with Adani had "zero to do with DoJ's actions in this case."
elements_required: Adani and co-defendants faced a pending federal indictment alleging a bribery scheme and fraud on U.S. investors
The defense, led by a lawyer who also represents the President, raised a $10 billion U.S. investment as part of a possible resolution before DOJ moved to dismiss
A single senior DOJ official decided on and signed the dismissal motion, without the prosecutors who brought the case
The presiding federal judge called the irregularities in the decision process concerning and the process apparently highly unusual in a written opinion, while granting dismissal
DOJ leadership has pressed to drop the remaining counts and did not answer senators' June questions about the investment offer

official: Linda McMahon, Secretary of Education
offense_category: Staffing a Federal Agency With Activists From Groups Whose Stated Goal Is Dismantling That Agency's Own Mission, Including the Secretary's Own Prior Leadership Role at One Such Group -- no criminal charge; an accountability claim about institutional capture and an undisclosed personal history rather than a specific statutory violation
incident_summary: Before becoming Education Secretary, McMahon chaired the America First Policy Institute (AFPI), a think tank co-founded by Stephen Miller that lists private-school vouchers and embedding 'biblical principles' in education among its priorities. ProPublica's investigation, published across a series of 2025-2026 reports, found McMahon has since brought at least 20 political appointees into the Education Department from ultraconservative advocacy groups and think tanks that share her department's own stated skepticism of public education's value, including at least nine from AFPI itself. Top adviser Lindsey Burke is a longtime Heritage Foundation policy director and the lead author of the education section of Project 2025, the conservative policy blueprint. Leaders from Moms for Liberty -- a group whose co-founder, Tiffany Justice (now with Heritage Foundation's political-advocacy arm), told ProPublica she hopes to drive public-school enrollment to 'zero' -- have joined McMahon for department roundtables and official events, and appointees with ties to Defending Education have also been placed in department posts. Under this leadership, the department has redirected hundreds of millions of dollars toward charter, private, and religious schools; released a formal 'Patriotic Education Supplemental Priority' tying federal funding preference to curricula emphasizing patriotic themes; and moved to protect school prayer. Separately, **the department's Office for Civil Rights (OCR) had its staff cut roughly in half early in Trump's second term and its nationwide regional office footprint reduced; OCR resolved 30% fewer discrimination complaints in 2025 than in 2024 and reached formal resolution agreements in fewer than 1% of its investigations**, while the administration's own subsequent budget proposal sought a further 35% cut to OCR's funding. In an apparent reversal reflecting the cuts' own dysfunction, the department later walked back hundreds of the OCR layoffs and paid approximately $38 million to the laid-off staff, even as OCR continued dismissing the large majority of complaints it received.
elements_required: McMahon personally led an organization (AFPI) advocating the same anti-public-school, pro-voucher, religious-curriculum agenda her department has since pursued, a direct personal continuity between her prior advocacy role and her official capacity

At least 20 political appointees, including at least nine from AFPI itself, were placed in the department from organizations whose stated goal is reducing or eliminating public school enrollment -- corroborated by named individuals' own statements to ProPublica, not merely inferred affiliation

The department's civil-rights enforcement function (OCR) was cut roughly in half in staffing and saw a documented, quantified decline in complaint resolutions during the same period the department pursued the appointees' shared ideological agenda

official: Linda McMahon, Secretary of Education
offense_category: Unauthorized Transfer of Congressionally Mandated Programs (potential separation-of-powers/ultra vires violation -- the Department of Education was created by Congress via the Department of Education Organization Act of 1979, and the statutes governing the transferred programs were separately enacted by Congress) — NOT criminally charged; addressed via formal impeachment articles (procedural, not expected to succeed given Republican control of both chambers) and ongoing political/legal dispute, not criminal prosecution
incident_summary: **Beginning May 2025, McMahon approved a series of interagency agreements transferring the administration of more than 100 programs and services (more than 140 by the impeachment sponsors' later count) -- governed by statutes including the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, Higher Education Act, Carl D. Perkins Career and Technical Education Act, Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, and civil rights enforcement under the Civil Rights Act, Title IX, the ADA, the Rehabilitation Act, and the Age Discrimination Act -- to the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, Justice, State, and Interior, without congressional authorization.** The impeachment resolution dates the approvals: May 21, 2025 (Perkins Act programs to Labor); September 30, 2025 (Elementary and Secondary Education Act and Higher Education Act programs to Labor, and Indian Education programs to Interior); February 20, 2026 (further Elementary and Secondary Education Act programs to HHS and Higher Education Act programs to State); and June 15, 2026 (special education and vocational rehabilitation to HHS, and civil rights enforcement to the Justice Department). Congress's fiscal 2026 appropriations law, passed in February 2026, did not prohibit the agreements, though its nonbinding explanatory statement said the department has no authority to transfer its fundamental responsibilities to other agencies. The Interior agreement moved Indian Education program administration to the Bureau of Indian Education; the transfer was announced in November 2025. At the only scheduled tribal consultation, on February 10, 2026, Cherokee Nation Principal Chief Chuck Hoskin Jr. said the agreements were already "at the execution stage," Navajo Nation Vice President Richelle Montoya said Executive Order 13175 requires timely and meaningful tribal consultation, and a Winnebago Tribe council member said the Bureau of Indian Education lacks the capacity to absorb the new grants. In May 2026, GAO told Sen. Warren it was expanding its existing review of the Education-Labor agreements to other agreements, including the transfer of student-loan default collections to Treasury, which Bloomberg Government reported covers more than 9 million borrowers in default and is the first step toward moving the full $1.7 trillion loan portfolio. In June 2026, the Education Department's Office of Inspector General reported that in the first three months of 2025 the department fired 1,277 employees, ended more than $500 million in grants and shut down 135 teams. On June 25, 2026, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici and 16 House Democrats introduced articles of impeachment (H.Res.1391) alleging the transfers violated the Department of Education Organization Act and that McMahon made false statements to the Senate at her February 13, 2025 confirmation hearing; the resolution was referred to the House Judiciary Committee. In September 2026, more than a hundred special education staff began reporting to an HHS building and dozens of civil rights staff moved to the Justice Department. The agreements are challenged in consolidated federal litigation in Massachusetts, which is in discovery with no ruling on their legality.

Whether 'interagency agreement' authority can lawfully accomplish what would otherwise require congressional action is the central legal question -- a genuine, unresolved point of administrative law, not a settled violation

status: Impeachment resolution H.Res.1391 has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since its June 25, 2026 referral, with no realistic path to conviction. The transfers are challenged in consolidated federal litigation in Massachusetts, now in discovery; no court has ruled on their legality.
rebuttal_anticipated: McMahon's own public response on X: it 'speaks volumes' that House Democrats treat 'working to improve student outcomes and reduce the federal bureaucracy' as impeachable, and they 'must not be bothered by chronic failures' such as historic low test scores and a failed FAFSA rollout; Rep. Burgess Owens, a supporter, called the effort 'completely unserious' and accused Democrats of protecting the 'entrenched bureaucracy.' At an April 2026 Senate hearing she said parents will 'still get the same treatment, the same funding' regardless of which agency administers programs.
comeback: Whether program administration is equally effective elsewhere is a policy question; whether the executive branch has legal authority to unilaterally relocate programs Congress assigned to a specific department by statute is a separate, legal question that policy arguments don't resolve. The documented OCR staffing cuts and the sharp decline in disability-discrimination investigations are concrete, measurable evidence of reduced capacity -- not merely a relocation with 'the same treatment,' as McMahon claims, but a demonstrated reduction in enforcement during the transition.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] By Trump's own public account, he appointed McMahon hoping she would 'put herself out of a job,' and McMahon has written that her mission is 'the responsible and permanent closure' of the department; the program transfers are consistent with a deliberate strategy to functionally dissolve the Department of Education without the congressional action that would formally be required to abolish it outright. Using interagency agreements to achieve through administrative action what hasn't been authorized through legislation is the same structural approach documented in the Vought entry (acting on legal theory courts haven't yet ratified) and the Sonderling/IMLS entry (sweeping agency dismantling via executive action before Congress can respond). This is an administration-wide pattern, not an isolated McMahon judgment call.

Impeachment articles have been introduced but have no realistic path to conviction, so 'McMahon was impeached' would overstate it. The GAO work is an expanding review of the agreements, not a finding; the staffing, grant and team figures come from the Education Department's Inspector General.

official: Donald Trump, President (issued and personally signed the veto message)
offense_category: Presidential Veto Power Used to Retaliate Against a Federally Recognized Tribe for Opposing an Unrelated Immigration Policy in Litigation -- an admitted-motive case rather than an inferred one
status: Veto sustained -- House override attempt failed
incident_summary: On December 31, 2025, Trump vetoed H.R. 504, the Miccosukee Reserved Area Amendments Act, a bipartisan bill (sponsored by Rep. Carlos Gimenez) directing the Interior Department to work with the Miccosukee Tribe to protect homes, water systems, and wastewater infrastructure at the tribe's Osceola Camp inside Everglades National Park from repeated flooding. **In his official veto message, published by the White House, Trump wrote that 'the Miccosukee Tribe has actively sought to obstruct reasonable immigration policies that the American people decisively voted for when I was elected' -- an explicit reference to the tribe's ongoing federal litigation opposing the administration's 'Alligator Alcatraz' migrant detention facility**, built in the Big Cypress National Preserve near tribal ceremonial sites and villages the tribe says the facility threatens. The veto message separately argued the federal government should not fund protections for 'an area that the Tribe has never been authorized to occupy' (Osceola Camp dates to 1935) and characterized the bill as 'special interests' funding 'unaligned with' the administration's immigration-enforcement policy. Tribal Chairman Talbert Cypress responded that the bill 'was not about special treatment, but about public safety, environmental stewardship, and honoring long-recognized tribal interests,' reflecting 'years of bipartisan work.' Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Trump's description of the tribe in the veto message was 'accurate.' The House attempted to override the veto on January 8, 2026, voting 236-188 in favor -- short of the 287 votes (two-thirds) required. This veto was issued the same day as a separate veto of H.R. 131, the Finish the Arkansas Valley Conduit Act (a Colorado water-infrastructure bill), which is documented separately in this tracker's entry on the Justice Department's intervention in Tina Peters's conviction, as part of a distinct retaliation pattern against Colorado over Tina Peters; the two vetoes share only a signing date, not a common grievance or target.

Congress passed, with bipartisan support, a bill addressing an unrelated matter (flood protection for existing tribal infrastructure) affecting that same tribe
The President vetoed the bill

The President's own official, published veto message -- not an inferred motive, an anonymous source, or a contested characterization -- cited the tribe's opposition to the unrelated immigration policy as a stated reason for the veto
The tribe and outside observers characterized the veto as retaliatory rather than a good-faith fiscal or authorization-based objection

official: Stephen Miller, White House Deputy Chief of Staff and Homeland Security Advisor (spoke at the FBI training and, per anonymous sources, pressed the bureau on threat cases involving his family; the agents' reassignment was ordered by FBI Washington Field Office head Darren Cox, who says it was made at the field office level alone)
offense_category: White House political interference in FBI criminal investigations -- a breach of the post-Watergate norm insulating Justice Department criminal cases from the White House, as former Justice Department officials describe it; a norm and policy concern, not an alleged crime, and the underlying cyberstalking charge is not itself in question
incident_summary: Stephen Miller, President Trump's deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, and his wife, conservative podcaster Katie Miller, have repeatedly asked the FBI's Washington Field Office to investigate political activists and others they say threatened or harassed them, CBS News reported, citing sources. In 2025 Miller asked the bureau to let agents go undercover in his Virginia neighborhood's political activist group, and after Arlington activist Barbara Wien protested outside the family's home, he pressed the Justice Department to act on that case, regularly calling the U.S. Attorney's Office in the Eastern District of Virginia for updates, sources told CBS; a magistrate judge twice rejected a federal search warrant, and the local prosecutor later declined charges, writing that "nothing in the proceeds of the search warrant supports criminal prosecution." Between August 3 and September 23, 2026, according to a later indictment, a caller using ever-changing phone numbers allegedly contacted the woman later identified as Katie Miller at least 40 times by phone and text. On Friday, September 25, 2026, the field office's counterterrorism chief, Special Agent in Charge Michael Burgwald, and his deputy, Courtland Rae, were demoted and sent to FBI headquarters, Bloomberg Law reported, citing three people familiar with the matter who said the orders from field office head Darren Cox stemmed from frustration shared by the Miller family that the probe was moving slowly. CNN, citing two sources, reported that the field office team had concluded the calls did not meet the threshold for an FBI investigation and found no nexus to terrorism. On September 29, Miller spoke at an FBI headquarters training conference for counterterrorism assistant special agents in charge, centered on the administration's domestic-terrorism directive, NSPM-7; according to an unnamed senior FBI official cited by CBS, **he told agents to be more proactive on threat cases and that no case is too small, whether the threats target a congressman, a spouse, friends, loved ones or a campus speaker.** Two days later, on October 1, the U.S. Attorney's Office in Boston announced a federal grand jury indictment charging John Anthony Proia III, 41, of Waltham, Massachusetts, with one count of cyberstalking a victim married to a "high-level federal government employee"; the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force arrested him, and Reuters and CBS identified the victim as Katie Miller. Proia has pleaded not guilty. Multiple former Justice Department officials told CBS that Miller's appearance ran afoul of post-Watergate norms and was unusual because he is an alleged victim and potential witness in the Boston case, and former Justice Department and FBI officials said they could not recall another White House official with such frequent, direct contact with the department's agents and prosecutors. The White House says the Millers never spoke with the reassigned agents or asked for the change, and that Miller's role as homeland security adviser includes carrying out the domestic-terrorism order; Cox says the reassignment was made at the field office level alone, and the FBI says it pursued the Millers' cases on "appropriate predicate" and evidence, "not because the White House ordered an investigation."
elements_required: Miller, a senior White House political official, addressed FBI counterterrorism supervisors at FBI headquarters on September 29, 2026, urging more proactive threat investigations under the administration's domestic-terrorism directive
Miller was at the time an alleged victim and potential witness in an open FBI cyberstalking investigation of threats to his own family, which was charged two days after his speech

official: Chad Mizelle, former DOJ Chief of Staff and senior adviser to Attorney General Pam Bondi
offense_category: Public Solicitation of Politically-Screened Hiring for Career (Nonpartisan) Federal Prosecutor Positions -- assistant U.S. attorneys are, by law and longstanding DOJ practice, career civil-service positions meant to be filled and evaluated apolitically, distinct from the political appointees at DOJ leadership
incident_summary: On January 31, 2026, Chad Mizelle -- who had been DOJ chief of staff and one of Attorney General Pam Bondi's top advisers until he left the department in September 2025 -- publicly called for lawyers who 'support President Trump' to apply for career federal prosecutor positions, telling them to 'DM me' and suggesting he could help such applicants secure the jobs. Assistant U.S. attorneys, who investigate and prosecute federal cases, are supposed to be nonpolitical and nonpartisan career civil servants, distinct from DOJ's political-appointee leadership. About forty minutes after Mizelle's post, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller amplified it, adding 'Patriots needed.' On February 2, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, Jason Reding Quinones, also reposted it, saying 'We are hiring!' The same day, on podcasts including Steve Bannon's, Mizelle said he had received 'hundreds and hundreds of inquiries' and that, as chief of staff, 'On Day 1 we dismissed about 100 people who we thought were working against Donald J. Trump.' The call came amid mounting DOJ turmoil over politically charged personnel decisions, including the firing of prosecutors and investigators connected to earlier Trump-related cases and the pursuit of investigations against several of the President's political opponents. A former federal prosecutor quoted in ABC News's reporting warned that explicitly recruiting career prosecutors on the basis of political loyalty could be 'dangerous' to the office's traditional independence. On February 7, 2026, The New York Times covered the department's recruiting problems under the headline 'Demanding Support for Trump, Justice Dept. Struggles to Recruit Prosecutors.' In March 2026, Bloomberg Law reported, and MS NOW and the ABA Journal relayed, that **DOJ had suspended its rule that newly hired federal prosecutors have at least one year of legal experience, citing an 'exigent hiring need,' so that some offices could hire candidates straight out of law school**, amid widespread departures and reported difficulty finding qualified replacements. Mediaite reported at the time that about 5,500 employees had left DOJ since the start of Trump's second term. On May 31, 2026, a New York Times analysis of federal employment data found that DOJ had lost more than 2,600 attorneys, a 21 percent decline in roughly 16 months. A related but analytically distinct legal challenge exists: AFGE, AFSCME, and NAGE sued over a broader federal civil-service 'loyalty question' job-application practice, unrelated to Mizelle's specific AUSA-hiring solicitation. On June 29, 2026, the First Circuit declined the unions' request to order the district judge to rule on their stalled challenge. On September 11, 2026, U.S. District Judge George O'Toole stayed the question's use on federal job applications, finding it likely violated applicants' First Amendment rights, but denied a broader preliminary injunction that would have barred agencies from considering answers already submitted; OPM then replaced the question. No legal action specific to Mizelle's own AUSA solicitation has been identified in sourcing reviewed.
elements_required: A former DOJ chief of staff and top adviser to the Attorney General, who had left the department months earlier, publicly solicited applicants for career (not political-appointee) federal prosecutor positions using explicit political-loyalty language ('support President Trump')
A senior White House official amplified the same call using similarly loyalty-coded language ('Patriots needed') within the same hour
Assistant U.S. attorney positions are, by design and longstanding DOJ norm, meant to be filled and evaluated on professional merit rather than political allegiance

The call occurred amid documented, separate instances of DOJ personnel actions against career staff connected to Trump-related investigations, providing context for concern that political-loyalty screening was already an operative practice, not merely rhetorical

rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: soliciting applicants who share the administration's general political outlook is not the same as excluding qualified candidates who don't, career hiring processes (background checks, bar standing, interview panels) remain formally in place regardless of who is encouraged to apply, and prior administrations have also been accused, at times, of favoring ideologically sympathetic hires within legal limits.
comeback: The specific language used -- explicitly conditioning the invitation on support for the President personally, rather than general qualifications or even broad philosophical alignment -- and its amplification by a senior White House official using loyalty-coded language ('Patriots needed') is a more explicit and public break from the norm that AUSA hiring should be conducted apolitically than prior administrations' informal, unstated preferences; the concern is not merely optics but that the Attorney General's former chief of staff offered to personally help such applicants secure positions, and a sitting U.S. attorney also publicly endorsed the call.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Fits a pattern this tracker documents of career prosecutors being pushed out of DOJ, such as the firings of January 6 prosecutors and the Minnesota U.S. Attorney's Office resignations over the Renee Good investigation. Here the pressure shows up on the hiring side: a former chief of staff who, by his own account, helped dismiss staff seen as working against Trump invited Trump supporters to apply for career prosecutor jobs, and a senior White House official and a sitting U.S. attorney amplified the call. DOJ's later waiver of its one-year experience rule is a separate act, reported as a response to departures, not as evidence that loyalty screening was applied.

MODERATE confidence on downstream impact: no source shows that the call itself changed who DOJ hired. The experience-requirement waiver is HIGH confidence (Bloomberg Law's report of the March 13 memo, relayed by the ABA Journal and MS NOW, and not denied by DOJ), but it is reported as a response to departures, not as a product of the post. The 21 percent / 2,600-attorney figure comes from the Times' May 31, 2026 analysis of federal employment data, read here through secondary coverage; the 5,500-employee figure is Mediaite's March 2026 figure, not the Times'. official: Markwayne Mullin, Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: Unverified Public Claims Undermining Election Confidence / Referral of State Election Partners to the Justice Department -- accountability concern, not alleged as a legal violation: the Homeland Security Secretary asked the Justice Department to investigate a state-run voter-roll consortium and an election nonprofit under a federal privacy law, and to examine whether widely used ballot-marking devices comply with federal law, on claims the groups dispute and with no reported example of the machines being manipulated in an election -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary: On Wednesday, September 2, 2026, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent Attorney General Todd Blanche a four-page letter asking the Justice Department to take up two election matters; the White House posted the letter on its website two days later. The first concerned the Electronic Registration Information Center, or ERIC, a nonprofit created and governed by state election officials that pools voter-registration and motor-vehicle records to help member states find inaccurate, duplicate and deceased registrations and people eligible to vote but not registered. Mullin wrote that "ERIC exposes millions of citizens' sensitive private data to unknown contractors, subcontractors, and agents of ERIC, potentially in violation of the DPPA," the federal Driver's Privacy Protection Act, and that before the 2020 election ERIC shared protected motor-vehicle data with the Center for Election Innovation & Research (CEIR), a nonprofit founded by ERIC co-founder David Becker that he said "received over $70 million from the Chan Zuckerberg 501(c)(3) organization." He also faulted ERIC's member agreement for barring states from sending records that indicate a person is not a citizen, citing a 2022 Colorado list of eligible-but-unregistered people that he said included 30,000 noncitizens who were invited to register; the letter did not say any of them registered or voted. Mullin wrote that DHS had first raised the data-sharing concerns with Justice Department officials the previous September. **The second request asked the department to ensure that ballot-marking devices, which print a voter's choices as text and as a barcode or QR code that a scanner then reads, comply with federal law, because DHS had found systems where the final paper record "may not be a reliable record for a manual audit."** The New York Times reported that critics have claimed hackers could in theory manipulate the codes, but election-integrity experts say there are no examples of that happening in an election, and that the request raised questions about whether it sought to lay the ground for claiming that some electronically cast or counted votes are invalid; such devices are widely used in states including Georgia and South Carolina. CEIR's Becker said the group "firmly rejects any suggestion that it receives motor-vehicle or voter data on an ongoing basis, conditions grants on access to sensitive information, or uses such information for partisan purposes," that the allegation concerned a 2020 study of state outreach to unregistered voters, and that DHS had not contacted CEIR before issuing the letter. ERIC's website says members submit Social Security and driver's license numbers only after they are cryptographically hashed. In June 2026 a federal judge had dismissed a Driver's Privacy Protection Act suit against ERIC and Becker brought by the group Citizen AG and sanctioned the lawyers who brought it. A DHS spokesperson said Mullin wanted the newly confirmed Attorney General to be aware of the concerns and that the referrals were made for the department "to determine if further investigation would be warranted." In a later letter, Georgia's Republican-controlled State Election Board, through its executive director, asked the Justice Department to declare the state's QR-code vote tabulation unlawful under the Help America Vote Act and to set a six-month deadline to replace it, copying Mullin; Democracy Docket, reporting that request, described Mullin's own letter as asking the department to declare bar- or QR-code machines unlawful under that law, and noted that the federal Election Assistance Commission has certified Georgia's machines and that the Justice Department has no authority to declare voting machines unlawful on its own. No Justice Department response or investigation has been reported.

offense_category: Reliance on an Error-Prone Federal Database / Unverified Public Claims Undermining Election Confidence -- DHS urged states to purge voter rolls using a system originally built for benefits-eligibility screening, whose USCIS fact sheet acknowledging its citizenship-verification limits has since been taken down, based on an unverified 250,000-noncitizen figure -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin urged state election officials to 'scrub' voter rolls using the expanded SAVE (Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements) system, claiming 250,000 noncitizens are registered to vote across four states -- California, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Nevada -- without explaining how DHS verified that figure. Mullin's letters to the four states said the numbers came from only a 'preliminary review' and asked the states to contact DHS by July 30. Copies of those letters obtained by The Hill showed that the 'preliminary review' had matched 118,000 people against names and other information in DHS's files -- less than half the 250,000 figure DHS publicized. The same July 17, 2026 announcement in which Mullin made the 250,000-noncitizen claim and sent the four states' letters also included, at a same-day press conference, explicit threats that noncompliant election officials could be 'held accountable by fines, by penalties, and even depending on how far it goes, prison time,' and that noncompliant states could lose federal election-related grant funding -- a materially more coercive characterization than 'urged,' corroborated across ABC News, Common Dreams, and States Newsroom/Herald and News coverage of the same speech and letters. SAVE was originally built to verify eligibility for government benefits, not to confirm citizenship for voter-registration purposes; the Trump administration expanded the system in 2025 to query voter registration data nationally using Social Security numbers and demographic information. A USCIS fact sheet that had acknowledged SAVE 'may not be able to confirm U.S. citizenship for individuals not designated as citizens in SSA records' has since been taken down. The expansion has also been challenged in court: the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia found it violated the Privacy Act, the Social Security Act and the Administrative Procedure Act and blocked its use, while a federal judge in Florida ruled weeks later that the government must keep providing access to four states. In a September 14, 2026 declaration in the D.C. case, the Social Security Administration's general counsel updated his earlier statement that SSA had reactivated its SAVE data connection with DHS for use 'solely for the four Plaintiff States' covered by the Florida order: SSA had since 'learned that the reactivated API connection was used by DHS for non-SAVE purposes,' in addition to SAVE checks for those states. The Justice Department's cover notice said those were DHS queries in support of federal law-enforcement investigations, not SAVE requests, and did not violate the D.C. court's order. The Social Security Administration itself has said its citizenship data provides only 'a snapshot,' not 'definitive information about citizenship status,' and a 2006 audit cited in a Fair Elections Center report found SSA's citizenship data wrong for seven percent of number holders it classified as noncitizens -- 3.3 million U.S. citizens. **Utah's own comprehensive 2025 SAVE-based review could not confirm nearly 9,000 people as citizens, but manual review found more than 5,600 of them -- most of those flagged -- were, in fact, U.S. citizens; just 27 were confirmed as noncitizens**. Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar called DHS's 250,000 figure 'wildly speculative at best,' and the Brennan Center's Sean Morales-Doyle said the results would be 'garbage in, garbage out' if DHS had used SAVE to cross-check public voter records, noting that publicly available voter data does not contain the Social Security numbers the letters said were matched. Former Texas Secretary of State Jane Nelson separately warned about SAVE's accuracy based on county registrars' experience obtaining citizenship documentation that contradicted SAVE's flags. Pennsylvania Secretary of State Al Schmidt formally demanded on July 30, 2026 that DHS disclose its methodology and data sources behind the 14,576 potential noncitizens DHS claimed for Pennsylvania specifically, citing reporting that SAVE had mistakenly flagged eligible voters as noncitizens in Texas and Missouri, and said he would not act to remove voters without that substantiation; Nevada officials raised similar objections. At an August 14 meeting, DHS officials told Nevada election staff that the state's 15,903 figure was 'preliminary,' a ceiling that had not had a full manual review; on August 20 a DHS official wrote that the agency had confirmed 185 of them were not U.S. citizens and that more than 14,000 still needed review, and DHS, which also sent a list of 6,218 unreviewed 'higher confidence' matches, declined Nevada's request for the names and other data points it had matched for the 185, providing only voter ID numbers. DHS officials also told Nevada they had made no criminal referrals against state election officials. In an August letter, Schmidt said DHS representatives had indicated they did not have 'high confidence' in Pennsylvania's figure. In September, Nevada deputy attorney general Greg Ott told DHS that the state's records showed the 185 were citizens and that DHS had 'provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise'; DHS told The New York Times that Nevada's characterization was 'false' and that the 185 were 'simply a subset of individuals that had gone through a rigorous manual review process.' After a divided D.C. Circuit panel declined on September 4, 2026 to pause that ruling, the Supreme Court on September 25, 2026, in an unsigned 6-3 order in Department of Homeland Security v. League of Women Voters, stayed the D.C. court's June 22 order pending appeal, allowing DHS to use the expanded SAVE system ahead of the midterms; the majority said the challengers' claims likely fail because a 1996 immigration law authorizes DHS to request and receive citizenship information from other agencies. The majority acknowledged that the National Voter Registration Act requires states to finish any program to systematically remove ineligible voters 90 days before a federal election, which limits the order's immediate effect, but said the expanded system can still be used for individualized checks in that period, and it left open whether the 90-day bar covers removing noncitizens, a question it will take up in a separate pending case. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan, dissented, writing that 'the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take.' The order does not require states to use the system, and within days Aguilar said Nevada would not use SAVE, saying 'It's widely known that the SAVE program flags eligible voters as ineligible at high rates.' On September 30, the watchdog group American Oversight sued DHS after the department failed to turn over records, requested under the Freedom of Information Act, to support Mullin's 250,000 claim. Internal Homeland Security Investigations reports from May and June, released October 7 by the legal group Democracy Forward, showed HSI drawing on 50.6 million records from a Justice Department dataset and 48.4 million records that Heather Honey, the department's 'election integrity' point person and a senior counselor to Mullin, obtained 'through independent sources of information'; the documents do not say where Honey's records came from, and The New York Times called them 'of unknown provenance.' CNN reported Honey's records may include public voter lists from the four states that DHS purchased and analyzed around that time. The same records show HSI reviewing more than 150 voter-registration nonprofits, by The New York Times' count, which TAP tracks in a separate entry. On October 9, in a separate case brought by Common Cause and voters whose registrations were canceled, U.S. District Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan -- whose June ruling against the expanded SAVE system the Supreme Court later paused -- set aside and vacated the Justice Department Civil Rights Division's 'Voter List Maintenance Policy' of obtaining states' voter rolls, running them through DHS's modified SAVE system and demanding that states remove the voters it flagged. She found that DOJ 'entirely failed to consider' the risk of removing eligible voters, though its agreement with USCIS acknowledged that the modified 'SAVE may only be able to verify acquired U.S. citizens in certain situations,' and that the policy 'has removed United States citizens from the voter rolls in their home states'; one plaintiff, a Texas voter, attested that his registration was canceled because of an erroneous SAVE result. The suit named only DOJ and the Attorney General; DOJ, which first said it was reviewing the decision, filed a notice of appeal to the D.C. Circuit on October 16, and TAP tracks the case in a separate entry. On October 15, the League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center and the League of United Latin American Citizens, represented by Democracy Forward and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, filed a new lawsuit against DHS in federal court in Washington over its collection of voter records. The 42-page complaint alleges that DHS obtained voter files from at least 47 states -- even as, the Associated Press reported, 30 states refused to turn their lists over to the administration -- combined voter records with information purchased from commercial data brokers, and sought to integrate processed voter data into an enforcement system used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, exceeding its legal authority and violating federal privacy protections. The plaintiffs ask the court to declare the collection illegal, block the policy, and order DHS to delete and stop using the voter data it has collected. DHS did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment.

rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: ensuring only eligible citizens are registered to vote is a legitimate government interest, and expanding an existing federal verification system to assist states in that effort -- while imperfect -- is a reasonable tool-sharing effort rather than a deliberate attempt to undermine election confidence; DHS has described the figures as preliminary and may argue they reflect a flag requiring further state-level verification, not a final claim of confirmed fraud. DHS itself later told Nevada its figures were preliminary, and Nevada says the first 185 voters DHS confirmed as noncitizens are citizens. The Supreme Court's stay order addressed whether federal law lets DHS share and use the data, not whether SAVE's matches are accurate or whether DHS's 250,000 figure holds up, and the dissent faulted the majority for weighing no harm to lawful voters; the majority itself accepted that one challenger, a naturalized citizen, had shown SSA's records did not reflect her citizenship. official: Elon Musk, former DOGE leader / Special Government Employee
offense_category: Evasion of Court-Ordered Testimony Regarding DOGE's Dismantlement of Federal Agencies -- a civil-litigation accountability claim, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: Beginning in mid-November 2025, **constables and private process servers made repeated attempts -- including at least four separate attempts at Musk's Brownsville, Texas property near SpaceX headquarters, and at his West Lake Hills, Texas residence -- to serve Musk with a subpoena for deposition testimony regarding his role in DOGE's dismantlement of federal agencies, including USAID**. Process servers were repeatedly denied entry to gated properties, and staff told servers Musk was not home and no one was authorized to accept paperwork on his behalf. U.S. District Judge Theodore D. Chuang ruled in early February 2026 that Musk and State Department officials must sit for depositions regarding USAID's dismantlement, rejecting a motion for a protective order that argued the testimony was barred by protections for high-ranking officials. The Justice Department, which represents Musk as an official-capacity defendant, asked the court to block his deposition. On March 4, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled 2-1 to grant Musk's petition, blocking the deposition from proceeding. As of CNN's April 13, 2026 reporting, whether Musk would ever be compelled to testify about his DOGE role remained unresolved. The Fourth Circuit directed a protective order "at this time" and wrote that its decision "does not mean that the depositions of Musk, Marocco and Lewin are barred for the remainder of these proceedings." Discovery has continued in the district court since then: plaintiffs moved in May 2026 for leave to depose Kenneth Jackson and Steve Davis, Judge Chuang granted in part a plaintiffs' motion to compel on September 3, 2026, and on October 1, 2026 he extended the time to complete discovery. On September 30, 2026, the plaintiffs and the government jointly asked Judge Chuang to say he would dissolve the March 2025 preliminary injunction, which the Fourth Circuit had stayed, with plaintiffs agreeing to seek final judgment at the close of discovery instead of preliminary relief. In an October 7, 2026 joint letter on the Jackson and Davis depositions, plaintiffs cited "the present unavailability of Lewin, Marocco and Musk," and on October 14 the Justice Department told the court that the Supreme Court's October 13 grant of review in a separate case over discovery from the U.S. DOGE Service, including a deposition of its head, supports denying the Davis deposition. The docket shows no renewed motion to depose Musk.
elements_required: A federal district court found that Musk's proposed deposition testimony regarding DOGE's dismantlement of USAID was justified and not barred by high-ranking-official protections
Musk personally evaded service of the underlying subpoena for approximately three months through repeated non-cooperation at his properties, documented across multiple specific attempts
The Justice Department, which represents Musk as an official-capacity defendant, sought to block his deposition
An appellate court blocked the deposition, for now, on a divided 2-1 vote, and more than a year after the litigation began, Musk had not been deposed
