official: Donald Trump, President (with the National Park Service, Department of the Interior, and General Services Administration named as co-defendants in their institutional capacity)
offense_category: Statutory Violation -- proceeding with major White House construction without congressional authorization, addressed here as a rule-of-law/separation-of-powers question rather than a criminal charge; a federal district court found the White House's own $2.5 million annual maintenance-and-repair appropriation does not authorize demolition and new construction of this scale
incident_summary:
President Trump ordered the 123-year-old East Wing and the Jacqueline Kennedy Garden demolished to build a roughly 90,000-square-foot ballroom, with its publicly announced cost escalating from an initial $200 million estimate to $300 million and then $400 million, which Trump said private donors -- including Amazon, Apple, Google, and other corporations with business before the federal government -- would pay for (a White House official said in October 2025 that $350 million had been raised).

The Washington Post reported on September 23, 2026 that White House meeting notes the Post reviewed had flagged life safety as a "big concern" on September 30, 2025, and that the ballroom's first architect, James McCrery II, left the project the week of October 20, 2025, when East Wing demolition began, after warning repeatedly that Trump's preferred design lacked adequate emergency exits and fire containment; **two people with knowledge of the discussions told the Post that Trump answered that building codes did not apply to White House construction because "I am the code."** A November 6 note, after McCrery left, said life safety still needed Trump's buy-in; the Post could not determine whether a formal code review was ever completed. The White House called any link between McCrery's departure and code issues "factually false" and said life-safety issues were "addressed and resolved continuously." The D.C. government has no code-enforcement authority over federal property.

On December 12, 2025, the National Trust for Historic Preservation -- the organization Congress itself designated to help protect historic federal sites -- filed suit in U.S. District Court for D.C., represented by former Clinton/Obama White House counsel Greg Craig, seeking to halt construction until the standard federal review and public-comment process was completed, arguing 'no president is legally allowed to tear down portions of the White House without any review whatsoever ... [or] construct a ballroom on public property without giving the public the opportunity to weigh in.' Separately, on December 16, 2025, Rep. Jamie Raskin introduced the People's White House Historic Preservation Act, which would remove what his office called the White House's "statutory exemption" from National Historic Preservation Act Section 106 review and require public review of future White House renovations; Raskin said the bill "returns power to the American people to protect the house we built for our presidents." The later court rulings did not rest on Section 106: they rested on Congress's constitutional control over federal property and on 40 U.S.C. section 8106, which bars erecting a building on federal grounds in D.C. "without express authority of Congress."

On March 31, 2026, U.S. District Judge Richard Leon enjoined construction of the ballroom until Congress authorizes it, ruling that 'no statute comes close to giving the President the authority he claims to have'; **Leon specifically found that 3 U.S.C. section 105(d)(1), which authorizes the White House's annual maintenance-and-repair appropriation (about $2.5 million in 2024), brings to mind 'things like replacing the lightbulbs, fixing broken furniture, and changing the wallpaper, not wholesale demolition of entire buildings and construction of new ones.'** On April 16 he narrowed the order to above-ground construction, leaving below-ground security facilities free to proceed, and on April 17, 2026, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals stayed Leon's injunction.

Congress has not authorized the project. On April 29, 2026, Sens. Lindsey Graham, Katie Britt and Eric Schmitt introduced the White House Safety and Security Act of 2026 (S. 4430), which would appropriate $400 million in federal funds, available until January 20, 2029, "to complete the East Wing Modernization Project, including a secure State Ballroom," paired with an extension of customs user fees; it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has had no further action. A separate bill from Sen. Rand Paul (S. 4486), which would treat such White House projects as authorized once the chairs of two congressional committees certify they have reviewed them, and which Paul said would let the ballroom proceed "without requiring additional taxpayer funds," was placed on the Senate calendar on May 12 and has not received a vote. A proposed $1 billion for the Secret Service, including "above-ground and below-ground security features" of the East Wing project, was dropped: the Secret Service chief reportedly told Republican lawmakers in May that only $220 million of it would fortify the ballroom, the Senate parliamentarian ruled against an earlier version, and Senate Republicans stripped it from an immigration enforcement reconciliation bill on June 3, 2026 (a White House spokesperson said that framing "is false as it implies that Republicans removed it deliberately rather than under parliamentary pressure"). On June 4, 2026, during debate on that bill, senators voted 53-46, with seven Republicans in the majority, to waive budget rules for Sen. Jeff Merkley's amendment to bar federal funds or private donations for the ballroom without congressional authorization; the motion failed because it needed 60 votes. Trump signed the bill without the Secret Service money on June 10.

The Washington Post reported on June 16, 2026, citing a March 5, 2026 project summary from the contractor, Clark Construction, that the project's estimated cost had reached $600 million, with $293 million from "private sources" and the remaining roughly $307 million from taxpayer-funded accounts: $155 million from the Secret Service, $149 million from the White House Military Office and $3 million from the Executive Residence. The White House says security features, including a hospital beneath the ballroom and a rooftop drone center, are separate from the ballroom itself; a spokesman said Trump and donors are funding it "to the tune of approximately $400 million," and in August 2026 Trump said it would cost "close to $400 million" with "no taxpayer money for the ballroom at all."

On August 7, 2026, the D.C. Circuit affirmed Leon's injunction, holding that 'Congress has exclusive authority to regulate the construction and demolition of White House structures.' The Supreme Court, in a 5-4 order on August 31, 2026, stayed the injunction pending the government's forthcoming petition for Supreme Court review, allowing construction to continue, on the grounds that the National Trust likely lacks legal standing to sue and that the balance of harms, citing national-security declarations from senior officials, favored the government -- a procedural ruling, not a merits finding that the project is lawful; the majority wrote, "Today, we do not pass upon the legality of the government's East Wing project." Chief Justice Roberts wrote the dissent, joined by Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson, arguing the ballroom construction 'is likely unlawful' and that the project likely requires congressional authorization -- meaning the Chief Justice himself agreed with the district court and D.C. Circuit's merits conclusion even while being outvoted on the separate standing question on which the stay's merits analysis turned.
elements_required: The White House's own annual congressionally-appropriated maintenance-and-repair fund (authorized by 3 U.S.C. section 105(d)(1); $2.475 million in the 2024 appropriation) is limited by its own terms to ordinary maintenance and repair, not demolition and new construction of this scale -- a federal district judge's own textual finding, not merely an advocacy characterization
No separate act of Congress specifically authorized the East Wing demolition or ballroom construction

The administration proceeded with demolition and continued construction notwithstanding the absence of that authorization, continuing under an appeals-court stay after a federal judge enjoined above-ground construction, and then under a Supreme Court stay

The Supreme Court's stay rests on the National Trust's likely lack of standing to sue, not on a finding that the underlying legal authority claimed by the administration is valid -- the merits question Judge Leon and the D.C. Circuit both resolved against the administration at the preliminary-injunction stage remains unreversed

status: Construction proceeds under the Supreme Court's Aug. 31, 2026 stay pending a forthcoming government certiorari petition; lower-court rulings that the project likely lacks authority stand unreversed, and Congress has not authorized it.
rebuttal_anticipated: The administration can argue the Supreme Court's stay vindicates its position, that the ballroom itself is paid for by private donors, with public money going only to separate security features, which distinguishes this from an appropriations-authority question, and that a sitting president has inherent authority over the White House complex as his official residence and workplace.
comeback: The Supreme Court's stay is expressly grounded in the National Trust's standing to sue, not a finding that the administration's claimed construction authority is valid -- both the district court and the D.C. Circuit, examining the merits at the preliminary-injunction stage, found the administration very likely lacks statutory authority for it (Judge Leon wrote that "no statute comes close" to supplying it), and Congress has not supplied that authority: a Senate bill to authorize and fund the project has sat in committee since April 2026; the government itself disclaimed "any explicit or implicit constitutional authority for their actions," the D.C. Circuit noted. The funding argument doesn't answer the question the courts ruled on, which concerned authority to alter federal property, not who pays: Judge Leon called the administration's route for spending the donations, through gifts to the Interior Secretary, "a far cry from affirmative congressional authorization." Its premise is also disputed: The Washington Post reported in June 2026 that the contractor's March 2026 estimate put the project at $600 million, with about $307 million from Secret Service, White House Military Office and Executive Residence accounts (the White House says that security work is separate from the ballroom). The donations also raise an unaddressed influence question, since several donors (Amazon, Apple, Google, and others) have significant pending business before federal regulators.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern this database documents of the administration proceeding with presidentially-favored capital projects (see also this tracker's Burgum entry, covering a separate D.C. monument project facing the same underlying congressional-authorization gap) through executive action first, treating litigation and congressional pushback as obstacles to route around rather than binding constraints to satisfy in advance.

official: Kristi Noem, then-Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: No-Bid Aircraft Purchase From a Donor-Chaired Contractor at Prices Above What the Seller Had Recently Paid -- framed under the federal procurement rule allowing non-competitive awards only for 'unusual and compelling urgency' (FAR 6.302-2) and the federal ethics standard that officials act impartially and give no private party preferential treatment (5 C.F.R. 2635.101(b)(8)); no criminal charge, inspector general finding or other official finding of wrongdoing has been reported
incident_summary: The New York Times reported in early October 2026, citing documents on the sale, that **on Kristi Noem's last morning as Secretary of Homeland Security in March 2026, DHS agreed to buy five aircraft from Daedalus Aviation Corporation** under a no-bid contract. DHS agreed to pay $108 million for a Boeing 737 converted into a private jet with a bar and two bedrooms, which Daedalus had bought months earlier from a seller who asked for less than $90 million; $106 million for two Gulfstream luxury jets, about $23 million more than the roughly $83 million Daedalus paid for them; and $45 million each for two 17-year-old Boeing 737 airliners, prices six aviation experts told the Times were above typical market value. According to the Times, Noem approved a significant change to the contract, covering the luxury jets, hours before leaving her post. Contracting records reviewed by the Times, first reported in August, show the contract grew by $303 million on the day her successor, Markwayne Mullin, was sworn in; with the five planes, the contract totals **$464 million for 10 aircraft, awarded without competitive bidding under the 'unusual and compelling urgency' exemption**. Daedalus, which had held no federal contract before 2025, is chaired by William Walters, who gave $10,000 in 2024 to American Resolve, a political committee connected to Noem; the company says Walters did not know the committee was tied to Noem. DHS said the planes were urgently needed for deportation flights, but the Times reported in August that most of the fleet had sat parked in Lake Charles, Louisiana for months because DHS lacked crews to fly them, and that one Gulfstream had been leased to the FBI. Two White House officials told the Times that Mullin looked into backing out of the deal but feared financial penalties, and that White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles advised him not to block it. Noem denies responsibility, says the purchase was finalized under Mullin, and has demanded a retraction; the Times stands by its reporting.
elements_required: DHS acquired the aircraft from Daedalus without full and open competition, citing the 'unusual and compelling urgency' exception (FAR 6.302-2), which permits a non-competitive award only when the government would otherwise be seriously injured

The prices DHS agreed to pay exceeded what Daedalus had recently paid for several of the same planes ($108 million vs. under $90 million; $106 million vs. about $83 million) and, per aviation experts, the typical market value of two older 737s

The firm's chairman had donated to a political committee connected to Noem, raising an appearance-of-favoritism question under the federal ethics impartiality standard; no source shows the donation influenced the award

Noem's personal role: the Times reports all five planes were bought on her last morning and that she approved a significant contract change for the luxury jets hours before leaving; Noem says the purchase was completed under her successor, so personal attribution of the final step is disputed
The stated urgency is undercut by later use: most of the fleet sat idle for months for lack of crews, and one jet was leased to the FBI rather than used for deportation flights

status: No official finding. Senators sought DHS records on the $464M no-bid deal in August and on Oct. 8, 2026 asked for the contracts and Walters's communications with Noem's DHS by Oct. 22. No inspector general probe of the purchase is confirmed. Noem denies blame; the Times stands by its report.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense (Noem's and Daedalus's stated positions): the purchase 'was not completed during' Noem's tenure and was 'finalized under Secretary Mullin's leadership'; Walters made no personal contribution to Noem and did not know the committee he gave to was tied to her, so calling him a 'donor' is misleading; the prices reflected a market with limited inventory of suitable planes and 'very tight time constraints'; and owning aircraft was meant to cut DHS's reliance on chartered deportation flights.
comeback: DHS itself says the Daedalus contract 'was made and approved by department leadership before Secretary Mullin was sworn in,' and the Times reports that Noem approved a significant change to the contract, for the luxury jets, hours before she left; Daily Wire's account of the Times report says the planes were purchased on her last morning and only formally changed hands in April. Campaign-finance records show the $10,000 gift to the Noem-connected committee. The urgency justification is undercut by the fleet sitting idle for months for lack of crews, and by Noem's leased luxury jet, which the Wall Street Journal reported in April the administration planned to keep for travel by select cabinet secretaries, with the first lady's office also to have access, rather than use for deportations (PunchUp, not the Journal, identifies it as the $108 million 737); DHS never substantiated the claimed $279 million in savings. None of this establishes a crime; the accountability question is whether the urgency exception and the prices paid can be justified.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Fits a pattern of DHS contracting under Noem that relied on awards made without full and open competition to politically connected firms, also documented in the Lewandowski contract-authority entry and the Noem perjury-referral entry. A New York Times analysis found the urgency exemption covered nearly two-thirds of DHS spending on contracts signed in 2026, up from under 1 percent in 2024, and that no other major agency used it as often; Walters's separate firm Salus Worldwide Solutions also won a large DHS contract under the urgency exception, through a limited competition, for the 'self-deportation' campaign, covered in the Salus self-deportation contract entry.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence that DHS bought 10 aircraft from Daedalus for $464 million without competition under the urgency exception, and that the contract grew by $303 million at the leadership handover: DHS, Noem's camp and a Senate letter all agree on the purchase and differ only on who completed it. MODERATE confidence on the markups and on Noem personally approving the final-day change, which rest on documents reviewed by The New York Times; the Times's October 4 article itself was paywalled and its figures here are as relayed by the Daily Wire, IBTimes UK and The New Republic. The donor link is a single $10,000 gift to a Noem-connected committee, and no source shows it influenced the award. No criminal or inspector general finding has been reported. Update 2026-10-16: The department-wide figures (urgency exemption at nearly two-thirds of DHS contract spending in 2026, under 1 percent in 2024) come from a New York Times analysis of federal data, read in a full repost of the August article; the 92 percent share attributed to the Congressional Research Service is as reported by MS NOW, and the CRS product itself was not located. Outlets describe the size of Walters's Salus contract differently, nearly $700 million (Times) or up to $915 million (MS NOW); a federal court opinion puts the contract's expected maximum value at $915 million, and USAspending.gov shows about $748 million obligated on its main delivery order. The luxury 737's price is reported two ways: a DHS spokeswoman told the Wall Street Journal in April that the jet Noem had leased cost about $70 million, while two senior administration officials told PunchUp it cost $108 million, the figure the Times reports for the bedroom-equipped 737. That the Journal's jet and the Times's $108 million Daedalus 737 are the same plane rests on PunchUp; the Journal names neither the model nor the seller. PunchUp's reports that DHS moved the jet from Daedalus to CSI Aviation in May and that the TSA is investigating a restricted-airspace paperwork lapse come from a single paywalled outlet, owned by the Daily Beast, and were not found in other reporting.

official: Kristi Noem, Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: Federal Records Act Compliance Failure and Contradictory Public Statements Over DHS's Preservation of Text Messages
incident_summary: In July 2025, watchdog group American Oversight submitted a FOIA request seeking text, Signal, and email communications of Secretary Kristi Noem and other top DHS officials related to the National Guard's deployment to Los Angeles and Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz' migrant detention facility. On July 23, 2025, **DHS responded that 'text message data generated after April 9, 2025, is no longer maintained' -- meaning DHS had stopped preserving senior officials' text messages for roughly three and a half months by the time of the request**. The New York Times first reported this response on August 22, 2025; DHS subsequently gave contradictory public assurances that it did continue to preserve text-message records, without explaining the discrepancy with its own written FOIA response. American Oversight said a failure to preserve records as described would violate the Federal Records Act and urged Noem to immediately recover any missing records and notify the National Archives of any unlawful destruction, as the statute requires. On October 20, 2025, American Oversight sued DHS, Noem, the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), and Acting Archivist Marco Rubio over the agency's failure to produce the requested records and the unresolved preservation question. A November 21-22, 2025 joint status report revealed DHS had issued a notice directing officials to preserve records relevant to the litigation, spurred by the lawsuit itself. In early April 2026, DHS admitted in a court filing that its original 'no longer maintained' assertion had been 'erroneous,' attributing it to a 'misunderstanding' tied to technology changes -- an explanation that, as of this entry's sourcing, had not been independently confirmed to demonstrate DHS actually complied with its Federal Records Act preservation obligations throughout the disputed period.
elements_required: DHS told a FOIA requester in writing that senior officials' text messages generated after a specific date were 'no longer maintained'
DHS subsequently gave contradictory public assurances that records were preserved, without reconciling the two statements
A federal lawsuit naming Noem personally, DHS, NARA, and the Acting Archivist followed, alleging Federal Records Act noncompliance
DHS later admitted in the litigation that its original non-preservation statement was 'erroneous,' without independently confirming full compliance during the disputed period

evidence.description: The New York Times first reported DHS's July 23, 2025 FOIA response stating text messages generated after April 9, 2025 were 'no longer maintained,' and DHS's subsequent contradictory public assurances

offense_category: Retaliation against protected federal whistleblowers -- potential violation of the Whistleblower Protection Act and First Amendment
incident_summary: On August 25, 2025, 14 FEMA employees sent Congress a formal dissent letter, later called the 'Katrina Declaration,' describing 'gross waste and mismanagement, abuses of authority, dangers to public health and safety' at the agency and warning that Trump administration and DHS Secretary Kristi Noem's policies were 'gutting critical reforms to FEMA's ability to respond to emergencies' put in place after Hurricane Katrina. The next day, August 26, 2025, DHS placed the public signers on indefinite administrative leave, ordered them to stop working, and imposed a communication blackout; at least one employee was terminated outright on a charge of 'Conduct Unbecoming a Federal Employee.' The employees, represented by the Government Accountability Project, filed for whistleblower protection. On December 1, 2025, **FEMA management reinstated the employees after its own legal counsel determined their conduct was protected under the Whistleblower Protection Act and the First Amendment** -- a resolution GAP's press release characterized as full reinstatement with no disciplinary action. Within hours of CNN reporting the reinstatement publicly, DHS reversed it, placing the workers back on administrative leave; a DHS spokesperson said they had been 'wrongly and without authorization reinstated by bureaucrats acting outside of their authority,' and the administration stated it 'will not tolerate rogue conduct, unauthorized actions, or entrenched bureaucrats resisting change.' Rep. Frank Pallone called the reversal 'retaliation in plain sight' and said Trump and Noem were 'tearing down the agency that protects Americans,' naming risk to coastal states including New Jersey. The employees filed a complaint with the Office of Special Counsel, with a further appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board possible if unresolved there. The dispute remained unresolved through the following months; on April 30, 2026, under new DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin -- who was simultaneously rolling back several other Noem-era FEMA policies (including a $100,000 spending-approval threshold) ahead of the 2026 hurricane season and the FIFA World Cup -- DHS offered all employees associated with the matter a return to duty, effectively ending the roughly eight-month saga with full reinstatement.

incident_summary: On March 16, 2026, Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin, the Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, and Rep. Jamie Raskin, the Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee, formally referred Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem to the Department of Justice for investigation into potential perjury and knowingly false statements to Congress, based on her testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee on March 3, 2026 and the House Judiciary Committee on March 4, 2026. The referral letter was addressed to Attorney General Pam Bondi. The referral identified four categories of allegedly false statements: (1) Noem testified that DHS complies with federal court orders, while the referral, citing federal court findings including Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz's February 26, 2026 finding of 210 ICE violations of court orders in Minnesota alone, says **DHS had repeatedly defied court orders to release individuals from ICE detention, in some cases failing to release people for days or weeks after a court-ordered release date**; (2) she made claims about the bidding process for a $220 million DHS television ad campaign contract that the referral disputes, and denied that adviser Corey Lewandowski had a role in approving DHS contracts; (3) she made claims about the detention of U.S. citizens by immigration agents, despite ProPublica having separately documented more than 170 U.S. citizens held by immigration agents in the administration's first nine months, an October 2025 count the referral cites; and (4) she made claims about detention conditions. The Lewandowski denial had been reported by ProPublica on March 4, 2026, the day after the Senate hearing, in an article the referral cites: when Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked whether Lewandowski had 'a role in approving contracts' at DHS, Noem answered 'No,' but internal DHS records reviewed by ProPublica showed Lewandowski personally approved a multimillion-dollar equipment contract, and current and former DHS officials said he had approved numerous contracts and was typically the last sign-off before Noem on contracts above $100,000. A DHS spokesperson responded that 'any claim that Secretary Noem committed perjury is categorically FALSE,' and a DOJ spokesperson said the department 'has received the latest political stunt from the Democrats.' Earlier, on March 5, 2026, one day after the March 3-4 testimony this referral concerns, Trump announced he was firing Noem as DHS Secretary and naming Sen. Markwayne Mullin to replace her; this tracker's separate DHS-dysfunction entry documents the firing and a related DHS OIG contracting investigation in fuller detail. The firing is not itself evidence the referral's specific perjury allegations are true, since reporting attributes it to the hearings' broader fallout rather than to the perjury question specifically. ProPublica's expanded tally, published October 6, 2026, counted 506 U.S. citizens detained by immigration agents between January 2025 and September 2026, a count it calls an undercount. A congressional criminal referral does not compel DOJ to open an investigation, and DOJ -- under the same administration Noem serves -- was not reported to have opened one as of the most recent reporting reviewed.

official: Donald Trump, President (reportedly at activist Laura Loomer's urging)
offense_category: Firing the Nation's Top Signals-Intelligence and Military Cyber Officials Reportedly at an Outside Activist's Urging on Loyalty Grounds, Leaving the NSA and Cyber Command Without Senate-Confirmed Leadership for Nearly a Year
incident_summary: On April 3, 2025, President Trump fired Gen. Timothy Haugh, the Senate-confirmed director of the National Security Agency and head of U.S. Cyber Command, and removed his civilian deputy, Wendy Noble, who was reportedly reassigned to the office of the under secretary of defense for intelligence -- roughly a year into what is traditionally a three-year term, and with no public explanation of an official reason. CNN and ABC News, citing sources, reported the firings followed a private April 2 Oval Office meeting in which far-right activist Laura Loomer presented Trump research on officials she deemed disloyal (CNN described a list of roughly a dozen names) and urged Haugh's removal; CNN's sources said she also urged Noble's. Loomer publicly took credit overnight, posting that Haugh and Noble 'have been disloyal to President Trump. That is why they have been fired,' and that Haugh had been 'HAND PICKED by General Milley, who was accused of committing treason by President Trump.' Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One on the afternoon of April 3, before Haugh's removal was reported, Trump called Loomer 'a very good patriot' who 'makes recommendations of things and people, and sometimes I listen to those recommendations,' said he makes the decisions, and denied she was involved in that week's National Security Council firings; asked about her posts on Haugh, the White House referred reporters back to those comments. Lt. Gen. William Hartman, Haugh's deputy at Cyber Command, was designated acting commander of Cyber Command and acting NSA director, and Sheila Thomas acting NSA deputy director. **The agency then went without a permanent, Senate-confirmed director for nearly a year: by November 2025, Nextgov/FCW (in a story republished by Defense One) reported that a leadership vacuum had produced sustained morale problems ('the morale inside the organization is rather depressed... that's what happens when your boss disappears'), a wave of additional senior departures -- including NSA's top lawyer, April Falcon Doss, reportedly also let go on Loomer's advice -- and a pause in recruiting for the NSA's Legal Honors Program, a key pipeline for the agency's legal talent.** The White House had reportedly considered elevating Hartman to the permanent post but backed off those plans. On August 21, 2025, the NSA announced that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard had designated Joe Francescon -- a former NSA analyst who held senior National Security Council roles in Trump's first term -- as the agency's next deputy director, with Trump's approval. Loomer attacked the pick almost immediately, accusing Francescon of having donated $500 to Democratic Rep. Jason Crow in 2023; The Record also reported resistance inside the administration, including from Sergio Gor, who led White House personnel until October, while Trump ally Kurt Olsen lobbied Trump for another candidate. In December 2025 the White House dropped Francescon -- the post does not require Senate confirmation, so no formal nomination had been sent -- leaving the deputy job in acting hands a while longer, and Loomer celebrated the reversal. Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) blamed the vacancies on 'infighting in the White House and the involvement of whacky Laura Loomer in hiring,' calling 'the inability to get leaders in place' 'gross negligence.' In December 2025, Trump nominated Army Lt. Gen. Joshua Rudd, then deputy commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command. On January 9, 2026, the NSA named former NSA and FBI official Tim Kosiba as deputy director. The Senate confirmed Rudd 71-29 on March 10, 2026, promoting him to four-star general, ending the vacancy. Some senators, most pointedly Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR), raised concerns during confirmation about Rudd's comparatively limited cyber-operations and signals-intelligence background relative to prior NSA/Cyber Command leaders.

The resulting leadership vacancy was documented, by current and former officials, mostly unnamed, speaking to multiple outlets, as producing concrete institutional harm (morale collapse, additional senior departures, paused recruitment) over an extended period (nearly a year)

status: Resolved as a personnel matter: Tim Kosiba was named NSA deputy director on January 9, 2026, and the Senate confirmed Gen. Joshua Rudd on March 10, 2026. Loomer's actual role and the firings' justification were never officially clarified. The NGA-Warner episode is a separate entry.
rebuttal_anticipated: The President publicly said Loomer only 'makes recommendations' and that he makes the decisions, denied she was involved in the same week's National Security Council firings, and no administration official has officially confirmed her account; the firings could alternatively be characterized as a normal exercise of the President's authority to select his own national-security leadership team, without requiring a stated cause.
comeback: The President's account is in tension with Loomer's own, repeated, contemporaneous public claims of credit and specific rationale, and with separately sourced reports (CNN, ABC News) describing the same Oval Office meeting and her advocacy against Haugh -- an unusual level of corroboration for an activist's private advocacy claim. Separately, whatever the true cause, the documented consequence (a nearly year-long vacancy in leadership of the nation's premier signals-intelligence agency and military cyber command, with reported morale collapse and further senior departures) is independently sourced and does not depend on resolving the Loomer-vs-Trump factual dispute.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of the pattern, also seen in the same week's National Security Council firings, of an outside activist with no formal government role reportedly shaping senior national-security personnel decisions outside any formal vetting process. Here the cost is documented: NSA and Cyber Command went nearly a year without a Senate-confirmed leader, and the NSA's deputy post stayed in acting hands after the White House dropped its August 2025 pick amid Loomer's attacks and opposition inside the administration. That cost stands regardless of which account of the April 2025 firings is correct.

official: Kurt Olsen, former White House Director of Election Security and Integrity (October 2025-May 2026); now senior counsel, U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida
offense_category: Abuse of Federal Investigative Power to Re-litigate the Settled 2020 Election, by an Official With a Court-Sanctioned Record of False Election Claims -- no criminal charge or court finding of wrongdoing against Olsen for his government work; making referrals was within his office. The concern rests on two courts' sanctions, an attorney-discipline finding, and a federal judge's criticism of the affidavit his referral produced
incident_summary:
Kurt Olsen, a Washington lawyer who spent much of his career in securities and product-liability litigation, entered election work after Trump's 2020 loss. According to congressional testimony by a top Justice Department official from Trump's first term, Olsen pressed the department to file a Supreme Court lawsuit challenging the results in battleground states, and he helped Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's bid to get the Supreme Court to overturn Joe Biden's win.

His later election litigation drew sanctions. Representing Kari Lake and Mark Finchem in a 2022 federal suit to ban electronic vote-counting in Arizona, Olsen and co-counsel Andrew Parker were sanctioned under Rule 11 and 28 U.S.C. 1927 and held jointly liable for $122,200 in fees; on March 14, 2025 a divided Ninth Circuit panel affirmed, finding they **made false, misleading, and unsupported factual assertions** and did not make a reasonable pre-filing inquiry. On May 4, 2023 the Arizona Supreme Court separately fined Olsen and co-counsel Bryan Blehm $2,000 for calling it an "undisputed fact" that 35,563 ballots were added at a vendor, a representation it called "unequivocally false." In 2024 Arizona's Presiding Disciplinary Judge ruled that Olsen had violated rules against false statements to a tribunal and dishonest conduct; in October a hearing panel found he had acted knowingly but admonished him, citing his clean record and remorse. In fairness, other reviews went his way: an Arizona disciplinary panel dismissed a separate complaint over the voting-machine suit (affirmed by the Arizona Supreme Court in May 2025, one justice dissenting in part), and six Ninth Circuit judges dissented from denial of rehearing, calling the sanctions a weaponization against disfavored litigation. On October 13, 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court declined to review the Ninth Circuit's ruling, denying a petition by Parker and his law firm; Olsen had not joined it.

In 2025 Olsen moved inside the government. Reuters reported that, while still holding no government post, he steered a June 2025 intelligence-agency inspection of a Dominion voting machine in Puerto Rico toward proving foreign vote manipulation; the inspection found no evidence of hacking or altered votes, and by late summer Olsen told Trump the contractor was secretly funded by George Soros, which the firm denied. Reuters reported that the effort grew into an investigation spanning the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security and the FBI, a search that later expanded into Georgia and Arizona; the White House said ODNI, then led by Tulsi Gabbard, had initiated it to identify vulnerabilities, not to revisit the 2020 election. In late October 2025 Trump appointed him White House Director of Election Security and Integrity, a temporary special-government-employee post.

On January 28, 2026, FBI agents seized about 650 boxes of Fulton County, Georgia's 2020 ballots and records. The FBI's sworn warrant affidavit, unsealed February 10, 2026, states: **"The FBI criminal investigation originated from a referral sent by Kurt Olsen, Presidentially appointed Director of Election Security and Integrity."** Judge Boulee's later order records that Olsen formally referred the matter to the FBI by 9:03 a.m. on January 5, 2026, and that Thomas Albus, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Missouri and Special Attorney to the Attorney General, received it that day. The affidavit was sworn by FBI Special Agent Hugh Raymond Evans, drafted from his witness interviews, and does not describe the referral's contents. On May 6, 2026, U.S. District Judge J.P. Boulee let DOJ keep the ballots, finding Fulton County had not shown "callous disregard" of its rights and that Olsen's referral came before the county clerk's motion that the county said the criminal case was a pretext to get around, a timing he said "cuts against" that claim. He found the affidavit "defective in some respects," one statement in it "misleading" and others "troubling," and called the seizure "certainly not perfect," but said this was not a case "where an officer intentionally lied." Reuters, citing three people familiar with his work, reported that in March 2026 Olsen oversaw DOJ's subpoena of the Arizona Senate for Maricopa County 2020 records; Reuters found his investigation turned up no evidence that foreign actors manipulated the 2020 election.

On May 18, 2026, eleven senators led by Democrat Alex Padilla demanded his removal, arguing he had exceeded the 130-day limit for special government employees; Olsen told Reuters he left the White House in May because "my 130 days were up." He then joined the Southern District of Florida as senior counsel on the "grand conspiracy" investigation of Trump's critics, where, according to a court declaration by John Brennan's lawyer, he told Brennan's team in September that Brennan was a "target" of a narrower investigation. On September 28, 2026 Olsen emailed that he was leaving that case. CNN and CBS first reported, citing sources, that he had quit DOJ; both later reported that DOJ officials had misread the email, and a DOJ official told CBS he remains senior counsel but is off the investigation. CBS also reported, citing two sources, that his security clearance had run into a problem before he stepped away. Reuters reported on October 7, citing two people familiar with the matter, that his DOJ security clearance had been terminated in September after he failed a polygraph test, which played a role though it was unclear whether other factors contributed; a DOJ spokesperson confirmed he has no active clearance with the department. Olsen said he holds an active clearance from an agency he did not name, that "any suggestion of a revoked clearance is false," and that his clearance was not relevant to his leaving the case; he did not address the polygraph. Reuters noted that a failed polygraph does not prove any offense and that it could not establish what he was asked.

rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: referring possible election-law violations to the FBI was squarely within the job of a White House election-integrity director, and a court issued the warrant; Judge Boulee later declined to order the ballots returned, found the referral came before the court clerk's motion whose delay the county said the criminal case was a pretextual response to, and said the affidavit was not a case "where an officer intentionally lied." Olsen's sanctions came from private advocacy for clients; a dissenting Ninth Circuit panel judge found "nothing they did was deceptive, intentionally false, or beyond the bounds of zealous advocacy," six Ninth Circuit judges called them a weaponization against disfavored litigation, an Arizona disciplinary panel cleared him on the voting-machine suit, and the panel that did discipline him chose the lightest sanction and credited his remorse.
comeback: The referral itself was lawful; the concern is who was given the power to make it and what it produced. Two courts found Olsen made false or unsupported factual claims about elections, and the Ninth Circuit upheld a finding of bad faith. He then set federal criminal process loose on Fulton County's 2020 ballots, and the judge who let DOJ keep them still found the resulting affidavit "defective in some respects," with one statement "misleading." His wider search, by Reuters' account, found no evidence the 2020 result was manipulated.

The pattern is a lawyer sanctioned for false election claims in private practice being handed the government's investigative tools to pursue the same claims, with no court yet finding the resulting investigations produced evidence of a crime.

official: Kristi Noem, then-Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: Forcible removal and physical restraint of a sitting U.S. Senator engaged in oversight activity, followed by a demonstrably false public agency statement mischaracterizing his conduct (potential First Amendment/congressional-oversight retaliation concern; no charges filed)
incident_summary: On June 12, 2025, Sen. Alex Padilla (D-CA) attempted to ask DHS Secretary Kristi Noem a question during her press conference at the Wilshire Federal Building in Los Angeles, held amid the administration's ICE/National Guard immigration-enforcement operation in the city. Video shows Padilla clearly stating 'I am Senator Alex Padilla. I have questions for the Secretary' as FBI and Secret Service personnel moved to remove him; **he was forced into a hallway, pushed face-forward to the ground, and handcuffed while officers ordered him to put his hands behind his back.** He was not arrested, charged, or detained afterward, and DHS said he and Noem spoke for 15 minutes following the incident. DHS's official account, posted on its X account, claimed Padilla 'interrupted a live press conference without identifying himself or having his Senate security pin on' and that he 'lunged toward Secretary Noem' -- both claims directly contradicted by video of the incident, which shows Padilla identifying himself verbally and does not show a lunge, instead showing him standing and speaking in a level tone as officers moved in. House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Rep. Jamie Raskin sent a formal letter to FBI Director Kash Patel on June 18, 2025 demanding an investigation into the FBI's role in what he characterized as the unlawful detention of a sitting member of Congress.
elements_required: A sitting U.S. Senator was physically restrained and handcuffed by federal law enforcement while attempting to ask a question of a Cabinet secretary at a public press conference -- documented on video, not disputed as to the physical facts
DHS's official public explanation contains at least two specific, checkable factual claims (failure to identify himself; lunging at the Secretary) that video evidence directly contradicts
No criminal charge, arrest, or detention followed, undercutting any characterization of Padilla's own conduct as warranting the level of force used
A formal congressional demand for investigation was made to the FBI director specifically over federal law enforcement's role in the incident

A senator asking a question in a level tone, having identified himself verbally, is a materially different situation than the one DHS's own public statement described to justify the response, regardless of whether interrupting the press conference itself was appropriate.

official: Sean Parnell, Assistant to the Secretary of Defense for Public Affairs; Steve Feinberg, Deputy Secretary of Defense; Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (Parnell announced the overhaul, his office issued the repeal rule and the ombudsman's removal notice, and his principal deputy Andrew Brey signed the journalists' separation notices; Feinberg issued the March 2026 memo; Hegseth is a defendant only in his official capacity as department head, and no source reviewed shows him personally directing the firings)
offense_category: First Amendment Retaliation Against Government-Employed Journalists (alleged; Pickering v. Board of Education / Garcetti v. Ceballos public-employee speech doctrine, under which two federal judges found the claims unlikely to succeed at the preliminary stage, though one declined to dismiss the ombudsman's suit) and Administrative Procedure Act Notice-and-Comment Violation (alleged) in removing the regulations that guaranteed Stars and Stripes' editorial independence -- civil litigation, not criminal
incident_summary: Stars and Stripes, the Defense Department-owned news organization that serves U.S. troops, military families and veterans and gets about half its budget from the department, had operated since 1994 under federal regulations (32 C.F.R. Part 246) requiring "a free flow of news and information to its readership without news management or censorship," adopted after a congressionally ordered GAO study of allegations of military censorship at the paper. On January 15, 2026, Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell, the Assistant to the Secretary of Defense for Public Affairs, posted on X that the department would "refocus [Stripes'] content away from woke distractions that syphon morale," with "no more Associated Press reprints." The same day, the department published a final rule (91 Fed. Reg. 1706) removing those regulations without notice and comment, on the ground that they covered internal procedures and their removal would not have "an impact or burden to the public." On March 9, Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg issued a "modernization" memo, effective immediately, that affirmed the paper's editorial independence while limiting wire-service content, barring comics and other syndicated features unless Parnell approved an exception, banning publication of "controlled unclassified information," requiring content to be consistent with "good order and discipline," routing the ombudsman's information for Congress through the department, and moving Parnell's office into an oversight role. The paper's congressionally created ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, who had criticized the changes in her columns, was then notified that her last day would be April 28; she wrote that the notice came from Parnell's office and gave no reason, and she sued in June. On June 3, two subscribers who sit on the paper's publisher's advisory board sued (Dardarian v. Department of Defense) to vacate the repeal and the memo under the Administrative Procedure Act; two veterans later joined them. On July 5, CBS Sunday Morning aired a segment on the dispute in which editor-in-chief Erik Slavin, who had his supervisor's approval for the interview, said that being told to drop "a perfectly accurate story" for one "written by the Pentagon" would be a red line, and Middle East reporter Lara Korte said she worked "for Stars and Stripes... not for the Pentagon." According to the journalists' later lawsuit, a July 28 performance review of publisher Max Lederer, approved by Parnell as his rater, faulted him because his "editor and another reporter participated in a network story they know was meant to criticize the DoW efforts with Stripes." The suit alleges that on August 12, the day after Stars and Stripes published a story on hardships aboard the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, Parnell's principal deputy, Andrew Brey, ordered Lederer to deliver separation notices to Slavin and Korte over their CBS remarks; the department says the notices were completed on August 6, before that story ran. Lederer refused and announced his retirement. **On August 21, the department issued notices of proposed separation to all three**: Slavin and Korte over their CBS remarks, citing a lack of authorization from Parnell's office even though their supervisors had approved the interview, and Lederer for refusing to deliver their notices and for his interview with his own paper about his retirement. The same day, it issued a revised DoD Instruction 5122.11 that carried forward most of the March memo's content restrictions. The three sued Parnell, Brey, Hegseth and the department on August 27 (Slavin v. Parnell), and the department agreed to hold off on the firings while the court considered their motion. On September 4, U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden denied a preliminary injunction, finding that Slavin and Korte likely spoke as part of their official duties, and so without First Amendment protection under Garcetti v. Ceballos, and that Lederer's refusal to deliver the notices was likely enough on its own to justify firing him. He wrote that the plaintiffs' "real complaint seems to be that they were victims of a cruel bait-and-switch," fired "for giving pre-approved interviews on their paper's behalf in which they largely toed the company line," and that whatever else that might violate, "it does not clearly offend the First Amendment." CBS News reported that all three were placed on administrative leave after the notices, and news coverage since the ruling has described all three as fired; the sources reviewed do not state the effective separation dates. In a statement he posted on X the day after the ruling, and later provided to the Ethics and Journalism Initiative, Parnell said the department has the authority and responsibility to keep the paper focused on the force "rather than becoming a platform for airing employee grievances." The journalists' lawyer said they would keep pursuing their procedural claims. In the subscribers' case, the plaintiffs added the new instruction to their suit and filed a consolidated summary-judgment motion on September 16, with briefing scheduled to run into December; in Smith's case, the government, citing Judge McFadden's ruling, argued she wrote as ombudsman and is unprotected. After a September 24 hearing at which Lederer testified for her, Judge Amit Mehta on October 6 denied her request to be reinstated, finding she had not shown that she wrote her April 8 column as a private citizen rather than as ombudsman. He also declined to dismiss her suit, questioning whether the public-employee speech test fits government-employed journalists: applied strictly, he wrote, it "would mean the First Amendment is but a hollow promise for Stars and Stripes journalists—and perhaps its Ombudsman." He gave the department until October 20 to renew its motion to dismiss or answer. A week after the ruling, Parnell appointed Christian Devine, an executive director and principal adviser in Parnell's own public affairs office, as the paper's acting publisher, as Military.com and Stars and Stripes reported on October 13. Devine keeps his Pentagon job and will split his time between the two roles until a permanent publisher is hired, with the department continuing to pay him. A Stars and Stripes official said he intends to let the acting editor-in-chief keep making routine coverage decisions while he directs business operations, including personnel actions; Devine said he is committed to preserving the paper's editorial independence. On October 19, at the department's request and over Smith's objection that a longer schedule would put at risk her return to the ombudsman post by December 19, Judge Mehta extended the department's deadline to respond to her suit to November 12, writing that whether she can be reinstated is a remedies question that will arise only if she prevails on the merits.

status: Litigation ongoing. Judges declined to block the firings of the editor, publisher and a reporter (Sept. 4) and to reinstate the ombudsman (Oct. 6), but her suit survived a dismissal bid; the department must respond by Nov. 12. Rules-repeal suit continues. A Pentagon official is acting publisher.
rebuttal_anticipated: The department would argue that Stars and Stripes is a Defense Department publication staffed by department employees, so it may set the paper's policies and discipline its staff like any other employer; that the 1994 regulation addressed internal procedures and could be removed without notice and comment; that the March memo and the revised instruction expressly preserve editorial independence; and that the separations punished insubordination and unauthorized media engagement, not viewpoint. A federal judge agreed at the preliminary stage that the editor and reporter likely spoke in their official roles, which Garcetti leaves unprotected, and that the publisher's refusal to deliver the notices justified his removal on its own; a second judge found the ombudsman had not shown she wrote her critical column as a private citizen rather than as ombudsman; the department also says the notices predated the USS Abraham Lincoln story.
comeback: The ruling was preliminary, and it did not endorse the firings: Judge McFadden described the plaintiffs' account as a "cruel bait-and-switch," fired for pre-approved interviews in which they "largely toed the company line," and said only that it does not clearly offend the First Amendment. In the ombudsman's case, Judge Amit Mehta refused to dismiss, writing that applying the public-employee speech test strictly "would mean the First Amendment is but a hollow promise for Stars and Stripes journalists." The department's own instruction still says the paper's editorial operations are independent of the military chain of command and free from censorship, yet the people it fired or removed, from the ombudsman Congress created to guard that independence to the editor and a reporter, were disciplined after defending it in public. The regulation it removed had been adopted through notice and comment after a congressionally ordered study of censorship at the paper, and whether it could be undone without the same process is before a separate judge.

offense_category: First and Fifth Amendment Violations Alleged in Retaliatory Firings of Career Agents, Plus a Separate Allegation of Illegal Grand Jury Secrecy Violations, and a Second Suit Alleging False Statements to Congress About the Firings -- civil lawsuits' allegations, not an adjudicated finding or criminal charge against Patel or Bondi
incident_summary: **Former FBI agents Jamie Garman, Blaire Toleman, and Michelle Ball -- who the lawsuit describes as having amassed 'exemplary' service records -- sued FBI Director Kash Patel, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, the FBI, and DOJ, alleging they were illegally purged from the bureau for having worked on 'Arctic Frost,' the FBI's investigation (opened in April 2022, later brought under special counsel Jack Smith) into the alleged criminal conspiracy to overturn Trump's 2020 election loss, which led to Trump's August 2023 indictment on four charges.** The suit alleges Patel and Bondi violated the agents' First and Fifth Amendment rights by firing them based on perceived political affiliation tied to their Arctic Frost work, without evidence of individual misconduct or due process. The named plaintiffs seek to represent a proposed class of all FBI employees fired since January 2025 over perceived political affiliation without due process -- at least 50 people by the complaint's estimate, a group that CBS News reported reaches beyond Arctic Frost to employees fired for other alleged political reasons. It was the second suit that month over the Arctic Frost firings: on March 19, 2026, two anonymous former agents had filed Doe 1 v. Patel, a related but separate case, and the Garman complaint was formally noticed as related to it. The lawsuit additionally alleges that Patel or people acting at his direction, and then-Deputy Director Dan Bongino, gave Congress Arctic Frost material protected by grand jury secrecy rules without court authorization, and that Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley then published some of it, including material naming Garman; disclosing grand jury material without court permission is a crime, so this is a separate legal issue beyond the firings themselves. This lawsuit is a direct legal-accountability consequence of the staffing purges documented separately in this tracker's Government Services database. On June 18, 2026, the government moved to dismiss both suits, arguing the agents were at-will employees removed over how they performed their assigned duties rather than for their perceived politics. Between July 29 and August 3, 2026, five sets of outside parties sought leave to file amicus briefs supporting the plaintiffs -- the FBI Agents Association; First Amendment scholars represented by the Campaign Legal Center and Yale's Media Freedom and Information Access Clinic; Lawyers for the Rule of Law; Justice Connection with 38 former FBI personnel; and former senior DOJ officials -- and the court granted each request. Briefing on the motion to dismiss closed August 18, 2026, and Judge Jia M. Cobb set an in-person hearing on the motions in both cases for October 21, 2026. On October 15, 2026, nine other former FBI employees filed a separate suit, Bacon v. Patel (No. 1:26-cv-03604, D.D.C.), against Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche, the FBI, and DOJ. Unlike the Arctic Frost plaintiffs, they were special agents, staff operations specialists and analysts on 'Plasmic Echo,' the FBI's investigation of Trump's handling of classified documents. Their complaint alleges that Patel fired eight of them on February 25, 2026 and the ninth the next day, in violation of the First and Fifth Amendments, with termination letters invoking 'Article II' and without any internal investigation or disciplinary process, and that Bacon was fired less than 48 hours after an agent on Patel's 'Director's Advisory Team' gained access to the case files containing their names. The suit also alleges that Patel later told House and Senate committees, in March and September 2026, that the firings followed internal investigations, which it says is untrue -- each plaintiff's personnel form recorded the termination as not 'for cause' -- and that the sensitive counterintelligence and counterterrorism cases they were working were not properly transferred when they were removed.

The firings are alleged to have occurred without the due process protections (Fifth Amendment) and free-association/political-belief protections (First Amendment) civil-service employees are normally entitled to

Separately, FBI materials from the Arctic Frost investigation protected by grand jury secrecy rules were allegedly disclosed to Congress without court authorization, a distinct potential federal crime independent of the firings themselves

In a separate suit, nine FBI employees assigned to the Plasmic Echo classified-documents investigation allege the same kind of firing, and allege that Patel told Congress the firings followed internal investigations, which they say is untrue

offense_category: Waiving Standard Security-Clearance Polygraph Requirements for the FBI's Deputy Director and Two Personal Aides, Granting Top-Secret/SCI Access Despite Unresolved or Inconclusive Results
incident_summary: ProPublica reported on November 24, 2025 that **FBI Director Kash Patel granted unprecedented polygraph waivers to three of his closest aides -- Deputy Director Dan Bongino, congressional-affairs liaison Marshall Yates, and Patel's personal assistant Nicole Rucker -- allowing all three to obtain Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) clearances, the level required for access to the nation's most sensitive intelligence, including presidential briefings, despite polygraph results that did not clear under normal standards.** Sources told ProPublica that Yates and Rucker did not clear their polygraph exams; Bongino's specific results were not established in reporting. Former FBI officials said they could not recall any senior official ever receiving such a waiver, with one recalling only a single such waiver in seven years, granted to an outside subject-matter expert -- not a sitting senior FBI leader. The FBI's own employment guidelines require all employees to pass a polygraph as part of obtaining Top Secret clearance. An FBI Security Division employee filed a formal internal complaint with the division's director, Robert Turner, alleging the waivers violated agency policy, and separately shared the complaint with the Justice Department's Office of the Inspector General. An FBI spokesperson denied that any of the three had 'failed' their polygraphs -- a characterization that leaves open whether the results were instead deemed inconclusive -- but declined to specify what, if anything, in ProPublica's reporting the FBI considered false.
elements_required: The FBI Director personally waived a standard, employment-guideline-mandated security-clearance requirement for his own deputy and two personal aides
At least two of the three did not clear their polygraph exams under normal standards, per multiple sources
The waivers granted access to SCI-level intelligence, the most sensitive tier, despite that unresolved vetting result -- a departure former officials said had no real precedent for senior leadership

An FBI Security Division employee formally objected internally and escalated the complaint to DOJ's Inspector General, indicating the waivers were controversial within the agency's own security apparatus, not merely from outside critics

evidence.description: ProPublica's original investigative report identifies all three waiver recipients (Bongino, Yates, Rucker), the SCI clearance level granted, the polygraph-clearance shortfall for Yates and Rucker, former officials' statements that such a waiver for senior leadership was unprecedented, the internal complaint to Security Division director Robert Turner and DOJ's Inspector General, and the FBI's on-record denial that anyone 'failed' their polygraphs
evidence.maps_to_element: Full incident: waiver recipients, clearance level, unprecedented nature, internal complaint, and FBI's response

status: Unresolved as of this entry. An internal complaint has been referred to DOJ's Office of the Inspector General; no OIG findings, and no reversal of the waivers, were identified in reporting reviewed.
rebuttal_anticipated: The FBI's on-record position is that none of the three 'failed' their polygraphs, implying inconclusive rather than disqualifying results, and that the Director has discretion to grant waivers for trusted senior personnel he has direct, ongoing working knowledge of.
comeback: The FBI's own employment guidelines make polygraph clearance a requirement for Top Secret access, not a discretionary formality, and former officials -- not partisan critics -- said they could recall no precedent for waiving it at this level for sitting senior FBI leadership; a single-source report of one prior waiver, for an outside expert rather than an internal official, is a materially different situation than exempting the Bureau's own Deputy Director and the Director's personal staff. The FBI's denial that anyone 'failed' notably does not address whether the results were inconclusive -- itself normally grounds for further review, not an automatic waiver -- and the agency declined to specify what else in the reporting it considered inaccurate.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern this tracker documents of Patel prioritizing personal loyalty and proximity over standard institutional vetting processes at the FBI, paralleling this tracker's separately-documented reduction of vetting standards for incoming special agents (see the Patel entry) -- here applied to the Bureau's own most senior leadership rather than new hires.

offense_category: Directing a Cross-Case Campaign to Manufacture Criminal Prosecutions Against Perceived Political Opponents, With Career Prosecutors Removed for Refusing to Proceed -- no criminal charge against Patel personally; this entry documents the pattern-level accountability claim underlying this tracker's separate, official-specific vindictive-prosecution entries for the Comey, Brennan, and James cases
incident_summary: New York Times reporting from June 2026 (syndicated by the Philadelphia Inquirer), based on interviews with multiple people with knowledge of the effort, describes FBI Director Kash Patel's pursuit of a "grand conspiracy case" against President Trump's perceived foes as the driving force behind a 2025-2026 effort to find prosecutors willing to charge them, despite evidence that career investigators found weak; the New Republic summarized that report. A whistleblower complaint filed with Senate Judiciary Committee members and reported in October 2026 by CNN and NBC News, from Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI's Los Angeles field office, alleges the pressure reached protesters as well: it says that after a February 2025 anti-ICE protest in Alhambra, California, Trump demanded an investigation of demonstrators he had seen in a TikTok video, Patel told top FBI leaders that the president "was angry about the incident, and he wanted those protesters investigated and arrested," and an FBI squad was ordered to run pre-assessment checks on them although it did not yet have evidence of a crime; NBC News reported that, according to Fields, the White House directive to Patel came after FBI agents had conducted a check into the protesters' conduct and declined to open an investigation, and that the Los Angeles office pulled agents off active cartel cases to satisfy what a supervisor described as "optics" designed to "make a show for the president." The complaint also says then-Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove demanded an investigation of anti-ICE protesters outside a federal building. Fields says she was stripped of her team and resigned. Sen. Alex Padilla wrote to Patel and Attorney General Todd Blanche that the allegations "raise grave concerns about the rule of law under your leadership, the diversion of resources from ongoing criminal investigations, and the testimony that you provided under oath to Congress," and asked officials to preserve information about the investigation. The White House called the allegations "FALSE," saying the First Amendment does not protect violent rioting or assaulting law enforcement, and a Justice Department spokesperson said DOJ and the FBI have a responsibility to investigate potential violations of federal law. Patel said on Joe Rogan's podcast in June 2025 that he had found documents inside FBI headquarters confirming his suspicions; those documents, found in FBI "burn bags," underpinned his push to have James Comey and John Brennan investigated for lying to Congress. The same account describes pressure on the Comey case also coming through deputies of then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, and pressure to charge New York Attorney General Letitia James coming from the White House after Blanche told a July 2025 meeting that the evidence did not support a case against her; in September 2025 Trump publicly complained that Comey, James, and Sen. Adam Schiff had not been charged. **Prosecutors who examined the evidence and declined to proceed were removed or saw their investigations transferred to more compliant colleagues. Todd Gilbert, interim U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Virginia, whom Patel personally directed on his first day in July 2025 to pursue the burn-bag case, resisted pressure to impanel a grand jury because his team did not believe there was a sufficient factual basis, and was pushed out after 37 days; his office's later declination memo concluded no charges were warranted.** Eastern District of Virginia U.S. Attorney Erik Siebert, who did not believe the evidence supported charging Comey, was fired in September 2025, and the grand conspiracy case moved to the Miami U.S. Attorney's office. In the Brennan probe there, CNN reported in March 2026 that career prosecutors who viewed the case as relatively weak were resisting pressure from top Justice officials to bring charges; in April 2026 DOJ removed the senior career prosecutor overseeing the case after she raised concerns about the strength of the evidence and put Trump ally Joe DiGenova in charge, and CBS News reported that two FBI agents assigned to it had served on Patel's Director's Advisory Team, one of whom had worked on the Comey prosecution. This tracker separately documents four of the resulting individual cases in more detail: the original Comey case, brought via Lindsey Halligan, an unlawfully-appointed interim U.S. Attorney, and dismissed without prejudice in November 2025 when a federal judge found Halligan's appointment invalid; a second, separate Comey prosecution filed April 28, 2026 in the Eastern District of North Carolina over a since-deleted Instagram post of seashells arranged as "8647," charged as a threat against the President; the Brennan grand-jury investigation, in which Brennan has been told he is a subject of the Fort Pierce conspiracy probe and a target of a separate probe into his testimony to Congress, but has not been charged; and the James case, also indicted by Halligan and dismissed on the same appointment defect, after which two grand juries declined to re-indict her. After the original Halligan-based Comey indictment collapsed on the appointment defect, DOJ did not close the matter: it filed the entirely new Eastern District of North Carolina indictment against Comey five months later, under a different legal theory (an alleged threat, rather than false statements or obstruction) -- direct, concrete evidence for this entry's own core thesis, that resistance or procedural setbacks redirect rather than end the underlying campaign, and the clearest single documented instance of it; the Times account adds that career prosecutors and agents had rejected the seashell case in 2025, after the Secret Service interviewed Comey and saw no point in a full investigation. In October 2026 The Atlantic, drawing on interviews with more than 40 current and former officials and others, reported (as summarized by Mediaite) that the White House was pressing the FBI for indictments in a sprawling set of election-related investigations before the midterms -- "The president wants indictments. He wants people in handcuffs," one former official said -- that Patel told staff to "look harder" when those probes turned up nothing new and, per a former senior FBI official, was willing to accommodate White House requests, and that prosecutors who recently left the grand conspiracy investigation had clashed with senior leadership over producing indictments before the midterms; DiGenova, who had overseen it, resigned in September, saying "If you want indictments where there's no evidence, you have an ethical problem." The White House denied dictating investigations or charges, and the FBI called election security one of its highest priorities. This entry documents the pattern-level claim that Patel's drive was central to the push across these cases, alongside pressure from Blanche's office and the White House, and that DOJ personnel who resisted were removed -- a distinct accountability claim from any single case's merits, since it concerns the process by which targets were selected and prosecutors were pressured, not any one prosecution's individual legal footing.
elements_required: Reporting based on current/former DOJ and FBI officials attributes a sustained, personal push to build criminal cases against Trump's perceived foes (the "grand conspiracy" case targeting Comey and Brennan) to Patel, alongside documented pressure from DOJ leadership and the White House on the Comey, James, and Schiff matters

At least one specific, named instance is documented of a prosecutor examining the evidence, finding an insufficient factual basis, and refusing to proceed (declining to impanel a grand jury) despite direct pressure to do so

Prosecutors and investigators who declined to pursue these cases were removed, reassigned, or had their investigations transferred to other personnel, establishing a documented consequence for resistance rather than a hypothetical chilling effect

The pattern spans at least four distinct targets across multiple DOJ components and time periods, and includes at least one instance (Comey) where an initial prosecution's dismissal on procedural grounds was followed by a new indictment of the same target via a different venue and legal theory rather than the matter being closed -- indicating a sustained campaign against specific individuals rather than four unrelated, one-off prosecutorial decisions

incident_summary: **FBI Director Kash Patel is set to eliminate the requirement that existing FBI support staff applying to become special agents complete an in-person interview and a writing assessment -- two long-standing vetting steps.** Under the new process, internal candidates who pass a written exam through an online portal can proceed directly to new-agent training at the FBI Academy in Quantico. offense_category: Alleged Hatch Act violation (5 U.S.C. §7323(a)(1), use of official authority or influence to affect the result of an election) and alleged misuse of government resources for partisan messaging -- NOT charged; the Hatch Act is enforced administratively through the Office of Special Counsel, which CREW says has opened an investigation on its complaint; no finding has been made
incident_summary: On Tuesday, October 6, 2026, the FBI's rapid response account on X posted a video of more than two minutes that, according to The Hill, labeled several prominent Democrats as part of the "defund the police crowd" and featured the faces of former Vice President Kamala Harris, Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar, and former Rep. Cori Bush. **It also featured Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan's Democratic Senate nominee, who appeared on screen as "Progressive Democrat, Senate Nominee."** The New Republic reported that the video decried "democratic socialist leaders" for calling to defund the police, with narration saying "Not reform. Defund the police as policy" and "What followed was a complete failure." The FBI's post accompanying the video said in part: "They sold slogans. We delivered handcuffs. CRIMINALS FEAR RESULTS, NOT HASHTAGS." Set to the beat of Michael Jackson's "Smooth Criminal," the video credited FBI Director Kash Patel with arresting violent criminals and seizing fentanyl and showed him walking away from a helicopter with Attorney General Todd Blanche; according to a thread by Donald Sherman, president of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), the narrator said "Kash Patel's FBI is taking safety back by force," and the video closed with the FBI's official seal. The Hill reported that the video does not mention the election outright, and that it came shortly after Patel said on Fox News in late September that viewers "may want to vote for people who back the blue, who fund law enforcement." Patel had already been named in an earlier Hatch Act complaint: on September 4, The Steady State, a group of former national security officials, asked the Office of Special Counsel (OSC) to investigate whether he and Blanche violated the Act by appearing under their official titles at an August 14 Garden City, New York, event headlined by President Trump and Republican gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman. CREW filed a Hatch Act complaint with OSC over the video, arguing that the video's message that the named candidates' policies "failed" and "Americans were left exposed" reflects advocacy against their election and that labeling El-Sayed, who holds no government office, a Senate nominee "is a clear invocation of the upcoming election." Delaney Marsco, director of ethics at the Campaign Legal Center, told The Hill that "It shouldn't shock anyone that this is not compliant with the Hatch Act." On October 7, Sherman wrote on X that OSC had opened an investigation at CREW's request, file HA-27-000006. By October 8 the FBI had deleted the post; it did not respond to The Hill's request for comment. El-Sayed's campaign also did not respond, though El-Sayed had earlier told Politico that "defund the police" is "a pretty dumb and unnuanced slogan" and that he would like to give local police departments more funding to recruit.

The content also promoted the FBI's record under Patel by name, weeks before the midterm elections

The Hatch Act bars covered federal employees from using their official authority or influence to interfere with or affect the result of an election, and the Office of Special Counsel is the body that investigates and can act on a complaint

Deleting it after the complaint does not settle whether posting it was lawful; that is for OSC to decide.
