official: Kash Patel, FBI Director
offense_category: Alleged politicization of federal law enforcement ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, including a refusal to rule out FBI agents at polling places (18 U.S.C. §592 bars federal personnel from ordering, bringing or keeping troops or armed men at a place where an election is held, unless needed to repel armed enemies of the United States) -- NOT charged; no court, inspector general or congressional finding; the core internal-concern claims are anonymous-source reporting that the FBI denies (DOJ denies one quoted message)
incident_summary:
At a contentious Senate Judiciary Committee oversight hearing on Tuesday, September 15, 2026, FBI Director Kash Patel refused to say whether FBI agents would be present at the polls during the midterm elections, Roll Call reported. Asked by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) whether he agreed that deploying FBI agents to the polls on Election Day would be illegal, Patel answered, **"I don't know that we can't legally do it,"** adding that agents and intelligence analysts would be housed in field offices for election security and that the Department of Homeland Security, not the FBI, takes the lead on monitoring elections. Later, asked by Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) about Michigan gubernatorial candidate John James's claim that Patel told him the FBI would "have a presence" across the state, Patel said, "We have an election crimes community coordinator at all 56 offices. So you bet we're gonna have them there ... for election interference matters," and called Welch's account of his earlier answer "just another lie." Asked to pledge not to interfere in the will of voters in November, Patel replied, "I pledge unequivocally that I will not participate in your charade of lies," while also saying, "We will always follow the law and the guidelines." Democracy Docket noted that the Election Assistance Commission does not indicate these coordinators normally act as a standing presence at poll sites, and that federal law bars armed federal officers at election sites.

On October 8, 2026, The Atlantic's Radio Atlantic podcast aired staff writer Sarah Fitzpatrick's reporting, drawn from what she said were "over 40 sources across the FBI and across Washington." According to The Atlantic, **"nervous agents have sought counsel in recent weeks about how to respond to FBI directives related to the midterms"**; the extensive Election Day preparation the FBI normally does, such as briefings and trainings on protecting election sites and workers, "has not happened thus far"; the one large-scale training, titled "Election Integrity," focused mostly on illegal-immigrant voting; and "There has been no specific guidance that has gone out," with sources describing orders framed as a White House "presidential priority." Fitzpatrick also said that over 200 agents were pulled from their duties this summer to review the 2020 Fulton County, Georgia ballots the FBI seized in January, a review she understood turned up nothing new or material, and that two people were walked out of the Atlanta field office after raising questions about the process; the FBI declined to comment on personnel. She quoted a message relayed between Justice Department officials: "I was told the Justice Manual isn't a thing ... There are no rules. Just make sure Republicans win." These are allegations from anonymous sources, not findings. DOJ said that message "is not and has never been department guidance"; FBI executives called the reporting false and the bureau "united"; an FBI spokesperson denied that any internal concerns were raised and said "Election security is and will continue to be one of this FBI's highest national security priorities"; and Patel answered detailed questions with a reference to a "golden Jet Ski." Patel is separately suing The Atlantic for $250 million over its April 2026 reporting on him.

incident_summary: Kash Patel began floating a UFC partnership with the FBI early in 2025, almost immediately after he became FBI director, according to Talking Points Memo. On March 12, 2026, the UFC and the FBI announced a two-day seminar at the FBI Academy in Quantico, Virginia, held March 14 and 15 and led by current and former UFC fighters. Patel called it "a tremendous opportunity for our FBI agents to learn and train with some of the greatest athletes on earth" and said the bureau was "extremely honored to be partnered with" UFC chief executive Dana White, a longtime friend and ally of President Trump. The FBI did not answer Talking Points Memo's questions about whether it paid for the seminar or received it as a gift from the UFC; ethics lawyer Virginia Canter told the outlet that federal employees generally cannot solicit a gift without advance approval from the attorney general or deputy attorney general. In June 2026 the UFC staged a fight on the White House South Lawn to mark Trump's 80th birthday. **On September 30, 2026, the FBI publicly posted a justification, dated June 2, for a one-year, firm fixed-price contract with the UFC to train special agents in defensive tactics built on mixed martial arts, without full and open competition.** It invoked the "only one responsible source" exception and stated that "this contract must be sole sourced to UFC, as they are the only vendor who can provide training that includes all of these styles at the level of expertise that is required by the FBI." The document says market research through internet searches, SAM.gov and the federal procurement database found no other vendor that could meet every requirement in the time allowed; that "Since the procurement was not advertised, no other companies have expressed an interest"; and that the one-year "bridge" contract would buy time for a competitive long-term contract later. The government's cost estimate is redacted. According to The Washington Sun, the notice set an October 15 deadline for responses. Rob D'Amico, a former FBI Hostage Rescue Team member who taught defensive tactics at the bureau, told MS NOW: "This is just Patel giving his friend Dana White a lucrative contract." The FBI did not immediately respond to The Daily Beast's request for comment, and no award has been reported.

incident_summary: Scrutiny of FBI Director Kash Patel's use of bureau resources for his girlfriend, country singer Alexis Wilkins, intensified in late October 2025, when public flight logs and Wilkins's own social-media posts showed that Patel had taken the FBI's $60 million Gulfstream jet on October 25, 2025 to watch Wilkins perform at a Penn State wrestling event, then flown with her to Nashville the next day. On November 17, 2025, MS NOW reported that Wilkins was being protected by SWAT agents from the FBI's Nashville field office, and on November 23, 2025 the New York Times reported that Patel had sent two SWAT agents from the FBI's Atlanta field office to guard Wilkins at the April 2025 National Rifle Association convention in Atlanta, where she performed the national anthem, and that current and former FBI officials called the use of SWAT agents to protect her 'highly unusual.' FBI spokesman Ben Williamson defended the arrangements to the Times, saying Wilkins had faced 'hundreds of credible death threats' tied to her relationship with Patel, stating that Patel's transportation spending was comparable to that of predecessors Christopher Wray and James Comey, and adding that 'bad faith criticisms of F.B.I. travel will not deter the bureau from our mission.' A New York Times investigation published May 15, 2026, and widely repeated by follow-on outlets, documented a pattern of Patel using federal jets, security resources, and FBI personnel for personal and leisure purposes involving Wilkins. On May 10, 2025, Patel and Wilkins flew from Washington, D.C. to Philadelphia on an FBI Gulfstream V jet to attend a Chris Stapleton/George Strait concert, watching from a private suite reported to cost between $35,000 and $50,000, while the FBI flight crew and Patel's security detail stayed on duty past 11 p.m. waiting for the concert to end, collecting overtime pay; through an FBI spokesperson, Patel declined to say who paid for the suite, and representatives for the performers did not confirm the FBI's claim that Wilkins was their invited guest. Separately, Wilkins -- who does not reside with Patel -- was assigned a full-time security detail made up of elite FBI agents previously assigned to the Nashville field office's SWAT team, reportedly the first time a senior FBI official's romantic partner (rather than spouse or dependent) has received a full FBI protective detail. The reporting also recalled the October 2025 Penn State jet trip. An earlier NYT report (Feb. 28, 2026) had already documented the security detail, additionally reporting that it was staffed by rotating FBI SWAT teams covering personal errands and events (not just concerts), and that FBI staffing in Nashville, where Wilkins lives, was increased around the same period -- former officials said this raised concerns about an unprecedented allocation of tactical resources. The May 15, 2026 NYT report also covered a 'VIP snorkel' excursion Patel joined at the USS Arizona Memorial around an official Hawaii trip, which the Associated Press had first reported on May 14, 2026 from government emails. Congressional scrutiny had begun earlier. On December 1, 2025, House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Jamie Raskin and Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove wrote to Patel demanding FBI and Justice Department aircraft travel records; their letter cited the Penn State trip and the flight with Wilkins to Nashville, a golf trip to Scotland, a Texas hunting retreat, earlier Senate Democratic criticism of his flights to hockey matches and fight nights, and Patel's move to shield the FBI jet from public flight tracking after his travel drew scrutiny. Patel has responded publicly that he is 'entitled to a personal life just like my other agency counterparts.' In April 2026, the New York Times reported that **FBI agents opened an investigation into Times reporter Elizabeth Williamson beginning around March 2026, after she wrote the story documenting Patel's use of FBI personnel to protect and transport Wilkins -- agents interviewed Wilkins, queried law-enforcement databases for information on Williamson, and moved toward assessing whether she had violated federal stalking law.** Some Justice Department officials, according to a person briefed on the matter, saw the inquiry as retaliation for an article that Patel and Wilkins did not like and determined there was no legal basis to proceed. The FBI denied that Williamson was personally investigated, said agents had interviewed Wilkins about a death threat made against her after the article, and said investigators 'were concerned about how the aggressive reporting techniques crossed lines of stalking' but pursued no further action. The Times called the inquiry an attempt to criminalize routine reporting. In a July 8, 2026 letter announced the next day, Raskin and Senate Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Dick Durbin launched a bicameral investigation into Patel's 'abuse of FBI jets and tax dollars,' following a private May 5, 2026 letter from Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley questioning his spending and travel; it cites other recreation on official trips, including the Hawaii snorkeling, helicopter tours in East Asia and a $100,000 trip to the 2026 Winter Olympics. Earlier, on February 24, 2026, Durbin had asked the Government Accountability Office to add whistleblower information to its ongoing review of Patel's aircraft use and asked the Justice Department's Inspector General to investigate.

official: Kash Patel, FBI Director
offense_category: First Amendment Retaliation Under Color of Law (potential civil/criminal exposure: 18 U.S.C. §242, deprivation of rights under color of law; misuse of federal investigative authority; possible Antideficiency Act / misuse-of-government-resources issues for the underlying security detail and transportation) — NOT charged, no criminal referral identified in available reporting
incident_summary: After New York Times reporter Elizabeth Williamson wrote in late February 2026 about Patel's girlfriend, Alexis Wilkins, receiving FBI security and transportation, including SWAT teams escorting her on her travels, the FBI under Patel began investigating Williamson in March 2026, the Times reported on April 22: agents interviewed Wilkins, queried databases for information on the reporter, and recommended moving forward to determine whether she broke federal stalking laws. Some Justice Department officials saw the inquiry as retaliation for an article Patel and Wilkins did not like and determined there was no legal basis to proceed; the FBI said it was not pursuing a case. The FBI called the account false, and Patel adviser Erica Knight said Williamson was never personally investigated and that agents asked Wilkins about her only as part of a threat case against a man later charged with threatening Wilkins after reading the article. Separately, after The Atlantic's Sarah Fitzpatrick reported on Patel's conduct, MS NOW reported in May 2026 that the FBI had launched a criminal leak investigation focusing on her, which the FBI denied, and **Patel later ordered polygraph examinations of more than two dozen of his own staff to identify sources who spoke to reporters.** As of June 2026, Democracy Forward's FOIA lawsuit seeking records on Patel's conduct was active, filed after the agencies missed FOIA response deadlines (Democracy Forward's April 21, 2026 request had given the FBI 20 days to produce documents); Democracy Defenders Fund had filed a separate FOIA suit over a previously undocumented $75,000 taxpayer-funded Italy/Olympics trip in February 2026. In a separate storyline, Patel filed a $250 million defamation suit against The Atlantic and staff writer Sarah Fitzpatrick over her April 17, 2026 article "The FBI Director Is MIA," which reported allegations of excessive drinking and unexplained absences (Patel v. Atlantic Monthly Group LLC, 1:26-cv-01329, D.D.C., filed April 2026); the suit is now contested on the merits. The case is assigned to Judge Emmet G. Sullivan. The Atlantic moved to dismiss on July 27, 2026, arguing Patel's own record makes the underlying drinking allegations "inherently plausible"; Patel filed his opposition brief on the August 17, 2026 deadline, contending the court must draw all inferences in his favor at the motion-to-dismiss stage. The discovery dispute's substance is now on the record: The Atlantic seeks internal DOJ/FBI records on Patel's absences and unreachability -- material Patel's own complaint relies on -- while resisting discovery into its own newsgathering process; Patel's team calls this "discovery for me but not for thee" and argues The Atlantic hasn't shown good cause for a stay. Defendants filed their replies in support of the motions to dismiss and to stay discovery on August 31, 2026; no ruling appears on the docket.
elements_required: Official acted under color of law (FBI investigative resources used under the Director's authority; whether Patel personally directed the inquiry is not established)
Action taken in retaliation for protected First Amendment activity (newsgathering/reporting)
Lack of legitimate law-enforcement justification for the investigation
Chilling effect on protected speech/press activity

Here, the bureau's inquiry into Times reporter Elizabeth Williamson followed her article on the security detail for Patel's girlfriend, and a reported leak probe focused on The Atlantic's Sarah Fitzpatrick, plus polygraphs of Patel's own staff, followed her reporting on his conduct; the FBI calls the Times account false and denies the Fitzpatrick probe. Patel also personally ran a White House-directed leak investigation into the Times's Air Force One reporting, and his FBI has fired agents over their assigned work on Arctic Frost, Jack Smith's election investigation. After four such firings in November 2025, the FBI Agents Association, the bureau's own agents' professional group, said Patel had "disregarded the law and launched a campaign of erratic and arbitrary retribution." Those purges of career staff also thin the internal pushback that would normally check an inquiry like the one into Williamson; the check that did surface there came from Justice Department officials who reportedly found no legal basis to proceed.

official: Kash Patel, FBI Director
offense_category: Retaliatory firing of federal law-enforcement employees for perceived political disloyalty, contradicting the agency's own prior clearance findings -- a pattern raising due-process and whistleblower/civil-service-protection concerns rather than a specific criminal statute
incident_summary: On June 4, 2020, a group of FBI agents in Washington, D.C. knelt during a protest following George Floyd's murder, an act they say was intended to de-escalate tensions with a hostile crowd rather than to express political solidarity with the broader movement. An FBI internal review at the time concluded the kneeling was a de-escalation tactic, not a political statement, and a Justice Department Inspector General review separately found no misconduct and no Hatch Act violation. **Despite both clearances, FBI Director Kash Patel fired 12 of the agents in September 2025. Their termination letters cited 'unprofessional conduct and a lack of impartiality' and accused the agents of 'weaponisation' of the FBI** -- the same word Patel and the administration have used to describe the conduct they say justified purging Trump-investigation-linked personnel elsewhere in the Bureau (see this project's Government Services entry on Patel's FBI field-office purge). On December 8, 2025, the 12 fired agents sued Patel in U.S. District Court, alleging their termination was part of a 'campaign of retribution' and that 'defendants targeted plaintiffs in particular because of plaintiffs' use of deescalation with civilians that defendants perceived as opposed to, or otherwise not affiliated with, President Trump.' The lawsuit further alleges that immediately upon becoming FBI Director on February 21, 2025, Patel began working to fire the agents, and that FBI senior leaders who spoke to him early in his tenure believed he had already decided to terminate them and that the decision had originated from the White House -- an allegation that, if proven, would mean the firings carried out a White House decision rather than an independent judgment of the underlying conduct.
elements_required: The June 2020 kneeling incident was reviewed twice before this firing -- an FBI internal review at the time, and a DOJ Inspector General review -- both of which cleared the agents of misconduct and found no Hatch Act violation

The termination letters' stated rationale ('unprofessional conduct,' 'lack of impartiality,' 'weaponisation') was issued years after both clearances, with no new fact identified in sourcing reviewed that would justify revisiting the prior findings

The lawsuit's central factual allegation -- that FBI senior leaders believed Patel had already decided on the firings early in his tenure and that the decision originated at the White House -- is a plaintiff-side pleading, not an independently adjudicated finding; no FBI or DOJ response to the lawsuit was identified in sourcing reviewed

The specific term 'weaponisation' used to justify these firings is the same term this administration has used to describe alleged misconduct by career FBI personnel elsewhere, creating an apparent inconsistency worth noting -- deescalating a protest is being characterized the same way as allegedly using the Bureau against political opponents

incident_summary: FBI Director Kash Patel traveled to Milan, Italy on a government jet during the 2026 Winter Olympics and was recorded in a roughly 45-second video celebrating in the U.S. men's hockey team's locker room after their gold-medal win over Canada, drinking beer, singing along to a Toby Keith song, and having a gold medal draped around his neck. When questioned by media, Patel said he was "extremely humbled" that his "friends" on the team invited him to celebrate, and separately defended the trip as an official visit to meet with Italian law enforcement to help provide security for American athletes and fans. According to a person familiar with the matter cited by NBC News on February 27, 2026, President Trump told Patel directly that he was displeased both with the viral locker-room video and with Patel's use of a government jet for the trip, though that disapproval did not result in a reported personnel consequence. CNN's follow-up reporting examined the FBI jet-use controversy and the practical constraints (security, communications needs) that shape how FBI directors typically travel. On February 24, 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Dick Durbin released whistleblower disclosures made to his staff alleging that **Patel's handling of FBI aircraft delayed responses to at least two major investigations: after the December 13, 2025 Brown University mass shooting, the FBI's shooting reconstruction team could not fly from Richmond, Virginia because, per a whistleblower, Patel had ordered the Hostage Rescue Team on standby, a hold that froze the aircraft's use by any other FBI team, so the team drove overnight from Quantico, Virginia to Providence, Rhode Island during a winter storm, arriving at 9 a.m. the next morning; and the shooting reconstruction team's deployment to Utah after conservative activist Charlie Kirk's assassination was delayed by at least a day by a plane and pilot shortage that Durbin attributed to Patel's personal flights, because the team could fly only after the pilots' mandated rest periods.** MS NOW, citing sources and the whistleblower's account, reported the same day that Patel had been flown on one of the FBI's two jets to south Florida and was there on the day of the Brown shooting. FBI spokesman Ben Williamson disputed the Brown account, saying it was initially a state-led homicide investigation with the FBI in an assisting role, that evidence response agents from the FBI's Boston field office reached the scene roughly two hours after the shooting, and that a plane to Rhode Island "wasn't needed." In the Feb. 24 letter that carried those disclosures, Durbin asked the DOJ Inspector General to investigate what he called Patel's "irresponsible joyriding" on DOJ and FBI aircraft and asked the Government Accountability Office to add the new information to its ongoing review of Patel's aircraft use, which Durbin first requested in May 2025; no outcome of either has been identified. A July 8, 2026 bicameral letter from House Judiciary's Raskin and Senate Judiciary's Durbin directly contradicts Patel's own official justification for the Olympics trip: Patel testified to the Senate Appropriations Committee on May 12, 2026 that the FBI "purposely planned" the trip around a wanted hacker's presence in Italian custody, but Patel had publicly announced his Olympics travel plans on July 3, 2025 -- the same date Italy took custody of that suspect, 218 days before the Olympics -- and DOJ's own records show the suspect was not extradited to the U.S. until April 27, 2026, over two months after the Olympics concluded. The letter also reveals Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, a Trump ally, separately raised similar spending and travel concerns in a private May 5, 2026 letter, and documents additional alleged incidents: a VIP snorkeling experience in Hawaii, a taxpayer-funded helicopter tour during a multi-country East Asia trip, and personnel demoted in Brussels for allegedly failing to keep Patel adequately entertained. At a September 15, 2026 Senate Judiciary Committee oversight hearing, Sen. Peter Welch questioned Patel about the locker-room celebration; Patel said the players, "who are my friends, invited me to the locker room," said no security incident occurred during the Games, and called the capture of "China's most prolific hacker" and his return to the United States the most important result of the trip.

official: Kash Patel, FBI Director
offense_category: Press Freedom / Politicization of Federal Law Enforcement -- FBI Director personally directing a criminal leak investigation from the White House at presidential direction, rather than through normal DOJ/FBI process insulated from political control
incident_summary: After the New York Times reported security concerns about President Trump's new Qatari-donated Air Force One (specifically, that Trump left a NATO summit in Turkey aboard the older presidential aircraft over Secret Service security concerns with the new plane), the White House directed FBI Director Kash Patel to personally oversee a leak investigation into the Times's sourcing. **Patel canceled a scheduled trip to Chicago and spent approximately eight hours at the White House itself -- not FBI headquarters -- personally running the investigation. On Friday, July 10, 2026, the investigation produced grand jury subpoenas, issued by Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton, to multiple New York Times reporters, with federal agents delivering some subpoenas directly to journalists' homes.** The Times's own reporting called Patel's running of the investigation from the White House rather than FBI headquarters a major departure from historical practice, and CNN described the White House's control over the probe as a significant breach of the Justice Department's historic independence. At his July 15, 2026 confirmation hearing to be Director of National Intelligence, Clayton testified that "we followed the procedures" and repeatedly called the subpoenas the "least intrusive" means possible, but declined to say whether the White House or top Justice Department officials ordered him to send the subpoenas. At his own confirmation hearing the same day, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche told the Senate Judiciary Committee that reporters were not targets but "material witnesses." At a July 23, 2026 hearing, U.S. District Judge Arun Subramanian repeatedly asked how subpoenas issued two days after the Times's first story could be the last resort that binding Second Circuit precedent and DOJ policy require, and said he would quash them if they were not withdrawn; prosecutors, who admitted "inadvertent errors" in their filings, withdrew them. A prosecutor also acknowledged, NBC News reported, that the government had mistakenly obtained phone records tied to reporters' relatives, including spouses and one reporter's mother, after a public-source database wrongly linked the numbers; The New York Times later described it as the administration having demanded that phone companies turn over the records of two of the reporters' wives and of one reporter's mother. A DOJ spokesperson attacked the judge's conduct and said the investigation "remains ongoing." On July 27, 2026, every Senate Judiciary Committee Democrat signed a letter to Blanche, who had acknowledged authorizing the subpoenas, demanding information on his and Clayton's roles. The Senate confirmed Clayton as Director of National Intelligence the next day, July 28, 2026, by a 51-47 vote.

incident_summary: **The FBI fired at least 10 agents and staff members who had been connected to obtaining 'toll records' (call timing and recipient logs, not call content) for phone numbers belonging to Kash Patel and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, sought in 2022-2023 as part of the Biden-era federal investigation into Trump's handling of classified documents at Mar-a-Lago.** Patel told Reuters the toll-record collection was 'outrageous and deeply alarming,' characterizing it as Biden-administration overreach. Legal observers noted that subpoenaing phone toll records -- which reveal only call metadata, not conversation content -- is a routine, unremarkable step in major federal investigations, including ones involving prominent officials' associates. It was not confirmed in sourcing reviewed whether the specific fired staff had personally sought, approved, or executed the toll-record request, or were terminated simply for having been assigned to the broader investigation.

official: Donald Trump, President of the United States
offense_category: Use of the pardon power to erase both criminal and civil consequences for a convicted ally -- clemency is a constitutional power, not itself unlawful, but its use here directly preceded a coordinate independent agency dropping its own separate civil enforcement action against the same person for the same underlying conduct
status: Closed as to both the criminal conviction (pardoned) and the SEC's civil suit (dismissed with prejudice, August 7, 2026) -- no remaining legal consequence identified in sourcing reviewed for the conduct a federal jury found to be insider trading and securities fraud.
incident_summary: Terren Peizer, founder and former CEO of healthcare company Ontrak, was convicted by a federal jury in 2024 of insider trading and securities fraud -- the first criminal case built on the theory that a pre-arranged stock-selling plan (normally used to shield executives from insider-trading liability) could itself be used to commit the fraud, since Peizer sold more than $20 million of Ontrak stock in mid-2021 while possessing material non-public negative information about the company's largest customer. He was sentenced to 3.5 years in prison. **President Trump pardoned Peizer in January 2026, erasing the criminal conviction and sentence. On August 7, 2026, the Securities and Exchange Commission moved to dismiss with prejudice its own separate, parallel civil enforcement action against Peizer and his company Acuitas -- the last remaining legal consequence for the conduct the jury had already found to be fraudulent.** No SEC reasoning independent of the pardon was identified in sourcing reviewed as justifying the civil dismissal.

Following the pardon, the SEC -- an agency independent of the pardon power and pursuing its own separate civil enforcement action -- moved on August 7, 2026 to dismiss that action with prejudice, ending the case permanently rather than merely pausing it.

No SEC statement or reasoning distinct from the pardon itself was identified in sourcing reviewed as the basis for dismissing the civil case, despite the civil action targeting the same underlying conduct a jury had already adjudicated.

official: Jeanine Pirro, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia
offense_category: Repeated Failure to Persuade D.C. Grand Juries to Indict in Cases Tied to Trump's Federal Policing Surge -- a pattern of prosecutorial overreach evidenced by citizen-juror rejection, not a single failed case
incident_summary: By early September 2025, D.C. federal grand juries had declined to indict at least six times in recent cases connected to Trump's federal policing surge and National Guard deployment in the city -- a pattern NBC News and other outlets characterized as a rebuke of prosecutors' charging decisions by ordinary D.C. citizens serving as jurors. Named examples include Nathalie Rose Jones, an Indiana woman whom a grand jury declined to indict over alleged threats against Trump (prosecutors said she had posted on Facebook about "disemboweling" the president; she allegedly called Trump a "terrorist" and a "Nazi" in a voluntary Secret Service interview on August 15, 2025, and was arrested on August 16 after joining a protest near the White House), and Sean Charles Dunn, whom prosecutors sought to charge with felony assault of a Customs and Border Protection officer for allegedly throwing a sandwich -- a case documented in more detail in this database's separate entry on his failed prosecution. A separate grand jury also declined to indict a second person accused of threatening to kill Trump, Edward Alexander Dana, who allegedly made the threat while being arrested on unrelated vandalism charges. The pattern extended to non-threat cases as well, including local residents accused of minor confrontations with federal agents during the crackdown. Prosecutors' office is led by Jeanine Pirro, whose office brought the underlying charges in these cases. A further named example: DC resident Sydney Lori Reid, arrested in late July 2025 while filming federal agents transferring detainees from DC jail to ICE custody, whom prosecutors accused of assaulting or impeding an immigration officer and an FBI agent. **A federal grand jury rejected the felony assault charge against Reid three separate times in the month after her arrest; on August 25, 2025, Pirro's office told the court it would charge her with a misdemeanor rather than drop the case, a charge that does not require grand jury approval.** Reid's public defenders said "three grand juries have now declined to indict Ms. Reid for felony assault on a law enforcement officer." Reid's arrest preceded the August federal takeover of D.C. policing, though outlets grouped her case with the surge-era refusals. Several of the named cases then collapsed: on September 4, 2025, prosecutors asked a magistrate judge to dismiss the federal case against Dana, recharging him with misdemeanors in D.C. Superior Court; on September 5, Pirro's office moved to dismiss the case against Jones "in the interests of justice" (by then, the Associated Press counted grand juries balking at least seven times in five cases since the surge began); on October 16, 2025, a jury acquitted Reid of the misdemeanor after less than two hours of deliberation; and on November 6, 2025, a jury acquitted Dunn of misdemeanor assault.

official: Jeanine Pirro, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia
offense_category: Failed Attempt to Criminally Indict Sitting Members of Congress Over Protected Legislative/Political Speech -- a grand jury's own refusal to indict is itself strong evidence the underlying prosecution theory lacked merit
incident_summary: In November 2025, six Democratic lawmakers -- Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Mark Kelly, and Reps. Chris Deluzio, Chrissy Houlahan, Maggie Goodlander, and Jason Crow -- released a joint video urging U.S. military servicemembers and intelligence community personnel to refuse illegal orders, following the administration's deadly boat strikes in the Caribbean. President Trump publicly called their statements "seditious" and demanded the lawmakers be "arrested and put on trial." Trump's actual November 20, 2025 Truth Social post was considerably more severe than that summary suggests -- **he wrote, 'SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!' Asked about it the next day on Fox News Radio, Trump said, 'I'm not threatening them, but I think they're in serious trouble.'** A group of former military lawyers, the Former JAGs Working Group, said the video "simply described the law as it pertains to lawful versus unlawful orders" and "did not suborn mutiny or otherwise encourage military members to disregard or disobey lawful orders issued to them." (Secretary Hegseth's February 2025 "Friday Night Massacre" firings of the Army, Navy, and Air Force's top Judge Advocates General are tracked separately in this database.) U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office subsequently sought to indict the six lawmakers for allegedly violating a federal law barring interference with the loyalty, morale, or discipline of the armed forces. On February 10, 2026, a federal grand jury in Washington, D.C. declined to return an indictment, reportedly without a single juror voting to charge -- the latest in a series of grand jury rebukes of Pirro's office's prosecution attempts in the capital. Bloomberg Law reported Pirro's office staffed the case with two Pirro hires with minimal federal prosecution experience, including Steven Vandervelden, a dance photographer who had worked for Pirro decades ago and still ran an active photography studio. On February 19, 2026, Reps. Robert Garcia and Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrats on the House Oversight and Judiciary Committees, asked DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility to investigate the conduct of Pirro and the two prosecutors who presented the case. On February 23 and 24, 2026, NBC News and CBS News reported, citing sources, that Pirro's office had decided to stop pursuing the case against the six lawmakers in Washington. On August 25, 2026, the Legal Accountability Center said it filed bar complaints in New York (against Pirro and Vandervelden) and Virginia (against prosecutor Carlton Davis), asking bar officials to investigate whether they violated professional-conduct rules in seeking the indictment. House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Jamie Raskin separately wrote to Pirro on August 26, 2026, describing her office as "one of the most significant and routine violators of basic legal and ethical standards" regarding candor to the court and compliance with judicial orders; that letter concerns the office's court conduct generally, not this case.
elements_required: The video's content -- reminding servicemembers of their existing legal duty to refuse illegal orders -- reflects established military law rather than incitement to disobey lawful orders

President Trump publicly and personally called for the lawmakers' arrest and prosecution before any indictment was sought, indicating the prosecution effort followed presidential direction rather than an independent prosecutorial judgment

A grand jury -- ordinary D.C. citizens, not a judge or the defendants' own attorneys -- independently declined to return an indictment despite hearing only the prosecution's evidence, the customary one-sided grand jury process

This was one of a documented series of grand jury rejections of Pirro's office's prosecution attempts in Washington, indicating a pattern rather than an isolated case of a good-faith theory that simply fell short

rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: DOJ has discretion to present cases to a grand jury even where the outcome is uncertain, urging servicemembers to consider disobeying orders during an active military operation could reasonably be viewed as raising legitimate morale/discipline concerns, and a grand jury's refusal to indict does not itself establish prosecutorial misconduct.
comeback: The specific facts distinguishing this from an ordinary close call are that the video's core content -- reminding servicemembers of their existing legal duty to refuse illegal orders -- restates established military law rather than urging disobedience of lawful orders, that the President personally and publicly called for the lawmakers' arrest before any charges were sought, and that this was one of a documented series of grand jury rejections of the same U.S. Attorney's office's prosecution attempts, suggesting a pattern of pursuing cases based on political direction rather than independent prosecutorial assessment of the merits.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with the broader pattern this tracker documents of DOJ prosecutorial power being turned on the administration's perceived political opponents after public presidential demands, rather than through independent case assessment (see also the Patel-driven prosecution-campaign entry). It also extends the run of D.C. grand juries refusing charges from Pirro's office, documented in the D.C. grand-jury refusals entry, from defendants swept up in the federal policing surge to sitting members of Congress.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the grand jury's refusal to indict, the six lawmakers' identities, Trump's public 'seditious'/arrest comments, and the characterization of this as part of a series of grand jury rejections are all independently corroborated by CBS News, NBC News, and Politico, with no facts disputed by any party. Trump's verbatim 'SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!' post is reported by NBC News and Al Jazeera, among others; his 'I'm not threatening them, but I think they're in serious trouble' remark, made on Fox News Radio on November 21, 2025, is reported by The Hill. The House Judiciary letter's quoted language matches the letter's PDF text verbatim. The end of the case rests on unnamed sources cited by NBC News and CBS News.

official: Jeanine Pirro, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia
offense_category: Use of Grand Jury Subpoena Power to Unmask Anonymous Political Speech -- no criminal charge has been identified against any of the targeted social media users; this is a First Amendment/investigative-power-abuse claim
incident_summary: By early March 2026, Homeland Security Investigations had sent administrative summonses, which need no judge's sign-off, to Reddit and X seeking to identify two anonymous users who had posted criticism of ICE; after each user's lawyers challenged the summons in federal court, DHS withdrew it. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia, led by Jeanine Pirro, then **issued grand jury subpoenas to Reddit (on March 31, 2026, four days after the Reddit summons was withdrawn) and to X (by early May) seeking the names, addresses, and banking information of the two anonymous users**, directing the companies to deliver the records to an ICE office. The subpoenas were signed by prosecutor Brendan Horan; the users have not been told what offense is under investigation, and DOJ declined to comment. The Reddit user's attorney, Lauren Regan of the Civil Liberties Defense Center (CLDC), said some of her client's posts were as simple as "expletive ICE," but that she suspects the post that drew the government's attention was one referencing the ICE officer who shot Minnesota protester Renee Good and where he had lived; The Intercept reported that the user had shared widely circulating biographical details of that officer, Jonathan Ross, adding "Hopefully he moves up to Stillwater State Penitentiary." The X user's attorney, Joshua Koltun, said his client's post was a sarcastic comment about donating to the same ICE officer, with an address the user had seen elsewhere on social media attached, and said the post "does not contain a trace or an inkling that any violence was intended." Both users, who learned of the subpoenas from the platforms and were given a short window to challenge them before Reddit and X would have to comply, moved to quash the subpoenas and to unseal the proceedings before Chief Judge James Boasberg. Judge Boasberg denied CLDC's motion to quash the Reddit subpoena and its motion to unseal the proceedings, in a ruling CLDC announced on June 17, 2026. Per CLDC's own July 13, 2026 statement, CLDC immediately appealed Boasberg's ruling to the D.C. Circuit, and the district court granted a stay pausing disclosure of the Reddit user's identity pending that appeal.
elements_required: A federal prosecutor's office sought highly sensitive personal identifying and financial information (names, addresses, banking information) to unmask anonymous social media critics, not merely content moderation or platform-level enforcement

No offense has been disclosed to the users, the Reddit subpoena names no specific post, and the posts the users' attorneys believe drew the government's attention repeated an ICE officer's personal details that were already circulating on social media, alongside commentary containing no explicit threat

The X post, per its author's attorney, was a sarcastic comment attached to an address the user had seen elsewhere on social media, not a genuine threat -- a characterization DOJ has not publicly disputed or confirmed, since it declined to comment
The targeted posts criticized ICE and its officers, supporting a viewpoint-based pattern rather than a neutral criminal investigation unconnected to the posts' political content

status: No ruling on the D.C. Circuit appeal has been identified, and no resolution of the X user's separate challenge, led by attorney Joshua Koltun, has been identified; no criminal charges against either targeted user have been identified, as of the most recent reporting reviewed.
rebuttal_anticipated: DOJ could argue that any post referencing a specific law enforcement officer alongside personal information (such as the officer's address) warrants investigation regardless of the poster's stated intent, and that identifying a poster through lawful subpoena process is not itself an infringement on speech absent a prosecution that never occurs.
comeback: The users have not been told what crime is under investigation, and DOJ has declined to say. The officer details both users are reported to have posted were already circulating widely on social media, and neither post, as described by the users' attorneys, contained a threat. The government first sought the same identities through DHS administrative summonses that need no judge's approval, withdrew each one once it was challenged in court, and then re-sought them through grand jury subpoenas -- in the Reddit case four days later -- a sequence the Reddit user's attorney calls "further proof that this is a bad faith attempt to unmask the user." Seeking to unmask the users without charging either one is itself the chilling effect the challengers describe.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] This entry is the DOJ step in a sequence that began at DHS: DHS used administrative subpoenas and summonses, which need no judge's sign-off, to try to identify critics of ICE (see the DHS administrative-subpoena entry and the broader DHS critic-subpoena entry) and repeatedly dropped them when challenged in court. Here, after DHS withdrew its summonses to Reddit and X, Pirro's office sought the same users' identities through grand jury subpoenas, a tool far harder to challenge, and the Reddit subpoena has so far survived a motion to quash. No charge has been reported against either user, so the effect so far is the exposure of anonymous critics rather than a prosecution.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the subpoenas' existence and scope: Bloomberg reviewed copies of the grand jury subpoenas, The Intercept separately obtained the Reddit subpoena, and CLDC's own statements document the Reddit challenge; Engadget, IBTimes UK and other outlets relayed Bloomberg's reporting rather than confirming it independently. MODERATE confidence on what the targeted posts said and why they were targeted: the Reddit subpoena named no post, no offense has been disclosed, and DOJ declined to comment, so accounts of the posts come from the users' own attorneys and from The Intercept's review of the Reddit user's posts. Judge Boasberg's denial of the motion to quash addressed the subpoena's validity, not whether the posts were threats, so it does not resolve this entry's First Amendment/viewpoint-targeting claim. The ruling, the D.C. Circuit appeal and the stay of disclosure are known from CLDC's own statements; the proceedings are sealed and no D.C. Circuit docket has been located. offense_category: Use of Federal Subpoena Power to Pressure Regulated Financial Institutions Over Lawful Account-Closure Decisions -- a novel application of FIRREA (a bank-fraud statute) to political "debanking" claims; no criminal charge has been identified against any bank
incident_summary: The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia, led by Jeanine Pirro, issued subpoenas to several of the nation's largest banks -- including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo -- as part of an investigation into alleged politically or religiously motivated "debanking" of customers. **Investigators are seeking the names of individuals and businesses who had accounts closed, plus internal records explaining the rationale for those closures. The Justice Department is examining whether the banks' conduct violated the Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery and Enforcement Act of 1989 (FIRREA), a statute historically used to prosecute bank fraud rather than customer-selection decisions.** The probe extends a broader Trump administration campaign against alleged debanking of conservatives and Trump allies; in August 2025 Trump signed an executive order directing regulators to examine "politicized or unlawful debanking."
elements_required: A U.S. Attorney's office issued subpoenas to major, systemically important banks demanding customer names and internal rationale for account closures -- not merely a regulatory inquiry, but a federal law-enforcement subpoena carrying the coercive weight of a criminal investigation

The legal theory invoked (FIRREA) is, per an outside consumer-finance expert, a "novel" application of a bank-fraud statute to ordinary account-closure business decisions, raising the question of whether the statute's elements can actually be met

The investigation follows a presidential executive order specifically directing scrutiny of banks' treatment of politically disfavored customers, establishing a direct line from a political grievance to a prosecutorial subpoena campaign

The scope targets banks' routine risk-management and compliance decisions (which customers to serve) rather than any specific allegation of fraud against a named victim, the conduct FIRREA was designed to reach

evidence.maps_to_element: Documents the contested legal theory and the coercive effect independent of a final legal ruling

Related context not previously incorporated: Trump personally sued JPMorgan Chase and CEO Jamie Dimon for $5 billion over alleged debanking on January 22, 2026 -- five months before this entry was written -- alleging the bank closed his accounts for political reasons after January 6, 2021; JPMorgan denies closing accounts for political or religious reasons. That personal suit is a separate civil matter from Pirro's DOJ subpoena investigation, but documents Trump's own direct financial stake in the debanking narrative underlying the subpoena campaign.
evidence.maps_to_element: The investigation follows a presidential executive order specifically directing scrutiny of banks' treatment of politically disfavored customers, establishing a direct line from a political grievance to a prosecutorial subpoena campaign

status: Ongoing -- subpoenas issued and banks responding as of this entry's sourcing (June 2026); no charges filed against any bank in reporting reviewed
rebuttal_anticipated: DOJ could argue banks have market power over access to the financial system and that politically or religiously motivated account closures, if proven, are a legitimate target for federal investigation regardless of which statute is used to pursue it, and that a subpoena is an investigative step, not a prosecution.

incident_summary:
Nikki Floris led the FBI's Foreign Influence Task Force, a unit created to address foreign influence campaigns, from mid-2019 to mid-2022, and Bradley Benavides was a section chief on the task force from mid-2019 through the 2020 election; the FBI disbanded the task force in February 2025. In August 2020 the two briefed Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley and Ron Johnson, who were investigating Hunter Biden's work in Ukraine; after news of the briefing leaked, the senators said the FBI had discredited their efforts and falsely linked them to Russian disinformation. In 2023 the House Judiciary Committee interviewed both, Floris on July 19 and Benavides on September 28. According to the criminal complaint, both told the committee the task force was not involved in the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations; Floris said she took part in no discussions about Hunter Biden while on the task force, and Benavides said he first learned the FBI had Hunter Biden's laptop from a Wikipedia article in 2023. Prosecutors say records, communications and witness accounts contradict that testimony: the complaint alleges Floris discussed the investigations for more than a year and Benavides regularly discussed the laptop with FBI officials before the 2020 election, and that the statements were material because they let the pair "escape" further questioning and hindered the committee's investigation.

**On Friday, October 23, 2026, Floris, 46, and Benavides, 56, surrendered after a criminal complaint charged each with one count of making a false statement in a matter within the jurisdiction of Congress.** U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro announced the case on X, saying they "allegedly lied to Congress about their roles in the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations, with one claiming they only learned about it from Wikipedia." The charges came less than two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, and prosecutors had not obtained a grand jury indictment; NBC News noted that D.C. grand jurors have been skeptical of cases brought in Trump's second term. At the initial appearance, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui noted both defendants' "sparkling backgrounds" in federal law enforcement and said charging conduct this "quite old" by complaint is unusual, and he set a preliminary hearing for the following Tuesday over prosecutors' request for more time. Floris's lawyers said DOJ "has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts" and that "It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election"; Benavides's lawyer Ronald Safer called it "a transparently political complaint." Trump told reporters that evening, "I heard they were bad people," calling them "Dirty cops, like Comey."

Overnight before the October 27 preliminary hearing, prosecutors posted to the docket an amended complaint adding an obstruction-of-Congress charge, without a judge's sign-off and without the swearing agent's signature. Faruqui called the filing "inappropriate" and said it "harms the defendant," and he struck it at the defense's request, continuing the hearing on the original complaint. Under cross-examination, FBI agent Bryan Witt, who was assigned to investigate the pair, testified that Patel directed the investigation be opened after a July primetime address by Trump (in which, the AP reported, Trump amplified debunked theories about the 2020 election), that Patel assigned the investigation of a list of former agents, including Floris and Benavides, to the FBI's Kansas City field office, and that he was directed to investigate Floris and other officials believed to have been involved in recalling a disputed FBI intelligence report on alleged Chinese election influence. Witt said Patel and FBI leadership "wanted us to investigate aggressively" and that "I had concerns that this would be political." Faruqui told prosecutors the government's conduct was "throwing enormous amounts of gasoline onto this fire" and "is making me more and more concerned that there's something to that," referring to the defense's claim the charges are politically motivated. The hearing continued on October 28, with the defense seeking dismissal; no probable-cause ruling had been reported.

Goodwin) -- Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell was never charged, and the underlying grand jury subpoenas were quashed by a federal court for lack of evidence; Pirro herself has not been personally charged with anything
incident_summary:
The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia, under Jeanine Pirro, opened a criminal investigation into Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell over a roughly $2.5 billion headquarters renovation project, tied to Powell's June 2025 testimony about the project before the Senate Banking Committee. Reported opening dates differ: CNBC dated it to November 2025 in May 2026 and to December 2025 in September 2026, while Forbes and a later CNBC report said it opened in January 2026. The Wall Street Journal reported that on Thursday, January 8, 2026, Trump confronted a group of dozens of U.S. attorneys gathered at the White House for what was meant to be a ceremonial photo event, calling them "weak" and complaining -- after Attorney General Pam Bondi introduced the group -- that they were moving too slowly to prosecute his chosen targets, including specifically that no case had yet been brought against Sen. Adam Schiff, part of the broader Patel-driven prosecution-campaign pattern tracked as its own entry in this database. The very next day, Friday, January 9, 2026, Pirro's office served the grand jury subpoenas on the Fed described below. Powell publicly called the investigation a pretext, saying it was not really about his testimony or the renovation but a consequence of the Fed setting interest rates independent of the president's preferences, amid Trump's escalating public pressure campaign for Powell to cut rates and eventually leave the Fed.

Sen. Thom Tillis, a swing vote on the Senate Banking Committee (split 13-11 Republican-Democrat), announced on January 12, 2026 that he would block all of Trump's Federal Reserve nominees -- including Kevin Warsh, Trump's reported pick to succeed Powell as chair -- until DOJ's criminal probe concluded, a position he reiterated in late January and again in February 2026 even as other Republicans sought an off-ramp. Trump shrugged off the threat: on February 2, 2026, he told reporters in the Oval Office that Pirro should "take it to the end and see." Separately, on January 13, 2026, central bank governors from the European Central Bank (Christine Lagarde), the Bank of England (Andrew Bailey), and the central banks of Canada, Brazil, Switzerland, Sweden, Denmark, South Korea, and Australia issued an unprecedented joint statement declaring they "stand in full solidarity" with Powell and the Federal Reserve, calling central bank independence "a cornerstone of price, financial and economic stability" that must be preserved "with full respect for the rule of law and democratic accountability."

In an opinion signed March 11 and unsealed Friday, March 13, 2026, **Chief Judge James Boasberg of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia quashed the subpoenas, finding they were issued for an improper purpose: "A mountain of evidence suggests that the Government served these subpoenas on the Board to pressure its Chair into voting for lower interest rates or resigning," while the government had produced "essentially zero evidence to suspect Chair Powell of a crime."** On March 18, 2026, Powell publicly stated he had "no intention of leaving the board until the investigation is well and truly over with transparency and finality" -- a pledge he repeated in April -- signaling he would remain past his term as chair, set to expire May 15, 2026, specifically to see the investigation through, a stance PBS NewsHour reported could itself "backfire" on Trump by keeping Powell in a position of influence longer.

The government had promptly asked Boasberg to reconsider; on April 3, 2026, he denied the motion, writing that the government's "cursory brief neither offers new evidence nor points to any material error" and that it "has presented no evidence whatsoever of fraud." In April 2026, Trump said he would "have to fire" Powell if he did not leave his post as the investigation continued. Around the same time, with the investigation "rapidly losing steam," as NBC News put it, three officials from Pirro's office made an unannounced visit to the Fed's headquarters construction site seeking a "tour" to "check on progress" of the renovation; they were turned away. On April 24, 2026, Pirro announced on X that she was closing the criminal probe, with the Fed's own inspector general taking over review of the renovation cost overruns, while writing that she "will not hesitate to restart a criminal investigation should the facts warrant doing so." On April 29, Powell announced he would remain on the Fed's Board of Governors -- a seat with its own separate term -- after his term as chair ended May 15, citing legal actions by the administration he called "unprecedented in our 113-year history," and in doing so blocked Trump from filling that board seat with a new appointee.

On May 3, 2026, appearing on CNN's "State of the Union," Pirro said her office would "continue to litigate the issue," promised to appeal Boasberg's ruling, and said whether the probe ended depended on what the inspector general found: "If there's something there, great. If there isn't, I'll go home." Contrary to her appeal pledge, her office did not appeal Boasberg's ruling: on Monday, May 4, 2026, the deadline to file a notice of appeal, the U.S. Attorney's office said it would not pursue an appeal, reasoning that one was likely to be dismissed as moot given the investigation's own closure. Instead, prosecutors asked Boasberg to vacate his prior rulings in the case.

Powell's chair term ended May 15, 2026, and he stayed on the board. On June 11, 2026, Boasberg denied the motion to vacate, writing that "Instead of appealing, the Government closed its investigation" and now proposed "a creative way to clear its loss from the books" -- leaving in place his March 2026 finding that the government had produced "essentially zero evidence" to suspect Powell of a crime.

A separate, non-DOJ development: Judicial Watch, a conservative government-transparency watchdog group unaffiliated with Pirro's office, filed a Freedom of Information Act suit (No. 1:26-cv-01113, D.D.C.) on April 2, 2026 -- per Judicial Watch's own case page, cited as a primary source -- and in an August 17, 2026 filing asked the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia to compel the Federal Reserve to release the two grand jury subpoenas at issue in the underlying investigation, arguing the Fed is improperly withholding them from public view; the Fed has resisted disclosure, asserting the subpoenas are protected from release. This is a public-records/transparency dispute distinct from Pirro's own prosecutorial decision-making.

On September 30, 2026, the Federal Reserve's inspector general, Michael Horowitz, released its 120-page evaluation of the renovation, which Powell himself had requested in July 2025. The report found that the Fed's board had not effectively managed the project: its approved budget grew from $1.317 billion in February 2020 to $2.381 billion in December 2024, and as of July 2026, more than four years after construction began the board still had not set a guaranteed maximum price with its construction manager. **But the inspector general wrote: "At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General," and it identified no administrative misconduct.** Pirro's office said that day that it was reviewing the report. Trump, undeterred, wrote on Truth Social that Powell "should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY!" from the Fed's board and that if he did not, he should be sued by the federal government "for either corruption or incompetence," adding that he had asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to "study" the report. On Friday, October 2, 2026, Blanche told Bloomberg News, "We're not reopening a criminal investigation into him," while not ruling out Justice Department action if an independent audit the Fed has committed to uncovers evidence of criminal wrongdoing.

official: Jeanine Pirro, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia
offense_category: Inflating a Minor Protest Incident Into a Felony Prosecution That Failed at Every Stage -- a grand jury's refusal to indict and a subsequent jury acquittal are themselves strong evidence the felony theory lacked merit
incident_summary: In August 2025, Sean Dunn, a former DOJ paralegal, threw a Subway sandwich at a Customs and Border Patrol officer participating in Trump's federal law-enforcement surge in Washington, D.C. -- an incident he characterized as a protest. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office sought a felony assault charge carrying up to eight years in prison. **A D.C. grand jury refused to indict Dunn on the felony charge, a step described in reporting as a notable rebuke joining a string of failed prosecutions against protesters arrested by the administration's militarized federal deployment. Rather than dropping the matter, Pirro's office then filed a misdemeanor assault charge against Dunn, which proceeded to trial. On November 6, 2025, a federal jury in Washington, D.C. found Dunn not guilty after only several hours of deliberation.** This case was one of at least six D.C. grand jury refusals to indict in crackdown-related cases by early September 2025 -- including a woman a grand jury declined to indict over an alleged online threat against Trump -- tracked as part of a broader pattern in this database.
elements_required: A minor incident (a thrown sandwich, no injury alleged) was charged at the felony level, carrying a multi-year prison exposure disproportionate to the conduct
A D.C. grand jury declined to return the felony indictment -- grand juries rarely refuse prosecutors, making this itself significant evidence the felony theory was not supported by probable cause
Rather than accepting that outcome, the U.S. Attorney's office pursued a misdemeanor charge instead of declining to prosecute, which also failed at trial by jury acquittal

rebuttal_anticipated: Pirro's office would characterize the felony charge as a legitimate application of the law to an assault on a federal officer regardless of the object thrown, argue that grand jury and jury outcomes reflect normal prosecutorial risk rather than misconduct, and note that some charge is not inherently improper simply because it is ultimately unsuccessful.
comeback: A grand jury's outright refusal to indict is a rare and significant check -- grand juries indict in the overwhelming majority of cases prosecutors bring -- and pursuing a second, lesser charge after that refusal, which also failed at trial, indicates the office was determined to obtain some conviction from a minor incident rather than exercising ordinary prosecutorial discretion to decline charges altogether; reporting situates this within a broader pattern of the same office pursuing and losing multiple protester-related cases from the same federal deployment.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Illustrates a pattern of using disproportionate criminal charges against protesters and critics of a federal law-enforcement deployment, with repeated failures at the grand jury and trial stages suggesting charging decisions driven by political messaging rather than the strength of the underlying case. This same grand-jury-refusal pattern is also cited, as one of several named examples, in the FBI street-policing entry in this database's government-services tracker, which documents FBI agents being diverted from fraud/corruption/counterintelligence casework to support the D.C. deployment itself -- a possible institutional-capacity contributor to the weak-case pattern this entry documents at the individual-prosecution level.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the felony charge, the grand jury's refusal to indict, the subsequent misdemeanor charge, and the jury's not-guilty verdict are all independently corroborated across NBC News, NPR, PBS NewsHour, CBS News, and CNBC. The characterization of the prosecution as politically motivated or a 'circus' is an editorial framing from reporting and commentary, not an adjudicated finding, and is flagged as contested accordingly.

official: Jeanine Pirro, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia
offense_category: Use of a rarely-invoked 'special' grand jury -- a type empowered to publicly name individuals and allege wrongdoing even when there is not enough evidence to bring criminal charges -- convened in the immediate aftermath of a public presidential rebuke over a separate dismissed prosecution; convening a special grand jury is a lawful prosecutorial tool, not itself unlawful, but its low evidentiary bar for public accusation and its timing relative to political pressure on Pirro's own position are the accountability-relevant concern

incident_summary:
In late July and early August 2026, Pirro's office moved to drop vandalism charges against several defendants -- including an Olympic canoeist -- accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, after determining the damage stemmed from faulty contractor construction rushed ahead of America 250 celebration events, not vandalism. President Trump publicly and repeatedly criticized Pirro over the dismissals, saying she 'choked' and 'folded like an umbrella, and people get away with things,' and did not rule out firing her; Pirro subsequently met with Trump at the White House, after which her position was reported safe for the time being. Shortly after this public clash, **reporting revealed Pirro's office had convened a rarely used 'special' grand jury in Washington, D.C. -- a type that, unlike a standard grand jury, can issue a public report naming individuals and alleging misconduct even when prosecutors lack sufficient evidence to bring charges -- overseen by prosecutor Steven Vandervelden**, a Pirro ally previously assigned to the separate investigations of Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell (tracked in this database's pirro-powell-vindictive-investigation entry) and D.C. police crime statistics. Later reporting (Washington Post, August 27, 2026) clarified the special grand jury's actual subject as an investigation into D.C. schools and the city's oversight of youth -- a distinct matter from both the Reflecting Pool dismissals and Vandervelden's earlier Powell assignment, which is otherwise unrelated to this entry beyond sharing the same overseeing prosecutor.

Update 2026-10-25: A judge later threw out the case against Hearn, which Pirro's office had moved to dismiss at the end of July, and barred the government from charging him again. In October 2026 Hearn's lawyers, among them former Justice Department inspector general Michael Bromwich, asked the Justice and Interior inspectors general to investigate the prosecution. They allege that prosecutors ignored evidence already in their possession and appear to have caused a grand jury witness to change his testimony on the dollar amount of damage needed for a felony charge; these are the defense's allegations, not findings. According to the lawyers' October 21 letter, Justice Department Inspector General Don R. Berthiaume declined to investigate, saying the matter belongs to the department's Office of Professional Responsibility. The lawyers, who asked him to reconsider, say that office lacks criminal jurisdiction, reports to the attorney general and deputy attorney general, and has had its staff cut in half. The letter says the Interior inspector general is investigating the allegations about Interior personnel.
elements_required: Pirro's office dropped vandalism charges tied to the Reflecting Pool after concluding a contractor's faulty, rushed construction -- not vandalism -- caused the damage, a decision Trump publicly and repeatedly criticized, including raising the possibility of firing her.

Within days to weeks of that public pressure, Pirro's office sought and obtained a rarely used special grand jury -- a tool distinguished specifically by its ability to publicly name individuals and allege wrongdoing without meeting the evidentiary threshold required to charge them, unlike a standard grand jury.

The special grand jury is overseen by Steven Vandervelden, the same prosecutor separately assigned to the Powell investigation and D.C. police crime-statistics review, indicating a pattern of using this prosecutor for politically salient inquiries.

No public report has been issued and no charges have been announced as of this entry's sourcing; the grand jury's confirmed subject (D.C. schools/youth oversight) has not been shown in any source reviewed to be causally connected to the Reflecting Pool clash, only temporally proximate to it.

incident_summary.base: In late July and early August 2026, Pirro's office moved to drop vandalism charges against several defendants -- including an Olympic canoeist -- accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, after determining the damage stemmed from faulty contractor construction rushed ahead of America 250 celebration events, not vandalism. President Trump publicly and repeatedly criticized Pirro over the dismissals, saying she 'choked' and 'folded like an umbrella, and people get away with things,' and did not rule out firing her; Pirro subsequently met with Trump at the White House, after which her position was reported safe for the time being. Shortly after this public clash, **reporting revealed Pirro's office had convened a rarely used 'special' grand jury in Washington, D.C. -- a type that, unlike a standard grand jury, can issue a public report naming individuals and alleging misconduct even when prosecutors lack sufficient evidence to bring charges -- overseen by prosecutor Steven Vandervelden**, a Pirro ally previously assigned to the separate investigations of Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell (tracked in this database's pirro-powell-vindictive-investigation entry) and D.C. police crime statistics. Later reporting (Washington Post, August 27, 2026) clarified the special grand jury's actual subject as an investigation into D.C. schools and the city's oversight of youth -- a distinct matter from both the Reflecting Pool dismissals and Vandervelden's earlier Powell assignment, which is otherwise unrelated to this entry beyond sharing the same overseeing prosecutor.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-25: A judge later threw out the case against Hearn, which Pirro's office had moved to dismiss at the end of July, and barred the government from charging him again. In October 2026 Hearn's lawyers, among them former Justice Department inspector general Michael Bromwich, asked the Justice and Interior inspectors general to investigate the prosecution. They allege that prosecutors ignored evidence already in their possession and appear to have caused a grand jury witness to change his testimony on the dollar amount of damage needed for a felony charge; these are the defense's allegations, not findings. According to the lawyers' October 21 letter, Justice Department Inspector General Don R. Berthiaume declined to investigate, saying the matter belongs to the department's Office of Professional Responsibility. The lawyers, who asked him to reconsider, say that office lacks criminal jurisdiction, reports to the attorney general and deputy attorney general, and has had its staff cut in half. The letter says the Interior inspector general is investigating the allegations about Interior personnel.

confidence_note.base: HIGH confidence for the sequence of events -- the Reflecting Pool dismissal, Trump's public criticism, and the special grand jury's existence and unusual public-report capability are independently corroborated by NBC News, NPR, and two separate Washington Post reports. MODERATE on whether the special grand jury's timing was actually caused by the Trump clash rather than coincidental prior planning -- no source reviewed shows internal DOJ deliberation establishing causation, only temporal proximity; the causal link is a reasonable inference from timing, not a proven fact.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-25: HIGH that the DOJ inspector general declined to investigate the Hearn prosecution and referred the matter to the Office of Professional Responsibility, but this rests on Hearn's lawyers' account of the IG's response (NBC News, AP); the inspector general's office had not commented. The misconduct claims against prosecutors are the defense's allegations, untested by any investigation or court. No report or charges from the special grand jury were found as of this date.

official: Jeanine Pirro, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia
offense_category: Substituting a Sanitized Filing That Omitted the Defendant's Jan. 6 Involvement After Two Career Prosecutors Were Suspended Within Hours, Reportedly by DOJ's Executive Office for United States Attorneys, for Accurately Describing January 6 as a 'Mob of Rioters' in a Court Filing
incident_summary: On October 28, 2025, two career DOJ prosecutors, Carlos Valdivia and Samuel White, filed a sentencing memorandum in the case of Taylor Franklin Taranto. Taranto was a former January 6 defendant who received clemency from President Trump. He was later separately convicted of weapons and hoax charges after being arrested near the Obamas' home in 2023 with firearms and ammunition in his van. The memo described the events of January 6, 2021 factually: 'thousands of people comprising a mob of rioters attacked the U.S. Capitol while a joint session of Congress met to certify the results of the 2020 presidential election.' **Within hours of the filing, both Valdivia and White were placed on administrative leave and locked out of their government devices.** The next day, the filing was marked 'entered in error' and replaced with a shorter 12-page memo, this time signed by Assistant U.S. Attorney Travis Wolf on behalf of Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia. **The substitute version omitted any reference to Taranto's involvement in the January 6 riot itself**, describing only his separate 2023 crimes near the Obama residence. At Taranto's sentencing hearing on Thursday, October 30, 2025, he received time served and 36 months of supervised release. He filed a notice of appeal to the D.C. Circuit on November 6, 2025 (No. 25-3110). From December 2025 the Probation Office filed petitions alleging he had violated his supervised release. On January 8, 2026, Judge Carl Nichols issued an order modifying his release conditions, and Taranto appealed that order too (No. 26-3008). A June 8, 2026 revocation hearing ended with the matter taken under advisement; the court later set a final revocation hearing, which was rescheduled to October 9, 2026, and the government moved on October 7 to continue it. No ruling on either appeal or on revocation appears on the dockets; the district docket's latest entry is the government's October 7, 2026 motion to continue. No public reversal of Valdivia's and White's suspension, and no independent explanation for the specific factual omission in the substitute filing, was identified in sourcing reviewed.
elements_required: Two named career prosecutors were placed on administrative leave, reportedly by DOJ's Executive Office for United States Attorneys, and locked out of their government devices within hours of filing a factually accurate court document describing January 6 as a riot carried out by a 'mob of rioters'
DOJ leadership, under U.S. Attorney Pirro, replaced that filing with a substantively altered version omitting the defendant's own January 6 conduct

The defendant whose sentencing memo was altered was a Trump-pardoned January 6 participant with a documented history of subsequent, separate violent-adjacent conduct (arrested near a former president's residence with firearms)
The altered filing's timing and content directly preceded and plausibly influenced a lenient sentencing outcome (time served) in a case involving weapons found near a former president's home
