official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services
offense_category: Ethics / Gift and Outside-Income Rules -- accepting more than $250,000 in travel and lodging from a major 2024 campaign backer, tested against the federal gift rules' personal-friendship exception (5 C.F.R. 2635.204(b)), plus $4 million in book advances paid during his tenure -- disclosed and approved by HHS ethics officials, NOT charged or found to violate any rule, contested, included for reference only; his wife's $210,000 in MAHA Action consulting fees is the subject of a Sept. 2026 Campaign Legal Center complaint to the HHS inspector general
status: Ongoing: Campaign Legal Center asked the HHS inspector general on Sept. 25, 2026 to investigate whether Kennedy broke conflict-of-interest law over his wife's $210,000 MAHA Action fees; no finding yet, and none on the de Becker gifts or Skyhorse advances. HHS says he complies with ethics rules.
incident_summary:
Gavin de Becker, a celebrity security adviser, served as Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s security adviser during his 2024 presidential campaign and was a major donor to a super PAC backing that campaign, The Daily Beast reported; the Guardian, citing Politico, reported that he gave that super PAC at least $10 million, $9.65 million of which was returned. In 2025, the year Kennedy became Secretary of Health and Human Services, **de Becker gave him free flights to and from Fiji and Greece and the use of a vacation home in Washington, D.C., gifts that Kennedy's own annual financial disclosure valued at more than a quarter of a million dollars** -- nearly $97,000 for roundtrip flights to Fiji, where de Becker owns a compound, and almost $45,000 for a roundtrip to Greece, according to The Wall Street Journal's reporting on the 2025 gifts as relayed by Mediaite and MS NOW; the filing values use of the D.C. home at $126,500. Counting smaller gifts on the same schedule, The New York Times put the total at more than $270,000 in gifts over the past year. De Becker also wrote a book, Forbidden Facts, published by Skyhorse Publishing, alleging government suppression of information about brain damage from childhood vaccines.

The same disclosure showed that Kennedy received two book advances of $2 million apiece from Skyhorse Publishing in the past year, while serving as secretary, against a secretary's salary of around $250,000. Skyhorse has published his earlier books and paid him $451,000 in consulting fees the year before he joined HHS; one of the new books will be called Unsettled Science, and the filing states that two of the three books in the Skyhorse agreement were completed before he entered government service. Skyhorse is owned by Tony Lyons, a longtime friend and business associate of Kennedy who also heads several groups built around Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda, and The New York Times reported that the filing dates the advance agreement to August 2024, the month Kennedy dropped his presidential bid and endorsed Donald Trump. The same filing shows that Kennedy's wife, Cheryl Hines, received $210,000 in consulting fees in 2025, through her production company, from MAHA Action, a nonprofit advocacy group also led by Lyons that backs health legislation including a federal bill to end vaccine makers' liability protection. In his ethics agreement Kennedy had pledged not to engage in any writing, editing or promotional activities associated with his Skyhorse books while in office, yet in July 2026 he posted on X about his 2021 Skyhorse book, The Real Anthony Fauci, which NPR described as defying that agreement.

The filing itself was late: due May 15, 2026, it was filed August 13 after an extension, revised four times in September, and signed by an HHS ethics official on September 17. NPR reported that HHS ethics officials had approved it but the separate Office of Government Ethics had not yet signed off. The Wall Street Journal obtained the amended filing through a records request and reported the gifts in mid-September, NPR reported on the filing on September 22 and 24, and The New York Times reported the advances and Hines's MAHA Action fees on September 23. On September 25 the Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint asking the HHS inspector general to investigate whether Kennedy violated the criminal conflict-of-interest law, 18 U.S.C. 208, and his ethics agreement by taking part in policy matters that could benefit his wife's consulting contract with MAHA Action.

On September 17, 2026, Kennedy gave the keynote address at a Washington, D.C. conference held by Children's Health Defense, an anti-vaccine group he co-founded that has filed dozens of lawsuits against federal agencies, state governments and companies over vaccine requirements and other policies. According to a federal ethics filing, the group paid him $326,056 in salary and bonuses in the year before he left his role as its board chairman and chief legal counsel to lead HHS. "You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House," Kennedy told the crowd. NPR called the appearance one of the ways Kennedy is pushing norms, and Jason Goldman, immediate past president of the American College of Physicians, told NPR that a secretary giving a keynote to an anti-vaccine group he helped found and continuing to promote his anti-vaccine agenda "is endangering the health, safety and lives of American citizens and the world at large."

HHS said Kennedy "complies with all applicable federal ethics laws, regulations, and financial disclosure requirements" and works with career HHS ethics officials to disclose his gifts and outside activities. De Becker told NPR that Kennedy is "my closest friend in the world for many years," that their families vacation together every year, that the gifts began "years before he was at HHS," and that "I have nothing whatsoever to do with HHS in any regard." Virginia Canter of Democracy Defenders Fund told NPR the gifts and advances were so large that they raise the question of a prohibited "supplementation of salary," and asked whether de Becker gives such gifts to all his friends or only to Kennedy; Washington University law professor Kathleen Clark called it "very weird" that Kennedy accepted $4 million in advances for two books he had promised not to write or edit while secretary. Kedric Payne of the Campaign Legal Center told The New York Times that de Becker's gifts appear to far exceed the exceptions for gifts from friends, and Richard Painter, a White House ethics counsel under President George W. Bush, said the MAHA Action fees to Hines "reeks of conflict of interest."

official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services
offense_category: Hatch Act Violation -- using the authority of a federal office to influence the outcome of an election by pressuring third-party candidates to withdraw from congressional races
incident_summary: Sen. Ron Wyden filed a complaint with the U.S. Office of Special Counsel (OSC) alleging that HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. violated the Hatch Act by placing phone calls urging two Libertarian congressional candidates in Iowa to withdraw from their races: a June 8, 2026 call to Marco Battaglia, running in Iowa's 3rd congressional district, and a June 11, 2026 call to Rick Stewart, running in Iowa's 2nd congressional district. **Donald Sherman, president of the nonpartisan watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), reviewed a recording of at least one call and said Kennedy invoked his official position and responsibilities as HHS Secretary multiple times during the conversation, calling it a 'clear violation' of the Hatch Act warranting OSC investigation.** The complaint seeks an OSC investigation into whether Kennedy improperly used his cabinet position to influence the composition of two competitive U.S. House races. Trump has separately taken steps during his second term to assert greater control over OSC, including firing the office's head earlier in the term, raising questions about whether the currently constituted office will investigate the complaint independently.
elements_required: A federal employee covered by the Hatch Act (a cabinet secretary) made direct contact with declared candidates in ongoing federal elections
The official invoked or referenced their federal office/authority during those contacts, rather than acting purely in a private political capacity
The purpose or effect of the contact was to influence the outcome of the election (here, by seeking candidate withdrawal)
The Office of Special Counsel is institutionally positioned to investigate and act on the complaint independently of the administration

comeback: The specific allegation is not that Kennedy expressed a personal political opinion, but that he invoked his HHS position and responsibilities during the calls themselves, which is the precise conduct the Hatch Act's use-of-official-authority provisions are designed to prevent -- and a nonpartisan ethics watchdog's independent review of the recording, not merely the complaining senator's characterization, supports that specific reading.

offense_category: Announcing That a Presidential Commission Would Investigate the Childhood Vaccine Schedule Despite Prior Assurances Not to Undermine Vaccine Confidence -- an institutional-credibility and consistency claim, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: On February 13, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14212 creating the President's Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) Commission, with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as its chair. On February 18, 2025, Kennedy told HHS staff in a closed-door meeting that the new commission would scrutinize the childhood vaccine schedule, along with electromagnetic radiation, glyphosate and other pesticides, ultra-processed foods, SSRIs and other psychiatric drugs, PFAS and microplastics, as possible causes of the country's chronic disease epidemic; 'nothing is going to be off limits,' he said, according to a video viewed by The Hill. The remarks drew scrutiny because they came despite assurances Kennedy had given during his confirmation process that he would not seek to undermine public confidence in existing, well-established vaccines. Kennedy's statement is the earliest-dated action in what became a documented, escalating chain of vaccine-policy actions this tracker follows separately in later entries -- including a January 2026 immunization-schedule overhaul and the May 2026 Executive Order 14407 realigning the childhood vaccine schedule based on a December 2025 HHS assessment. The commission's own first deliverable undercut its credibility on release. Its 'Make America Healthy Again' assessment report, published in late May 2025, **was found by NOTUS, which first reported the problems on May 29, 2025, to cite at least seven sources that do not appear to exist, plus other citations that misrepresented real studies' findings; ABC News, Rolling Stone and PolitiFact followed, and experts quoted by PolitiFact said the nonexistent titles were a hallmark of AI-generated citations. Dr. Katherine Keyes, cited as the first author of a paper on teen depression and anxiety during the pandemic, told NOTUS and ABC News she never wrote it; the American Academy of Pediatrics and JAMA Pediatrics both told ABC News they could not locate certain cited papers in their own publications.** White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt attributed the errors to 'some formatting issues' while stating the administration had 'complete confidence' in Kennedy's team. On June 2, 2025, Rep. Stephen Lynch, the House Oversight Committee's acting ranking Democrat, sent Kennedy a letter demanding information on how the report was drafted, reviewed, published and later amended, including whether AI was used. At a June 24, 2025 House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing, Kennedy called the fabricated citations 'wrong' and a 'mistake,' said he had not personally fact-checked the report, and maintained that its 'foundational assertions' were accurate.
elements_required: Kennedy, as HHS Secretary and chair of the newly created presidential MAHA Commission, publicly stated that the commission would investigate the childhood vaccine schedule, among other subjects

Kennedy had given assurances during his confirmation process that he would not seek to undermine vaccine confidence, creating a specific, citable prior commitment against which this action can be measured
This action is the documented starting point of a subsequent, escalating chain of vaccine-schedule-related policy actions tracked separately elsewhere in this database

evidence.description: The Hill reported that Kennedy told HHS staff in a closed-door meeting on Tuesday (Feb. 18, 2025) that the new presidential MAHA commission, which Trump launched by executive order the previous week with Kennedy at its helm, would scrutinize the childhood vaccine schedule, pesticides, psychiatric drugs and other possible factors, saying 'nothing is going to be off limits'; it noted that Cassidy voted to confirm Kennedy after saying he had received commitments from Kennedy about not undermining vaccine safety efforts

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard later acknowledged some of the citation inconsistencies, with Hilliard calling them 'minor citation and formatting errors' that had been corrected.

I will do that,' and a 'yes' commitment not to impound or divert vaccination-program funding -- against specific subsequent actions: firing all the incumbent ACIP members, the CDC's pullback of $11 billion in COVID-era grants that local health departments used partly for vaccination programs, cancellation of a half-billion dollars of mRNA vaccine research, and new CDC website language questioning the vaccines-autism consensus, although the page technically kept the 'vaccines do not cause autism' statement he had pledged not to remove

status: Kennedy's February 2025 statement is a completed, dated event and the starting point of a longer chain of vaccine-policy actions; see the separately tracked rfk-jr-vaccine-autism-reexamination-2026 and trump-childhood-vaccine-eo-2026 entries for downstream outcomes through 2026.
rebuttal_anticipated: Kennedy and HHS have publicly defended the administration's health policy changes as necessary reforms, and could argue the commission itself was framed broadly rather than as a vaccine-specific inquiry. Kennedy's on-record position is that he has kept his confirmation commitments: he testified at a June 2025 House budget hearing that he is 'complying with all the agreements' he made with Cassidy, and HHS spokesperson Andrew Nixon told PolitiFact in February 2026 that Kennedy 'continues to follow through on his commitments' to Cassidy. HHS did not respond to CBS's request for comment on Cassidy's June 2026 accusation.
comeback: This entry does not allege the commission itself was unlawful -- the accountability question is the tension between Kennedy's specific, on-record confirmation-process assurances and his statement, within a week of taking office, that the presidential commission he chairs would scrutinize the childhood vaccine schedule. That tension is no longer inferred from a single contemporaneous report: PolitiFact's February 2026 fact-check documented the specific quoted promises against the specific actions that followed, and Sen. Cassidy -- one of the Republican senators who personally extracted those commitments and voted to confirm Kennedy on the strength of them -- said on national television in June 2026 that they 'have been violated' and that Kennedy built public health policy 'upon a foundation of lies.' Kennedy disputes this and maintains he has kept his word.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Illustrates a policy-level consistency/credibility question about Kennedy's confirmation-process assurances on vaccines, rather than a specific legal violation. The commission's first report, whose fabricated citations the White House attributed to formatting issues, raises a separate question about the reliability of the commission's own work product. The vaccine-schedule inquiry Kennedy flagged in February 2025 is an early step toward the schedule directives documented in the trump-childhood-vaccine-eo entry.

Kennedy's February 2025 statement of the commission's scope and its tension with Kennedy's confirmation-process assurances is no longer sourced to a single contemporaneous report alone: PolitiFact's dated, sourced fact-check documents the specific promises and the specific actions that broke them, and Sen. Cassidy -- a Republican who helped confirm Kennedy and personally extracted several of the commitments -- has since gone on the record agreeing they were broken. This entry's significance still rests substantially on hindsight as the documented starting point of a much larger, separately-tracked chain of subsequent vaccine-policy actions elsewhere in this database. official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services
offense_category: Misuse of Government Resources for Political/Campaign Travel -- Hatch Act and appropriations-purpose concerns raised by using a taxpayer-funded military aircraft to campaign for candidates in the midterms -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary: On August 17, 2026, **according to people cited by The Washington Post, an Air Force-operated Gulfstream jet flew HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from the Washington, D.C. area to Des Moines, Iowa, arriving hours ahead of his first scheduled event. The Defense Department charges roughly $9,000 per hour to operate that aircraft, compared with approximately $250 for a commercial ticket on the same route under the government's own discount travel program.** During the trip, Kennedy appeared alongside Republican candidates in contested 2026 midterm races -- Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, seeking reelection in Iowa's 1st congressional district, and Zach Lahn, the Republican gubernatorial candidate -- while also conducting official HHS business, announcing an initiative to help parents battling addiction and touring a community health center. The White House and HHS's own lawyers signed off on the arrangement in advance. Internally, Chris Klomp, Trump's nominee for HHS deputy secretary, questioned whether military-jet use was necessary on at least one other occasion; Kennedy agreed with the concern and opted not to use a jet for that trip, indicating the department itself recognized the practice as discretionary rather than operationally required.
elements_required: A federal official used a taxpayer-funded military aircraft, rather than a far cheaper commercial or government-discount alternative, for travel that included campaign appearances alongside declared candidates
The travel combined official government business with political/campaign activity in a way that makes the aircraft's cost attributable, at least in part, to campaign-adjacent purposes
Government lawyers (White House and HHS) signed off on the plan in advance, and the Post reports that protocols exist for deciding whether to use a government plane
The practice was not operationally necessary, as shown by HHS's own deputy-secretary nominee successfully persuading Kennedy to forgo a military jet on a separate occasion

evidence.description: The Washington Post's original reporting that Kennedy used military aircraft for domestic travel, including the Iowa trip, with the White House and HHS lawyers approving the arrangement
evidence.maps_to_element: A federal official used a taxpayer-funded military aircraft for travel that included campaign appearances

evidence.description: Syndicated copy of The Washington Post's report (via Yahoo News) confirming the August 17, 2026 flight, the ~$9,000/hour Gulfstream cost against a ~$250 commercial-ticket alternative, the specific candidates (Miller-Meeks, Lahn) Kennedy appeared with, and the official HHS business (addiction initiative, community health center tour) conducted the same trip
evidence.maps_to_element: The travel combined official government business with political/campaign activity

evidence.description: White House and HHS lawyers signed off on the plan to let Kennedy use military jets, per the same syndicated Washington Post report
evidence.maps_to_element: Government lawyers reviewed and approved the arrangement in advance

evidence.description: Chris Klomp, HHS deputy secretary nominee, questioned the necessity of military-jet use on at least one other occasion, and Kennedy agreed not to use a jet for that trip
evidence.maps_to_element: The practice was not operationally necessary

status: Reported September 10, 2026; no OSC complaint, IG referral, or other formal accountability action has been identified over the jet use. Separate from the Wyden Hatch Act complaint over Kennedy's June 2026 calls urging Libertarian candidates to quit Iowa races.
rebuttal_anticipated: Cabinet secretaries routinely travel on military aircraft for security and scheduling reasons, and this trip did include genuine official HHS business (the addiction initiative announcement, the health center tour); the White House and HHS's own lawyers reviewed and approved the arrangement in advance, which is exactly the process meant to catch a genuine legal problem before it happens.
comeback: Advance legal sign-off and the existence of travel protocols show the arrangement was reviewed, not that it was actually necessary -- and HHS's own deputy-secretary nominee, Chris Klomp, is on record successfully talking Kennedy out of using a military jet on a separate occasion, which undercuts any claim that paying about $9,000 per flight hour instead of a roughly $250 commercial ticket was operationally required rather than a matter of discretion exercised in favor of the more expensive option on trips that happened to include campaign stops.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Fits a broader pattern of cabinet officials campaigning for midterm candidates using government resources and platforms, raising the same use-of-office concerns as the separate Hatch Act complaint against Kennedy over his Iowa candidate-withdrawal calls -- worth watching whether this becomes a pattern across other cabinet officials as the midterms approach, not just Kennedy.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core facts -- the August 17, 2026 flight, the cost comparison, the candidates Kennedy appeared with, the concurrent official business, the advance legal sign-off, and the Klomp pushback episode all come from The Washington Post's original reporting (read in full via its Yahoo News syndicated copy), which relies on anonymous sources; later outlets only repeat the Post's story. MODERATE confidence on how this should ultimately be characterized legally, since no Hatch Act complaint, IG referral, or other formal proceeding has been filed over this specific conduct as of this entry (unlike the separate, already-filed Wyden complaint over Kennedy's Iowa candidate calls).

official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., HHS Secretary
offense_category: False Statement to Congress (potential concern under 18 U.S.C. §1001 if made with knowledge of falsity; not charged, no criminal referral identified) -- misrepresenting a specific constituent's documented medical circumstances to deflect accountability for NIH staffing cuts
incident_summary: At a May 14, 2025 Senate hearing, Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA) confronted HHS Secretary Kennedy with the case of her constituent Natalie Phelps, a Bainbridge Island mother of two with stage IV colorectal cancer enrolled in an NIH Clinical Center immunotherapy trial. Murray said Phelps's own NIH doctors had told her twice that her treatment was being delayed roughly four weeks because of NIH staffing cuts from the reduction-in-force, and asked Kennedy for a personal update within 24 hours. Following a recess, **Kennedy told the committee Phelps had actually been found 'medically ineligible' for the trial and that her situation had nothing to do with the RIF, adding that NIH was trying to place her in a different trial instead. Murray immediately and directly disputed this on the record, stating Phelps was already enrolled in the trial -- eligibility was not in question** -- and that the delay was a care-delivery problem, not an eligibility determination, per Phelps's own doctors' statements to her twice.
elements_required: A specific, checkable factual claim was made to Congress by a Cabinet secretary (Phelps's 'medical ineligibility') that is capable of being true or false, not mere rhetorical spin
The claim directly contradicts a first-hand account -- the patient's own doctors, relayed by the senator who had spoken with the patient directly -- rather than only a policy disagreement
The claim served to deflect responsibility for a specific, documented harm (a cancer patient's treatment delay) attributable to the secretary's own department's staffing reduction
No public correction or retraction from Kennedy or HHS was identified in reporting reviewed

evidence.description: CNN's May 14, 2025 report on Phelps's case, published the same day as the hearing, documents her doctors warning that NIH staffing cuts from the RIF were the reason for the treatment delay, before Kennedy's ineligibility claim was made later that day
evidence.maps_to_element: Establishes the pre-existing, contemporaneous doctor-sourced account of the delay's cause

evidence.description: Sen. Patty Murray's official Senate statement disputing Kennedy's 'medically ineligible' claim on the record: Phelps was already enrolled in the trial, so eligibility was not the issue, and her NIH doctor told her twice, directly, that her care was delayed by the staffing cuts
evidence.maps_to_element: Direct, on-record rebuttal of the specific factual claim, sourced to the patient's own doctors relayed by her senator

evidence.description: A separate, earlier Murray Senate statement documents Kennedy separately acknowledging, when pressed, that NIH staffing cuts generally 'will hurt' clinical care -- a broader admission in tension with his specific denial that Phelps's individual case was RIF-related
evidence.maps_to_element: Kennedy's own general admission that staffing cuts harm clinical care, in tension with his specific denial in Phelps's case

evidence.description: Fox News/PJ Media coverage of the same hearing exchange, presenting Kennedy's characterization that Murray was 'playing politics' with a terminally ill constituent -- the administration's contemporaneous framing of the exchange, included for balance
evidence.maps_to_element: Contested characterization/rebuttal context from sympathetic coverage

status: Documented via direct, on-record congressional exchange; no correction, retraction, or independent adjudication of which account is accurate identified in reporting reviewed. No criminal referral or charge.
rebuttal_anticipated: Kennedy's stated position is that Phelps was found medically ineligible for reasons unrelated to the RIF and that NIH was working to place her in an alternative trial -- a good-faith clinical determination, not a fabrication, and that Murray was using a sympathetic patient's story for political point-scoring rather than engaging the underlying eligibility facts.
comeback: The specific, falsifiable claim in dispute is not whether NIH staffing cuts harm clinical care generally -- Kennedy has separately admitted that they do -- but whether Phelps herself was actually already enrolled (making 'ineligible' factually incoherent) and whether her own doctors' twice-repeated, direct statement to her that the RIF caused her specific delay is true. Kennedy offered no documentation or named clinical reviewer supporting the ineligibility claim in the available record, while Murray's account is anchored to the patient's own treating physicians relayed through direct contact with the patient.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] An instance of a broader pattern this database documents in other RFK Jr. entries (see the Kennedy entry): specific, checkable public claims that conflict with contemporaneous documentation, in service of minimizing the disruptive effects of HHS/NIH staffing reductions.
confidence_note: MODERATE-HIGH confidence: the core factual dispute (enrolled-vs-ineligible) is unusually clean and checkable -- if Phelps was already enrolled in the trial, as Murray states and CNN's contemporaneous reporting is consistent with, 'medically ineligible' is not merely disputed but internally incoherent as an explanation. However, this entry relies on Sen. Murray's account of what Phelps's doctors told her (relayed secondhand through the senator, not a doctor's own public statement or medical record), and Kennedy's HHS did not have its own detailed rebuttal captured in the sourcing reviewed beyond his hearing statement. Present as a direct, documented factual dispute between a senator's account and the secretary's own testimony, not as an independently adjudicated finding of falsity.

offense_category: Installing an Unqualified, Research-Compromised Figure to Lead a Federal COVID Vaccine Safety Review -- distinct from this tracker's David Geier entry (a data-access hiring) in that this concerns leadership of the safety-review process itself
incident_summary: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. installed Retsef Levi -- an MIT professor of operations management with no epidemiology, immunology, or clinical medical background -- to lead a federal task force reviewing COVID-19 vaccine safety. Levi has been a vocal public critic of COVID-19 vaccines. **A Guardian investigation found that more than a dozen scientists and public health experts, reviewing Levi's own published research underlying his vaccine-safety claims, concluded it failed to meet basic scientific standards.** The appointment follows the broader pattern this tracker documents of Kennedy installing ideologically aligned but professionally unqualified figures into roles with direct influence over federal vaccine policy and safety findings, rather than credentialed specialists in the relevant clinical or epidemiological fields.
elements_required: Levi lacks epidemiological, immunological, or clinical medical credentials relevant to leading a vaccine-safety review
Levi has a documented public record as a vocal critic of COVID-19 vaccines prior to his appointment, indicating a pre-formed conclusion rather than a neutral review posture
Independent scientific review of Levi's own published research found it failed to meet basic scientific standards, per more than a dozen scientists and public health experts cited by The Guardian
Kennedy personally selected and installed Levi to lead a federal task force with direct influence over vaccine-safety findings and, by extension, national vaccine policy

official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services
offense_category: Personal Financial Conflict of Interest in Pursuing Policy That Could Weaken Vaccine Manufacturers' Legal Liability Shield -- no criminal charge; an accountability claim regarding undisclosed/documented conflicts shaping federal health policy
incident_summary: AP reported a specific, named instance of the conflict this entry documents: in June 2025, HHS awarded a **$150,000 contract** to an Arizona law firm for "expertise" on the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP), whose attorney Andrew Downing had a leading role in product-liability lawsuits against Merck over its Gardasil HPV vaccine, including claims of a rare movement disorder; Downing was listed in HHS's own staff directory for a time. In a podcast the year before joining the effort, Downing had criticized the VICP for taking "a hard line" against such cases, pushing attorneys like himself toward civil lawsuits instead -- the same civil-liability exposure this entry's central conflict concerns. On July 28, 2025, Kennedy announced in a post on X that he would overhaul the VICP, saying it "has devolved into a morass of inefficiency, favoritism, and outright corruption," and that, working with Attorney General Pam Bondi, "we will steer the Vaccine Court back to its original congressional intent" -- an announcement Reuters noted came after Kennedy had fired all 17 members of the CDC's vaccine advisory committee in June 2025 and replaced them with members including known vaccine skeptics. Kennedy is pursuing changes to the VICP -- a federal system Congress created in the 1980s, after lawsuits drove vaccine manufacturers out of the U.S. market, to provide no-fault compensation for rare, serious vaccine side effects and, in exchange, shield manufacturers from direct liability litigation. In January 2026, STAT News reported that Kennedy's slashing of the federally recommended childhood vaccine schedule, documented separately in this tracker, created new uncertainty about manufacturers' legal protections; HHS said the liability shield remained in place, but STAT reported that Kennedy's allies were hopeful the move opens the door to stripping vaccine makers of their liability shields -- a longtime aim of Kennedy's, which he pursued for years before joining the administration, as an attorney who represented plaintiffs in vaccine-injury lawsuits and, per this tracker's separately-documented measles entry, personally collected referral fees from such litigation. On January 27, 2026, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal, Ed Markey, and Angela Alsobrooks sent Kennedy a formal letter raising conflict-of-interest concerns about his role overseeing VICP policy given this financial history and his ties to vaccine-injury lawyers, including Downing, whose firm's HHS contract, the letter said, grew from $150,000 in June 2025 to $400,000 by September 2025; they asked for answers by February 10, 2026. In March 2026, ProPublica noted that the program covers only immunizations the CDC recommends for routine administration to children or pregnant women, leaving shots moved to other categories open to injury lawsuits. ProPublica warned that if the liability shield collapses, manufacturers could exit the U.S. market as they did in the 1980s -- a risk with heightened stakes given the CDC's March 2026 warning that polio was circulating in 28 additional countries, and a diphtheria outbreak that began in Western Europe in 2022, the largest rise in cases there in 70 years. Merck agreed in June 2026 to pay about $50 million to settle more than 200 Gardasil product-liability lawsuits, including cases in which Kennedy had been an attorney of record before joining HHS and cases brought by Wisner Baum, the firm to which he had referred Gardasil plaintiffs and where his son Conor works. Separately, on a distinct legal track, on June 30, 2026 HHS announced that Kennedy had signed determinations terminating the COVID-19 emergency use authorization (EUA) declarations first issued in 2020, for drugs and biological products (effective June 29, 2027) and for medical devices (effective December 26, 2026), with HHS saying the circumstances that justified those emergency authorities no longer exist. HHS's announcement concerned the EUA declarations and did not address the separate PREP Act declaration that gives makers of COVID-19 countermeasures liability immunity; either way, this is a different mechanism from the VICP shield that is this entry's central subject. In a letter dated July 28, 2026, Sens. Warren, Alsobrooks, Blumenthal, and Andy Kim wrote to Kennedy about the Merck settlement, asking by August 11, 2026 whether he played any role in it, how many of the settled Gardasil cases he had referred to Wisner Baum, whether his son received his share of the fees, and how much money he has received from vaccine-injury lawsuits while serving as Secretary. Wisner Baum managing partner Brent Wisner told Reuters that "at no time" will Kennedy or his son receive fees from a Gardasil settlement. During his confirmation, Kennedy had initially said he would keep a 10% fee from Gardasil cases he referred to Wisner Baum; after Warren and other lawmakers raised conflict concerns, his February 1, 2025 amended ethics agreement said he would assign that stake to a non-dependent adult family member, which he told the Senate Finance Committee would be his adult son, and on May 12, 2025 he certified that he had completed the divestitures in his ethics agreement. In an August 1, 2026 post on X, Kennedy said that neither he nor anyone in his family had "received a penny" from the settlement and that before taking office he had "relinquished any interest in potential Gardasil fees back to the Wisner Baum law firm." On August 24, 2026, Sens. Warren, Wyden, Blumenthal, and Alsobrooks wrote that this statement suggested he had either modified his ethics agreement or strayed from it, noting that their staff found no amendment to his public financial disclosures or ethics documents reflecting a change, and asked for answers by September 9, 2026. In an August 25, 2026 reply on Kennedy's behalf, HHS Assistant Secretary for Legislation Gary Andres wrote that on February 11, 2025 Kennedy had irrevocably assigned his outstanding Gardasil contingency-fee interests directly to Wisner Baum rather than to a non-dependent adult family member, and that HHS's ethics official had reported his compliance with his ethics agreement on May 14, 2025. On September 24, 2026, the same four senators, noting that Kennedy was confirmed on February 13, 2025, two days after the change, wrote that the reply was, to their knowledge, the first disclosure to Congress of the change, called his apparent failure to report it to ethics officials "deeply alarming," questioned whether any agreement with Wisner Baum about future payments accompanied the transfer, and requested answers by October 8, 2026. HHS spokeswoman Emily G. Hilliard told the AP that HHS had confirmed Kennedy's compliance with his ethics agreement in May 2025 and said, "Any claim that Secretary Kennedy maintained a financial interest in this litigation after taking office is false." Separately, NPR reported on September 24, 2026 that Kennedy's latest annual financial disclosure listed a payment of nearly $7,000 from Wisner Baum, described as "final payment at termination of agreement of Referral Fees On Contingency Fee Case"; the firm told NPR the payment was not related to the Gardasil case and said Kennedy and his family had not received any fees recovered from the Gardasil cases. This Gardasil-specific dispute concerns a different, though related, category of vaccine-litigation financial interest than the VICP liability-shield policy conflict that is this entry's central subject.

official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., HHS Secretary; Donald Trump, President (nominated Casey Means for Surgeon General despite her lacking an active medical license or completed residency)
offense_category: Public Health Service Commissioned Corps qualification standards disregarded in nomination -- not itself illegal (a presidential nomination and Senate confirmation are a political process, not a prosecutable act), but a documented, unprecedented departure from every prior Surgeon General's clinical qualifications
status: Concluded: Trump withdrew the nomination April 30, 2026 after it stalled in the Senate for nearly a year. His replacement pick, Dr. Nicole Saphier, a radiologist and former Fox News contributor, cleared the HELP Committee 12-11 on Sept. 30, 2026; no full Senate vote yet.
incident_summary: Trump's Surgeon General nominee, Dr. Casey Means, was a close ally of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a leading figure in his 'Make America Healthy Again' movement. On May 15, 2025, AP reported that she had publicly promoted unproven psychedelic therapies, including crediting psilocybin mushrooms with helping her find romantic love, raising questions about her fitness to serve as the nation's top public-health spokesperson. Her confirmation hearing before the Senate HELP Committee was initially postponed after she went into labor. It was ultimately held February 25, 2026, and she was pressed there on vaccine skepticism. During the confirmation process, reporting by STAT News, PBS and Healthbeat surfaced that Means's Oregon medical license had been **inactive since 2024** and that she had not completed her five-year surgical residency at Oregon Health and Science University after earning her M.D. at Stanford. If confirmed, she would have been the first U.S. Surgeon General in history to hold neither an active medical license nor board certification, a departure from the longstanding policy and tradition that Public Health Service Commissioned Corps physicians complete residency and maintain active licensure. Former Trump-administration Surgeon General Jerome Adams publicly said in a STAT News piece that Means 'does not meet basic standards' for the role. The nomination stalled in the Senate through early 2026 without a committee vote being scheduled. On April 30, 2026, nearly a year after she was nominated, Trump withdrew it and nominated Dr. Nicole Saphier, a board-certified radiologist and former Fox News Channel contributor, as his new Surgeon General pick instead. On September 30, 2026, the Senate HELP Committee advanced Saphier's nomination on a party-line 12 to 11 vote; a full Senate vote was not expected until after the November midterm elections.

Means held neither at the time of her nomination and confirmation hearing (inactive Oregon license since 2024; incomplete surgical residency)
The concern was substantive, raised by a named former Surgeon General and reflected in the Senate's failure to advance the nomination, not merely a partisan objection

incident_summary: Dr. Harvey A. Risch, professor emeritus and senior research scientist in epidemiology at the Yale School of Public Health, announced on X on December 4, 2025 that President Trump had appointed him to chair the President's Cancer Panel -- the body that monitors the National Cancer Institute's National Cancer Program and reports directly to the president -- succeeding Elizabeth M. Jaffee, who had served since January 2023. HHS did not make the appointment official until December 16, 2025, eleven days after Risch's own announcement; HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in the official statement, 'Dr. Risch brings the expertise and resolve needed to identify the root causes of cancer in America.' That statement did not mention Risch's COVID-19-era public record: he was an early and vocal proponent of hydroxychloroquine and ivermectin as COVID-19 treatments, currently serves as chief epidemiologist for The Wellness Company (which commercially sells ivermectin), and has, per Wired's reporting, speculated about a possible connection between COVID-19 vaccines and so-called '**turbo cancer**' in young people -- a claim without established scientific support. Risch's own research background is in cancer etiology, prevention, and early diagnosis across ovarian, pancreatic, lung, bladder, esophageal, and stomach cancers, per HHS's official biography of him.

evidence.description: Just the News's report documents the December 4/December 16, 2025 announcement timeline, HHS's official statement and Kennedy's quote, Risch's academic biography, and (citing Wired) his ivermectin/hydroxychloroquine advocacy, Wellness Company role, and 'turbo cancer' speculation

official: Brooke Rollins, Secretary of Agriculture
offense_category: Potential First Amendment Establishment Clause Violation (government endorsement/coercion of religion) and related APA claims — active federal civil litigation (not criminal); filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California
incident_summary: USDA employees filed a lawsuit against Rollins over a series of escalating religious messages sent department-wide, culminating in an April 2026 Easter email referencing "sin," being "destroyed," and Christ's resurrection as "the foundation of our faith." The formal complaint, National Federation of Federal Employees, et al. v. U.S. Department of Agriculture (No. 3:26-cv-04406, N.D. Cal., filed May 13, 2026), was brought by the National Federation of Federal Employees (representing more than 19,000 USDA employees) together with seven individual USDA employees from Jewish, Buddhist, Pagan, and atheist backgrounds. One of them, Adam Diamond, voluntarily dismissed his claims on May 19, 2026, leaving six individual plaintiffs. Plaintiffs allege the messages, which grew markedly more explicitly Christian over a roughly 10-month period beginning July 2025, were "unconstitutionally coercive" and left non-Christian or non-religious employees feeling "unwelcome, excluded and like outsiders," with one plaintiff, Lanette Dietrich, reporting that when she asked to be removed from the distribution lists used for religious messages she was told this was not possible and that elevating her request would "create trouble" for her, and another stating he felt the messaging conveyed he was "going to hell" for not sharing Rollins's beliefs. **The complaint notably cites USDA's own November 2025 internal memorandum, which explicitly forbids officials from using "official authority to pressure subordinates" regarding religious beliefs, arguing Rollins's own department policy contradicts her conduct.** Rollins has responded to the lawsuit publicly and unapologetically rather than disputing the underlying facts, and has continued sending agency-wide religious content (Memorial Day, Independence Day 2026) during the pendency of the suit. A separate ethics complaint is pending with the USDA Inspector General regarding unrelated conflict-of-interest allegations, which USDA disputes as frivolous. Plaintiffs filed a motion for a preliminary injunction and stay on July 22, 2026 seeking to bar further religious messaging while the case proceeds, first noticed for an August 27, 2026 hearing before Magistrate Judge Laurel Beeler. That hearing never took place. On July 27, 2026 Judge Beeler approved the parties' stipulation to brief the motion together with a government motion to dismiss and moved the hearing to October 29. On July 28 the case was randomly reassigned to U.S. District Judge Trina L. Thompson, and the hearing was reset for October 27, 2026 before her. On August 21, 2026 the government filed a combined motion to dismiss and opposition, arguing that the plaintiffs lack standing, that the emails are not agency action reviewable under the Administrative Procedure Act, and that the emails fit the nation's history and tradition of religious invocations in official discourse and coerce no one. Plaintiffs filed their opposition on September 21, 2026; the government's reply is due October 5.

In its August 21, 2026 filing, the government argued that the plaintiffs lack standing because offense at seeing religious messages is not a cognizable injury, that the emails are not "agency action" under the APA, that holiday emails with religious references fit the nation's history and tradition of religious invocations in official discourse, and that the emails "do not request, much less coerce, anyone to do anything" and establish no denominational preference.
comeback: The legal distinction the plaintiffs are drawing isn't about Rollins's personal beliefs -- it's about using a government-funded platform (USDA agency email reaching roughly 100,000 employees) to deliver theologically specific Christian content in the context of ongoing federal agency business, then failing to follow the department's own internal policy against pressuring subordinates on religious matters. The complaint's citation of USDA's own November 2025 memo is significant: this isn't only an outside legal theory being applied to Rollins's conduct, it's an allegation that her own department's written rules were violated. An active federal lawsuit exists with specific named plaintiffs describing concrete fear of career retaliation -- the question of whether this crosses the Establishment Clause line is before a court, not yet settled in the administration's favor, and Rollins's public 'He is Risen' response to the lawsuit suggests no intention to change course pending that ruling.

Whether the emails are coercive under the Establishment Clause has not been decided by the court.

incident_summary: Former CNN journalist Don Lemon, civil rights attorney Nekima Levy Armstrong, and seven others were federally charged over a January 18, 2026 incident in which anti-ICE protesters disrupted a service at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minnesota. Lemon and eight co-defendants each face two federal charges, first brought in the original indictment: conspiracy to violate someone's constitutional rights, and violating the FACE Act (which prohibits force or threats interfering with someone's First Amendment religious-exercise rights). Lemon has said he was present to chronicle the protest as a journalist, not to participate in it. The grand jury indictment followed an earlier, failed DOJ attempt to secure charges via a federal magistrate judge, who found no probable cause to arrest Lemon. When Magistrate Judge Douglas Micko signed only three of the eight arrest warrants DOJ presented on January 20, U.S. Attorney Rosen personally called the court to demand district-court review of the other five. **Patrick Schiltz, then Chief Judge of the federal district court in Minnesota, wrote to the Eighth Circuit on January 23, 2026 that two of those five -- Lemon and his producer -- were "not protesters at all" and that "[t]here is no evidence that those two engaged in any criminal behavior or conspired to do so."** A three-judge Eighth Circuit panel then denied DOJ's request to order the five warrants signed (one judge, L. Steven Grasz, wrote separately that he saw probable cause). DOJ turned to a grand jury, which indicted Lemon and eight others on January 29, 2026, and Lemon was arrested in Los Angeles while covering the Grammy Awards, according to his attorney. Schiltz's letter addressed the evidence DOJ offered for the warrants, not the later grand jury case, and he is not the judge presiding over the prosecution; the charges have not been dropped. Lemon, Levy Armstrong and three other defendants pleaded not guilty at a February 13, 2026 arraignment in St. Paul; journalist Georgia Fort, also charged, pleaded not guilty on February 17. On February 23, 2026, Magistrate Judge Micko refused the government's request to designate the case "complex" under the Speedy Trial Act, which would have excluded at least 90 days from the speedy-trial clock, finding that nine defendants charged with the same offenses from "the same discrete course of conduct" was "not particularly complex"; he did give the government 30 more days for discovery. A superseding indictment unsealed February 27, 2026 charged 30 more people with the same two counts, bringing the case to 39 defendants; on March 23, 2026 Judge Provinzino granted the government's motion to dismiss the charges against one of them, Heather Danae Lewis. Magistrate Judge Micko denied defense requests for grand jury materials on June 10, 2026. On August 7, 2026, Lemon's attorneys filed three motions to dismiss: one alleging vindictive prosecution, one arguing his newsgathering was protected by the First Amendment, and one arguing that the FACE Act's house-of-worship provision exceeds Congress's Commerce Clause power. Fort had filed three dismissal motions the day before, on First Amendment, vindictive-prosecution and failure-to-state-an-offense grounds. On objections from Lemon, Fort and 32 co-defendants (Lemon's team cited grand jury "irregularities"), U.S. District Judge Laura Provinzino, who presides over the case, ordered DOJ on August 18, 2026 to produce by August 25, for her own private (in camera) review, the transcripts and evidence of its January 29 and February 26, 2026 grand jury presentations; the government filed a notice of an in camera submission on August 21. On September 24, 2026, with 101 defense pretrial motions pending, including the dismissal motions, Micko gave the government until October 16 to respond and moved the motions hearings to November 3, 5, 9 and 10, 2026. Court records reported by WIRED on October 13, 2026 show that judges in Minnesota (January 30) and Pennsylvania (January 31) signed warrants letting agents use cell-site simulators, devices that impersonate cell towers, to target the phone of defendant Jerome Richardson, a Temple University student who, WIRED reports, helped produce Lemon's coverage, for the purpose, his lawyers wrote, of "locating and arresting him"; Richardson voluntarily surrendered at a federal courthouse in Philadelphia and was released on bond that afternoon. Agents also applied for simulator warrants targeting Fort and Jamael Lundy, then a Minnesota State Senate candidate, and sought pen register orders for Fort and a number WIRED traced to Lemon; it is unclear whether a judge approved any of those applications. The affidavits claimed video showed Fort, Lemon, Richardson and others "chanting with agitators"; prosecutors have since conceded that Lemon and Fort did not chant, and according to Fort's lawyers the government acknowledged the false claim appeared in at least 15 warrant affidavits. DHS also demanded journalists' telephone and YouTube records under a customs authority that requires no prior judicial approval (defense attorneys have identified 92 customs summonses and are challenging them), and agents sought records of everyone who bought a particular beanie at REI in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area over more than two years. DOJ told WIRED it "speaks through its court filings"; DHS declined to discuss investigative methods.

incident_summary: On June 16, 2026, U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen announced a federal indictment, filed under seal on June 11, against 15 people, described by prosecutors as members of two Minneapolis groups (Direct Action Minnesota and Black Cat Workers Collective) with alleged "antifa" ties, on charges including conspiracy to impede or injure a federal officer, assault on a federal officer, and destruction of government property, tied to protests at the Whipple federal building -- which houses the regional ICE field office and a detention facility -- on January 23 and March 1, 2026. **Among those charged is Erik Davis, chair of Macalester College's religious studies department; the indictment cites a Signal message in which he asked people with AFL-CIO connections to focus organizing on the Whipple building, and prosecutors say he moderated organizing meetings, described himself as an anarchist, and attended an anti-ICE rally where others wore "Antifa"-branded sweatshirts.** His attorney, Jordan Kushner, said the only thing Davis is accused of is participating in meetings, and Cato Institute analyst David Bier, reviewing the 94-page indictment, found only one documented, charged act of violence against an agent's person, by a different defendant. Rosen's announcement explicitly invoked NSPM-7 -- one of the first known instances of DOJ citing that presidential memorandum as a basis for arrests -- as part of a stated effort to prosecute perceived antifascist organizing as domestic terrorism-adjacent conduct. Davis faces up to six years in prison if convicted. The defendants were arraigned beginning July 1, 2026, and the court designated the case complex in August. On August 13, 2026, Kevin Riach, attorney for co-defendant Isaac Sant, filed a discovery motion with dozens of government exhibits showing how DOJ and DHS put NSPM-7 into practice, and asked the court to order the government to disclose more. The documents revealed HSI surveillance operations -- "Operation Puppet Master," opened January 28, four days after federal agents killed protester Alex Pretti, and "Project Whipple Shield," begun two weeks later, both launched under NSPM-7's authority according to the filing -- that used undercover infiltration of meetings, license-plate tracking, and administrative subpoenas for years of financial records from labor unions and nonprofits, none of which has been charged. The filing was reported by the Associated Press (carried by CBS Minnesota), KSTP, Democracy Now and The Hill. On August 25, Protect Democracy filed an amicus brief on behalf of the Cato Institute, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression and the Society for the Rule of Law, groups spanning the ideological spectrum, urging Magistrate Judge David T. Schultz to order the government to reveal more about how NSPM-7 was put into practice in Minnesota; Schultz granted leave to file it on August 26 and heard the discovery motion on August 27. Talking Points Memo reported on September 2 that emails produced in discovery show HSI agents using PATRIOT Act Section 314(a) -- which lets investigators learn which banks hold an entity's accounts without a warrant, subpoena, or grand jury -- though the target of the search is not clear and the search terms are not revealed, and a former prosecutor told TPM the government would now know which banks every group on HSI's "conspiracy" chart uses, a chart that prosecutors and HSI told the grand jury included public-sector unions, the Democratic Socialists of America, the AFL-CIO and SEIU. Also on September 2, Schultz allowed the government to file supplemental briefing describing "Operation Keyhole," another HSI initiative named in the case; the government filed it on September 10, describing Operation Keyhole, a certified undercover operation run by HSI's St. Paul office, as "a funding source, not an investigative tool." Sant responded on September 25, seeking only Keyhole records tied to Puppet Master, Whipple Shield and other surveillance of protesters, unions and progressive groups, and arguing that using Keyhole funds for that surveillance would violate the federal Purpose Statute and that he had already made "a credible showing" of vindictive and selective prosecution; he filed further exhibits on October 12. On October 7, District Judge Katherine M. Menendez vacated a pretrial release condition barring contact among codefendants for ten defendants, including Davis, finding it was not the least restrictive option and not necessary to protect the community, and noting that, as the government's brief highlighted, none of those defendants is alleged to have used physical violence. WIRED reported on October 16, 2026 that an HSI report titled "Antifa Roadshow," released by the defense, details how an HSI Chicago task force of six local police officers and eight HSI agents surveilled an April 2 talk in Chicago where Minnesota organizers spoke, using two undercover agents, a live audio transmission and license-plate-reader data, and that one defendant's remarks there are included in the indictment; the Chicago Police Department told WIRED its work with HSI is permitted under Illinois law because it pertained to criminal enforcement, not immigration. On October 19, Menendez vacated the same condition for the remaining five defendants, including Sant, after the government filed no objection. On October 20, Schultz held an evidentiary hearing on the discovery motion; the docket says the motion requires supplemental briefing and will be taken under advisement after it. At the same hearing he heard a motion by Matthew Deates, an assistant federal defender with no connection to the case, to correct the record over an April ICE memo that prosecutors had sent to the defense in this case's discovery and that, MPR News reported, falsely accused him of helping a client evade immigration arrest. According to MPR, Assistant U.S. Attorney Tory Sailer called the memo's inclusion "an oversight by our office," said Deates is not under investigation, but said the office would not make a determination on the memo's allegation; Schultz apologized to Deates, said "it's clear that Mr. Deates did not and could not have committed any crime," and said he would order prosecutors to destroy all copies of the memo and replace them with a version redacting Deates' name, while saying he was unsure he had authority to grant Deates' request for a legal finding that he did not violate the law. offense_category: Appearance of Pay-to-Play Foreign-Influence Access -- not itself unlawful (the Secretary of State has discretion to waive Section 7031(c) sanctions designations), but a State Department policy reversal that followed a $6 million lobbying campaign built specifically around access to Trump-administration insiders, raising the same access-for-money concern this tracker documents elsewhere
incident_summary:
**In April 2025, Sali Berisha -- Albania's indicted former president and prime minister -- signed a two-year, $6 million lobbying contract with Continental Strategy, a Republican consulting firm.** Berisha had been barred from the U.S. since 2021 under Section 7031(c) of the State Department's annual appropriations act, over Biden-era State Department findings that he misappropriated public funds to enrich relatives. Continental's roster included Alberto Martinez (a former chief of staff to then-Senator Rubio) and Katie Wiles (daughter of White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles), though AP reporting specifically found Katie Wiles was not staffed on the Berisha account. Berisha's party separately hired Chris LaCivita (a co-manager of Trump's 2024 campaign) as an electoral adviser; LaCivita has said he is not lobbying U.S. officials for Berisha. The Associated Press reported the arrangement was funded in part through a New Jersey-based group called the 'Make Albania Great Again Foundation,' whose donors were not publicly disclosed at the time.

A little over a year later, on June 12, 2026, the State Department confirmed it had issued 'waivers for several 7031(c) [non-grata] designations imposed under the previous administration because granting the waivers serves a compelling national interest.' Berisha said that 'following an in-depth review of my case by the Department of State,' he and his family were 'no longer barred from traveling to the United States of America.' Berisha announced the reversal himself, telling Albania's parliament 'I am back,' and told the Daily Signal he wanted 'to thank President Trump's administration and Secretary [of State Marco] Rubio for correcting this unfair decision.' He remains under a separate corruption prosecution in Albania and remains persona non grata in the United Kingdom.

In September 2026, Berisha attended the Republican Party's 'midterm convention' in Dallas, which Mother Jones reported the waiver had allowed him to travel to. In its October 2026 report, Mother Jones said Continental's Justice Department filings 'have noted extensive contacts with the State Department, including with' Dan Holler, a longtime Rubio aide who works as counselor in the department, and that Continental said it had been paid $750,000 for the work. Mother Jones wrote that Continental's lobbying 'appeared to bear fruit' with the waiver, but also reported that while Berisha has said the waiver resolved his U.S. designation, the State Department has not confirmed that, has not taken down its 2021 designation, and did not answer questions about the designation's status. A Continental spokesperson said the firm had 'complied with all requirements under the Foreign Agents Registration Act' and 'played no role' in Berisha's Dallas visit.

No sourcing reviewed directly quotes Rubio or any other State Department official connecting the lobbying campaign to the waiver decision, and none of the June 2026 reports on the reversal reviewed mention Continental Strategy or the lobbying contract at all. No State Department statement acknowledges the lobbying campaign as a factor; the department's only stated basis is that the waivers serve 'a compelling national interest.' The connection here is a documented, well-sourced temporal and access relationship (a paid lobbying campaign built specifically around Trump-administration proximity, followed just over a year later by a State Department waiver letting Berisha travel to the U.S., the relief it was hired to obtain), not a proven quid pro quo.

incident_summary:
In May 2022 Congress passed the Additional Ukraine Supplemental Appropriations Act (P.L. 117-128). It gave the Foreign Military Financing Program, which pays for partner countries to buy U.S. military equipment, an extra $4 billion "for assistance for Ukraine and countries impacted by the situation in Ukraine." Section 505(d) lets the title's foreign military financing, narcotics-control and nonproliferation funds be transferred among those accounts "to respond to the situation in Ukraine and in countries impacted by the situation in Ukraine," and section 505(f) makes such transfers subject to "prior consultation with, and the regular notification procedures of," the appropriations committees. Section 505(e) says these transfer authorities are "in addition to any other transfer authority provided by law."

On Tuesday, September 15, 2026, the State Department notified Congress that it would reprogram $52 million in foreign military financing from Slovakia, North Macedonia, Tunisia and Iraq to Panama, Peru, Ecuador and Colombia, the Associated Press reported. Secretary of State Marco Rubio had visited Colombia, Ecuador and Peru the week before and pledged them more support. The department said the money would "combat narcoterrorism in our backyard and help continue to secure the Panama Canal" and that the existing split did "not align with the administration's prioritization of" the Western Hemisphere. The AP noted the shift did not end military financing for the four original recipients; Slovakia and North Macedonia are NATO members.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen and Rep. Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrats on the Senate Foreign Relations and House Foreign Affairs committees, placed a hold on the transfer. In their later letter to Rubio, they wrote that **the majority of the $52,100,000 had been appropriated through the 2022 Ukraine supplemental**, that section 505(d) lets those funds be transferred only for the Ukraine-related purpose, and that "The Executive Branch does not have unlimited discretion to redirect these funds toward unrelated Administration policy priorities or countries." They said department briefers cited the National Security Strategy and National Defense Strategy but did not explain how the money would serve the statute's purpose, and that the department's September 29 written answers gave "no compelling explanation" for why the four Latin American countries were "impacted by the situation in Ukraine." They added that the department "confirmed that Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, and Peru have not provided meaningful security assistance to Ukraine" or to other affected European partners.

Late on Wednesday, September 30, the administration told Congress it would go ahead despite the hold, three U.S. officials told the Washington Post, which reported the move on October 1. The same day, Shaheen and Meeks wrote to Rubio that the hold "remains in effect" and that they would "consider a breach of this hold and the transfer of funds to violate statutory requirements and to have consequences for the Department's relationship with our committees." Their committees' October 1 releases say Rubio "diverted the funds." The State Department told the Post that "Reprogramming money away from [the] Middle East and Europe to the Western Hemisphere is consistent with the National Security Strategy"; per the Post, as relayed by UNN, it did not answer the lawmakers' claim that the move breaks statutory requirements.

offense_category: Misleading Congress About Military Intentions Toward Venezuela, Then Launching an Unauthorized Special-Forces Raid That Captured a Foreign Head of State Without Any Advance Congressional Notification -- a War Powers Resolution consultation-and-notification dispute; not itself criminally charged
incident_summary: On January 3, 2026, more than 200 U.S. special operations forces raided Fuerte Tiuna military base in Caracas (Operation Absolute Resolve), capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, after Maduro failed to reach a safe room; **Venezuela's Defense Ministry reported 83 deaths in the raid, including 47 Venezuelan troops and 32 Cuban soldiers.** Trump announced the capture from Mar-a-Lago. This was a dramatic escalation of the Caribbean/Pacific counter-narcotics boat-strike campaign already tracked in this database (this tracker's entry on the failed war-powers resolutions covers the preceding months' congressional votes on that campaign). Neither Trump nor Secretary of State Rubio notified any member of Congress in advance. In a November 2025 classified briefing to lawmakers, ahead of that month's Senate war-powers vote, Rubio -- per the Washington Post's and CNN's reporting on the briefing, as summarized in Reason's own analysis of the episode -- indicated the administration was not currently preparing to target Venezuela directly and did not believe it had a proper legal argument for doing so; CNN separately reported officials told lawmakers the U.S. was not currently planning to launch strikes inside Venezuela. After the raid, Democrats accused Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth of having lied in that briefing: Sen. Andy Kim said 'Secretaries Rubio and Hegseth looked every Senator in the eye a few weeks ago and said this wasn't about regime change. I didn't trust them then and we see now that they blatantly lied to Congress,' and Rep. Gregory Meeks told the Post 'Rubio said that there were not any intentions to invade Venezuela. He absolutely lied to Congress.' Rubio's own subsequent defense was inconsistent on its face: he characterized the raid as a 'law enforcement operation' not requiring congressional authorization, a characterization Trump's own public description of it as an 'extraordinary military operation' contradicted. Al Jazeera's post-raid fact-check of Trump's separate public justifications for the broader campaign found several did not hold up: his claim that each U.S. strike on suspected drug boats (32 strikes since September 2025, killing roughly 115 people) saves 25,000 American lives was contradicted by experts who note Venezuela plays a minor role in U.S. drug trafficking, with no drug evidence provided for the strikes; his claim that Maduro 'sent savage and murderous gangs' (Tren de Aragua) to terrorize American communities was contradicted by an April 2025 National Intelligence Council report finding the Maduro government 'probably does not have a policy of cooperating' with the gang; his claim Venezuela had 'stolen' U.S. oil ignored that Venezuela nationalized its oil industry in 1975; and his claim that Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodriguez, was 'willing' to cooperate was contradicted by her own public denunciation of the operation, on Venezuelan state television, as 'brutal aggression.' The raid prompted a further round of Senate action (following the Nov. 6, 2025 procedural vote on S.J.Res. 90 already documented in this database's companion entry on those war-powers votes): per the Senate's own official roll call record, a motion to discharge a new joint resolution, S.J.Res. 98 -- like S.J.Res. 90, directing removal of U.S. armed forces from unauthorized hostilities against Venezuela, but introduced in the new (2nd) session of the 119th Congress -- succeeded 52-47 on January 8, 2026, with Sens. Rand Paul, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Todd Young, and Josh Hawley joining Democrats. On January 14, 2026, a subsequent procedural vote to advance toward final passage failed as Sens. Josh Hawley and Todd Young, who had joined Democrats on the January 8 vote, reversed course after Rubio personally assured Hawley 'point blank, we're not going to do ground troops' and gave Young a written commitment to seek congressional authorization in advance of any future 'major military operations,' 'circumstances permitting.' That vote ended in a 50-50 tie, broken by Vice President JD Vance against the resolution. On January 28, 2026, weeks after the raid, Rubio told the same Senate Foreign Relations Committee 'we are not postured to, nor do we intend or expect to have to take any military action in Venezuela at any time' regarding further action -- language nearly identical to his pre-raid assurances, this time as a forward-looking statement rather than one later proven false by an already-completed operation. Maduro and Flores were flown to the United States and held at Brooklyn's Metropolitan Detention Center; on January 5, 2026 they were arraigned before U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in Manhattan on federal narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine-importation conspiracy, and weapons charges, pleading not guilty -- Maduro interrupted the proceedings to declare 'I am innocent... I am still president of my country' and separately said he had been 'kidnapped.'

incident_summary: In 2016, Dahud Hanid Ortiz -- a U.S. military veteran and dual Venezuelan-American citizen -- killed two Cuban women and an Ecuadorian man at a law office in Madrid, Spain, and fled to Venezuela afterward. Spain convicted him in absentia and requested his extradition, but Venezuela's constitution bars extraditing its own citizens, so Venezuela prosecuted him itself: he was arrested in 2018 and sentenced by a Caracas court on January 9, 2024 to 30 years in prison. In 2023, the Biden administration, aware of Ortiz's criminal record, chose not to include him when it negotiated a different prisoner swap with Venezuela that year. On July 18, 2025, the Trump administration completed a three-way exchange: El Salvador returned 252 Venezuelan migrants to Venezuela (the number Venezuela's government confirmed) -- men the U.S. had deported to El Salvador, 137 of them under the Alien Enemies Act, and paid El Salvador to hold at the CECOT mega-prison -- and in return Venezuela released 10 Americans (U.S. citizens and legal permanent residents), including Ortiz. Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly announced the released Americans were "on their way to freedom." **Of the 10 people released, 8 were officially classified by the U.S. government as "wrongfully detained" -- the stated criterion used to justify prioritizing Americans for return -- but Ortiz was not among them.** The New York Times reported that at least some people in the Trump administration knew of Ortiz's criminal past when he was flown out, a U.S. official told ABC News the U.S. was aware of his past but decided to bring him out anyway, and the Times later obtained a State Department email in which a senior official wrote "we did ask for and receive 10." Venezuela's Justice Minister, Diosdado Cabello, said U.S. officials were told of the conviction and still wanted him released. No U.S. official has since explained, on the record, why a convicted violent felon who did not meet the swap's own wrongful-detention criterion was included. Ortiz has been reported living freely in Orlando, Florida since his return.

incident_summary: After The Atlantic revealed on March 24, 2025 that Rubio had participated in an auto-deleting Signal chat with other senior national-security officials discussing Yemen strike war plans (the chat at the center of this tracker's separate Hegseth Signal/Yemen entry), Democracy Forward filed a FOIA request two days later for Rubio's and then-chief of staff Mike Needham's Signal messages about the administration's El Salvador renditions, and for the names, participants and deletion timelines of the Signal groups they used for official business; it sued in May 2025 (Democracy Forward Foundation v. DOJ, D.D.C., Judge Amit Mehta). Separately, in June 2025, Judge James Boasberg, ruling in American Oversight's Federal Records Act suit over the Yemen chat, ordered the agency heads to notify Rubio, as acting archivist, of any Signal chats holding federal records at risk of deletion, and ordered Rubio to ask the Attorney General to start a recovery action for those records and to notify Congress. Opposing Democracy Forward's motion for a preservation order, State filed a July 22, 2025 declaration by Agency Records Officer Mallory Rogoff stating that, as of July 21, 2025, LeapXpert software on Rubio's government-issued phone archives "all messages sent and received, regardless of whether the sender configures a message to 'auto-delete,'" and that the Office of the Secretary had confirmed "Secretary Rubio does not use the auto-deletion functions in third party messaging applications when sending communications that may include federal records." State repeated that sentence under penalty of perjury in declarations by Susan Weetman (September 9, 2025) and Timothy Kootz (October 2025), filed under a stipulated preservation order. **About two months after the Weetman declaration, Rubio changed the settings in a Signal chat about administration matters with other senior officials so that messages would automatically delete, according to a person familiar with the exchange who spoke anonymously to The Atlantic; a State Department official contested the idea that Rubio made a practice of it but said he could not address the specific instance.** In April 30, 2026 declarations filed under a settlement with American Oversight, State did not repeat its claim that Rubio does not use disappearing messages, instead stating that an application on his device collected messages "even if those messages otherwise have a deletion timeline setting enabled." On June 22, 2026, under court order, State produced to Democracy Forward undated screenshots of the settings of 16 Signal chats, collected by August 2025, that show Rubio as a member of chats with disappearing messages enabled -- including a chat with Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman Caine named "SS/APNSA,SD,CJCS" set to delete messages after eight hours, and a redacted-name chat set to one week; the newly disclosed chats date from the first half of 2025. On August 12, 2026, Democracy Forward asked the court to reinstate a hearing or allow limited discovery into State's candor and its compliance with the preservation order. On September 11, 2026, State opposed, reaffirmed that Rubio "does not use" the auto-deletion functions, noted that any member of a chat can set a deletion timeline, and cited a Deputy Assistant Secretary's review finding no preserved record showing Rubio enabling auto-delete in any thread. Democracy Forward replied on September 23, 2026; no ruling had been entered as of late September.
