offense_category: Alleged political-affiliation discrimination in Foreign Service promotions -- reported questioning of promotion candidates about how they voted, which would conflict with the Foreign Service Act's bar on political-affiliation discrimination (22 U.S.C. 3905(b)(1)) and the prohibited-personnel-practice rule it cross-references (5 U.S.C. 2302(b)(1)(E)). Anonymously sourced and denied by the State Department; no official finding
incident_summary: On October 22, 2026, The Washington Sun reported that the State Department had asked some Foreign Service officers up for promotion who they voted for in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 presidential elections. Citing six current and former State Department officials, three of whom had spoken directly with people who were asked the questions, **the Sun reported that top department officials made clear only candidates who voted for President Donald Trump would be eligible for mid- to upper-level Foreign Service roles**, and told candidates their campaign donation history would be examined, with any donation to Democrats disqualifying. The report names no official who asked the questions and gives no dates for them. **The department denies it.** It first declined to comment on the voting-history questions, saying in a statement that its "fidelity" standard "is not about partisan behavior but rather about executing the president's vision for foreign policy"; about seven hours after publication, a spokesperson added that the department rejects "this absurd premise that individuals are being asked about their political affiliations, and even more so for promotions." Federal law directs the Secretary of State to ensure that Foreign Service members and applicants are free from discrimination on the basis of political affiliation, and promotions and assignments are personnel actions under that law. The policy backdrop is documented: since July 2025, the department's tenure and promotion criteria have graded Foreign Service officers on "fidelity," including "protecting and promoting executive power" and, for senior officers, "quickly and completely aligning oneself and one's team to the most current USG goals." Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, told the Sun the committee is working with the House and other committees "to thoroughly investigate all such claims," and The Hill reported that the American Foreign Service Association has heard anecdotes of senior officers not getting jobs after interviews with questions that were political in nature, and is exploring legal options.

It says "fidelity" means upholding the Constitution and the law and executing policy with loyalty to the American people, "not about partisan behavior." The report names no official who asked the questions and cites no document, and spokesperson Tommy Pigott told the Daily Beast that "those bureaucrats who are complaining to the press prove the point that they shouldn't have, and can't be, trusted with sensitive information." comeback: The denial came late: by the Sun's account, the department declined in several exchanges before and after publication to address the voting questions directly, and issued its blanket denial only seven hours after the story ran. Six sources, three of whom spoke with people who were questioned, is more than a single leak, and the Sun says it heard from more people familiar with the questioning after publication. The positions involved are career Foreign Service roles, not political appointments, and the department's own written criteria already grade senior career officers on "quickly and completely aligning" with "the most current USG goals." Whatever the label, the law bars political-affiliation discrimination in Foreign Service promotions and assignments; any records of the promotion interviews would show whether the questions were asked.

official: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State (heads the department that announces and carries out the revocations and has said "Every time I find one of these lunatics, I take away their visas," while Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau directed the Charlie Kirk-related revocations)
offense_category: First Amendment viewpoint discrimination (found by two federal district courts) and Administrative Procedure Act violations (found by one) in the subset of visa revocations based on protected political speech; revoking visas for crimes, overstays or fraud is a lawful discretionary power under the Immigration and Nationality Act and is not itself alleged to be unlawful. Both speech rulings are on appeal
incident_summary:
Since President Trump returned to office in January 2025, the State Department under Secretary of State Marco Rubio has revoked visas at a rate it says no earlier administration has matched. Its own running totals: about 80,000 nonimmigrant visas by November 2025; more than 100,000 by January 12, 2026, which the department called a record and a 150% increase over 2024; more than 175,000 by August 10, 2026; more than 250,000 by September 30; and more than 300,000 on October 20, 2026, an increase of roughly 125,000 in just over ten weeks. Announcing the latest figure, spokesman Tommy Pigott said the administration "has revoked more visas at a faster pace than any administration in history." The department says most revocations follow crimes or other violations: an official told Al Jazeera the majority were for criminal activity or public safety concerns, including 25 percent for assault and related crimes and 22 percent for driving under the influence, and that more than 4,000 were tied to birth tourism. In 2025 it said it was reviewing the status of more than 55 million current visa holders, and it has set up a Continuous Vetting Center.

A smaller share, which the department has never counted publicly, is at the center of the free-speech challenges. In March 2025, asked about Tufts doctoral student Rumeysa Ozturk, whose visa State had revoked and who was detained a year after co-writing a student-paper op-ed criticizing her university's response to Israel's war in Gaza, Rubio said: **"It might be more than 300 at this point. We do it every day. Every time I find one of these lunatics, I take away their visas."** He said visas would be pulled from students who joined actions such as "vandalizing universities, harassing students, taking over buildings," but did not say what Ozturk had done. In August 2025 a State official said about 200 to 300 of more than 6,000 revoked student visas were pulled for "support for terrorism," without saying which groups. In October 2025 the department revoked six visas over social media posts about the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, after Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau directed consular officials to act and asked social media users to send him such posts.

Two federal courts have ruled against the speech-based campaign. On September 30, 2025, after a trial, U.S. District Judge William Young in Boston found that Rubio and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem had "intentionally and in concert implemented" two executive orders "in a viewpoint-discriminatory way to chill protected speech." His January 22, 2026 judgment declared the enforcement policy void and vacated it, and let noncitizens who were members of the plaintiff groups from March 25 through September 30, 2025 bring their own court actions in which any change to their immigration status since January 20, 2025 is presumed to be retaliation unless the government proves otherwise. The government appealed to the First Circuit. On August 28, 2026, U.S. District Judge Noël Wise of the Northern District of California ruled that the statutes Rubio used to revoke visas and deport legal immigrants over their speech were unconstitutional as applied to protected speech, while declining to bar future revocations; the government had appealed to the Ninth Circuit by October 14.

official: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State and, since September 2026, National Security Advisor (acting from May 2025); also served as Acting Archivist of the United States and Acting USAID Administrator in 2025
offense_category: Potential Federal Vacancies Reform Act (FVRA, 5 U.S.C. §3345 et seq.) compliance issues — concentration of multiple statutorily limited acting roles in one individual; NOT charged, no formal violation finding identified, but Rubio's exit from the Archivist role, which NARA says came at the Act's 300-day limit, indicates an internal recognition the statutory clock applied
incident_summary: Beginning in 2025, Rubio simultaneously held Secretary of State plus, at various points, Acting USAID Administrator (February to August 2025), Acting Archivist of the United States, and Acting National Security Advisor (from May 1, 2025). **Rubio became acting Archivist on February 16, 2025, after Trump fired Archivist Colleen Shogan on February 7. NARA and Rubio's staff say he gave up the role on December 4, 2025, just within the Vacancies Act's 300-day limit for vacancies early in a new administration (210 days is the usual limit), after delegating the Archivist's functions to senior adviser James Byron rather than to a Senate-confirmed successor.** The change was not made public until February 4, 2026, when a NARA spokesperson told Federal News Network that Rubio was no longer serving as acting Archivist. Trump nominated Bradford Wilson for the post on March 2, 2026. In late March 2026, Sen. Tammy Duckworth asked GAO to investigate whether Rubio overstayed the limit, raising the prospect that his departure had been backdated; NARA and GAO confirmed the vacancy had not been reported to GAO until January 23, 2026. Georgetown law professor David Super said the late report at a minimum violated the Act's reporting requirement; NARA called his conclusions inaccurate. The Senate confirmed Wilson on August 7, 2026, and NARA announced him as the 12th Archivist on August 21. On September 22, 2026, three administration officials told Fox News Digital that Trump had signed a commission formally making Rubio national security adviser, ending his acting status in a post that does not require Senate confirmation.

comeback: Complying with a statutory deadline isn't the same as complying with the statute's purpose. By NARA's account, Rubio relinquished the Archivist role on the 300th day of the vacancy, exactly at the FVRA limit -- a precision that's harder to characterize as coincidental than as deliberate deadline management. And delegating the Archivist's functions to a non-Senate-confirmed adviser, while Rubio also served as Secretary of State and acting national security adviser, raises a distinct question: whether the practical effect of stacking acting designations on one confirmed official is to bypass Senate confirmation for multiple roles simultaneously, achieving through sequencing what the FVRA's confirmation requirements were designed to prevent through Senate oversight.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with the Sonderling entry's five acting and deputy roles, several held at once: a pattern of piling acting designations onto a few trusted officials, which lets them run agencies whose leaders need Senate confirmation without the Senate's participation and stretches one person's reach across several agencies beyond what any single confirmation authorized. Rubio's case shows the pattern at the National Archives, a Senate-confirmed post that went without a confirmed leader for about eighteen months after Colleen Shogan's firing; by NARA's account Rubio left it at the Vacancies Act's 300-day limit, delegating its functions to an adviser rather than to a nominee. The national security adviser post is different: it needs no confirmation, so its September 2026 conversion from acting to permanent raises no Vacancies Act question, though it keeps two full-time jobs in one person's hands.

incident_summary: **White House adviser David Sacks personally called President Trump between the night of May 20 and the morning of May 21, 2026, ahead of a planned May 21 signing ceremony, and persuaded him to abruptly shelve a draft executive order that would have set up a voluntary framework for AI companies to submit their most advanced models to national-security agencies for testing up to 90 days before public release (industry had sought a 14-day window, according to reports cited by Seoul Economic Daily).** According to Politico's account, as relayed by Fortune, Sacks told Trump he feared the voluntary vetting would act as a de facto licensing regime; the Wall Street Journal reported he warned the order could slow the AI industry and put the U.S. at a disadvantage against China. Sacks, a venture capitalist whose firm holds AI-industry investments, had separately been the subject of a September 2025 letter from Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Rep. Melanie Stansbury and six other Democratic lawmakers questioning his ethics waivers and whether he had exceeded his 130-day limit, and of December 2025 reporting (NPR, following a New York Times investigation) on his "vast AI investments" while serving as a White House adviser on AI policy. Earlier in his tenure as the formal White House AI and Crypto Czar (a Special Government Employee position, subject to a 130-day time limit), Sacks received a blanket ethics waiver from White House Counsel David Warrington, issued in March 2025, covering conflicts of interest in matters "of general applicability concerning the digital asset industry" -- a waiver specific to crypto. A second, AI-specific ethics waiver from Warrington, undated but made public by the White House in June 2025, followed. Sacks stepped down from the formal AI/Crypto Czar role in March 2026 after reaching the 130-day SGE limit, moving on to co-chair PCAST, a post the council's January 2025 executive order had assigned to the Special Advisor for AI and Crypto and to which the White House announced his appointment in March 2026; he held it at the time of the May 2026 AI executive order intervention. The draft AI-safety executive order was shelved. On June 2, 2026, Trump signed a different order that asks AI companies, on a voluntary basis, to give the government access to covered frontier models up to 30 days before release, rather than the draft's 90 days. Warrington later left the administration for the private sector; Trump announced in August 2026 that Will Scharf would replace him as White House Counsel, effective September 1, 2026 (PBS NewsHour, August 10, 2026).

incident_summary:
Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old political appointee who began as senior adviser to DRL -- the State Department bureau that selects and distributes human-rights grants -- on Trump's second inauguration day, spent his first 18 months in the role courting far-right political movements in Europe, which he has publicly described the U.S. as sharing a 'common civilizational struggle' with, including in a State Department Substack post titled 'The Need for Civilizational Allies in Europe' criticizing Europe as a 'hotbed of digital censorship, mass migration, restrictions on religious freedom.' **With Samson a key figure in the grants, DRL staff were told to begin awarding funds to Lex Libertas, a South African organization founded by a prominent figure in the country's white Afrikaner movement -- occurring alongside the administration's separate, parallel policy fast-tracking refugee status for white South African Afrikaners.** DRL officials also traveled to Paris in support of Marine Le Pen after a French court barred her from office over a conviction the administration characterized as politically motivated 'lawfare' against conservatives; DRL subsequently excluded French organizations from a related grant program, citing foreign-interference concerns, even as the bureau's broader posture favored right-wing European causes. This redirection occurred concurrently with a much larger cut: an OMB-produced Foreign Assistance Review recommended cutting all but two of DRL's 391 active grants (sparing one program each in China and Yemen), affecting nearly $1.3 billion, per Guardian reporting.

Update 2026-10-08: On September 30, 2026, the last day of the fiscal year, the State Department obligated its Human Rights and Democracy Fund awards hours before the money would lapse, despite congressional holds, according to unnamed sources cited by the Guardian and CNN. The Guardian reported that critics focused on 43 awards totaling $176.9 million -- most of the $205 million Congress appropriated for the fund -- including a $40 million award to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a $1 million award opposing what it calls judicial overreach by Brazil's supreme court, and a $2 million 'Promoting Western Civilization Allies' program naming possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and the Balkans. The Guardian described Samson as the deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee's top Democrat, had held 10 awards worth $22 million; a Democratic congressional aide told the Guardian that Rubio personally signed a memo to disregard the holds and obligate the funds. Shaheen said the proposals 'would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies.' The State Department declined to tell the Guardian whether it had obligated the funds; spokesperson Tommy Pigott told CNN the department 'will never apologize for defending Western civilization.'

incident_summary.base: Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old political appointee who began as senior adviser to DRL -- the State Department bureau that selects and distributes human-rights grants -- on Trump's second inauguration day, spent his first 18 months in the role courting far-right political movements in Europe, which he has publicly described the U.S. as sharing a 'common civilizational struggle' with, including in a State Department Substack post titled 'The Need for Civilizational Allies in Europe' criticizing Europe as a 'hotbed of digital censorship, mass migration, restrictions on religious freedom.' **With Samson a key figure in the grants, DRL staff were told to begin awarding funds to Lex Libertas, a South African organization founded by a prominent figure in the country's white Afrikaner movement -- occurring alongside the administration's separate, parallel policy fast-tracking refugee status for white South African Afrikaners.** DRL officials also traveled to Paris in support of Marine Le Pen after a French court barred her from office over a conviction the administration characterized as politically motivated 'lawfare' against conservatives; DRL subsequently excluded French organizations from a related grant program, citing foreign-interference concerns, even as the bureau's broader posture favored right-wing European causes. This redirection occurred concurrently with a much larger cut: an OMB-produced Foreign Assistance Review recommended cutting all but two of DRL's 391 active grants (sparing one program each in China and Yemen), affecting nearly $1.3 billion, per Guardian reporting.

official: Mel Gunewardena, senior markets adviser to the CFTC chairman and head of the CFTC Office of International Affairs (reportedly ordered staff to retract the referral, per anonymous sources; did not respond to Bloomberg); Michael Selig, Chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (the adviser works for the chairman's office; no reporting says Selig himself directed the retraction)
offense_category: Integrity of an insider-trading inquiry -- a senior adviser to the chairman reportedly pulling back career staff's enforcement referral on trades placed minutes before a market-moving presidential post. The Commodity Exchange Act (7 U.S.C. 6c(a)(4)) bars trading on nonpublic government information, but no one has been shown to have done so, and the retraction itself is not alleged to break a specific rule
incident_summary: On March 23, 2026, in a two-minute window starting at 6:49 a.m., traders sold oil futures equal to at least 6 million barrels of Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude, more than 8.5 times the volume traded at that time of morning over the prior week, and billions of dollars' worth of contracts betting oil would fall and the S&P 500 would rise were placed, Bloomberg reported. About 15 minutes later, President Trump posted on Truth Social that he was postponing strikes on Iranian power plants and energy infrastructure for five days, and Brent fell as much as 14%. On April 9, Senators Elizabeth Warren and Sheldon Whitehouse asked CFTC Chairman Michael Selig to have the Division of Enforcement investigate the March 23 trading and an approximately $950 million bet on falling oil placed hours before Trump's April 7 ceasefire announcement. On April 16, Selig told the House Agriculture Committee that anyone engaged in insider trading would "face the full force of the law," and later that month the Justice Department was reported to be examining the trades as well. On October 13, 2026, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that career analysts in the CFTC's Division of Market Oversight had referred the March 23 trades to the enforcement division, and that **Mel Gunewardena, a senior adviser to Selig, then told a supervisor to retract the referral**. Gunewardena, a former Goldman Sachs and State Street executive who had joined weeks earlier as head of the Office of International Affairs, later assembled his own team to redo the analysis. By July the supervisor had left the agency, and other team members resigned or were moved, though Bloomberg said it is not clear whether those changes were related. Former CFTC enforcement director Aitan Goelman, asked generally about such a move, said it had "never" been done in any administration he knew. An agency official told Bloomberg the review was broadened internationally because the original findings were U.S.-focused, and that enforcement is still examining the March 23 trading. Who placed the trades, and whether anyone had inside information, has not been reported.

A senior adviser to the CFTC chairman reportedly ordered the referral retracted and took over the analysis himself, an intervention a former enforcement director called unprecedented
The CFTC says enforcement is still examining the trades; who placed them, whether anyone had nonpublic information, and whether the chairman directed the retraction are all unreported

official: Keith Sonderling, Secretary of Labor (confirmed September 30, 2026; previously Acting Secretary); also Acting Director, Office of Government Ethics; concurrently held acting roles at IMLS and Commerce during the relevant period
offense_category: Administrative Procedure Act Violation (5 U.S.C. §706(2)(A), arbitrary-and-capricious agency action) and Impoundment Control Act concerns (unilateral termination of congressionally-appropriated grants) — per Rhode Island v. Trump (D.R.I.), in which the court found the IMLS dismantlement actions arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law, and the separate ALA v. Sonderling (D.D.C.); NOT criminally charged, resolved via civil litigation (permanent bar, withdrawn appeal, settlement and stipulated dismissal)
incident_summary: **As acting director of the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) beginning March 2025, Sonderling placed many agency staff members on administrative leave, sent termination notices to most of them, began canceling grants and contracts, and fired all members of the National Museum and Library Services Board -- actions carrying out Executive Order 14238, which directed that IMLS be cut to the minimum functions required by law.** A federal judge later blocked these actions. In a suit brought by 21 state attorneys general (Rhode Island v. Trump), the federal district court in Rhode Island found the dismantling actions arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law, set them aside, and permanently barred further steps to carry out the order on November 21, 2025; on April 6, 2026, a federal court granted the administration's request to withdraw its appeal of that ruling. In a separate case in federal court in Washington, D.C., brought by the American Library Association and AFSCME (ALA v. Sonderling), the plaintiffs and DOJ signed a settlement agreement, binding on all parties, on April 9, 2026 that keeps IMLS intact, confirms that terminated grants were reinstated and staff reductions reversed, and records the administration's representation that it will take no further steps to carry out the executive order against IMLS; the parties filed a stipulation dismissing that case without prejudice the same day. Trump announced on June 29, 2026 that he would nominate Sonderling as permanent Labor Secretary, and Sonderling testified at his Senate HELP Committee confirmation hearing on July 16, 2026; the IMLS matter did not derail his nomination or confirmation process. The Senate HELP Committee approved Sonderling's nomination 12-11 on a party-line vote on July 30, 2026 (after an earlier scheduled July 23 vote was postponed for lack of attendance), advancing it to the full Senate floor; the IMLS matter does not appear to have been a stated factor in the committee vote. The full Senate confirmed Sonderling as Secretary of Labor on September 30, 2026, by a 47-41 vote.

At IMLS the speed did not outrun the courts: judges blocked the layoffs within weeks, and the agency was restored by the November 2025 ruling and the April 2026 settlement described in the companion IMLS dismantlement entry. The pattern reflects an administration-wide approach to agencies targeted for elimination rather than a practice specific to Sonderling.

official: Leland Dudek, Acting Commissioner of the Social Security Administration
offense_category: Canceling a State's Vital-Records Service Contract as Admitted Political Retaliation Against Its Governor -- an abuse-of-power and improper-use-of-office claim, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: On February 27, 2025, Acting SSA Commissioner Leland Dudek ordered the cancellation of the agency's longstanding contracts with the State of Maine that automatically processed Social Security numbers for newborns at hospitals and death certificates from funeral homes -- contracts whose termination, which took effect March 6, required Maine parents to go to a federal Social Security office in person to register a newborn. Emails later obtained by House Oversight Committee Democrats showed Dudek ordered the cancellation over a staffer's warning of improper payments and identity theft; Dudek has said he made the decision after watching Democratic Governor Janet Mills publicly clash with President Trump over transgender-athlete policy at a White House event -- **Dudek wrote to staff, 'Please cancel the contracts. While our improper payments will go up, and fraudsters may compromise identities, no money will go from the public trust to a petulant child,' and separately told The New York Times he had been 'ticked' at Mills for 'not being real cordial to the president.'** SSA reinstated both contracts on March 7 amid bipartisan backlash, and Dudek apologized to Mainers; Democrats later called for his resignation. Dudek has since offered other explanations, including a September 2025 claim that he deliberately worded his order so it would be reversed.

official: John Thune, Senate Majority Leader
offense_category: Inserting an Undisclosed Self-Benefiting Provision Into Must-Pass Government Funding Legislation, Creating a Personal Financial Remedy for Himself and Colleagues Whose Records Were Lawfully Subpoenaed in a Federal Investigation
incident_summary:
In November 2025, as Congress finalized the legislative package ending the 43-day government shutdown, **Senate Majority Leader John Thune personally directed staff to insert language into one of the package's full-year spending bills allowing senators (and at least one House member) to sue the federal government for up to $500,000 in statutory damages per violation if their phone or electronic records were subpoenaed or obtained without their knowledge.** The provision followed an October 2025 disclosure, via documents released by Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, that then-Special Counsel Jack Smith's 2023 investigation into efforts to overturn the 2020 election had obtained phone records for eight Republican senators -- Lindsey Graham, Bill Hagerty, Josh Hawley, Dan Sullivan, Tommy Tuberville, Ron Johnson, Cynthia Lummis, and Marsha Blackburn -- around the time of the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack, plus at least one House member, all via lawful grand jury subpoena. The provision was inserted without a standalone vote or public debate and signed into law along with the rest of the funding package. It drew immediate bipartisan criticism once discovered: House Speaker Mike Johnson said he was 'surprised and very frustrated,' calling it 'way out of line' and saying he was 'very angry about it'; Senate Finance Committee Democrat Ron Wyden called it a 'tax dollar giveaway to Republican senators.' Johnson announced the House would hold a standalone vote to strip the provision. The House did so, voting 426-0 to repeal the provision -- a second unanimous House repeal vote followed weeks later after the first stalled -- but Thune refused to bring the repeal to a Senate floor vote, and Sen. Graham personally blocked a Democratic attempt to force one, arguing that he and the other senators whose records were obtained were 'wronged' and deserved a 'remedy.'

Update 2026-10-26: On January 22, 2026, the House unanimously attached a repeal of the provision to a must-pass funding package. Graham, who had said he planned to sue under the law, held up the package; on January 30 he lifted his hold in exchange for future votes, which he said Thune supported, on ending sanctuary city policies and on letting groups and private citizens, "not members of Congress," harmed by the Jack Smith investigation have their day in court. The repeal, which also removed the requirement that phone companies notify senators, was signed into law on February 3, 2026, according to Sen. Martin Heinrich, whose repeal bill it carried. Graham died in July 2026.

The provision created a specific financial remedy (up to $500,000 per violation) for a defined class of people that includes the inserting official's own colleagues, following a lawful federal investigative action (grand jury subpoenas) that the underlying prosecutors were legally entitled to pursue without notifying the targets in advance
Once discovered, the provision drew bipartisan public criticism, including from the inserting official's own party's House leadership

The House voted unanimously, twice, to repeal the provision, but the Senate leader who inserted it refused to allow a floor vote on repeal, and a directly financially-interested senator (Graham) personally blocked an attempt to force one

official: Scott Bessent, Treasury Secretary / White House
offense_category: Enhanced Financial Surveillance Framed Around an Ethnic Community, Over Internal Treasury Objections -- a facially geographic order (Hennepin and Ramsey counties) launched and publicly framed as a crackdown on alleged fraud in Minneapolis's Somali community, raising civil-liberties and discriminatory-targeting concerns about blanket reporting imposed without individualized suspicion
incident_summary: **John Hurley, Treasury's Under Secretary for Terrorism and Financial Intelligence (the sanctions and anti-money-laundering chief), began telling associates in recent weeks that he was leaving his post after privately objecting to White House-backed plans to crack down on alleged fraud in Minnesota's Somali immigrant community, The Washington Post reported February 25, 2026, citing seven people familiar with the matter.** Bloomberg News had reported on February 15 that Hurley was set to leave after friction with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Per the Post, Hurley had recently conveyed his concerns to Bessent about a project to enhance federal monitoring of international payments from the Minneapolis area, and two of the people said he raised data-privacy concerns; ACAMS's moneylaundering.com, summarizing the Post's report, said he did so before the surveillance commenced. The project was FinCEN's Minnesota Geographic Targeting Order, issued January 8, 2026 and in effect from February 12, 2026, which requires banks and money transmitters in Hennepin and Ramsey counties to report added information on transfers of $3,000 or more going abroad. Career officials who helped formulate the order also objected, viewing it as clumsy and an inefficient way to root out fraud (one person said some saw it as an overtly partisan use of Treasury resources); Hurley shared at least some of their concerns, but they were effectively overruled, two people told the Post. Hurley denied the premise of the Post's article, calling his team "the tip of the spear pushing back to stop Somalia fraud in Minnesota," and an administration official told the Post the Minnesota disagreement was not the only reason he was leaving and that he and Bessent had mutually agreed the role was not the right fit. The Post wrote that his departure underscores how some Trump allies in the federal government are uneasy with the extent of White House directives to deploy law-enforcement tools against Minneapolis's Somali community, part of the administration's broader crackdown on alleged benefits fraud in the state. Hurley's departure follows several other senior Treasury exits since August 2025, including Deputy Treasury Secretary Michael Faulkender and two successive Bessent chiefs of staff. By April 28, 2026, the Post reported that Hurley had left his post and was expected to be nominated as U.S. representative to the OECD. The underlying financial-surveillance program has continued: FinCEN renewed the order on August 7, 2026, effective August 11, 2026 through February 6, 2027, per FinCEN's order and Treasury's press release; a February 27, 2026 FinCEN order exempting banks from recording or reporting transfers by certain categories of originators was carried into the renewal, which is otherwise unchanged -- the program remains active and has been formally extended past its original term, not ended. The Senate confirmed Hurley as U.S. Ambassador to the OECD on August 7, 2026.

The surveillance program, though facially geographic (Hennepin and Ramsey counties), was launched and publicly framed as a crackdown on alleged fraud in Minneapolis's Somali community rather than as a general anti-fraud measure
Hurley's objection was reportedly overruled, and per the Post's sources he left his post over it rather than continue implementing the program
Reporting indicates some administration allies themselves expressed unease with the program's scope, suggesting the concern was not limited to political opponents

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Categorical Clemency for 2020 Election-Subversion Co-Conspirators (Fake Electors, Legal Architects, and Aides), Issued via Sweeping, Ambiguously-Worded Proclamation Language -- clemency is a constitutional presidential power, not itself unlawful; the accountability claim concerns the pardon's non-individualized scale, its later-rejected attempted extension beyond its intended targets, and its practical inability to reach the parallel state prosecutions it was seemingly meant to shield.
incident_summary:
On November 7, 2025, Trump signed a proclamation granting 'full, complete, and unconditional' federal pardons to 77 people over conduct connected to efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss; U.S. Pardon Attorney Ed Martin posted it online late on Sunday, November 9. Named recipients included Trump's former personal lawyer Rudy Giuliani, former chief of staff Mark Meadows, attorney Sidney Powell, former Justice Department official Jeffrey Clark, who championed Trump's efforts to challenge his loss, and lawyers Kenneth Chesebro, Jenna Ellis, and John Eastman, alongside dozens of Republican 'fake electors' from Michigan, Arizona, Nevada, Georgia, and Wisconsin. **The proclamation's operative language was sweeping rather than individualized, granting pardon for conduct relating to the 'advice, creation, organization, execution, submission, support, voting, activities, participation in, or advocacy for or of any slate or proposed slate of Presidential electors, whether or not recognized by any State or State official, in connection with the 2020 Presidential Election,' as well as for 'any conduct relating to their efforts to expose voting fraud and vulnerabilities in the 2020 Presidential Election.'**

Because the presidential pardon power under Article II reaches only federal offenses, and none of the named recipients had been charged with a federal crime over their 2020-election conduct (Special Counsel Jack Smith's federal case charged Trump himself, not these co-conspirators as defendants), the pardon left the parallel state prosecutions of many of the same people legally untouched. Those included Georgia's 2023 racketeering indictment of Trump and 18 others (including Giuliani, Meadows, Chesebro, Ellis, and Eastman), Arizona's fake-elector indictment of 18 people, Nevada's refiled fake-elector case, and Wisconsin's forgery case against three Trump aides, including Chesebro. Several had already run into roadblocks, but all sat under state authority the federal pardon has no power to reach. Michigan's fake-elector charges against its 15 remaining defendants had already been dismissed in September 2025 by a state judge who said there was not enough evidence to prove intent.

Harrison Floyd -- an ex-Marine and MMA fighter who worked on Trump's 2020 campaign, and one of the 77 people named on the pardon list for his role in the Georgia fake-electors racketeering case -- also faced a separate federal charge. It stemmed from a February 2023 incident in which he allegedly rushed at and assaulted two FBI agents (spitting in their faces, per reporting) sent by then-Special Counsel Jack Smith to serve him a subpoena in the federal 2020-election-subversion investigation, an incident with no direct connection to the fake-electors conduct itself. Floyd's attorney, Carlos Salvado, told ABC News in November 2025 that the pardon's broad 'any conduct relating to their efforts to expose voting fraud' language might extend to the unrelated assault charge, saying only 'there is an argument.'

Legal scholars, including Loyola Law School's Justin Levitt (a former DOJ official), warned at the time that the proclamation's broad, non-individualized wording could unintentionally sweep in people Trump did not intend to cover. That warning proved accurate: Matthew Laiss, federally charged in September 2025 with double voting in the 2020 election (in person in Florida and by mail in Bucks County, Pennsylvania), invoked the proclamation's broad language as a defense. The Justice Department itself told the federal court it did not consider Laiss covered, stating it had consulted the Office of the Pardon Attorney and could 'explicitly confirm' Laiss fell outside the proclamation's intended scope.

By January 2026, Georgia's racketeering case had been dropped by the prosecutor who took it over after the Fulton County district attorney was disqualified. Floyd's case went the other way from Laiss's. On January 7, 2026, federal prosecutors moved to dismiss Floyd's assault charge, a decision reporting tied to the clemency order; DOJ did not publicly explain its decision or address the apparent inconsistency with its Laiss position. Six days later, on January 13, a federal judge ruled the pardon did not apply to Laiss, finding he had not applied for or received the pardon certificate the proclamation's own terms require. Within a week, the same ambiguous pardon language was allowed by DOJ itself to end a federal prosecution for allegedly assaulting FBI agents in the line of duty, and rejected by a federal judge as a shield for Laiss's alleged double voting.

Laiss was subsequently found guilty of the underlying voter-fraud charges by a federal jury in March 2026. That same month, on March 9, Michigan's attorney general said she would not appeal the September 2025 dismissal, ending that state's prosecution. In June 2026, Arizona's attorney general dismissed her office's case against the 18 defendants, vowing to bring it back to a grand jury. On July 15, 2026, Laiss was sentenced to six months of house arrest and three years of probation. In August 2026, a Nevada judge dismissed that state's case against its six electors, finding a lack of evidence that they intended to deceive government officials; the attorney general's office plans to appeal. A fake-electors case remains ongoing in Wisconsin.

offense_category: Pardon of and Reported Consideration of a Diplomatic Appointment for a Convicted Public-Corruption Felon Turned Political Ally -- clemency and appointment power are constitutional presidential prerogatives, not themselves unlawful; the accountability claim concerns rewarding political loyalty from a convicted corrupt official rather than any specific legal violation
incident_summary: Rod Blagojevich, the former Illinois governor convicted on 17 corruption charges -- including trying to sell Barack Obama's vacated U.S. Senate seat -- had his 14-year prison sentence commuted by Trump in 2020, during Trump's first term. Blagojevich subsequently rebranded himself as a vocal Trump supporter, describing himself as a 'Trump-ocrat.' **On February 7, 2025, Politico reported Trump was reportedly considering Blagojevich for U.S. ambassador to Serbia, noting Blagojevich had recently met with Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić. Days later, on February 10-11, 2025, Trump went further and granted Blagojevich a full pardon, forgiving the corruption convictions for which his sentence had previously only been commuted.**

Trump then granted Blagojevich a full pardon, forgiving the underlying convictions rather than merely ending the remaining sentence

official: Donald Trump, President (signed Executive Order 14168, whose Sec. 4(c) ordered the change); William K. Marshall III, Director, Federal Bureau of Prisons (approved the February 2026 replacement policy)
offense_category: Accountability concern, not alleged as a legal violation by Trump personally: a presidential order directing the Bureau of Prisons to stop spending federal funds on hormone therapy and other gender-affirming care for transgender federal inmates. A federal judge found the Bureau's implementing policy likely arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act and pretextual; the inmates' Eighth Amendment (cruel and unusual punishment) claims are undecided. Preliminary findings only; litigation ongoing
incident_summary: On January 20, 2025, his first day back in office, President Trump signed Executive Order 14168, which recognizes only two sexes. Its Section 4(c) directs the Attorney General to ensure that the Bureau of Prisons revises its medical-care policies and "that no Federal funds are expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate's appearance to that of the opposite sex." The Bureau issued two memoranda in February 2025 to carry it out, the second stating that "no Bureau of Prisons funds are to be expended" on such care. A federal judge later found that the named plaintiffs' "access to hormone medications and social accommodations was subsequently cut off or reduced"; **one, Alishea Kingdom, went forty days without her hormone medication**, and she described anxiety, panic attacks and suicidal ideation. On March 7, 2025, Kingdom and two other transgender inmates, Jas Kapule and Solo Nichols, represented by the ACLU and the Transgender Law Center, sued in federal court in Washington, D.C. On June 3, 2025, Senior U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth certified a class of Bureau inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria and blocked the order and the memoranda as applied to their care, finding the memoranda likely arbitrary and capricious for lack of a reasoned explanation. By then the named plaintiffs' hormone access had been restored, though not their social accommodations. On February 19, 2026, Bureau Director William K. Marshall III approved a replacement policy, Program Statement 5260.01, "Management of Inmates with Gender Dysphoria." It says psychotherapy "should be prioritized," ends sex trait modification surgeries, bars starting anyone on hormones, puts every inmate now receiving hormones on a "tapering plan," and ends social accommodations such as clothing, makeup and wigs, which the Bureau will "remove or confiscate" when practicable. The Bureau said it adopted the policy "independently of" the order and supported it with a 43-page memo citing "the latest scientific information" and security concerns. On June 17, 2026, Lamberth blocked the new policy as well, writing that "despite providing gender-affirming care to inmates in its custody for years, the government cites in the Program Statement zero evidence from its own medical or mental health professionals to support its conclusions," and finding that the policy appears pretextual and "reverse engineered" to implement the order. Because such prison injunctions expire after 90 days, he renewed it on August 26, 2026, barring enforcement from September 15 to December 14, 2026. On September 18, a divided D.C. Circuit panel refused to pause that order, finding the government unlikely to defeat the claim that the Bureau failed to adequately consider "its own experience providing gender-affirming care under its prior policy"; Judge Walker dissented. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the Supreme Court to step in on September 28. On October 21, 2026, the Court denied the application in a one-sentence order that gave no reasons; Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito would have granted it. The Bureau said in court records that about 600 inmates were receiving hormone therapy in 2025; the ACLU says the class covers about 1,000 people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. The case continues in the district court and on appeal.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Using Official U.S. Trade and Sanctions Authority to Attempt to Shield a Foreign Political Ally From a Legitimate Foreign Prosecution -- not itself a domestic criminal charge, addressed here as a foreign-policy/abuse-of-power accountability concern
incident_summary: In a July 9, 2025 letter to Brazil, Trump threatened a 50% tariff on Brazilian goods, explicitly citing and denouncing the ongoing coup-plot prosecution of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro -- an ally Trump has publicly supported -- as a politically motivated "witch hunt." **Trump followed through by executive order, imposing a 40% additional tariff (bringing total duties on many Brazilian goods to 50%) and separately invoking the Global Magnitsky Act -- a sanctions law designed for human-rights abusers and corrupt officials -- against Alexandre de Moraes, the Brazilian Supreme Court justice overseeing the Bolsonaro case, freezing his U.S.-based assets and barring his travel to the United States.** The administration also revoked U.S. visas for 8 of Brazil's 11 Supreme Court justices and other Brazilian officials. In August 2025 the State Department separately revoked the visas of Health Ministry officials tied to the Mais Médicos program, which had brought Cuban doctors to Brazil, citing what it called a Cuban forced-labor scheme, and then the visas of Health Minister Alexandre Padilha's wife and 10-year-old daughter; Padilha's own visa had already expired. Despite this pressure campaign, a five-justice panel of Brazil's Supreme Court convicted Bolsonaro by a 4-1 vote and on September 11, 2025 sentenced him to 27 years and three months in prison; Justice Moraes, the case's lead judge, pointed to "overwhelming evidence" of a plot to assassinate then-President-elect Lula and Moraes himself, part of which he said was printed inside the presidential palace. On September 22, 2025, the U.S. extended the Magnitsky sanctions to Moraes's wife, Viviane Barci de Moraes, and a family-linked company, and revoked the visas of more Brazilian officials, including Attorney General of the Union Jorge Messias, which the White House framed as a further response to the conviction. Brazilian President Lula publicly framed his government's refusal to intervene in the judiciary as a defense of national sovereignty, and his domestic popularity rose amid the confrontation, while Brazil simultaneously expanded trade ties with China as U.S.-Brazil relations strained. In October 2025, the first formal U.S. proposal for negotiating the tariffs, later revealed by O Estado de S. Paulo, contained 21 demands, mostly on trade but including that Brazil hold "free and fair" 2026 elections and not arrest or arbitrarily restrict the participation of "political dissidents," which Brazil's government read as a reference to Bolsonaro; Brazil refused to negotiate those points. Relations then thawed: after an October 26, 2025 Trump-Lula meeting on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit in Kuala Lumpur, which Lula described as "surprisingly good," Lula said Trump had assured him an agreement would be reached, and in November 2025 Trump signed Executive Order 14361 exempting coffee, beef, and certain other agricultural products from the 40% tariff. Bolsonaro began serving his sentence in November 2025 after Justice Moraes declared the case closed at the end of the appeals period. On December 12, 2025, the Treasury removed Moraes, his wife, and the linked company from its sanctions list. On February 20, 2026, after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the emergency-powers law (IEEPA) does not authorize tariffs, Trump signed an order ending all IEEPA tariffs, a category that included the 40% Brazil tariff. In March 2026, Justice Moraes granted Bolsonaro temporary humanitarian house arrest after he was hospitalized with pneumonia, and he extended it in July 2026. A new dispute followed a May 2026 White House meeting that Lula said had improved relations: on June 1, 2026, the U.S. Trade Representative, concluding an investigation opened at Trump's direction in July 2025 under Section 301 of the Trade Act, proposed a 25% tariff on many Brazilian products, citing alleged unfair practices in areas including electronic payments, digital trade, ethanol, anti-corruption enforcement and illegal deforestation. The proposal became entangled with Brazil's October 2026 presidential race: Lula accused Bolsonaro's son Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, a presidential candidate, of lobbying Washington for the tariffs, while Flávio Bolsonaro denied it and asked the administration to delay any decision until after the election. On June 16, 2026, Brazil's Supreme Court sentenced Bolsonaro's son Eduardo Bolsonaro, a former congressman living in the U.S., to four years and two months in prison after finding him guilty of courting U.S. interference in his father's trial through sanctions on the court's justices and tariffs on Brazilian goods; he said he had not been properly notified of the proceedings. On July 15, 2026, USTR imposed the 25% tariff, effective July 22, with exemptions including beef, coffee, rare earths, energy products and aircraft; Lula called it unjustified and said Brazil would invoke its Reciprocity Law and the WTO. On October 24, 2026, Reuters, citing 10 current and former U.S. officials, reported that two State Department political appointees, Darren Beattie, a senior advisor overseeing Brazil policy, and Ricardo Pita, since promoted to deputy assistant secretary, led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power. According to three of those officials, the pair told U.S. diplomats in Brazil it was U.S. policy to restore Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil's leader, pivoted to backing Flávio Bolsonaro's candidacy after the September 2025 sentence, and told embassy staff not to interact with rival conservative contenders; the 10 officials said the pair successfully pushed punitive measures including the sanctions on Moraes and the designation of Brazil's PCC and Comando Vermelho gangs as terrorist groups. Reuters could not determine how far they acted on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio, or how much their influence decided the gang designation, and a State Department spokesman did not address the specific claims. Flávio Bolsonaro led the October 4, 2026 first round, but Lula won the October 25 runoff with about 51.8% of the vote, according to Brazil's electoral court. The next day Trump, saying he had not endorsed anyone, told reporters it "looked like another rigged election" without offering evidence, while demurring when asked whether he would take any action over the result. Flávio Bolsonaro called for the result to be annulled and, Reuters reported, left for the United States despite a Brazilian Supreme Court order to surrender his passports in a money-laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing; the White House press office said the State Department would issue visas to him and his family. A Trump adviser told CNN that Trump had approved letting him into the United States and that administration officials, aware he had roughly 24 hours to surrender his passports, made clear he would be allowed entry. He landed in Miami with his wife and two daughters on October 28, and Trump told reporters, "I know that we gave him a pass to come into the country." This Brazil-specific pressure campaign was part of a broader pattern this tracker documents in a companion entry, which covers parallel U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court and its judges over the Netanyahu/Gallant arrest warrants, and informal pressure on France over Marine Le Pen's conviction.

offense_category: Presidential Pardon of Political Allies Convicted of Federal Corruption, Accompanied by a Factually False 'Biden Over-Prosecution' Narrative -- clemency is a constitutional power, not itself unlawful; the accountability question is the falsity of the administration's own stated justification for it
incident_summary: Former Tennessee House Speaker Glen Casada and his top aide Cade Cothren were convicted on 17 federal charges, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering, for operating a fake consulting firm ('Phoenix Solutions,' run under the false identity 'Matthew Phoenix') that funneled taxpayer and campaign money -- including a $52,000 legislator-mailer program -- back to themselves. Casada was sentenced to 36 months in prison in September 2025; Cothren received a shorter sentence. On November 10, 2025, Trump granted both men pardons. A White House official justified the pardons by claiming 'the Biden Department of Justice significantly over-prosecuted these individuals for a minor issue involving constituent mailers -- which were billed at competitive prices, never received a complaint from legislators, and resulted in a net profit loss of less than $5,000.' **This framing is contradicted by the case's own timeline: the investigation began during Trump's first term, FBI raids on Casada's and Cothren's properties occurred in January 2021 while Trump was still president, and the judge who oversaw the case and sentenced Casada was a Trump first-term appointee -- meaning no part of the prosecution, investigation, or sentencing occurred under a Biden-appointed official or during the Biden administration's DOJ leadership.**
elements_required: Casada and Cothren were convicted at trial (not merely charged) on 17 felony counts including wire fraud and money laundering conspiracy
Casada received a 36-month federal sentence, indicating the convictions were for substantive, not de minimis, offenses

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Presidential Directive Overriding Scientific Advisory Process on Childhood Vaccine Policy -- no criminal or civil legal violation established; the order was issued while a separate court stay (see this tracker's separate ACIP litigation entry) already blocks implementation of a related prior vaccine-schedule overhaul, raising a legal-authority question about the order's practical effect
incident_summary: The May 2026 executive order documented here had two direct antecedents in late 2025. On November 7, 2025, NPR reported that a CDC committee hand-picked by RFK Jr. was scrutinizing the childhood vaccine schedule after Trump's own complaint that "they pump so much stuff into those beautiful little babies", and that the CDC was investigating splitting up the combined MMR shot; some public-health experts worried the review was part of Kennedy's campaign against vaccines, amid new measles and whooping cough outbreaks. Then, on December 5, 2025, Trump signed a memo directly ordering federal health agencies to reconsider the childhood vaccine schedule and potentially align it with "peer, developed countries," after praising advisers for scrapping the longstanding hepatitis B birth-dose recommendation for newborns; the memo instructed the HHS Secretary and CDC director to revise U.S. standards if they deemed foreign practices "superior" -- the same "peer nations" framing and hepatitis B rollback that recur in the December 2025 HHS assessment and executive order below. On May 29, 2026, Trump signed Executive Order 14407, directing the CDC and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) to realign the U.S. childhood vaccine schedule with that December 2025 HHS assessment, which had called for reducing the number of recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11, reasoning that the U.S. recommends more childhood vaccines than "peer nations" such as Denmark and more than twice as many vaccine doses as some European countries. The order followed the CDC's January 2026 overhaul of the immunization schedule under HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a memo by then-acting CDC Director Jim O'Neill that cut the vaccines recommended as routine for children from 17 to 11, limited several to high-risk groups, and moved rotavirus, COVID-19, influenza, hepatitis A, hepatitis B and meningococcal shots to shared clinical decision-making -- an overhaul the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts stayed on March 16, 2026, along with the appointments of 13 ACIP members Kennedy named between June 2025 and January 2026 and all votes the panel had taken, leaving the recommendations in place before June 2025 in effect pending litigation (the same underlying ACIP litigation this tracker documents in detail in a separate entry, which should be checked for that litigation's current status rather than this entry). **EO 14407 steers CDC/ACIP toward a specific numerical and substantive vaccine-schedule outcome via presidential directive, notwithstanding that a federal court has already found the government's process for changing the schedule, including bypassing ACIP, disregarded the scientific method, and that the schedule remains under an active judicial stay.** On August 10, 2026, Trump signed a second executive order, EO 14420 ("Delivering Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations for Americans"), which reaffirms rather than supersedes EO 14407 and elaborates it into three specific categories: vaccines recommended for all children (including measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, and polio), vaccines for high-risk groups only (including RSV and dengue), and vaccines moved into a shared clinical-decision-making category between parents and doctors (including hepatitis A/B, rotavirus, influenza, and COVID-19). It also states that the combined MMR vaccine should be given as three separate single-disease shots once domestically available (while keeping combination vaccines available), and that childhood immunizations should be given at separate visits where feasible. According to an October 1, 2026 vaccine-policy column published by CIDRAP, Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump's nominee to lead the FDA, helped develop that order, and flu vaccines remain recommended for everyone 6 months and older this season because the order's call to end that recommendation for children has been held up by a legal challenge. EO 14420 is not self-executing: Section 3 directs an HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines to deliver an implementation plan within 90 days, and the order itself states it creates no enforceable right or benefit against the government. The order explicitly acknowledges that implementation of the administration's prior vaccine-schedule directives "has been delayed due to litigation over the composition" of ACIP -- the same litigation covered in detail in the separate entry noted above, which covers the litigation side of the dispute while this entry covers the presidential-directive side. EO 14420 assigns that 90-day implementation plan to the statutory Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines, which HHS had revived in August 2025 after it lay dormant since 1998, naming NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya chair, with CDC and FDA representatives. The 90-day deadline runs to approximately November 8, 2026. HHS published a formal Request for Information in the Federal Register on August 24, 2026 (Docket No. HHS-OS-2026-0332), seeking public comment on whether the three categories used in federal vaccine recommendations (routine/universal, risk-based, and shared clinical decision-making) are adequate or should be revised -- a direct follow-on to EO 14420's 90-day implementation-plan mandate. The comment period closed September 20, 2026. On September 18, 2026, speaking in the Oval Office with Kennedy beside him, Trump said his administration would be "demanding" that drug companies split certain childhood vaccines into five smaller doses given at six-month intervals, "so that a small amount of the vaccine gets pumped into the body," and claimed the change would bring a "massive reduction in autism." He offered no evidence, did not say which vaccines he meant, and HHS did not answer CNN's request for details. **Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, told CNN the plan "would not work" and would give vaccines "in a manner in which they wouldn't be protective," and extensive scientific studies have found no evidence linking vaccines to autism.** The remarks came a day after Kennedy told a conference of Children's Health Defense, the anti-vaccine group he founded, "you have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House."
elements_required: The order steers a scientific advisory process that traditionally operates at arm's length from direct presidential or political direction toward a predetermined, quantified outcome: it names an HHS assessment calling for recommended childhood vaccines to be cut from 17 to 11 as "a guiding resource" and directs CDC/ACIP to take "any appropriate steps" to update the schedule in line with it

The order was issued while a federal court stay from the same underlying litigation already blocks implementation of a substantively similar prior schedule change, raising a documented tension between the executive order's direction and the current legal status of childhood vaccine policy

The order's stated justification (international comparison to 'peer nations') is a policy argument, not itself evidence the underlying scientific/evidentiary process was followed -- the same arbitrary-and-capricious concern already found by a federal court regarding the related ACIP panel decisions

Trump, as the official directly issuing the order, is the accountable official for its content and timing, distinct from Kennedy's separate, already-documented role in the underlying ACIP panel dispute

offense_category: Attempted unilateral executive takeover of an independent, statutorily bipartisan watchdog commission, circumventing 42 U.S.C. § 1975's requirement that the President designate the Commission's chair only "with the concurrence of a majority of the Commission's members" -- NOT charged; a political/institutional dispute, not a criminal matter
incident_summary: **In April 2025, the White House sent a 'de-designation' email to Rochelle Garza, the Democratic chair of the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights (a term she had held since March 17, 2023), seeking to demote her and elevate Republican commissioner Peter Kirsanow as the new chair. Garza refused to step down, citing 42 U.S.C. § 1975's requirement that a chair be designated only with the concurrence of a majority of the Commission's members -- not by unilateral presidential letter -- and declined to recognize a vote on new leadership as procedurally in order.** The White House renewed the attempt in March 2026, when the deputy director of the Office of Presidential Personnel sent a similar letter seeking the same change; Garza again resisted, and the Commission's own website continued to list her as chair as of at least June 12, 2026 (she is documented moderating an official Commission hearing on immigration enforcement in Minnesota that month). The dispute sits against the backdrop of a major, unrelated Supreme Court ruling: on June 29, 2026, the Court decided Trump v. Slaughter 6-3, overruling the 91-year-old Humphrey's Executor v. United States precedent and holding that for-cause removal protections for heads of independent multi-member agencies exercising executive power violate separation of powers. That case arose from Trump's firing of two Democratic FTC commissioners, not from the Civil Rights Commission, but its reasoning substantially strengthens the legal argument that Trump could lawfully remove or override Garza going forward -- a development not yet resolved as of this entry's creation.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: First Amendment Viewpoint Discrimination — Denial of Press Access (established precedent: Sherrill v. Knight, D.C. Cir. 1977, holding that White House press credential denials must not be arbitrary or based on viewpoint) — civil litigation, not criminal
incident_summary:
On Friday, September 18, 2026, Trump announced on Truth Social that he was banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House over their "constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" The next day, journalists from all three outlets had their credentials pulled and were blocked from entering the White House. **After the outlets sued on September 21, Trump personally defended the ban in Truth Social posts, baselessly claiming the outlets' coverage posed "a threat to our National Security," and wrote that the White House was "instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS,"** adding "Why should I have to give 'access' to such people?" Before the suit, the White House had also removed CNN from its scheduled turn as White House pool representative -- the network had been set to accompany Trump to New York for the United Nations General Assembly -- and the five-network television pool declined to replace it: pool chair Bryan Boughton of Fox News wrote that there would be "no replacement pool put in place," and ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC said in a joint statement that "the public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government" and that "no administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting." On September 22, letters from the White House Press Office, filed in court that day with the Justice Department's opposition to the outlets' motion, accused them of behavior "in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information." The letters listed stories on the Iran war, U.S. munitions and missile-interceptor stocks, the East Wing bunker, security funding for the White House ballroom, and a Politico Playbook item on the Republican midterm convention, and gave the outlets until 5 p.m. on September 25 to contest the decision. The Justice Department's brief argued that "access to the White House is a privilege—not a right," asked that the 1977 Sherrill v. Knight precedent be overruled, and urged that the appeals court's reasoning in the AP case, which, in a stay ruling, let the White House weigh viewpoint in the Oval Office and similar restricted spaces, be applied to the whole White House complex. **One of the Politico stories the letters cited, a June report quoting a "senior administration official" who put the odds of a preliminary Iran deal at 80 to 85 percent, reportedly came from Vice President JD Vance speaking on a background press call the White House itself hosted**, according to the media newsletter Status and to HuffPost, which cited a Washington Post report on a recording of the call; on September 21, Vance had publicly called the ban "totally appropriate." Early on September 24, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly granted a 14-day temporary restraining order requiring the White House to restore the revoked hard passes, finding the outlets likely to succeed on their Fifth Amendment due-process claim because the passes were revoked without notice or a chance to be heard, and writing that he was skeptical, on the record before him, that national security was the actual motivation; he also noted that, in most cases, the reporters who wrote the stories cited in the letters did not hold hard passes. Reporters from all three outlets were turned away again that morning and began getting back onto the complex around noon. The five-network pool resumed coverage on September 25, but that night White House guidance left CNN off Air Force One for Trump's September 26 trip to Tennessee, a flight on which it had been scheduled to fly as the TV pool network; the Associated Press noted that Kelly's order addressed hard passes and did not directly address pool duties; the outlets' lawyer said they believe it does. On September 27, Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the ban on ABC, saying of the White House, "It is a privilege, and not a right, to be there," and the next day the outlets asked Judge Kelly for a preliminary injunction to keep their access in place after the restraining order expires on October 8, citing CNN's exclusion from pool duty.

Update 2026-10-11: On Monday, October 5, 2026, the White House kept Politico off Air Force One for Trump's trip to Nebraska; Politico had been scheduled to serve as the out-of-town print pool reporter, who reports on the president's movements and activities for other outlets. CNN, citing sources, reported that the White House offered the seat to other outlets in the travel-pool rotation and that they uniformly declined, so the trip had no primary print pooler, and that since the restraining order the White House had repeatedly barred CNN from Air Force One on its turns as TV pool representative. Judge Kelly's order required the White House to restore the outlets' hard passes; as The Washington Post noted, it does not extend beyond the White House grounds or mention the traveling press pool. The White House's position is that pool spaces are different: communications director Steven Cheung said the judge "basically ordered them to renew their access back to the White House, but that's different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One," and a spokesperson said traveling aboard Air Force One "is a privilege not a right." That night, the outlets' final brief on the preliminary injunction cited the CNN and Politico Air Force One exclusions. At an October 8 hearing, Kelly extended the restraining order through October 13 and said he expected to rule on the injunction by then; the Justice Department asked that any injunction be limited to restoring the hard passes and be put on hold during an appeal.

Update 2026-10-13: The Justice Department's Antitrust Division is investigating whether ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC, the five networks that make up the White House TV pool, violated federal antitrust law when they briefly suspended pooled coverage after CNN was removed from its pool turn. A Justice Department official told NBC News the department sent "civil investigative demands" on Friday, October 9, 2026, and The New York Times, citing people with knowledge of the action, reported that officials demanded communications and materials related to the pool. Department spokeswoman Emily Covington said on October 10: "Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws." The reports did not name the official who directed the probe or tie it to Attorney General Todd Blanche personally; according to The Washington Post, the division has no Senate-confirmed head, since Trump ousted his first pick, Gail Slater, and his nominee, FCC general counsel Adam Candeub, has not been confirmed. The Post also noted that Laura Loomer, a far-right activist close to the administration, had urged an antitrust investigation of the networks after they suspended pool coverage, though it said it was not clear whether she played any role. Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, called the probe "another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists."

Update 2026-10-14: On October 13, 2026, Judge Kelly granted the outlets' motion for a preliminary injunction, barring the defendants other than Trump from enforcing the September 18 decision to revoke the outlets' hard passes while the case proceeds. In a 26-page opinion he found the outlets likely to succeed not only on their due-process claim but also, for the first time in the case, on their First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint-discrimination claims, writing that "President Trump's own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes to alter their reporting on him" and, of the ban, "Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination." He found "no evidence in the record" that Trump made the decision on national security grounds "from the get-go," and said the record suggests that rationale was "merely a post-hoc justification," while adding that no one should read the ruling to suggest Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded. He denied the Justice Department's request to stay the injunction pending appeal and required the outlets to post a $1 bond. As CNBC noted, the order does not compel the White House to restore the outlets' access to the Oval Office or Air Force One; Trump had said in September that he would appeal any ruling blocking the ban.

Update 2026-10-16: On Wednesday, October 14, 2026, the Justice Department filed a notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit from Judge Kelly's October 13 opinion and order. According to States Newsroom, the notice contained no legal arguments, the administration's brief outlining its case is due November 13, and the outlets' response is due by the end of November. As TheWrap noted, the appeal does not automatically suspend the injunction, so the outlets keep their White House credentials for now. In a background statement, the White House said "The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President's Oval Office" and that the outlets are "completely capable of reporting from directly outside." States Newsroom also reported that, according to a court filing, the ban ousted 78 journalists from the three outlets.

Update 2026-10-25: The White House has kept CNN off Air Force One on its turns as the TV pool network, even after the preliminary injunction. In a letter to Justice Department attorney Michael K. Velchik late on Monday, October 19, 2026, CNN attorney Theodore J. Boutrous Jr. wrote that the White House had denied CNN access to the plane no fewer than four times, each time when CNN was the scheduled pool network, according to the Associated Press: for Trump's trip to the U.N. General Assembly, a football game in Knoxville, Tennessee, a trip to Texas and Oklahoma, and, most recently, a trip to Georgia and Florida. He wrote that the White House had given no explanation, called the exclusions "efforts to retaliate and discriminate against CNN based on the content of its news coverage" that are "mistaken, counterproductive, and unlawful," and gave the White House two days to respond: "If these actions persist, CNN will have no choice but to return to the court to defend its rights, and it is prepared to fight as long as is necessary to secure them." The Justice Department did not respond to the AP's request for comment, but a White House official told TheWrap on October 20 that "No person and no journalist have a constitutional right to access to the President's Oval Office, Air Force One, or other sensitive and private facilities."

Update 2026-10-29: On Monday, October 26, 2026, six citizens who say they rely on White House reporting -- human rights advocate Kenneth Roth, media and political journalist Daniel Froomkin, Yale historian Beverly Gage, New York City high school civics teacher Peter Schmidt-Nowara, Lawfare editor-in-chief Benjamin Wittes and Daily Pennsylvanian editor-in-chief Ethan Young -- filed a separate lawsuit, Roth v. Trump, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, represented by the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University and Yale Law School's Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic, and moved for a preliminary injunction. According to the Associated Press, the suit names Trump, Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Communications Director Steven Cheung and Secret Service Director Sean M. Curran as defendants. It challenges what the Knight Institute calls the administration's policy of restricting or revoking the access of White House journalists whose reporting the president says is "false" or "fake," arguing that the spaces opened to White House journalists are a "public forum" under the First Amendment and that the policy deprives the plaintiffs and the public of those journalists' independent reporting. Unlike the outlets' suit, it seeks a broad injunction protecting the entire White House press corps from retaliation. Asked about the suit, the White House responded with a statement attributed to an unidentified official: "No person may demand access to the Oval Office."
