rebuttal_anticipated: The administration's defense in court: access to the White House is "a privilege, not a right"; Sherrill and Karem were wrongly decided and should be overruled; the appeals court's reasoning in the AP case should extend to the whole White House complex; the ban was not retaliatory because other outlets equally critical of the President kept their access; letters sent to the outlets on September 22 gave adequate after-the-fact notice and a chance to respond; and the outlets' reporting threatened national security and breached "standards of professionalism and decorum" -- a broad claim of executive discretion over access rather than a factual rebuttal of the outlets' account. Outside court, the White House has said the order restored hard passes, not pool access to the Oval Office or Air Force One, where travel "is a privilege not a right," and in court it asked that any injunction be limited to the hard passes; after CNN threatened to return to court over its Air Force One exclusions, a White House official said "No person and no journalist have a constitutional right to access to the President's Oval Office, Air Force One, or other sensitive and private facilities." On the pool, the Justice Department says the networks' suspension of coverage was a group boycott: "Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act," and the Antitrust Division is "simply investigating" whether the networks broke the antitrust laws. After the preliminary injunction, the White House said in a background statement that "The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President's Oval Office" and that the outlets are "completely capable of reporting from directly outside," and the Justice Department appealed the ruling. Asked about a separate suit filed by six citizens on October 26, the White House said in a statement attributed to an unidentified official, "No person may demand access to the Oval Office."
comeback: Sherrill v. Knight holds that once a general practice of press access exists, it cannot be withdrawn from specific outlets based on the content of their reporting or editorial decisions -- and here the viewpoint-based motive is unusually explicit and self-documented: Trump's own Truth Social post cited "constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" as the reason, and his subsequent Truth Social posts offered no evidence for the separately claimed national-security rationale. The same judge, Timothy Kelly, previously found a materially similar credential revocation (Acosta, 2018) likely unlawful and ordered access restored on an emergency basis. On September 24, 2026, he did so again here, finding the outlets likely to succeed on their due-process claim under Sherrill and Karem v. Trump, and noting that nothing in the record predating the suit suggested national security motivated the revocations, and that most of the reporters behind the stories the White House cited did not hold hard passes. On October 13 he granted a preliminary injunction, finding the outlets likely to succeed on their First Amendment claims as well: "Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination." One of the Politico stories the White House cited to justify the ban reportedly quoted Vice President JD Vance himself, speaking anonymously on a background call the White House arranged. The outlets argue the pool exclusions are the same viewpoint-based ban by other means: "The President may not use Air Force One as a flying press briefing room and then claim standardless discretion to exclude news organizations based on the content of their reporting or their perceived editorial viewpoint." When Politico was barred, the outlets the White House offered its seat to all declined it, according to sources cited by CNN. The Justice Department then opened an antitrust investigation of the five pool networks over their suspension of pool coverage after CNN's removal; Jonathan Kanter, the Biden administration's antitrust chief, said, "This is not even in the same zip code of an antitrust violation. ... It's literally freedom of speech."
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of a documented pattern of White House press-access restrictions aimed at outlets whose coverage the President objects to, following the earlier Wiles/AP press-access case, in which the Associated Press was shut out of the Oval Office, Air Force One and other pool spaces after refusing to adopt the "Gulf of America" name. This case is larger in scale -- three outlets' hard passes revoked and their reporters barred from the White House complex entirely, rather than one outlet excluded from specific restricted spaces -- and more direct in how it was announced: in the AP case, Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt conveyed the exclusion and told the AP it came at President Trump's direction, while here Trump announced the ban himself on Truth Social and defended it in public remarks. Chief of Staff Susan Wiles is a named defendant in the AP lawsuit, the outlets' lawsuit and the citizens' suit. In court, the Justice Department asked that the appeals court's AP-case reasoning be extended from the Oval Office and similar spaces to the whole White House complex, and that the 1977 precedent protecting reporters' access be overruled, relying in part on a Pentagon press secretary's declaration and an appeals court stay order favoring Pentagon escort rules for reporters. The national-security rationale was raised only after the outlets announced their suit, and Judge Kelly, granting a preliminary injunction, said the record suggests it was "merely a post-hoc justification." The pool networks' refusal to replace CNN then drew a Justice Department antitrust investigation, extending the dispute from the outlets' access to the networks' own coordination.

incident_summary.base: On Friday, September 18, 2026, Trump announced on Truth Social that he was banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House over their "constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" The next day, journalists from all three outlets had their credentials pulled and were blocked from entering the White House. **After the outlets sued on September 21, Trump personally defended the ban in Truth Social posts, baselessly claiming the outlets' coverage posed "a threat to our National Security," and wrote that the White House was "instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS,"** adding "Why should I have to give 'access' to such people?" Before the suit, the White House had also removed CNN from its scheduled turn as White House pool representative -- the network had been set to accompany Trump to New York for the United Nations General Assembly -- and the five-network television pool declined to replace it: pool chair Bryan Boughton of Fox News wrote that there would be "no replacement pool put in place," and ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC said in a joint statement that "the public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government" and that "no administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting." On September 22, letters from the White House Press Office, filed in court that day with the Justice Department's opposition to the outlets' motion, accused them of behavior "in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information." The letters listed stories on the Iran war, U.S. munitions and missile-interceptor stocks, the East Wing bunker, security funding for the White House ballroom, and a Politico Playbook item on the Republican midterm convention, and gave the outlets until 5 p.m. on September 25 to contest the decision. The Justice Department's brief argued that "access to the White House is a privilege—not a right," asked that the 1977 Sherrill v. Knight precedent be overruled, and urged that the appeals court's reasoning in the AP case, which, in a stay ruling, let the White House weigh viewpoint in the Oval Office and similar restricted spaces, be applied to the whole White House complex. **One of the Politico stories the letters cited, a June report quoting a "senior administration official" who put the odds of a preliminary Iran deal at 80 to 85 percent, reportedly came from Vice President JD Vance speaking on a background press call the White House itself hosted**, according to the media newsletter Status and to HuffPost, which cited a Washington Post report on a recording of the call; on September 21, Vance had publicly called the ban "totally appropriate." Early on September 24, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly granted a 14-day temporary restraining order requiring the White House to restore the revoked hard passes, finding the outlets likely to succeed on their Fifth Amendment due-process claim because the passes were revoked without notice or a chance to be heard, and writing that he was skeptical, on the record before him, that national security was the actual motivation; he also noted that, in most cases, the reporters who wrote the stories cited in the letters did not hold hard passes. Reporters from all three outlets were turned away again that morning and began getting back onto the complex around noon. The five-network pool resumed coverage on September 25, but that night White House guidance left CNN off Air Force One for Trump's September 26 trip to Tennessee, a flight on which it had been scheduled to fly as the TV pool network; the Associated Press noted that Kelly's order addressed hard passes and did not directly address pool duties; the outlets' lawyer said they believe it does. On September 27, Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the ban on ABC, saying of the White House, "It is a privilege, and not a right, to be there," and the next day the outlets asked Judge Kelly for a preliminary injunction to keep their access in place after the restraining order expires on October 8, citing CNN's exclusion from pool duty.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-11: On Monday, October 5, 2026, the White House kept Politico off Air Force One for Trump's trip to Nebraska; Politico had been scheduled to serve as the out-of-town print pool reporter, who reports on the president's movements and activities for other outlets. CNN, citing sources, reported that the White House offered the seat to other outlets in the travel-pool rotation and that they uniformly declined, so the trip had no primary print pooler, and that since the restraining order the White House had repeatedly barred CNN from Air Force One on its turns as TV pool representative. Judge Kelly's order required the White House to restore the outlets' hard passes; as The Washington Post noted, it does not extend beyond the White House grounds or mention the traveling press pool. The White House's position is that pool spaces are different: communications director Steven Cheung said the judge "basically ordered them to renew their access back to the White House, but that's different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One," and a spokesperson said traveling aboard Air Force One "is a privilege not a right." That night, the outlets' final brief on the preliminary injunction cited the CNN and Politico Air Force One exclusions. At an October 8 hearing, Kelly extended the restraining order through October 13 and said he expected to rule on the injunction by then; the Justice Department asked that any injunction be limited to restoring the hard passes and be put on hold during an appeal.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-13: The Justice Department's Antitrust Division is investigating whether ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC, the five networks that make up the White House TV pool, violated federal antitrust law when they briefly suspended pooled coverage after CNN was removed from its pool turn. A Justice Department official told NBC News the department sent "civil investigative demands" on Friday, October 9, 2026, and The New York Times, citing people with knowledge of the action, reported that officials demanded communications and materials related to the pool. Department spokeswoman Emily Covington said on October 10: "Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws." The reports did not name the official who directed the probe or tie it to Attorney General Todd Blanche personally; according to The Washington Post, the division has no Senate-confirmed head, since Trump ousted his first pick, Gail Slater, and his nominee, FCC general counsel Adam Candeub, has not been confirmed. The Post also noted that Laura Loomer, a far-right activist close to the administration, had urged an antitrust investigation of the networks after they suspended pool coverage, though it said it was not clear whether she played any role. Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, called the probe "another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists."

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-14: On October 13, 2026, Judge Kelly granted the outlets' motion for a preliminary injunction, barring the defendants other than Trump from enforcing the September 18 decision to revoke the outlets' hard passes while the case proceeds. In a 26-page opinion he found the outlets likely to succeed not only on their due-process claim but also, for the first time in the case, on their First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint-discrimination claims, writing that "President Trump's own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes to alter their reporting on him" and, of the ban, "Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination." He found "no evidence in the record" that Trump made the decision on national security grounds "from the get-go," and said the record suggests that rationale was "merely a post-hoc justification," while adding that no one should read the ruling to suggest Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded. He denied the Justice Department's request to stay the injunction pending appeal and required the outlets to post a $1 bond. As CNBC noted, the order does not compel the White House to restore the outlets' access to the Oval Office or Air Force One; Trump had said in September that he would appeal any ruling blocking the ban.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-16: On Wednesday, October 14, 2026, the Justice Department filed a notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit from Judge Kelly's October 13 opinion and order. According to States Newsroom, the notice contained no legal arguments, the administration's brief outlining its case is due November 13, and the outlets' response is due by the end of November. As TheWrap noted, the appeal does not automatically suspend the injunction, so the outlets keep their White House credentials for now. In a background statement, the White House said "The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President's Oval Office" and that the outlets are "completely capable of reporting from directly outside." States Newsroom also reported that, according to a court filing, the ban ousted 78 journalists from the three outlets.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-25: The White House has kept CNN off Air Force One on its turns as the TV pool network, even after the preliminary injunction. In a letter to Justice Department attorney Michael K. Velchik late on Monday, October 19, 2026, CNN attorney Theodore J. Boutrous Jr. wrote that the White House had denied CNN access to the plane no fewer than four times, each time when CNN was the scheduled pool network, according to the Associated Press: for Trump's trip to the U.N. General Assembly, a football game in Knoxville, Tennessee, a trip to Texas and Oklahoma, and, most recently, a trip to Georgia and Florida. He wrote that the White House had given no explanation, called the exclusions "efforts to retaliate and discriminate against CNN based on the content of its news coverage" that are "mistaken, counterproductive, and unlawful," and gave the White House two days to respond: "If these actions persist, CNN will have no choice but to return to the court to defend its rights, and it is prepared to fight as long as is necessary to secure them." The Justice Department did not respond to the AP's request for comment, but a White House official told TheWrap on October 20 that "No person and no journalist have a constitutional right to access to the President's Oval Office, Air Force One, or other sensitive and private facilities."

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-29: On Monday, October 26, 2026, six citizens who say they rely on White House reporting -- human rights advocate Kenneth Roth, media and political journalist Daniel Froomkin, Yale historian Beverly Gage, New York City high school civics teacher Peter Schmidt-Nowara, Lawfare editor-in-chief Benjamin Wittes and Daily Pennsylvanian editor-in-chief Ethan Young -- filed a separate lawsuit, Roth v. Trump, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, represented by the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University and Yale Law School's Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic, and moved for a preliminary injunction. According to the Associated Press, the suit names Trump, Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Communications Director Steven Cheung and Secret Service Director Sean M. Curran as defendants. It challenges what the Knight Institute calls the administration's policy of restricting or revoking the access of White House journalists whose reporting the president says is "false" or "fake," arguing that the spaces opened to White House journalists are a "public forum" under the First Amendment and that the policy deprives the plaintiffs and the public of those journalists' independent reporting. Unlike the outlets' suit, it seeks a broad injunction protecting the entire White House press corps from retaliation. Asked about the suit, the White House responded with a statement attributed to an unidentified official: "No person may demand access to the Oval Office."

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Contested Exercise of D.C. Home Rule Act Emergency Authority -- Section 740 permits the President to direct D.C.'s police for limited emergency purposes, but the scope, duration, and factual predicate ('crime emergency') of this invocation raised separation-of-powers and home-rule concerns rather than an established statutory violation
status: Federal control of D.C. police lapsed Sept. 10, 2025. Judge Jia Cobb found the Guard deployment likely unlawful Nov. 20, 2025, but the D.C. Circuit stayed that ruling Dec. 17 pending an appeal still unresolved; the deployment is extended through January 2029.
incident_summary: On August 11, 2025, President Trump announced he was placing Washington, D.C.'s Metropolitan Police Department under direct federal control and deploying the National Guard, invoking Section 740 of the D.C. Home Rule Act to declare a "crime emergency." Within about a week, roughly 800 D.C. National Guard troops had been mobilized, with additional state National Guard units en route, alongside roughly 500 newly deployed immigration and other federal agents patrolling the streets and operating checkpoints. Trump said he was acting "to rescue our nation's capital from crime, bloodshed, bedlam and squalor, and worse," but the city's own crime data showed violent crime had been declining for two consecutive years before the declaration: homicides fell 32% in 2024 (from a 2023 peak of 274, the city's highest since 1997, to 187) and continued falling roughly 12% further into 2025. D.C. officials and local commentators characterized the declared emergency as a pretext rather than a response to worsening conditions, noting that the district's justice system was already strained -- including by the administration's own purge of senior federal prosecutors who had worked on January 6 cases, documented separately in this database, and a years-long judicial vacancy backlog in the D.C. courts, which remained short-handed into 2026 (the Senate confirmed six Superior Court and two D.C. Court of Appeals judges on August 7, 2026); according to the D.C. Sentencing Commission, felony case filings in the Superior Court rose 44% in 2025, an increase Bloomberg Law reported coincided with the administration's push for more control over D.C. police and more federal prosecutions in the district. A documented case of wrongful detention arose within the same crackdown-era criminal-justice system: Kristal Rios Esquivel was arrested August 20, 2025 at the National Zoo, accused of trying to enter a restricted birdhouse staff entrance and spitting on a police sergeant during her arrest. She should have been brought to court on August 22 but was not brought before a federal magistrate judge until August 25 -- a three-day delay -- and at that hearing prosecutors did not seek her detention, instead recommending release on minimal conditions. She was ordered released but remained jailed for more than 19 hours afterward, until the afternoon of August 26, about six days after her arrest. **U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui wrote that the D.C. Department of Corrections had refused to release her over a "hit" in the warrant system from the very warrant for which she had appeared on August 25 -- a failure Faruqui called "false imprisonment," noting it was not the first time in the past four months that the court had encountered the problem.** The Department of Corrections said a routine database check had turned up an FBI warrant and that it held her until that warrant was cleared. A DOJ prosecutor ultimately intervened to clear the erroneous database entry. Faruqui questioned why compliance with a release order required such extraordinary effort. Reuters reported on September 4, 2025, based on interviews with nine current and former FBI employees, that the surge pulled FBI agents who normally work out of the public eye into routine, highly visible police work, emerging from unmarked cars in tactical gear -- the employees said as many as 1,000 unmarked FBI vehicles had been used in Washington during highly public scenes. FBI employees said the exposure risked burning vehicles the bureau relies on for undercover work against cartels, violent gangs, and foreign intelligence services; one employee said, "We can't use these cars to go undercover, we can't use them to surveil narcotraffickers and fentanyl suppliers or Russian or Chinese spies or use them to go after violent criminal gangs or terrorists." An FBI spokesman denied the employees' assertions. The surge, justified by the administration as a violent-crime crackdown, drew criticism for featuring many arrests for minor offenses while creating this operational-security cost to the FBI's own national-security and counterintelligence capacity. On September 4, 2025, D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb sued over the National Guard deployment. Federal control of the Metropolitan Police Department lapsed on September 10, 2025, when the 30-day Section 740 period ended without a congressional extension, after Mayor Muriel Bowser ordered continued cooperation with federal law enforcement; the National Guard deployment, which is not subject to that time limit, continued. On November 20, 2025, U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb ruled that the deployment was likely unlawful and blocked it, pausing her order for 21 days to allow an appeal. On November 26, two West Virginia National Guard members were shot while on patrol near the White House; Army Spc. Sarah Beckstrom died the next day, and Trump ordered 500 more troops to Washington. The D.C. Circuit administratively stayed Cobb's ruling on December 4 and, on December 17, a unanimous panel of Judges Patricia Millett, Gregory Katsas and Neomi Rao stayed it pending appeal, finding the president likely to succeed in arguing that he holds a unique power to mobilize the Guard in the federal district; the appeal remained pending as of September 2026. By August 2026 the deployment had been extended through January 2029, an extension a Defense Department estimate put at about $1.4 billion, and more than 4,600 military personnel from D.C. and 24 states and territories were still deployed as of August 4, 2026. Crime kept falling: Metropolitan Police Department figures showed overall crime down 20% and homicides down 32% (from 97 to 66) through August 7, 2026 compared with the same period of 2025, though how much of the decline was owed to the surge rather than longer-running local efforts remained disputed.
elements_required: Section 740 of the D.C. Home Rule Act authorizes the President to direct the Mayor to provide D.C. police services for federal purposes he determines are of a special nature and emergency circumstance, but was designed around brief, narrowly-defined emergencies -- its application here to a broad, open-ended 'crime emergency' declaration is the contested legal question, not a settled violation

The declared factual predicate (an ongoing crime crisis) is directly contradicted by the district's own published crime statistics, which showed two consecutive years of declining violent crime, including a 32% homicide drop in 2024 and continued decline into 2025

The scale of the federal response -- ~800 National Guard troops and ~500 federal agents -- and its timing followed, rather than preceded, documented strain on D.C.'s own justice-system capacity, including the administration's purge of federal prosecutors and a years-long local judicial vacancy backlog

official: Donald Trump, President (said he would personally be "the arbitrator" of who receives rewards under the Justice Department's fraud tip program); JD Vance, Vice President of the United States (chairs the administration's fraud task force; co-announced the program and presented its first payment to Nick Shirley)
offense_category: Accountability concern, not alleged as a legal violation: the President claiming personal, "binding" control over who receives cash rewards from a Justice Department program whose published rules leave every award to the department's "sole discretion" under 28 U.S.C. 530C(b)(1)(L), and promising payouts (a 1 percent commission, no limit, no criminal charges needed) that its published terms do not include. TAP notes that the reward statute names the President only for approving rewards of $250,000 or more and caps rewards at $3,000,000 unless another statute allows more. The concern is political control of a law-enforcement payment program, with its first payment going to an allied influencer. No lawsuit, ethics complaint or investigation has been reported
incident_summary: In December 2025, Nick Shirley, a 24-year-old right-wing YouTuber, posted a video alleging that Somali-run childcare centers in Minnesota were collecting public money without caring for children. The video drew national attention and the administration's interest; the Associated Press reported that inspectors said the centers were operating as expected, and a CBS News review of state records found that all but two had active licenses and "no recorded evidence of fraud" as of December 30, 2025. Shortly after the video was posted, federal officials announced about 2,000 more agents for the immigration enforcement surge in Minnesota. One woman featured in the video, the former head of a childcare center, pleaded guilty in July 2026 to wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud the United States. On October 20, 2026, Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who chairs the administration's fraud task force, announced in the Oval Office the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, or WHIP, run by the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division. The department's announcement and published rules say tips that lead to criminal charges in health care fraud and fraud on federal benefit programs (eight agencies' programs in the announcement, seven in the rules) can earn a reward of $10,000 to $30,000, awarded "in its sole discretion" under its reward authority, 28 U.S.C. 530C(b)(1)(L), and that its decisions are "neither appealable nor subject to judicial review." The Treasury committed $25 million to the three-year pilot. **At the announcement Trump said: "I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions. In other words, I'll determine whether or not the person is deserving, and I will be very generous, believe me."** He called it "binding arbitration," said tipsters would get a 1 percent commission on the fraud they uncover, and, asked about the gap with the department's terms, said there was no limit and criminal charges were not necessary. The White House referred reporters' questions back to his remarks. Vance said he and Trump created the program to encourage more people to report fraud like Shirley, and the White House said Trump would present Shirley a $10,000 check, which MPR News called the program's first payment; CBS Minnesota reported that Trump handed it to him in the Oval Office, while the Associated Press reported that no check was given in front of journalists. The department's rules require tips to contain original information that does not merely repeat news media or other public sources. By October 24, Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald, who leads the fraud division, said thousands of tips had come in; NewsNation reported that he described tipsters as also standing to receive "a potential 1% commission," a term the department's published rules do not contain. On October 26, Trump separately posted on Truth Social that "Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud!" He did not say where the money would come from, who would decide whether a tip qualified, or whether the offer was part of an existing federal program; a White House spokesperson referred NBC News to the post, and the Justice Department, asked whether it would administer the reward, told Newsweek, "We defer to the White House." NBC News noted there is no evidence of widespread voter fraud in U.S. elections.

incident_summary: Over 2025, NPR and OPB reported Trump had pardoned or commuted the sentences of more than 20 people convicted of serious drug-trafficking offenses, even as the administration escalated its rhetorical and military 'war' on drug trafficking. Notable examples include Ross Ulbricht, founder of the Silk Road dark-web drug marketplace, pardoned January 21, 2025 (tracked in this database's crypto-pardon pattern entry); Larry Hoover, founder of the Chicago Gangster Disciples gang tied to one of the largest drug-trafficking syndicates in the country, whose federal life sentences were commuted in May 2025 (Hoover remained in custody on a separate state murder conviction); Garnett Gilbert Smith, pardoned in May 2025 after a 25-year federal sentence for conspiring to distribute cocaine in Baltimore; and former Honduran president Juan Orlando Hernández, whose 45-year sentence for a large-scale cocaine-trafficking conspiracy was pardoned in December 2025, an episode that included Federal Bureau of Prisons staff providing him bespoke post-release logistical assistance (tracked in this database's Hernández pardon entry). At the same time this individualized-leniency pattern was unfolding, **the administration was expanding a lethal strike campaign against vessels merely suspected -- not charged, tried, or convicted -- of drug trafficking: beginning with a September 2, 2025 Caribbean strike in which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth allegedly gave a verbal 'leave no survivors' order before a follow-up strike killed two survivors clinging to wreckage** (tracked in this database's Hegseth boat-strike entry), the campaign grew to more than 60 strikes and over 200 deaths by mid-2026, with no captures, charges, or judicial review of the underlying trafficking allegations in any of the strikes.

offense_category: Exceeding presidential authority over state and federal election administration -- multiple federal courts have found provisions of the order unconstitutional or beyond executive power (separation of powers) -- NOT charged; a civil/constitutional dispute, not a criminal matter
incident_summary: On March 25, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14248, 'Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections,' which directed the Election Assistance Commission to require documentary proof of citizenship on the federal voter registration form, directed the Secretary of Defense to add the same requirement to the form military and overseas voters use, directed the Department of Homeland Security to review state voter rolls against federal immigration databases, and directed the Attorney General to act against states that count mail/absentee ballots received after Election Day even when cast on time. **A military-family group, the Secure Families Initiative, was among the plaintiffs in a lawsuit filed March 31, 2025, arguing the receipt-deadline change and citizenship-documentation requirements would disproportionately burden servicemembers and their families stationed abroad or deployed, who face mail delays and have long relied on postmark-based deadlines.** Multiple federal courts subsequently ruled against key provisions: in Washington, D.C., Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly permanently blocked the proof-of-citizenship requirement for the federal registration form in October 2025 and later the military-voter-form and public-assistance-agency provisions; in January 2026 a federal judge in Washington state permanently blocked key provisions for Washington and Oregon; and in June 2026 Judge Denise Casper in Massachusetts ruled for a coalition of 19 state attorneys general, permanently blocking the citizenship-documentation provisions and, for most of the plaintiff states, the funding-condition and ballot-receipt-deadline provisions (Wisconsin and states without post-Election Day receipt deadlines were excluded from parts of the ruling for lack of standing). The administration has appealed. Trump's second elections order, signed March 31, 2026, targets mail voting through the Postal Service and is being litigated separately.
elements_required: The order directs changes to how states administer federal elections, an area the Constitution's Elections Clause assigns primarily to state legislatures and Congress, not the President
Multiple federal courts have found specific provisions exceed presidential authority or are otherwise unconstitutional

incident_summary: On January 20, 2025, his first day back in office, Trump signed Executive Order 14148, rescinding a list of Biden-era executive orders and actions, including Executive Order 13989. **That Biden order had required every executive-branch appointee to sign an ethics pledge committing them not to accept gifts from lobbyists or lobbying organizations, and imposing a two-year "revolving door" ban preventing new appointees from working on regulations or contracts tied to their immediately prior employer or clients. The pledge also barred departing appointees from lobbying senior executive-branch officials until the end of the administration or for two years, whichever was later, and for senior appointees lengthened the one-year ban on contacting their former agency to two years. Rescinding it removed these restrictions for Trump's incoming appointees.** One immediate effect was lifting restrictions that would otherwise have continued to apply to former Biden-administration appointees after they left government, which Politico reported could make it easier for them to move into lobbying and other private-sector jobs. Trump did not issue a replacement ethics pledge or comparable restriction of his own for his administration's appointees, despite this being a step new administrations have typically taken, and none had been issued as of July 2026. That month, a Sludge review of second-quarter lobbying disclosures named former Trump administration officials who had moved into lobbying after leaving: three of them, from the Interior Department, the White House press office and the Vice President's office, were lobbying the agency they had recently left or the White House offices of their recent colleagues, and a fourth, a former White House Senate liaison, was lobbying senators and the Energy and Treasury Departments. Sludge wrote that none of this was illegal, because no ethics pledge or revolving-door restriction of Trump's own was in place to prevent it.

incident_summary: Extremity Care LLC, which sells 'skin substitute' wound-care products made from placental and other tissue, donated $5 million to the pro-Trump MAGA Inc. super PAC on February 24, 2025 -- a donation not publicly disclosed until July 31, 2025, buried on page 18 of the PAC's mid-year filing. The Biden administration had proposed a CMS rule limiting Medicare coverage of skin substitutes to products 'supported by evidence' of effectiveness, which CMS itself found would have excluded 92% of currently covered products (identifying only 17 with proven scientific validity) -- including Extremity Care's, which cost $7,812 to $11,051 per square inch, compared to $75 to $195 for proven alternatives. Days after the donation, Extremity Care co-owner Oliver Burckhardt attended a Mar-a-Lago donor dinner and spoke with Trump. The next morning, March 1, 2025, Trump posted on Truth Social attacking the rule and claiming, without evidentiary support, that it would cause '431,429 lost limbs annually and 187,286 additional deaths.' CMS, which had already pushed the rule's original effective date from February to April 13, 2025, announced on April 11, 2025 -- 40 days after Trump's post -- a further delay to at least January 1, 2026. **Between April and July 2025 alone, Medicare spent an additional $2.3 billion on skin substitutes while the rule remained blocked, on top of a broader spending surge in the category from a negligible amount in 2014 to more than $10 billion in 2024.** Extremity Care separately retained Trump fundraiser Brian Ballard as a lobbyist for $320,000 annually; Ballard's former employee, Susie Wiles, is Trump's White House Chief of Staff. In October 2025, Burckhardt attended a second Trump donor dinner, this one at the White House Rose Garden, and the New York Times later reported Extremity Care had been an anonymous $2.5 million donor to Trump's White House ballroom construction fund.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Executive Order Stripping Collective Bargaining Rights From Two-Thirds of the Federal Workforce, Allowed to Proceed After an Appeals Court Vacated an Injunction on a Retaliation Challenge -- documents a contested administration action still in litigation, not an allegation of illegality
incident_summary: President Trump signed Executive Order 14251, "Exclusions from Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs," on March 27, 2025, excluding roughly 40 agencies and subdivisions (including Defense, State, Treasury, HHS, and Veterans Affairs) from the Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute on stated national-security grounds, eliminating collective bargaining rights for wide swaths of the federal workforce. Federal employee unions sued, arguing the order was actually issued to retaliate against unions for challenging other administration policies, in violation of their free-speech rights. U.S. District Judge James Donato in San Francisco preliminarily enjoined the order on June 24, 2025, but after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals stayed that injunction on August 1, 2025, allowing enforcement to proceed, agencies moved through August 2025 to terminate union contracts covering hundreds of thousands of workers in quick succession: the EPA said on August 8, 2025 that it would no longer recognize its unions (AFGE, the National Association of Government Employees, the Engineers and Scientists of California, and the National Association of Independent Labor) and that all its contracts were terminated; **USDA notified union leaders on August 12, 2025 that it was ending contracts covering roughly 6,500 FSIS food-safety inspectors and about 1,650 APHIS employees, including roughly 1,500 plant inspectors, prompting a separate union lawsuit arguing that inspection work has nothing to do with national security**; and by August 31, 2025, VA, EPA, and Agriculture Department contracts had all been voided in the same wave (VA's termination specifically is documented in greater depth in this tracker's separate entry on the department's union defiance). Trump then expanded the order's scope: Executive Order 14343, "Further Exclusions From the Federal Labor-Management Relations Program," signed August 28, 2025 (published in the Federal Register September 3, 2025), added agencies including NASA, the U.S. Agency for Global Media, the Patent and Trademark Office's patents office, and the National Weather Service -- NASA's own implementation notice confirmed the agency would stop recognizing certain unions as exclusive bargaining representatives and halt collection of union dues on their behalf. On September 25, 2025, Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William K. Marshall III terminated the agency's collective bargaining agreement covering more than 30,000 correctional officers among its nearly 35,000 employees, represented by the Council of Prison Locals/AFGE, calling the union "an obstacle to progress instead of a partner in it." In Congress, a bipartisan effort to protect Defense Department civilians' bargaining rights via the FY2026 NDAA -- which had passed the House 231-196 in September 2025 -- was stripped from the final compromise bill in December 2025; a source familiar with the negotiations told Government Executive that only Sen. Lisa Murkowski among Senate Republicans ultimately pushed to keep the provision. On December 11, 2025, the House passed standalone legislation, the Protect America's Workforce Act (H.R. 2550), 231-195 with 20 Republicans in favor, to nullify both executive orders and restore bargaining rights; the National Active and Retired Federal Employees Association described the orders as having taken bargaining rights from about one million federal employees. The bill was received in the Senate on December 15, 2025, with no Senate vote recorded in the congressional bill-status records reviewed. On February 26, 2026, a three-judge panel of the 9th Circuit vacated Donato's preliminary injunction, concluding that on the preliminary record the unions had not shown a likelihood of success on their retaliation claim: assuming without deciding that they had made out a prima facie case, the panel found that the order had a legitimate grounding in national security concerns and that the government had shown Trump would have taken the same action even without the unions' protected speech. Judge John Owens, concurring, noted that because the panel was reviewing a preliminary injunction, a fully developed factual record could be materially different. The orders affect the bargaining rights of an estimated two-thirds of the federal civilian workforce. The panel amended its opinion on June 17, 2026, in an order that constituted the mandate of the court and directed that no petition for panel rehearing or rehearing en banc would be permitted, ending Ninth Circuit review of the injunction; no certiorari petition was filed. The panel expressly declined to address the unions' separate claim that the order exceeded the President's authority under 5 U.S.C. Section 7103(b)(1). That claim, the merits of the First Amendment retaliation claim, and the unions' Fifth Amendment claims all remain pending before Donato, where the parties are disputing whether the government must answer the unions' discovery requests before any motion to dismiss. A parallel challenge by the National Treasury Employees Union, argued before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in December 2025, remained undecided as of September 2026.

offense_category: Using U.S. Sanctions Authority to Punish or Pressure Foreign Judges and Courts Over Rulings Touching U.S. Personnel or Political Allies -- a pattern spanning the ICC, Brazil, and France, not itself a domestic criminal charge
incident_summary: Beyond the Brazil-specific sanctions on Justice Alexandre de Moraes over the Bolsonaro prosecution -- documented in full in this tracker's separate entry on that campaign, and lifted on December 12, 2025, when the Treasury removed Moraes, his wife and a linked company from its sanctions list -- Trump's administration built a broader pattern of using U.S. sanctions authority against foreign judges and courts whose rulings touched U.S. personnel or affected political allies. On February 6, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14203 authorizing sanctions against the International Criminal Court, in response to ICC arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant; the order's annex, published February 10, named ICC Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan as its first target. **On June 5, 2025, Secretary of State Rubio named four sitting ICC judges for sanctions -- Beti Hohler (Slovenia) and Reine Alapini-Gansou (Benin), over their role in authorizing the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants, and Solomy Bossa (Uganda) and Luz del Carmen Ibanez Carranza (Peru), over authorizing the ICC's investigation into U.S. personnel in Afghanistan.** The ICC, Amnesty International, and Human Rights Watch condemned the sanctions as an attack on international judicial independence. On July 18, 2025, U.S. District Judge Nancy Torresen in Maine barred the government from penalizing two American human rights advocates who had sued, Matthew Smith and Akila Radhakrishnan, for providing speech-based services to the ICC, finding the order likely violated the First Amendment; the injunction covers only those two plaintiffs and does not lift the sanctions on the designated ICC officials. Rubio added four more designations on August 20, 2025 -- judges Kimberly Prost (Canada) and Nicolas Guillou (France) and Deputy Prosecutors Nazhat Shameem Khan (Fiji) and Mame Mandiaye Niang (Senegal) -- and two more judges, Gocha Lordkipanidze (Georgia) and Erdenebalsuren Damdin (Mongolia), on December 18, 2025, three days after they voted with the majority to reject an Israeli appeal. On August 18, 2026, the State Department sanctioned ICC President Tomoko Akane and Senior Trial Lawyer Abdoulaye Seye; the ICC said nine of its eighteen judges, both deputy prosecutors, the former prosecutor and one staff member were by then under U.S. sanctions. On September 20-21, 2026, the Wall Street Journal and Reuters reported that the administration was preparing sanctions against the court itself that would prohibit most transactions with it after a grace period. Separately, after a French court convicted National Rally leader Marine Le Pen of embezzling European Union funds and barred her from running for office (March 31, 2025), Trump called her office ban a "very big deal" and wrote on Truth Social, "FREE MARINE LE PEN!" On May 28, 2025, according to French magistrate Magali Lafourcade -- secretary general of France's National Advisory Commission on Human Rights (CNCDH) -- two advisers from the State Department's Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor, Samuel D. Samson and Christopher J. Anderson, met her in Paris and steered a conversation that began on human rights toward Le Pen's case, seeking "elements indicating that this was a purely political trial to stop her running for president." Lafourcade made her account public in January 2026, on France 5's En societe program (reported by Newsweek) and in an interview with AFP (reported by the Guardian and republished by the Irish Times). She told AFP she immediately reported the exchange to the French foreign ministry -- "which is something I never do, as we are an independent institution and don't report the exchanges we have with diplomats" -- fearing a potential "manipulation of the public debate in France." The State Department did not comment in those reports. On July 7, 2026, the Paris Court of Appeal upheld Le Pen's conviction but cut her ban on holding office to 45 months, 30 of them suspended, leaving her formally eligible to run in 2027; she said she would appeal to the Court of Cassation. No U.S. sanctions against the French judges who tried Le Pen were identified in sourcing reviewed, distinguishing this instance from the ICC and Brazil actions. A Washington Post report (Sept. 12, 2025) said Trump's rebukes of judges and courtroom prosecutors had "extended far beyond the United States' borders," as he and his officials questioned the fairness of foreign court systems, including those of long-standing allies, whose rulings displeased him.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Selective Clemency Pattern -- Pardoning Convicted Fraudsters (Many Donors/Allies) While Publicly Launching a New Anti-Fraud Enforcement Initiative -- clemency is a constitutional presidential power, not itself unlawful; the accountability claim concerns the pattern's inconsistency and its ties to political/financial support
incident_summary:
The New York Times reported Trump has granted clemency to more than 70 people convicted of fraud across his two terms, including numerous donors and allies, with those pardoned owing a combined $700 million in restitution and fines that the clemency wiped out. Specific documented cases include Philip Esformes, sentenced to 20 years for a $1.3 billion Medicare/Medicaid fraud scheme prosecutors called the largest-ever criminal health care fraud case brought against individuals; Salomon Melgen, a Palm Beach doctor sentenced to 17 years for stealing more than $42 million from Medicare; Trevor Milton, founder of electric-vehicle startup Nikola, pardoned after he and his wife donated $1.8 million to the Trump campaign; and Julio Herrera Velutini, granted clemency after his daughter Isabela Herrera donated $2.5 million in December 2024 and $1 million in July 2025 to the pro-Trump PAC MAGA Inc. Trump's pardon of Republican donor Adam Kidan, and the pardon of former Tennessee state Sen. Brian Kelsey -- a campaign-finance-fraud case rather than a financial-fraud-against-victims case -- are tracked separately in this database as fitting the same pattern.

On April 23, 2025 -- two weeks after being sentenced to 18 months for willfully failing to pay over $10 million in employment and income taxes -- Trump pardoned healthcare executive Paul Walczak. Walczak's mother, GOP donor Elizabeth Fago, had helped spread Ashley Biden's stolen diary during the 2020 campaign to benefit Trump; the New York Times reported Walczak applied for the pardon days after Trump's inauguration, citing his mother's fundraising for Trump and other Republicans, and that Fago was then invited to a $1-million-per-person Mar-a-Lago fundraising dinner less than three weeks before the pardon came through. The sentencing judge had ordered Walczak to pay roughly $4.4 million in restitution alongside his 18-month sentence, declaring there is not a get-out-of-jail-free card for the rich; Trump's pardon relieved Walczak of both the prison time and the entire restitution obligation.

On May 28, 2025, Trump pardoned reality-TV stars Todd and Julie Chrisley, convicted of defrauding banks of more than $30 million and evading federal taxes -- part of a broader late-May 2025 pardon wave tracked in fuller detail in a companion entry in this database. In July 2025, Tim Leiweke, former CEO and co-founder of entertainment-venue developer Oak View Group, was indicted on a federal conspiracy charge for allegedly rigging the bidding process for the $375 million Moody Center arena at the University of Texas at Austin -- allegedly agreeing with a competitor that it would withdraw from the bidding in exchange for subcontracts; Leiweke pleaded not guilty, and Oak View Group itself, not formally charged, separately agreed to pay $15 million in penalties over the underlying conduct. Also in August 2025, former Puerto Rico Governor Wanda Vazquez Garced pleaded guilty to a reduced campaign-finance-violation charge over a scheme to finance her 2020 gubernatorial campaign, in a case that had begun 10 days after she endorsed Trump in October 2020.

**On November 26, 2025 -- less than two weeks after GPB Capital founder David Gentile reported to federal prison to begin a seven-year sentence for a $1.6 billion investor-fraud scheme -- Trump commuted his sentence and eliminated his $15.5 million restitution obligation to more than 10,000 defrauded investors**, per Politico's December 3, 2025 reporting; the sentencing court had received thousands of victim-impact statements, many from elderly retirees describing losing their life savings. The commutation is tracked in fuller detail, including a since-halted DOJ investigation into whether payments were made to secure it, in a companion entry in this database. On December 2, 2025, Trump granted a full and unconditional pardon to Leiweke. The Wall Street Journal reported, per an account Billboard separately confirmed, that a friendly round of golf between Trump and former Republican Congressman Trey Gowdy -- whom Leiweke had hired to lobby on his behalf in the criminal case -- factored into the pardon decision; Billboard reported that neither Leiweke nor OVG were major donors to Trump or either party, though OVG gave $250,000 to Trump's inauguration, so no campaign or PAC donation link comparable to this entry's other cases was identified, making this case's main documented connection to Trump personal/lobbying access rather than campaign contributions.

The Washington Post's December 19, 2025 investigation put a specific restitution figure on the Milton case for the first time -- prosecutors had argued Milton should pay defrauded investors $660 million, a calculation the sentencing judge never had the chance to finalize before Trump's pardon eliminated the obligation entirely, along with any prison time. The same investigation surfaced a further, previously undocumented case: Marian Morgan, sentenced in 2013 to nearly 34 years for running a Ponzi scheme and ordered to pay $17.5 million to dozens of defrauded investors, most of which remained unpaid -- despite Morgan having told a court in 2021, in a sworn statement, "I want to pay restitution to my victims so they know I am truly sorry for the damage I caused." The Post's reporting also identified at least 20 people who received Trump clemency in 2026 alone who were also forgiven of financial penalties totaling tens of millions of dollars, and quoted Elizabeth Oyer, who served as U.S. Pardon Attorney for three years until being fired two months into Trump's second term, on the pattern's effect: "It's having a detrimental effect on victims and taxpayers, and it's a windfall to the people who committed crimes."

The New York Times reported on October 20, 2026 that, with Herrera Velutini still unhappy with his misdemeanor plea, he had brought in Christopher Kise, a former member of Trump's personal legal team, to press for clemency, and that his daughter's $3.5 million in pro-Trump super PAC donations had not produced a pardon by fall 2025. In late October 2025, Isabela Herrera registered a Florida company, Concord Partners, and within days Alina Habba -- Trump's former personal lawyer, then still acting U.S. attorney for New Jersey and an adviser to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi -- agreed to become its general counsel at $10 million a year for four years plus bonuses, a deal guaranteeing her more than $50 million, per the Times; the firm "has no public profile and its business remains unclear" even to some people tied to the family's businesses. Habba formally started on January 1, 2026, while still a senior Justice Department adviser, and Trump pardoned Herrera Velutini on January 15, issuing an amended clemency order five days later that specifically covered his misdemeanor. People familiar with Habba's contract told the Times they believed she was hired to help with the pardon effort. Habba said any insinuation that her employment, which she said had been vetted and disclosed to the Justice Department, had anything to do with securing a pardon is false; the Justice Department said she never discussed clemency with anyone there, and a White House official said she played no role in the decision. Herrera Velutini's clemency was granted as part of a single pardon covering Vazquez Garced and her two co-defendants, Herrera Velutini and Mark Rossini, in the federal bribery/campaign-finance case described above. A White House official told CBS News the MAGA Inc. donations had nothing to do with the pardon, and the administration's pardon materials characterized the underlying prosecution as politically motivated. The Washington Post later reported, from an internal donor spreadsheet for Trump's White House ballroom, that a month after Herrera Velutini's charges were reduced to a misdemeanor in August 2025, his daughter had pledged $2.5 million to the ballroom and paid a first installment of $835,000, with a second payment due in October 2026; the Post said its reporting does not show the donations led to any government action. The ballroom donations are tracked in a companion entry in this database. On March 16, 2026, Trump signed an executive order establishing a new "Task Force to Eliminate Fraud," to be led by Vice President JD Vance, publicly framing fraud enforcement as an administration priority even as the pardon pattern continued. A further documented example: in November 2025, Trump pardoned nursing home operator Joseph Schwartz, who ProPublica reported had served just three months of a three-year sentence for a $39 million fraud scheme tied to his collapsing chain of care facilities. Families of patients who died or were harmed under Schwartz's ownership had won multimillion-dollar civil judgments against him, but ProPublica found many have recovered nothing, a debt now further complicated by his truncated sentence and clemency.

In May 2026, Trump commuted Marian Morgan's sentence "to time served with no further fines, restitution, probation or other conditions." A bicameral congressional oversight investigation (Sen. Welch, Reps. Min and Ruiz) launched that same month, sending pay-to-play inquiry letters to 17 pardon recipients including several named in this entry; the White House has denied any impropriety. The investigation escalated in June 2026: Welch and Min sent formal records-preservation requests to DOJ's Pardon Attorney, the White House Records Management office, the White House Pardon Czar, and the Secret Service, with a July 24, 2026 compliance deadline.

In letters sent October 6, 2026, Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Peter Welch and Reps. Dave Min and Mary Gay Scanlon asked HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin to answer questions by October 20 about any role they played in Trump's pardons, so Congress can "better understand the extent to which influence and access have overridden the standard pardon review process." The letter to Kennedy concerned Milton, who with his wife had given almost $2 million to a committee aligned with Trump's reelection and $750,000 to the Make America Healthy Again Alliance PAC aligned with Kennedy's agenda, per Federal Election Commission records CBS News cited, and it cited a June Reuters report that Kennedy advocated for Milton's pardon; a source close to Kennedy told CBS News he has privately said he will not advocate for any pardons. The letter to Zeldin concerned the pardon of Troy Lake, a Colorado diesel mechanic convicted in 2024 under the Clean Air Act, citing a statement from Lake's wife that appeared to credit Zeldin; a senior EPA official, speaking anonymously, said Zeldin "did not make a recommendation or suggestion." Rep. Jamie Raskin said in September that Democrats are gearing up to investigate "everybody along the assembly line of clemency for cash" in the next Congress.

A substantial share of those pardoned are documented donors or personal/political allies, with specific pardons following documented campaign or PAC contributions from the recipient or their family
The pardons collectively wiped out approximately $700 million in court-ordered restitution and fines owed to defrauded victims and taxpayers

offense_category: Nominating a Cabinet-Level Law-Enforcement Official (Attorney General) Who Faced Credible, Independently-Corroborated Allegations of Statutory Rape and Sex Trafficking of a Minor
incident_summary: On November 13, 2024, President-elect Trump nominated former Rep. Matt Gaetz to be Attorney General, the nation's top law-enforcement post overseeing federal sex-trafficking and civil-rights enforcement. Gaetz had faced a federal sex-trafficking investigation beginning in 2021 -- DOJ ultimately declined to bring charges -- but the House Committee on Ethics had separately been conducting its own investigation, effectively derailed when Gaetz resigned from the House the day after his nomination. **The Ethics Committee nonetheless later released its findings, concluding there was 'substantial evidence' Gaetz violated Florida's statutory rape laws, among other findings.** Newly unsealed court records reported by the New York Times on November 13, 2025 (one year after the nomination) detailed the vulnerable circumstances of the minor victim at the center of the case: she was a homeless high school junior living in a shelter with a parent, working at McDonald's, who joined a 'sugar dating' website in an effort to save money for braces, falsely listing her age as 18. She testified she was 17 when she met Greenberg -- a Gaetz associate later convicted in a broader sex-trafficking scheme -- through the site in April 2017, and that she first had sex with Gaetz, who paid her, in July 2017 at a party hosted by lobbyist Chris Dorworth. Gaetz has consistently denied the allegations, telling the Times the account was 'fiction' and that he 'never had sex with this person,' who he said had instead threatened to sue him for $2.3 million. Gaetz withdrew his AG nomination on November 22, 2024, nine days after it was announced, citing a desire to avoid becoming 'a needlessly protracted Washington scuffle' and 'a distraction' to the transition; CNN and other outlets reported the more direct proximate cause was that Trump personally told Gaetz he lacked the Senate votes for confirmation, amid senators' concerns over the same allegations.

The nomination collapsed specifically because Senate Republicans, aware of the same allegations, would not provide the votes for confirmation -- not because the White House withdrew it on the merits

The underlying allegations involve a documented pattern of vulnerability (homelessness, poverty, a minor's use of an adult 'dating' platform under a false age) that later, independently-sourced reporting corroborated in additional detail a year after the nomination collapsed

status: Gaetz was never confirmed and never served as Attorney General; DOJ's 2021-2023 sex-trafficking investigation ended without charges, and no subsequent criminal charge has been reported. The House Ethics Committee's 'substantial evidence' finding on statutory rape stands as an official congressional finding, contested by Gaetz's continued denial. Trump has not publicly commented on the November 2025 unsealed-records reporting as of this entry.
rebuttal_anticipated: Gaetz's own defense, on the record, is a categorical denial -- he says he never had sex with his accuser and that she instead attempted to extort him for $2.3 million -- and DOJ's own multi-year investigation, informed by the same underlying facts, did not result in criminal charges.
comeback: DOJ's decision not to charge and a House Ethics Committee's independent 'substantial evidence' finding of a specific state-law violation are not in tension -- criminal charging decisions turn on proof beyond a reasonable doubt and a range of prosecutorial-discretion factors, while the Ethics Committee applied its own, different evidentiary standard and concluded the evidence supported the violation regardless. Trump's own team's stated reason for the nomination's collapse -- insufficient Senate votes -- was itself a direct consequence of sitting Republican senators finding the same underlying allegations disqualifying, undercutting any characterization of the episode as adequately vetted or resolved in Gaetz's favor before the nomination was made.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Presidential Directive Withholding Federal Funding to Restrict Gender-Affirming Medical Care for Minors -- no criminal or civil legal violation established against Trump personally; the accountability question is the order's legal authority and its practical effect given sustained, largely successful court challenges
incident_summary: **On January 28, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14187, 'Protecting Children from Chemical and Surgical Mutilation,' directing federal agencies to withhold grant funding from medical institutions that provide gender-affirming care -- including puberty blockers, hormone therapy, and certain surgical procedures -- to patients under 19, and directing exclusion of these treatments from Tricare (military health coverage) and calling for restrictions under Medicare and Medicaid.** The order was challenged almost immediately: Lambda Legal filed suit on behalf of PFLAG in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland on February 4, 2025, and on March 4, 2025 the court issued a nationwide preliminary injunction barring the federal government from withholding funding from institutions on the basis that they provide this care to minors. The order's funding-cutoff provision has not been enforceable since that injunction. A second front opened in late 2025: a coalition of 19 states and the District of Columbia sued HHS and other federal defendants, adding Hawaii and Nevada and filing a motion for summary judgment on January 6, 2026 that challenged an HHS report (referred to in litigation as the 'Kennedy Declaration,' after HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.) cited to justify the restrictions; at oral argument on March 19, 2026 the presiding judge indicated an intent to partially grant the states' request to invalidate that declaration. On April 18, 2026, the judge instead fully vacated the declaration and permanently enjoined HHS from enforcing it, or any materially similar policy, against providers in the plaintiff states.
elements_required: Executive Order 14187 directed federal agencies to withhold funding from institutions providing specified gender-affirming care to minors, and to restrict coverage of that care under Tricare, Medicare, and Medicaid
A federal court issued a nationwide preliminary injunction within roughly five weeks of the order, finding sufficient legal basis to block its enforcement pending litigation
The order's funding cutoff has remained judicially blocked since that injunction, with no reporting found of it taking practical effect

A second, separate multi-state lawsuit specifically challenges the scientific/administrative basis (the HHS 'Kennedy Declaration') the administration has relied on to justify the underlying restrictions, which a federal judge vacated in full on April 18, 2026

CMS likewise maintains that its August 2026 Medicaid/CHIP rule rests on independent statutory authority and does not rely on the enjoined sections of the order.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Presidential Imposition of an Unauthorized Tax Via Proclamation -- a federal court found the $100,000 H-1B visa fee exceeded executive authority, violated the Administrative Procedure Act, and violated separation-of-powers principles by usurping Congress's exclusive taxing authority
incident_summary: In September 2025, Trump announced by proclamation a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions, dramatically increasing the cost of hiring highly skilled foreign workers. A coalition of 20 Democratic state attorneys general sued, and **on June 8, 2026, U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin in Boston ruled the fee unlawful, finding it constituted a tax Trump imposed without congressional authorization -- an authority the Constitution reserves to Congress -- and that the administration's implementation violated both the Administrative Procedure Act and constitutional separation-of-powers principles.** Despite the ruling, the court's order blocking the fee was temporarily paused on June 12, 2026 to allow an appeals court to consider the government's request for a stay; as a result, USCIS was again permitted to collect the $100,000 fee while the First Circuit considered that request, even after a federal court had found it unlawful. On July 24, 2026, the First Circuit Court of Appeals denied the government's request to stay Judge Sorokin's ruling, finding the administration had not shown it was likely to succeed on the merits; as a result, the fee has been unenforceable nationwide since that denial. Separately, a different lawsuit (brought by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the Association of American Universities) produced the opposite result: in December 2025 the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia upheld the fee, leaving two district courts in direct conflict; that ruling is on appeal before the D.C. Circuit, which heard oral argument on March 9, 2026 and had issued no ruling as of late September 2026. As of August 12, 2026 reporting, the administration was expected to seek emergency relief from the Supreme Court, but no such application had been reported as of late September 2026. Separately, on August 25, 2026, DHS proposed a new $103,265 fee on H-1B cap-subject petitions via notice-and-comment rulemaking rather than presidential proclamation, with comments due September 24, 2026 -- a different mechanism and different actor from the proclamation fee this entry tracks, noted here as forward-looking context. Proclamation 10973's 12-month restriction was due to lapse on September 21, 2026; on September 18, 2026, Trump signed Proclamation 11069 extending it, including the $100,000 payment requirement, for another 12 months, until September 21, 2027. The extension did not revive collection: the vacatur of the implementing agency policy remains in force while the government's First Circuit appeal proceeds, and USCIS has said it will comply with the court's order.
elements_required: Trump imposed the $100,000 H-1B fee via presidential proclamation rather than through congressional legislation, a documented procedural fact

A federal court (Judge Sorokin, D. Mass.) issued a reasoned ruling -- not merely a preliminary characterization -- finding the fee constituted an unauthorized tax exceeding executive authority, in violation of the APA and separation of powers

The fee's practical effect (a $100,000 per-petition cost) was substantial enough to function as a de facto barrier to H-1B hiring, relevant to assessing the fee as a policy lever rather than a routine administrative charge

Despite the unlawfulness finding, the fee remained collectible from June 12, 2026, when the district court administratively stayed its own ruling, until the First Circuit denied a stay on July 24, 2026 -- meaning the policy the court had found unlawful continued to have real-world effect for several weeks after that ruling

rebuttal_anticipated: The administration could argue the fee was a legitimate exercise of the President's authority to regulate immigration and protect domestic labor markets, that the proclamation followed established precedent for immigration-related fee-setting, and that the pending appeal could still vindicate the fee's legality.
comeback: A federal court's specific finding that this was an unauthorized tax -- not merely a disputed policy choice -- distinguishes this from ordinary immigration-fee-setting; the fee was collected for several more weeks during the appeal despite that finding, and in September 2026 the President extended the proclamation for another year while the court's vacatur of its implementing policy remained in force.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of the broader pattern in this tracker of executive actions that courts have found to exceed statutory or constitutional authority. More specifically, it parallels the IEEPA tariff program the Supreme Court struck down in February 2026: in both, a court found that the executive had imposed a revenue-raising charge without clear authorization from Congress, which holds the taxing power, and Judge Sorokin relied on that tariff decision in treating the $100,000 payment as a tax (a D.C. district court has ruled the other way on the H-1B fee, and both rulings are on appeal). The September 2026 one-year extension of the proclamation, signed while the vacatur of its implementing policy remained in force, keeps the policy on the books pending appeal rather than letting it lapse, though collection remains blocked.

official: Donald Trump, President of the United States
offense_category: 26 U.S.C. § 7217 -- federal law making it a felony for the President or other executive branch officials to request the IRS conduct, terminate, or otherwise influence an audit or investigation of a specific, named taxpayer
status: Threatened in April and May 2025 but not carried out: no sourcing reviewed shows the IRS opened a revocation proceeding against Harvard. Treasury and the IRS proposed rules on Sept. 3, 2026 that the Harvard Crimson said could give a new avenue to target Harvard's tax exemption.
incident_summary: After Harvard rejected a series of Trump administration demands in an April 11, 2025 letter -- including governance and leadership changes, altered hiring and admissions practices, and ending DEI programs -- Trump signaled on April 15, 2025 that he wanted Harvard to lose its tax-exempt status, and **multiple outlets (Washington Post, CNN, Inside Higher Ed) reported the next day that the administration had directly asked the IRS to revoke it. Legal experts immediately flagged that this appeared to violate 26 U.S.C. § 7217, the statute Congress passed specifically to bar the President and other officials from directing the IRS to investigate or act against a named taxpayer** -- a George Mason University tax law professor said he was unaware of any prior administration attempting something like this. Harvard filed suit April 21, 2025 to halt a related federal funding freeze. Trump renewed the threat publicly on May 2, 2025, saying revocation was 'what they deserve.' Harvard President Alan Garber called the threatened action 'highly illegal' in a Wall Street Journal interview the same day. Reporting in April 2025 indicated the Treasury Department separately made an inquiry to the IRS's then-acting chief counsel, Andrew De Mello, regarding rescinding Harvard's status, and that a formal revocation would require the IRS to first open a full audit and issue notice to Harvard -- a process with no sourcing reviewed confirming it was ever formally initiated. Harvard's own communications office stated 'there is no legal basis to rescind Harvard's tax-exempt status.' This action ran concurrently with, but is legally and factually distinct from, the administration's separate SEVP-certification revocation and its $2.6 billion research-funding freeze against the same university, each covered in its own TAP entry (the Harvard SEVP entry is on the DHS and ICE tab).
elements_required: Trump personally and publicly called for Harvard to lose its tax-exempt status, naming the specific institution rather than speaking generally about nonprofit tax policy
Multiple independent outlets reported the administration directly asked the IRS to act on this specific request, which is the conduct 26 U.S.C. § 7217 was written to prohibit
The timing directly followed Harvard's public refusal of the administration's broader demands, supporting a retaliatory rather than a routine tax-enforcement motive
Legal experts and Harvard's own leadership publicly characterized the threat as illegal, not merely controversial

evidence.maps_to_element: Documents the targeted institution's own legal characterization of the threat

evidence.maps_to_element: Shows the April 2025 threat was not carried out as a revocation, and that the administration's pressure on Harvard's tax status continued through new rulemaking

rebuttal_anticipated: The administration could argue Trump's public comments were political rhetoric rather than a formal presidential directive to the IRS, that any IRS review of Harvard's tax-exempt status could be independently justified on the university's own conduct (e.g., alleged failure to adequately address campus antisemitism, a legitimate basis for IRS scrutiny of a 501(c)(3)'s tax-exempt activities), and that no formal audit or revocation was ever actually opened, so no completed statutory violation has occurred -- only a threat.
comeback: Section 7217 by its own text criminalizes requesting IRS action against a named taxpayer, not only a completed revocation -- multiple outlets independently reported the administration directly asked the IRS to act, which is the prohibited conduct itself, not merely rhetoric about tax policy in the abstract. The timing (immediately following Harvard's public refusal of unrelated governance and DEI demands) undercuts a good-faith, viewpoint-neutral tax-enforcement rationale, and Trump's public framing ('what they deserve') was explicitly retaliatory rather than a stated tax-compliance concern.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of the same broader campaign against Harvard documented in the Harvard SEVP entry (international-student enrollment) and the Harvard funding-freeze entry (research funding) -- three separate federal levers (immigration, research funding, tax status) deployed against the same institution in the same several-week period after it refused the administration's governance demands.

MODERATE confidence on whether this rises to a prosecutable Section 7217 violation specifically, since no sourcing reviewed confirms the IRS ever formally opened an audit or issued a revocation determination -- the entry documents a well-corroborated threat and request, not a completed enforcement action.
