official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Pardon Followed by Federal Bureau of Prisons Special-Treatment Assistance to a Convicted Foreign Drug Trafficker -- extends this tracker's pardon-power pattern (see the Kidan donor pardon entry) to include post-pardon logistical favoritism by a federal agency
incident_summary: On November 28, 2025, Trump announced he would pardon Juan Orlando Hernández, the former president of Honduras, who had been convicted by a U.S. federal jury in March 2024 on cocaine-trafficking-conspiracy and related firearms charges and sentenced in June 2024 to 45 years -- a case Bloomberg called a landmark U.S. drug case. Trump's announcement came two days before Honduras's presidential election and was paired with an endorsement of Nasry "Tito" Asfura -- the candidate of Hernández's own National Party -- and a warning that if Asfura lost, "the United States will not be throwing good money after bad"; in a separate Truth Social post Trump had written, "Tito and I can work together to fight the Narcocommunists, and bring needed aid to the people of Honduras." Trump justified the pardon by claiming Hernández had been "treated very harshly and unfairly" and had been the victim of a "Biden setup," echoing a claim in Hernández's own letter to Trump that he had been politically persecuted by the Biden administration rather than legitimately prosecuted -- a characterization the underlying 2024 federal jury conviction on cocaine-trafficking and firearms charges directly contradicts. Trump formally granted the pardon on December 1, 2025, and Hernández was released the same day; on December 12 his lawyer asked the federal appeals court, where his appeal was pending, to dismiss the appeal as moot, vacate the judgment and send the case back for dismissal of the indictment; with the government not opposing, the Second Circuit granted the motion on April 8, 2026, vacating the judgment and remanding with instructions to dismiss the case as moot. ProPublica's investigation found that despite Hernández having an active ICE immigration detainer in place at the time of his release -- a formal request for law enforcement to hold a noncitizen for pickup by ICE -- **the Federal Bureau of Prisons scrambled for several hours to get the detainer removed (records show immigration officials lifted it just after 11 p.m. that night) so Hernández could walk free rather than be transferred to ICE custody. BOP then activated a four-man tactical team, paying at least three of its members overtime, to drive Hernández roughly six hours from a West Virginia high-security facility to the Waldorf Astoria hotel in Manhattan, rather than providing standard transportation.** Before he left, according to a source ProPublica cited, Hernández was allowed to use the prison captain's government phone to speak with BOP deputy director Joshua Smith, himself a Trump pardon recipient; Hernández's lawyer, Renato Stabile, told ProPublica that Smith then called him about a release plan. Immigration attorney Lena Graber of the Immigrant Legal Resource Center told ProPublica, "Most people with drug convictions would never get their ICE detainer removed just because the conviction was pardoned." Farmers protested the pardon in Tegucigalpa on December 4, 2025, and on December 8, 2025, Honduras's attorney general ordered domestic authorities and asked Interpol to execute a 2023 Honduran arrest order against Hernández -- signed by a Supreme Court magistrate and written to take effect if U.S. authorities freed him -- tied to the "Pandora" public-funds diversion case, in which prosecutors allege officials funneled more than 288 million lempiras (about $10.7 million) in public money through foundations toward political campaigns between 2010 and 2013, including at least 62 million lempiras (about $2.3 million) to movements tied to Hernández's 2013 presidential campaign. That arrest order and Interpol notice were not enforced while Hernández remained in the United States; a Honduran judge suspended both in late June 2026 after admitting his request to surrender voluntarily, allowing him to return to Honduras on July 26, 2026, at which point the "Pandora II" fraud and money-laundering prosecution began in earnest. That Honduran proceeding concerns Hernandez's own conduct rather than any U.S. official's, and is a separate accountability track from this entry's focus on the U.S. pardon and BOP conduct: at an August 3, 2026 hearing the Public Ministry, which had initially sought pretrial detention, did not oppose the defense's request for release, the state attorney's office (PGR) maintained its detention request, and a judge of the organized-crime and corruption court ordered him to face the case free under non-custodial measures; the case's initial hearing, rescheduled multiple times, opened August 12, 2026, resumed August 18 (defense presented 36 evidence items and moved for absolute nullity of the proceedings) and again August 24, 2026, before the court issued a definitive dismissal (sobreseimiento definitivo) on September 1, 2026, finding that the money's trail to Hernandez's campaign had not been established and that the relevant budget decisions belonged to the executive branch, which he did not then head; charges have also been dropped against former President Porfirio Lobo and ex-finance minister Wilfredo Cerrato. The Public Ministry and the PGR have appealed the dismissal.

official: Donald Trump, President (personally offered Ingrassia the unconfirmed GSA post after Ingrassia's Senate-confirmed nomination collapsed)
offense_category: Circumventing Senate Advice-and-Consent Review by Installing a Rejected Nominee in an Unconfirmed Position of Authority
incident_summary:
Trump nominated Paul Ingrassia, then DHS's White House liaison, to lead the Office of Special Counsel on May 29, 2025. During a July 2025 business trip to Orlando, Ingrassia allegedly arranged for a female colleague's hotel room to be canceled so she would share his room, Politico later reported. The complaint prompted an investigation by DHS's career human resources personnel, which found no wrongdoing. Accounts of the underlying complaint itself conflict. Ingrassia's attorney denied any last-minute room change occurred. The woman herself later told Politico she "never felt uncomfortable" and had not made a complaint, saying "a colleague misjudged the situation." Other reporting described her as having filed an HR complaint she later retracted, citing fear of retaliation.

In October 2025, Politico published text messages in which Ingrassia allegedly wrote that he has "a Nazi streak," called MLK Day something that should be "tossed into the seventh circle of Hell," and made other racist and antisemitic remarks. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the nomination was "not gonna pass," and Ingrassia withdrew before his confirmation hearing.

**Rather than abandon the appointment, Trump personally offered Ingrassia the GSA deputy general counsel post -- a position that does not require Senate confirmation -- in the Oval Office the evening before the November 13, 2025 announcement. Less than three weeks later, on December 1, 2025, Ingrassia was elevated again, to acting general counsel, GSA's top in-house legal position.** On December 3, 2025, Senate Homeland Security Committee Democrats led by Gary Peters (joined by Slotkin, Hassan, Blumenthal, Gallego, and Kim) sent a formal letter to GSA calling Ingrassia's continued employment "unacceptable" and demanding his removal. They cited both the unresolved text-message controversy and the hotel-room allegation. As of September 2026, Ingrassia remained GSA's acting general counsel. No removal in response to the senators' demand, and no DHS Inspector General outcome on the hotel-room allegation, have been identified in sourcing reviewed.
elements_required: Trump nominated Ingrassia to a Senate-confirmed post that collapsed specifically because of documented racist/antisemitic remarks, not an unrelated or partisan objection
Trump personally selected and offered Ingrassia an alternative post structured to require no Senate confirmation, rather than abandoning the appointment
Ingrassia was further elevated to GSA's top legal position within weeks, without any additional confirmation check on the way up
The pattern drew a formal, on-record removal demand from sitting senators on the relevant oversight committee, not just informal criticism

rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: the GSA deputy and acting general counsel posts are legitimate, lower-visibility administrative roles, distinct from the Senate-confirmed Special Counsel post. Trump has broad Article II latitude to staff non-confirmed positions as he sees fit. Ingrassia's own attorney disputes the authenticity of the text messages, and the hotel-room allegation was investigated and no misconduct was found.
comeback: The defense doesn't address the sequence. The Senate leader of the nominee's own party said the nomination could not pass over documented bigoted remarks. Within weeks, a presidential decision placed that same nominee into GSA's top legal post: the exact kind of appointment the Senate confirmation requirement exists to screen, reached instead through a position structured to avoid that screen. The authenticity dispute and the no-misconduct finding go to the strength of the underlying allegations, not to whether Trump chose to elevate Ingrassia specifically because the confirmed route had failed.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] An example of a broader pattern of using non-Senate-confirmed positions to install personally loyal appointees the confirmation process has already rejected or would likely reject.

MODERATE confidence on the sexual-harassment element specifically. The allegation and the resulting investigation are well-documented, but accounts conflict on whether the woman ever filed a complaint (some reporting describes one filed and later retracted; she told Politico she made none). The internal investigation reportedly found no misconduct, and Ingrassia's attorney separately disputes the authenticity of the racist/antisemitic texts. None of these disputes is settled fact. official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Unlawful Mass Removal of Inspectors General Without Statutorily Required Congressional Notice -- a federal judge later called the firings an "obvious" violation of the Inspector General Act, without a final merits ruling; a civil/administrative matter, not a criminal one
incident_summary: On January 24, 2025, Trump fired inspectors general at 17 federal agencies in a single night, including at the Department of Labor and other major departments. The Inspector General Act of 1978, as amended in 2022, requires the President to give Congress 30 days' advance notice of an IG's removal along with substantive, case-specific reasons -- neither was provided. Sen. Jon Ossoff warned in early February that the firings likely violated federal law and asked that they be rescinded. Eight of the fired inspectors general sued on February 12, 2025, seeking reinstatement. **On September 24, 2025, U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes wrote that Trump's violation of the law was "obvious," but declined to order reinstatement, reasoning that Trump could simply re-fire the same inspectors general after providing the 30-day notice the law required the first time, and stayed the case without deciding the merits or back pay.** Separately, in October 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a memo overhauling the Pentagon's own inspector general complaint process, requiring inspector general offices to decide within seven days whether complaints are backed by 'credible evidence' and directing that 'repeat complainants' be tracked -- changes oversight advocates said would discourage legitimate whistleblowing, coming as the broader 17-IG purge remained unremedied.
elements_required: Trump removed inspectors general at 17 federal agencies simultaneously, without the 30-day advance congressional notice the Inspector General Act requires
No case-specific substantive rationale for the removals was provided to Congress at the time, as the amended statute also requires
A federal court found the statutory violation "obvious," while leaving the final merits, including the constitutional question, undecided
Despite that finding, the court declined to reinstate the fired IGs, leaving the practical effect of the mass removal in place
A subsequent agency-level action (Hegseth's Pentagon IG memo) narrowed the Pentagon's IG complaint-handling procedures, in the same period the broader firings remained unremedied

status: Pending. A judge found it "obvious" in September 2025 that the firings broke the Inspector General Act but denied reinstatement and left the merits undecided. In August 2026 both sides readied summary-judgment motions; the government says Trump v. Slaughter lets the president fire IGs at will.
rebuttal_anticipated: The administration argues that, after the Supreme Court's 2026 Trump v. Slaughter decision, Article II gives the President unfettered authority to remove inspectors general, so the Inspector General Act's notice requirement cannot limit the firings, and that the fired IGs' APA, ultra vires and mandamus claims fail. It can also note that the court declined to order reinstatement, which some officials may cite as evidence the practical harm was limited.
comeback: This entry does not dispute that a president can remove an inspector general through the lawful process -- the accountability question is that Trump fired 17 of them simultaneously, without the congressional notice or case-specific justification the law explicitly requires. offense_category: Use of a DOJ Settlement Fund to Enable Taxpayer-Funded Payments to January 6 Defendants -- no criminal charge; a public-integrity and appropriations-propriety concern given Trump's personal financial interest in the underlying settlement and his own public support for compensating people convicted of crimes committed in his name
incident_summary: **The Justice Department created a $1.776 billion "anti-weaponization" fund as part of a settlement, announced May 18, 2026, of Trump's own $10 billion lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service, part of the executive branch he oversees, over the leak of his tax returns, together with his pending administrative claims over the 2022 Mar-a-Lago search and the Russia investigation -- a settlement of claims brought by the government's own boss, under which Trump received a formal apology but no money and the Attorney General agreed to create the fund.** The fund was intended to compensate people claiming harm from what the settlement called "Lawfare and Weaponization" by the government, and was widely reported to be positioned to include payments to January 6 Capitol riot defendants. After congressional Republicans balked and critics labeled it a "slush fund" benefiting Trump allies, and after a federal judge in Alexandria, Virginia had temporarily blocked it in a lawsuit filed May 22, 2026 by a fired former federal prosecutor and others, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche told a House Appropriations hearing on June 2, 2026 that DOJ was "not moving forward with the Fund, period." Despite the fund's abandonment, lawyers for Capitol rioters said in early June 2026 that they had filed at least 600 separate claims under the Federal Tort Claims Act seeking taxpayer-funded payouts, which would come from the government's permanent Judgment Fund. When asked directly in a June 2026 NBC "Meet the Press" interview, Trump said he supports compensating January 6 defendants and refused to rule out taxpayer-funded payments to people convicted or charged in connection with the Capitol attack. On June 12, 2026, U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema, presiding over that Virginia lawsuit, Floyd v. Department of Justice, entered a preliminary injunction barring the government from taking any action to create or operate the fund, expressly including "reconstituting the Anti-Weaponization Fund under a different name", and ordered that, to end the litigation, Blanche, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declare under penalty of perjury that the fund would not proceed "in any manner, or under any name"; they filed no such declaration, so the case went forward, and DOJ reported to the court on June 22 that no payments had been made and no money had been transferred to the fund. On July 13, 2026, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Williams in Miami, ruling in the IRS case whose settlement created the fund, found the suit had been brought for an improper purpose -- "to gain the imprimatur of judicial legitimacy" for the settlement -- and wrote that "there was never adverseness between the Parties; there was never a case or controversy"; appeals are pending. On August 2, 2026, Blanche issued an order formally rescinding the fund; the order did not include language barring government restitution or payouts to convicted January 6 rioters. The next day, DOJ moved to dismiss a related FTCA class action, Sullivan v. United States in federal court in Florida, filed in March 2026 by three January 6 defendants who allege police used excessive force on the crowd that day and who list 46 class members who had filed administrative claims. DOJ argued the claims are "forever barred" because the two-year deadline for administrative claims over those January 6, 2021 injuries ran out on January 6, 2023. The plaintiffs filed an amended complaint on August 24, 2026 arguing the deadline should be equitably tolled, and on August 26 the judge found DOJ's motion moot, allowed DOJ to file a renewed motion, and kept the case stayed. The class action is a distinct proceeding from the individual claims; if a court accepts DOJ's timeliness theory, the same reasoning could reach other claims over injuries suffered on January 6, 2021 itself. In the Virginia case, DOJ moved to dismiss, arguing the challenge targets a fund "that has never existed and will not exist." At a September 18, 2026 hearing, Brinkema took that motion under advisement without ruling and left her injunction in place. "The issues that underlie this case are still alive and kicking, in my view," she said, pointing, according to ABC News, to statements by administration officials suggesting payments were still on the table for January 6 rioters and for anti-abortion protesters convicted under the FACE Act. "I think the 'Anti-Weaponization Fund' -- that entity, is gone. But is there a functional equivalent of that going on?" she asked, and she raised, as a hypothetical remedy once the case is resolved, an independent monitor over payments from the Judgment Fund.

offense_category: Categorical Clemency for January 6 Capitol Attack Defendants, Including Violent-Offense and Seditious-Conspiracy Convictions, and Its Downstream Effects -- clemency is a constitutional presidential power, not itself unlawful; the accountability claim concerns the scale/non-individualized nature of the grant, its erosion of the public case record, and the pattern of political and paramilitary rehabilitation it enabled
incident_summary:
On January 20, 2025, hours after his inauguration, Trump issued clemency covering roughly 1,500-1,600 people charged or convicted over the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack -- pardons for most, and sentence commutations for several leaders of extremist groups convicted of seditious conspiracy, including Oath Keepers founder Stewart Rhodes. Many recipients had been convicted of violent offenses (assaulting police officers) or were leaders of the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys. Within days, DOJ took offline its searchable public database of January 6 case records, making it substantially harder for the public to verify what exactly had been pardoned, even though DOJ press releases and court records remained accessible at the time. Michael Romano, a deputy chief of the DOJ section that prosecuted the cases, resigned because staying had become "untenable" given the pardons, and in an April 2025 interview with the Associated Press warned they could embolden right-wing extremists and encourage future political violence.

By May 2025, downstream effects were already visible: pardoned Proud Boys leader Enrique Tarrio personally thanked Trump at Mar-a-Lago -- by his own account, "for giving me my life back" -- and Trump replied "I love you guys"; later that month, Trump's pardon attorney Ed Martin met with Peter Ticktin, an attorney seeking full pardons for the small remaining group of January 6 defendants whose convictions still stood, including Rhodes and several Proud Boys members whose sentences had only been commuted. Over the following year, other pardoned defendants began appearing at Republican events and floating political runs, and by late 2025, Rhodes -- his sentence commuted -- was attempting to relaunch the Oath Keepers as an explicitly pro-Trump paramilitary organization, claiming that "president Trump can call us up as the militia" and casting the group as a counter to what he called an "insurrection by the left" (though experts, former members and online chatter suggested little to no interest).

In December 2025, Brian Cole Jr. -- accused of planting pipe bombs near the Republican and Democratic national committees' headquarters, close to the Capitol, the night before the riot -- was charged, nearly a year after the pardon proclamation. In January 2026, legal commentators flagged that the proclamation's broad "related to" language could be read to cover him, despite DOJ's own effort to prosecute that case as unrelated to January 6, and in March 2026 Cole's lawyers moved to dismiss all charges on exactly that ground. On July 6, 2026, U.S. District Judge Amir Ali ruled that Cole is not covered by the pardon and declined to dismiss the charges against him -- but on narrow, textual grounds specific to his case (the pardon covers only those already "convicted of offenses," and Cole was not charged until nearly a year after the proclamation), not by resolving the pardon's broader language itself; Cole has pleaded not guilty, and his trial is currently set for February 16, 2027. That broader scope question remains theoretically live for anyone convicted by January 20, 2025 whose conduct might fall under similarly sweeping language. Separately, in May 2026, DOJ deleted thousands of remaining January 6 pages from its websites -- including the D.C. U.S. Attorney's Office's individual case press releases, the remaining pages of its Capitol Breach case database, and the FBI's "wanted" pages for Capitol rioters -- according to a Lawfare archive project that reconstructed most of the deleted records.

Also in January 2026, Adam Johnson -- pardoned after being photographed carrying House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's lectern during the riot -- filed to run as a Republican for a Manatee County, Florida commission seat, using the Capitol photo in his campaign branding; in the August 18, 2026 Republican primary he finished fourth of six candidates, with about 12 percent of the vote. On September 3, 2026, Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, with Reps. Ted Lieu and Joe Neguse as cosponsors, introduced the No Pardon Paydays Act (H.R. 10290) as part of a legislative package; the bill would require DOJ's Pardon Attorney to submit a criminal-history review to Congress for any pardon recipient and would bar recipients from making large political contributions to committees associated with the president who pardoned them. Its sponsors cited Trump's blanket January 6 pardons, along with pardons for donors and allies; the bill has not been voted on. (Separate entries in this database track new criminal charges against three pardoned defendants, including Andrew Paul Johnson, and a $1.776 billion DOJ settlement fund, since abandoned, that January 6 defendants had been expected to claim from.)

incident_summary:
This entry documents three named, unrelated Jan. 6 defendants covered by Trump's January 2025 clemency who later faced serious new criminal charges -- Christopher Moynihan, John Banuelos, and Andrew Paul Johnson -- reported as part of a broader pattern of pardoned rioters facing new prosecutions.

John Banuelos -- the only Jan. 6 defendant accused of firing a gun on Capitol grounds -- had his pending federal Capitol riot case (charged in March 2024; he had pleaded not guilty and never stood trial) dismissed and was released from custody in January 2025 after Trump's January 20, 2025 clemency grant. During 2024 proceedings before his Jan. 6 case's judge, Tanya Chutkan, Banuelos said, "Trump is going to be in office in six months, so I have nothing to worry about" -- an explicit anticipation of impunity voiced before the pardon was even granted. According to prosecutors' charging document, an August 2025 DNA test linked him to a June 2018 attack in the Salt Lake City area. Prosecutors charged him in Salt Lake County's 3rd District Court with aggravated kidnapping and eight counts of aggravated sexual assault, all first-degree felonies, and a Utah arrest warrant issued October 1, 2025; he was located in Cicero, Illinois on October 17, 2025. He pleaded not guilty, was ordered detained pending trial, and as of August 2026 was jailed in Salt Lake County awaiting a three-day trial scheduled to begin December 1, 2026.

Christopher Moynihan, convicted in 2022 for obstructing an official proceeding after breaking through a security perimeter and entering the Senate Gallery on Jan. 6, 2021 (sentenced to nearly two years), received a full pardon within hours of Trump's inauguration in January 2025 along with over 1,500 other Jan. 6 defendants. **On October 18, 2025, Moynihan was arrested and charged with making a terroristic threat after sending text messages on October 17, 2025 reading "Hakeem Jeffries makes a speech in a few days in NYC I cannot allow this terrorist to live," "Even if I am hated he must be eliminated," and "I will kill him for the future," referring to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries ahead of a scheduled New York speech.** Reporting described him as the first pardoned Capitol rioter arrested over alleged political violence. Jeffries said he was "grateful to state and federal law enforcement for their swift and decisive action to apprehend a dangerous individual"; Rep. Jamie Raskin said the case illustrated Trump granting pardons "without obviously studying the details of each individual case." In February 2026, under a plea deal, Moynihan pleaded guilty to a reduced misdemeanor charge of aggravated harassment and agreed to three years of probation, with sentencing set for April 2, 2026.

Andrew Paul Johnson, who received a full pardon from President Trump for his role in the January 6, 2021 Capitol riot as part of Trump's blanket pardon of hundreds of Jan. 6 defendants in January 2025, was arrested in August 2025 -- roughly seven months after his pardon -- and subsequently convicted by a Hernando County, Florida jury in February 2026 on five charges, including molesting a child under 12, molesting a child under 16, and lewd and lascivious exhibition. Johnson was sentenced to life in prison in March 2026. According to a Hernando County Sheriff's Office police report, Johnson attempted to bribe one victim using money he claimed he would receive as restitution owed to Jan. 6 defendants. NPR's reporting characterized this as the latest in a documented pattern of pardoned Capitol rioters committing new crimes after receiving clemency.

offense_category: Privacy Act Violation (5 U.S.C. § 552a) -- unauthorized disclosure of protected personal records
incident_summary: On January 23, 2025, Trump ordered the immediate, unredacted release of all remaining classified John F. Kennedy assassination records, and the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) published more than 60,000 pages within about 24 hours -- bypassing the extensive review process NARA had previously used under the JFK Records Act to withhold Social Security numbers and other personal data of living individuals. **The rushed release publicly exposed the Social Security numbers and other personal data of more than 200 former congressional staffers and other former officials, including at least two still-living individuals identified in press reporting: Joseph diGenova (Trump's own former personal attorney) and Christopher Pyle (a former Church Committee investigator).** More than 80 additional people with birthdates placing them in their 70s, 80s, or 90s also had SSNs and birthdates exposed. Asked about the disclosure, Trump told reporters, 'We even released Social Security numbers, I didn't want anything deleted' -- a direct, on-the-record statement that the unredacted release, including the SSN exposure, was his personal instruction rather than a lower-level processing error. NARA and the Social Security Administration said they were working to identify and contact affected individuals; diGenova said he intended to sue NARA, stating 'They violated the Privacy Act.'

The official ordering the release is on the record confirming the unredacted release, including SSN exposure, was intentional and not accidental
Documented harm/risk resulted: named living individuals face identity-theft and fraud exposure, and at least one has stated intent to pursue legal action

incident_summary: Former Tennessee state Sen. Brian Kelsey pleaded guilty in November 2022 to secretly funneling $91,000 from multiple sources, including his state Senate campaign committee, through a national political organization to support his failed 2016 U.S. House bid, and to causing false contribution and expenditure reports to be filed with the FEC -- a scheme prosecutors said was designed to evade federal contribution limits. U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw denied Kelsey's repeated attempts to withdraw his guilty plea or otherwise reopen the case, as recently as February 2025, and Kelsey reported to federal prison to begin his 21-month sentence. On March 11, 2025 -- just two weeks into that sentence -- Trump granted Kelsey a 'full and unconditional pardon.' In a public statement, Kelsey said 'God used Donald Trump to save me from the weaponized Biden DOJ,' explicitly echoing Trump's own rhetoric about his personal legal cases, despite having pleaded guilty rather than being convicted at trial. Tennessee Democratic state Rep. Gloria Johnson responded, 'Dude plead guilty, but sure.' **Within a month of his release, Kelsey began lobbying sitting Tennessee state lawmakers to amend a pending campaign-finance bill (SB 229) to let him use leftover funds in his state campaign account to pay his personal legal fees from the case -- after Tennessee's own Bureau of Ethics and Campaign Finance had already denied his request to do so.** State Sen. Brent Taylor drafted the requested amendment at Kelsey's request; state Sen. Richard Briggs confirmed Kelsey called him personally to press for it.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Board Plans Held to Violate a Federal Court Injunction (Kennedy Center Naming) and Unilateral Alteration of a Federal Cultural Institution Through Board Control
incident_summary: In February 2025 Trump purged the Kennedy Center's bipartisan board and installed loyalists, then had himself elected board chairman; in December 2025 the board voted to rename the institution in Trump's honor, even though Congress, which created the center in 1958 and named it for John F. Kennedy in 1964, never authorized a renaming. **Rep. Joyce Beatty sued, and in May 2026 U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that only Congress can rename the Kennedy Center and ordered Trump's name removed, writing "Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it." After the Trump-chaired board voted on August 13, 2026 to inscribe "renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump" on the building and rename the grounds "President Donald J. Trump Plaza," Cooper held on September 15 that both plans violate that injunction and blocked them; Trump and the other defendants appealed the same day.** The dispute then escalated: the Trump-installed board voted to close the building, citing "acute risks to public safety" from a partial ceiling collapse and a roof-terrace canopy problem, and Trump said the closure would be "immediate." The next day, photographs showed Trump reviewing a placard that appeared to read "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED" over a demolition image, despite Kennedy Center officials insisting nothing was being demolished. Beatty asked the court to block any demolition; on September 17 Cooper ordered the administration to give 30 days' notice before any major physical change to the building, "including but not limited to any 'demolition' of the Center's main building," and to file a detailed status report on the closure and repairs. Trump later said Congress's $257 million appropriation for the renovation would not proceed unless the naming ruling is overturned and his name is added to the building. On September 18 the Justice Department moved to dissolve the May 29 preliminary injunction blocking the board's closure of the main building, citing the board's renewed votes to close it for two years; briefing runs to November 6. Beatty moved on October 5 to compel discovery of Trump's communications with Kennedy Center management, and on October 14 the White House formally invoked presidential communications privilege over them. Neither motion had been ruled on as of October 21.
elements_required: A federal court (Judge Cooper) had already enjoined Trump's name from appearing on the Kennedy Center, on the ground that only Congress -- which chartered and named the institution -- can rename it
Cooper found that the Trump-chaired board's planned inscription and grounds renaming honoring Trump would violate that injunction, and enjoined them
The same board Trump installed after purging the prior bipartisan board then voted to close the building, and Trump himself said the closure would be immediate
Photographic evidence showed Trump reviewing material referencing demolition of the building, contradicting Kennedy Center officials' public statements that nothing was being demolished
The court found sufficient concern about unauthorized alteration to order 30 days' advance notice before any major physical change, including demolition

rebuttal_anticipated: Building closures for documented structural hazards -- a partial ceiling collapse and a roof-terrace canopy problem -- are a routine facilities-safety decision, not a renaming or demolition act, and the board (which Trump chairs) has the authority to make facility decisions; the placard photograph is not itself an order to demolish the building.
comeback: This entry does not rest on the placard photo alone -- a federal judge has already held that the Trump-installed board's planned inscription honoring Trump and its renaming of the grounds for him would violate a standing injunction over the Kennedy Center's name, and the same board Trump installed after purging its prior bipartisan membership then moved, on Trump's own statement that closure would be "immediate," to shut the building down citing safety concerns Kennedy Center officials had not previously flagged as urgent. The court's own response -- ordering 30 days' notice before any major physical change, specifically naming demolition -- reflects the same pattern of concern, not manufactured advocacy framing.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Pardon Power Used as Political/Financial Patronage -- no criminal charge implicated by the pardon itself; this tracks accountability for the timing and apparent quid pro quo pattern of the President's clemency decision
incident_summary: **President Trump pardoned Adam Kidan, a Republican megadonor and former business partner of lobbyist Jack Abramoff who pleaded guilty to conspiracy and wire fraud over the fraudulent 2000 purchase of the SunCruz casino-boat fleet (sentenced in March 2006 to 70 months in prison and $21,701,015.45 in restitution), on July 3, 2026 -- three days after Kidan donated $2,600 to a leadership PAC affiliated with Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-PA).** Trump had personally campaigned in Mackenzie's eastern Pennsylvania district on June 23, about a week before the donation. Mackenzie's office said the congressman did not speak with the White House or Trump about the pardon, but declined at first to say whether he would keep the donation; after the timing became public, Mackenzie returned it. The pardon releases Kidan from any restitution he has not paid.
elements_required: The President personally exercised the pardon power for a convicted political donor
The donation preceded the pardon by a short, specific, documented interval (three days)
The pardon followed the President's own campaign visit to the donation recipient's district shortly before the donation was made
The pardon relieves the recipient of a substantial, court-ordered financial obligation (restitution) in addition to the underlying conviction

evidence.description: NOTUS reporting establishes the specific timeline: Trump campaigned with Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in his Pennsylvania district on June 23, 2026; Kidan donated $2,600 to Mackenzie's leadership PAC on June 30; Trump pardoned Kidan on July 3, three days after the donation
evidence.maps_to_element: Donation preceded the pardon by a short, documented interval

evidence.description: Florida Bulldog's reporting on the pardon says the pardon dissolved Kidan's felon status and his restitution obligation ($21.7 million plus interest), that his Miami court file shows no indication he paid any of it, that his name does not appear in a search of the Office of the Pardon Attorney's clemency cases, and quotes the White House's stated rationale crediting his post-prison staffing career

status: Pardon granted July 3, 2026; it is final and releases Kidan from any unpaid share of his $21.7 million restitution order. Rep. Mackenzie returned the $2,600 donation. No congressional, DOJ Inspector General or other formal inquiry into this pardon has been identified.
rebuttal_anticipated: The White House's stated rationale credits Kidan's post-prison career in staffing businesses that it says secured entry-level jobs for over 250,000 people. Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said pardons go through "a rigorous review process involving the Department of Justice and the White House Counsel's Office" and that "The President finds it detestable that anyone would even attempt to profit off pardons." Mackenzie's spokesperson called any link between the contribution and the pardon "ridiculous." Other likely defenses: presidents have unreviewable constitutional pardon power, the $2,600 donation was a routine political contribution below the amount likely to constitute an explicit quid pro quo under bribery statutes, and timing alone does not prove the donation and the pardon were causally connected.
comeback: The specific facts distinguishing this from an ordinary pardon are the tight, documented three-day window between donation and clemency, the President's own campaign visit to the donation recipient's district a week beforehand, and the fact that the recipient congressman's office would not initially say whether it would keep the money -- returning it only after the timing was reported. The White House's only stated rationale is Kidan's post-prison business career; it did not respond to NOTUS's questions about Mackenzie and Kidan, and Florida Bulldog reported that Kidan's name does not appear in a search of the Justice Department's Office of the Pardon Attorney clemency cases, suggesting he did not go through the usual application process.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern of this administration's pardon power benefiting donors, political allies, and supporters rather than being reserved for cases involving claims of wrongful conviction, excessive sentencing, or demonstrated rehabilitation.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the pardon date, sentence and restitution amount are on the Justice Department's own clemency list; the donation and campaign-visit dates come from NOTUS's reporting (based on FEC records), which Spotlight PA republished and the Daily Beast followed; and Mackenzie's office's own responses (declining then reversing course on the donation) are on the record rather than disputed. Re-verified 2026-08-19: no Kidan-specific congressional inquiry, DOJ Inspector General probe, or other formal oversight action identified in follow-up searches -- a July 30, 2026 opinion piece calling for such oversight (published after this pardon and before this entry's own write date) confirms none existed as of that date either. A broader, pre-existing bicameral 'pay-to-play pardons' oversight investigation by Sen. Welch and Rep. Min (launched May 2026, covering 17 other clemency recipients, with a records-preservation demand to DOJ's Pardon Attorney, the White House, and the Secret Service due July 24, 2026) runs parallel to and predates this pardon, but has not been confirmed to name Kidan specifically as of this update. Update 2026-10-15: the Justice Department's clemency list puts Kidan's restitution at $21,701,015.45, matching Florida Bulldog and LNP | LancasterOnline; the "$217 million" figure in NOTUS's reporting appears to be a decimal error. Follow-up searches found no congressional, Inspector General or other formal inquiry naming this pardon, and no report that the Welch-Min pay-to-play pardons probe has added it.

official: Donald Trump, President (memorandum ordering the actions; carried out by Attorney General Pam Bondi/DOJ and DHS/CBP)
offense_category: First Amendment Retaliation Under Color of Law -- using presidential and federal investigative authority to punish a private citizen for prior truthful government speech (Krebs' on-the-record 2020 statement that the election was 'the most secure in American history'), rather than for any alleged wrongdoing; not charged criminally, and no allegation Krebs committed a crime has been substantiated in sourcing reviewed
incident_summary: **On April 9, 2025, President Trump signed a memorandum revoking any security clearances held by Chris Krebs.** Trump himself had appointed Krebs CISA director in 2017, then fired him by tweet in November 2020 after Krebs publicly affirmed the 2020 election was secure and debunked fraud claims. The memorandum directed the Attorney General and DHS Secretary to review Krebs' and CISA's conduct, specifically citing CISA's work with social media platforms during the 2020 campaign. A White House fact sheet said the review would include a 'comprehensive evaluation of all of CISA's activities over the last 6 years' and identify any instances where Krebs' or CISA's conduct 'appears to be contrary to the administration's commitment to free speech and ending federal censorship.' It also revoked security clearances for any employee of SentinelOne, the cybersecurity firm where Krebs then served as Chief Intelligence and Public Policy Officer, and directed a review of Krebs' handling of classified information during his government tenure. A nearly identical memorandum the same day targeted Miles Taylor, a former DHS chief of staff who had anonymously authored a 2018 New York Times op-ed critical of Trump and later publicly confirmed authorship. That parallel action against a second named former official is tracked here as context rather than as this entry's primary subject. On April 16, 2025, Krebs resigned from SentinelOne specifically to contest the action, telling colleagues 'this is my fight, not the company's' and that it was 'a fight for democracy, for freedom of speech, for the rule of law.' On April 30, 2025, CNN reported that Krebs had discovered his Global Entry trusted-traveler membership was revoked. The next day, DHS confirmed the revocation, and a DHS spokesperson told CBS News that Krebs was 'under active investigation by law enforcement agencies,' which the spokesperson described as 'a fact disqualifying him for Global Entry.' DHS was using the still-pending investigation the same memorandum had ordered as the stated justification for a further, concrete consequence against him. Krebs remains out of government service. No charge, formal finding or public report resulting from the investigation has been identified in sourcing reviewed, and no confirmation that his Global Entry membership or security clearance status has since been restored was identified either.
elements_required: Krebs' conduct that triggered these actions was truthful, on-the-record government speech in his official capacity (affirming 2020 election security) -- not private conduct or any alleged crime
A presidential memorandum, not a routine agency personnel or clearance-review process, directly ordered the security-clearance revocation and DOJ/DHS investigation, naming Krebs personally

The investigation the memorandum ordered was then itself cited by DHS as the justification for a separate, concrete consequence (Global Entry revocation) -- the ordered investigation's mere existence, not any finding from it, produced real-world harm
No sourcing reviewed identifies any substantiated finding of wrongdoing by Krebs from the ordered DOJ/DHS review as of this writing

status: Investigation pending: sourcing reviewed shows no charge, formal finding or public report from the DOJ/DHS probe the April 9, 2025 memorandum ordered, and no confirmation that Krebs' security clearance or Global Entry membership has been restored.
rebuttal_anticipated: The administration's stated position is that the investigation concerns whether CISA, under Krebs, exceeded its mandate by coordinating with social media platforms in ways that amounted to government-directed censorship of protected speech (including downplaying the Hunter Biden laptop story) -- a legitimate oversight question about agency conduct, not retaliation for Krebs' personal statements.
comeback: The memorandum itself frames the investigation's trigger as Krebs' specific public statements affirming 2020 election security, not a general CISA oversight inquiry that happened to include him; it was issued by presidential order rather than through any standard inspector-general or congressional process, targeted Krebs and his current private employer's clearances by name, and its mere existence -- with no finding yet reached -- was then cited by DHS as sufficient grounds to revoke a benefit (Global Entry) requiring no criminal charge, let alone conviction. Using an investigation's existence as its own punishment, before any finding, is a materially different posture than ordinary oversight.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern this tracker documents of using federal investigative and clearance authority against named individuals whose past official conduct angered Trump personally, rather than in response to evidence of wrongdoing discovered through ordinary process.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on all core facts -- the memorandum's issuance, text, and scope are corroborated across TechCrunch, The Record, Axios, and wide additional wire coverage; Krebs' SentinelOne resignation is corroborated across CNBC, The Register, and CyberScoop, including his own on-record statement; the Global Entry revocation is corroborated across CNN and CBS News, and DHS's stated justification is on record in a DHS spokesperson's statement to CBS News; Votebeat documented the fear the memorandum caused among election officials. `contested: true` reflects that the administration has a stated, on-the-record justification (alleged CISA censorship overreach) for ordering the investigation, even though this entry's own reading is that the memorandum's text and the subsequent Global Entry action support the retaliation framing more directly than the censorship-oversight framing.

incident_summary: Rep. Barry Loudermilk (R-GA) was named in January 2025 to lead a new House Judiciary subcommittee continuing to investigate Jan. 6, following a December 2024 interim report in which Loudermilk recommended a criminal (FBI) investigation into former Rep. Liz Cheney, accusing her of witness tampering for staying in contact with hearing witness Cassidy Hutchinson during the original House Jan. 6 committee's work. Authorization of the new subcommittee stalled for months amid disputes between Loudermilk and other committee chairs over how broad its jurisdiction should be. **Trump personally intervened to push the panel through, and by July 2025 Loudermilk had secured everything he sought, including an agreement letting the subcommittee investigate matters outside its normal jurisdiction and full subpoena power (CNN, July 25, 2025).** The House formally voted to stand up the Loudermilk-led subpanel on September 3, 2025 (Roll Call). Its stated mission -- reinvestigating the original House Jan. 6 committee, Cheney specifically, and law enforcement's handling of the Capitol attack -- is aimed at discrediting the body that had documented Trump's own role in the events of Jan. 6, 2021. The subcommittee is composed of five Republicans appointed by Speaker Mike Johnson and three Democrats appointed by Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, and is required to issue a final report by the end of the 119th Congress (Dec. 31, 2026).

offense_category: Alleged Federal Election Campaign Act soft-money violation (52 U.S.C. § 30125(e)(1)(A), which bars federal officeholders from directing or spending funds raised outside federal contribution limits, and bars entities they control from raising or spending such funds) -- alleged in a civil FEC complaint, not a criminal charge, with no FEC finding
incident_summary: MAGA Inc., a hybrid super PAC that registered with the FEC in November 2024 right after Trump's election, reported just over $400 million in its unlimited-contribution (super PAC) account in its August 20, 2026 filing, and no money in its limited, hard-money account. Its donors include corporations and individuals giving in the millions, including $35 million from one company, Foris DAX. Federal law has barred federal officeholders since 2002 from directing or spending such "soft money," and bars groups an officeholder controls from raising or spending it. In a Punchbowl News interview published August 7, 2026, when Jake Sherman described MAGA Inc. as controlled by Trump's allies, Trump interjected: "Not my allies, I control it." On August 21, before boarding Air Force One, he said: "I'll be spending a lot of that money for candidates that I think are good, Republican candidates." In the Oval Office on September 4, Trump told reporters he would allocate $400 million to $500 million of the PAC's money to the midterms and said, as Reuters reported it, "This is money from MAGA Inc. This is money that I control" (the Campaign Legal Center's transcript renders it "my money that I control"). Asked how he decides where it goes, he said, per that transcript: "I sit down and I say, 'let's do this, let's do that.'" That week MAGA Inc. made a $10 million ad buy supporting Ken Paxton's Texas Senate campaign. On the basis of those statements, the Campaign Legal Center filed an FEC complaint dated September 14, 2026, made public September 18, alleging that Trump directed or spent soft money and that MAGA Inc., as an entity he controls, unlawfully raised and spent it; it asks the FEC to investigate and seek civil penalties and an injunction. MAGA Inc. spokesperson Alex Pfeiffer called the complaint "frivolous" and said "MAGA Inc. fully complies with the law"; the White House did not immediately respond to The Washington Sun. **The FEC cannot act on the complaint: it has lacked a quorum since May 2025 and has had only two of its six commissioners since October 2025, below the four votes needed to open an investigation, and the Senate had not scheduled a hearing on Trump's two February 2026 nominees.**

official: Donald Trump, President; David Steiner, Postmaster General (the Postal Service under Steiner wrote and finalized the mail-ballot rule the order directed; he answers to the USPS Board of Governors, not the President)
offense_category: Exceeding presidential authority over federal election administration -- an executive order directing the Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to voters on state-submitted lists and DHS to compile state citizenship lists; federal judges found the order and the Postal Service rule implementing it likely unconstitutional or beyond the agency's authority (Elections Clause, separation of powers, Administrative Procedure Act) -- NOT charged; a civil/constitutional dispute, not a criminal matter
incident_summary: On March 31, 2026, President Trump signed Executive Order 14399, 'Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections,' his second elections order after a March 2025 order that courts had largely blocked. It directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, with the Social Security Administration, to compile and send each state a 'State Citizenship List' of adult citizens; directs the Attorney General to prioritize investigating and prosecuting election officials who issue ballots to ineligible people; and directs the Postmaster General to propose a rule under which states would submit lists of their mail voters at least 60 days before a federal election, ballot envelopes would carry unique Postal Service barcodes, and the Postal Service would not transmit mail ballots for anyone not enrolled on a state list. Twenty-three states and the District of Columbia, voting-rights groups led by the League of Women Voters, and Democratic Party organizations sued. **At a June 24 Senate Homeland Security & Governmental Affairs Committee hearing, Sen. Gary Peters asked Postmaster General David Steiner whether the Postal Service would still mail ballots for a state that refused to turn over its absentee voter list under the proposed rule; Steiner replied, 'Under our proposed regulation, no.'** He said the Postal Service would obey a court order blocking the rule. U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston then declared Sections 2 and 3 of the order 'legally void as they are ultra vires and unconstitutionally violate the separation of powers' and barred federal agencies from implementing them in the plaintiff states, and in late July the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals refused to pause that ruling. In a separate case, U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan in Washington, D.C., blocked the proposed rule on July 1 as a likely violation of the Postal Service's 2021 settlement with the NAACP; on July 17 a D.C. Circuit panel paused his order, finding the Postal Service likely to succeed in arguing the challenge was premature and the rule would not breach the settlement, and on Oct. 1, at the NAACP's request, the appeals court vacated his ruling and dismissed the appeal as moot because the NAACP had effectively abandoned the challenge for the 2026 election. On Aug. 11, in the voting-rights groups' case, Talwani issued a preliminary injunction barring the Postal Service from taking any steps to implement the order before the midterms. The Postal Service finalized its rule anyway, effective Aug. 21, saying it would not apply the rule in 2026 while the injunctions stood. On Aug. 24 the Supreme Court, 6-3, paused Talwani's June ruling, finding the states likely could not yet challenge what it called 'an internal directive from the President to his subordinates'; it did not decide the order's legality ('On that score, time will tell'), and Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, dissenting, called it a 'blatantly unconstitutional Order.' Talwani found the Postal Service had 'feigned compliance' with her injunction by issuing the rule but declined to block it, and on Aug. 26 canceled her Aug. 11 injunction in light of the Supreme Court's ruling. Twenty-four states and D.C. sued over the final rule that day; Talwani blocked its mandatory envelope, voter-list portal and ballot-verification provisions with a temporary restraining order on Aug. 27 and a preliminary injunction on Sept. 4, writing that 'Congress has never delegated its Elections Clause power to the USPS.' On Sept. 13, U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols in Washington, D.C., separately enjoined the rule. On Sept. 14 the Supreme Court refused to lift Talwani's injunction, saying the administration was unlikely to succeed on the merits; Justice Brett Kavanaugh, concurring, wrote there is 'at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority' but that applying it in the 2026 elections 'would be arbitrary and capricious,' and Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas would have granted the stay. Trump called the ruling 'a big loss for Republicans.'

offense_category: Presidential Pardon of a Convicted Agent of a Foreign Transnational-Repression Campaign, Overturning the First Jury Conviction in a Chinese 'Operation Fox Hunt' Case
incident_summary: Michael McMahon, a retired 14-year NYPD sergeant turned private investigator, was hired to locate Xu Jin, a former Chinese city official living as a dissident in suburban New Jersey, as part of China's 'Operation Fox Hunt' -- a global campaign to forcibly repatriate fugitives and dissidents. McMahon searched law enforcement databases, conducted surveillance, and fed information to the operation's organizers that prosecutors said fueled a pressure campaign against Xu's family: disparaging Facebook messages sent to his daughter's friends, letters to relatives, and an intimidating visit from Xu's elderly father, flown in from China specifically for the purpose. **Xu's wife discovered a note threatening: 'If you are willing to go back to the mainland and spend 10 years in prison, your wife and children will be all right.'** Following a two-week trial in June 2023, a federal jury unanimously convicted McMahon of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government and interstate stalking -- the first jury conviction obtained in a Fox Hunt prosecution. He was sentenced in spring 2025 to 18 months in prison; the sentencing judge described his conduct as part of 'a campaign of transnational repression.' On November 7, 2025, Trump pardoned McMahon. A White House official said McMahon claimed he was 'unwittingly used' and misled into believing he was working for a Chinese construction company rather than the Chinese government, and the administration highlighted his NYPD career, commendations, and a 2001 line-of-duty injury, casting the pardon as correcting a trial the administration said 'had issues' despite the unanimous jury verdict. McMahon's attorney called the pardon a correction of 'a horrible injustice.' Republican Reps. Mike Lawler and Pete Sessions had previously supported clemency for McMahon; the Brooklyn U.S. Attorney's Office, which had prosecuted the case, declined to comment on the pardon.

The sentencing judge characterized the underlying conduct in explicitly serious national-security terms ('a campaign of transnational repression'), not as a minor or technical offense
The President personally pardoned the convicted defendant, overturning that unanimous jury verdict's practical consequences

The White House's stated justification for the pardon does not address or dispute the underlying national-security conduct (aiding a foreign government's repression campaign against a dissident family), instead focusing on the defendant's claimed lack of awareness and his separate, unrelated law-enforcement career

official: Donald Trump, President (personal public claims); Chris Klomp, HHS chief counselor, Deputy Secretary nominee, and a lead MFN deal negotiator
offense_category: Sustained Public Mischaracterization of Voluntary 'Most Favored Nation' Drug-Pricing Deals as Delivering Historic Price Relief, Contradicted by Contemporaneous List-Price Data -- an institutional-accountability and public-transparency claim, not a criminal charge
status: Ongoing -- MFN deals now cover 26 manufacturers (~89% of the branded market, per the White House) while deal companies keep raising list prices; the only two contracts released so far (Pfizer, Lilly) are heavily redacted and show terms never announced
incident_summary:
Beginning with a May 12, 2025 executive order, 'Delivering Most-Favored-Nation Prescription Drug Pricing to American Patients,' the Trump administration negotiated a series of voluntary agreements with pharmaceutical manufacturers to sell certain drugs at prices closer to what other wealthy nations pay, marketed through a planned TrumpRx.gov platform directing consumers to manufacturers' direct-purchase discount channels. By the end of 2025, 16 manufacturers had signed such deals; the administration's own January 15, 2026 'Great Healthcare Plan' touted these as a signature achievement. Trump personally described a later round of deals (announced August 31, 2026, bringing the total to 26 manufacturers, which the White House said cover 89% of the branded drug market) as 'as big as it gets medically' and 'the largest drug discount, the largest price reductions in the history of medicine.' However, NPR reported that in January 2026 -- the time of year drugmakers typically implement annual list-price increases -- all 16 of the companies that had signed MFN deals nonetheless raised list prices on at least some of their drugs; **a contemporaneous analysis by drug-pricing research firm 46brooklyn found companies (including all 16 deal-signers) raised prices on 872 brand-name drugs in the first two weeks of 2026 alone, spanning cancer, diabetes, and heart-disease medications, a pace matching the prior year's increases**. Separately, a March 18, 2026 review by the New York Times and German news partners found untrue Trump's claim that he had taken drug prices 'from the highest price in the entire world to the lowest': of 24 TrumpRx drugs it could compare, Germany's public health system paid less than the TrumpRx price in more than half the cases, and consistently less for the six patent-protected drugs. The MFN deals are voluntary and apply only to specific, administration-negotiated drugs/channels (often cash-pay, direct-to-consumer purchases bypassing insurance) -- they do not cap or bind each company's list prices generally, which is the mechanism that allowed simultaneous 'historic price reduction' marketing and continued list-price increases across hundreds of other products from the same companies.

Update 2026-09-29: On September 19, 2026, the watchdog group Public Citizen released nearly 120 pages of heavily redacted Pfizer and Eli Lilly MFN agreements, obtained through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit it filed in January 2026 after HHS and the Commerce Department did not answer its requests; the other deals remain confidential. The documents show terms the administration had not announced. Pfizer's September 30, 2025 White House deal was only a letter of agreement committing both sides to 'diligent and good faith negotiations'; the definitive agreement was signed February 23, 2026, and ends January 20, 2029, the end of Trump's term. Bloomberg reported that the contract spells out a term the White House had announced only in general form in 2025: Pfizer agreed to share with HHS an undisclosed portion of the extra revenue it earns from charging higher prices abroad, from January 1, 2026, through January 20, 2029, with the rate and the drugs covered redacted; White House spokesperson Kush Desai said 'Foreign prices are going to increase,' and Trump had said 'We had to get their prices up in order to get our prices down.' **Public Citizen reported that Lilly's agreement lets the company stop supplying a drug to a reference country and then have that country's price dropped from the U.S. benchmark, and that it excludes Lilly's Zepbound and Mounjaro from Medicaid MFN pricing; an analysis by Harvard Medical School's Thomas Hwang provided to the group estimated that excluding Lilly's and Novo Nordisk's GLP-1 drugs could cost the Medicaid pricing model $1 billion to $1.7 billion in first-year savings.** The released MFN agreements themselves do not mention the tariff relief tied to the deals. Pfizer's deal came with a three-year reprieve from threatened pharmaceutical tariffs, and an April 2, 2026 proclamation set a 100% tariff on imported patented drugs, cut to zero until January 20, 2029 for companies that have both MFN pricing agreements and Commerce-approved onshoring plans; Public Citizen said the Commerce Department documents on Pfizer's tariff exemptions it received were not the final agreement, and Lilly's tariff agreement was produced only as a draft. At a September 15, 2026 Senate Finance Committee hearing on his nomination as HHS Deputy Secretary, Chris Klomp, a lead negotiator on the deals, told Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who demanded 'Show me the receipts,' that the administration was 'not hiding anything'; the committee advanced his nomination 15-12 on September 24. A Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker analysis published the same day compared 32 brand-name TrumpRx drugs with listed prices in 11 wealthy peer countries: the TrumpRx price was below the peer average for 17 and above it for 15, the lowest of all for five and the highest for 13.
elements_required: The administration publicly and repeatedly claimed the MFN deals represented historic, large-scale drug-price relief for American patients
The deals themselves are voluntary and narrow in scope (specific drugs/channels), not binding price caps across each company's full product line

Independent, contemporaneous data (46brooklyn's analysis, NPR's reporting) found the same deal-signing companies raised list prices on hundreds of other drugs during the same period the deals were being marketed as a price-relief achievement

Independent reviews (the New York Times with German partners; later Peterson-KFF) found TrumpRx prices for many drugs were higher than prices paid in other wealthy countries, contrary to the platform's 'world's lowest prices' claim
The administration's public description of the deals did not distinguish this narrow, voluntary scope from a general claim of falling drug prices

The administration kept the deal contracts confidential; the first two released under a FOIA lawsuit were heavily redacted and contained terms (drug carve-outs, supply-withdrawal and end-date terms) absent from the public announcements

The administration did not give the Times enough detail to check its adjusted figures, and its own promise was the 'world's lowest prices,' not the lowest after adjustment. Nothing in the public announcements clarified that the deals leave the vast majority of each company's list prices, and general market pricing, untouched. On secrecy, Public Citizen found that text redacted in Pfizer's agreement is visible in Lilly's, and that some redacted definitions had already been published in a White House economic analysis, which cuts against the claim that the redactions protect trade secrets.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Illustrates a pattern of an administration announcing narrowly-scoped voluntary industry agreements in maximalist, historic-achievement language, while independent data contemporaneously shows the underlying pricing behavior driving most consumers' actual costs is unchanged or continuing to worsen, and while the contract terms that would let the public test those claims, including what the companies received in return, are kept confidential -- a gap between marketing claims and measurable outcomes rather than a specific statutory violation.

Separately, a March 18, 2026 review by the New York Times and German news partners found untrue Trump's claim that he had taken drug prices 'from the highest price in the entire world to the lowest': of 24 TrumpRx drugs it could compare, Germany's public health system paid less than the TrumpRx price in more than half the cases, and consistently less for the six patent-protected drugs. The MFN deals are voluntary and apply only to specific, administration-negotiated drugs/channels (often cash-pay, direct-to-consumer purchases bypassing insurance) -- they do not cap or bind each company's list prices generally, which is the mechanism that allowed simultaneous 'historic price reduction' marketing and continued list-price increases across hundreds of other products from the same companies.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-09-29: On September 19, 2026, the watchdog group Public Citizen released nearly 120 pages of heavily redacted Pfizer and Eli Lilly MFN agreements, obtained through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit it filed in January 2026 after HHS and the Commerce Department did not answer its requests; the other deals remain confidential. The documents show terms the administration had not announced. Pfizer's September 30, 2025 White House deal was only a letter of agreement committing both sides to 'diligent and good faith negotiations'; the definitive agreement was signed February 23, 2026, and ends January 20, 2029, the end of Trump's term. Bloomberg reported that the contract spells out a term the White House had announced only in general form in 2025: Pfizer agreed to share with HHS an undisclosed portion of the extra revenue it earns from charging higher prices abroad, from January 1, 2026, through January 20, 2029, with the rate and the drugs covered redacted; White House spokesperson Kush Desai said 'Foreign prices are going to increase,' and Trump had said 'We had to get their prices up in order to get our prices down.' **Public Citizen reported that Lilly's agreement lets the company stop supplying a drug to a reference country and then have that country's price dropped from the U.S. benchmark, and that it excludes Lilly's Zepbound and Mounjaro from Medicaid MFN pricing; an analysis by Harvard Medical School's Thomas Hwang provided to the group estimated that excluding Lilly's and Novo Nordisk's GLP-1 drugs could cost the Medicaid pricing model $1 billion to $1.7 billion in first-year savings.** The released MFN agreements themselves do not mention the tariff relief tied to the deals. Pfizer's deal came with a three-year reprieve from threatened pharmaceutical tariffs, and an April 2, 2026 proclamation set a 100% tariff on imported patented drugs, cut to zero until January 20, 2029 for companies that have both MFN pricing agreements and Commerce-approved onshoring plans; Public Citizen said the Commerce Department documents on Pfizer's tariff exemptions it received were not the final agreement, and Lilly's tariff agreement was produced only as a draft. At a September 15, 2026 Senate Finance Committee hearing on his nomination as HHS Deputy Secretary, Chris Klomp, a lead negotiator on the deals, told Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who demanded 'Show me the receipts,' that the administration was 'not hiding anything'; the committee advanced his nomination 15-12 on September 24. A Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker analysis published the same day compared 32 brand-name TrumpRx drugs with listed prices in 11 wealthy peer countries: the TrumpRx price was below the peer average for 17 and above it for 15, the lowest of all for five and the highest for 13.

confidence_note.base: HIGH confidence on the factual sequence: the executive order and the deal announcements are primary-sourced via White House fact sheets, and Trump's August 31 quotes are verbatim in the Washington Examiner's report of the Oval Office event (CNBC also covered the announcement but does not carry the quotes). The 872-drug price-increase figure comes from 46brooklyn, an established, frequently-cited drug-pricing research firm, via NPR's direct reporting. The TrumpRx price comparison is read directly from the New York Times's March 18, 2026 review; it compares TrumpRx prices with what Germany's health system pays and with pharmacy cash prices for two weight-loss drugs in eight countries, in U.S. dollars unadjusted for national income, a method the White House and drugmakers dispute. The later Peterson-KFF analysis uses listed prices in 11 peer countries, also unadjusted, and finds a mixed picture.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Using the Federal Government's Contracting Relationship With a Private Company as Public Leverage to Demand the Firing of a Named Employee Over Her Prior Government Service and Perceived Political Disloyalty
incident_summary: Lisa Monaco served as a homeland-security and counterterrorism aide under President Obama and then as Deputy Attorney General under President Biden; as Deputy AG she helped coordinate DOJ's response to the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack. In July 2025 she joined Microsoft as President of Global Affairs. On September 26, 2025, one day after former FBI Director James Comey's indictment, President Trump posted on Truth Social demanding that Microsoft immediately fire her. **Trump called Monaco 'a menace to U.S. National Security, especially given the major contracts that Microsoft has with the United States Government,' explicitly invoking Microsoft's federal contracting relationship as leverage in the same post demanding her termination.** He claimed the government had stripped her of her security clearances, cut off her access to national security intelligence and banned her from federal properties because of unspecified 'many wrongful acts.' Microsoft declined to comment publicly on the demand, and it never publicly complied or substantively responded. In May 2026, a conservative advocacy group, the American Accountability Foundation, separately sent DOJ a referral letter asking its inspector general to review whether Monaco and other former officials complied with federal ethics and recusal rules. The letter said DOJ never brought a cyber-fraud action against Microsoft during her tenure as Deputy AG, despite at least five major intrusions between 2019 and 2023 involving Russian and Chinese state-linked hackers and Russian cybercriminals, and that she joined the company months after leaving DOJ; Breitbart characterized this as an allegation that she buried investigations into Microsoft. That revolving-door allegation is distinct from Trump's demand. It has been covered primarily by conservative outlets, and no independent confirmation was found that DOJ opened a formal investigation based on the referral. As of mid-2026 reporting, Monaco remained employed at Microsoft in her role.

The company did not comply, and the employee remained employed there as of mid-2026 reporting

official: Donald Trump, President (accepted a Qatari-government-gifted Boeing 747 for use as Air Force One, with a stated plan to transfer it to his post-presidency library foundation)
offense_category: Foreign Emoluments Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, sec. 9, cl. 8) -- accepting a present or gift from a foreign state without the consent of Congress
status: Ongoing: the Qatari jet has been accepted, retrofitted and is in active use as Air Force One without congressional consent. Neither 2025 emoluments resolution passed, and no court has ruled on the constitutional question.
incident_summary:
Bloomberg reported May 13, 2025 that the government of Qatar was preparing to gift Trump a luxury Boeing 747. The jet has been valued at roughly $400 million. The administration planned to use it as a temporary Air Force One while Boeing's long-delayed permanent replacement jets (expected 2028) are finished. Intelligence officials and lawmakers quoted at the time warned that, given its origin, the aircraft could be difficult to fully secure against foreign surveillance ('bugged'), and that stripping and rebuilding it to U.S. presidential security standards would be costly and technically demanding.

On May 21, 2025, Sen. Richard Blumenthal introduced S.Res.244. The resolution affirmed that accepting and transferring the plane without explicit congressional consent would be an illegal emolument, and demanded that any such plane be transferred to the permanent control of the U.S. government rather than Trump personally. It was referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and did not receive a floor vote. A companion House measure, H.Res.410, expressed the sense of the House that Trump must comply with the Emoluments Clause by submitting his plans for the jet to Congress; it likewise did not pass.

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink later told Congress the retrofit would likely cost under $400 million. Other estimates put the cost near or above $1 billion once security systems, secure communications equipment and structural upgrades are included, and reporting found Air Force officials privately acknowledged shifting funds from other defense programs to help cover the overhaul.

Trump took his first flight aboard the retrofitted jet on July 1, 2026, traveling to North Dakota, and it remains in active use as Air Force One. The aircraft was repainted in Trump's preferred navy-and-red-and-gold color scheme, with lie-flat seats, wood paneling, and a presidential seal on the seatbelts, which Trump called 'maybe the greatest commercial plane ever built.'

**Trump has said the jet will be transferred to the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation once his term ends**; as of August 2026 a White House official said 'no final decision has been made yet' on the plane's post-presidency disposition. No congressional consent has been given, and no court has ruled on the underlying constitutional question.
elements_required: A 'present' or 'gift' of value from a foreign state ('King, Prince, or foreign State') to a U.S. federal officeholder
Acceptance without the explicit consent of Congress, as the Foreign Emoluments Clause requires
The recipient holds a federal 'Office of Profit or Trust' (the presidency)

The benefit accrues personally to the officeholder, not permanently and exclusively to the U.S. government -- the central factual dispute, given the plan to transfer the plane to Trump's own post-presidency library foundation

Trump has said the plane was donated to the Air Force and the Defense Department, not to him personally, and that after his term 'I wouldn't be using it, no.' On that view the Emoluments Clause is satisfied because no individual officeholder receives a personal benefit. Officials also point to the absence of any passed resolution from either chamber of Congress as evidence that Congress has not withheld its consent, treating legislative inaction as sufficient. The Justice Department also reportedly concluded, in a May 2025 memorandum reportedly signed by Attorney General Pam Bondi, that accepting the jet was legally permissible; the memo has not been made public, and a Freedom of Information Act suit seeking it remained open in federal court as of October 2026.
