official: Russell Vought, Director of the Office of Management and Budget
offense_category: Impoundment Control Act Violations (2 U.S.C. §681 et seq.) — the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan congressional watchdog, has opened dozens of investigations and formally determined the administration committed violations in several instances (seven decisions finding violations and two mixed as of October 2026); NOT criminally charged, GAO impoundment findings are enforced via the ICA's own mechanisms (notification requirements, potential GAO litigation) rather than criminal prosecution, and no GAO lawsuit has been reported (Comptroller General Dodaro declined to sue before retiring in December 2025)
incident_summary: Beginning shortly after Trump's second term started, Vought directed OMB to freeze, delay, or withhold congressionally appropriated federal funding without following the Impoundment Control Act's required notification procedures, arguing the ICA itself is unconstitutional. **As of July 2025, GAO had opened at least 46 impoundment investigations; by April 2026 it had issued five decisions finding violations and two with mixed outcomes (and four finding none), with violations found for the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program, museum and library grants, Head Start, NIH grants and FEMA federal-assistance grant funds, and a mixed decision on the Department of Energy's Renew America's Schools Program.** In late August 2025, the White House sent Congress a roughly $4.9 billion foreign-aid rescission request timed so the money would expire on September 30 before the law's 45-day window for Congress to act had run -- a "pocket rescission" that GAO has said the ICA does not permit -- and on September 26, 2025 the Supreme Court, in an unsigned emergency order that was not a final ruling on the merits, allowed about $4 billion of it to lapse. OMB's general counsel told GAO the office would cooperate only where its demands did not get in the way of Trump's agenda, and told the Transportation Department to ignore GAO's NEVI ruling. Separately, on January 28, 2026, a federal judge ordered OMB to make public legally binding "spend plans" it had incorporated by reference through footnotes in apportionment documents, in a lawsuit brought by CREW (represented alongside Public Citizen Litigation Group). The NEVI-program litigation reached a January 23, 2026 summary judgment finding DOT/FHWA acted unlawfully (roughly $1 billion released to 20 states and D.C.), and a separate second lawsuit over two other EV-charging programs (~$2.15 billion combined) was filed December 16, 2025 -- both tracked in fuller detail in a companion entry on the Government Services tracker. In September 2025, Vought said he does not think GAO -- which he called a "quasi-legislative independent entity" -- should exist at all, and in March 2026 he escalated the conflict, issuing OMB internal-controls guidance saying earlier guidance had "overly deferred" to external entities "such as the Government Accountability Office." In April 2026 testimony, Vought told the House Budget Committee that GAO's decisions were "typically wrong and very partisan" and told the Senate Budget Committee "We have not impounded anything." On August 6, 2026, Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove introduced two articles of impeachment against Vought, for abuse of power through improper impoundment and failure to faithfully execute the law. In a separate suit by the National Center for Learning Disabilities and other education groups against OMB, Vought and the Education Department, U.S. District Judge Allison D. Burroughs (D. Mass.) on September 17, 2026 granted partial summary judgment, setting aside OMB apportionment footnotes that conditioned education research funds on compliance with two Trump executive orders, and ordered the government to report by September 28 on whether the remaining funds would be obligated before they expire on September 30. On September 25, 2026, five days before the fiscal year ended, the White House sent Congress another pocket rescission, proposing to cancel about $810 million in appropriated funds across six departments and international assistance programs; **the largest piece, $567 million, came from HHS's Refugee and Entrant Assistance account, which pays for the Office of Refugee Resettlement's programs, including services for refugees and asylees and the care of unaccompanied migrant children, and which the White House called "overfunded."** Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, a Republican, said the move showed OMB "intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation of appropriations." On September 29, 2026, GAO told congressional leaders that the special message did not permit the administration to withhold the funds beyond the end of the fiscal year, when all 11 affected accounts were due to expire, writing that "the President may not force the expiration of budget authority Congress has already enacted and did not rescind." Vought dismissed the conclusion the same day in a post on X, writing that "GAO has become hyper partisan" and "They make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House." With the House in recess until after the elections, there was no practical way for the House to consider the package before the funds expired at the end of the fiscal year on September 30. That day, seven states led by California sued President Trump, Vought and others in the Northern District of California, arguing that the impoundment of federal funding, including the pocket rescission, violates the Constitution and the Administrative Procedure Act; their complaint covers the $567 million in refugee and entrant funds. A national association of migrant-education grantees sued the same day over $24.9 million for two migrant-student programs. Also on September 30, in a suit filed the day before by the National Urban League and other housing nonprofits, U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb (D.D.C.) suspended the September 30 deadline for the $57.5 million Congress appropriated for HUD's housing-counseling program (the package proposed rescinding $56.1 million of it) so the funds would not lapse before she rules on the groups' request for preliminary relief, writing that the court was "not presently in a position to grant or deny" that request. On October 7, 2026, GAO issued two more decisions finding violations: EPA had violated the Impoundment Control Act by pausing payments for, and then terminating, Community Change Grants representing over $1.5 billion in obligated environmental justice funds, and HHS had violated it by leaving more than $78 million of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's fiscal 2025 funds unobligated after cutting the staff who ran its grants. A third decision that day found no violation in the Education Department's handling of a campus child-care grant program, bringing GAO's count since early 2025 to seven decisions finding violations, two mixed and five finding none.

rebuttal_anticipated: Vought's own stated position: the ICA is unconstitutional, the administration's actions are 'programmatic delays' rather than impoundments requiring notification, and reducing spending below appropriated levels when achievable for less money is fiscally responsible, not unlawful. Vought has publicly dismissed individual GAO findings as 'non-events with no consequence. Rearview mirror stuff.' On pocket rescissions specifically, the White House argues they are allowed under the 1974 law because the law does not expressly prohibit them, and when GAO concluded on September 29 that the September 2026 package did not permit withholding the funds past their expiration, Vought wrote on X that "GAO has become hyper partisan and Congress recently attempted to cut their spending because of it" and "They make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House."
comeback: Vought's defense pairs two claims -- that the administration has 'not impounded anything,' and that the law restricting impoundments is unconstitutional anyway -- and the second undercuts the first: an official who says the law doesn't bind him gives little reason to accept his word that he complied with it. An official's personal belief that a duly enacted, never-overturned statute is unconstitutional doesn't entitle that official to act as though it doesn't apply; that's a determination for courts to make. His March 2026 move to formally reduce OMB's deference to GAO's own internal-control authority, on top of dismissing individual findings, shows this has moved beyond disputing specific determinations into disputing GAO's institutional legitimacy altogether -- itself the kind of unilateral executive-branch assertion of power over a co-equal branch's oversight function that the ICA was designed to prevent. official: Mike Waltz, then-National Security Advisor
offense_category: Federal Records Act / federal information-security compliance -- Waltz used TM SGNL, a modified Signal clone marketed as preserving federal records while still using end-to-end encryption, for official government communications; the product in fact stored plaintext copies of messages on an insecure archive server that was subsequently breached -- NOT charged, no criminal exposure identified in reporting reviewed, included for reference only
incident_summary: TeleMessage, an Israeli company, sells TM SGNL (also called Archive Signal), a modified version of Signal marketed to U.S. government agencies as a way to satisfy federal records-retention requirements without giving up Signal's end-to-end encryption. Then-National Security Advisor Mike Waltz was photographed by Reuters photographer Evelyn Hockstein using TM SGNL on his phone during a Cabinet meeting on Wednesday, April 30, 2025. On May 1, the day Trump removed Waltz as National Security Advisor and said he would nominate him as U.N. ambassador, 404 Media and the Washington Post reported that the app in the Reuters photos was TM SGNL; visible parts of the screen showed messages from contacts named Rubio and JD Vance, an apparent call to Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, and an "NSC Scheduling" message about the President's Daily Brief. The photos became the public trigger for the technical scrutiny that followed. On May 3, security researcher and journalist Micah Lee republished TM SGNL's Android source code, and that night an anonymous hacker told him they had breached TeleMessage. The hacker said the break-in took "about 15-20 minutes" and later described exploiting client-side MD5 password hashing on TeleMessage's admin panel and an exposed /heapdump URL on its archive server that returned snapshots of the server's memory, including plaintext chat logs. On May 4, Lee and Joseph Cox reported the breach in 404 Media: the stolen data included message contents from TeleMessage's modified Signal, WhatsApp, Telegram, and WeChat clients, government officials' names and contact information, usernames and passwords for TeleMessage's backend panel, and data tied to Customs and Border Protection, Coinbase, and other financial institutions; the hacker had not obtained the messages of Waltz, cabinet members, or the people Waltz spoke to. On May 5, NBC News reported that a second hacker claimed to have downloaded a large cache of files from a TeleMessage server, and TeleMessage's owner, Smarsh, temporarily suspended all TeleMessage services. **On May 6, Lee published an analysis of TM SGNL's source code, corroborated by the hacked data, finding that it transmitted decrypted, plaintext copies of chat logs to TeleMessage's archive server -- directly contradicting the product's end-to-end-encryption marketing claims.** On May 12, 2025, CISA added the underlying flaw (CVE-2025-47729, cleartext storage of messages contradicting the app's encryption claims) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and under Binding Operational Directive 22-01 ordered federal civilian agencies to remediate by June 2, 2025. On May 19, the transparency group Distributed Denial of Secrets published 410 GB of TeleMessage heap dumps taken May 4, sharing them only with journalists and researchers. Reuters, reviewing that cache, identified more than 60 unique government users, including disaster responders, customs officials, several diplomatic staffers, at least one White House staffer, and members of the Secret Service, and messages tied to at least one financial services firm. On July 1, 2025, CISA added two more actively exploited TM SGNL flaws (CVE-2025-48927 and CVE-2025-48928) to the catalog.

rebuttal_anticipated: The White House, asked about the Cabinet-meeting photos, said: "As we have said many times, Signal is an approved app for government use and is loaded on government phones," without addressing TeleMessage. Smarsh, TeleMessage's owner, said it was investigating a potential security incident, had engaged an outside cybersecurity firm, and suspended TeleMessage services out of caution. The implicit defense is that the product was adopted for records-compliance purposes and that the flaws were in TeleMessage's own infrastructure, not the result of any individual official's misuse.
comeback: The Federal Records Act rationale for using an archiving tool doesn't excuse the underlying failure: officials chose a specific product marketed as preserving end-to-end encryption while archiving, and that marketing claim was false. Compliance-motivated tool selection is not a defense when the tool itself created the exposure the encryption claim was supposed to prevent -- a CISA Known Exploited Vulnerability catalog entry and mandatory federal remediation directive are not marks of a merely theoretical risk.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Structural: a records-compliance requirement (Federal Records Act) collided with officials' preference for encrypted messaging apps, producing demand for a third-party product promising both -- TM SGNL -- that in practice could not deliver both properties simultaneously: it copied plaintext messages to an archive server that was then hacked in minutes. The same underlying tension (secure, ephemeral-feeling communication vs. official recordkeeping obligations) runs through this tracker's Hegseth Signal/Yemen entry, the Waltz NSC Signal-chat entry, and the Rubio Signal auto-delete entry, each a separate episode; together they suggest senior officials adopting consumer or quasi-consumer messaging tools without adequate security vetting.
confidence_note: Strong sourcing: the core vulnerability and breach are corroborated by Micah Lee's original technical research, reporting by 404 Media, NBC News, the Washington Post, CSO Online, Security Affairs, and Reuters (via a secondary summary), and -- most authoritatively -- CISA's own Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog entries for three TeleMessage CVEs (CVE-2025-47729 in May 2025; CVE-2025-48927 and CVE-2025-48928 in July 2025) with Binding Operational Directive remediation orders, the strongest possible source type per this tracker's sourcing priorities. The photo's date (the April 30, 2025 Cabinet meeting), venue, and Reuters credit are HIGH confidence: the Washington Post and NBC News both place it at Wednesday's Cabinet meeting, and 404 Media reported Reuters published it Thursday, May 1. What's less certain: any personal disciplinary consequence for Waltz specifically tied to this incident (as opposed to the separate, earlier Yemen-strike Signal-chat controversy that preceded his removal as National Security Advisor) -- reporting reviewed does not establish that connection, so this entry treats them as related but distinct episodes.

official: Mike Waltz, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations
offense_category: Potential Law of Armed Conflict Violation (Geneva Conventions Additional Protocol I, Art. 52, protecting civilian objects from attack; potential War Crimes Act, 18 U.S.C. §2441, if implemented) — NOT charged; this entry documents a PUBLIC STATEMENT asserting a legal position, not the later strikes on the named targets; the statement itself is the documented conduct
incident_summary: On April 19, 2026, during a ceasefire in the U.S.-Iran war and the same day Trump threatened to "knock out every single Power Plant, and every single Bridge, in Iran" if Tehran rejected a U.S. deal, Waltz, the U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations, went on ABC's This Week, NBC's Meet the Press and CBS's Face the Nation to argue that U.S. strikes on Iranian bridges and power plants would not constitute war crimes, citing their dual military use and IRGC control. A Just Security analysis by Michael Schmitt, Tess Bridgeman and Ryan Goodman found a basis in law for some of his claims but called them exaggerated and incomplete. Waltz spoke 17 days after an April 2 U.S. strike hit the unfinished B1 bridge linking Tehran and Karaj, which Iran said killed eight people and wounded 95; Trump had shared footage of that strike. Strikes on those target categories have since occurred: after the ceasefire collapsed in July 2026, U.S. strikes hit at least six bridges around the port of Bandar Abbas, and Iran acknowledged attacks on its power infrastructure, according to Iranian state media as reported by NBC News on July 17. On July 22, Trump declared that the U.S. would destroy one bridge or power plant for each Iranian attack on a ship in the Strait of Hormuz. **Iran's Health Ministry said on July 22 that U.S. strikes over the previous 11 days had killed 53 people and wounded nearly 600.**
elements_required: Law of armed conflict generally protects civilian objects (infrastructure not serving a direct military function) from deliberate attack
Bridges and power plants can have 'dual-use' status (civilian and military) depending on specific circumstances, which is the central legal complexity in applying this principle
Whether Waltz's statement reflected a legally defensible dual-use analysis specific to Iranian infrastructure, or a blanket assertion that such targets are categorically permissible regardless of use
Whether any such strikes were actually carried out following the statement -- a separate factual question from the legality of the stated position itself

evidence.description: On CBS's Face the Nation on April 19, 2026, Waltz stated: 'And by the way, bridges, power plants that are run by the IRGC, which runs the entire military, are absolute legitimate military targets, not only now, but have been historically. That is a false, fake and ridiculous notion that this is some type of war crime.'
evidence.maps_to_element: The primary-source statement this entry previously lacked -- Waltz grounded the claim in a dual-use/IRGC-control theory rather than a blanket 'all civilian infrastructure' assertion

evidence.description: On ABC's This Week on April 19, 2026, when Jonathan Karl said Trump was threatening every bridge and every power plant in Iran and asked, 'That wouldn't be a war crime?', Waltz responded: 'That would be an escalatory ladder. And if you go back in the history of warfare, go all the way back to World War II, of course we bombed and took down bridges, other infrastructure, power plants that, yes, could be used for civilian, but also are used to manufacture drones and missiles'
evidence.maps_to_element: Direct acknowledgment the targets have civilian use ('yes, could be used for civilian'), qualified by a claimed military-manufacturing purpose -- the central factual dispute for the dual-use analysis

evidence.description: Just Security's April 22, 2026 legal analysis (by Michael Schmitt, Tess Bridgeman and Ryan Goodman) notes that on Meet the Press Waltz justified targeting 'power plants, the grid, and other things that are being used to power Iran's war economy, which, oh, by the way, the IRGC controls an estimated 40% to 50% of,' calls this 'a remarkable admission,' asks 'What about the other 50-60% that the President and Secretary of Defense threatened to destroy?', and says it fails to see the legal significance of IRGC control, since the IRGC may also control purely civilian institutions and facilities. The analysis also calls Waltz's World War II bombing analogy 'an anachronism at best,' noting that the destruction of Dresden and the firebombing of Tokyo to terrorize the civilian population is precisely what led to those methods of warfare being outlawed through Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law.

The report says Iran's Health Ministry says U.S. strikes over the past 11 days have killed 53 people, including six women and three children, and wounded nearly 600 people.

rebuttal_anticipated: Waltz's own stated position: international humanitarian law permits strikes on infrastructure serving a genuine military function under the dual-use doctrine, bridges and IRGC-run power plants meet that standard, and the WWII precedent shows infrastructure targeting with civilian secondary uses has long been an accepted feature of warfare when the military use is real.
comeback: Waltz's own figure does less work than he suggests. On Meet the Press he said the IRGC controls an estimated 40% to 50% of Iran's war economy; Just Security asks what would justify destroying the other 50-60% the President and Defense Secretary threatened, and adds that IRGC control of an asset does not by itself make it a military objective -- the IRGC may also control purely civilian institutions. The law of armed conflict requires each target to qualify on its own as a military objective, with proportionality and precautions judged strike by strike; beyond military equipment, Just Security notes, no category of target universally qualifies. Asked on ABC whether destroying every power plant and bridge in Iran would be a war crime, Waltz answered that it 'would be an escalatory ladder' and pointed to World War II. Just Security calls that analogy 'an anachronism at best': the destruction of Dresden and the firebombing of Tokyo to terrorize civilians are precisely what led to those methods of warfare being outlawed under Additional Protocol I and customary international humanitarian law, so the citation is to the practice that got outlawed, not a precedent for its legality.

The documented conduct is a UN Ambassador publicly defending a legal theory for targeting Iranian infrastructure while the President threatened to destroy every power plant and bridge in Iran -- not a confirmed law-of-war violation or a war-crimes finding.

official: Susie Wiles, White House Chief of Staff
offense_category: First Amendment Viewpoint Discrimination — Denial of Press Access (established precedent: Sherrill v. Knight, D.C. Cir. 1977, holding that White House press credential denials must not be arbitrary or based on viewpoint) — civil litigation (Associated Press v. Budowich), not criminal
incident_summary: After the Associated Press declined to adopt the administration's preferred 'Gulf of America' naming convention in its stylebook, Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt told the AP on February 11, 2025 that, at President Trump's direction, it would no longer be permitted in the Oval Office as part of the press pool until it revised its Stylebook, and AP reporters and photographers were then blocked from press events and locations including the Oval Office and Air Force One. **On February 18, 2025, responding to the AP's complaints, Wiles emailed the AP that its Stylebook had 'misused, and at times weaponized' its 'influence' to 'push a divisive and partisan agenda'; three days later the AP sued her, Deputy Chief of Staff Taylor Budowich and Leavitt in Associated Press v. The same report said, citing people familiar with the matter, that Wiles met AP Executive Editor Julie Pace in February to discuss the standoff and told her, 'You have to give us something.'
elements_required: Government actor restricted press access previously granted on a generally available basis
Restriction was based on the content/viewpoint of the press outlet's editorial decisions, not a neutral, generally applicable rule
Established case law (Sherrill v. Knight and progeny) holds White House press access cannot be denied arbitrarily or based on viewpoint once a general practice of access exists
Documented connection between the official's own communications and the access restriction

status: Judge McFadden granted AP a preliminary injunction April 8, 2025; a 2-1 D.C. Circuit panel stayed it June 6, 2025 except as to the East Room, and the full court denied en banc reconsideration July 22, 2025. Circuit's June 2025 stay order partially credited as to those specific spaces.
comeback: Sherrill v. Knight holds that once the White House opens press facilities to journalists generally, access can't be denied arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting; the district court applied that principle to the AP's exclusion, though the stay-panel majority said it does not reach the Oval Office and similar restricted spaces. The administration's own justification -- Wiles's email saying AP's Stylebook had 'misused, and at times weaponized' its 'influence' to 'push a divisive and partisan agenda' -- is an explicit statement that access was revoked because of editorial viewpoint, not a neutral logistical reason. The district court found AP likely to succeed and granted a preliminary injunction; the D.C. Circuit's partial stay on appeal turned on a different, narrower legal question -- whether specific restricted spaces are First Amendment fora at all, not whether viewpoint discrimination occurred. The district court's preliminary finding that AP was excluded for its editorial choices has not been overturned -- the stay majority itself noted officials announced that as the reason -- and what's stayed is only the remedy as to certain spaces while the forum question is litigated.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of the press-access and speech-retaliation pattern this tracker documents (cross-reference the reported FBI inquiry into a Times reporter under Patel and Zeldin's dissent-letter retaliation): an administration-wide approach of treating editorial independence -- whether in a news organization's stylebook or federal employees' public letter -- as grounds for punitive action. The Wiles/AP case is distinctive in that the rationale was stated openly: Wiles's email tied the dispute to AP's Stylebook, alongside the Press Secretary's message to the AP and the Deputy Chief of Staff's and President's public statements, making the viewpoint rationale unusually well documented compared to cases where motive must be inferred. The appeals court's stay majority said the White House is likely free to choose journalists for the Oval Office and similar restricted spaces even on the basis of viewpoint, the question the pending merits appeal will settle. A later, separate act -- Trump's September 2026 ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House -- applied the same approach to whole outlets' credentials.

Circuit) -- these are documented in the district court's April 8, 2025 opinion, the D.C. Circuit's orders and courtroom minutes, and the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse docket. Sherrill v. Knight is longstanding D.C. Circuit precedent for press facilities opened to journalists generally, but the stay-panel majority said it does not reach the Oval Office and similar restricted spaces, where it said the White House may choose journalists even on the basis of viewpoint. AP won a preliminary injunction; the appeal produced a partial, space-specific stay (en banc reconsideration denied July 22, 2025), and the merits remain undecided more than ten months after the November 24, 2025 argument. offense_category: Accountability concern, not alleged as a legal violation: a senior Justice Department official using the department's antitrust power to pressure the American Bar Association's law school accreditor over a faculty rule his letter reportedly says limits his own teaching. TAP notes that federal ethics rules bar employees from using public office for private gain (5 C.F.R. 2635.702) and direct employees whose circumstances would raise a question about their impartiality to seek a recusal determination (5 C.F.R. 2635.502(a)(3)); the letter also raises the risk of retaliation against an organization that is suing the administration. incident_summary: The Trump administration has been in open conflict with the American Bar Association for more than a year. The ABA sued the administration in 2025 over the executive orders targeting several large law firms, and that case is ongoing. In August 2026, Education Department career staff recommended that the ABA's accreditation council lose the federal recognition it has held as the national law school accreditor since 1952, finding it failed 26 of the department's criteria; a decision is expected by year's end. On October 7, 2026, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr., the Justice Department's third-ranking official, who oversees its Antitrust Division and has taught as an adjunct law professor at Catholic University, signed a letter to the council warning it could face an antitrust investigation over its standard requiring full-time faculty to teach "substantially all of the first one-third of each student's coursework." According to The Wall Street Journal, which reviewed the letter and reported it on October 13, Woodward wrote that the standard appears to restrict his own ability to teach first-year students. He argued that adjuncts cost less and often bring more real-world experience, so limiting their teaching hurts education and pushes up tuition, and that the limits "cannot be clearly explained by differences in real or perceived quality in the instruction of full-time or adjunct faculty." **The letter gave the council 15 days to change the standard or explain why it does not violate antitrust law; the Wall Street Journal reported it warns that the department "may proceed with additional investigatory steps" if the answer is insufficient.** The Wall Street Journal also reported that the letter faulted the ABA's positions on abortion rights, affirmative action and transgender health care. In September the council had already proposed dropping the first-third rule while still requiring full-time faculty to teach more than half of credit hours or two-thirds of student contact hours; according to the Wall Street Journal, Woodward's letter said that would not fully resolve the department's concerns. A council spokesperson confirmed the letter arrived and said "we will respond."

official: Chris Wright, Secretary of Energy
offense_category: Federal Advisory Committee Act Violation (5 U.S.C. §§ 1001-1014, enacted 1972) — a federal court has actually ruled on the merits that Wright and DOE violated this statute, the strongest evidentiary posture of any entry involving a 'secret committee' style violation in this dataset; NOT criminally charged, FACA violations are addressed via civil litigation/injunctive relief, not criminal prosecution
incident_summary: Wright convened a DOE "climate working group" to produce a report evaluating climate change science and the EPA's endangerment finding, operating without the transparency requirements (public meetings, balanced membership, chartering, public reporting) FACA imposes on federal advisory committees. Wright disbanded the working group by a letter dated September 3, 2025, while the FACA lawsuit against it (EDF and Union of Concerned Scientists v. Wright, D. Mass.) was pending. On September 17, 2025, Judge William G. Young ruled that the group was not exempt from FACA. His January 30, 2026 judgment declared that the group was a federal advisory committee that gave DOE substantive policy advice, and that its violations of FACA's requirements on establishing and using an advisory committee, open meetings, open records and fair balance were "established as matter of law," because the government had argued only that the claims were moot, not that the violations did not happen. The judgment dismissed EPA as a defendant, finding no persuasive evidence of FACA violations by anyone outside DOE and Secretary Wright. Earlier, EPA's August 2025 proposal to repeal its 2009 endangerment finding had said the group's draft report was "reviewed and relied upon in formulating this proposal." **But when EPA finalized the repeal in February 2026, two weeks after the judgment, the final rule stated that EPA "is not relying on" either the draft or the final working-group report "for any aspect of this final action,"** citing in part concerns commenters raised about the draft. The repeal itself is being challenged in the D.C. Circuit, covered in the Deregulation tracker's endangerment-finding entry. A second, separate case -- EDF v. Wright, D.D.C., filed March 17, 2026 -- alleges DOE appointees used personal email to conduct the working group's business in violation of the Federal Records Act. EDF filed an amended complaint on August 6, 2026 -- adding Edward C. Forst as a named defendant -- and defendants sought a further extension to respond on August 14, 2026, which Judge Carl J. Nichols granted on August 24, 2026, setting a new response deadline of September 17, 2026. On that date, defendants moved to dismiss, arguing that EDF lacks standing, that its claims are unripe or moot, and that it fails to state a claim.
elements_required: FACA requires federal advisory committees -- groups providing advice/recommendations to agencies -- to operate with chartering, balanced membership, public meeting notice, and public reporting requirements
The DOE climate working group functioned as the kind of advisory body FACA covers, rather than purely internal agency staff work exempt from the Act
A court found, as a matter of law, that the group's operation violated FACA's requirements

The resulting report was used in a separate major agency action: EPA said it relied on the draft report in proposing the endangerment finding repeal (August 2025), though the final repeal (February 2026) disclaimed reliance on it

evidence.maps_to_element: Context on Wright's public stance on renewable energy before the working group's report, not itself a legal element

evidence.description: A separate DOE Inspector General audit, flagged before Wright's confirmation, found the department's loan office was 'not managing organizational conflicts of interest in compliance with regulations,' with the IG recommending new loan issuance potentially be suspended until safeguards were implemented; Wright committed during his confirmation hearing to 'immediately engage' on the issue
evidence.maps_to_element: Separate, distinct conflict-of-interest concern at DOE -- included as a related but separate matter, not part of the FACA finding itself

evidence.description: Environmental Defense Fund v. Wright, No. 1:26-cv-00928 (D.D.C.), filed March 17, 2026 against DOE, Secretary Wright, the National Archives and Records Administration and Acting Archivist James Byron, alleges that DOE political appointees, including Seth Cohen, Travis Fisher, and Joshua Loucks, extensively used personal email accounts to conduct government business related to the Climate Working Group, in violation of the Federal Records Act. The Clearinghouse lists the case as ongoing.
evidence.maps_to_element: A second, still-open legal action targeting the same working group's conduct, distinct from the FACA violation already documented

evidence.description: EDF filed an amended complaint in the Federal Records Act case (EDF v. Wright, D.D.C., No. 1:26-cv-00928) on August 6, 2026; defendants filed a motion for an extension of time to respond to the amended complaint on August 14, 2026. No ruling on the merits has been issued; the case remains in early procedural stages.
evidence.maps_to_element: Updates the status of the second, still-open Federal Records Act case -- an amended complaint and a new response-deadline extension, not yet a ruling

evidence.description: The August 6, 2026 amended complaint in EDF v. Wright added Edward C. Forst as an additional named defendant. On August 24, 2026, Judge Carl J. Nichols granted defendants' extension motion, setting a new deadline of September 17, 2026 for their response to the amended complaint.
evidence.maps_to_element: Confirms the extension was granted (not merely requested) and identifies the new defendant and the specific new response deadline

evidence.description: Judge William G. Young's January 30, 2026 judgment in Environmental Defense Fund v. Wright (D. Mass., No. 25-12249) declares that the Climate Working Group was not exempt from FACA and was a federal advisory committee that provided substantive policy advice and recommendations to DOE; states that the defendants argued only mootness and that the alleged violations of FACA's requirements for establishing and using an advisory committee, open meetings, open records and fair balance are "now established as matter of law"; and dismisses EPA as a defendant, finding no persuasive evidence of FACA violations by any entity outside DOE and Secretary Wright.
evidence.maps_to_element: Direct judicial finding of the FACA violations -- the primary court record for the central element

evidence.description: Judge Young's September 17, 2025 order denied the plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction but granted summary judgment on whether the Climate Working Group was exempt from FACA as a group assembled to exchange facts or information with federal officials.
evidence.maps_to_element: Court's threshold ruling that the working group was covered by FACA

evidence.description: EPA's proposed rule to rescind the 2009 endangerment finding (90 FR 36288, August 1, 2025) states that the Administrator received and evaluated the DOE Climate Working Group's May 27, 2025 draft report and, in footnote 10, that the draft report "was reviewed and relied upon in formulating this proposal."
evidence.maps_to_element: Shows the working group's draft report was relied upon in EPA's repeal proposal

evidence.description: NPR (September 13, 2025) reported that Energy Secretary Chris Wright disbanded the Climate Working Group, confirming that Wright wrote a letter on September 3 to the group's five members thanking them for their service, as a hearing was held that week in the EDF and Union of Concerned Scientists lawsuit.
evidence.maps_to_element: Dates the working group's dissolution, relevant to the mootness defense

evidence.description: On September 17, 2026, the defendants in Environmental Defense Fund v. Wright (D.D.C., No. 26-0928) filed a motion to dismiss arguing that the claims should be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction (standing, ripeness, mootness) and that EDF has failed to state a claim for relief on the merits.
evidence.maps_to_element: Current status of the still-open Federal Records Act case

status: A court declared on Jan. 30, 2026 that DOE's Climate Working Group was a FACA committee and its violations were established; the group was disbanded in Sept. 2025. In the Federal Records Act suit (EDF v. Wright), defendants moved to dismiss on Sept. 17, 2026. Civil cases only; no criminal charges.
rebuttal_anticipated: [DRAFT] Likely defense: the working group functioned as internal agency deliberation/staff work product rather than a formal advisory committee, the FACA finding addressed a procedural technicality rather than the substance or accuracy of the report's findings, and the group was already disbanded before the ruling, making the violation moot in practical effect. They can also point out that EPA's final endangerment-finding repeal expressly did not rely on the group's reports.
comeback: [DRAFT - needs your input] The 'already disbanded, so moot' framing doesn't address the more significant problem: by EPA's own account, the group's draft report was "reviewed and relied upon" in formulating the August 2025 proposal to repeal the endangerment finding -- one of the most consequential deregulatory actions in EPA history -- and the public was asked to comment on a proposal built partly on work a federal court has since found was produced through an unlawful process. EPA disclaimed reliance on the report only in its final rule, two weeks after the court's judgment. A procedural violation in how scientific input was generated is exactly the kind of defect that should call the substance of what was produced into question, not be dismissed as a technicality.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Possible cause: convening a working group outside FACA's requirements may have been a deliberate choice to avoid the balanced-membership and public-scrutiny rules that would have applied to a formally chartered advisory committee, since the group's draft report fed a policy outcome already in motion (EPA's proposal to rescind the endangerment finding, which said it relied on the draft) rather than functioning as genuinely open scientific inquiry. EPA's decision to drop the report from its final rule does not undo that: the draft had already been used to build the proposal the public was asked to comment on.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the FACA violation: it rests on a federal court's declaratory judgment (D. Mass., Jan. 30, 2026), not contested allegations -- though the violations were established because the government contested only mootness, not the violations themselves. Frame the endangerment-finding link carefully: EPA said it relied on the group's draft report in its August 2025 proposal, but its February 2026 final rule states that it did not rely on either working-group report for any aspect of the action. The separate Federal Records Act case (EDF v. Wright, D.D.C., filed March 17, 2026, over DOE appointees' personal-email use) awaits a ruling on defendants' September 17, 2026 motion to dismiss; there is no ruling on the merits. The repeal itself is being litigated in the D.C. Circuit by health and environmental groups and a 24-state coalition, covered in the Deregulation tracker's endangerment-finding entry.
pull_quote: “These violations are now established as matter of law.” -- Judge William G. Young, judgment declaring that DOE's Climate Working Group violated FACA (D. Mass., Jan. 30, 2026)

official: Lee Zeldin, Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency
offense_category: First Amendment Retaliation Against Federal Employees (protected speech in personal capacity); potential Whistleblower Protection Act issues — NOT charged criminally; being challenged via litigation and MSPB appeals, not criminal prosecution
incident_summary: On June 30, 2025, approximately 270 current and former EPA employees published a "Declaration of Dissent" criticizing the administration's treatment of agency science and staff, many signing with their job titles but stating explicitly they signed in their personal capacity, on their own time, without agency resources. EPA's own ethics staff internally reviewed the letter and found the signatories were within their rights to do so. Despite this internal finding, EPA placed close to 150 signatories on administrative leave on July 3, 2025, searched their work computers and email accounts, and required them to complete a survey about government-resource use related to the letter. After weeks on leave, EPA suspended many of them and fired some by the end of that summer. Counts differ by source: a June 2026 letter from 22 senators put the toll at 20 fired (including seven probationary employees) and more than 140 suspended, while the employees' union, AFGE Council 238, counted nine removals, six probationary terminations and over 50 two-week unpaid suspensions. The internal ethics finding was not made public until POLITICO's E&E News obtained it via a FOIA request months later; subsequent FOIA-obtained emails, disclosed in April 2026, further revealed that **an EPA assistant general counsel, Nate Nichols, had separately advised in a July 2, 2025 email -- sent to senior human resources officials and forwarded that day to political appointees -- before the disciplinary action that "taking any such action would present significant legal risk, as the letter is likely protected speech under the First Amendment."** That warning, separate from the ethics office finding, further contradicts Zeldin's stated justification for the disciplinary action. According to the advocacy group PEER, of the several federal agencies whose employees signed comparable dissent/solidarity letters, EPA is the only one that continued disciplining signatories -- NIH, NASA, and NSF took little or no adverse action (or reinstated the one NIH employee placed on leave), and FEMA reinstated over a dozen signatories after an eight-month paid-leave period.
elements_required: Federal employees engaged in speech in their personal capacity on a matter of public concern (the EPA's treatment of science and staff)
Agency's own ethics review found no rules violation
Agency's own legal counsel separately warned the disciplinary action carried significant First Amendment legal risk
Adverse employment action (administrative leave, computer searches, suspension, termination) taken against the employees despite the ethics office's clearance and the legal counsel's warning
Documented intent/effect of chilling future employee speech

evidence.description: EPA ethics staff internally reviewed the Declaration of Dissent shortly after it was published and found no rules violation by the signatories, as documented in internal emails later obtained via FOIA request; a senior EPA official responded to receiving this assessment by writing 'This is helpful and I think I have what I need... we are standing down for now'
evidence.maps_to_element: Agency's own ethics review found no violation -- the central, strongest piece of evidence

evidence.description: A subsequent FOIA-obtained email, apparently accidentally divulged by EPA's own FOIA office, showed EPA assistant general counsel Nate Nichols separately and explicitly warned leadership before the disciplinary action that 'taking any such action would present significant legal risk, as the letter is likely protected speech under the First Amendment'
evidence.maps_to_element: Second, separate internal legal warning disregarded before disciplining employees -- strengthens the pattern beyond the ethics-office finding alone

evidence.description: Despite the ethics office's finding, close to 150 staffers who signed the letter were placed on administrative leave on July 3, 2025, the day Zeldin issued his statement, and kept in that status for almost two months; EPA ultimately suspended over 50 employees for two weeks without pay and fired at least 15, according to AFGE Council 238 (nine removed for misconduct, six probationary workers terminated), charging staffers with 'Conduct Unbecoming of a Federal Employee'; Zeldin publicly characterized the signatories as 'agency bureaucrats' whose letter was 'riddled with misinformation'
evidence.maps_to_element: Adverse employment action despite the internal ethics and legal findings

evidence.description: One of the disciplined signatories, Wesley Ingwersen, was the creator and lead scientist behind USEEIO, EPA's widely-used open-source greenhouse-gas emissions database that hundreds of companies rely on to calculate supply-chain emissions; the New York Times reported in August 2025 that EPA would stop updating USEEIO after suspending Ingwersen over the Declaration of Dissent, leaving the tool publicly available but increasingly outdated. Ingwersen left EPA for a position at Stanford University. This is a concrete, named illustration of the disciplinary campaign's downstream public cost: beyond the employment action itself, it degraded a specific piece of federal data infrastructure third parties depended on.
evidence.maps_to_element: Adverse employment action despite the internal ethics and legal findings -- illustrates a specific, quantifiable public-facing consequence of the disciplinary campaign beyond the affected employees themselves

evidence.description: Six former EPA employees filed appeals with the Merit Systems Protection Board in December 2025 challenging their terminations, with the help of Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility; in April 2026, Lawyers for Good Government and the Government Accountability Project separately announced they would represent additional disciplined EPA staffers in MSPB proceedings
evidence.maps_to_element: Formal legal challenges via the administrative appeals process available to non-probationary employees

evidence.description: On June 30, 2026, seven additional former EPA employees who were probationary at the time of termination -- and therefore lacked MSPB appeal rights -- filed new lawsuits, represented by Democracy Forward and law firm James & Hoffman, arguing their firings for personal-capacity speech violated the First Amendment; the suits seek reinstatement and back pay
evidence.maps_to_element: New, separate legal track specifically for probationary employees excluded from MSPB appeal rights, testing whether probationary status can be used to route around civil-service speech protections

evidence.description: Senators Slotkin and Van Hollen, joined by 20 Senate colleagues, sent a letter to Zeldin (announced July 1, 2026) demanding reversal of the disciplinary actions, citing 'recent revelations from EPA legal counsel,' writing that EPA 'has not produced any evidence that would indicate that EPA employees used official resources or otherwise were acting in their professional capacity' and that 'speaking the truth is not a fireable offense'
evidence.maps_to_element: Documents continued, escalating political pressure on EPA following the internal-counsel-warning revelation, though this is advocacy from one party's senators rather than an independent finding

evidence.description: An EPA spokesperson stated the agency 'has a zero-tolerance policy for career bureaucrats unlawfully undermining, sabotaging, and undercutting the administration's agenda,' and the agency's statement did not address whether Zeldin was aware of the ethics office's conclusion that there was 'no ethics concern'
evidence.maps_to_element: Agency's public justification, notably silent on the ethics office's finding

evidence.description: E&E News reported on April 2, 2026 that Nate Nichols, assistant general counsel of EPA's employment law practice group, advised in a July 2, 2025 email that the agency should not take personnel actions against signers, writing that 'taking any such action would present significant legal risk, as the letter is likely protected speech under the First Amendment'; the email went to senior HR officials and was forwarded that day to political appointees; EPA's press office said it was preliminary staff-level advice that should not have been released.
evidence.maps_to_element: Agency's own legal counsel separately warned the disciplinary action carried significant First Amendment legal risk

evidence.description: A June 30, 2026 letter to Zeldin signed by 22 senators (Van Hollen, Murray, Wyden, Sanders, Whitehouse, Shaheen, Slotkin, Alsobrooks and others), copied to the Office of Special Counsel, states that EPA put approximately 140 signers on administrative leave on July 3, 2025 and, after 80 days or more, fired 20 (including seven on probation) and suspended the rest; it cites E&E News's April 2026 report that an EPA personnel lawyer warned discipline would trample First Amendment rights, and demands reinstatement and reversal of all discipline.
evidence.maps_to_element: Adverse employment action despite the internal ethics and legal findings; documents the scale of discipline as counted by the senators

evidence.description: In a September 1, 2026 motion to seal in Harris v. EPA (N.D. Ill., No. 26 C 7640), EPA states that the lawsuit challenges the plaintiffs' terminations, that other former employees' MSPB proceeding is ongoing, and that EPA mistakenly produced an email in that MSPB proceeding (attached as Exhibit D to the complaint) which it says is privileged and is seeking to claw back there.
evidence.maps_to_element: Confirms the MSPB track is ongoing as of September 2026 and that EPA is contesting use of a later internal legal email attached to the complaint

evidence.description: Of the several federal agencies whose employees signed similar dissent/solidarity letters, EPA is the only one that continued disciplining signatories. NIH took no adverse action against nearly all signers (one employee placed on paid leave roughly six months, then reinstated); NASA and NSF signatories faced no discipline; FEMA placed over a dozen signatories on paid administrative leave for eight months but has since reinstated them. PEER's May 6, 2026 statement, quoting Executive Director Tim Whitehouse, characterizes EPA as 'the only remaining agency that fired, suspended, or otherwise disciplined employees who signed a dissent letter.'
evidence.maps_to_element: Strengthens the pattern claim: EPA's disciplinary campaign was not a shared, agency-wide administration response to similar letters, but a singular outlier even among other agencies whose employees took the same action

evidence.description: Complaint in Balani v. EPA (D.D.C., filed June 30, 2026) by former probationary EPA employees Claire Balani, Lane To and Alexis Wright, represented by Democracy Forward Foundation and James & Hoffman, P.C., alleging their terminations after signing the Declaration of Dissent violated the First Amendment and noting that as probationary employees they cannot appeal to the MSPB.
evidence.maps_to_element: New, separate legal track for probationary employees excluded from MSPB appeal rights

status: MSPB appeals by fired non-probationary signers are pending; there, EPA seeks to claw back a later (Aug. 28, 2025) email from EPA lawyer Nate Nichols. Probationary employees' suits filed June 30, 2026 (Balani v. EPA, D.D.C.; Harris v. EPA, N.D. Ill.) are at the pleading stage. No merits ruling.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: even if the ethics office found no ethics concern and internal counsel warned the discipline carried legal risk, Zeldin retains independent management authority to discipline employees who publicly undermine agency leadership and policy direction using their official titles, and the agency's stated 'zero-tolerance' position reflects a legitimate management judgment distinct from those internal assessments.
comeback: The 'separate management judgment' defense was already weak when only the ethics office's clearance was known; it is considerably weaker now that a second, separate internal voice -- EPA's own assistant general counsel -- explicitly warned in writing that disciplining the signatories carried 'significant legal risk' under the First Amendment, and that warning was disregarded too. Two different internal offices, applying two different kinds of institutional expertise (ethics compliance and legal risk), both concluded the same thing before leadership proceeded anyway. The scale also continues to matter: by the senators' count, more than 140 employees suspended and 20 fired (the union's tally is lower), and now two separate parallel legal fights -- MSPB appeals and, as of June 2026, federal lawsuits from probationary employees specifically routed around MSPB's appeal process. That's not a management response to a tone problem; it's a sustained disciplinary campaign that the agency's own ethics office had found no ethics concern with, and its own employment lawyer had warned against in advance.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] EPA's handling of the Declaration of Dissent fits a pattern seen in other entries where officials answered criticism or resistance with punitive action, such as the FBI's inquiry into a New York Times reporter who wrote about Patel's girlfriend (as the Times reported; the FBI disputes it), and the ouster of CDC Director Susan Monarez, whose lawyers said she was targeted after she refused to 'rubber-stamp unscientific, reckless directives'. What sets this case apart is that EPA leadership went ahead after its own ethics office found no ethics concern and its own employment lawyer warned the letter was likely protected speech, and that, according to PEER, EPA is the only agency still disciplining signers of such letters: NIH, NASA and NSF took little or no action, and FEMA reinstated its signers. That points to a choice by EPA's leadership rather than a uniform government-wide rule. The agency's own stated rationale is a 'zero-tolerance policy for career bureaucrats unlawfully undermining' the administration's agenda. Whether the discipline was unlawful retaliation is for the MSPB and the courts to decide.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the internal contradiction (an ethics-office clearance and a separate legal-risk warning, both followed by discipline anyway) is documented through FOIA-obtained internal EPA emails reported by POLITICO's E&E News, not press characterization or anonymous sourcing, making this one of the more concretely evidenced entries in the dataset. In September 2026, EPA told a federal court that it had mistakenly produced a later email from the same lawyer (dated Aug. 28, 2025, per the complaints) in the MSPB proceeding and is seeking to claw it back there as privileged. The two legal tracks (MSPB appeals and the probationary employees' federal lawsuits) are documented through named plaintiffs, filing dates, counsel and court dockets. Discipline counts differ by source: the senators' June 2026 letter cites 20 firings and more than 140 suspensions, while AFGE Council 238 counts 15 removals or terminations and over 50 two-week suspensions; the entry reports both rather than choosing. The Wesley Ingwersen/USEEIO example was reported by the New York Times and summarized by Daily Climate and SEJ, so it rests on one original report. The EPA-as-sole-outlier comparison rests on PEER's May 6, 2026 statement; PEER also represents fired signers. A separate, broader EPA headquarters facility-conditions story (broken elevators, extreme heat, a firing-range basement relocation) affects the general workforce rather than these signatories and is tracked as its own entry.
pull_quote: Zeldin publicly dismissed the signatories as ‘agency bureaucrats’ whose letter was ‘riddled with misinformation’ -- a characterization at odds with his own agency's ethics office, which found ‘no ethics concern,’ and its employment lawyer, who called the letter ‘likely protected speech.’
